COMMENT FORM TEXT:
The July 31, 2026 OCC/FDIC CRA proposal, OCC-2026-0694, is very disappointing because it fails to address the central reason CRA modernization became necessary in the first place: the growth of digital and branchless banking since CRA’s last major reform in 1995.

CRA was enacted to combat redlining by encouraging banks to help meet the credit needs of the communities from which they gather deposits. Today, however, increasingly large amounts of deposits are gathered electronically from communities where banks maintain no physical branches. 

I estimate that roughly 10 percent of U.S. bank deposits, or approximately $2 trillion, are now gathered electronically outside traditional branch footprints. Yet, the current branch-based CRA framework, which is maintained in this most recent proposal, leaves those communities without a corresponding CRA reinvestment obligation.

I was fortunate to have the opportunity to know and work with Senator Proxmire, the "Father of CRA," and he always emphasized the importance of reinvesting deposits back into the communities from which they were sourced, which is why he called it the "Community REINVESTMENT Act."

The OCC itself previously recognized this problem. In its June 2020 CRA Final Rule under Comptroller Joseph Otting, the OCC expressly stated that the growth of internet banks and internet platforms for collecting deposits made deposit-based assessment areas increasingly relevant. 

That rule required certain banks receiving more than half of their retail domestic deposits outside their facility-based assessment areas to establish additional deposit-based assessment areas in geographic markets accounting for at least 5 percent of their retail domestic deposits. That 2020 CRA Final Rule was later rescinded, illustrating the unfortunate politicization of CRA across administrations.

Comptroller Otting’s approach reflected the principle behind what I have long called the "5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule:" a bank has a CRA reinvestment requirement in any area sourcing 5% or more of its deposits. 

The absence of a physical branch by branchless banks, including credit card, internet, fintech, and other banks with electronic delivery systems, should not make the communities sourcing those deposits invisible under CRA.

This is the modern form of the problem CRA was intended to address. Traditional redlining was tied to physical neighborhoods and branch networks. In the digital era, the comparable danger is what I have labeled "weblining," namely the ability of branchless banks to gather substantial deposits electronically from communities without a meaningful corresponding CRA responsibility to reinvest in those communities.

Weblining is most adversely impacting our biggest cities sourcing large amounts of deposits to branchless banks, like my home community of South Florida. There is no commensurate reinvestment requirement for the more than $100 billion of estimated deposits these branchless banks harvest from South Florida. Rather, the CRA benefits flow to the area surrounding the single home-office location of these branchless banks, most notably in Delaware, South Dakota, and Utah.

Comptroller Otting’s 2020 OCC rule demonstrated that this problem can be addressed in a targeted manner with deposit-based assessment area, without imposing nationwide CRA obligations on every bank or simply following lending wherever it occurs. 

Unfortunately, the July 31 proposal ignores this critical issue. By retaining a framework centered on physical facilities, the proposal misses an important opportunity to modernize CRA for the realities of digital banking.

CRA modernization should preserve Senator Proxmire’s fundamental principle in a modern banking system: follow the deposits. If 5% or more of a bank’s deposits come from a community, that community should not disappear from CRA simply because those deposits arrived through a computer or smartphone rather than through a branch door.

With all due respect, the OCC and FDIC should reconsider this serious omission and specifically request comment on a targeted deposit-based assessment-area framework, including a modern version of the 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule previously reflected in the OCC’s 2020 CRA Final Rule.

Better yet, the prudential regulators, including the Fed, if and when it comes out with its own CRA reform package, should follow the KISS rule: maintain the current 1995 regs and update them with the 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule and the best ideas from the rescinded 2023 CRA Final Rule, such as the list of qualified CD activities.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment.

Kenneth H. Thomas, Ph.D.

FYI, full disclosure: I was the only individual to submit an Amicus Brief opposing the 2023 CRA Final Rule in the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit in Texas Bankers Association, et al. v. Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, et al., No. 24-10367.

Dear Sir or Madam,
The San Joaquin Valley Housing Collaborative appreciates the opportunity to comment on the
proposed amendments to the agencies' Community Reinvestment Act regulations published in
the Federal Register on August 12, 2026. The Collaborative is a regional nonprofit serving the
eight counties of California's San Joaquin Valley. Our members include affordable housing
developers, local governments, lenders, and community organizations working together to
expand the supply of safe, affordable homes in one of the most housing-burdened regions in the
country.
Some context on our region may be helpful. The San Joaquin Valley is home to more than four
million people and produces much of the nation's food, yet it has some of the lowest household
incomes and highest poverty rates in California. Large philanthropic institutions are scarce here.
Bank participation motivated by CRA is not a supplement to other capital in our region. In many
cases it is the capital. That is why we are writing about two elements of the proposal that would,
in our experience, pull investment and support away from the very communities the statute
directs banks to serve.
First, we are concerned about the proposal to reclassify banks with assets between $1.65 billion
and $10 billion as intermediate banks no longer subject to the investment test. The Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit is the primary tool for building affordable homes in our region, and the
banks that invest in Valley LIHTC projects are disproportionately mid-size and regional
institutions in this asset range. The investment test is a meaningful part of why they do. If these
banks can receive the same CRA consideration for ordinary market-rate lending, many will have
little reason to continue purchasing housing credits. Fewer investors mean weaker equity
 pricing, and weaker pricing means fewer homes built per credit dollar. Our region already sees
thinner LIHTC pricing than coastal markets, so we would feel this change first and hardest. We
ask the agencies to retain a community development investment component for banks above the
current large bank threshold, or at minimum to structure the intermediate bank evaluation so
that LIHTC and other community development investments receive distinct, meaningful
recognition rather than being blended into general lending performance.
Second, we are concerned about the proposed treatment of community development grants.
Limiting consideration to grants directly used for a specific plan, project, or initiative, and
requiring banks with assets over $10 billion to document that grantees hold overhead costs to 15
percent or less, would sharply curtail bank support for organizations like ours and for the
housing counselors, CDFIs, and community-based nonprofits we work alongside. General
operating support is often the most valuable grant a community organization can receive,
because it funds the staff who put projects together in the first place. The 15 percent overhead
figure has no basis in how effective nonprofits actually operate, and it penalizes small rural
organizations that run lean but cannot spread fixed costs across a large budget. In practice, we
expect the documentation burden would lead many banks to simply stop making grants rather
than police their grantees' cost structures. We ask the agencies to withdraw the overhead
documentation requirement and to preserve CRA consideration for grants, including operating
support, made to organizations whose work has a community development purpose.
We recognize and support the agencies' goals of clarity, continuity, and reduced burden for
community banks. But these two provisions would not reduce burden on communities. They
would reduce investment in them. We would welcome the chance to discuss our experience in
the San Joaquin Valley with agency staff, and we thank you for considering these comments.
Sincerely,
Miguel Arambula
Executive Director
San Joaquin Valley Housing Collaborative

To Whom It May Concern,
On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community
Reinvestment Act.
OFN is the nation's leading network and intermediary focused on community development
investment, managing over $1 billion in total assets and a membership of more than 500
community development financial institutions (CDFIs). OFN's membership includes community
development loan funds, credit unions, banks, and venture capital funds, many of whom
partner with banks who are motivated by the CRA to invest in low- and moderate-income
(LMI) communities.
Since its founding in 1986, OFN members have originated $136 billion in financing, helping to
create or maintain more than 3.8 million jobs, start or expand more than 1.2 million
businesses and microenterprises, and support the development or rehabilitation of nearly 3
million housing units and more than 16,000 community facility projects in rural, urban, and
Native communities across the United States. With cumulative net charge-off rates near one
percent, OFN members lend prudently and productively in the LMI communities.
The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking spans over four hundred pages and proposes significant
changes to the CRA framework with far-reaching implications for banks, community
development partners, and the low- and moderate-income communities they serve. In
addition, the review period covers the final month of Summer when significant portions of
Washington D.C.-based policy organizations are short staffed due to summer vacations ahead
of back-to-school obligations. Given these factors, the proposed 60-day comment period
at this time, and for a regulation of this complexity, does not provide sufficient time
for stakeholders to fully analyze, assess, and understand a rulemaking of this
magnitude. While the agencies have spent considerable time developing the proposal,
regulated institutions and community stakeholders require adequate time to evaluate its

Page 3

operational, economic, and community impacts, consult with internal and external experts, and
develop meaningful, evidence-based feedback.
Previous major CRA rulemakings have provided 90 days for public comment. For instance, in
2022, when the federal banking regulators jointly proposed substantial changes to the CRA
regulations, they provided a 90-day comment period. A rulemaking of this scope with a 60-
day comment period would be insufficient to meaningfully evaluate the proposal, consult
affected parties, and develop data-driven recommendations. For organizations like ours and
the CDFIs we represent, a meaningful review also requires engaging with members nationwide
to understand how the proposal would affect institutions of varying sizes, business models,
and markets. Providing additional time for this analysis will ultimately result in comments that
are more substantive, data-driven, and useful to the agencies as they consider a final rule.
Accordingly, we respectfully urge the agencies to extend the comment period by at
least 30 days. An extension would encourage broader participation from banks, community
organizations, CDFIs, and other stakeholders, leading to a more complete administrative
record and a more informed final regulation.
The CRA is one of the nation's most consequential community development statutes, shaping
billions of dollars in lending, investment, and services that support low- and moderate-income
communities. Changes to its implementing regulations warrant careful deliberation and
meaningful stakeholder engagement. Experience has shown that complex regulatory overhauls
developed under compressed timelines are more likely to require subsequent revisions,
clarification, or litigation. Allowing additional time for public input will help ensure that any
modernization of the CRA framework is thoughtful, durable, and effective for both regulated
institutions and the communities the Act was designed to serve.
Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Sincerely,
Dafina Williams
EVP, Chief Policy Officer and Head of Government Affairs
Opportunity Finance Network

To the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
For Small Business Only LLC strongly supports the agencies' proposed amendments to the Community
Reinvestment Act regulations. The proposal appropriately returns the focus of CRA administration to
demonstrable community credit needs, direct local benefit, transparent use of grant funds, and clear
standards for banks and community organizations.
For Small Business Only LLC (FSBO) is a Virginia limited liability company and a technical-assistance and
capital-readiness intermediary working with nonprofit organizations and financial institutions to prepare
small businesses to become bankable, creditworthy, and lender-ready. FSBO develops and delivers
business-credit, cash-flow, compliance, financial-literacy, and capital-readiness programming. Our
operating premise is straightforward: access to capital improves when businesses receive disciplined
technical assistance before they apply for financing.
Strong support for capital-readiness technical assistance
FSBO particularly supports the proposed economic-development category covering technical assistance
and support services for qualifying small businesses and farms. The proposal recognizes an operational
fact seen across community-development ecosystems: many viable small businesses are not yet
prepared to obtain traditional bank financing and require structured assistance before they can present
an underwriter-ready application.
This clarification should be retained in the final rule. Capital-readiness assistance can improve
compliance, financial records, cash-flow management, credit profiles, loan documentation, and
understanding of lender requirements. These activities reduce preventable application failures and
create a more qualified pipeline for responsible lenders. They advance CRA's objective more directly
 CRA Comment | For Small Business Only LLC
For Small Business Only LLC | Page 2
than programming that promotes access without preparing applicants to use credit safely and
successfully.
Strong support for direct community-development grants
FSBO also strongly supports the proposal's express recognition that a grant or donation to a local
nonprofit providing small-business technical assistance or financial-literacy programming may receive
CRA consideration. This language gives banks greater confidence to support organizations that directly
serve communities and gives nonprofit recipients a clearer standard around which to design programs,
budgets, records, and outcomes.
We likewise support requiring a direct connection between grant funds, qualifying activities, and the
bank's assessment area. The written commitment, program budget, geographic evidence, and closeout
documentation contemplated by the proposal will help distinguish direct service from pass-through
arrangements in which excessive administrative layers reduce the resources reaching businesses and
residents.
Strong support for the 15% indirect-cost guardrail
FSBO supports the proposed 15% indirect-cost limit for community-development grants made by large
banks. A clear ceiling protects community benefit, disciplines program design, and permits reasonable
recovery of necessary operating expenses. The use of the Uniform Guidance framework or a comparable
standard also gives recipients a recognizable method for classifying costs.
The final rule should preserve this guardrail. To improve consistent implementation without weakening
the standard, FSBO respectfully requests that the agencies clarify the following points in final regulatory
text, official commentary, or implementation guidance:
•
New nonprofit documentation. A newly formed nonprofit that has not yet filed an IRS Form 990
should be permitted to substantiate compliance through its current operating budget, program
budget, board-approved cost-allocation policy, recent financial statements, formation
documents, and written attestation.
•
Specialized curriculum and intellectual property. A reasonable, documented, arm's-length
license fee for curriculum actually used to deliver the funded program should be treated as a
direct program cost when the license is necessary to provide the qualifying service, separately
stated, properly approved, and supported by a written agreement.
•
Outcome measurement and required reporting. Costs incurred to collect eligibility, assessment-
area, service-delivery, and outcome evidence required by the bank or agencies should be
treated as direct costs when they are allocable to the funded program.
•
Related-party safeguards. Where a nonprofit licenses curriculum or purchases services from an
affiliated entity, the agencies should recognize the cost if the relationship is disclosed, the
interested director or officer recuses, the governing body determines the terms are fair and
reasonable, and the recipient maintains documentation supporting the programmatic necessity
and value.
 CRA Comment | For Small Business Only LLC
For Small Business Only LLC | Page 3
•
Comparable standards. The final rule should confirm that a recipient may use a consistently
applied cost-allocation methodology comparable to 2 CFR part 200 even when the recipient is
not a federal grantee.
Financial literacy and workforce development
FSBO supports the continued treatment of financial-literacy and workforce-development activities as
community development when they serve low- or moderate-income individuals and families. Financial
capability affects employment stability, household resilience, responsible credit use, and the ability to
retain income gains from workforce participation. The proposal appropriately preserves these activities
while improving categorical clarity.
Recommended final-rule implementation
The agencies can strengthen implementation by encouraging banks and recipients to use a standardized
but scalable evidence package. At minimum, that package should identify the qualifying purpose,
assessment-area nexus, eligible population or business size, approved budget, direct and indirect costs,
service outputs, outcomes, and budget-to-actual reconciliation. Smaller organizations should not be
required to create costly systems disproportionate to the grant, but every recipient should be capable of
demonstrating where the funds went and whom they benefited.
The final rule should also continue to make clear that technical assistance does not require or guarantee
a subsequent loan. The value of capital-readiness programming lies in improving the quality of the
applicant, the completeness of the documentation, and the appropriateness of the financing request.
Individual lending decisions must remain with lenders applying safe and sound underwriting standards.
Conclusion
For Small Business Only LLC strongly supports the proposed rule because it recognizes that community
credit needs are not met by capital alone. Communities also need local organizations capable of
preparing residents and small businesses to understand, qualify for, obtain, and responsibly use financial
products. The proposal's recognition of technical assistance, financial literacy, direct nonprofit grants,
assessment-area benefit, and transparent indirect-cost limits provides a sound framework for
accountable bank-community partnerships.
We urge the OCC and FDIC to adopt the proposal with the limited implementation clarifications
described above. Those clarifications would preserve the proposal's guardrails while enabling newly
formed and specialized nonprofit providers to demonstrate compliance through reliable, proportionate
documentation.
Respectfully submitted,
Sandy E. Day, MSL, PA, CFEI®
Managing Director
For Small Business Only LLC | FSBOnly.com | seday@fsbonly.com

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
I urge the OCC and FDIC to clarify that CRA consideration should support community development financing that creates durable, place based economic opportunity and reduces household vulnerability in low and moderate income neighborhoods, designated disaster areas, and distressed or underserved rural communities.

Communities across Missouri, the St. Louis region, and southern Illinois face overlapping challenges: repeated disaster exposure, high household energy burdens, aging housing and commercial buildings, limited access to patient capital, and the loss of locally rooted businesses. CRA policy should recognize financing that addresses these interconnected needs.

The agencies should expressly clarify that qualifying community development activities can include financing for locally rooted brick and mortar businesses; small business facilities; workforce oriented AI, robotics, advanced manufacturing, research, laboratory, repair, and fabrication spaces; and related equipment and technical assistance, when those activities primarily promote economic development for small businesses, create accessible jobs for low  and moderate income people, or revitalize and stabilize eligible geographies.

The agencies should also recognize financing for affordable housing and community facility improvements that reduce utility costs and improve resilience, including weatherization, efficient electrification, solar, battery storage, geothermal systems, resilient microgrids, flood resilient construction, and other high performance building measures. These investments can preserve affordability by reducing ongoing operating and household energy costs, not merely initial construction costs.

CRA consideration for technology intensive projects should be tied to measurable community benefit. Relevant evidence should include local hiring; quality jobs and apprenticeships; contracts with local and minority , women, and veteran owned businesses; affordable access to facilities or services; documented energy and water impacts; utility bill savings; and long term benefits to eligible communities. CRA should not reward projects whose benefits bypass local residents or whose energy and infrastructure demands worsen affordability.

Finally, the agencies should provide clear recognition for regional partnerships that serve connected rural and metropolitan markets. Banks in the St. Louis metropolitan area and banks serving southern Illinois and rural Missouri should be encouraged to collaborate on projects that demonstrably benefit their assessment areas or broader regional areas that include them.

Clear standards for these activities would help banks direct capital toward businesses and infrastructure that remain in communities, reduce household costs, increase resilience, and build a stronger local economic base.

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations – Joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking

Dear Sir/Madam:

The National Association of Development Companies (NADCO) submits these comments
in response to the joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking and request for comment from the
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and Department of the Treasury, Office of
the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC).

NADCO represents over 190 Certified Development Companies (CDCs) and their industry
partners that deliver the Small Business Administration (SBA) Development Company
Program, commonly known as the 504 Loan Program (and referred to as the "SBDC"
program in the proposed rule). Since 1986, CDCs have provided over 224,000 small
businesses with $146 billion in Section 504 financing, representing a total capital
investment of over $418 billion and creating or retaining over 3.4 million jobs in local
communities throughout the United States.

The SBA Development Company Program is authorized by Section 501(a) of the Small
Business Investment Act of 1958, P.L. 85-699, as amended, which states: "The Congress
hereby finds and declares that the purpose of this title is to foster economic development
and to create or preserve job opportunities in both urban and rural areas by providing long-
term financing for small business concerns through the development company program
authorized by this title."

The 504 Loan Program advances this congressionally established economic development
mission through a public-private partnership. In a typical 504 financing, a private-sector
lending institution provides a first mortgage loan in conjunction with financing provided
through a CDC and backed by an SBA-guaranteed debenture. This structure enables small
businesses to obtain long-term financing for major fixed assets, including land, buildings,
machinery, and equipment, while leveraging private-sector capital to support economic
development and job creation in communities throughout the country.
 Page 2 of 3


Proposed Economic Development Definition
NADCO strongly supports the agencies' proposed revisions to the definition of "economic
development." In particular, NADCO supports the proposed third category of economic
development, which would include "Federal, State, local, or Tribal government programs,
projects, or initiatives that serve small businesses or small farms, as defined by those
programs."

NADCO particularly supports the agencies' specific identification of the SBA Development
Company Program as an example of a federal program meeting this economic
development category. The 504 Loan Program is a congressionally established economic
development program specifically designed to foster economic development and create or
preserve employment opportunities through long-term financing for small businesses.

As the agencies recognize in the proposed rule, expressly identifying these government
programs will provide greater clarity and encourage continued participation in and support
of programs providing small business and small farm financing. The agencies further
recognize that aligning CRA economic development activities with government programs
addressing identified small business needs can encourage coordination among banks,
government agencies, and other program participants. NADCO strongly agrees with this
approach.

This clarification is particularly appropriate for the 504 Loan Program because the program
is built upon precisely this type of public-private coordination. Bank lending partners are
integral to 504 financing, providing private-sector capital alongside CDC/SBA financing to
support small-business investment and economic development. Greater certainty
regarding CRA consideration for qualifying 504-related lending can encourage continued
bank participation in the program and expand access to long-term capital for small
businesses in communities throughout the country.

Elimination of the Purpose Test
NADCO also supports the agencies' proposal to eliminate the existing "purpose test"
applicable to economic development activities. Under current guidance, an otherwise
qualifying small-business activity must satisfy additional requirements related to job
creation, retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income individuals or in
qualifying geographic areas.

The proposed approach would instead establish more objective criteria for determining
whether an activity qualifies as economic development. As the agencies explain, banks
would no longer need to demonstrate, for example, low- or moderate-income job creation
for a qualifying small-business loan and could instead demonstrate that the activity or
government program through which the activity was made is identified as economic
development under the regulation.

 Page 3 of 3

For the SBA 504 Loan Program, this approach appropriately recognizes the economic
development purpose of a federal program specifically established by Congress to foster
economic development and create or preserve employment opportunities, while providing
greater certainty for participating banks.

Response to Question 26
In response to Question 26, NADCO strongly supports retaining the SBA Development
Company Program in the non-exhaustive list of Federal, State, local, or Tribal government
programs, projects, or initiatives included in the proposed definition of economic
development.

Explicit recognition of the SBA Development Company Program will provide greater
regulatory certainty to bank lending partners, encourage continued bank participation in
the 504 Loan Program, and help expand access to long-term capital for small businesses
throughout the United States. It also appropriately recognizes the role of CDCs and their
bank lending partners in carrying out a congressionally established federal economic
development program.

NADCO therefore urges the agencies to adopt the proposed revisions to the economic
development provisions and retain the specific reference to the SBA Development
Company Program in the final rule.

NADCO appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments and the agencies'
recognition of the important role the SBA Development Company Program, Certified
Development Companies, and their bank lending partners play in supporting economic
development in communities throughout the United States.

Sincerely,


Wayne Williams
Executive Vice President
Regulatory Affairs & Training

0014:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Individually, I support the OCC and FDIC's proposed rule, particularly its express recognition of the SBA Development Company Program as a qualifying federal economic development program. Greater CRA certainty for bank loans made with Certified Development Companies (CDCs) under the 504 Loan Program is welcome. At the same time, the final rule should ensure this recognition continues to reflect the LMI and underserved-community focus that gives CRA's community development framework its purpose.

My CDC serves Missouri (urban and rural) and the St. Louis Metro area of Illinois, including lending in distressed rural counties in the Bootheel, Central and Northern Missouri and LMI metro neighborhoods including Jefferson City, Cape Girardo, St. Louis County/City and the Metro East in Illinois. I’ve also worked in conventional business and commercial banking in the same area. This experience informs my general view on finalizing the economic-development category.

CRA credit should recognize economic-development activities because they direct private bank capital toward underserved people and places, not merely because an activity fits within a government program. Any final rule should:

1. Preserve the connection between the economic-development category and underserved communities. The proposed elimination of the current purpose test removes the requirement that a qualifying small business loan create, improve, or retain jobs for LMI individuals or areas. Recognition of the SBA Development Company Program (see proposed rule at 76) should reflect not only its status as a federal program, but its demonstrated role in expanding capital access in underserved communities.

2. Recognize 504 lending as a proven tool for reaching underserved businesses. Our lending in Missouri's distressed rural counties and LMI metro neighborhoods illustrates how the 504 program channels capital where conventional financing often falls short. CRA should recognize this structure, including both interim financing and the Third Party Loan, as directly advancing community-development objectives.

3. Avoid a system where underserved communities become incidental rather than central beneficiaries. If any qualifying small-business loan can receive economic-development consideration regardless of LMI status, banks have less incentive to direct capital where credit needs are greatest. The final rule should expressly tie CRA recognition of the 504 program to its role in expanding economic opportunity for those underserved by conventional credit markets.

504 loans should receive CRA credit because Congress created both CRA and the 504 program to close gaps in private credit markets. Based on our direct experience serving distressed and LMI communities across Missouri and the St. Louis region, we urge the agencies to finalize a rule that provides regulatory certainty while preserving the 504/CDC model's measurable community impact.

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
I am writing regarding the OCC and FDIC's proposed Community Reinvestment Act regulations. Proposed Sec. __.13(a)-(b) codifies a publicly available illustrative list of community development activities and a 90-day agency confirmation process for novel activities. That change directly answers a documented pain point: under current guidance, banks often cannot learn whether an activity qualifies until documentation is reviewed at examination, well after resources are committed.

That same goal of pre-commitment certainty is worth extending to the new "community development grant" definition. For large banks, proposed Sec. __.12 and Sec. __.42(a)(3) cap a grant recipient's indirect costs at 15 percent, "calculated consistent with the Uniform Guidance for Federal Awards, 2 CFR part 200." But 2 CFR 200.414's de minimis rate is defined as a share of modified total direct costs, not as a share of the grant or donation's own dollar amount, which is how the preamble's discussion and examples apply it. A bank and a nonprofit recipient cannot tell from the rule text which base governs, which recreates the exact uncertainty the confirmation process is meant to close, this time for the activity type the agencies identify as most exposed to rent extraction. Specifying the calculation base directly in Sec. __.42(a)(3), rather than by cross-reference to a standard built for a different purpose, would let the safeguard work as intended without turning every large-bank grant into a documentation dispute.

A second gap sits underneath the entire proposed size framework. The small ($1 billion), intermediate ($1-10 billion), and large (over $10 billion) bank categories all turn on undefined "assets." The preamble's own Question 3 asks whether assets should be defined by reference to Call Report Schedule RC or the foreign-bank Schedule RAL, which suggests the agencies see the gap themselves. Resolving that question in the final rule, rather than leaving it to case-by-case interpretation, would let the threshold structure the agencies are building around function predictably from day one.

Proposed Sec. __.21(g) also offers two structurally different major product line methods (a bank-level quantitative standard and an assessment-area qualitative standard) without indicating a preferred path. Banks cannot build the data systems and lending strategies the rule anticipates while both options remain live; identifying a lead option, even provisionally, would let institutions begin preparing before the comment period closes rather than after a final rule issues.

Proposed Sec. __.13(d)(3) allocates CD activity that benefits more than one assessment area either by recipient address or by a deposit-weighted formula, and it also lets a bank propose "another reasonable methodology" for agency approval. That flexibility is useful for cross-regional funds of the kind the preamble describes, but without illustrative criteria for what makes an alternative methodology reasonable, approval could vary examiner to examiner in ways the recipient-address and deposit-weight options were designed to avoid. Adding two or three worked examples of an acceptable alternative, alongside the ones already given for the default methods, would let banks propose allocation approaches with a reasonable expectation of how they will be evaluated.

Finally, proposed Sec. __.13(e)(2) measures the geographic flexibility standard for CD activity outside assessment areas as a percentage of tier 1 capital. The agencies themselves invite comment on exactly this gap, asking when tier 1 capital should be treated as an insufficient measure of capacity for a bank with a large foreign deposit base, since tier 1 capital does not track domestic lending capacity for such institutions. Pairing the tier 1 capital measure with a domestic-deposit-based alternative for banks in that position would keep the standard meaningful across business models rather than only for the typical case.

These points are offered to sharpen provisions the agencies have already identified as central to reducing burden and improving clarity, not to oppose the recodification effort. The asset threshold increases and the public file's shift to a website-based model are reasonable responses to the burden the current rules impose on smaller institutions, and the changes above would help that same objective reach the CD grant, sizing, and lending-test provisions consistently.

suggested by the proposal necessitate a comment period of at least one hundred
and twenty (120) days.

comment on the over 350 pages of material and over 60 questions posed in this
complex proposed rule. We are concerned that many of the numerous proposed

reinvestment in the low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities meant to be

proposed changes will lead to significant outcomes, including: less support for

investments that support small businesses, and less capacity for community based
organizations to play their critical role in supporting communities and the financial
service ecosystem.

one-hundred twenty (120) days in total.

To Whom It May Concern:

The [Independent Bankers Association of Texas ("IBAT") appreciates the
opportunity to submit this comment letter regarding the joint Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) on July
31, 2026, to amend the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.

Representing community banks across Texas, IBAT is dedicated to preserving
the health and vitality of local financial banks that serve as the economic
engines of our communities.

IBAT and its member banks have a long, proven track record of meeting the
credit needs of our local communities, long predating the original 1977 CRA
statute. While we appreciate the agencies' intent to modernize the
framework, reduce unnecessary burdens, and provide greater transparency,
we have both positive feedback and significant concerns regarding the
specific structural impacts of this proposal on community banking.

Support for Regulatory Relief and Streamlined Frameworks

IBAT welcomes several provisions within the proposal that offer necessary
relief to community banks:

Realignment of Asset Thresholds: Raising the asset thresholds is a highly
consequential and positive adjustment. Re-categorizing small banks to
include banks under $1 billion in assets (up from the previous $412 million
threshold) and establishing the intermediate bank category between $1
billion and $10 billion provides critical regulatory relief. Exempting banks
under $10 billion from excessive data collection, maintenance, and reporting
requirements represents a substantial reduction in unnecessary overhead.

Refocus on Core Lending Activities: Community banks excel at traditional relationship-based lending. By
refocusing the evaluation framework more heavily on measurable lending activities and primary credit
products, the proposal aligns evaluations with what community banks do best: funding local families, small
businesses, and agriculture.

Exclusion of Retail Deposit Services: Limiting the retail service test to primary credit products and explicitly
excluding retail deposit services from evaluation acknowledges that digital and physical deposit gathering
have evolved significantly. This eliminates subjective and burdensome evaluations of retail service metrics
that do not accurately measure community impact.

Objective Qualification Criteria: The effort to bring greater clarity, transparency, and objectivity to what
qualifies for community development consideration will provide community banks with greater certainty
prior to making long-term investment or lending commitments.

Critical Concerns with the Joint Proposal

Despite these positive developments, IBAT is deeply concerned by several structural aspects of the
proposal that threaten to disrupt the banking ecosystem and introduce operational challenges:

A Fractured Regulatory Framework: The most glaring deficiency of this proposal is that the Board of
Governors of the Federal Reserve System did not join it. A fractured framework where OCC- and FDIC-
supervised banks operate under a new rule while Federal Reserve-regulated state member banks remain
under the legacy 1995 framework is unworkable. This division disrupts competitive equity, complicates
holding company supervision, and creates confusion for community partnerships that rely on consistent
interagency rules.

Regulatory Whiplash and Uncertainty: The banking industry has endured substantial regulatory shifting
since 2020, ranging from the 2023 final rule to subsequent litigation, rescission proposals, and now this
completely new framework. Community banks require a durable, long-term, and fully unified interagency
standard. This cyclical rulemaking forces community banks to redirect finite compliance resources away
from actual community lending to handle continuous administrative changes.

Constraints on Community Development Infrastructure: While community banks support verifying that
community development funds reach their intended beneficiaries, specific new restrictions—such as rigid
indirect cost caps or narrow definitions of qualifying economic development—may inadvertently penalize
long-standing partnerships with local nonprofits. Local nonprofits in rural or smaller Texas markets heavily
depend on general operating support grants from community banks, and overly restrictive tracking
mandates could choke off this vital infrastructure.

IBAT urges the OCC and the FDIC to pause finalization of this proposal until a fully unified, interagency rule
can be reached in conjunction with the Federal Reserve. While the tiered asset thresholds and lending
focus represent positive steps toward meaningful regulatory relief, a split regulatory landscape
undermines the core statutory goal of providing a consistent, predictable environment for community
investment. We look forward to ongoing engagement with the agencies to establish a workable, durable
CRA framework that truly supports economic growth across Texas.

 Sincerely,

/s/

Christopher Williston
President and CEO
Independent Bankers Association of Texas

Dear Chief Counsel, 

Community Housing Network, Inc. is a nonprofit organization that provides housing that helps close Central Ohio’s housing affordability gaps for extremely-low-income households, particularly those with disabilities. In advance, we share our gratitude for your review and consideration of these comments. 

The proposed rule will significantly reduce investment capacity in proven housing creation strategies that are critical for reducing Central Ohio’s housing shortage, including the federal Low Income Housing Tax Credit, the Ohio Low Income Housing Tax Credit (rural and preservation focused), and others. It would restrain the State’s proposed Promise Land tax credit which will support faith-based housing providers working to advance homeownership opportunities. As demonstrated by this list of tax credit programs funding critical bipartisan supported housing initiatives, tax credit investment is fundamental to getting the missing housing that Ohio needs.  The proposed rule changes will disincentivize Banks from making these investments and will significantly reduce the impact of these critical housing programs.

Central Ohio’s booming economy means that we need nearly 200,000 new homes over the next ten years to accommodate job growth. Over the past decade, the community produced housing at half the pace we now need and pressure is mounting as more than 80,000 residents experience severe housing cost burden (signified by paying more than half their incomes to housing, leaving little money to pay for other basic needs). The suite of equity investment programs that will be negatively impacted by the proposed rule are essential to correcting this market imbalance. 

Additionally, the proposed rule will impede service delivery, especially those designed to advance economic self-sufficiency for low- and moderate-income households. Specifically, portions of the rule that restrict nonprofit grants and donations or impose administrative fee caps that are out of alignment with actual costs will result in inefficiencies, increased administrative burden, and funding shortfalls for high-priority initiatives, many of which were recently promoted in the bipartisan supported 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. 

In Central Ohio, the following program types are likely to experience operating shortages and/or risk closure should this rule become effective in its current form: 

•Technical assistance and education to reduce zoning barriers to housing creation; 
•‘Libraries’ with pre-approved housing construction plans to reduce permitting delays and construction costs;  
•Capacity building for faith-based housing providers; 
•Risk tolerant lending for emerging building types, like manufactured and ADU housing; 
•Innovative down payment strategies; 
•Housing counseling to promote self-sufficiency and/or sustainable homeownership; 
•Home modifications to support senior independence and aging in community;
•Public safety-based programs to remediate blight and reduce housing vacancies; 
•Housing research to assess and monitor supply shortages and document best practices. 

The rule changes would contract these programs and lead to increased housing supply shortages, housing quality barriers, or neighborhood stability needs. Housing alone can help stabilize people and give them opportunities to thrive.  But our residents struggle to stay housed if they do not have supportive services as it is hard work to lift oneself out of poverty and our residents cannot do this work alone.  They need collaborative partners to provide services and support to our residents.  This work will not happen without the rules directing Banks to create the environment needed to foster these collaborations.

Community Housing Network requests that the proposed rulemaking process be suspended or delayed pending further research and community engagement into these acute harms. Alternately, we recommend modifications that both (1) strengthen the LIHTC program and similar public-private partnerships and (2) protect the current incentive structure that supports local, place-based responses to the nation’s housing challenges. 

Thank you for your time and consideration. 

Sincerely,

Central Bank appreciates the opportunity to comment on the OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding
the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

Central Bank is an FDIC-supervised community bank with approximately $2.1 billion in assets, 13 branches, and
operations concentrated within a single metropolitan statistical area. We currently maintain a CRA rating of Satisfactory
and conduct more than 80 percent of our lending activity within our assessment area.

We generally support the proposal and commend the agencies for pursuing a framework that more closely aligns with
the CRA's statutory purpose of helping banks meet the credit needs of their local communities while reducing
unnecessary regulatory burden.

We strongly support the proposed asset thresholds creating Small Banks (under $1 billion), Intermediate Banks ($1
billion to $10 billion), and Large Banks (over $10 billion). The current thresholds no longer reflect the structure of today's
banking industry. Institutions in our asset range continue to operate as community-focused banks but are subject to
compliance expectations originally designed for significantly larger organizations.

We also support the proposal's increased emphasis on lending activities. Lending remains the most direct and
measurable way banks meet community credit needs. The proposal appropriately rebalances CRA evaluations toward
lending performance while continuing to recognize community development activities.

Central Bank further supports retaining the traditional assessment-area framework tied to physical banking facilities and
local communities. This approach provides important regulatory certainty and better reflects the statutory focus on local
communities served by deposit-taking institutions.

We support efforts to reduce data collection, reporting, and administrative burden for banks below $10 billion in assets.
Resources devoted to regulatory administration can instead be directed toward additional lending and community
development activities.

While we generally support the proposal's treatment of community development grants, we encourage the agencies to


preserve flexibility for effective nonprofit organizations that provide meaningful community services and community
development benefits.

Overall, we believe the proposal will better align CRA requirements with bank size and complexity, place appropriate
emphasis on lending, preserve the traditional community-based CRA framework, and reduce unnecessary regulatory
burden. For these reasons, Central Bank generally supports the proposal and encourages the agencies to proceed with
finalizing the rule.

Sincerely,


Niki Christensen
Chief Compliance Officer
Central Bank

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
I oppose the proposed rule changes noted for the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) since it moves away from the reason why the CRA was in acted in the first place.  The proposed rules will impact millions of people depriving them of community support, redevelopment activities, housing, and so many other important financial activities now available to them.  These smaller communities, non-profits, communities of color and low- and moderate-income people are the backbone of our country. These rule changes won't improve consumer bank fees, but will improve the profit margin for banks making the rich even richer.
Examples of this unfair change in the rules:
>Eliminating or weakening CRA requirements for hundreds of banks by raising asset thresholds will result in hundreds of banks to no longer have obligations to report their investments, services and small business loans, resulting in significant reductions in activities serving low- and moderate-income people. Banks have and should continue to have an obligation to support the communities that support and trust them with their hard earned cash. This rule making tries to reduce this community responsibility by just changing the asset thresholds of who has to report giving most of the banks a free pass to overlook any community responsibility. 

A reverberation of this rule change affects more than 5,000 bank branches in low- and moderate-income (LMI) census tracts (30% of all LMI branches nationwide and more than 4,000 branches in majority-people-of-color census tracts).  CRA’s branching obligations are a major reason that banks have maintained the share of their branches located in LMI communities at relatively steady levels — roughly 24% nationwide. Without branch evaluations, the number and share of branches maintained by affected banks in LMI areas will decline precipitously further challenging LMI communities to have access to financial institutions that treat them fairly.

The proposed rule would restrict the service test to credit services and exclude deposit services, such as checking and savings products, from CRA consideration. For large banks still subject to the service test, examiners would no longer evaluate whether checking and savings accounts are affordable, reducing incentives to offer the basic products that help unbanked (5.6 million households) and underbanked households (19 million households). These are real people being left behind in our banking system.

The proposal also weakens the standard for earning CRA credit for economic development activities. Under current guidance, an activity must generally satisfy both a size test and a purpose test, including showing that it creates, retains or improves jobs for low- and moderate-income people, benefits low- and moderate-income areas or works through qualifying intermediaries. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test, allowing banks to receive CRA credit for business financing without showing that it creates, preserves or improves jobs for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. By removing the focus on LMI communities, the proposal could allow a bank to receive CRA credit for financing a limited liability company (LLC) established by a wealthy business owner in an upper-income census tract — even if the business creates no jobs for low- and moderate-income people. 

The rule change should not dilute, remove, or reward banks for not supporting the communities!

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
I am submitting this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).  In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

Dear Comptroller and Members of the Board of Directors of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
Lord Santiago LLC appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's proposed amendments to the regulations implementing the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), published at 91 Federal Register 52114 on August 12, 2026.
Lord Santiago LLC is a fractional executive consulting business that serves Community Development
Financial Institutions (CDFIs) certified by the U.S. Department of the Treasury. These organizations provide

Lord Santiago LLC has provided risk-analytics services to the banking industry, including developing the IRA

Drawing on that experience, Lord Santiago LLC fully supports the regulators' decision to return to
