Since 2022, Lord Santiago LLC has participated in the OCC's Project REACh program and contributed to its
homeownership preservation, small-business, special-purpose credit program, and minority depository
institution revitalization initiatives.
Lord Santiago LLC's homeownership-preservation work produced a theory paper examining innovative uses
of shared-equity structures. That work helped develop the policy foundation for government-assisted,
lower-cost shared-equity down-payment assistance of the kind now embodied in California's Dream for All
program.
In contributing to the small-business special-purpose credit program initiative, Lord Santiago LLC
advocated using CDFIs as bank partners for small-business loan applications that regulated depository
institutions could not serve because the applicants fell outside traditional five-Cs credit guidelines. This
 Page 2
work identified several regulatory and process problems, including the risk that banks could be penalized
for formally denying an application as a predicate to transferring the file to a CDFI. Constructive discussions
led by Lord Santiago LLC have identified better pathways for addressing this regulatory obstacle while
improving net access to capital for borrowers who do not meet conventional bank underwriting standards.
The regulators' current initiatives are broadly compatible with this constructive process.
Lord Santiago LLC's involvement in minority depository institution revitalization also highlighted the need to
provide smaller institutions with achievable pathways for maintaining safety and soundness, recognizing
that they do not possess the internal infrastructure available to their larger counterparts. We are pleased
that regulators are increasingly sensitive to this economies-of-scale challenge and to the need for
supervisory expectations that remain rigorous but proportionate to institutional capacity.
Lord Santiago LLC's founder, Dennis Santiago, also authored a substantial response to the June 3, 2022,
interagency notice of proposed rulemaking on Community Reinvestment Act regulations while serving as a
member of the Board of Directors of the National Diversity Coalition. That response provided detailed input
on numerous specific questions posed by the regulators and reflected direct engagement with the
proposal's major policy choices.
We support the regulators' objective of ensuring that CRA-qualified activities demonstrably benefit the
communities Congress intended the CRA to serve. We also support efforts to make CRA qualification more
predictable and to focus CRA evaluation on the provision of credit and meaningful community-development
activities.
In particular, we support the concept underlying Options 1 and 2 for determining major product lines: CRA
retail lending evaluation should concentrate principally on the lending products that represent meaningful
components of a bank's business. We believe this approach can make CRA evaluation more relevant to
how financial institutions actually operate while allowing banks and regulators to devote greater attention
to activities capable of producing meaningful community impact.
We also agree with the regulators that rent extraction is a legitimate concern in evaluating community-
development grants. CRA consideration should not encourage structures in which successive layers of
intermediaries consume grant resources without producing commensurate benefits for the communities
the CRA is intended to serve.
These two policy objectives are related. If banks are encouraged to concentrate their direct retail lending
efforts on the major products in which they possess scale, systems, expertise, and demonstrated capacity,
Treasury-certified CDFIs can provide a complementary channel for reaching borrowers and credit needs
that fall outside those products or below conventional bank underwriting standards.
Direct bank partnerships with Treasury-certified CDFIs can therefore improve the efficacy of CRA programs
while simultaneously addressing the regulators' concern about unnecessary intermediary costs.
I. Treasury-certified CDFIs should be distinguished from generic intermediaries.
CDFIs are not simply intermediaries between banks and ultimate beneficiaries. A certified CDFI is a
specialized financial institution whose primary mission is community development and whose certification
is subject to standards administered by the U.S. Department of the Treasury.
CDFIs perform financial functions that conventional lenders frequently cannot perform economically at
comparable scale. These functions include borrower identification and development, technical assistance,
underwriting of nontraditional credits, loan origination, loan servicing, portfolio monitoring, compliance,
loan-loss management, and recycling of repaid capital into subsequent community-development loans.
These functions are not ancillary to community-development lending. They are the process by which
community-development lending occurs.
 Page 3
Banks appropriately establish credit standards—or "buy boxes"—designed to define borrowers and
transactions that satisfy their risk, underwriting, profitability, regulatory and portfolio requirements.
Inevitably, otherwise viable borrowers exist whose financial condition, collateral, credit history, transaction
size, stage of development or other characteristics place them below those conventional bank financing
thresholds.
Serving that population is one of the essential functions of a CDFI. A CDFI identifies prospective borrowers,
prepares them for financing, provides technical assistance where appropriate, performs underwriting
adapted to the characteristics of underserved markets, originates and services loans, monitors credit
performance, and works with borrowers after closing.
The objective is not merely to make loans that conventional banks will not make. It is to develop qualified
borrowers and viable credits in markets where conventional bank underwriting alone may not economically
support that development process.
We recommend that the regulators establish a rebuttable presumption or safe harbor under which a loan,
investment, grant, or other qualifying financial commitment to a Treasury-certified CDFI is considered to
have a community-development purpose when the funds are committed to activities otherwise qualifying
under the CRA and the CDFI maintains reasonable records demonstrating the use and geographic
distribution of those funds.
II. Major product lines: We support the fundamental direction of Options 1 and 2
We support the regulators' proposal to focus CRA retail lending evaluation on a bank's major product lines.
Banks differ substantially in business model, market, expertise, and lending capacity. A bank substantially
engaged in small-business lending should be evaluated meaningfully on its small-business lending
performance. Similarly, an institution whose principal retail credit activity consists of mortgage lending
should receive appropriate scrutiny of that activity.
Requiring equal regulatory attention to incidental lending activities can consume both bank and regulatory
resources without necessarily producing a corresponding community benefit.
Accordingly, we support the fundamental concept reflected in both Options 1 and 2: CRA evaluation should
identify and meaningfully evaluate the lending activities that are actually significant to the institution or the
markets in which it operates.
At the same time, concentrating evaluation on major products should not cause credit needs outside those
products to disappear from CRA policy.
This is precisely where strategically working with U.S. Treasury-certified CDFIs can improve the
effectiveness of a bank's CRA program. CDFIs can complement the bank's major product lending by
reaching qualified community-development borrowers and activities outside the bank's primary business
lines and by serving prospective borrowers below the bank's conventional credit thresholds.
III. Response to Question 4: A de minimis threshold is reasonable.
Question 4 asks whether the regulators should establish a de minimis threshold for determining major
product lines, including whether a threshold such as 30 loans would appropriately exclude incidental
lending.
We believe a de minimis threshold is reasonable and appropriate.
A bank may originate a small number of loans in a particular category for reasons unrelated to a sustained
product strategy. Inadvertently, treating such incidental activity as a major product line could distort CRA
 Page 4
evaluation and impose examination and compliance costs disproportionate to the community significance
of the activity.
The threshold should distinguish a genuine lending business from incidental activity while avoiding a level
so high that it excludes meaningful lending by smaller institutions. We encourage the regulators to consider
both loan count and the institution's overall lending activity when defining the threshold and to evaluate
experience under the final rule to determine whether the chosen threshold produces the intended result.
Importantly, exclusion of incidental lending from the major-product test should not imply that the
corresponding community credit need is unimportant. Banks should be encouraged to address credit
needs outside their major products through community development lending and strategic partnerships
with Treasury-certified CDFIs possessing specialized capacity in those markets. This provides a practical
means of focusing on major products while preserving broader CRA impact.
IV. Response to Question 5: Consumer lending should be evaluated by individual type.
We recommend that consumer lending be evaluated by individual product type rather than treated as a
single undifferentiated category.
Consumer lending encompasses a particularly broad variety of credit structures, purposes, borrower
populations, risk characteristics, and pricing models.
Historically, "consumer lending" has often functioned as a catch-all reporting category, including for
regulatory Call Report purposes. That broad categorization may be useful for certain financial-reporting
purposes, but CRA evaluation requires a more granular understanding of how credit is actually being
provided to communities.
For example, automobile lending, credit-card lending, other revolving credit, unsecured installment
lending, and other forms of consumer credit can present substantially different borrower populations,
pricing structures, underwriting criteria, and community impacts.
For CRA purposes, consumer lending should therefore be examined with a finer degree of product-level
differentiation. This would allow regulators to determine whether a particular consumer product represents
a meaningful component of the bank's lending activity rather than allowing a broad aggregate category to
obscure the significance—or insignificance—of individual lending products.
Here again, Treasury-certified CDFIs can serve as strategic partners. Where a particular consumer-credit
need is material to a community but does not constitute a major product for the bank, a qualified CDFI with
appropriate lending authority and expertise may provide a more effective channel through which the bank
can support responsible access to credit.
V. Response to Question 6: Both dollar volume and loan count should determine major
product lines.
Question 6 asks whether regulators should rely on dollar volume, loan count, or both in determining a
bank's major product lines.
We recommend using both dollar volume and loan count. Neither metric alone adequately captures the
significance of a lending product.
This is particularly evident in small-business lending. Small-business loans frequently have substantially
smaller principal balances than residential mortgages and other large-balance credit products. A bank
could originate a significant number of small-business loans, serve a substantial number of businesses,
and generate meaningful community impact, while the aggregate dollar balance of those loans remains
relatively modest compared with its mortgage portfolio.
 Page 5
A dollar-volume-only test could consequently understate the importance of small-business lending.
Conversely, loan count alone could understate the significance of a product involving fewer but
substantially larger extensions of credit.
Using both metrics provides regulators with a more complete picture of the bank's actual lending business
and avoids systematically penalizing products characterized by smaller, more numerous loans.
This principle is particularly relevant to CDFI partnerships. CDFI lending frequently consists of
comparatively small loans whose aggregate community impact is better reflected by considering both
dollars deployed and borrowers served. Banks working strategically with Treasury-certified CDFIs should
therefore be encouraged to report both dollar volume and loan count, together with appropriate information
concerning borrower characteristics and community impact.
VI. Response to Question 7: Apply Option 1 to small and intermediate banks and consider
Option 2 for large banks.
Question 7 asks whether, if Option 1 is adopted, major product lines should be determined by assessment
area rather than at the institution level.
We believe the answer should depend substantially on institution size and geographic complexity.
For small and intermediate banks as defined under the proposed rule, we believe the institution-level
methodology contemplated by Option 1 is generally the preferable approach. These institutions are more
likely to have relatively cohesive business models and geographic footprints. Determining their major
product lines at the institution level should provide regulators with meaningful information while avoiding
unnecessary compliance and examination burden.
For large banks, particularly institutions operating across numerous and materially different geographic
markets, the assessment area analysis contemplated by Option 2 may provide useful additional
information.
A large geographically dispersed institution may operate in markets with significantly different economic
conditions, demographic characteristics, credit needs, and product demand. A product that is relatively
insignificant at the consolidated institution level may nevertheless be important in a particular assessment
area. Accordingly, an assessment-area approach may provide greater insight into whether the bank is
responding to the credit characteristics of particular communities.
However, this additional analytical granularity comes at a cost. The regulators should therefore evaluate the
cost-benefit relationship associated with imposing assessment-area-level major-product analysis on large
institutions.
The relevant question should be whether the additional data collection, systems, compliance activity,
examination work, and regulatory resources required by the assessment-area methodology produce a
commensurate improvement in community outcomes and CRA effectiveness.
We recommend that the regulators incorporate a mechanism to assess this return on regulatory investment
after implementation. Such an assessment could examine whether the additional analytical work materially
improves identification of unmet credit needs, changes bank lending behavior, or produces measurable
benefits for communities.
If experience demonstrates that assessment-area analysis produces meaningful incremental benefits, its
continuation would be supported by evidence. If the additional burden produces little difference in
community outcomes, the regulators should retain the flexibility to simplify the methodology.
Treasury-certified CDFIs can also contribute to this analysis. Because CDFIs frequently possess detailed
knowledge of credit gaps within individual communities, strategic bank-CDFI relationships can provide
 Page 6
banks and regulators with market information that may complement quantitative assessment-area
analysis.
VII. Further Regarding Questions 4 to 7: The major product framework strengthens the
case for direct bank-CDFI partnerships.
Questions 4 through 7 should not be considered independently from the community development
provisions addressed later in the proposal.
A major product framework necessarily acknowledges that no bank can specialize in every form of lending
required by every community it serves.
The logical regulatory objective should therefore be twofold: first, evaluate banks rigorously on the lending
products that constitute meaningful components of their business; second, provide effective channels
through which banks can address legitimate community credit needs outside those major products.
Treasury-certified CDFIs provide one such channel.
Bank major-product lending supports direct lending in areas where the bank possesses scale, systems, and
expertise. Bank-CDFI partnerships support specialized borrower development, technical assistance,
underwriting, and lending in areas outside the bank's principal products or conventional credit parameters.
The major product framework and CDFI partnerships should therefore be viewed as complementary
components of an efficient CRA architecture rather than unrelated policy questions.
VIII. Response to Question 9: Address rent extraction by distinguishing intermediaries
from direct CDFI financial activity
Question 9 asks: "Are there alternative standards the regulators should consider relying on in the context of
limiting indirect costs for CD grants? Do the proposed guardrails do enough to ensure the majority of grant
and donation funds go directly towards benefiting the bank's assessment area(s)?"
We agree with the regulators' underlying concern. CRA consideration should not encourage arrangements
in which organizations function principally as intermediaries, transferring resources through multiple layers
while extracting administrative costs at each stage. Regulators have a legitimate interest in ensuring that
CRA-motivated grants actually produce measurable community-development benefits.
We believe that direct relationships between banks and Treasury-certified CDFIs engaged in actual
economic-development lending provide one appropriate regulatory response to this concern.
A Treasury-certified CDFI that identifies borrowers, develops those borrowers, performs underwriting,
originates loans, services those loans, and monitors their performance is not merely passing funds to
another organization. It is performing the financial activity for which the community-development resources
were provided.
The distinction between intermediation and financial production is therefore critical.
Where an organization merely receives a grant and passes substantially the same funds through to another
organization, the regulators' concern about intermediary costs may appropriately receive heightened
scrutiny. Where a certified CDFI uses bank resources to identify, prepare, underwrite, finance, service and
monitor borrowers that fall outside conventional bank credit parameters, those expenditures are
fundamentally different. They are costs incurred to produce community-development credit.
 Page 7
IX. The 15 percent limitation should principally address true general-and-administrative
costs.
We believe the regulators' proposed 15 percent limitation is better understood and more appropriately
applied as a limitation on general and administrative (G&A) costs, rather than as a broad limitation on all
operating expenditures that do not directly become loan principal.
A distinction should be drawn between (1) general institutional overhead, consisting of costs that are not
reasonably allocable to a particular lending or community-development program, and (2) direct program
costs, consisting of expenditures necessary to identify, prepare, underwrite, originate, service, monitor and
manage qualifying community-development credit.
The regulators' concern regarding rent extraction is most relevant to the first category. True G&A expenses
may include corporate governance, certain executive and administrative functions, general office
administration, non-program-specific legal or accounting expenses, and other costs supporting the
organization as a whole without a direct nexus to qualifying community-development activity.
The second category represents the operational cost of producing and maintaining the very financial activity
the CRA is intended to encourage.
We therefore recommend that any percentage limitation adopted in the final rule apply principally to true
general-and-administrative costs, and not to reasonable direct program costs necessary to create,
administer and monitor qualifying community-development loans.
X. Borrower development, lending infrastructure and technology are direct program
costs.
For a CDFI loan fund, borrower development, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, portfolio
management, loan-loss monitoring, impact reporting, and appropriate financial controls are essential
components of the lending process.
A dollar cannot responsibly be deployed as a small-business loan merely by transferring it from a bank to a
borrower. The prospective borrower must be identified. The business must be evaluated. The borrower may
require assistance with financial statements, bookkeeping, cash-flow projections, or other elements
necessary to be prepared for financing.
The credit must then be underwritten, approved, documented, and closed. After closing, the loan must be
serviced and monitored. Delinquencies and credit deterioration must be identified and managed. These are
direct costs of producing and maintaining community-development loans.
The technology supporting those functions is equally integral. Direct program costs should expressly
include reasonable expenses associated with:
• loan application platforms used for borrower intake and document collection.
• underwriting platforms used for credit analysis, risk assessment, and approval.
• loan servicing platforms used to administer loans after closing; and
• portfolio surveillance systems used to monitor credit performance, covenant compliance, delinquency,
concentration, and risk migration.
These systems are not administrative conveniences. They are lending infrastructure. A platform used to
originate or monitor hundreds of qualifying loans should not become an indirect expense merely because
the technology supports multiple borrowers.
 Page 8
XI. Banks should document CDFI performance rather than rely solely on an overhead
percentage.
The regulators can address rent extraction through accountability for outputs and outcomes, rather than
relying exclusively on an overhead ratio.
Banks receiving CRA consideration for CDFI support could reasonably request periodic reports concerning:
• number and dollar amount of loans originated.
• communities and populations served.
• borrower characteristics relevant to CRA qualification.
• borrowers receiving technical assistance.
• borrowers prepared for financing.
• lending to borrowers outside conventional bank underwriting thresholds.
• geographic distribution.
• loan and portfolio performance.
• direct program expenses associated with borrower development and lending.
• technology costs reasonably allocable to qualifying lending; and
• where practicable, borrowers subsequently graduating to conventional financial products.
The CDFI-bank relationship is inherently symbiotic. Banks provide capital, grants, investments, and
financial expertise. CDFIs provide specialized market access and the borrower-development, underwriting
and servicing capabilities necessary to responsibly extend credit deeper into underserved markets.
The appropriate regulatory question therefore should not simply be: "What percentage did the CDFI spend
on administration?"
A more meaningful question is: "What did the CDFI produce with the bank's support, whom did it
finance, what financial-development activities and systems were required to produce those loans,
and did the resulting activity demonstrably benefit the communities the CRA is intended to serve?"
XII. The proposed 15 percent indirect cost limitation should be modified for certified
CDFIs. G&A costs should be controlled. Certain program costs should be classified as
direct costs.
We appreciate the regulators' objective of preventing excessive administrative expenses from absorbing
funds intended for community development. However, a rigid 15 percent test does not accurately reflect
the economics of community-development finance.
The Uniform Guidance de minimis indirect-cost rate provides a mechanism for recognizing and recovering
legitimate indirect costs. Its existence should not imply that organizations exceeding that percentage are
inefficient or engaged in rent extraction.
We recommend that the 15 percent limitation apply principally to G&A expenses after reasonable direct
program costs have been identified and allocated.
For Treasury-certified CDFIs, direct program costs should include reasonable expenses associated with
borrower identification and preparation, technical assistance, underwriting, origination, closing, servicing,
portfolio surveillance, loan-loss management, and lending technology—including loan applications,
underwriting, servicing, and portfolio-surveillance platforms.
This concept is similar to the use of cost allocation agreements used in other areas of federal contracting.
We believe they principles are applicable and recommend regulators consider codifying this guidance as
part of the final rule.
 Page 9
Alternatively, the regulators could establish 15 percent as an administrative safe harbor rather than an
absolute ceiling. Organizations within the safe harbor would require no additional demonstration. A
certified CDFI exceeding it could establish qualification through documentation demonstrating the nature
of its costs and the qualifying lending produced.
XIII. Response to Question 10: Grants and donations should remain eligible.
Question 10 asks: "As an alternative, should the regulators eliminate all grants and donations from CRA
consideration?"
We strongly recommend that grants and donations remain eligible.
Loan capital finances assets expected to produce repayment. Grants finance many of the activities
required to create the pipeline through which that loan capital can responsibly reach underserved
borrowers.
These include borrower preparation, technical assistance, underwriting assistance, outreach, loan-loss
support, post-closing assistance, lending systems, and institutional capacity.
Eliminating CRA consideration for grants could therefore reduce precisely the activities that help
prospective borrowers become capable of obtaining responsible financing and, ultimately, conventional
financing.
XIV. Geographic flexibility for CDFI activities
CDFI service territories frequently do not correspond precisely with bank assessment areas.
CDFIs may manage lending programs across metropolitan, regional, or statewide markets. Excessively
narrow geographic restrictions can fragment capital pools, increase reporting burdens, and inhibit
deployment based on actual borrower demand.
CDFIs should therefore be permitted to establish geographic benefit through reasonable methodologies
including loan-level information, portfolio allocations, borrower addresses, census-tract data, or
proportional allocation.
Exact tracing of every dollar should not be required where a reasonable methodology reliably demonstrates
community benefit.
XV. Strategic plans should incorporate CDFI knowledge.
CDFIs work directly with borrowers who frequently cannot obtain conventional financing and therefore
possess information about unmet credit demand that may not appear in traditional bank lending data.
We recommend expressly recognizing consultation with certified CDFIs as potentially relevant evidence
when banks identify community credit needs and develop measurable CRA strategic-plan objectives.
Such consultation should not be mandatory or exclusive, but it represents a meaningful source of market
intelligence.
XVI. Recommended CDFI safe harbor
We encourage the regulators to consider language substantially similar to the following:
Certified CDFI Safe Harbor
A loan, investment, grant, deposit, or other financial commitment provided to a Community
Development Financial Institution certified by the U.S. Department of the Treasury shall be
 Page 10
presumed to have a community-development purpose to the extent that the recipient CDFI commits
the funds to activities satisfying the community-development requirements of this part.
Reasonable costs directly associated with identifying and preparing prospective borrowers and with
originating, underwriting, closing, administering, servicing, monitoring, or providing technical
assistance in connection with qualifying community-development loans shall constitute direct
program costs.
Direct program costs shall include reasonable costs allocable to loan application platforms,
underwriting and credit-analysis platforms, loan servicing platforms, portfolio-surveillance and risk-
management systems, and other technology infrastructure necessary to originate, manage and
monitor qualifying community-development credit.
Any percentage limitation on indirect costs should apply principally to general-and-administrative
expenses remaining after reasonable direct program costs have been identified and allocated.
A certified CDFI may establish geographic benefit through loan-level information, portfolio
allocations, proportional methodologies, beneficiary information, or another reasonable and
consistently applied methodology.
A regulated financial institution relying upon this safe harbor should maintain reasonable
documentation of the recipient CDFI's qualifying activities and outcomes, including lending volumes,
borrower and geographic characteristics, technical-assistance activity, portfolio performance, and
direct program expenditures.
XVII. The future role of national intermediaries
National intermediaries remain a valuable resource within the broader ecosystem serving communities.
Their value should increasingly be understood not as that of rent-extracting conduits, but as outcome-
enhancing resources capable of improving the efficiency, reach, and accountability of community-
development activity.
We believe national intermediaries can reduce friction costs for both regulators and banks by helping
identify opportunities for direct relationships with Treasury-certified CDFIs, facilitating appropriate
introductions and due diligence, and monitoring the efficiency and outcomes of service delivery to the
American public. Properly structured, this role can complement rather than displace direct bank-CDFI
relationships.
We therefore recommend that the regulators initiate a study of how national intermediaries can best be
utilized on a going-forward basis. We respectfully suggest that this study be conducted as a public-private
partnership between regulators and banks, with structured input from CDFIs and national intermediaries,
and that it focus on measurable outcomes, reduced transaction friction, and the efficient delivery of capital
and services to communities.
XVIII. Conclusion and recommendations
We support the regulators' movement toward a CRA framework that concentrates examination resources
on meaningful lending activity while improving accountability for community-development expenditures.
We respectfully recommend that the regulators:
1. adopt the major product concept reflected in Options 1 and 2.
2. establish a reasonable de minimis threshold under Question 4 to exclude truly incidental lending.
3. under Question 5, evaluate consumer lending by individual product type rather than as a single catch-all
category.
4. under Question 6, use both dollar volume and loan count when identifying major product lines.
 Page 11
5. under Question 7, generally employ Option 1's institution-level methodology for small and intermediate
institutions while considering Option 2's assessment-area methodology for large, geographically dispersed
institutions.
6. evaluate whether the incremental compliance and examination costs of assessment-area analysis for large
institutions produce commensurate improvements in community outcomes.
7. recognize strategic partnerships with Treasury-certified CDFIs as a complementary mechanism for
addressing credit needs outside banks' major products and conventional underwriting parameters.
8. retain grants and donations as CRA-eligible community-development activities.
9. address rent extraction by distinguishing unnecessary intermediary costs from the direct costs of producing
community-development credit.
10. apply the proposed 15 percent limitation principally to true G&A expenses.
11. recognize borrower identification, preparation, technical assistance, underwriting, origination, servicing and
monitoring as direct program costs.
12. expressly recognize reasonable loan-application, underwriting, servicing, and portfolio-surveillance
technology as direct program costs.
13. create a safe harbor or rebuttable presumption for qualifying activity conducted directly through Treasury-
certified CDFIs.
14. encourage outcome-oriented reporting by CDFIs receiving CRA-motivated bank support.
15. preserve reasonable geographic flexibility for qualifying CDFI activity; and
16. recognize CDFIs as an appropriate source of information concerning community credit needs.
17. initiate a public-private study, in partnership with banks and informed by CDFIs, on how national
intermediaries can reduce transaction friction, facilitate direct bank-CDFI relationships, and
strengthen outcome monitoring.
These recommendations share a common principle: CRA regulation should concentrate resources where
they can produce measurable credit outcomes.
We agree with regulators that banks should be evaluated for CRA performance with an emphasis on the
lending they either directly provide or leverage delivering to the community. Direct partnerships with
Treasury-certified CDFIs should complement in-house activity, extending the financial system's reach to
borrowers, products and communities that fall outside conventional bank credit channels.
That division of labor can simultaneously improve regulatory efficiency, reduce opportunities for rent
extraction, strengthen accountability, and increase the amount of responsible credit ultimately reaching
underserved communities.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill,

Kent Attainable Housing (KAH) submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced
above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the
complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed
changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to
comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment
deadline by 60-days.

KAH is a small nonprofit emerging developer in rural Kent County, Maryland. We provide financial literacy education
to working low- and moderate-income residents designed to help them find pathways to homeownership. We also construct
affordable homes and pair them with families who have participated in our programs, ensuring that their housing costs do
not exceed 30% of their household budget. Kent County's population is just under 20,000 residents, the smallest county in
Maryland. There are numerous pockets of poverty, and ALL public schools qualify for federal Title I funding, meaning at
least 40% of our students come from low-income households as measured by the number of students who qualify for free
or reduced-price meals.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks meet the credit
needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that
communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in
very rural communities like ours that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access
to mainstream financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how regulators evaluate
community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes
are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income
communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in communities. For example, it suggests
that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would
be enough to receive a passing CRA rating2. However, that percentage is far lower than the percentage the National
Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the largest banks currently devote to community investments and
loans.


Page 2 of 3


NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the OCC and FDIC supervised banks
in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in
community development loans and investments inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of
annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital, and a median of 3.6% of tier 1
capital for annual CRA qualified investments3.

If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for
community development lending and investments, combined activity would fall to approximately $14.9 billion
annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use
strategic plans to make their CRA compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set
strategic plan benchmarks for CRA performance well-below historical levels of community development activity.4
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination – like
ours on Maryland's Eastern Shore – cannot withstand such a reduction in community development
investments and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the
communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for our rural communities.
It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs. Before finalizing the rule, the
agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or investment available to low-
and moderate-income communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.
We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit
organizations like ours.
Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling, workforce programs,
neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships
with nonprofit organizations. These resources can be particularly important to local organizations like ours that have
deep relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new documentation
requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations. For smaller nonprofit organizations
like ours, a 15 percent cap on indirect costs is simply unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance
and other operating expenses are necessary to deliver the underlying program itself, and in our rural community we
have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based
nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial records, budgets or program documentation in
the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller
organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose
activities are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can play in supporting
community development. Our local banks such as PNC, Truist, and Hanscom Federal Credit Union provide
critical grants as well as housing counseling and financial literacy programming support for our limited staff
of two providing critical, tangible benefits for our rural residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and
community development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond the banks
themselves.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed documentation requirements
and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or redirect bank support away from smaller nonprofit
organizations, especially those with limited administrative capacity. The agencies must also determine whether those
effects would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.
More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of reducing perceived regulatory
burden on financial institutions. They must also determine what the changes mean for the communities CRA
is intended to serve.

Page 3 of 3

Finally, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
•
identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under the proposal;
•
quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development activities
subject to CRA evaluation;
•
assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations, including rural
communities and communities of color;
•
consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing meaningful
community accountability.
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, KAH believes that the OCC and FDIC should
rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public
comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting community credit
needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating
that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low-
and moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The proposal is
more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to bank classifications, community
development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from community organizations,
civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is
warranted. An extension would allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical
consequences, gather examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13,
2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; FDIC
RIN 3064-AG31

Attention: Jennifer M. Jones, Deputy Executive Secretary, Attention: Comments—RIN
3064–AG31, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, 550 17th Street NW, Washington,
DC 20429

Dear Ms. Jones,

The national nonprofit Cities for Financial Empowerment Fund (CFE Fund) appreciates
the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC's) proposed changes to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. The CFE Fund's comments focus specifically on
the important role that safe and affordable deposit accounts play in connecting
consumers with low and moderate incomes to the financial mainstream and ultimately
to opportunities to bank, build credit, borrow, and fully participate in the economy.
Consumers generally do not begin their financial lives with a mortgage or small
business loan. Safe and affordable transaction accounts provide an entry point into the
mainstream financial system and can create a pathway to the savings, financial
stability, and financial institution relationships that support successful borrowing and
longer-term asset building.

Over the past decade, financial institutions, local governments, community
organizations, and federal regulators have worked together to dramatically expand
access to safe and affordable banking. The CFE Fund's experience leading the national
Bank On movement shows that these efforts work. More than 500 financial institutions
– representing more than two thirds of the national deposit market share – now offer
safe and affordable accounts meeting the Bank On National Account Standards; local
and state governments across the country are integrating account opening into
programs and services; and at least 23 million consumers have opened these accounts
to date.

Importantly, access to a safe and affordable banking account is foundational to
consumers' ability to access safe and affordable credit and build assets. Evidence from
our network of Financial Empowerment Center (FEC) municipal partners reveals that
even when working repeatedly with a professional financial counselor, people without
a mainstream bank or credit union account were only half as likely to be able to save

money and only one-third as likely to improve their credit score compared to those
with accounts. Counseling clients who newly opened a mainstream account became
eight times more likely to improve their finances than those who did not.

As the agencies gather information on the CRA framework, we urge them to keep this
important connection in mind.

The CFE Fund and Bank On

The CFE Fund is a national nonprofit organization that has worked with over 100 cities
and counties to help them implement large-scale, systemic financial empowerment
initiatives for their residents, including access to safe and affordable banking accounts,
one-on-one financial counseling, asset building, and consumer financial protection.

The CFE Fund's national Bank On initiative is a multi-sector partnership to create
pathways for un- and underbanked individuals to enter, or re-enter, the financial
mainstream. At the core of the initiative are the Bank On National Account Standards
for basic banking accounts, designed to address critical pain points for consumers and
limit risk for financial institutions. Certification under the Standards prohibits
overdraft or insufficient fund fees and requires low monthly fees, a low opening
deposit, and bill pay functionality. The 15 required core features in the Standards
address the issues identified by the FDIC as primary reasons that individuals are
unbanked.

The CFE Fund also supports more than 100 local Bank On coalitions across the country
to expand banking access and connect consumers to these Bank On certified accounts,
both by encouraging more financial institutions to offer certified accounts and by
developing programmatic integration opportunities to connect people to those
accounts at scale. Bank On certified accounts are widely available to people receiving
federal payments. There are more than 500 banks and credit unions with a certified
account; certified accounts are available at over 60% of bank branches across the
country.

Federal banking regulators have played an important and constructive role in the
progress the country has made in expanding access to mainstream banking. The FDIC's
longstanding research and outreach on unbanked and underbanked households has
helped policymakers, financial institutions, local governments, and community
organizations understand both the scale of financial exclusion and the reasons
households remain outside the banking system. The FDIC's Safe Account Pilot in 2011
also provided an important foundation for the development of safe account models and
helped inform the Bank On National Account Standards.


Regulators also have provided important technical assistance and regulatory clarity as
the market for safe and affordable accounts has developed. In 2016, the federal
banking regulators specifically recognized low-cost deposit accounts in their
Interagency Questions and Answers Regarding Community Reinvestment as an
example of retail banking services that improve access to financial services or decrease
costs for low- and moderate-income individuals.

Banking Access Benefits Consumers, Communities, Governments, and Financial
Institutions

For households, a safe and affordable account provides the basic infrastructure
necessary to manage daily financial life. Consumers can safely receive income and
benefits, pay bills, store funds, save, and begin building a relationship with a
mainstream financial institution. As our FEC data demonstrates, having an account also
is closely connected to consumers' ability to improve savings, build credit, and achieve
broader financial outcomes.

Banking access also benefits communities and governments. Across federal, state, and
local programs, there are recurring points at which individuals receive income or
engage with public systems, including tax refunds, benefit payments, emergency
assistance, and workforce-related earnings. Connecting consumers to safe accounts at
these moments can help governments deliver payments more quickly and safely,
reduce the costs associated with paper payments, and reduce risks associated with
lost, stolen, or fraudulent checks.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, the CFE Fund worked with federal
partners in the Trump Administration, Bank On coalitions, and other local leaders to
harness the banking access opportunities represented by Economic Impact and Child
Tax Credit payments. Partners deployed messaging about how direct deposit could
help consumers receive funds faster, safer, and more affordably and directed
consumers to Bank On certified accounts. According to the Internal Revenue Service
(IRS), more than 10 million households entered new or modified banking account
information for the first series of stimulus payments. The FDIC's unbanked survey
subsequently found that almost half (44.8%) of recently banked households who
received a government benefit payment cited the payment as contributing to their
decision to open an account.

This existing banking infrastructure also supports current federal efforts such as the
Executive Order 14247 (EO14247) to move payments away from paper checks and
toward electronic delivery. For consumers to receive payments electronically through
mainstream financial institutions, they need access to accounts that are safe,
affordable, federally insured, and fully transactional. The nationwide availability of

Bank On certified accounts provides governments with an existing private-sector
infrastructure to help accomplish this goal.

Financial institutions benefit from this infrastructure as well. Bank On certified
accounts meet demonstrated consumer demand for low-cost, checkless checking
products and complement financial institutions' increasingly digital product offerings.
They also provide institutions with an entry point for consumers who may ultimately
use additional savings, credit, and lending products.

Bank On accounts are particularly effective at bringing new customers into
mainstream financial institutions. Data reported through the Federal Reserve Bank of
St. Louis' Bank On National Data Hub (BOND Hub) found that 84% of Bank On accounts
opened at reporting institutions in 2023 were opened by customers new to that
financial institution. A safe and affordable checking account is at the beginning of a
broader and longer-term banking relationship.

Bank On also creates efficiencies for participating financial institutions and their
government and community partners. Rather than developing different products or
approaches for individual local programs, financial institutions can offer one nationally
certified account that municipal governments, financial counselors, workforce
programs, benefits programs, and community organizations can confidently integrate
into their work.

Banking Access as a Foundation for Credit and Asset Building

The CFE Fund recognizes the agencies' focus on ensuring that CRA encourages financial
institutions to meet the credit needs of the communities they serve. Our experience
working with consumers, local governments, and financial institutions demonstrates
that safe and affordable deposit accounts support this objective.

For consumers outside the financial mainstream, opening an account is often the first
step toward a broader financial relationship. A mainstream bank account allows a
consumer to safely receive and manage income, pay bills, accumulate savings, and
establish a relationship with a regulated financial institution. These basic building
blocks can help consumers improve their overall financial stability and position
themselves to successfully access and use credit.

Relationships with financial institutions also decreases the use of high-cost fringe
financial services, which deter savings and hurt local economies. Data from the BOND
Hub shows that millions of customers are safely making payments, debit card swipes,
deposits, and withdrawals.


Conclusion

The CFE Fund appreciates the opportunity to share our experience with the role that
deposit accounts – and financial institution and regulator synergies – play in
supporting CRA objectives, and we therefore urge you to incorporate those learnings
and successes in your efforts.

Sincerely,


Jonathan Mintz
President and Chief Executive Officer
Cities for Financial Empowerment Fund

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
See attached file from Cindy Miles, President/CEO, Urban League of Kansas, regarding objections to proposed rule on the CRA.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0036_09000064b95bc853.pdf:
September 23, 2026

Dear Comptroller,
On behalf of the Urban League of Kansas, I write to express serious concern regarding the proposed changes to regulations
implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). For nearly fifty years, CRA has served as a cornerstone of federal
efforts to ensure that federally regulated banks meet the credit needs of the entire communities they serve, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods that have historically experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch closures, and unequal
access to mainstream financial services. The proposed rule would narrow consideration of certain banking services, restrict how
community development grants receive CRA credit, and impose new requirements on nonprofit organizations that could
significantly reduce community investment in the places that need it most.
Given the significance of these proposed changes, we respectfully request that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation extend the public comment period and conduct a thorough analysis of the likely
consequences for low- and moderate-income communities before moving forward. The agencies should provide stakeholders
with an opportunity to assess and comment on the evidence supporting such substantial changes to CRA implementation.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments, and partnerships can play in supporting community
development. These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into tangible benefits
for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community development activities receive CRA consideration can
therefore have consequences well beyond the banks themselves.
Why This Matters in Kansas
The proposed changes could have profound consequences for communities across Kansas that continue to face barriers to
homeownership, affordable housing, access to capital, neighborhood investment, and economic mobility.
In Wichita, Kansas City, Topeka, Hutchinson, Salina, Dodge City, Liberal, and rural communities throughout our state, nonprofit
organizations work alongside financial institutions to address challenges that cannot be solved through lending alone. These
efforts include financial coaching, housing counseling, foreclosure prevention services, support for first-time homebuyers, small-
business development assistance, workforce development, neighborhood revitalization, and community development initiatives
that strengthen local economies.
At the Urban League of Kansas, we have seen that access to credit is only one component of successful community
development. Families seeking to purchase homes often require months of financial education, credit repair assistance,
budgeting support, savings strategies, and individualized counseling before becoming mortgage-ready. Likewise, aspiring
entrepreneurs frequently need business planning assistance, bookkeeping support, cash flow training, and lender readiness
coaching before they are in a position to qualify for financing.
These services help create successful borrowers, homeowners, and business owners. They are often funded through grants
and partnerships supported by CRA incentives. If banks receive less CRA consideration for supporting these activities,
community organizations may be forced to reduce services that help individuals and families achieve financial stability and long-
term economic success.

Impact on Housing and Homeownership
Kansas continues to face a shortage of affordable housing that affects working families, seniors, veterans, and first-time
homebuyers. Nonprofit organizations, housing counseling agencies, and community development entities play a critical role
in helping families access homeownership opportunities, avoid foreclosure, and remain stably housed.
A reduction in CRA incentives for grants and community development activities could result in:
•
Fewer homebuyer education classes.
•
Reduced housing counseling services.
•
Less foreclosure prevention and loss mitigation assistance.
•
Fewer resources to support affordable housing development and rehabilitation.
•
Reduced support for housing stability programs serving vulnerable populations.
Communities across Kansas are already struggling with rising housing costs and limited affordable housing supply.
Weakening incentives for banks to invest in organizations addressing these challenges risks undermining years of progress.
Impact on Minority-Owned and Small Businesses
Kansas entrepreneurs, particularly minority-owned, women-owned, and low-income businesses, often rely on nonprofit
technical assistance providers before they are ready to access conventional financing.
Many organizations help business owners:
•
Develop business plans.
•
Establish bookkeeping and accounting systems.
•
Build business credit.
•
Prepare loan applications.
•
Navigate procurement opportunities.
•
Improve long-term financial sustainability.
These organizations help bridge the gap between aspiring entrepreneurs and traditional lenders. Many of these services are
made possible through bank partnerships and CRA-supported investments. Reducing incentives for these partnerships
could result in fewer entrepreneurs becoming loan-ready and fewer small businesses being created and sustained in
underserved communities.
Impact on Neighborhood Revitalization and Community Development
Neighborhood revitalization requires far more than financing buildings. Successful revitalization requires resident
engagement, community planning, leadership development, housing rehabilitation, financial literacy programming, youth
development opportunities, community organizing, and collaboration among residents, nonprofits, governments, and
financial institutions.
In Wichita's historically underserved neighborhoods and in older neighborhoods throughout Kansas, nonprofit organizations
often serve as the backbone institutions coordinating these efforts. CRA-supported grants frequently provide the resources
necessary to engage residents, coordinate stakeholders, implement projects, and ensure sustainable outcomes.
The proposed restrictions fail to recognize that effective neighborhood revitalization requires staff, technology, data
systems, compliance functions, outreach efforts, facility costs, and organizational infrastructure. Those investments are
essential components of successful community development, not unnecessary overhead.



Concerns Regarding the Proposed 15 Percent Administrative Cost Limitation
We are particularly concerned about the proposal that would limit CRA consideration for community development grants
when nonprofit recipients have indirect or administrative costs exceeding 15 percent and would require large banks to
document compliance with that threshold.
While intended to ensure funds reach communities directly, this approach misunderstands the realities of nonprofit service
delivery.
Administrative costs support:
•
Program management.
•
Financial accountability.
•
Compliance and reporting.
•
Technology and cybersecurity.
•
Staff supervision and training.
•
Data collection and impact measurement.
•
Facility operations.
Without these functions, programs cannot effectively serve residents.
For many small and mid-sized nonprofits in Kansas, particularly those serving rural communities or historically underserved
populations, a 15 percent cap is unrealistic. Smaller organizations often lack the economies of scale available to larger
institutions. As a result, banks may be discouraged from supporting smaller community-based organizations if doing so
jeopardizes their ability to receive CRA credit.
The result could be fewer resources flowing to the very organizations that possess the strongest relationships and deepest
trust within the communities CRA was designed to benefit.
Impact on the Operating Capacity of Nonprofit Organizations
The proposed rule appears to assume that administrative and operating costs are separate from community impact. In
reality, the opposite is true.
Every successful housing counselor, foreclosure prevention specialist, financial coach, neighborhood organizer, small-
business advisor, and community development professional requires training, supervision, technology, office space,
financial management systems, and organizational support.
Strong organizations require:
•
Qualified staff.
•
Secure technology systems.
•
Financial controls.
•
Compliance infrastructure.
•
Data management and reporting capabilities.
•
Strategic planning and evaluation.




Limiting support for these functions weakens the nonprofit sector that banks rely upon to deliver measurable outcomes in
low- and moderate-income communities.
In Kansas, where nonprofit organizations frequently serve large geographic regions with limited resources, the proposed
changes could undermine partnerships that have taken decades to establish and that continue to generate meaningful
results for families and neighborhoods.
CRA Must Continue to Support Comprehensive Community Development
The agencies should not evaluate these proposed changes solely through the lens of reducing regulatory burden on
financial institutions. CRA was enacted to ensure that banks serve the entire community, particularly those neighborhoods
and populations historically excluded from access to capital and financial services.
Community development is about more than loans alone. Effective community development requires housing counselors,
community development corporations, nonprofit service providers, neighborhood organizations, workforce development
programs, and financial capability initiatives that transform financial investments into measurable improvements in people's
lives.
If adopted, the proposed changes could reduce incentives for banks to invest in the nonprofit infrastructure that makes
community development possible. This risk is especially significant in Kansas, where many nonprofit organizations operate
with limited resources while addressing substantial housing, economic, and social challenges.
The OCC and FDIC should not finalize the rule without first doing the following::
•
identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under the proposal;
•
quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development activities subject to
CRA evaluation;
•
assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations, including rural
communities and communities of color;
•
consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing meaningful community
accountability; and
•
respond directly to evidence submitted by community and civil rights organizations about likely real-world
consequences.
Where precise quantification is not possible, the agencies should not simply assume that community effects are
insignificant. They should identify the available evidence, explain its limitations, assess reasonably foreseeable
consequences and explain why the benefits of the proposed changes outweigh those risks. The agencies should allow for
public comment on the agencies' analysis.
CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting community credit needs. The
agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes
are consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods.

Conclusion
The Urban League of Kansas respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to:
•
Extend the public comment period.
•
Conduct a comprehensive analysis of impacts on low- and moderate-income communities.
•
Reconsider the proposed 15 percent limitation on indirect and administrative costs.
•
Preserve strong CRA incentives for community development grants and nonprofit partnerships.
•
Evaluate proposed changes based on their impact on communities as well as the burden imposed on financial
institutions.




The ultimate question should not be whether a nonprofit's overhead exceeds an arbitrary percentage. The question should
be whether families become homeowners, whether foreclosures are prevented, whether small businesses are created,
whether neighborhoods improve, and whether economic opportunity expands.
For nearly fifty years, CRA has helped achieve those goals by fostering partnerships between financial institutions and
community organizations. Weakening incentives for those partnerships threatens progress not only in Wichita, but in
communities across Kansas that continue to depend on collaborative investments to create opportunity and improve quality
of life.
Thank you for your consideration of these comments.
Respectfully,
Cindy Miles
President & CEO
Urban League of Kansas
Wichita, Kansas

My name is Tamika Rose, and I am submitting this comment as an individual from ZIP code 10523.
I recently applied for a mortgage and was denied. What concerned me most was not simply being denied, it was what happened when I asked what I could do next.
I asked what I needed to improve, what steps I could take to become qualified, and whether someone could help me understand how to get there. I was simply told that I did not qualify. I was not given meaningful guidance about what I could do differently or what pathway might help me become mortgage-ready.
I left feeling as though I had wasted their time rather than feeling like a customer who could potentially become qualified in the future.
I understand that not every applicant will qualify for a mortgage. My concern is what happens after the “no.”
I encourage regulators to consider whether banks are providing consumers with clear, accessible information about why they were denied and meaningful guidance about available resources or next steps.
A denial should not be the end of the conversation. People should have enough information to understand what they can work toward so they have a fair opportunity to come back better prepared.
Thank you for considering my experience.
