COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Please accept the attached comment as my comment on the proposed CRA rule.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0040_09000064b95c365a.pdf:
1

September 24, 2026

Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
FDIC ID: RIN 3064-AG31

To Whom it May Concern:
Just as in the medical field, the first rule for federal agencies proposing a rule must be a
Hippocratic oath to do no harm. The FDIC's and OCC's proposed changes to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulation would cause massive harm by reducing the requirements for
banks to finance affordable housing, economic development, community facilities and
neighborhood revitalization. The result will likely be significant reductions in lending and
investing in community revitalization activities across the country. The proposed changes will
also lessen accountability for banks by eliminating small business and farm loan reporting
requirements for hundreds of banks.
In addition to lessening reinvestment requirements, the proposed changes will diminish the
amount of financing for community revitalization by damaging the infrastructure that supports
CRA-related lending and investing. The proposed changes will reduce the amount and variety of
partnerships among banks and community organizations by imposing unnecessary and
burdensome reporting requirements on large banks and community organizations when banks
provide vital grants for CRA-related activities like counseling or housing development. The
proposal will also reduce the importance of public comments on CRA exams. The essence of
CRA is responding to community needs and banks will not be as effective in responding to
community needs if the value CRA exams place on public comments is diminished instead of
enhanced.
The proposed changes to CRA also include a gratuitous request to the U.S. District Court for the
Northern District of Texas to rule that in the future, the federal agencies cannot legally consider
expansions in assessment areas (geographical areas on CRA exams) beyond branch bank
networks or examine the provision of deposit accounts. I believe that the CRA statute permits the
agencies to consider activities in areas beyond bank branches, and banks themselves desire that
their community development financing beyond their branch footprint be considered. There are
likewise compelling reasons for retail lending to be considered beyond branch networks as some
past CRA exams for non-traditional banks have already done. Likewise, since needs for deposit
services are directly mentioned in the CRA statute, the agencies have the discretion to examine


2

the provision of deposit services, which also helps banks become more effective at making loans
in low- and moderate-income communities.
It is also unclear that any judgement in a single District Court about future CRA regulations
would have any significant impact since the regulatory agencies in the future could go to court
regarding any judgement of this nature. This gambit amounts to a ploy to erect a judicial
roadblock to future CRA reforms that might be desired by both banks and community groups. It
is not appropriate for agencies to attempt to straitjacket policymakers and stakeholders from
pursuing evolutions of CRA rules to match future community needs.
For almost three decades, I worked at the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC)
in various research and policy capacities. I now consult for NCRC as a Senior Fellow. I am also
the author of Ending Redlining through a Community-Centered Reform of the Community
Reinvestment Act. This comment letter will offer insights that I have gleaned over the decades. I
also urge the agencies to seriously consider the well-researched and reasoned positions in
NCRC's comment letter. The views expressed in this letter are my own and do not represent the
official position of NCRC.
Proposed Counterproductive Treatment of Assessment Areas Could Significantly Diminish
CRA-Related Bank Lending and Investing
By trying to freeze any consideration of retail lending outside of assessment areas, the current
proposal forecloses possibilities of agreement or compromising among stakeholders on this
important issue. A compromise on retail lending and community development activity outside of
assessment areas is possible and would be more effective in increasing community development
lending and investing than the proposed rule.
The proposed rule would allow large banks to make community development (CD) loans and
investments outside of assessment areas if:
• The dollar amount of their CD lending exceeded .625 percent of their Tier I capital (CD
lending divided by Tier 1 capital)
• And the dollar amount of CD investments exceeded .625 percent of Tier 1 capital.
For intermediate banks, the ratio would be 1.25 percent.
To estimate the adequacy of these proposed ratios, I examined the 2025 OCC CRA exam for
First National Bank of Omaha. The bank had an overall Outstanding rating but the percentage of
CD lending or CD investing per Tier 1 capital nevertheless varied across nine assessment areas.
For CD lending, the percentage of Tier 1 capital ranged on the high end of 27 percent and 18


3

percent to 2 percent or 1 percent on the low end. The median for the assessment areas was 6
percent. CD investment was even better, ranging from 35 percent and 14 percent at the high end
to no lower than 5 percent on the low end.
Despite the proposal's protestations to the contrary, the message that the geographical flexibility
standard (of .625 percent for large banks or 1.25 percent for intermediate small banks) would
send to good performing banks is that they can relax and aim for much lower ratios. In fact,
NCRC estimates that if banks aim for the lower geographical flexibility standard, the losses
could total in the tens of billions of dollars in decreased community development financing for
economically challenged communities.
There is a much better way than the geographical flexibility standard. NCRC proposes that banks
can extend up to 25 percent of their community development financing outside of their
assessment areas if they at least maintain past levels of community development financing inside
of their assessment areas. NCRC would also allow percentages above 25 percent provided any
portion above 25 percent was directed to high needs areas. This proposal presents no danger of
banks decreasing their community development financing and, in fact, encourages them to
increase their financing levels.
Moreover, this proposal would seem to accommodate even the most aggressive banks in terms of
seeking outside assessment area CD financing opportunities. In a report for NCRC, I examined
the CD lending and investing of the top 50 banks in terms of asset size. I found just three
aggressive banks making 15 to 25 percent of their CD lending outside of their assessment areas,
and I found that the median percentage of CD lending outside of assessment areas was 7.4
percent. Likewise, the median investment outside of assessment areas was 14 percent of current
investments and 13 percent of total investments (prior plus current). Four banks with a high
percentage of investments outside of assessment areas included one bank at 71 percent, one bank
at 31 percent, two banks at about 30 percent.
The NCRC proposal is grounded in recent history of CRA activity and would accommodate a
wide range of banks with different strategies. I would add a few wrinkles to the NCRC proposal.
I would suggest that any bank that makes more than 25 percent of its retail lending outside of its
assessment areas would be required to have this lending evaluated on its CRA exams. CRA is
aimed at ensuring that banks are responding to the totality of needs, not just needs for
community development financing inside and outside assessment areas. Omitting any
consideration of retail lending outside of assessment areas would amount to the agencies falling
short on their responsibilities to ensure that banks are responding to community needs.


4

Would banks balk at the notion that retail lending outside of assessment areas needs to be
examined? Perhaps some would, but others would conclude that evaluation of a reasonable
portion of lending outside of assessment areas is an acceptable quid pro quo for allowing
community development financing outside of assessment areas to count. Moreover, procedures
that are unfair such as no examination of outside assessment area retail lending but generous
consideration of outside community development financing will be controversial, and will
ultimately fail and be repealed. Unjust and one-sided proposals create unstable and unpredictable
CRA rules whereas sensible compromises will create more durability and predictability of how
banks are expected to perform.
The 25 percent benchmark for consideration of retail lending outside of assessment areas is also
based on empirical research. In 2022, the Urban Institute found that about 20 percent of retail
bank loans are outside assessment areas. They found that a significant number of banks exceeded
20 percent but were usually under 30 percent outside of assessment areas. In previous research
for NCRC, I found that of the top 100 banks by asset size, most were making the vast majority of
their loans in their assessment areas but that eleven banks made less than 50 percent of their
home loans in their assessment areas and 7 made less than 50 percent of their small business
loans in their assessment areas.
In total, consideration of retail lending outside of assessment areas would not apply to most
banks but it would be important in capturing lending by a minority of banks, some of which are
among the top 100 banks. Also, procedures could be created that would adjust the weight of
outside assessment area retail lending on CRA exam ratings to consider the business models of
banks. CRA exams could weigh outside assessment area lending based on the percentage of
lending that is outside of assessment areas. In this manner, traditional banks that rely on bank
branches for lending would have relatively small weights on their lending test for outside
assessment area lending while non-traditional banks would have higher weights for outside
assessment lending.
One approach would be a weighted average of outside assessment area and inside assessment
area lending. If one bank made 25 percent of their loans outside of assessment areas, their
outside assessment area lending performance would have a 25 percent weight on the lending test
rating and their inside assessment area performance would have a 75 percent weight. The reverse
weights would apply to a bank that made 75 percent of its loans outside of assessment areas.
This seems like a fairer approach than trying to freeze out all outside assessment area retail
lending from CRA exams for all time. Freezing a testing procedure is akin to creating
government safety tests for coal or wood steam powered boats when boats today are powered by


5

gas engines and tomorrow's boats could be powered by renewable energy. Likewise, an
unwillingness to evolve with technological developments renders government intentions to
ensure anti-discriminatory and safe and sound loans increasingly ineffective. And over time, it
appears more bank lending will be made outside of bank branch networks so all stakeholders
must figure out how to factor that into CRA ratings.
Legislative history and regulatory precedent also support evolving the lending test for
consideration of lending outside of assessment areas. In the CRA statute, §2903 requires the
federal bank agencies to "assess the institution's record of meeting the credit needs of its entire
community, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with the safe and
sound operation of such institution." The mandate is to assess whether needs in the entire
community are being met, not just needs in some of the communities a bank serves.
In addition, the Riegle-Neal Interstate Banking and Branching Efficiency Act in 1994
significantly expanded the geographical scope of CRA exams. To enable CRA to consider the
expanding geographical reach of banks, Section 110 of Riegle-Neal required federal agencies to
conduct CRA evaluations in each state in which a bank has a branch and to reach conclusions
about performance for metropolitan and non-metropolitan areas of each state where banks have
branches. Evaluations were also to be conducted for multistate metropolitan areas in which
banks have branches.
Since Riegle-Neal anticipated that banks would serve multiple states, it insisted that CRA retain
a local focus and conduct evaluations in metropolitan and rural parts of each state they served.
Congress did not want CRA evaluations to be confined to only a few states where banks did
business but wanted CRA exams to consider bank activities in all states in which they did
business. It would be inconsistent with this Congressional intent that CRA exams would stop at a
state border because retail lending was outside of assessment areas.
It would be inconsistent that activity could only be examined in geographical areas with branches
since Riegle Neal stipulated that evaluations would occur at a state, metropolitan or non-
metropolitan level even in parts of these geographical areas that did not have branches. Non-
metropolitan areas of states are large areas, and the branches of a bank can be in one or a few of
the non-metropolitan counties. Likewise, metropolitan areas can be large areas with branches not
in all counties. The vagueness of the Riegle Neal language suggests that the law favors a broader
geographical reach for CRA exams. (As amended by Riegle Neal, the CRA's statute stipulates
that as long as one branch is in a state or the smaller geographical areas, the state or other areas
are to be included. This is codified in § 2906 (d) (1) (2) (3) of the CRA statute).


6

The agencies have incorporated assessments of lending outside of traditional branch-based
assessment areas on CRA exams. For example, the former Office of Thrift Supervision (OTS)
2009 CRA exam of Citicorp, a non-traditional thrift located in Wilmington, Delaware, that made
loans through 77,000 agents located throughout the country, included analyses of 10
metropolitan areas and three non-metropolitan areas with the largest percentage of lending
outside of the Wilmington assessment area. Likewise, the OTS examined Capital One's lending
in 20 areas beyond its one assessment area. These 20 areas comprised 25 percent of the thrift's
lending.
More recently, a 2018 OCC CRA exam of State Farm FSB considered lending beyond the thrift's
headquarters in Bloomington, IL since the thrift has no branches and makes loans through its
18,000 insurance agents located throughout the country. The OCC designated expanded review
areas outside of Bloomington, Illinois including the states of Alabama, Alabama, Arizona,
Georgia, and New York. These states accounted for 20 percent of the thrift's loans.
While these precedents are incomplete in terms of consistent methodologies, they nevertheless
reveal that the agencies over several years and administrations seriously considered lending
outside of branch-based assessment areas, believing that they had the statutory authority to do so.
They considered this an important part of assessing bank's responsiveness to all the communities
they serve. By breaking with precedent in a manner that will not allow CRA to evolve with
changes in banking and technology, this proposed rule is not effective or durable and will likely
create chaos and consternation among stakeholders since it will likely be rescinded in a few
years.
Unnecessary Reductions in Data Reporting Would Cloud Picture of Access to Credit
The FDIC's and OCC's proposed rule not only constrains geographical areas on CRA exams but
will curtail the ability of the agencies and the public to assess access to credit in the remaining
geographical areas on CRA exams. Proposing unnecessary reductions in small business and farm
data therefore impedes the agencies' ability and duty to evaluate bank's responsiveness to
community needs for credit.
Since only large banks report small business and farm data, the FDIC's and OCC's proposal to
shift about 417 banks from large banks to intermediate banks would significantly reduce the
number of banks required to report this vital data. If this proposal is implemented, only 155
banks out of 4,200 would be considered large banks for CRA purposes. In other words, only 3.6
percent of the banks will be reporting data on the number of small business loans they issued in
low- and moderate-income census tracts and to the smallest businesses.


7

According to NCRC, almost 11 percent of the small business and small farm data reported in
2024 would no longer be reported in future years if the agencies implement their proposal. While
the percentage may seem relatively small, further analysis indicates that impacts are large and
significant in terms of clouding the picture on access to a type of loan that is critical for wealth
building and economic growth in low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. The loss of
about 11 percent of loans (10.6 percent to be precise) amounts to more than 897,000 small
business loans and more than 17,000 small farm loans issued across the country in 2024, the
most recent year for which data is available.
The loss of hundreds of thousands of loans in the publicly available CRA database will reduce
the accuracy and effectiveness of CRA exams of hundreds of banks. The reliability of industry-
wide data used for comparing performance of individual banks against their peers will decrease
significantly particularly in states that will experience large reductions in data. According to
NCRC, North Dakota will lose 30 percent of its reported data and Maine will lose 25 percent.
Additional states with significant losses of about 20 percent of their data include South Dakota,
Iowa, Nebraska, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama. These include states with
weaker economies and higher poverty rates than several of their peers. Reducing data on whether
small businesses and farms are receiving loans not only diminishes the effectiveness of CRA
exams in motivating increases in lending and wealth-building but also imperils other public and
private sector efforts to revitalize the economies in those states.
The loss of data reporting for the 417 banks moving from large to intermediate small would also
reduce the reporting of community development loan data. This diminishes the public's ability to
monitor these banks' commitments to financing affordable housing and other community
development projects in LMI communities.
Ironically, the FDIC and OCC are proposing that large banks publicly report community
development data similar to the small business and farm data they report. In other words, the
public would, under the proposal, experience a reduction in the available amount of community
development data, but the data that remains will be more detailed and informative. This amounts
to a pyrrhic victory at best. The agencies understand the importance of sufficiently detailed data
to better assess banks' responsiveness to needs but will nevertheless provide the public with less
of the data. Their assertions of reducing costs for banks are not valid since banks still must
collect and report this data to their CRA examiners but would not take the next step involving
minimal to no extra cost of reporting it in a form that the agencies then make available to the
public.


8

Finally, another part of the proposal would result in a diminished amount of data not even being
used in significant numbers of CRA exams. The FDIC and OCC are proposing to evaluate only
two major product lines of a bank that consists of the largest number of loans. Because small
farm lending is a lending type with smaller volumes, small farm loans would often not be among
the two major product lines for several banks. This would even be the case when a particular
bank is an important small farm lending in rural communities. Len Suzio shows that CRA exams
may not evaluate the small farm lending of very large banks such as JP Morgan Chase and Bank
of America because the number of small farm loans which are in the thousands are dwarfed by
small business lending. This will reduce the ability of CRA exams to assess whether small farms
in rural America are receiving access to credit, contrary to the purpose of CRA.
Proposed Changes to CRA Portend Dramatic Reductions in Affordable Housing and
Community Development Financing
Across the country, the proposed changes to the asset thresholds for small, intermediate small,
and large banks would endanger hundreds of millions, if not billions of dollars, in community
development financing and could imperil access to branches for traditionally underserved
communities.
CRA exams include various subtests for evaluating banks reinvestment activities. Large banks
have the most comprehensive exams that include separate tests for lending, investments, and
services. Intermediate banks have less complex exams that assess retail lending and community
development activities including financing for affordable housing and economic revitalization.
Small banks have the most streamlined exams assessing retail lending only.
Purporting to reduce regulatory burden, the FDIC and OCC are adjusting the asset thresholds for
determining which banks undergo which exams. Under the proposal, the small bank asset
threshold qualifying banks for the most streamlined exam would be moved from $412 million to
$1 billion. The intermediate bank asset range would be $1 billion to $10 billion, changed from
$412 million to $1.649 billion. The large bank threshold would move from $1.649 billion to
above $10 billion.
Nationally according to NCRC, raising the small bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion
would eliminate community development evaluations and requirements to provide community
development financing for roughly 814 banks, or about 40% of the banks currently subject to
that requirement. In addition, raising the large bank asset threshold from $1.649 billion to $10
billion would move 417 banks to the intermediate category and would eliminate their service test
and would therefore eliminate the scrutiny of their branches. These 417 banks have established
more than 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts — 30% of all LMI


9

branches nationwide. After the elimination of their service test, it is probable that the number of
their branches in LMI branches could decrease significantly.
In addition to destructive impacts on a national level, the proposed rule would imperil state
efforts to bolster affordable housing and community development. I have recently participated in
efforts in Connecticut to promote fair housing that could be set back by the CRA proposal.
Over the last year, lawmakers in Connecticut and the United State Congress have passed
significant legislation facilitating increases in affordable housing. Connecticut is in the process of
implementing HB 8002, An Act Concerning Housing Growth, which requires towns and regional
bodies to estimate needs and goals for affordable housing. This will be aided by the 21st Century
ROAD to Housing Act that provides federal financial incentives along with regulatory reforms
aimed at boosting affordable housing production. At a time of housing shortages nationally and
in Connecticut, these are well-timed and needed initiatives.
A harmful result of the proposed CRA rule would be to sharply reduce the number of banks
expected to engage in affordable housing and community development finance in Connecticut.
By moving the small bank threshold to $1 billion, nine banks headquartered in Connecticut
would no longer have any obligations to engage in community development financing. This
would involve banks ranging from Jewett City Savings Bank on the lower end of the asset range
to Torrington Savings Bank that is just shy of $1 billion in assets. Based on a review of their
CRA exams, I estimate that these banks made approximately $3.7 million annually in community
development financing. Over the CRA exam cycle of about three to four years, the banks
combined made a total of $144 million in community development financing. Their community
development financing equals about 2.5 percent of their assets.
If the proposed changes are implemented and CRA examiners no longer assess community
development financing for the nine banks, the banks may very well continue some of this
financing because they have found it is profitable business. But would the finance continue at the
same level of 2.5 percent of assets? The prudent approach is not to find out. Reductions by
significant amounts, even if they are just one fourth or one third less, would likely frustrate and
possibly stymie efforts in Connecticut to build affordable housing as required by HB 8002.
A micro analysis further shows the innovation and responsiveness of the community
development financing undertaken by the banks. Some examples of community development
financing found on the CRA exams included a $9.5 million loan for 400 units in multifamily
housing in Bridgeport for which 40 percent of the units were reserved for low- and moderate-
income households. Not only does this provide needed affordable housing, it also promotes
integration within the building and in the neighborhood.


10

Other projects involved mixed-income housing in Torrington and energy efficiency upgrades in
affordable housing. Non-housing financing included a line of credit to an organization providing
transportation to modest income households and investing in small business loan pools. CRA has
encouraged financing a wide array of community needs, which helps promote holistic
development enabling neighborhoods to thrive.
Another harmful change triggered by the asset threshold adjustments is moving nine other
Connecticut-based banks from the large to the intermediate category. They would still have
community development finance responsibilities, but they would no longer be subject to a
service test examining their branching patterns and provision of affordable deposit products.
Together, these nine banks have 162 branches, of which 36 or 22 percent are in low- or
moderate-income census tracts.
While it is unlikely that these banks would close most of their branches just because they no
longer have a service test, they would not have to contemplate CRA implications if any of them
are thinking about branch closures, including when they want to merge with other institutions.
Research has found that CRA has encouraged banks to maintain branches in modest income
neighborhoods. Again, the prudent course of action is not to find out what happens to branches
for small businesses and residents in economically challenged neighborhoods should these
changes be implemented.
A third agency, the Federal Reserve Board, did not join the FDIC and OCC in these proposed
changes. Perhaps the Federal Reserve believed that the harmful impact of the proposal exceeded
the benefits of reduced costs for banks. After all, since the last major changes to CRA in 1995
and 2005, banks have been subjected to the current exams for decades. They have learned how to
make profitable loans, investments, and services under CRA that benefit them and communities.
Proposed Changes to CRA Imperils Bank-Community Partnerships and Neighborhood
Revitalization by Stigmatizing Nonprofit Organizations
A further means by which the proposed rule would curtail the variety and amount of affordable
housing and community development is the proposal's discouragement of bank grants to
nonprofit organizations that are key partners in community revitalization projects.
Enacted in 1977, CRA combats redlining or discrimination against working class neighborhoods
and communities of color by requiring banks to serve community needs. The input of
community-based organizations and neighborhood residents is an integral part of banks
successfully responding to needs since these stakeholders have unique insights into how banks
can structure and deliver their products and programs to most effectively respond to needs. Over


11

the decades of CRA's existence, the law and its accompanying regulation has stimulated growth
in a vital nonprofit infrastructure that has helped banks provide financing for affordable housing,
small businesses, health centers, childcare facilities, and cultural and recreational centers.
Despite the daily experience of the benefits of hundreds if not thousands of bank and nonprofit
partnerships, the FDIC and OCC harbor suspicions of the activities of nonprofit organizations.
The proposed rule states that, "In their supervisory experience, the agencies have found that the
latter type of activities (donations and grants to non-profit entities) may be susceptible to rent
extraction, in which entities divert funds away from local communities, including low and
moderate-income (LMI) individuals, small businesses, and small farms." Hence, in order to limit
so called "rent extraction," the agencies are proposing that if large banks wish to receive
favorable CRA consideration for grants to nonprofits, they must obtain documentation from the
nonprofit recipients that no more than 15 percent of the grant amount is used for operating costs.
This proposal is offered without any thoughtful analysis of whether abuses are rampant in the
nonprofit sector and whether a 15 percent threshold is reasonable in terms of preventing
inefficient management. The proposal states that the threshold is consistent with Office of
Management and Budget (OMB) guidelines but while that might be accurate, the proposal does
not indicate whether the OMB derived at that guideline in a careful manner.
Operating costs are indirect costs necessary for managing a nonprofit organization and include
rent, costs for accounting, technology, and insurance, and salaries for staff not directly involved
in program delivery. Typically, they range from 15 to 35 percent of a nonprofit organization's
budget. An academic paper recently scrutinized the criticism of excessive operating costs. While
a high percentage of operating costs might indicate inefficiencies, the paper concluded that low
percentages could starve nonprofit organizations and deprive them of capacity that would enable
them to thrive such as resources for marketing and tracking program outcomes. Gathering data
on nonprofit arts and cultural institutions, the paper's econometric analysis concluded that these
organizations were more successful in attracting audiences as their operating costs grew to about
35 percent of total costs. Beyond that threshold, the effectiveness declined.
The paper's conclusions debunk the proposal's rationale for a 15 percent limit. Without any
analysis to support this proposed threshold, the threshold is arbitrary and could very well impair
a nonprofit organization's ability to engage in homeownership counseling, small business
technical assistance, or building affordable housing and other community infrastructure. The
paper concluded that additional research is needed to see if a threshold is reached in terms of
effectiveness in other sectors beyond arts and culture. Yet, the FDIC and OCC did not wait for or
engage in such research before issuing this proposal. Indeed, if measuring outcomes such as the


12

number of clients of housing counseling that improve their credit scores or purchase homes, bank
grants to nonprofit organizations for this type of outcomes measurement would need to be
robust, not stingy.
A further harmful aspect of the proposal is to require complicated documentation that nonprofit
organizations would provide to the bank making the contribution. The proposal suggests that an
IRS 990 form could be used. The difficulty with this form is that it is an annual accounting for
various items in a budget of nonprofit organization. In other words, documentation in a 990 form
would result in a nonprofit limiting all of its operating costs to 15 percent, not just those
associated with the bank grant. The FDIC and OCC proposal does not consider whether this
overall limit is conducive to nonprofit growth, health or effectiveness.
An outcome of the proposed 15 percent would be hesitancy on the parts of both banks and
nonprofit organizations to engage in grants as part of their partnerships. The question is how
many worthy neighborhood projects would be starved of resources, how many nonprofit
organizations would cease receiving bank grants, and how many neighborhood residents would
no longer receive services from trusted and long-established neighborhood-based nonprofit
organizations.
An alternative approach is readily available. Why not encourage banks to report to their CRA
examiners more data on outcomes associated with the projects in general and those with their
nonprofit partners. These outcomes would be housing units built, small business expansions or
hires of employees, clients counseled and whether they purchased homes or started small
businesses and countless other results. Overtime, the stakeholders (banks, nonprofit
organizations, and CRA examiners) could use outcomes data to separate effective programs and
projects from those that are not achieving their goals. CRA evaluations could encourage banks to
expand upon their successful partnerships and discard those that are not delivering. Data
collection and transparency is a more effective approach to improving CRA-related outcomes as
opposed to arbitrary limits on operating costs. And guess what – it might involve more bank
grantmaking or banks assisting in collecting the data than would be allowed under a 15 percent
limit.
I have recommended this type of approach in my book Ending Redlining through a Community-
Centered Reform of the Community Reinvestment Act. In particular, Chapter 6 discusses an
earlier iteration of 15 percent caps called CRA sunshine, that was more akin to extinguishing the
thousands points of light, the phrase of George H. Bush in describing the role of nonprofits in
society.


13

CRA depends on banks and community organizations working together to identify and respond
to community needs. Needless reporting requirements, particularly when data on impacts could
be collected, must not imperil decades of partnership building between banks and communities.
Removing Consideration of Responding to Customer Concerns from CRA Exams Does Not
Make Sense
Banks listening to and responding to community concerns about bank performance in meeting
needs is critical to improving bank reinvestment performance. Inconceivably, the FDIC and
OCC would diminish the weight of community input on CRA exams. This is another aspect of
the proposal that would decrease banks' abilities to meet community needs. When considered
together, aspects of the proposal such as diminishing the importance of community input on
exams and new reporting requirements for nonprofit organizations could magnify each other's
detrimental impact.
Intuitively, one of the most important methods of responding to neighborhood needs is listening
to neighborhood residents as they describe their needs and the larger needs of the community.
These can include easier access to home mortgage loans, small business loans, home repair
loans, or financing for community facilities such as day care or recreational parks.
Recognizing the importance of responding to community needs as articulated by the residents
themselves, the federal bank agencies have formally incorporated consideration of bank
responsiveness to community comments and complaints as part of their CRA evaluations. In
particular, the small and intermediate bank exams have an explicit criterion in their lending test
that considers, "The bank's record of taking action, if warranted, in response to written
complaints about its performance in helping to meet credit needs in its assessment area(s)."
Consumer complaints and comments about smaller and intermediate-sized banks are key to
assessing their compliance with CRA. Local residents are not only intimately familiar with the
needs in their communities but also have a high level of knowledge about the business practices
and culture of their local banks. They have insights that are unlikely to occur to federal CRA
examiners. Thus, the explicit criterion asking examiners and banks to listen to residents'
comments and concerns makes eminent sense.
The FDIC and the OCC are proposing to remove the consumer comment criterion on small and
intermediate bank lending tests because they believe that their consideration of a bank's
responsiveness to needs on the subtests of a CRA exam will be sufficient, rendering an explicit
criterion of responding to consumer and residents' concerns redundant. The agencies, however,
do not offer a convincing rationale about how removing explicit consideration of public


14

comments, which has been a feature of the lending test of smaller banks for decades, will better
enable them to measure banks' responsiveness to needs. How can the agencies better assess
responsiveness if they demote the importance of public comments on responsiveness?
All banks, including larger ones, have a part of their CRA exam called performance context
which considers factors like economic conditions and demographics in considering bank
performance. Consideration of public comments is also part of performance context. This aspect
of considering public comments will remain for all banks, as it should.
However, the removal of the explicit criterion of a smaller or intermediate-size bank's
responsiveness to concerns about its lending activity is still not justified. If anything, this
criterion should be added to large bank exams. Due to the structure of CRA exams, responding to
consumer concerns as part of the lending test elevates the importance of those comments,
concerns, or praise when warranted. If CRA's objective is to ensure responsiveness to needs as
seen by community residents, why would the agencies remove an exam criterion that insists on
the importance of responding to needs as articulated by the public?
Banks have made important progress in designing home mortgage and small business loan
products and other community programs after soliciting and listening to community comments.
A central vision of CRA is establishing partnerships between banks and their communities to
design products and programs that are profitable for banks and that successfully respond to
community needs. Consideration of public comments on CRA exams likely motivated the
creation of partnerships between banks and their communities.
In Ending Redlining through a Community-Centered Reform to the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA), I emphasize that CRA's effectiveness is improved if it is made more responsive to the
views and needs of communities. I suggest that more formal incorporation of community views
on CRA exams and during consideration of bank mergers and branch expansions is needed. Now,
the agencies are proposing the opposite in diminishing CRA evaluations' consideration of
community views during different parts of the exam.
Proposed Changes to CRA Could Facilitate Displacement of Longterm Lower Income
Neighborhood Residents
Yet another aspect of not heeding community concerns is diminishing the attention CRA exams
devote to ensuring projects financed by banks do not displace residents of economically
distressed and vulnerable communities. The OCC and FDIC are ignoring the history of urban
planning and renewal that often displaced long-term neighborhoods by proposing to not carefully
examine large scale projects receiving bank financing. Advocates from urban neighborhoods


15

that helped secure passage of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) in 1977 were fighting
destructive institutional forces that were threatening to displace long-term neighborhood
residents and intensify racial segregation.
Not considering this history, the FDIC's and OCC's proposed rule could qualify large-scale and
disruptive economic development projects for CRA. These are projects that transform
neighborhoods, provide upscale housing, commercial, or entertainment amenities, but that
eventually displace lower income residents who cannot keep up with rising rents or property
taxes.
The CRA regulation encourages financing for community development by qualifying projects
that revitalize and stabilize low- and moderate-income (LMI) census tracts and economically
distressed neighborhoods. The current interagency guidance includes the proviso that the projects
must retain or attract businesses and residents. The word "retain" is key in that it establishes an
expectation that the community development projects would include affordable housing that
eases housing cost pressures for modest income residents or small business financing that helps
local businesses remain in their current neighborhoods.
The FDIC and OCC are proposing to drop the requirement of retaining residents and businesses
because they assert that "essential infrastructure projects are often community-wide projects for
which it is not feasible to allocate the benefit to specific populations or areas." This explanation
is not convincing, considering that the current interagency guidance provides clear and detailed
instructions for examiners of how to gauge whether plans assist longer term residents and
businesses to remain and prosper in their current neighborhoods. For example, the examiners are
to consult "formal and informal" community plans for specifics regarding the beneficiaries of the
plans. Current guidance also places more weight on "those activities that are most responsive to
community needs, including the needs of low- or moderate-income individuals."
Contrary to the assertions of the FDIC and OCC, it is not difficult for examiners to determine the
quality of community or economic development projects. First, CRA works best if it helps
motivate projects that feature a high level of community input and involvement. If long-term
residents have considerable input in the creation of the projects, it is more likely that the projects
will include substantial amounts of affordable housing and assistance to small businesses. Well-
conceived community plans will describe extensive community input mechanisms ranging from
surveys, town hall meetings, charrettes, and other techniques for gathering suggestions.
Secondly, if a project is making a good faith effort to benefit a wide constituency, it will be in a
community plan describing in detail the various aspects of the project including any


16

transportation infrastructure, housing (with counts of housing for various income groups), and
the numbers and types of small businesses assisted.
Any updates to the CRA regulation that relaxes requirements for examiners to determine the
quality of community and economic development projects contradicts CRA's purpose to preserve
and revitalize existing communities, not replacing them with upscale developments.
In her recent book, After Redlining, the Urban Reinvestment Movement in the Era of Financial
Deregulation, Rebecca Marchiel describes how Gail Cincotta and National People's Action
(NPA) engaged in advocacy in the late 1960s and early 1970s to combat unscrupulous real estate
agents and unregulated lenders that would prey on racial fears of working-class whites in
Chicago neighborhoods. These actors would convince the whites to sell their homes at discounts
which would be marked up and sold to unsuspecting African Americans moving into the
neighborhoods. NPA sought to achieve integration by welcoming the newcomers while
preventing widespread panic selling by the neighborhood residents.
Cincotta and NPA reasoned that if the bad actors could be replaced by mainstream banks making
responsible loans and serving all neighborhoods as required by CRA, then the predatory activity
would subside. Likewise, Dan Holland in Communities of Resistance and Resilience in the Post-
Industrial City documents how advocates in Pittsburgh likewise saw CRA as an antidote to large
scale government-led urban renewal and private sector projects that destroyed existing
neighborhoods to make way for downtown business districts.
More recent examples of projects threatening displacement are described by Dan Immergluck
and Sharon Cornelissen. In Red Hot City: Housing, Race and Exclusion in the Twenty-First
Century Atlanta, Immergluck describes the Beltline, a light rail project which included tax
increment financing by the City of Atlanta. Political and economic elites planned the Beltline in a
top-down manner that did not engage neighborhood residents in a significant manner. The result
were developments that did not provide enough affordable housing and facilitated gentrification
and displacement of modest income African American residents. In their proposal, the FDIC and
OCC would provide favorable CRA consideration for government funded projects without
ensuring that they explicitly benefit long-term residents. CRA must not end up funding more
projects like the Beltline.
Similarly, Cornelissen's, The Last House on the Block: Black Homeowners, White
Homesteaders, and Failed Gentrification in Detroit, describes Brightmoor, an economically
distressed neighborhood in Detroit, where homeowners struggle to maintain dilapidated housing.
Over the decades, governments at all levels failed this and other neighborhoods in Detroit. The
lack of federal anti-predatory lending regulation in the years preceding the 2008 financial crisis


17

facilitated high levels of abusive lending and foreclosures that caused massive amounts of vacant
housing in Brightmoor. The local and state government did not then implement forbearance
plans, causing even more damage.
Towards the end of her book, Cornelissen discusses plans for large-scale infrastructure
development that is unlikely to benefit community residents. After decades of laissez faire
policies, a new round of urban renewal policies and programs without community input and
possibly blessed by an ill thought-out CRA reform would likely compound the economic harm
and displacement suffered by community residents.
Even keeping the word "retain" does not guarantee revitalization initiatives that are helpful for
residents struggling economically. Some banks and CRA examiners can still make the wrong
decisions in certain situations. However, this language will help avoid repeated mistakes,
particularly if accompanied by a preamble in a final rule explaining the intent behind the word
"retain" as avoiding displacement. Moreover, robust interagency training for examiners will also
help, especially if it includes contributions by community-based organizations, local
governments, and banks that have revitalized neighborhoods and preserved opportunities for
long-term residents to remain and prosper.
FDIC and OCC Propose to Diminish the Role of Anti-Discrimination Reviews as part of
CRA Evaluations
Just as the FDIC and OCC are not being careful in avoiding displacement under their proposed
rule, they are also diminishing attention to any discriminatory activity by banks, which again is
contrary to the purposes of the CRA statute.
Congress passed and President Carter signed the Community Reinvestment Act in 1977 to
prevent redlining, or discrimination against modest income neighborhoods and communities of
color. To enforce CRA's anti-discriminatory purpose, the exam will check to make sure that the
bank is not committing any illegal or discriminatory practices.
Now, the FDIC and the OCC are proposing to narrow the anti-discriminatory review
accompanying CRA exams. This undermines the central purpose of the law to make sure that
banks are not redlining.
Under the current CRA regulations, a CRA rating can be downgraded and a bank can fail its
CRA exam based on findings of discrimination. A federal agency (the Consumer Financial
Protection Bureau (CFPB) in the case of banks over $10 billion dollars in assets or the FDIC,
OCC, or Federal Reserve Board for banks with fewer assets) will conduct a fair lending review
at about the same time as the CRA exam. If the fair lending review uncovers a pattern and


18

practice of discrimination or violation of a consumer protection law, the CRA rating can be
downgraded. A section of the CRA exam reports whether a downgrade occurred due to any
illegal activity; it can also describe the nature and extent of the activity.
In their proposed changes to the CRA regulation, the FDIC and the OCC are suggesting as one of
the possible options for adoption that only an enforcement action by a federal or state agency (or
judicial order including a Federal or state agency) involving discrimination or illegal action can
result in a possible downgrade of a CRA rating. Enforcement actions are not as frequent as
ongoing fair lending compliance exams. Thus, the incidence of downgrades or failed ratings due
to discrimination or other illegal activity will probably be less frequent.
Overall, the current Administration is lessening its investigation and enforcement of civil rights
law. The CFPB has even tried to return funding to a lender that had provided funds to the federal
government as part of a discrimination settlement.
The consideration of public comments highlighting racial or gender disparities in lending and
asking the agencies to further investigate them is in doubt. Currently, the agency regulating a
bank that receives this type of comment would likely consider evidence of disparities in lending
when conducing a fair lending review of a bank. If the FDIC and OCC proceed to consider
downgrades of ratings only in the wake of enforcement actions, would the agencies even
consider public comments that were submitted to the bank's public file before the enforcement
actions.
In addition, would the fair lending review, if it uncovered significant evidence of discrimination,
influence the bank's rating under the option being considered by the FDIC and OCC that only
enforcement actions influence a bank's rating. Enforcement actions can occur significantly after
the completion of the CRA exam. Therefore, a bank can enjoy the privileges of passing its CRA
exam such as agency approval of its merger applications without being penalized for its
discriminatory conduct which an enforcement action addresses months or years later.
Instead of proposing diminishing the importance of fair lending reviews, the federal bank
agencies should be boosting their influence. The agencies should explicitly state that public
comments will be considered on fair lending reviews. As I recommended in my book, Ending
Redlining Through a Community-Centered Reform of the Community Reinvestment Act, the
agencies should also explain the methodologies they employed on fair lending reviews and the
products they tested to make sure no discrimination occurred as they used to in the early years of
the public release of CRA exams.


19

More transparency in fair lending reviews and their findings would increase efficiency and
efficacy. The public, for instance, can monitor the area of lending that the agencies tested in
future years to see if the bank's fair lending performance improved, remained constant, or
worsened. The public could also suggest that the agencies consider other lending products or
disparities that they might not have examined.
Finally, the current regulation states that the effect of discriminatory or other illegal action on the
CRA rating depends on the "nature, extent, and strength of the evidence of the practices." The
proposed rule removes this phrase, which removes an objective consideration determining
whether a downgrade will occur. Banks themselves may wonder at the increased possibility of
arbitrary decisions if this sensible guideline is removed. For instance, widespread discrimination
practiced across markets should result in downgrades as opposed to one rogue loan officer
practicing discrimination that the bank subsequently fired.
Going backwards on the consideration of discriminatory or illegal activity is not the way to
enforce an anti-redlining law. Diminishing the role of public comments about racial or gender
disparities in lending removes an important resource for the FDIC and OCC. In sum, this
proposed change is likely to increase the incidence of redlining.
Proposed CRA Rule Diminishing Attention to Bank Branching and Deposit Accounts
Would Result in Less Lending
A relatively unnoticed aspect of the FDIC's and the OCC's proposed changes to the CRA
regulation is the decrease in attention that would be devoted to measuring banks' branching and
deposit services in LMI communities. Over time, a lack of attention to bank branches and
services will decrease bank retail lending to LMI borrowers and communities.
Currently, CRA exams, in addition to evaluating lending and investing, will scrutinize bank
branches and deposit services in a comprehensive manner for large banks and to a lesser extent
for intermediate-small (ISB) banks. As described by NCRC, 417 banks that are currently
classified as large banks will be re-classified as ISB banks. This means that they would no longer
have a separate service test that evaluates the number and percentages of their branches in LMI
census tracts. If the proposed rule is adopted, only 155 banks out of more than 4,200 banks (or
only about 3.6 percent) in this country would have a CRA exam that evaluates bank branching.
To make matters worse, the OCC and FDIC under their proposal would no longer evaluate the
number and quality of bank deposit products on CRA exams. Instead, the agencies would focus
on just considering the range of credit services (or lending products) on CRA exams, something
that is already done now. The agencies explain the cutback by stating, "In the agencies' view, this


20

limitation is appropriate in light of the agencies' statutory mandate to assess a bank's "record of
meeting the credit needs of its entire community."
This is a significant change from FDIC's and OCC's views just a few years ago when they
finalized a revised CRA rule in February of 2024 that is now being rescinded. Back then the
agencies reasoned, "While the operational provisions of the CRA instructs the agencies to
evaluate a bank's record of meeting the credit needs of its communities, the agencies have found
that there is a sufficient nexus between deposit products and the provision of credit." In other
words, the agencies were asserting a relationship exists between providing deposit accounts and
lending. They cited academic studies showing that customers in LMI communities are more
likely to receive loans if they have deposit accounts that enable them to save, improve their
credit scores, and otherwise become ready to receive loans.
When I was the research director at NCRC, we conducted studies for the Appalachian Regional
Commission that confirmed the relationship between branching and lending, and reviewed the
literature that discussed the practice of relationship lending in which banks would make loans
based on their daily interactions with small business owners at branches.
A narrow reading of the CRA statute to restrict CRA evaluations of most banks to mainly focus
on retail lending is contrary to CRA practice over the decades that has also included robust
examination of a variety of activities related to services and investments. CRA evaluations have
included non-lending activities because they help a bank make retail loans to LMI borrowers.
For example, community development investments that provide affordable rental housing or
revitalize a downtown business district will help banks make home and small business loans to
people who want to live near and operate businesses in the revitalized part of town. Likewise,
evaluating the provision of deposit services would help banks make retail loans by creating more
creditworthy borrowers.
One could argue that if a CRA exam mainly focusses on retail lending, it will still encourage
banks to make branches and deposit products available because these services enable them to
make loans to LMI borrowers. However, this line of argument misses the impact of industry-
wide changes that would be prompted by reduced examinations of deposit products on the
lending part of CRA exams.
Because most banks would no longer be evaluated under the proposal based on their branching
and no banks will have deposit products assessed, over time, several banks may reduce their
branching and deposit provision in LMI communities. This will reduce their abilities to make
loans to LMI borrowers and communities. On a CRA exam, a bank's percentage of loans to LMI
borrowers and communities is compared to the percentage of loans made by peer banks to LMI


21

borrowers and communities in a county or metropolitan area. The peers' percentage would likely
decrease after they reduce their branching and deposit products, meaning that individual banks
would realize they would not need to work as hard to match their peers' lending performance.
The result of less comprehensive CRA exams will be less access to credit for LMI borrowers and
communities. Under the CRA statute, the agencies are to assess banks' records in meeting credit
needs of communities. If the FDIC and OCC finalize their proposal, their exams would likely
result in reductions in the provision of credit to LMI borrowers and communities. This is the
opposite of their statutory responsibilities.
Just as in the medical field, the first principle of Hippocratic rulemaking should be to do no
harm. Why would the FDIC and OCC propose radical changes to CRA exams that banks have
been undergoing for decades that would mainly cause harm? Their explanation of reducing
regulatory costs is unconvincing since the banking industry has thrived over the last decades of
CRA's implementation. The issue of regulatory cost is addressed next.
FDIC Cost-Benefit Analysis on Changes to CRA is Sorely Lacking
When federal agencies propose changes to regulations, including those implementing CRA, they
conduct cost-benefit analysis. Such analyses usually show that the benefits of the proposed
change outweigh the costs for all parties. In this case, the FDIC, one of the agencies proposing to
weaken the CRA rules, conducted a cost-benefit analysis that is so misleading that it cannot
withstand scrutiny.
I looked at one aspect of the proposed changes to CRA – eliminating community development
financing responsibilities for intermediate banks with assets ranging from $412 million to $1
billion that would be re-classified as small banks. Community development financing refers to
financing affordable housing (often multifamily), economic development financing small
business growth, or large-scale revitalization projects such as a light rail line designed to increase
access to jobs and other benefits for LMI communities.
For this analysis, I sorted FDIC banks in descending order of assets and documented the
community development financing of the ten largest banks that would change from intermediate
small to small. These banks each had assets of around $1 billion. They were generally located in
smaller cities or rural areas in several states including California, Missouri, and Maryland. These
communities will have a harder time replacing community development financing if the banks
sharply curtail this financing if they no longer are required to provide it.
On an annual basis, the ten banks combined provided approximately $158 million in community
development loans and $29 million in investments for affordable housing, economic


22

development, community facilities, and revitalization activities. In total, 625 FDIC-supervised
banks would move from intermediate to small and so would no longer be required to provide
community development financing.
The FDIC estimated that these banks would save about $10.8 million annually in reduced costs
related to community development financing including underwriting, origination, and
documentation costs. From a societal perspective, the community development financing levels
of just ten banks overwhelm the savings achieved by a factor of 17 ($187 million in community
development lending and investing divided by $10.8 million). If I had retrieved the community
development financing levels of all 625 banks (which an analyst has to do one exam at a time
since there is no central database for community development financing), the community
development financing would have been exponentially greater than the savings for the banks.
While the banks would not eliminate all their community development financing, reductions of
half or a third would nevertheless be devastating on a societal level.
These rough calculations do not even account for other benefits including job creation. Daniel
Ringo, a Federal Reserve economist, found that $80,000 in community development lending
creates one job. A loss of $187 million annually in community development lending would equal
about 1,976 fewer jobs. Other benefits include property value appreciation minus any
displacement of modest income residents due to higher housing costs that are not included in this
analysis. My back of the envelope analysis suggests that the agencies could do much better in
generating a comprehensive cost-benefit analysis given their access to scores of economists
skilled in such analysis.
In addition to societal benefits, a cost-benefit analysis should consider the impact of the changes
on an individual bank basis. I calculated that the FDIC's estimate of total savings of $10.8
million for 625 banks would equal about $17,280 per bank. A quick scan of the profits of
affordable housing lending (for multifamily housing) suggests that a lender's profit is about 1
percent of the total loan amount. The median amount of annual affordable housing lending was
about $1.398 million for the banks in my sample. One percent of that is approximately $13,978.
This means that just one type of community development financing, affordable housing lending,
almost equals the amount of reduced costs should these banks cease all community development
financing. Overall, this analysis suggests that the banks benefit much more in terms of profit than
they lose in terms of costs for engaging in community development financing.
Although the agencies announced their intentions to change the CRA regulations more than a
year ago, they did not attempt to conduct a thoughtful cost-benefit analysis. The FDIC states that
"it does not have the information necessary to quantify, accurately, the effects of the proposal on


23

consumers and businesses, including depositors and/or borrowers. However, the FDIC notes that
the proposal's provisions are intended to better achieve statutory objectives." How exactly does
the proposal enable better achievement of CRA's goals --- by reducing requirements and
expectations for banks to engage in a range of financing that is aimed at revitalizing
neighborhoods?
My analysis does not assess the OCC's cost-benefit analysis, which is similarly lacking. The
OCC states "Ideally, a cost-benefit analysis would be able to identify and monetize, with
certainty, all costs and benefits of a regulation, which would then allow policymakers to evaluate
different regulatory options by comparing dollar amounts of costs and benefits and pursuing
those options with the greatest net benefits. Many financial regulations, however, include both
cost and benefit components that cannot be expressed in monetary units with adequate certainty."
Put together, the OCC's and FDIC's assertions amount to an admission that their cost-benefit
analysis is incomplete because costs and benefits are difficult to identify. Is this a red herring,
however? Is it more accurate to say that the agencies simply cannot defend a proposal that would
relieve hundreds of banks from community development financing responsibilities? And by
doing so, the banks would be encouraged to focus more on retail lending. A narrower focus and
fewer product lines are generally not a good idea for financial institutions which traditionally
diversify their portfolios in order to mitigate an over-exposure to risk in any product line or
financial activity.
In the final analysis, the FDIC's and OCC's cost-benefit analysis is woefully short in terms of
documenting benefits to banks or communities and therefore cannot support the proposed
changes to CRA.
Conclusion
The proposal fails on the principle of the Hippocratic oath of doing no harm. Multiple harms
would be endured by communities losing access to possibly billions of dollars of community
development financing, less access to retail lending and branching, more exposure to projects
receiving favorable CRA consideration that displace long-term residents, and increased chances
that CRA exams will not catch discrimination or redlining. Harms would also affect banks as
they may not be as effective in making profitable loans since CRA will not push them as much to
do so and they may expose themselves to more risk by focusing on fewer product lines and types
of financing.


24

Any reasonable cost benefit analysis would have concluded that the costs of this proposal
exponentially overwhelm the meager benefits. Any reasonable cost benefit analysis would have
stopped this proposal immediately.
CRA's intention to provide the means of communities to lift themselves up through more access
to credit and bank services is thwarted should this proposal be adopted. This is the opposite of
Ending Redlining through a Community-Centered Reform of the Community Reinvestment Act
that would elevate the input of communities into the CRA process, not throttle it.
Thank you for this opportunity to comment on this important matter. If you have any questions,
please contact me at endredline77@gmail.com.
Sincerely,
Josh Silver

I support the OCC and FDIC in their attempt to limit indirect cost rate charges for banks receiving and distributing grant funding to 15%. As a grant writing professional, I understand that indirect costs play a vital role in allowing organizations and institutions to administer programs by covering overhead costs. Given that the current federal de minimis rate is 10%, a 15% cap is both reasonable and necessary. This cap will allow banking institutions to cover their administrative costs while maximizing the amount of funds that are put directly to work for community development initiatives. 

Additionally, reducing the middlemen in grant fund allocation will also be a positive step towards ensuring that grant funding is maximized and utilized by direct-service nonprofits working within a bank's community. This further reduces the indirect cost drain on limited grant funds. Similarly, by creating a community development grant definition and instating clear guidelines on what qualifies and how funds are used, our communities will be better served. 

Overall, I believe these amendments to be a critical step towards funneling more grant funding to community development activities without straining the organizations and institutions involved. Indirect cost caps, discouraging funding nonprofits that fund other nonprofit programs, and creating a clear community development grant definition will direct more vital funding to communities in need. Failure to adopt these proposed rules will allow grant funds to be whittled away by general operating costs and programs that do not directly benefit our communities.

Dear Chief Counsel, Ms. Jones, and Leadership of the OCC and FDIC,

The Affordable Housing Alliance of Central Ohio is a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization that provides
research, education, technical assistance, and support to efforts that close Central Ohio's housing
affordability gaps. We analyze housing opportunities through an economic development lens and are
guided by nearly forty organizational members with significant professional expertise in housing
development, finance, and service delivery.

While we have not previously engaged in federal rulemaking activities, we feel compelled to share two
important concerns regarding the proposed Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA") rule and seek
modifications to better align with broader federal policy objectives and statutory intent. In advance, we
share our gratitude for your review and consideration of these comments.

First, by reducing the number of lenders who are subject to the most comprehensive aspects of the
rule, this proposal will significantly reduce investment capacity in proven supply-side housing
strategies. These at-risk investment tools, which are critical for reducing Central Ohio's housing
shortage, include the federal Low Income Housing Tax Credit, the Ohio Low Income Housing Tax
Credit (rural focused), Welcome Home Ohio (homeownership focused), and the Single-Family Tax
Credit (homeownership focused). It would also restrain the State's proposed Promise Land tax credit
which, if passed, would support faith-based housing providers working to advance homeownership
opportunities and is particularly well suited to smaller banking partners. Disincentivizing mid-sized
banks from investing in these bipartisan equity programs will limit Ohio's ability to resolve its housing
deficit.





While AHACO agrees that in many cases, "a community's credit needs are best and most directly met
through activities that involve lending," we caution against a one-size-fits-all approach. In reality, a mix
of both debt and equity tools has proven most effective at increasing housing inventory and restoring
balance in the market. The CRA's current configuration supports this diversified approach while also
flexibly accommodating the distinctive needs of local housing markets.

This is evident in Central Ohio where a booming economy means that we need to build nearly 200,000
new homes over the next ten years. With traditional financing vehicles for workforce housing strained,
our region consistently fails to meet annualized benchmarks, building only half of what is needed to
accommodate record job gains. As these pressures mount, more than 80,000 residents are now
experiencing severe housing cost burdens.

However, even with local reforms to zoning and permitting, debt alone remains insufficient to support
construction needs. Pro formas without a robust equity component increasingly fail to pencil out. CRA
has bridged some of this gap but, even today, more investment is needed. Our members report that
thousands of units are stalled due to reduced credit demand. Not only is our region unable to realize
the stabilizing impact of those homes, but we are also unable to capture the economic boon of
hundreds of millions of dollars in complementary lending that would accompany it. Weakening the
CRA will further destabilize this suite of "off budget" equity investments and hinder our Ohio's ability to
protect and expand housing affordability.

Secondly, the proposed rule will frustrate and impede the nonprofit delivery model for critical housing
services, especially those designed to advance economic self-sufficiency for low- and moderate-income
households. See: § __.12. Specifically, portions of the rule that restrict nonprofit grants and donations
or impose administrative fee caps that are out of alignment with actual costs will result in inefficiencies,
increased administrative burden, and funding shortfalls for high-priority initiatives, many of which were
recently promoted in the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act.

In Central Ohio, the following widely acclaimed program types are likely to experience operating
shortages and/or risk closure should this rule become effective in its current form:

•
Technical assistance and education to reduce zoning barriers to housing creation;
•
'Libraries' with pre-approved plans to reduce permitting delays and construction costs;
•
Capacity building for faith-based housing providers;
•
Concessionary lending programs required to leverage external resources;
•
Risk tolerant lending for more naturally affordable building types, like manufactured,
Accessory Dwelling Unit, and "missing middle" housing;
•
Temporary housing programs that require clients to participate in career education;
•
Innovative down payment strategies, including shared appreciation mortgage loans;
•
Housing counseling to promote self-sufficiency and/or sustainable homeownership;
•
Home modifications to support senior independence and aging in community;
•
Public safety-based programs to remediate blight and reduce housing vacancies; and
•
Local research to assess and monitor supply shortages and document best practices.
 Each of these initiatives gives a range of constituencies an opportunity to thrive, including our rural and
suburban communities. Either directly or indirectly, they all expand access to credit.
These programs work because of strong public-private partnerships between builders, like those in
AHACO's membership, investors subject to the CRA rules, and the determined oversight of federal
regulators. It is these robust collaborations that sustain affordable housing construction and support a
durable services ecosystem. Unfortunately, the proposed changes weaken that tripartite system and
will increase housing supply shortages, reduce housing quality, and intensify neighborhood instability.
For these reasons, AHACO respectfully requests that the proposed rulemaking process be suspended
or delayed pending further research and community engagement into these acute harms. Alternately,
we recommend modifications that both (1) strengthen the LIHTC program and similar public-private

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31; 91 Fed. Reg. 52114 (Aug. 12, 2026)
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
We represent a Community Action Agency that is also a Community Development Corporation. We urge the Office of the Comptroller (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to withdraw the proposal to change the Community Reinvestment Act regulations. In our view, it would weaken support for affordable housing, community organizations, and residents with low incomes.
Our organization works with individuals and families seeking stable housing and greater financial security. We see how affordable housing, access to basic banking, and support from trusted local organizations contribute to lasting stability. Banks are important partners in this work. Their loans, investments, grants, and services help community organizations respond to needs that cannot be met through public funding alone.
The proposal would change how smaller and midsize banks are evaluated under CRA. Banks with less than $1 billion in assets would no longer receive a separate review of their community development activities, while banks with less than $10 billion would no longer receive the full review now applied to large banks. Local and regional banks can be vital partners in affordable housing and other community projects. Reduced scrutiny could weaken their incentive to participate.
We ask the agencies to preserve meaningful review of community development lending, investments, and services. Public reporting should also continue so communities can see where bank resources are reaching residents and where needs remain unmet.
Affordable housing projects often require several sources of financing. A bank loan alone may not close the gap. Bank investments, including those connected to the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, help make homes affordable to families with limited incomes. If CRA examinations place less weight on these investments, housing organizations may find it harder to assemble the financing needed to build or preserve homes.
We are also concerned that the proposal’s low minimum level of community development activity, intended for recognizing work outside a bank’s local service area, could become a broader benchmark. Although the agencies say it is not a general passing score, banks should be evaluated in light of the needs of the communities they serve and the work they are capable of doing.
The proposed limits on grants to nonprofits are of particular concern. The proposal would generally require a bank grant to support a specific project or program. A grant designated for one housing program might still count toward a bank’s CRA performance, while a flexible grant that an organization could use where the need is greatest, such as supporting staff or keeping several services running, could be harder for the bank to count. That could make banks less willing to provide the flexible support community organizations need. The agencies further ask whether grants should receive CRA consideration at all. We strongly oppose eliminating that consideration.
Nonprofits need staff, facilities, coordination, and sound administrative systems to serve residents effectively. These are necessary costs of service, even when they do not fit neatly within a single project budget. Flexible grants allow organizations to respond as needs change. We urge the agencies to continue recognizing grants that support nonprofits serving low-income communities, including general operating support.
The proposal would also exclude checking and savings accounts from the review of certain bank services. For many residents, an affordable account makes it easier to receive wages or benefits, pay rent, and save for emergencies. Access to a branch nearby can also matter. We urge the agencies to continue evaluating whether banks offer affordable, accessible accounts and services in low-income neighborhoods.
For these reasons, we urges the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the proposal. If the agencies proceed, they should preserve meaningful expectations for community development lending and investment; continue recognizing grants to nonprofits, including operating support; consider affordable accounts and branch access; and retain public information needed to identify gaps in service. We also request a fuller assessment of the proposal’s effects on low-income communities and additional time for those communities to comment.
Thank you for considering our views and the needs of the residents and communities we serve.
