whether those activities will receive CRA consideration.
7. Make the strategic plan option a genuinely practical alternative
I support the proposed prefiling consultation process, clearer standards for measurable goals, written
notice when a plan is technically complete, a defined process for denial and resubmission, and greater
flexibility to amend plans after material changes. These changes could make strategic plans useful for
institutions whose business models are not appropriately evaluated under standard tests.
To make this option workable, the agencies should provide model plan elements, examples of acceptable
performance measures and levels, and transparent standards for determining whether goals are
substantially met. Prefiling feedback should be timely and sufficiently substantive to identify material
concerns without implying preapproval. Where an amendment is narrow or results from circumstances
outside the bank's control, the agencies should not require the bank to repeat the entire public
participation and approval process.
8. Promote examination consistency, transparency, and reasonable implementation
Even well-designed rules can produce uncertainty if examination procedures, examiner training, and
performance evaluations are not aligned. The agencies should issue coordinated examination procedures
and training before the final rule becomes applicable. Banks should receive clear notice of the data,
product lines, assessment areas, and analytical standards that will be used in an examination, along with

identified.

improve the evaluation of CRA performance.

transparency, and effectiveness of the Community Reinvestment Act framework.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0096_09000064b9625366.pdf:
My name is Kent M Franzen VP of Compliance for Henderson State Bank. We are a
small community Bank with thirteen locations across Nebraska and have recently grown
past the $500 million asset mark. My own personal experience is that I have worked for
several community Banks in Nebraska since beginning my Banking career in 1985. I
have experience in lending, compliance, operations as well as IT.
Over my career I have observed that the number of total bank charters in Nebraska
has fallen dramatically from over 300 in 1985 to under 150 at present. Part of this is
market driven, in that as agriculture has consolidated into fewer hands with larger
financial needs Banks have also needed to do the same to service these customers.
However, part of the Bank charter consolidation is driven by the burden of Government
Regulation of which the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) is a part.
Over the years I have come to appreciate that most regulation was initiated to
manage a certain problem or promote a goal. In my opinion the CRA was originated to
ensure that deposits sourced in a Banks geographic trade area were loaned out
primarily within this same geographic area. Overall, this is a philosophy we agree with.
However, in my personal opinion politics has gradually transformed the CRA into a
mechanism that forces funds to flow towards social programs that have little to no
economic value to the American Society as a whole by control over the donations and
subsidization of lending that political agitators. I will attempt to identify the portions of
the regulation proposal in italics and follow with the comment Henderson State Bank
desires to make in regard to the Small Bank directives in the proposal.
Asset Thresholds: The proposed rule would increase the asset threshold of a small
bank to below $1 billion (up from less than $412 million), or alternatively, to $850 million
or below in alignment with the Small Business Administration ("SBA") standard for
commercial banks (to be automatically adjusted when the SBA size threshold changes);
The small bank threshold would continue to be adjusted annually based on changes in
the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers.
Henderson State Bank (HSB) is extremely glad to see the regulators adjusting these
asset size-based regulations in such a fashion. We support the proposed adjustment to
the $1 Billion asset level for small banks and find the periodic inflation adjustment of this
threshold a vital provision for the future.
Lending Test:
 The Proposed Rule reflects an increased focus on lending activities consistent with the
requirements of the CRA. This change reflects the agencies' view that a community's
credit needs are most directly met through activities that involve lending.
Under the small bank lending test, the agencies would consider only a bank's major
product line(s) when assessing its retail lending. The agencies propose two potential
options for determining a bank's major product lines. Under one option, the agencies
would use a quantitative, bank-level approach to evaluate a bank's retail lending in two
of the four retail lending product lines, and those would be considered the major product
lines. The other option would use an assessment-area-level approach that qualitatively
and quantitatively determines major product lines, similar to the current methodology for
small and intermediate small banks. Under either approach, the agencies would
consider consumer lending to be a major product line only if it constitutes a majority of
the bank's retail lending by both dollar amount and loan count, or at the bank's option.
The Proposed Rule would codify that 30 loans are generally sufficient for a meaningful
lending-performance assessment but permit the agencies to consider fewer loans
where a smaller sample can still support a meaningful assessment. If loan data are
insufficient for a meaningful assessment, the agencies would rely on other lending
criteria that can be meaningfully assessed or on applicable performance-context factors.
In our opinion as long as a small Bank shows that the majority of its lending is done
inside its designated trade area that should be sufficient to satisfy the CRA. The minutia
of looking at consumer lending versus commercial loans or any other parsing of the
data diverts the overall focus from what the CRA is intended to do, and that is keeping
the deposits supplied by the residents of a trade area at work within that same trade
area. Please keep this analysis simple and direct in the regulation.
Service Test:
This change would exclude deposit services and the distribution and availability of an
institution's retail banking facilities, which are currently considered retail banking
services.
HSB supports removing deposit services from the CRA evaluations. It is our experience
that community Banks AKA small banks under the CRA, will need more flexibility to
attract deposits, such as so-called brokered deposits, from outside our trade area for
lending within our trade area, and this change would be a good step in this direction.
Community Development Activities:
Henderson State Bank in regard to the proposed changes to the Community
Development Activities requests that donations made to political subdivisions, such as
school districts or rural fire districts be recognized fully under the CRA without further
 need for any analysis or complicated record keeping. Overall HSB finds these
community development activity rules the most burdensome of the proposed CRA
changes. We encourage the agencies to do all they can to promote CRA credit to
intuitions without the penalty of busy work accounting.
Strategic Plan:
HSB comments on the small bank CRA strategic plan process are that we welcome the
proposed changes to make the process less burdensome. At the risk of "looking a gift
horse in the mouth" we also ask for any further changes that the agencies can make to
ensure this mandate is structured to be as simple as possible for small community
banks. HSB would like to point out that every day we are working to document and
satisfy a regulation requirement such as this strategic planning, is a day we are not
working with and for our clients. We ask that this principle be a major consideration of
those writing this final regulation.
 Public File and Notice Requirements:
As I said, my personal banking experience began in 1985. Excluding requests by
examination staff, I have been asked for the Bank's CRA public file precisely two times
over more than 4 decades. Both of those requests were from other Banker's, looking to
oppose an application to establish a new branch location by our Bank. With awareness
that quarterly call reports, with over eighty pages of detail each, are available online
from the FFIEC, on any Bank, the public file does not seem to be of important use to the
citizenry. If regulators must retain this requirement to satisfy law, then please keep the
burden of meeting this requirement to the absolute statutory minimum, especially for
small Banks. We welcome the ability to retain the public file electronically as this is a
way we can provide the information at any HSB location within a few minutes of a
request. So, if this public file information is not highly sought after, what is the purpose
of the public file? Does the public file exist solely to be wielded as a cudgel upon the
Banks by political opportunists looking to force funding of their personal whims by a
privately held Bank?
Point not evident in the request:
HSB would like to bring up one issue in regard to CRA not directly addressed in the
proposed regulation and that is the effect that the internet, internet banking, email,
electronic transactions, electronic signatures, and mobile device deposits are having on
the concept of an identified trade area (AKA Community) for a Bank. At some point in
the not-too-distant future our collective definition of community as a concept in CRA will
 need to adapt to our evolving society. When I joined Henderson state Bank in 2015 we
had five locations in four Nebraska towns. Today we have thirteen locations in twelve
Nebraska towns, literally stretching from the Colorado border to the Iowa border. HSB
has several clients that began their relationship with us as residents of our trade area
but are now residing internationally or in other states, obviously outside our designated
trade area. We have been able to continue to serve them using the technology
mentioned. However, retaining these relationships actually works against us in our CRA
evaluation as these customers are now "out of our trade area." My point is to ask
Regulators and or Lawmakers to ponder how the CRA regulation and/or underlying
legal definitions should be adjusted into the future to take customer relationships like
these into account. If this is not done, the CRA will become a choke collar on the
community reinvestment growth it was intended to foster.
Conclusion:
Henderson State bank agrees wholeheartedly with the general goal of the Community
Reinvestment Act, that the deposits gathered within a community should be used to the
advantage of that community. The cliché "A rising tide lifts all boats" comes to mind.
However, we believe that the proof of this concept for a small community Bank should
be measured by its actual lending activity. If most of its activity is being done in its
designated trade area, or even its home state, in the case of rural agricultural banks
then we believe the Bank should be given a satisfactory CRA grade without extensive
accounting tracking of unrelated charity donations or other complicated, time intensive
requirements. We should all be more concerned with meeting customers' needs than
we are with filling out forms, composing public files and writing strategic plans that no
one but regulators and political agitators ask to see or use.
Thank you for your time and attention to our concerns.
Kent M Franzen VP
Henderson State Bank

Henderson NE 68371
kfranzen@hendersonstate.bank

I am the Executive Director of Clare Housing, an HIV Housing organization that has built and operates over one hundred units of deeply affordable housing for Minnesotans living with HIV, thanks to the current structure of the Community Reinvestment Act Regulations. Like most nonprofit housing providers, partnerships and lending practices with community banks lead to increased availability of housing units and development of multi-family units. However, if the changes to the Community Reinvestment Act Regulations are implemented, nonprofit housing developers, families with low incomes, and small business communities nationwide will be economically harmed. 

With the implementation of the significant changes to the CRA, Minnesota will be the second most impacted state with one hundred seven (107) banks losing requirements for community reinvestments. The changes will mean that the already barrier-laden landscape of securing investments for nonprofit housing developments will become more challenging. According to the 2026 MHP State of Housing Report, there is a gap of over 100,000 available low-income units in Minnesota, and that gap will continue to grow as wage-growth has slowed. With less housing developed and reduced access to dollars to make reinvestments in existing housing for low-income people over time, housing waitlists and competition for affordable and deeply affordable housing will increase. 

It is also critical to consider the role deeply affordable and non-profit owner developers play in our communities. Non-profit developers are able to make units affordable because they are not built to maximize profit, meaning we can provide fair-market rent. Every single person in our community is better off when people are housed – but someone or some organization has to do that work. The lack of affordable housing leads directly to dangerous situations, impacts education, public safety, future job opportunities, and health. All of our social structures relate to housing. The current CRA program is unique, and if the proposed changes take effect there is no replacement program or alternative way forward.

Due to the considerations that will impact housing development, we urge the significant changes to the Community Reinvestment Act not be implemented.

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

LaunchPad Collective, Inc. objects to the harmful changes proposed to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. Congress passed the CRA in 1977 in
response to redlining, and it creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help
meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities, including low- and
moderate-income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged
banks to lend, invest, and provide services in underserved communities, challenges
related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of access remain.
LaunchPad Collective, Inc. is a San Bernardino-based nonprofit community
development organization focused on creating affordable housing and expanding
economic opportunity, particularly for transitional-age youth and young people
aging out of foster care. Our developments bring housing together with workforce
development,
entrepreneurship, childcare, healthy food access, and other
community-serving resources.


LaunchPad Collective, Inc. | 330 N. D Street, Ste. 526 | San Bernardino, CA 92401 |
www.launchpadcollective.org | robert@launchpadcollective.org | 909-521-8432


We work with banks and other financial institutions to identify financing,
investment, and philanthropic resources that can help make affordable housing and
community development projects possible in historically underserved communities.
CRA-motivated
lending,
investment,
grants,
and
partnerships
can
help
organizations like ours access construction and permanent financing, support
community-serving facilities and programs, and attract capital to neighborhoods
where conventional financing alone may not be sufficient. As we expand our work in
San Bernardino, strong relationships between banks and community-based
organizations are essential to increasing affordable housing, supporting small
businesses and entrepreneurs, and creating greater economic opportunity for local
residents.
The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift.
The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on
LMI communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional
60 days so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost
to communities because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not
conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing
and small businesses will drop dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development
projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as
they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate," and "Large"
Banks, so many banks would face substantially less CRA scrutiny and fewer
expectations to meet community development needs.[1] According to National
Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70 California banks would see
their reinvestment obligations reduced under the proposal. Twenty-five California


LaunchPad Collective, Inc. | 330 N. D Street, Ste. 526 | San Bernardino, CA 92401 |
www.launchpadcollective.org | robert@launchpadcollective.org | 909-521-8432


banks would shed their Community Development Test responsibilities entirely, and
45 California banks would no longer be subject to the Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs), which are a
key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC), which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity
equivalent investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach,
and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative
market.

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from
CRA-motivated banks.[4] Regulators will further weaken CD obligations if they
adopt the alternative proposal that defines Large Banks as those with over $30
billion in assets.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests a
bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just 0.625% of its Tier 1 capital were
devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower than what
the NCRC determined banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet the proposed
thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]

Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business
development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.

2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.


LaunchPad Collective, Inc. | 330 N. D Street, Ste. 526 | San Bernardino, CA 92401 |
www.launchpadcollective.org | robert@launchpadcollective.org | 909-521-8432


The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain
branches in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a
"Large Bank" to over $10 billion, forty-five banks in California will no longer be
subject to the Services Test and will be reviewed to ensure their branches serve LMI
communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI areas
and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure due to
this proposal.[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities.
Fewer branches will result in less small business lending. These changes will be
particularly hard-hitting in rural areas of our state where smaller banks originate a
larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also remove the long-standing obligation for banks to offer
deposit products accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are a gateway to
credit access, financial stability, and wealth building, especially for families who are
otherwise preyed upon by predatory financial institutions. For example, the BankOn
program has provided access to no- or low-fee bank accounts for over fourteen
million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn coalitions that establish
effective partnerships among banks, community-based organizations, and local
governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million
are underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of
dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone,
state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million) in OD and
NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm,
and community development lending activities. Such data is critical to
understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA
data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The


LaunchPad Collective, Inc. | 330 N. D Street, Ste. 526 | San Bernardino, CA 92401 |
www.launchpadcollective.org | robert@launchpadcollective.org | 909-521-8432


loss of such data is particularly harmful as the Administration walks back efforts to
collect and disclose detailed small business lending data under Section 1071 of the
Dodd-Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately impact rural communities in
our state, where banks with up to $10 billion in assets make up a larger share of
the small business and small farm lending markets.

4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see
sufficient benefits.
The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs
of Native American communities and Tribal Nations, which have been poorly served
by banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations on areas where banks have
branches, even though far fewer bank branches exist near Tribal lands and in rural
areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this CRA
gap by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related
activities in "Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of
bank CRA assessment areas. But many members of Tribes in California will not
benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or
Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within
particular geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with historic
dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should also consider
whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct
benefits to, federally recognized Tribes and non-federally recognized Tribes.
Non-federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and can access
programs and contracts with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes
exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit
organizations or other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses
that are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by
providing:
●​ Active outreach and engagement
●​ Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and
economic development projects


LaunchPad Collective, Inc. | 330 N. D Street, Ste. 526 | San Bernardino, CA 92401 |
www.launchpadcollective.org | robert@launchpadcollective.org | 909-521-8432


●​ Small farm and small business loans
●​ Home mortgage loans
●​ Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes
and support for Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
●​ Support for cultural, health and other programs
●​ Bank branches
●​ Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
●​ The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship
programs, and technical assistance support

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities
outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to
encourage banks to engage in CRA-related activity to directly benefit Tribes,
nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned
businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks
whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with Tribes, Tribally
controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work
with Tribes.

5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will
suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating
that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more
than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and
OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to
nonprofits entirely.



LaunchPad Collective, Inc. | 330 N. D Street, Ste. 526 | San Bernardino, CA 92401 |
www.launchpadcollective.org | robert@launchpadcollective.org | 909-521-8432


Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze the impact of such draconian
measures beyond acknowledging that community groups, including smaller groups,
may be affected.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They can also be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit, and
investment products into communities that tend to trust long-established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as down payment
assistance programs, that support CRA-related activity, rely on bank contributions
to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful bank contributions for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps
in their own capacity – seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job
training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can
attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and
focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can more easily meet their new
FDIC- and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even when nonprofits secure grants from Large Banks, the 15% overhead
restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. For example,
to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to pare down costs for
critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing, compliance,
technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower technical
assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions, organizations
are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the minuscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large


LaunchPad Collective, Inc. | 330 N. D Street, Ste. 526 | San Bernardino, CA 92401 |
www.launchpadcollective.org | robert@launchpadcollective.org | 909-521-8432


negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more leniency for banks.
Several provisions in the proposal will further weaken the link between CRA and LMI
impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, regulators must evaluate lending by banks,
subsidiaries, and affiliates. Further, certain products, such as small farm and
consumer loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a
bank's largest product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller
product lines from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how
they offer those products.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and builds greater
community trust in banks. Eliminating categories of loan products from scrutiny will
have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would remove the purpose test,
which has encouraged financing projects that create LMI jobs, from the definition of
economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for banks to
support the creation of jobs that pay family-sustaining wages for LMI workers and
in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide CRA credit for
job creation and economic development that may only benefit middle- and
upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the purpose of
CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large-scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Expanding what qualifies for CRA credit


LaunchPad Collective, Inc. | 330 N. D Street, Ste. 526 | San Bernardino, CA 92401 |
www.launchpadcollective.org | robert@launchpadcollective.org | 909-521-8432


can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities. For
example, banks might choose to earn CRA credit more profitably by financing
larger-scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, instead of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry-pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessment
areas,[15] where they face more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an exception
to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks are not currently
doing enough to meet credit and deposit needs in the areas where they have CRA
responsibility, a problem regulators tried to address in the 2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet
the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit for projects in areas away
from their branches, lending, and CRA responsibility. This will allow banks to get
credit for activity outside their assessment areas, with no accompanying CRA
obligation to better serve those areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, is a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can drive bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA credit


LaunchPad Collective, Inc. | 330 N. D Street, Ste. 526 | San Bernardino, CA 92401 |
www.launchpadcollective.org | robert@launchpadcollective.org | 909-521-8432


should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and operated by
mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI tenants, and
the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are compliant with
tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents can reasonably
be expected to retain their housing.

7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
rating downgrades.
The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what counts as evidence of discrimination for the purpose of
downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should consider any evidence
that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in discrimination, redlining, or
illegal credit practices in their lending, deposit, branching, or other activities.
Regulators should consider this evidence regardless of its source (public or private
parties) or its form (informal complaints, data-based research, testing results,
comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation, etc.). We also urge the
regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity Act authorizes Special
Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage banks to develop SPCPs to
better serve communities that have been redlined, excluded, and underserved. This
is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information
for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of entities
and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities the CRA was meant to
support. If finalized substantially in the same form as proposed, communities will
suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and CDFI support,
more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer community-serving
nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and redlining, with no
CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its purpose of
encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and the OCC to
reconsider this proposal.



LaunchPad Collective, Inc. | 330 N. D Street, Ste. 526 | San Bernardino, CA 92401 |
www.launchpadcollective.org | robert@launchpadcollective.org | 909-521-8432


Thank you for considering this request.

Very Truly Yours,


Robert Carrillo
Founder & President
LaunchPad Collective, Inc.

RE: Comments Regarding RIN 1557-AF57, RIN 3064-AG31

Chief Counsel, Deputy Executive Secretary Jones, and Leadership of the OCC and FDIC:
The Greater Ohio Policy Center (GOPC) is a nonpartisan, not-for-profit organization operating
statewide. We advance strong local economies and community revitalization across Ohio by
equipping communities and leaders with place-based research, collaboration, and advocacy.
Our vision is a revitalized Ohio.
Through our work, GOPC stewards several peer-learning networks that share information on
community revitalization and housing. These networks include leaders from Ohio's small legacy,
or postindustrial, cities; and leaders who finance, build, and champion housing for Ohio's low
and moderate income residents. GOPC also supports Ohio's community development financial
institutions, which provide needed lending to borrowers and projects that otherwise can not
access traditional financing.

Our vision of a revitalized Ohio compels us to share our concerns with the proposed Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules as outlines in RIN 1557-AF57 and RIN 3064-AG31.

(1) Limits on Reviewed Lenders. We are concerned that by reducing the number of lenders
who are subject to the most comprehensive aspects of the rule, this proposal will significantly
reduce the investment capacity of proven supply-side housing strategies. Communities
throughout Ohio utilize a number of investment tools, including the federal and state Low
Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC), state Single-Family Housing Tax Credit, and the Welcome
Home Ohio (WHO) program, to name just a few.

We are also concerned that faith-based housing providers, who are working to create and
advance homeownership opportunities, will access less equity and debt if CRA rules change.

Ultimately, in a state like Ohio where development costs exceed what the market can bear, debt
is hard to access and equity investments are often needed. The flexible and diversified
approach that financial institutions take to investing in community projects and housing remains
a cornerstone to community development financing.

 2 | P a g e

(2) Impediments to Critical Community Development and Housing Services. We believe
the proposed rules will impede critically needed housing and community development services,
such as self-sufficiency trainings to Ohioans in need. These services are largely delivered by
non-for-profits throughout Ohio; restrictions on grants and administrative fees will make it
financially difficult to cover the actual costs of those services.

Examples of housing and community development services that could be shuttered if the
proposal CRA rules are implemented include:

•
Technical assistance and education that improves the success and longevity of
entrepreneurs and small businesses
•
Financial Empowerment Centers, which teach Ohioans how to budget, financially plan
for the future, and prepare to be responsible homeowners
•
Preapproved housing plan catalogs that reduce permitting delays and construction
costs—a priority in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act
•
Risk tolerant lending to emerging housing types that can provide stable housing and
homeownership opportunities to Ohioans, including manufactured homes, Accessory
Dwelling Units, and "missing middle" housing

These initiatives have immense benefit to urban and rural communities throughout Ohio, and
they rely on expanded access to credit and the training and expertise needed to successfully
utilize credit. The implementation of the new proposed CRA rules risks these, and other needed,
initiatives.

Given the recent enactment of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, we believe it would be
prudent to delay action on these rules in order to ensure that they do not conflict with new
initiatives designed to strengthen access to affordable housing and incentivize place-based
work to address the national housing challenge.

GOPC respectfully requests that the proposed rules for the CRA program be suspended or
delayed for further consideration and engagement with the concerns we and others have raised.

Thank you for your consideration. We are happy to address these directly with you should you
have any questions.

With regards,

Alison Goebel
Executive Director
Greater Ohio Policy Center

community development evaluation, and 417 banks would move from the large-bank
framework to the less demanding intermediate-bank framework. Those institutions would
also no longer face separate investment and service tests. Yet community needs do not
diminish because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Across southeast Michigan,

accountability. For the residents MiWealth serves, access to a branch, an affordable
checking account, and a trusted banking relationship can determine whether they can
safely receive income, build savings, establish credit, and prepare for homeownership. Our
housing counselors and financial coaches routinely help clients address credit barriers and
connect with appropriate financial products.

in low- and moderate-income census tracts from the full large-bank service test. That

checking and savings products, fees, and accessibility would weaken incentives for banks to
address these persistent barriers.

services. Bank grants and partnerships help MiWealth provide housing counseling,
financial education, workforce services, and other supports that translate capital into
measurable results for residents. The proposed 15 percent cap on indirect costs and new
documentation requirements could push banks away from smaller organizations—even
when those organizations have the strongest community relationships and the clearest
understanding of local needs.
For MiWealth, operating capacity is inseparable from program delivery. Qualified
counselors, technology, compliance, outreach, data systems, and facilities are essential to
providing responsible, accessible services. The agencies should determine whether the
proposed cost limits and documentation requirements would reduce support for
community-based organizations—and, in turn, reduce resources available to low- and
moderate-income households.
CRA examinations and reporting should not obscure local lending gaps. Home
mortgage lending remains a critical need in the communities we serve. Although demand
for homeownership has increased across Metro Detroit, many prospective borrowers still


face barriers involving credit, affordability, down-payment resources, and access to
responsible mortgage products. The proposal presents two alternatives for concentrating
large-bank lending evaluations on designated major product lines. Under either approach,

that product is essential to the local community.

percent. Community organizations use these data to determine where credit is available,

narrowing examinations or reporting requirements, the agencies should analyze the
impact on local mortgage, small-business, small-farm, and community development
lending.

regulatory burden. The central question is whether the rule would strengthen or weaken
banks' responsibility to meet the credit needs of their entire communities. As written, the
proposal creates a substantial risk that low- and moderate-income communities would
receive less lending, fewer services, less investment, and less transparent information.

provide the public a meaningful opportunity to respond. At a minimum, any revised

Gutting the Community Reinvestment Act would mean fewer financing options for aspiring homeowners, nonprofits and small businesses. In a time where high prices and interest rates make buying a home or growing a business harder than ever, the OCC and FDIC efforts to end CRA are damaging to the communities we work in.

CRA was passed nearly 50 years ago to keep banks from discriminating against people on racial grounds through practices like redlining, when they used race to deny loans to residents of certain neighborhoods. As you know CRA compels banks to provide mortgages, small business loans, and maintain branches in previously redlined neighborhoods, and support other community services by financing affordable housing development and providing grants to nonprofits.

CRA obligations brought $85.5 billion in small business lending and mortgages to the Denver Metro Area in the last 15 years alone. Local nonprofits like Urban Land Conservancy, use these funds to buy and preserve a community assets, like the Mosaic Community Campus, build affordable housing, like the Irving at Mile High Vista, and renovate buildings like the Tramway Nonprofit Center, which houses more than a dozen nonprofits serving the community. Letting roughly 97% of banks off the hook for most of their CRA obligations, means fewer resources for nonprofits that are keeping people housed and fed, fewer financing options for small businesses, and dramatically less dollars getting spent in our communities.

Please don't gut CRA!

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Introduction

My name is Arisbett Adame I am currently an MPA student and work in local government specifically in housing development for affordable housing in the state of North Carolina. I am interested in this proposal because bank support plays an important role in developing and preserving affordable housing.
Background

I understand the need to make CRA rules easier for banks to follow, but these changes could reduce their support for affordable housing and nonprofits. My comments focus on which banks receive simpler evaluations, keeping incentives for both loans and investments, and limiting the administrative expenses allowed for certain nonprofit grants to count toward a bank’s CRA rating.

Analysis

Through my work in housing development, I have come to see the importance of partnerships between local governments, developers, nonprofits, and banks. Local governments have limited funding and cannot address housing needs alone. Bank loans and investments help housing projects move forward.

These changes would let more banks follow simpler requirements. I worry this could lead to less bank investment in affordable housing, especially in smaller communities. Developers could have trouble getting funding, which could delay projects or require more public money.

On most occasions affordable housing projects need both loans and investments. CRA rules should continue to encourage banks to provide both.

I am also concerned about limiting the administrative costs allowed for nonprofit grants to receive CRA credit. In my place of employment, we partner with many nonprofits, and I fear this change could affect them. Nonprofits need staff and technology to provide services and manage their funding. By placing a strict limit, this could discourage banks from supporting organizations that provide housing counseling and other services.

Recommendations

I ask the agencies to consider on how these changes could affect affordable housing funding. The CRA rules should continue encouraging banks to provide both loans and investments. The agencies should also reconsider the 15% limit on nonprofit grant expenses. The rules should continue focusing on the needs of low to moderate income families.

Conclusion

I support making CRA rules easier to follow, but they should still encourage banks to support affordable housing and nonprofit services.

To Whom It May Concern:

The Advocacy Alliance for Corporate Social Responsibility ("AACSR" or "the Alliance") submits these
comments on the joint notice of proposed rulemaking issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to amend their regulations implementing the
Community Reinvestment Act.

The Advocacy Alliance for Corporate Social Responsibility is a joint coalition of organizations serving
and led by California's minority communities. Our members collectively represent the voices of more
than one million Californians. The Alliance's core advocacy initiatives address corporate social
responsibility, economic and community development, environmental sustainability, and equitable
access to resources for underserved communities, which we pursue through public policy
engagement, community outreach and strategic partnerships.

This rulemaking sits at the center of two of those initiatives. In first place, the Community Reinvestment
Act is the principal federal mechanism directing private capital toward economic and community
development in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, and it substantially determines whether
the communities our members serve have equitable access to credit, to banking services, and to the
community-based organizations that deliver programming in those neighborhoods. When the CRA
framework changes, the consequences reach our members' communities directly.

These comments are submitted on behalf of the Alliance and its member organizations. They draw on
the collective experience of our membership. Where concrete illustration is useful, we describe the
experience of OASIS Center International, the Alliance's convening organization, whose
circumstances are representative of our membership generally.

OASIS Center International ("OASIS") submits these comments on the joint notice of proposed
rulemaking issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation to amend their regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act.
 2

OASIS is a community development organization established in 2012 and based in Santa Ana,
California. Through our Art Leads® program, we deliver arts education and youth development
programming to students in Title I schools across Orange, Los Angeles, Contra Costa and Fresno
Counties. In the 2024–2025 school year we served more than 4,500 students through thirty programs
at fourteen schools, in partnership with six public school systems: Santa Ana Unified School District,
Orange Unified School District, the Orange County Department of Education, Los Angeles Unified
School District, Fresno Unified School District, and the Contra Costa County Office of Education.

Our position throughout this letter follows a single principle. We support changes that reduce
compliance friction without reducing what reaches communities. We oppose changes that reduce what
reaches communities, whether they also reduce regulatory burden. We apply that principle
consistently below, including where it leads us to support the agencies' proposals.

I.
Community Development Grants

A. Grant provisions impose new compliance obligations rather than reducing them

Under the current rules, a bank that makes a grant to an organization with a community development
purpose receives consideration without any prescribed documentation process. Under the proposal,
a large bank would need to obtain from the recipient: (1) a written commitment to use the funds for
specific qualifying activities in the bank's assessment area; (2) a written attestation that the recipient's
indirect costs for administering the grant will not exceed 15%; and (3) supporting documentation for
both. 91 Fed. Reg. at 52129.

The proposed rules impose new regulatory obligations on banks and grant recipients, as both groups
would be required to collect, review and retain the documentation. They apply to every qualifying grant,
including small ones, and nothing in the proposal scales the requirement to the size of the grant.

We do not think banks will respond to this by making better grants. We think a substantial number will
respond by making fewer of them. Community development grants are a modest component of a large
bank's CRA performance relative to lending and investment, and a compliance process attached to a
low-weight activity is the kind of cost an institution eliminates rather than absorbs. The result would be
no improvement in how funds reach communities and the loss of the funding stream altogether.

B. The 15% cap misapplies the federal standard the agencies identify as its source

In the discussion preceding Question 9, the agencies request comment on whether the indirect cost
rate from the Uniform Guidance for Federal Awards would be an appropriate standard for is evaluating
a grant recipient's indirect costs. 91 Fed. Reg. at 52129. From our perspective, the Uniform Guidance
is an appropriate reference, but the proposal uses the wrong figure from it.

Under 2 C.F.R. § 200.414(f), 15% is the de minimis indirect cost rate, the floor that an entity without a
federally negotiated rate may charge without documentation or negotiation. Them, it is not a limit. An
entity with a federally negotiated indirect cost rate applies that rate, and negotiated rates are commonly
and legitimately higher. The Uniform Guidance treats 15% as the minimum an organization may
recover in the absence of anything more specific.

We therefore request, that the final rule align the treatment of indirect costs with federally negotiated
rates under the Uniform Guidance. An organization with a negotiated rate should be permitted to apply
it. An organization without one should be permitted the de minimis rate. In the alternative, we ask that
15% be treated as a safe harbor, rather than as a cap.

This request is consistent with the agencies stated objective. A standard that tracks the federal
government's own framework is easier for banks to apply, easier for examiners to review, and
 3
defensible on its face. A threshold with no counterpart in any other federal program is none of those
things.

C. The proposal is ambiguous as to whether the cap applies to the grant or to the organization

In its text, the proposal does not make clear whether the 15% limit applies to the indirect costs charged
to the grant or to the recipient organization's overall indirect cost structure. The language refers to "a
recipient whose indirect costs for administering the grant or donation" do not exceed 15%, which reads
as organization-level. The illustrative example in the preamble describes a grant of which
"approximately 25%... was reported to be used for the organization's internal expenses," 91 Fed. Reg.
at 52119, which reads as grant-level. The attestation the recipient must provide is framed grant-by-
grant.

The difference is substantial for both banks and recipients. A grant-level test permits an organization
to allocate indirect costs across funding sources and accept a bank grant at a lower rate. An
organization-level test disqualifies the organization entirely, regardless of how the grant is structured.
Banks cannot design a compliant grant program without knowing which test applies, and recipients
cannot tell whether they are eligible.

D. Question 10: the agencies should not eliminate grants from CRA consideration

Question 10 asks: "As an alternative, should the agencies eliminate all grants and donations from CRA
consideration?" 91 Fed. Reg. at 52129. We urge the agencies not to adopt that alternative.

We acknowledge at the outset that eliminating the category would reduce regulatory burden, and that
this is the one place in this letter where we ask the agencies to accept burden rather than remove it.

On our perspective, three considerations support retaining grant consideration. The first is consistency
with the agencies' own stated objective. The proposal's purpose, as described throughout the
preamble, is to ensure that community development grants reach the communities they are intended
to benefit. Eliminating the category does not accomplish that objective. A final rule that adopts a means
directly opposed to the end the agency identified would be difficult to sustain as reasoned decision-
making.

The second is the length and consistency of the contrary practice. The agencies acknowledge that
consideration of community development activities has been a component of their CRA rules since
those rules were first promulgated in 1978. 91 Fed. Reg. at 52127. Nothing in the statute requires the
elimination of grant consideration, and nothing in the Texas Bankers litigation addresses it. Reversing
nearly fifty years of continuous practice based on a question posed in the alternative would not give
the public the notice that reasoned rulemaking requires.

The third is effect. Grants are the only CRA channel that reaches organizations of our kind. A
community development loan requires a borrower with debt capacity and a repayment source. A
structured investment requires an entity that can issue one. A youth arts organization operating in Title
I schools has neither. If grants are removed from CRA consideration, the practical consequence is not
that banks support our work through a different instrument.

II.
The Community Development Definition and the Illustrative List

The proposal would organize the community development definition around four components:
(i) affordable housing; (ii) civic assistance for low- and moderate-income individuals; (iii) economic
development; and (iv) revitalization and stabilization of targeted areas. The category presently
described as community services targeted to low- and moderate-income individuals appears as civic
assistance.

 4
We read this as a change in nomenclature rather than scope. The low- and moderate-income qualifier
is retained in the category name, and the agencies describe the change as clarifying the components
of a principles-based definition. We ask that the final rule confirm that reading expressly, and confirm
that educational, youth development and cultural services targeted to low- and moderate-income
individuals remain within the category.
The proposal would codify a public, non-exhaustive illustrative list of activities that do and do not qualify
for community development consideration, together with a process by which a bank may seek advance
confirmation that an activity qualifies. We support both measures. They are the clearest example in
this rulemaking of a change that reduces compliance uncertainty without reducing what reaches
communities.

Thus, we suggest that educational, youth development and arts-integrated programming serving low-
and moderate-income young people be named among the qualifying examples on that list. Inclusion
on the list costs the agencies nothing and resolves a question that banks currently answer
conservatively. It is worth more to organizations like ours than any amount of favorable language in
the preamble.

III.
Data Collection and Reporting

As it is, the proposal would limit data collection, maintenance and reporting requirements to banks
with more than $10 billion in assets. 91 Fed. Reg. at 52120. We oppose this change, and we do so
from a perspective that is not primarily about grants.

OASIS participates in the public comment process on bank merger applications. That work depends
on public CRA data. A comment asserting that an institution has underserved a particular community
carries weight only if it can be substantiated, and substantiation comes from small business lending
data, community development lending data, and assessment area reporting. Without those data, a
commenter can assert a lending gap but cannot demonstrate one, and an agency has no obligation
to credit an assertion it cannot verify.

The effect on peer benchmarking is equally significant and cuts in favor of banks as well as
communities. A bank that wishes to understand whether its own performance is adequate compares
itself to peers. Removing most reporting institutions from the data set removes the basis for that
comparison. Institutions that remain subject to reporting would be benchmarked against a shrinking
and unrepresentative sample, and examiners would have correspondingly less context for judging
whether performance in each market is strong or weak.

IV.
Retail Banking Services

The proposal would amend the retail banking services criterion to consider only "the range of credit
services" provided across low-, moderate-, middle- and upper-income geographies, excluding deposit
services from the evaluation. 91 Fed. Reg. at 52126. The change would supersede the Interagency
Questions and Answers to the extent they treat deposit products as part of that evaluation.

In this context, the families of our students are disproportionately unbanked and underbanked. For a
household in that position, the threshold question is not the availability of credit but whether a deposit
account can be opened and maintained at a cost the household can bear. Minimum balance
requirements, monthly maintenance fees and overdraft terms determine whether a family enters the
banking system at all. Credit access follows from that relationship; it does not precede it. An evaluation
that examines credit services while disregarding whether a bank offers an affordable transaction
account measures the second step and not the first.

We note that the statute itself does not compel the narrower reading. Congress found, in the findings
codified at 12 U.S.C. § 2901(a), that "the convenience and needs of communities include the need for
credit services as well as deposit services." The agencies quote this finding in the preamble. 91 Fed.
 5
Reg. at 52115. We recognize that the operative assessment provision speaks of credit needs, and we
do not suggest the agencies lack discretion here. We suggest that the discretion runs in both
directions, and that the findings support retaining deposit products in the evaluation.

On the other hand, the proposal retains the branch distribution criterion, and we support that. But
raising the large bank threshold to $10 billion would remove the service test entirely for the great
majority of banks now subject to it, and with it the evaluation of branch distribution and the record of
opening and closing branches. For a community like Santa Ana, the presence or absence of a physical
branch is not a secondary consideration. It's determinative of whether residents transact with a bank
or with a check casher.

V.
Affordable Housing

Affordable housing is retained as a component of the community development definition, and the
agencies describe the treatment of that component as a clarification. The significant effect of this
proposal on affordable housing does not come from the definition. It comes from the thresholds.

Raising the large bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion would remove the investment test
obligation from most institutions that carry it today. Using the agencies' own figures, approximately
3,577 banks with CRA obligations are supervised by the OCC and FDIC; of these, 2,040 are small
banks that are not intermediate small banks and 1,060 are intermediate small banks, leaving
approximately 477 institutions presently evaluated as large banks. Under the proposal, 86 institutions
would be large banks. 91 Fed. Reg. at 52120–52122.

The investment test is the principal regulatory driver of bank equity investment in Low-Income Housing
Tax Credit transactions. Bank equity is the mechanism by which the LIHTC program converts federal
tax credits into housing. Removing the investment test obligation from roughly four-fifths of the
institutions now subject to it removes the regulatory reason for a significant share of that equity
participation. Affordable housing developers and syndicators have identified reduced LIHTC equity as
their principal concern with this proposal, and we share it.

We ask that the final rule preserve an affordable housing investment obligation for institutions in the
range between the current and proposed large bank thresholds, whether through the investment test,
through a community development test applicable to intermediate banks, or through another
mechanism the agencies identify.

We separately support the revision to the community development loan definition permitting a
multifamily dwelling loan or a low-cost education loan to receive consideration as both a retail loan
and a community development loan. 91 Fed. Reg. at 52127–28. This codifies a treatment that
presently exists in guidance, reduces uncertainty, and does not diminish what reaches communities.

VI.
Removal of the Appendix A Rating Factors

The agencies propose to remove from Appendix A the factors requiring specific consideration of a
bank's record of serving the credit needs of highly economically disadvantaged areas and of low-
income individuals, reasoning that "highly disadvantaged areas" is not a defined term and that the
considerations are captured by the borrower and geographic distribution criteria. 91 Fed. Reg. at
52127.

We ask the agencies to reconsider, and we think the reasoning does not support the result in either
instance. That a term is undefined is a reason to define it. The agencies are engaged in a rulemaking
and could supply a definition. Removing the factor because the term lacks one resolves the ambiguity
by eliminating the obligation rather than by clarifying it. The rationale for removal provided by the
agencies also fails to acknowledge or address the original purpose behind promulgating such a
provision.
 6

The reasoning has a further difficulty as applied to the low-income factor. "Low-income" is a defined
term in the rule. And the borrower distribution criteria that are said to capture the consideration
aggregate low- and moderate-income categories. Removing a factor directed specifically at low-
income individuals therefore permits adequate performance with moderate-income borrowers to offset
the absence of performance with low-income borrowers, within a single aggregated measure that
shows neither.

VII.
Small Business and Economic Development

We support an increase in the gross annual revenue threshold defining a small business for CRA
purposes, from $1 million to $5 million, subject to the condition described below. The $5 million figure
is the definition the agencies themselves adopted in the 2023 final rules. The preliminary injunction
ordered in Texas Bankers Association v. OCC rested on the interpretation of "entire community," the
required nexus between a bank's community and its physical locations, and the Major Questions
Doctrine. Tex. Bankers Ass'n v. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, 728 F. Supp. 3d 412, 416
(N.D. Tex. 2024). It did not address the small business revenue threshold. The agencies retain
authority to adopt it.

We note for the record that the present $1 million criterion dates to the 1995 rules rather than to the
statute's enactment in 1977. It has been in place for approximately thirty years, not fifty. Even on the
shorter figure, it has not been adjusted for inflation across a period in which the nominal revenue of
an unchanged business has roughly doubled, and it now captures a materially smaller set of
enterprises than it did when adopted.

VIII.
Asset Size Thresholds

We do not object to the baseline adjustment of the asset size thresholds. The current figures were set
against a banking industry that has since consolidated substantially, and the agencies are right that
the distribution of institutions across evaluation categories has drifted from what the 1995 framework
contemplated. Adjusting the thresholds is legitimate, and we say so notwithstanding that the
adjustment produces consequences we oppose elsewhere in this letter. Our objection is to the
magnitude of the alternative the agencies describe, not to the concept.

We do object to the alternative described in Question 1, which would raise the intermediate bank
threshold to $30 billion and, correspondingly, the small bank threshold to $10 billion. 91 Fed. Reg. at
52122–23.

Under that alternative, the number of institutions subject to the full large bank evaluation would fall to
a figure that bears no relationship to where banking activity occurs. Regional banks with tens of billions
of dollars in assets, substantial branch networks and meaningful market share in California
communities would be evaluated under standards designed for institutions a fraction of their size.
Banks with $10 billion in assets would be treated as small banks and evaluated under the streamlined
lending test alone. A threshold set at that level would leave the CRA with no meaningful evaluative
application to regional banking. We ask that the agencies not adopt it.

We would welcome the opportunity to provide additional information about the effect of this proposal
on community development funding in Orange County and Southern California, and we are available
to the agencies' staff at their convenience.

A few years ago, many federal agencies, financial institutions and community organizations worked together to improve the CRA.   Unfortunately, that work was rescinded and the new better CRA was not put into law.   Now we have a new CRA proposal that would put many communities at risk of losing substantial financial assistance, bank services, and support for nonprofit organizations.  We have worked for years to build strong relationships with our local banks and the CRA is what brought them to the table.  I admit that good business keeps them there, but as banks change and people change, we still need to have the CRA has an incentive.  It has helped us find first mortgages for our families, helped us keep families away from predatory lending, bought our Section 42 tax credits so we could develop affordable rental housing, and made banking accounts available for those who have struggled in the past or simply do not have enough funds to maintain a large checking balance.   We have used banks to help us teach financial education and introduced our banks to people who thought conventional banking was not for them.  The CRA act has brought good business to the banks and has helped countless communities thrive, whom otherwise would have been left behind.   We need to strengthen the CRA, not make it more lenient.   This new proposed act would substantially decrease the number of banks that are required to help their communities by significantly increasing the asset thresholds that determine how most banks are analyzed for CRA compliance.  It would also significantly reduce bank demand for qualified investments and reduce transparency of how banks serve small business, farms and low-to-moderate income families.  As a small organization, we are also concerned about the 15% indirect costs proposed for organizations receiving a grant.  Many smaller organizations may not be able to meet that threshold and banks may find it easier to just donate to large national organizations, again leaving our small communities behind.

A fundamental aspect of CRA is that it has, for decades, created motivation and incentive for financial

Community Development Partnership submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC)
and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the
changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze
the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on
the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment
deadline by 60-days.
The Community Development Partnership's Vision is a strong and diverse year-round population for the
Lower and Outer Cape Cod, MA that can afford to live, work, and thrive here. Our Mission is to create a
thriving year-round community on the Lower and Outer Cape through accessible and stable housing, and
economic opportunity through bold systemic change.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks
meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These
protections remain especially important in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment,
branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. We are
concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on
low- and moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination
and disinvestment.
We are particularly troubled by the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit
organizations.
Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling, workforce
programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through grants, investments,
loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These resources can be particularly important to local
organizations that have deep relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their
communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new
documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.2 For smaller
nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting,
compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself.
Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In
addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial
records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA
eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document,
they may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can play in
supporting community development. Our small business programming is partially funded through our local
banks. Many of them use the CRA to fund us. If we were to lose this funding, it would be challenging to fill
those gaps.

benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community development activities receive
CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond the banks themselves.

smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with limited administrative capacity. The agencies must

income communities.
More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of reducing perceived
regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine what the changes mean for the
communities CRA is intended to serve.

identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under the
proposal;

quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development
