Agency Name: FDIC; RIN 3064-AG31

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Pathward, N.A. ("Pathward") appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
("FDIC") (collectively, the "Agencies")' proposed amendments to their regulations
implementing the Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA").
Pathward is a national bank headquartered in Sioux Falls, South Dakota. Unlike a
traditional branch-based institution, Pathward provides banking and lending products
through specialized business lines and third-party relationships. Its deposits, lending
activities, and community-development opportunities therefore are not concentrated in
the same geographic markets. The strategic plan framework gives Pathward a practical way
to translate that business model into concrete, measurable CRA commitments. Pathward's
current plan does so through goals for community-development investments and loans,
donations, and service hours in Sioux Falls, together with substantial regional community-
development investment and lending.
Pathward also has a substantial record of community-development activity. In fiscal year
2025, Pathward invested $7.4 million in community development in its CRA assessment
area, financed $203.3 million in Small Business Administration loans, made $180,000 in
direct contributions to nonprofit community partners advancing financial inclusion, and its
employees contributed more than 900 volunteer hours to community-development and
financial education activities.
Pathward supports the Agencies' effort to reduce unnecessary burden and improve the fit
of the CRA framework for banks with different business models. Based on its experience
operating under an OCC-approved strategic plan, Pathward offers the following
recommendations.
 2

I. Strategic Plans Should Permit Measurable Community-Development Goals Outside
a Bank's Assessment Area (Responds to Question 43)
Pathward strongly supports preserving the ability of a bank operating under an approved
strategic plan to establish measurable goals for community-development activity outside
its assessment area.
Pathward's only CRA assessment area is the Sioux Falls metropolitan statistical area.
Because Pathward has no traditional branches or deposit-taking ATMs, its assessment area
is based on the location of its main office. At the same time, Pathward's branchless
business model and the limited number of qualifying community-development
opportunities in Sioux Falls make it impractical to confine all meaningful community-
development activity to that market.
Pathward's current strategic plan combines measurable goals in Sioux Falls with
substantial community-development lending and investment throughout a seven-state
Broader Statewide or Regional Area. In its proposed 2027–2031 strategic plan, Pathward
has sought to continue that structure with significant annual regional investment and
lending goals outside the Sioux Falls assessment area.
The Agencies specifically request comment on whether strategic plans should permit
measurable goals for community-development activity outside a bank's assessment area
and whether such goals should be limited to the Outstanding level. Pathward recommends
that the final rule expressly permit such goals at both the Satisfactory and Outstanding
levels. Limiting measurable community-development goals outside assessment areas to
the Outstanding level could discourage banks from making broader community-
development commitments and would not fully reflect the CRA's purpose of encouraging
banks to help meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods.
Limiting outside-assessment-area goals to the Outstanding level would create uncertainty
about how substantial commitments outside the assessment area will be treated. A
strategic plan should be able to state clearly, in advance and subject to public comment
and agency approval, how both Satisfactory and Outstanding performance will be
measured.
This approach would preserve strong expectations within a bank's assessment area while
allowing the strategic plan framework to account for institutions whose business models
and community-development opportunities do not fit neatly within a single local market.
II. The Agencies Should Adopt a $30 Billion Intermediate Bank Threshold and Index It
Prospectively for Inflation (Responds principally to Question 1)
 3

Pathward supports the Agencies' proposal to raise the asset threshold separating
intermediate banks from large banks. Pathward recommends that the Agencies adopt the
$30 billion threshold identified in Question 1 of the proposal rather than the proposed $10
billion threshold, and adjust that threshold prospectively for inflation.
The Agencies themselves have recently used $30 billion to distinguish community banks
from larger institutions. The OCC's 2026 community-bank licensing rule applies
streamlined procedures to qualifying institutions with less than $30 billion in assets, and
the FDIC has similarly increased from $10 billion to $30 billion the asset threshold used for
presumptive inclusion in its continuous examination process. The proposal accordingly
asks whether $30 billion should also serve as the upper bound for intermediate banks
under the CRA.
By contrast, among the Agencies' stated reasons for selecting $10 billion is Congress's use
of that amount in other federal banking statutes. The proposal cites several provisions
enacted through the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act,
including the $10 billion small-issuer threshold established by the Durbin Amendment. The
repeated use of a nominal threshold enacted more than 15 years ago does not establish
that the same amount remains an appropriate dividing line for CRA purposes today, nor
does reuse of the nominal figure preserve the economic significance of the original
threshold. Adjusted for inflation, $10 billion in 2010 is approximately $15 billion today. A
$10 billion threshold adopted in 2026 therefore would be roughly one-third lower in real
terms than the threshold Congress selected in 2010.
The banking system has changed substantially as well. FDIC-insured institutions held
approximately $13.3 trillion in assets at year-end 2010; by the first quarter of 2026, that
figure had risen to approximately $26.3 trillion, while the number of insured institutions
declined significantly. A $10 billion institution therefore represents a materially smaller
share of the banking system today than it did in 2010. Applying the same nominal threshold
today would extend the large-bank framework to institutions that are relatively smaller than
the $10 billion benchmark captured when it was first adopted.
The proposal itself recognizes the need to account for these changes. Existing CRA asset
thresholds have been adjusted annually for inflation, and the Agencies cite growth and
consolidation in the banking industry in support of increasing the current thresholds. Yet
the proposal would leave the new intermediate-bank ceiling fixed at $10 billion in part
because other statutes and regulations using that amount are themselves fixed. That
rationale would perpetuate the erosion of the threshold rather than address it.
 4

The Agencies should instead calibrate the CRA threshold to the current structure of the
banking industry and to the scale and complexity that warrant application of the large-bank
framework. The $30 billion threshold identified in Question 1—and already employed by
the OCC and FDIC in other community-bank contexts—provides a current, administrable
benchmark. Pathward therefore recommends that the Agencies define an intermediate
bank as a bank with assets of $30 billion or less and a large bank as a bank with assets
greater than $30 billion. Pathward also does not believe the alternative $3.252 billion
threshold discussed in the proposal would provide an appropriate dividing line between
intermediate and large banks. At that level, institutions such as Pathward would be treated
as large banks despite operating at a materially different scale from the institutions
traditionally subject to the large bank CRA framework.
Pathward further recommends that the $30 billion threshold be adjusted prospectively for
inflation. A bank should become subject to the large-bank CRA framework because its
growth reflects a meaningful change in scale or complexity, not because a fixed nominal
threshold becomes progressively smaller in real terms. The existing CRA framework already
applies that principle to other asset thresholds, and the Agencies should do the same here.
The Agencies should also provide an appropriate transition period for banks that cross the
intermediate-bank threshold, recognizing the time needed to adjust data collection,
reporting, examination preparation, and other CRA processes associated with large-bank
status. A reasonable transition period would help avoid disruption to ongoing CRA
programs and strategic plan commitments.
III. Community-Development Grant Rules Should Preserve Legitimate Operating and
Capacity Building Support (Responds to Questions 9 and 10)
Pathward supports the Agencies' objective of ensuring that grants receiving CRA
consideration have a genuine community-development purpose. At the same time,
Pathward's experience with nonprofit partners demonstrates why banks need reasonable
flexibility in how that support is structured and used.
In 2025, for example, a fire caused extensive damage to the warehouse of the Furniture
Bank of Metro Atlanta, a Pathward community partner. Pathward authorized the
organization to reallocate existing grant funds to address its most urgent recovery needs.
Those funds helped the organization hire two graduates of its workforce program, purchase
beds for families in need, and resume deliveries within one week of the fire. The
organization later cited that flexibility as an important part of Pathward's support.
Although this particular grant was not treated as CRA-qualified because the recipient was
outside Pathward's assessment area and designated regional area, the experience
 5

illustrates why flexibility in the use of grant funds can help community organizations
respond quickly to urgent needs. Pathward's broader Community Impact Program reflects
the same approach: in fiscal year 2025, Pathward made $1.2 million in charitable
investments to nonprofit community partners, while employees contributed nearly 5,000
volunteer hours across more than 180 organizations.
The proposed rule would require a community-development grant to be directly used for a
program, project, or initiative having a primary purpose of community development. For
large banks, the proposal would also impose a 15 percent cap on recipient indirect costs,
calculated under the OMB Uniform Guidance, and require documentation including the
recipient's IRS Form 990 and operating and program budgets. The Agencies acknowledge
that this standard could reduce CRA incentives for general operating support, capacity-
building grants, and grants made through intermediaries.
Pathward agrees that grants receiving CRA consideration should have a clear community-
development nexus. But the final rule should not exclude general operating or capacity-
building support where a bank can reasonably document that the recipient has a qualifying
community-development mission and that the funds support qualifying activities. In many
cases, the ability to use grant funds flexibly is what allows nonprofit organizations to
respond quickly to changing conditions, sustain programs, and continue serving low- and
moderate-income individuals and communities. Many small and community-based
nonprofits, particularly those serving hard-to-reach populations, may have indirect-cost
ratios that reflect the realities of small-scale operations rather than inefficiency. A rigid 15
percent cap could therefore make it more difficult for banks to support some of these
organizations.
The final rule should preserve that flexibility while maintaining appropriate documentation
and accountability.
IV. Pathward Supports the Proposed Treatment of Employee Expertise as a
Community-Development Service (Responds to the proposed clarification of
community-development services)
Pathward supports the proposal's clarification that a community-development service may
include volunteer activity related either to financial services or to an employee's area of
professional expertise.
That clarification reflects the way Pathward employees already serve their communities.
Pathward's employees do more than contribute their time; they bring the skills, experience,
and judgment developed in their professional roles to organizations working directly with
individuals and families in need.
 6

In fiscal year 2025, for example, Pathward employees developed and delivered a
customized financial-literacy curriculum for students, whose average assessment scores
increased from 60% to 100%. Employees later expanded that work through a partnership
with the Veterans Community Project in Sioux Falls, designing and facilitating a four-week
financial-literacy series for houseless veterans focused on personal finance fundamentals
and debt management.
That commitment extends well beyond financial education. Pathward's 2025 Volunteer of
the Year contributed approximately 400 hours across 18 organizations and 24 volunteer
events, supporting causes ranging from housing and food insecurity to education and
veterans' services. That work included board service and skills-based support, and reflects
the initiative Pathward employees take in identifying needs and finding ways to put their
experience to work on behalf of their communities.
Pathward encourages that engagement by providing paid volunteer time and supporting
both individual and team-based service opportunities. The proposed clarification
appropriately recognizes what Pathward has seen in practice: community-development
service is often most valuable when employees are able to contribute not only their time,
but also the expertise and capabilities they have developed through their work.
Pathward therefore recommends that the Agencies retain this clarification in the final rule.
V. The OCC Should Expressly Preserve Every OCC-Approved Strategic Plan that is in
Effect on the Final Rule's Applicability Date through the Plan's Stated Expiration Date
(Addresses transition provisions for existing strategic plans)

Pathward has submitted a proposed CRA strategic plan for the period 2027 through 2031
that, if approved, will be in effect prior to the applicability date of the new CRA rule. To
ensure regulatory continuity and honor the commitments already undertaken through the
public participation and agency approval process, the final rule should expressly provide
that any OCC-approved strategic plan in effect on the rule's applicability date will remain in
effect through the plan's stated expiration date.

An existing strategic plan represents the agency's prior determination that specified
measurable goals adequately serve that objective for the bank and its communities. This
treatment is consistent with the OCC's own precedent: the 2021 transition rule and the
Agencies' 2023 CRA transition provisions both preserved approved strategic plans through
expiration subject to limited exceptions. Grandfathering would not exempt any bank from a
CRA examination or guarantee any rating. Each bank would remain accountable for the
 7

measurable goals in its approved plan. Because existing plans are time-limited, successor
plans would be governed entirely by the new rule.

Requiring an already approved plan to be rebuilt, republished, and reapproved before
expiration would impose additional process-related burden and could disrupt the planning
of banks, communities, and nonprofit partners that have organized their activities around
the plan's commitments.
Pathward's Recommendations
Pathward supports a CRA framework that maintains meaningful community-reinvestment
obligations while recognizing differences in bank business models, geographic footprints,
and available community-development opportunities.
For the reasons discussed above, Pathward recommends that the Agencies: preserve the
ability of strategic plan banks to establish measurable community-development goals
outside their assessment areas at both Satisfactory and Outstanding levels; adopt a $30
billion intermediate-bank threshold, index that threshold prospectively for inflation, and
provide an appropriate transition period for banks that cross the threshold; preserve CRA
consideration for qualifying operating and capacity-building grants without imposing overly
rigid indirect-cost limitations; retain the proposed recognition of employee professional
expertise in community-development services; and preserve OCC-approved strategic
plans that are in effect on the final rule's applicability date through each plan's stated
expiration date.
Taken together, these changes would preserve meaningful CRA standards while better
aligning the regulatory framework with the scale, structure, and business models of the
institutions subject to it.
Pathward appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposal and to share its
experience operating under the CRA strategic plan framework.
Sincerely,


Brett Pharr
CEO
Pathward, N.A.

Proposed changes to CRA, taken together, could significantly reduce community development activity and the lending, investment, grants, and other critical resources available for low- and moderate-income communities. Dramatic drops in CRA-motivated community development activity would hurt local economies and businesses, exacerbate the affordable housing shortage, reduce local jobs, and weaken affordability for households, especially in rural communities and smaller markets, at a time when our country is focused on those very priorities. The scale of CRA’s impact is significant. In 2024 alone, CRA incentivized more than $430 billion in loans and investments in low- and moderate-income communities, nearly six times the combined federal budgets of HUD, USDA’s Rural Housing Service, the Small Business Administration, and the CDFI Fund. For nearly 50 years, CRA has helped bring private capital into communities and strengthen partnerships between banks and the organizations that serve them. Through these partnerships, banks have financed affordable housing and homeownership, small businesses, community facilities, health care, childcare, economic development, and other essential community needs. At a time when communities face significant affordable housing shortages, rising costs, and constrained public resources, the CRA framework should continue to support and strengthen these partners.

I urge you to ensure that the final rule does the following:
I. Maintain meaningful community development responsibilities for banks of all sizes. Raising the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA would significantly reduce the number of institutions subject to community development expectations. 
II. Preserve strong expectations for community development lending and investment. Communities need different types of capital to meet different needs.
Loans are critical, but they are not interchangeable with investments. Equity investments and other forms of capital support affordable housing through the Low- Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit), economic development through the New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC), CDFIs, and other activities that often cannot be supported through conventional lending alone. Proposed changes to the evaluation framework, including how community development performance contributes to a bank's overall CRA rating, could reduce the relative importance of community development investments. The final rule should
III. Protect grants and other support for nonprofit and community-based organizations. Across the country, families, older adults, veterans, and small businesses are served by nonprofit and community-based organizations that rely on grants to operate. CRA-qualifying grants support housing counseling, financial education, small business assistance, food access, health and human services, and other essential activities.
Operating support and capacity building through grants are critical for nonprofit organizations that are a lifeline to hard-to-serve communities and that take on difficult to develop projects. These organizations are also important local employers. Nonprofits employ 12.8 million workers nationwide, accounting for nearly 10 percent of all private-sector jobs.3 Reducing support for these organizations could affect both the services communities rely on and local jobs.
IV. Keep low- and moderate-income people and communities at the center of CRA as intended by statute. CRA was enacted to address persistent gaps in access to credit and investment. Low- and moderate-income communities represent a significant share of the country, with more than one in four Americans living in a low- or moderate-income census tract. The need for affordable housing, access to small business financing, and support for other economic and community development remains most acute for low- and moderate-income families and communities.
Expanding CRA’s focus to increasingly broader populations or a wide array of new activities could unintentionally shift critical private capital away from low- and moderate-income households and leave underserved communities behind. Taken together, changes to income targeting, community development definitions, evaluation standards, and other provisions could significantly shift where CRA-motivated capital flows and reduce the focus on low- and moderate-income communities, resulting in less affordable housing supply, fewer jobs for low- and moderate-income workers, and reduced access to vital community resources. The final rule should preserve a clear and meaningful focus on the low-and moderate-income households and communities CRA was intended to serve.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
The St. Louis Equal Housing and Community Reinvestment Alliance (SLEHCRA) submits
this comment to express our concern that the proposed changes to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) could reduce incentives for banks to maintain and expand
meaningful banking services in low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.
SLEHCRA is a St. Louis regional coalition that has worked since 2009 to increase
investment in LMI communities and communities of color by ensuring that banks meet their
obligations under the CRA and fair lending laws. Our members have worked directly with
financial institutions and regulators to expand access to branches, responsible lending,
financial products, and community development investment.
One of our most significant concerns is the potential effect of the proposed rule on bank
branches serving LMI communities. Over the years our collaboration with banks has led to
19 bank branches in LMI communities that otherwise would not have them. We are
concerned that communities in the St. Louis region, could be at risk of reduced support,
relocation, closure, or reduced community-service expectations if the proposed changes
weaken CRA scrutiny and incentives. These branches are more than physical locations. For
many residents, they provide access to deposits, personal assistance, financial education,
small-business relationships, and other services that cannot always be replaced by online
banking.
SLEHCRA has seen firsthand the value of CRA incentives in encouraging banks to
establish and maintain branches in underserved communities. In addition to new bank
branches, our coalition's work has contributed to community benefits agreements that
 included commitments to establish new service locations in partnership with nonprofits and
maintain existing branches in LMI and minority communities. These experiences
demonstrate that meaningful CRA expectations can translate into tangible improvements in
financial access.
We are concerned that raising the asset thresholds for CRA examinations and reducing
data collection and community-development scrutiny could make it more difficult for
regulators and community organizations to identify when banking access is being reduced
in neighborhoods that need it most. The proposed changes should not unintentionally create
an environment in which banks can reduce their physical presence or community services
without meaningful consideration of the impact on LMI residents.
From SLEHCRA's experience, the size of a financial institution does not necessarily
determine the importance of that institution to a particular community. A bank with a smaller
asset base may have a significant presence in a particular metropolitan area, neighborhood,
or underserved community.
SLEHCRA's experience demonstrates why community-level information matters. The
coalition examines individual banks' assessment areas, lending patterns, branch locations,
and other activities to understand whether communities are being adequately served.
SLEHCRA therefore urges the OCC and FDIC to carefully evaluate the potential impact of
the proposed rule on existing branches in LMI communities, including the 19 St. Louis-area
branches we have identified as potentially vulnerable. The agencies should examine branch
openings and closures, changes in branch hours and services, and whether affected
communities have reasonable access to alternative banking services.
We also urge the agencies to preserve meaningful community input in CRA examinations.
Community organizations such as SLEHCRA have direct knowledge of neighborhood
conditions and can identify changes in banking access that may not be apparent from
aggregate data alone.
The CRA was created to ensure that banks serve the credit and financial-service needs of
the communities in which they do business. Any regulatory changes should strengthen—not
weaken—that connection. SLEHCRA respectfully asks the agencies to reconsider
provisions that could reduce accountability for banking access in LMI communities and to
conduct a thorough analysis of the potential effects on branch access before finalizing the
rule. As an NCRC member, we support their comments and efforts to protect LMI and
communities of color through maintaining a strong CRA.
Thank you for considering SLEHCRA's concerns and our experience working in the St.
Louis region, and other areas including Kansas City, East St. Louis IL, and other LMI
communities throughout Missouri.
Sincerely,
Jackie Hutchinson, Co-Chair & Rose Eichelberger, Co-Chairs
St. Louis Equal Housing and Community Reinvestment Alliance (SLEHCRA)

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN
1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Tacony Together submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and
the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of
the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes,
carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide
an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any
changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.
Tacony Together is a Community Development Corporation providing small business,
residential, and community engagement services in the Tacony neighborhood in Northeast
Philadelphia. Our organization serves over 300 small business owners and a population of
23,000+ residents - all of whom are considered either low- or moderate- income. The community
we work with has been historically underserved by traditional financial services, and continues to
face considerable difficulties accessing credit needs. Our organization works directly with small

business owners and residents to build loan and grant applications and to offset our constituents'
financial difficulties.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access
to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in
communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to
mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia
metro area, from 2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to
LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small
businesses. Investments such as these benefited our community by allowing microenterprises to
access necessary funding for things like emergency repairs, moving into brick-and-mortar
locations, and scaling up their businesses. With the success of small business comes the success
of community, and by providing our small business owners with access to capital these
investments brought more buying power into the neighborhood as a whole; increased perceptions
of safety; and encouraged active participation in community services and events.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a
passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote
to community investments and loans and we fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling
instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually, but
under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million – an 80% loss.
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If
regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the
communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example, in

our community, small business owners and residents who are already struggling to access the
financial capital needed to acquire property will face even more barriers. When the people living
and working in a community are unable to purchase homes and commercial properties, those real
estate opportunities go to property management companies, corporations, and outside investors
who do not have the same community buy-in or incentive to work towards the goals of the
neighborhood. Already, our neighborhood struggles with apathetic commercial property owners,
first-time homebuyers facing obstacles to homeownership, lack of affordable housing
development, and disinvestment into preserving historic properties.
It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities
like ours. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.
The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less
demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to
large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business,
community development lending.
A number of banks that operate in Philadelphia will now be considered either intermediate or
small banks under the proposed rule and therefore subject to less rigorous requirements. These
reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development obligations for over 800
banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks across the country, may worsen the
housing crisis by reducing investor interest in buying Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC), and reducing access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers or access to credit for
home repairs.
Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service
test. Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information
about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this criterion to credit
services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts from direct
evaluation under the service test. As such, examiners would no longer evaluate whether those
products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though approximately 15% of
Philadelphians – over 100,000 households – remain unbanked or underbanked. Moreover,

according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, these households are overwhelmingly
low-income, black, or disabled. CRA review of the cost and features of deposit products has
played an important role in encouraging banks to address these disparities by providing
affordable products, and it must continue to do so.
For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from
access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely
receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit. Our
neighborhood has already lost bank branches – residents and business owners need to travel 20+
minutes outside of the area to access their banking needs. As a community without easy access to
financial services and institutions, we have already seen a reduction in bank investments into our
housing stock and small businesses.
This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and
moderate-income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to
affordable mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible
small-business financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing,
small businesses and other community development.
The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income
communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other
community-based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit
organizations. These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep
relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.
For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology,
accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the

underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources
over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with
limited staff and may not maintain financial records or program documentation in the precise
format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller
organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand what it can mean to community development when banks do
not feel an obligation to serve smaller, community-based nonprofits and businesses. Our
businesses face barriers to accessing capital that business owners in other parts of the country do
not; our residents feel uneducated and pessimistic about their chances of owning their own
homes; our community facilities and non-profits rely on more competitive, state-wide and
national funding resources and are often passed over; and our youth have little to no financial
literacy or access to financial education.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into
tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community
development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond
the banks themselves. These rules should be motivated by the needs of the communities CRA is
intended to serve and not by the perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions.
To be considered economic development under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying
small business must promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation,
retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income
communities.
The proposed rule would eliminate this "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could
earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs
for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. This
change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-development credit and the
people and communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying
business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an
underserved neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a
qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to
demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.

We are also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and
report data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while
the proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Banks
with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report CRA
data on small business loans and community development loans.
Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information
to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs
are being met. Local community leaders and elected officials depend on this data for decision
making and for ensuring that the needs of residents are being addressed. This proposed change is
inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and should not be in the
final rule.
Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
●​ identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
under the proposal;
●​ quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
●​ assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
including rural communities and communities of color; and
●​ consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability.

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the
OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is
prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to
prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity. ​
​
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods. ​
​
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days.
The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes

to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit
grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on
October 13, 2026. ​
​
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not
have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected
organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the
communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base
any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment
deadline by at least 60 days.​
​
Sincerely,

Amarynth Ruch
Corridor Manager
Tacony Together

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill: 
Greater Twin Cities United Way opposes the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). The proposed changes would weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), a law that helps ensure banks meet the needs of all communities, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods.
Because these changes are broad and complex, we encourage the OCC and FDIC to carefully examine their impact on LMI communities before moving forward. We also encourage the agencies to publicly share their analysis and supporting evidence, provide an opportunity for additional public review and comment, and extend the current comment period by 60 days.
The proposal would reduce bank responsibilities to invest in, lend to, and serve LMI communities. It would also weaken community development requirements, reduce transparency, and limit accountability.
The impact in Minnesota would be significant. Minnesota ranks second among states and territories in the share of banks that would lose community development obligations. Nearly 47% of Minnesota banks (50 of 107) would no longer be required to support activities such as affordable housing, small business development, workforce training, and community services. In addition, 170 of the 343 bank branches serving LMI communities (49.6%) could lose CRA coverage, compared with a national rate of 30.3%.
CRA exists because many communities have historically been excluded from lending, investment, and banking services. Strong CRA requirements encourage banks to invest in underserved communities and support local economic development. Weakening those requirements could mean less support for affordable housing, small businesses, workforce programs, and other resources that help families and neighborhoods thrive.
These changes would be especially harmful for people who already face barriers to accessing financial services. In Minnesota, many low-income households, people with limited credit histories, and justice-impacted individuals struggle to obtain affordable loans and other banking products. CRA encourages banks to serve these communities and work with organizations that help people build credit, become homeowners, start businesses, and improve their financial stability.
CRA does more than encourage lending. It also helps strengthen partnerships between banks and nonprofit organizations. Across Minnesota, these partnerships connect people to financial education, homeownership counseling, workforce development programs, small business support, and other services that create opportunity and financial stability. While many banks offer affordable loan products and make charitable contributions through their foundations, CRA helps keep community investment and local partnerships a priority. Weakening CRA could reduce incentives to maintain these collaborations over time, making it harder for banks, nonprofits, and community partners to work together to address local needs and expand opportunity in LMI communities.
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to review and modernize CRA regulations. As this process moves forward, we encourage the OCC and FDIC to ensure that any changes strengthen, rather than diminish investment, partnership, and opportunity in low- and moderate-income communities. Minnesota communities need continued access to capital, strong community partnerships, greater access to financial services, and meaningful accountability to support long-term economic opportunity for all residents.

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
As executive director of Old Brooklyn Community Development Corporation in Cleveland, Ohio, I am concerned that the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act would make it harder for neighborhood organizations like ours to secure the resources needed to deliver lasting community investment.

OBCDC works to improve housing conditions, support small businesses and move challenging redevelopment projects forward. This work requires sustained capacity, often years before a project is ready for a construction loan or a private developer. At Memphis and Pearl, our organization has helped coordinate environmental remediation, demolition, building stabilization and public investment to prepare a major neighborhood site for redevelopment. Projects like this require an organization willing and able to manage the work long before it generates revenue.

Restricting CRA consideration for grants and imposing a 15% overhead threshold would undervalue the infrastructure that makes this work possible. Financial management, insurance, technology and organizational leadership are necessary to manage public and private dollars responsibly. An overhead ratio alone does not tell regulators whether an organization is effective, accountable or meeting community needs.

For OBCDC, reduced access to flexible bank support could mean less capacity to assist residents, support neighborhood businesses and advance redevelopment. Requiring more narrowly restricted funding could also leave us with resources for individual activities but insufficient support to coordinate and sustain them.

I urge the agencies to preserve meaningful CRA consideration for operating support that advances eligible community development work, remove the proposed overhead threshold and evaluate investments based on their community benefit. Banks should be encouraged to invest in the long-term capacity of neighborhood organizations. Our ability to turn investment into results depends on it.

RE: Comment on Notice of Proposed Rulemaking Regarding Community Reinvestment Act Regulations – OPPOSE ROLLBACK OF 2023 CRA RULES

Dear Regulators,

I am writing as a professional in real estate development, with direct experience in affordable housing, to strongly oppose the proposed rescission of the 2023 Community Reinvestment Act rules. I have witnessed firsthand how CRA-funded investments transform lives of residents, and I urge you to maintain the 2023 framework.

In my work in housing development, I have seen residents of low-income housing seize opportunities made possible by CRA-funded programs. They are neighbors who have used CRA-supported homes, clinics, clinics, to build a platform of stability, and go on to start businesses, purchase their first homes, and support their families. 

For example, Banner Bank's CRA-driven investments in demonstrate the typical impact: a $10 million in 2021 financing affordable housing and homeless services in King County; $4 million for 51 affordable units in Skagit County; $10 million in 2022 for housing in Snohomish County; and $5.2 million in 2024 renovating 217 affordable units in King County. The millions of dollars in investments represent hundreds of families with stable homes and vulnerable community members receiving critical services. Rolling back the 2023 rules threatens this pipeline of capital.

* The 2023 Rules Reflect Modern Banking Reality

The 2023 update was the first modernization of CRA rules since 1995. It accounted for the shift toward online and mobile banking, ensuring CRA obligations follow banks' actual market activity rather than being tied solely to physical branch locations. Capital flows differently today than three decades ago; the 2023 rules captured this reality. Reverting to the pre-2023 framework would allow institutions to evade responsibility by shifting away from brick-and-mortar presence in the very communities they are meant to serve.

Additionally, the proposed asset threshold reclassification would eliminate community development obligations for an estimated 8.9% of Washington State banks. For large banks, 28.1% would lose "large bank" status, eliminating separate investment and service tests. This would directly reduce the incentive for banks to pursue the kinds of high-impact community development activities I cited above.

* Recommendations

I urge the FDIC, OCC, and Federal Reserve to:
Keep the 2023 rules, don't turn back the clock
Don't let banks underserve by closing branches or getting reclassified
Judge banks by their actual impact on communities, not by checking boxes
Don't bury community groups in paperwork, they're the ones connecting money to people who need it
Pay attention to race, not just income, because redlining was always about both
Get the Federal Reserve on board with the other regulators so banks aren't playing catch with different rulebooks

The 2023 CRA rules represented hard-won progress. Rolling them back would undermine affordable housing development and betray communities that have historically faced systemic discrimination. I urge you to protect these rules and continue moving forward, not backward.

Respectfully,
Chris Govella

On behalf of the board, staff, and constituencies of the Louisville Urban League–residents of Jefferson County, Kentucky, and the many surrounding counties we serve–I urge that any changes to the Community Reinvestment Act strengthen, rather than dilute, the impact on communities it was designed to serve. Attached to this letter is a detailed list of problematic proposed changes and recommendations to adopt instead. 

Title VIII of the Housing and Community Development Act provided a powerful platform for financial institutions, local governments, and developers to work together to expand investment in the nation's small businesses, workforce, and housing infrastructure. Billions of dollars have been directed to highly leveraged projects that have revitalized thousands of neighborhoods and local economies. 

By raising asset size thresholds, the proposed changes to the CRA would significantly reduce the expectations and accountability placed on banks to invest in and serve low- and moderate-income communities. The reclassification of hundreds of financial institutions into lower-rigor examination categories will result in fewer banks being subject to CRA requirements, reduced community development investment, fewer incentives for banks to maintain branches in underserved neighborhoods, and less reporting on how banks are meeting their community reinvestment obligations.

These changes will directly affect affordable housing, small-business lending, community development, financial education, and access to banking services. Nonprofit organizations could also face reduced access to CRA-supported grants, with additional restrictions on how grant funds can be used, including limitations on administrative and indirect costs.

At the Louisville Urban League, we see the impact of CRA-supported grants firsthand. Last year, we provided homebuyer education to 161 participants and helped 80 new homeowners access over $15 million in mortgages. Our Center for Entrepreneurship served 675 business owners and helped participants access more than $400,000 in loans and grants. These outcomes demonstrate what is at stake.

Reduced CRA requirements will weaken accountability for banks and make it more difficult for communities to demonstrate when banks are not adequately reinvesting in the neighborhoods where they collect deposits. This could disproportionately affect communities that already experience limited access to capital, particularly low- and moderate-income communities and communities of color.

From the perspective of many local and national organizations, the proposed changes will ultimately mean fewer resources for programs that help families purchase homes, build financial stability, support small businesses, develop affordable housing, and create generational wealth. They will have a direct downstream impact on the resources, services, and economic opportunities available to the communities we serve. Our collective responsibility is to protect the progress we have made, safeguard our communities, and work together to ensure that every community continues to have access to the investment and opportunities needed to thrive. The Louisville Urban League is committed to doing our part to protect that progress, and we urge Federal regulators to do the same and withdraw these regressive proposals.

CONCERNING PROVISIONS IN THE PROPOSED CRA REGULATORY CHANGES
The following items outline significant issues with the proposed regulatory changes.

Drastic Reduction in Bank Accountability and Reporting Transparency
The reclassification of hundreds of financial institutions into lower-rigor examination
categories will result in fewer banks being subject to CRA requirements, reduced community
development investment, and less reporting on how banks are meeting their community
reinvestment obligations:
●​ Small Bank Threshold Expansion: Increases the small bank threshold from $412 million
to $1 billion in assets.

●​ Intermediate Bank Threshold Expansion: Increases the intermediate bank threshold
from $1.649 billion to $10 billion in assets.

●​ Large Bank Threshold Expansion: Elevates the large bank threshold to institutions with
over $10 billion in assets.

●​ Loss of Community Development Duties: Over 800 banks with less than $1 billion in
assets would no longer have any community development responsibilities.

●​ Exemption from Full Large-Bank Tests: Over 400 banks between $1 billion and $10
billion would no longer face full, rigorous large-bank examinations.

●​ Elimination of Data Collection and Reporting: Banks with $10 billion or less in assets
would no longer collect or report CRA data on small-business, small-farm, or community
development loans.

●​ National Data Loss: Eliminating data collection for banks under $10 billion removes
approximately 11% of small-business lending data nationwide, and nearly 25% of
available data across six states.

Severe Capital Reductions and Lost Branch Access in LMI Neighborhoods
The proposed changes establish benchmark targets that significantly lower the standard for
acceptable community reinvestment, risking a massive collapse of capital in underserved
neighborhoods:

●​ Drastic Benchmark Reductions: The proposal sets passing benchmark targets as low
as 0.625% of Tier 1 Capital (or 0.12%–0.24% of assets), compared to current bank
activity levels averaging 0.6%–1.0% of assets.


Page 3 of 5
 COMMENT ON THE PROPOSED CRA CHANGES

●​ Collapse in CD Lending: Annual community development lending would drop from
$59.1 billion to $7.44 billion, representing an 87.4% decrease.

●​ Collapse in Qualified Investments: Annual qualified investments would fall from $42.9
billion to $7.44 billion, representing an 82.7% decrease.

●​ Total Capital Loss: Combined annual community development financing would collapse
from $102.0 billion to $14.88 billion (an $ 87.14 billion loss).

●​ Risk to LMI Branches: Over 5,000 branches in LMI census tracts (30% of all LMI
branches nationwide) would lose CRA incentives to stay open.

●​ Risk to Branches in Communities of Color: Over 4,000 branches in
majority-people-of-color census tracts (23% of all such branches) would lose CRA
branch presence incentives.

●​ Long-Term Economic Impact: Branch closures depress local small-business lending for
up to six years and undermine investments in Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC)
projects that support housing choice voucher holders, families with children, and
communities of color.

Onerous Restrictions on Community Nonprofits and Grantmaking
Nonprofit organizations, fair housing agencies, and community development entities face
major administrative hurdles that restrict operational sustainability and direct community
assistance:

●​ 15% Indirect Cost Cap: For banks over $10 billion, CRA credit for grants to community
nonprofits would cap administrative and indirect cost support at 15%.

●​ Project-Specific Mandates: Grants would need to be tied directly to specific projects or
programs, eliminating essential general operating support.

●​ Pre-Clearance and Public Databases: Rules would require public reporting of funded
nonprofits, allow confidential "pre-clearance" of grants without public oversight, or
consider eliminating CRA credit for nonprofit grants entirely.

●​ Disproportionate Harm: These limitations create severe hardship for smaller nonprofits,
newer grassroots organizations, and groups serving hard-to-reach populations.


Page 4 of 5
 COMMENT ON THE PROPOSED CRA CHANGES
Louisville Urban League


Weakened Protections Against Redlining and Civil Rights Violations
The proposed rule undermines protections against redlining and consumer harm, shielding
institutions from accountability:

●​ Exclusion of Redlining Penalties: Subtle language changes exclude redlining violations
from automatically downgrading a bank's CRA performance rating.

●​ Exclusion of Private Litigation: Regulators would only consider formal federal or state
enforcement actions—ignoring private litigation—at a time when federal enforcement
has significantly decreased.

●​ Omission of Special Purpose Credit Programs: The proposal fails to award CRA credit
for Special Purpose Credit Programs (SPCPs), despite universal stakeholder support in
prior rulemakings.

●​ Stripped Consumer Protections: The rule eliminates consideration of key Truth in
Lending Act protections and ignores the severity, root cause, duration, and
pervasiveness of consumer violations.

RECOMMENDATIONS FOR THE PROPOSED CRA REGULATORY CHANGES
To safeguard economic opportunity, affordable housing, and fair access to credit in Kentucky
and across the nation, regulators must incorporate the following core demands:

1.​ Maintain CRA Rigor Below $10 Billion: Retain current asset thresholds to ensure small
and intermediate banks continue to meet explicit community development, service, and
reporting obligations.

2.​ Reject Restrictive Grant Rules: Eliminate the proposed 15% administrative cap and
project-specific mandates, preserving flexible general operating support for community
nonprofits and fair housing organizations.

3.​ Maintain Strong Fair Lending Penalties: Ensure that findings of redlining, civil rights
violations, consumer protection breaches, and private litigation explicitly downgrade
banks' CRA performance ratings.

4.​ Incorporate Special Purpose Credit Programs: Provide explicit CRA credit for SPCPs to
expand credit access in LMI neighborhoods and communities of color.

5.​ Protect Branch Incentives and Data Transparency: Preserve strong regulatory
incentives to maintain physical branches in LMI areas and maintain mandatory data
collection for small-business, small-farm, and CD loans.

strengthening Black-owned businesses, advancing economic opportunity, and building pathways to
business growth, capital access, commercial property participation, and long-term wealth creation.

CRA obligations create an important incentive for financial institutions to invest, lend, and build
partnerships in communities that have historically received insufficient capital. The proposed rule could
substantially reduce those expectations.
The proposal suggests that a total of just 0.625 percent of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to
community-development loans or investments could be sufficient to meet certain CRA benchmarks.2
NCRC's analysis of OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks among the nation's 100 largest banks found

organizations that have deep relationships with residents and businesses and understand the specific needs

cap may not reflect the actual cost of delivering effective community-development programs. Staff,
facilities, technology, accounting, insurance, compliance, evaluation, and other operating expenses are not
peripheral to the work; they are part of the infrastructure required to perform it.
Smaller community-based organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources over which to
spread these expenses. Additional documentation requirements could compound this problem. If financial
institutions determine that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document for
CRA purposes, funding may migrate toward larger institutions with greater administrative capacity rather

Economic-Development Credit Should Produce Meaningful Community Benefit
We are also concerned about the proposal to eliminate the existing "purpose test" for
economic-development activities.
Under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business does not automatically constitute
economic development. The activity must also promote economic development through outcomes such as
permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or
moderate-income communities.5
The proposed rule would eliminate this requirement and allow financing to qualify based more heavily on
characteristics of the business and whether the financing expands, improves, or preserves productive
capacity, physical presence, or employment.6
As an organization whose mission centers on business development, BBA strongly supports increased
access to responsible financing for small businesses. But small-business financing and community
development should not automatically be treated as synonymous.
The fundamental question should remain: Who benefits?
Financing that expands a business can be valuable while still producing limited benefit for low- and
moderate-income workers or communities. CRA credit should continue to prioritize activities that
demonstrate meaningful connections between capital deployment and community outcomes—including
job creation and retention, neighborhood investment, business ownership, commercial development, and
economic opportunity.
Removing the purpose test risks shifting CRA from an outcomes-oriented community-development
framework toward one in which financing receives credit without sufficient consideration of whether the
communities CRA was created to serve actually benefit.
Before eliminating this test, the agencies should identify what additional activities would qualify, where
those activities are likely to occur, and whether financing could shift away from investments that produce
measurable economic benefits in low- and moderate-income communities.

Behind The Leaf submits this comment in opposition to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

Behind The Leaf is a 501(c)(3) philanthropic organization powered by Flourish Media that works to strengthen financial readiness, access to capital, and economic opportunity for women business owners. Through financial education, investor-readiness programming, small-business grants, community conversations, and connections between entrepreneurs and potential funders, we see firsthand the importance of responsible financial institutions and meaningful community investment.

The CRA has long helped ensure that banks meet the credit needs of the communities they serve, including low- and moderate-income communities. We are concerned that the proposed rule would substantially weaken this accountability and reduce incentives for banks to invest in communities.

The proposal could significantly reduce community development lending and investment. The NCRC's analysis included in the comment template indicates that if banks conducted only the proposed 0.625% benchmarks for community development lending and investments, community development activity could decline by approximately 85%. Such a reduction could have serious consequences for affordable housing, small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and community development.

Access to responsible capital is particularly important for small-business owners and entrepreneurs. Women entrepreneurs and other small businesses often depend on financial institutions, community organizations, grants, and responsible financing to build sustainable businesses, create jobs, and contribute to local economic development. Lowering banks' incentives to invest in these communities could make existing barriers to capital even more difficult to overcome.

We are also concerned about the proposed treatment of nonprofit organizations. Community-based nonprofits often have the relationships, trust, and local knowledge necessary to translate financial resources into meaningful community outcomes. Proposed limits on indirect costs and additional documentation requirements could make it more difficult for smaller organizations to receive bank support. Banks may consequently redirect resources toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to document.

The proposal's elimination of the economic-development "purpose test" is another significant concern. CRA credit should remain connected to meaningful economic benefits for low- and moderate-income people and communities. Business financing should not automatically receive CRA credit simply because it expands or strengthens a business if there is no demonstrated connection to job creation, retention, or economic opportunity for the communities CRA is intended to serve.

We are also concerned about reducing CRA data collection and reporting requirements. Meaningful data allows communities, regulators, and researchers to identify lending gaps, evaluate bank performance, and determine whether local credit needs are being met. Reducing transparency would make it more difficult to hold financial institutions accountable and identify communities where additional investment is needed.

For these reasons, Behind The Leaf urges the OCC and FDIC to rescind the proposed rule until the agencies conduct and publicly release a thorough analysis of its likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities, small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and community development.

The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken CRA accountability without demonstrating that those changes are consistent with the CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period by at least 60 days to allow community organizations and other stakeholders sufficient time to evaluate this significant proposal and provide meaningful input.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Sincerely,

Behind The Leaf
A 501(c)(3) philanthropic organization powered by Flourish Media

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN
1557-AF57; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Behind The Leaf submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation (FDIC) concerning the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).
Behind The Leaf is a 501(c)(3) philanthropic organization powered by Flourish Media that works
to strengthen financial readiness, access to capital, and economic opportunity for women
business owners. Through financial education, investor-readiness programming, small-business
grants, community conversations, and connections between entrepreneurs and potential
funders, we see firsthand how important responsible financial institutions and community
investment are to the ability of entrepreneurs and families to build sustainable economic futures.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. These protections remain especially important for
communities and entrepreneurs that have historically experienced barriers to capital, unequal
access to financial services, and disinvestment.
 We are particularly concerned that the proposed rule would reduce meaningful accountability for
banks while potentially decreasing the resources available to small businesses, nonprofit
organizations, affordable housing, and other community development efforts.
Reduction in Community Investment Expectations
CRA obligations help incentivize banks to invest in the communities they serve. The proposed
rule would substantially lower the level of community development activity that could be
sufficient for banks to receive CRA credit. The NCRC template notes that the proposal could
effectively reduce community development lending and investment by approximately 85% if
banks conduct only the proposed 0.625% benchmarks.
For organizations like Behind The Leaf, this is concerning because community investment is not
an abstract concept. Capital from financial institutions can translate into grants, sponsorships,
financial education, small-business support, affordable housing, and opportunities for
entrepreneurs to build sustainable businesses.
Women entrepreneurs, particularly those operating small and growing businesses, need access
to responsible capital and financial institutions that understand the communities they serve.
Reducing incentives for banks to invest in those communities could make it more difficult for
entrepreneurs to obtain financing, build assets, create jobs, and contribute to local economic
development.
The agencies should therefore analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending,
services, and investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether
communities that have experienced historic barriers to capital would be disproportionately
affected.
Protect Support for Community-Based Nonprofits
We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations.
Community-based nonprofits often have the relationships, trust, and knowledge necessary to
translate financial resources into meaningful outcomes for residents and entrepreneurs.
Organizations such as Behind The Leaf work directly with communities to provide education,
connections, resources, and opportunities that may otherwise be difficult to access.
The proposed 15 percent limit on indirect costs for grants from large banks, along with
additional documentation requirements, could create significant challenges for smaller
organizations. Staff, technology, accounting, compliance, facilities, and other operating
expenses are not separate from the programs nonprofits provide—they are part of the
infrastructure required to deliver those programs effectively.
 If banks determine that supporting smaller nonprofits is more difficult or costly to document, they
may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify. That could
reduce resources available to community-based organizations that are closest to the people and
entrepreneurs they serve.
We urge the agencies to analyze whether these proposed documentation requirements and
administrative-cost limitations would redirect bank support away from smaller nonprofit
organizations and ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-income
communities.
Preserve the Connection Between Economic Development and Community
Benefit
Behind The Leaf is particularly concerned about the proposed elimination of the existing
"purpose test" for economic development.
Under current CRA guidance, qualifying economic-development activities must have a
meaningful connection to job creation, retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income
people or communities. The proposed rule would eliminate this purpose test and allow a
broader range of business financing to qualify for CRA credit without requiring banks to
demonstrate that the financing creates or improves economic opportunity for low- and
moderate-income people or communities.
This change could weaken the connection between CRA credit and the communities CRA is
intended to benefit.
Supporting a business is important, but economic development should also be measured by
whether that investment creates opportunity, strengthens communities, supports employment,
and expands access to economic mobility. A bank should not be able to receive CRA credit
simply because financing increases the productive capacity of a business if there is no
meaningful connection to underserved people or communities.
The agencies should analyze what additional activities would qualify under the proposed
definition and whether bank financing could shift away from activities that create or retain jobs
and economic opportunities for low- and moderate-income people and communities.
Maintain Transparency and Accountability
We are also concerned about changes that would reduce CRA data collection and reporting
requirements.
Meaningful data allows communities, regulators, and researchers to understand where credit is
flowing, identify gaps, and determine whether banks are meeting local needs. The proposed
rule would eliminate annual CRA data collection and reporting requirements for more than 400
banks with assets of $10 billion or less, according to the NCRC template.
 For organizations working to improve financial readiness and access to capital for
entrepreneurs, less information about lending and community development activity makes it
more difficult to understand where barriers exist and where additional investment is needed.
The agencies should not reduce transparency before analyzing how the loss of CRA data would
affect communities' ability to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance, and understand
whether local credit needs are being met.
Conclusion
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not adequately:
●​ Identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny;
●​ Quantify changes in branches, lending, investments, services, and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
●​ Assess whether the effects would be concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations;
●​ Consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability.
Given these concerns, Behind The Leaf believes the OCC and FDIC should rescind the
proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public
comment.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
the credit needs of the communities they serve. Changes that materially weaken that
accountability should not be finalized without demonstrating that they are consistent with the
CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period by at least 60 days. The
proposed rule is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant
changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations,
nonprofit grants, reporting, and other core elements of CRA implementation.
Thank you for considering this comment and for your continued commitment to ensuring that
financial institutions remain accountable to the communities they serve.
Sincerely,
Behind The Leaf​
A 501(c)(3) philanthropic organization powered by Flourish Media
