Comptroller Gould, Chairman Hill, Ms. Janes, to whom it may concern:
The Cambridge Housing Authority (CHA) submits these comments in response to the proposed amendments to
the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and
the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. CHA appreciates stated goals of improving clarity, reducing
unnecessary burden, and ensuring that community development resources reach the communities they are
intended to benefit. At the same time, as the CRA plays a critical role as one of the only tools supporting
affordable housing production in the United States, CHA is concerned that several elements of the proposal
could weaken that financing ecosystem at a time when communities across the country are facing an acute and
worsening housing crisis. Cambridge, Massachusetts' experience reflects that national reality: the impact of the
proposed CRA regulation changes would be devastating.
CHA urges the agencies to revise the proposed rule to preserve the strong CRA incentives for affordable
housing lending, Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) investment, community development grants, and
nonprofit partnerships that directly support low- and moderate-income households. More specifically, CHA
recommends that the final rule maintains robust consideration for community development investments and
grants, avoid reducing accountability for banks that play an important role in local affordable housing finance,
and ensure that any new documentation requirements are workable for public housing authorities and
nonprofit housing providers.
The proposed rule will detrimentally impact affordable housing development in Cambridge, MA.
CHA relies on a complex mix of public subsidy, private debt, tax credit equity, and community development
capital to develop and preserve affordable housing. Capital investment motivated by the CRA has long been an
important part of this ecosystem. Banks subject to meaningful CRA evaluation often provide construction loans,
permanent loans, acquisition financing, tax credit equity, grants, and other flexible resources that help close
financing gaps and make deeply affordable housing feasible.
In Cambridge and similar high-cost markets, affordable housing developments routinely face funding gaps
driven by land costs, construction costs, operating pressures, and the need to serve households with very low
incomes. Even modest reductions in CRA-motivated investment demand, concessionary lending, or grant
support can affect whether projects proceed, how deeply affordable they can be, and how much additional
public subsidy is required.

For a recent project, there was over $0.11 difference per dollar of credit between CRA-driven LIHTC pricing and
non-CRA-driven pricing. Eleven cents may not sound like a lot to someone unfamiliar with the LIHTC program,
but it amounted to over $4 million, or over $59,000 per unit, on this recent project. When that cost difference
is factored over the 1000 affordable homes in our development pipeline, the shortfall from losing CRA-
motivated LIHTC pricing reaches over $59,000,000. A financing gap this large cannot be covered by other
sources. If adopted, the proposed changes to the CRA will grind CHA's efforts to expand affordable housing to a
halt.
To avoid that end, we respectfully request that the proposed rules be revised to ensure:
1. Preservation of strong CRA incentives for affordable housing investment
The proposal would raise the large bank threshold to more than $10 billion in assets and would subject
banks with $10 billion or less in assets to fewer data collection, maintenance, and reporting
obligations. CHA is concerned that this change could reduce CRA incentives for a significant group of
mid-sized banks that currently participate in affordable housing finance and make up the bulk of the
LIHTC motivated investors in the market. If these institutions face less robust evaluation of community
development activity, they may have reduced motivation to provide LIHTC equity, community
development loans, grants, and other financing commitments essential to these transactions.
2. Avoidance of weakening the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit market
LIHTC remains the primary federal tool for producing and preserving affordable rental housing. CRA-
motivated bank investment is a major driver of LIHTC demand and pricing. If fewer banks are subject to
meaningful investment expectations, demand for LIHTC equity could soften, reducing equity proceeds
and increasing financing gaps. For public housing authorities and mission-driven affordable housing
developers, this would likely translate into greater reliance on scarce local, state, and federal subsidy
sources. As noted earlier, CHA calculates the loss in LIHTC equity from this change to be over $59,000
per unit, or more than $59 million in funding for projects in Cambridge's affordable housing
development pipeline.
3. Maintenance of meaningful consideration for grants and nonprofit partnerships
CHA supports the goal of ensuring that community development grants benefit intended communities.
However, the proposed limitation on grant consideration, including the requirement that large banks
document that recipients do not have overhead costs above 15 percent, could create practical barriers
for public agencies and nonprofit housing organizations. Affordable housing development requires
organizational capacity, planning, predevelopment, resident engagement, compliance, asset
management, and project administration. These activities are not incidental to community
development; they are often essential to delivering and sustaining affordable housing.
4. Recognition of the full continuum of affordable housing finance
The proposal's greater emphasis on lending may preserve CRA consideration for construction loans,
acquisition loans, permanent loans, and other project-level credit facilities. CHA supports continued
and clear CRA recognition for those activities. However, affordable housing finance depends on a
broader continuum of support, including equity investment, credit enhancement, grants, technical
assistance, and operating support for mission-driven sponsors. The final rule should not inadvertently

privilege debt over other forms of capital that are equally necessary to meet the credit and housing
needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
5. Retention of accountability while reducing unnecessary burden
CHA recognizes the importance of clear, predictable, and appropriately tailored CRA evaluation
standards. Reducing unnecessary compliance burden can be a legitimate goal, particularly for
community banks. However, burden reduction should not come at the expense of transparency,
accountability, or incentives to serve low- and moderate-income communities. The agencies should
ensure that any revised asset thresholds and examination procedures continue to encourage banks of
all sizes to respond to demonstrated local needs, including affordable housing production and
preservation.
Requested revisions
CHA requests that the agencies revise the proposed rule to:
1. Preserve strong CRA consideration for LIHTC equity investments and other community development
investments that support affordable housing;
2. Maintain meaningful incentives for mid-sized banks to participate in affordable housing finance;
3. Ensure that grants, predevelopment support, technical assistance, and capacity-building resources
remain eligible when they directly support affordable housing outcomes;
4. Avoid rigid overhead standards that may exclude effective public and nonprofit housing partners; and
5. Retain sufficient reporting and examination transparency to allow communities to evaluate whether
local credit and housing needs are being met.
For the past 15 years in Cambridge and surrounding communities, the CRA has played a vital role in
encouraging financial institutions to help meet the credit needs of low- and moderate-income communities
and has been a critical tool in CHA's $1.5 billion investment in affordable housing. During that time, investors
motivated by the CRA have provided over $500 million in equity funding for this effort.
Amid the ongoing national housing affordability crisis, the Community Reinvestment Act should remain a
strong and reliable tool for bringing private capital to bear on the urgent need for affordable homes. A final rule
that provides clarity while preserving robust incentives for lending, investment, grants, and partnerships will
better advance the statutory purpose of the CRA and help communities address urgent housing needs.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule.
Respectfully submitted,

To the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
HVN Development, LLC respectfully urges the agencies to keep the CRA investment test in place for banks with assets above the current $1.649 billion large-bank threshold. The proposal would move banks between $1.649 billion and $10 billion into a new intermediate category with no investment test. For affordable housing developers like HVN, that change would remove a meaningful share of the bank demand that prices Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit) equity, at the moment Congress has expanded the program.
About HVN Development
HVN Development is a California affordable housing developer focused on Housing Credit communities in Los Angeles and the surrounding region. Most of our pipeline is 4% Housing Credit transactions financed with tax-exempt private activity bonds allocated by CDLAC. Each development combines bank construction and permanent lending, tax-exempt bond financing, and Housing Credit equity provided by bank investors directly or through multi-investor syndicated funds.
Why the Investment Test Matters to Our Transactions
CRA demand sets the price of the equity that closes our deals. According to the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), banks supply roughly 75 to 80 percent of Housing Credit equity, and at least 71 percent of that is CRA-motivated. AHTCC's survey found at least 108 banks below $10 billion in assets invested about $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over five years, or roughly $2 billion when extrapolated to the full market.
Those banks matter to us even when they are not the named investor. The syndicated funds that invest in our partnerships pool capital from many banks, and regional and community banks deepen the bidding for each transaction. Fewer CRA-motivated buyers means less competition and lower credit pricing.
In California's high-cost markets, small pricing changes create large financing gaps. On a development generating $30 million of federal credits, a five-cent decline in pricing removes $1.5 million of equity. That gap must be filled with scarce state and local soft funds or more deferred developer fee, or the project does not proceed.
The timing compounds the risk. The 2025 federal tax law lowered the tax-exempt bond financing test for 4% transactions from 50 to 25 percent and permanently increased 9% credit allocations. More 4% transactions will need equity just as the proposal would weaken a key source of investor demand.
CRA investment also anchors the rest of the capital stack. Banks that invest in our equity often provide the construction loan or purchase the bonds on the same transaction. We support the proposal's recognition that a CD investment forming part of a multicomponent financing involving a loan is complex; Housing Credit transactions are a clear example.
Our Requests
1.Keep the investment test for banks above $1.649 billion. If the agencies raise the large-bank threshold, we ask that they adopt the $3.252 billion alternative described in the proposal rather than $10 billion.
2.Keep the intermediate bank CD test meaningful. We ask the agencies to retain the requirement that an intermediate bank earn at least a "satisfactory" CD test rating to receive an overall "satisfactory," rather than allowing the lending test alone to carry the rating.
3.Name Housing Credit equity as a responsive and complex CD investment. This should include equity held through multi-investor funds and equity paired with a construction loan or bond purchase on the same transaction.
4.Preserve credit for statewide and regional benefit. Fund investments spread across a state should continue to receive consideration once a bank has served its assessment areas.
5.Lower the risk weight on Housing Credit investments. In the parallel capital rulemaking, we support AHTCC's request to reduce the risk weight from 100 percent to 20 percent, and in no case above 50 percent.
Conclusion
The investment test has built a deep, efficient market for Housing Credit equity, and California renters benefit directly from it. We support the comments of the AHTCC and ask the agencies to preserve that market as they finalize the rule. Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
Respectfully submitted,
JP Sciammarella
Chief Financial Officer
HVN Development, LLC

Irvine, CA 92618

October 7, 2026

As an employee in the banking industry, I recognize the importance of a CRA framework that is transparent, objective, administrable, and appropriately tailored to a bank’s size, business model, market conditions, and community needs. I support the agencies’ stated objectives of aligning CRA implementation with the statutory purpose of encouraging banks to help meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with safe and sound operations and respectfully offer the following comments and recommendations for the OCC’s consideration.

Data Collection, Reporting, and Disclosure
The proposal appropriately recognizes the relationship between CRA small business and small farm data requirements and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s Section 1071 small business lending data rule. However, the practical overlap between the two regimes appears likely to affect a limited number of banks, because Section 1071 applies only to financial institutions that meet its coverage criteria pertaining to covered small business lending activity. Additional information is needed to determine the number of small and intermediate banks subject to duplicative collection, maintenance, or reporting obligations under both frameworks.

CRA data collection, maintenance, and reporting remain important because they provide regulators, financial institutions, and communities with a consistent basis for evaluating whether banks are helping meet the credit needs of the communities they serve, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, in a safe and sound manner. CRA small business and small farm data also support transparent performance evaluations, help identify lending patterns and community development needs, and provide an established public framework distinct from the fair lending and market-monitoring purposes of Section 1071.

My recommendation is that banks identifying as an intermediate bank under the proposed asset threshold should continue to collect, maintain, and report CRA data. Continuing these requirements for intermediate banks would preserve meaningful CRA performance information, avoid creating gaps in data used to evaluate community credit needs, and ensure that the agencies have adequate information to assess the impact of any future changes intended to reduce duplicative reporting. Before discontinuing or narrowing CRA data requirements, the agencies should provide additional analysis showing the number and type of institutions subject to both CRA and Section 1071 reporting and the extent to which Section 1071 data would provide an adequate substitute for CRA-specific data.

Retail Banking Services
Consideration of banking services is particularly important for low- and moderate-income individuals, who may have less flexibility to travel to a more distant branch, conduct banking during limited hours, absorb higher transaction fees, or qualify for products that require higher minimum balances. Access to conveniently located branches, suitable operating hours, affordable deposit and credit products, and reasonably priced transaction services can affect an individual’s ability to establish and maintain a banking relationship, manage household expenses, build savings, obtain credit, and avoid reliance on higher-cost alternative financial services. Reviewing material differences among branches also helps identify whether low- and moderate-income communities receive a level and cost of service reasonably comparable to that available elsewhere in a bank’s market.

I recommend and strongly support that, under the service test, the agencies retain a review of the general services offered by a bank, including hours of operation, available loan and deposit products, and transaction fees, as well as, where applicable, any material differences in the availability or cost of services at particular branches. This review would ensure that CRA evaluations continue to consider whether retail banking services are reasonably accessible and responsive to the needs of the communities a bank serves. 

In closing, I appreciate the OCC and FDIC’s consideration of my comments.

Respectfully,
G. Jones

Dear Deputy Executive Secretary Jones and Others This May Concern:
On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide loans, investments, grants,
and services in communities that have historically lacked access to capital.
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations, and we support some of the
agencies' provisions that could improve the CRA framework and increase responsible capital in
underserved communities. However, we have concerns about the increases in the asset
thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA and the restrictions on operating
grants. Additionally, several interacting provisions could further weaken community development
incentives, impairing the flow of much needed capital in the most underserved communities.
Community Ventures Corporation (CVC) is a statewide CDFI headquartered in Lexington,
Kentucky, providing small business lending, affordable housing finance, homeownership
counseling, and entrepreneurship support to rural and low-income communities and individuals
across the Commonwealth.
Banks are critical partners in our work. We currently have relationships with banks that provide
term loans, lines of credit, subordinated (EQ2) debt, and grants. These partnerships provide
approximately $22.7 million (24%) of our total debt and grant capital support. Two examples of
the work that these investments allow are Wells Fargo's commitment to serve 30,000+ individuals
and 5,000 renter households through a housing counseling program and a U.S. Bank-funded
program in Lexington's East End, committing to assisting us to create 30+ new jobs/businesses and
helping at least 8 small businesses secure SBA loans every year.


These partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical capital and resources
to CDFIs, banks rely on CDFIs to reach underserved communities, develop borrowers, and
cultivate future bank customers. The CRA has long helped create incentives for banks to build and
sustain these relationships, strengthening the broader community development ecosystem. We
are therefore concerned that several provisions in the proposal could weaken these incentives,
reducing bank engagement with CDFIs and ultimately the flow of capital to the communities we
serve.
Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance: Section IV.A, "Asset
Thresholds"; Questions 1–3
The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate
banks as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as institutions with
more than $10 billion. About eight hundred banks that currently face a separate community
development test as intermediate small banks would become small banks and lose that
requirement. Another approximately four hundred banks that are currently evaluated as large
banks would become intermediate banks, losing the separate large-bank lending, investment, and
service tests and many associated data-reporting requirements.
In the Commonwealth of Kentucky where we serve, it is estimated that 30 banks, comprising 38.0%
of all the banks in the state would no longer be required to reinvest in local community
development projects such as affordable housing, small business support, workforce
development, community healthcare and education services. Additionally, fourteen (14) banks,
comprising 41.2% of all banks in the state would lose their large bank status, thereby jeopardizing
168 low- and moderate-income (LMI) bank branches in Kentucky.1
The consequences may be especially significant in rural and smaller markets, where there are
fewer financial institutions and fewer alternative sources of capital. CVC's own federally funded
small-business program serves eighty-five rural Kentucky counties, illustrating the scale of markets
with limited conventional banking access. In these communities, the loss of even one or two CRA-
motivated bank partners can materially affect whether projects are financed. For communities with
fewer financial institutions and fewer sources of private capital to begin with, losing even a handful
of CRA-motivated lenders and investors could have an outsized effect on whether affordable
housing, small businesses, and community facilities get financed.
Harm to Communities from Loss of Community Development Finance
These thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development performance is
evaluated and therefore affect the strength of banks' incentives to engage in community
development. The agencies acknowledge in the proposal that when banks become subject to a CD
test under the current framework, the explicit evaluation of their CD activities typically results in
banks adjusting their CRA programs.
Banks moving down asset sizes and losing incentives for community development activities would
have a direct impact on our partnerships. We estimate that a combined $15.5 million of debt and
grant funding would be at risk from our bank funders that are currently considered large or
intermediate that would transition into lower asset categories. This represents 68% of our
total bank funding. Specifically, $12.2 million is with Republic Bank & Trust, $1.5 million with


Central Bank & Trust, $1.4 million with Traditional Bank, and $379,000 with Farmers National Bank
of Danville — all currently Large or Intermediate banks that would move to a lower CRA size class
under the proposal — plus a $10,000 at-risk grant from Woodforest National Bank.
Laura Schwarz's journey illustrates why Community Ventures' Rural Homeownership Program is so
important to rural Kentucky. As a single mother, she faced significant barriers to homeownership,
including credit challenges and limited financial knowledge. Through counseling, education, credit
repair assistance, and affordable financing, Community Ventures helped her purchase a safe,
energy-efficient home in Jessamine County, providing the stability, security, and wealth-building
opportunity she wanted for her children. Today, she hopes to pass that home on to the next
generation and serves as a volunteer leader helping other families achieve the same dream.
Laura's story demonstrates that bank investments in CDFI's like ours are not merely transactions.
They create a lasting community impact. Bank investment in Community Ventures helps transform
renters into homeowners, strengthens local workforce stability, builds generational wealth, and
creates community leaders. Without continued access to this capital, fewer families like Laura's
will have the opportunity to build assets, achieve long-term housing stability, and contribute to the
economic vitality of rural communities across Kentucky.
CDFIs frequently rely on regional and community banks for patient debt, deposits, investments,
lines of credit, grants, and other forms of capital that allow us to reach borrowers and projects that
conventional financial institutions cannot efficiently serve directly.
Misalignment with Congressional Priorities on Affordable Housing and New Markets Tax
Credit (NMTC)
The change also undermines Congress's recent efforts to strengthen Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit (LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC), which are two bipartisan, popular federal tax
tools with a long track record of success in our communities. While Congress expanded LIHTC and
made NMTC permanent, the proposal undermines these important investment tools.
LIHTC and NMTC are considered equity investments that are evaluated under the standalone
investment test for large banks which currently have a distinct 25%-weighted component of their
CRA evaluation devoted to qualified investments. Moving banks into the lower size category would
mean these transitioned banks would only be subject to a diluted evaluation that considers all CD
in one test. This means a bank may have greater ability to emphasize CD lending rather than
maintain the same level of LIHTC or NMTC investment because investment performance no longer
receives a separate rating. Through this weakened regulatory incentive, bank demand for these
investments would decrease.
A powerful example of the impact of bank investment through Community Ventures can be found
in Millersburg, Kentucky. Through Community Ventures' New Markets Tax Credit program, with
support from Fifth Third Bank, the historic 404 Main Street building is being restored as part of the
Jan Wagoner Preservation Fund, a $6 million initiative created to save and repurpose some of
Millersburg's most important historic properties. Once a vacant and deteriorating structure with a
collapsed floor and shifting walls, the 1919 building is being transformed into a mixed-use
development featuring new commercial space and upper-floor apartments, bringing new
economic activity, housing opportunities, and life back to the community's downtown core.


The significance of this investment extends far beyond a single building. The restoration of 404
Main is part of a broader strategy to strengthen Main Street, support local businesses, create
housing, expand the tax base, and preserve the historic character that makes rural Kentucky
communities unique. Local leaders have pointed to Millersburg's growing business activity and
renewed momentum as evidence that patient investment and innovative financing can help small
towns compete, attract visitors, and create opportunities for future generations.
This is exactly the type of community transformation that Community Reinvestment Act
investments help make possible. Bank investments in Community Ventures' New Markets Tax
Credit activities provide critical capital for projects that conventional financing often cannot
support in rural and economically distressed communities. Without these investments, projects
like the Jan Wagoner initiative and the restoration of 404 Main would be far more difficult to
accomplish. The result would be fewer revitalized downtowns, fewer housing opportunities, less
private investment, and fewer economic opportunities in communities that are working hard to
write their own comeback stories.

Significance of CRA data and transparency: Section IV.G, "Data Collection, Reporting, and
Disclosure"
The threshold changes would also substantially reduce the number of institutions subject to large-
bank CRA data requirements. This would make it harder for communities, CDFIs, policymakers,
and regulators to identify credit gaps, compare bank performance, assess geographic disparities,
and understand whether community credit needs are being met. We are concerned that aggregate
community development finance data is already difficult to track and the proposal would
exacerbate the coverage of data, making it difficult to identify and understand where credit is
flowing.
CVC is also building an organization-wide process to track the demographics of the clients we
serve and the community-level impact of our work, an active investment in the kind of community
development data capacity this section describes.
Recommendation
For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and reject all
alternatives offered (especially the substantially higher thresholds raised for consideration in
Question 1). The current thresholds are already annually indexed to CPI-W, so they are not
beholden to 1995 asset levels. Moreover, the justification of "restoring proportionality to 1995" that
the agencies use in the proposal does not adequately explain why raising asset thresholds better
serve the statutory intent of the CRA—which is to ensure that credit needs of LMI communities are
met. For the small bank threshold, the proportionality metric rests on the distribution of the
number of banks such that nearly 80% of all banks would be considered small, similar to what it
was in 1995. While that is true, by the same logic, nearly 20% of banks in 1995 were considered
large whereas under the proposed large bank threshold, only a little over 2% of all banks would be
considered large. Instead, the agencies selectively use total banking industry share to justify the
large bank threshold saying large banks would be under this proposal, and similar to 1995, cover
about 85% of all total bank industry's assets. Matching a 1995 distribution through either method
does not necessarily demonstrate that the resulting categories are appropriate for the modern
banking system. The industry has consolidated dramatically; bank business models and


geographic reach have changed. Banks with several billion dollars in assets today may have
substantially greater lending, investment, data, and operational capacity than institutions that
were treated as small or intermediate, three decades ago. The fact that assets happen to sit above
a chosen threshold does not by itself establish that banks below that threshold should lose the
separate investment/service tests or associated data requirements.
Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community Development
Activities — CD Grants"; Questions 9–11
We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants which: 1)
requires a qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative
with a primary purpose of community development; 2) for large banks, caps grant recipient's
indirect administrative costs to 15%; 3) requires that large banks obtain documentation from grant
recipients including written commitments regarding use of funds, indirect-cost attestations, IRS
Form 990s, and operating and program budgets. We also strongly oppose the alternative
contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and donations from CRA consideration entirely.
While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit
communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of effective grantmaking and
misunderstand the role that flexible operating support plays in community development finance.
For CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, risk management, data
systems, financial management, technical assistance, and product development are not ancillary
to community development. They are the infrastructure that makes community development
lending possible.
CVC uses operating grants to fund core program investments like our Wells Fargo-supported
eHome America housing counseling program, our Truist- and PNC-supported Women's Business
Center, and our Old National Bank-supported Chef Space culinary incubator, which help residents
become homeowners, help entrepreneurs start and grow businesses, and help food entrepreneurs
launch ventures.
Moreover, we oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA eligibility. An
organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for community impact.
Costs vary depending on an organization's size, geography, product mix, regulatory obligations,
technical-assistance model, and populations served. The cap could disproportionately affect
small and emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-dollar loans, organizations providing
intensive borrower technical assistance, CDFIs developing new products or entering underserved
markets and organizations making necessary investments in technology, compliance, data, and
risk management.
Recommendation
The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building
grants as currently is in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage flexibility for
banks to provide the form of support that best responds to the identified community needs instead
of imposing undue compliance burdens.
Interacting Provisions That Could Further Reduce Community Development Incentives


Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance: Section IV.B,
"Performance Tests — Intermediate Bank Ratings"
Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a
Satisfactory rating on both its lending test and its CD test to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
The proposal would require a Satisfactory or better lending-test rating but would allow lending
performance to compensate for weaker CD performance.
This change is particularly concerning when combined with the proposed asset thresholds, which
would move hundreds of banks currently evaluated under the large-bank framework into the
intermediate category. If weak CD performance does not prevent an overall Satisfactory rating,
banks may have less regulatory incentive to make CDFI loans and investments, provide grants, or
undertake other community development activities. We urge the agencies to retain a requirement
that intermediate banks demonstrate at least Satisfactory CD performance to receive an overall
Satisfactory rating.
Complexity definition anchored to lending is too narrow: Section IV.C, "Qualitative Factors";
Questions 12–17
The proposal would define complexity for CD investments, grants, and services largely by whether
an activity is a necessary or beneficial component of a multicomponent financing transaction
involving a loan. We oppose establishing a lending-centric definition of complexity. Investments in
CDFIs can involve specialized expertise, layered capital, subordinate positions, public subsidies,
risk sharing, guarantees, tax-credit structures, patient repayment terms, or other features that
make transactions complex even when they are not directly paired with a particular bank loan. We
also oppose requiring CD investments or services to be complex as contemplated in Question 14
or treating complexity as categorically more responsive than innovation, flexibility, or impact as
contemplated in Question 15.

The agencies should assess complexity, innovativeness, flexibility, impact, and responsiveness
based on the characteristics and community value of the activity itself, rather than its association
with a lending transaction.
Prevent ordinary retail lending from substituting for specialized CD lending: Section IV.B,
"Retail Lending Product Lines," Questions 4–7; and Section IV.C, "CD Loans"
The proposal would evaluate retail lending only in a bank's major product lines. It will also allow a
loan in a retail product line that is not evaluated as a major product line to receive consideration as
a CD loan if the loan otherwise satisfies the community development definition. We agree that
genuinely community-development-oriented financing should not lose CRA consideration simply
because a product line is excluded from the retail evaluation.
However, this interaction creates a risk that ordinary-course small-business, small-farm, or other
retail lending could substitute for more specialized community development lending that depends
more directly on CRA incentives. The agencies should require a meaningful community
development nexus and ensure that the provision does not allow banks to satisfy CD expectations
primarily through activity they would undertake in the ordinary course of business.


Essential community infrastructure and facilities should retain a meaningful CD nexus:
Section IV.D, "Community Development Definition — Revitalization and Stabilization",
Question 25
We support CRA consideration for essential community facilities and infrastructure, particularly in
rural communities, Indian Country, distressed areas, and other markets with limited access to
conventional capital. The proposal, however, would broaden eligibility for essential community
infrastructure and facilities serving specified targeted areas. These activities would no longer
necessarily need to demonstrate that they help attract or retain businesses or residents, and
community-wide infrastructure may receive consideration without allocating a particular share of
the benefit to LMI individuals.
We are concerned that large infrastructure transactions routinely financed in the conventional
market could compete with affordable housing, CDFI financing, small-business lending, and other
activities more dependent on CRA incentives. The agencies should preserve flexibility where
infrastructure addresses a genuine community development or financing gap while ensuring that
ordinary-course infrastructure transactions do not displace more targeted CD activity.
One example is Millersburg, Kentucky, a small Bourbon County community where CVC has
financed the acquisition and rehabilitation of blighted and historic properties, several of which sat
at $0 assessed value as tax-exempt parcels for years. That investment is measurably rebuilding the
town's own tax base: six previously tax-exempt properties are now taxable, and CVC's own
occupational tax filings accounted for roughly 22% of Millersburg's entire occupational tax revenue
in a recent year. This kind of structural revitalization work — removing blight, returning properties to
the tax rolls, and preserving historic structures — produces a provable, measurable community
benefit, rather than simply qualifying because a project sits inside a targeted area.
Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas: Section IV.E,
"Consideration of Community Development Activities — CD Activities Outside Assessment
Areas"; proposed § __.13(e); Question 34
We support the goal of enabling CRA-motivated capital to reach communities with significant
unmet needs but relatively few bank assessment areas. Greater geographic flexibility could be
particularly beneficial for reaching CRA deserts.
CVC serves rural small-town Kentucky communities across all of Kentucky's 85 rural counties,
including markets like Millersburg, where conventional bank presence is non-existent.
However, flexibility should supplement rather than displace CD activity in banks' own assessment
areas. The agencies are considering both quantitative and qualitative approaches for determining
when a bank has sufficiently served its assessment areas to receive consideration for outside-AA
activity.
With respect to Question 34, we support greater geographic flexibility where it can help direct CRA-
motivated capital to rural communities, Indian Country, and other underserved areas that may fall
outside traditional assessment areas. However, that flexibility should only become available after a
bank has demonstrated meaningful community development performance within its own
assessment areas.


We are concerned that the quantitative standard proposed under Option 1 is too low to meet that
objective. For large banks, the proposal would allow outside-assessment-area consideration once
a bank reaches 0.625 percent of allocated Tier 1 capital in community development loans and
0.625 percent in community development investments and grants. The agencies themselves
explain that these thresholds generally reflect the minimum level of activity needed to avoid a
"Needs to Improve" rating and are not, by themselves, sufficient to demonstrate satisfactory
community development performance.
Recent analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition further illustrates the gap
between the proposed thresholds and current bank activity. Among sixty-nine large OCC- and
FDIC-supervised banks analyzed by NCRC, current annual assessment-area community
development lending, investments, and grants totaled approximately $102 billion. Applying the
proposed 0.625% Tier 1 capital thresholds to those same institutions yielded a benchmark of
approximately $14.8 billion—roughly 85% below current activity. NCRC also found median
assessment-area community development lending equal to 6.83% of Tier 1 capital and median
qualified investments and grants equal to 3.5%, both substantially above the proposed 0.625%
benchmarks.
A standard intended to determine when a bank has adequately served its own communities should
therefore be calibrated to meaningful, satisfactory community development performance—not
merely the minimum necessary to avoid a failing rating. We encourage the agencies to adopt a
more rigorous standard that considers both the level of activity and its responsiveness to identified
community needs. We further caution against allowing a broadly defined "substantially met"
standard to weaken this safeguard. Any exception should be narrowly tailored to circumstances in
which a documented lack of community development opportunities or other performance-context
factors explain the shortfall, rather than simply allowing weaker community development
performance in individual assessment areas to be offset by activity elsewhere.
Allocation of CD activities across assessment areas: Section IV.E, "CD Activities in
Assessment Areas, Assessment Area Allocation, Assigning Assessment Area Weights"
We support greater flexibility in allocating CD activities that benefit or serve multiple assessment
areas. This could better accommodate statewide and regional CDFIs whose community impact is
not accurately represented by the physical location of their headquarters.

Support for Provisions That Could Strengthen Community Development Finance
Consider prior-period community development loans: Section IV.C, "CD Loans"; Question 8
We strongly support providing CRA consideration for qualifying CD loans that remain outstanding
from prior evaluation periods, like the existing treatment of prior-period investments. Community
development borrowers frequently need long-term, patient financing. CRA should encourage
banks to structure loans around community needs rather than examination cycles.
With respect to Question 8, we recommend evaluation period-based consideration because it
better recognizes patient, long-term CD financing and provides a more representative measure of
capital committed throughout the CRA examination period than an annual snapshot and brings
parity to the treatment of loans and investments. The agencies should base consideration on the


average outstanding balance or otherwise account for both the amount and duration of the
outstanding exposure and should treat repeated renewals of substantially the same loan as a
single exposure.
Recognize disaster preparedness and resilience: Section IV.D, "Revitalization and
Stabilization — Designated Disaster Areas"; Question 31
We support expressly recognizing qualifying activities that help communities prepare for, adapt to,
and withstand natural disasters. CDFIs frequently provide financing before and after disasters to
affordable housing developments, homeowners, small businesses, and community facilities. CRA
should recognize responsible investments that strengthen vulnerable communities before
disasters occur, not only financing provided after damage occurs.
With respect to Question 31, we recommend broadening consideration for FEMA category A/B
disaster areas, given CVC's own direct disaster-recovery work in Western Kentucky, including a
Truist-funded Western KY Disaster Relief grant and a line of credit from Paducah Bank for housing
production, where CRA-motivated capital played a direct role.
Conclusion
CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities we
serve. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and flexibility. Modernization,
however, should result in more responsible capital reaching communities with unmet credit needs,
as the CRA statute was intended.
We urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the raised asset thresholds proposed and to withdraw the
restrictions on CD operating grants and to adopt the additional recommendations above regarding
intermediate-bank CD ratings, CD-grant eligibility criteria, and assessment-area flexibility.
Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed
changes on the communities we serve.
Sincerely,


Kevin R. Smith
President and CEO

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

Two Valleys Community Land Trust in West Marin writes to object to the
harmful changes proposed to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules.
The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and
creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit,
and banking needs of communities, including low and moderate income
(LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged banks to
lend, invest and provide services in underserved communities, challenges
related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of access
remain.

TVCLT's mission is to preserve, create, and manage affordable housing in
the San Geronimo Valley, Nicasio Valley, and beyond. Our vision is for a
culturally diverse and vibrant San Geronimo and Nicasio Valley communities
that retain their unique rural and natural qualities, while offering housing
opportunities for people of all income levels and walks of life.

The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant
to uplift. The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their
expected impact on LMI communities. We request an extension of the
comment period for an additional 60 days so we have time to better
understand how much CRA activity may be lost to communities because of
this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not conduct or provide.
 The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in
underserved communities in several ways.

1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable
housing and small businesses will drop dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development
activities that support critically needed affordable housing and economic
development projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA
impact in communities as they strengthen economic stability and mobility,
quality of life, and social health of residents and communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and
"Large" Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less
CRA scrutiny and expectation to serve the community development needs of
their communities. [1] According to National Community Reinvestment
Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70 California banks would see their reinvestment
obligations reduced under the proposal. Twenty-five California banks would
shed their Community Development Test responsibilities entirely, and 45
California banks would no longer be subject to the Investment Test. [2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which
are a key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits
(NMTC) which fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas;
and EQ2 equity equivalent investments in Community Development Financial
Institutions (CDFIs) that provide small business lending in underserved
areas that banks cannot reach, and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that
take property off of the speculative market.

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors,
highlighting the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the
financing of affordable housing. [3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI
funding comes from CRA motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even
further weaken CD obligations if they adopt the alternative proposal that
Large Banks be defined as those with over $30 billion in assets.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD
finance even where they remain subject to the Community Development and
Investment Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do
significantly less CD lending and investment and still pass their CRA
examinations, all while seeking CRA credit for activity outside of their CRA
assessment areas. The proposal suggests that a bank could receive a
passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1 capital were devoted
to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower than the
percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount
necessary to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by
approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]

 Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California
will have tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small
business development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.

2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and
maintain branches in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset
threshold for a Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five banks in California
will no longer be subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that
their branches are serving LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC
estimates that 245 branches in LMI areas and 497 branches in
neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure due to this proposal.
[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in
communities. Fewer branches will result in less small business lending.
These changes will be particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our state
where smaller banks originate a larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for
banks to offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents. [7]
Deposit accounts are a gateway to credit access, financial stability, and
wealth building, especially for families who are otherwise preyed upon by
predatory financial institutions. As one important example, the BankOn
program has provided access to no or low fee bank accounts for over
fourteen million people. [8] California is home to several BankOn coalitions
that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based
organizations, and local governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19
million are underbanked. [9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged
billions of dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in
California alone, state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars
($56 million) in OD and NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that
fewer banks will be required to report data regarding their small business,
small farm, and community development lending activities. Such data is
critical to understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the
needs of local markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations
routinely analyze this CRA data when meeting with banks and commenting
on CRA exams and mergers. The loss of such data is particularly harmful at
a time when the Administration is walking back efforts to collect and disclose
detailed small business lending data under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank
Act. These changes will disproportionately impact rural communities in our
state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make up a larger part of the
small business and small farm lending markets.

 4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see
sufficient benefits.
The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the
needs of Native American communities and Tribal Nations which have been
poorly served by banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations in areas
where banks have branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches
near Tribal lands and in rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The
proposal seeks to address this CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in
community development and related activities in "Indian Country" and on
"Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of bank CRA assessment areas. But
many members of Tribes in California will not benefit from this proposal as
they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring
within particular geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated
with historic dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations
should also consider whether banks have established meaningful
relationships with, and provided direct benefits to, federally recognized
Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes. Non-federally recognized
Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access programs and
contracts with, various local and state entities. [11] Such processes exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes,
nonprofit organizations or other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-
owned businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native
American entrepreneurs by providing:
● Active outreach and engagement
● Community development loans and investments for affordable housing
and economic development projects
● Small farm and small business loans
● Home mortgage loans
● Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for
Tribes and support for Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
● Support for cultural, health and other programs
● Bank branches
● Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
● The provision of financial services such as financial literacy,
apprenticeship programs and technical assistance support

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for
activities outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions
should be made to encourage banks to engage in CRA related activity to
directly benefit Tribes, nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled
by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses that are majority owned and
controlled by Native American entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and
tracks whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with Tribes,
 Tribally controlled entities and Native owned businesses. [12] If banks know
they will be examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually
beneficial ways to work with Tribes.

5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will
suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits
by requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and
mandating that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees
will not use more than 15% of these grants on overhead. [13] As if this
wasn't enough, the FDIC and OCC question whether they should end CRA
eligibility for bank grantmaking to nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such
draconian measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups,
including smaller groups, may be impacted. [14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of
local needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit,
credit and investment products into communities inclined to trust long
established local organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs,
such as downpayment assistance programs, that support CRA related
activity, rely on bank contributions to operate. Smaller, local, and rural
organizations will be least able to meet new reporting obligations, and they
risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal would also end impactful
contributions from banks for general operating support, sponsorships, and
capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of
their communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill
in the gaps in their own capacity – seeking assistance with community
outreach, borrower education, credit building and repair, technical
assistance, legal services, job training and placement, tax assistance,
affordable housing and other services and programs which help residents
become stable and bankable so that banks can attract new deposits and
make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall
and will focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more
easily meet their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational
success. As one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks,
CDFIs will need to pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as
underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, impact measurement,
product development, and borrower technical assistance. With less support
to sustain these operational functions, organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of
CRA activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA
 activity), the large negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations
that rely on bank funding, the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are
meant to benefit from the CRA, and the disruption it will cause to
constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for
their top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan
products in, and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks,
subsidiaries and affiliates must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such
as small farm and consumer loans, are important in many communities, but
may not be among a bank's largest product lines. If regulators give banks a
pass and exempt smaller product lines from CRA oversight, banks will have
less incentive to consider how those products are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank
safety and soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and
engenders greater trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories
of loan products from scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the
purpose test, which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI
jobs, from the definition of economic development. The CRA should create
greater incentives for banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family
sustaining wages for LMI workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to
provisions that would provide CRA credit for job creation and economic
development that may only benefit middle- and upper-income workers and
communities. Such provisions ignore the purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would
provide CRA credit for large scale community infrastructure products that
generate profits for banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and
provide only incidental benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an
expansion of what qualifies for CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's
impact on LMI residents and communities. For example, banks might choose
to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing larger scale infrastructure
projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative, smaller CDFI-led
projects that better meet local community needs (such as childcare facilities,
health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The
CRA should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA
assessments areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory
oversight (with an exception made to encourage banks to better serve
Tribes, as noted above). Banks are not doing enough currently to meet the
credit and deposit needs in the areas where they have CRA responsibility, a
problem the regulators tried to address in the 2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the
proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit for projects in areas
 away from their branches, lending and CRA responsibility. This will enable
banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while
providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal
goes out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan
option to meet their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for
financial institutions that operated under a unique business model that the
CRA rules were not designed to address. The Strategic Plan option provides
for minimal public input and regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to
determine the level of reinvestment activity they need to engage in to earn a
passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with Strategic Plans tend to
reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways. The OCC's
guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable
Housing, where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered
by deed or rent restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But
CRA rules should not give banks credit for financing such activities where the
benefit to LMI residents and communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be
a resource for LMI residents, or it can be a driver of bank investment in
problematic landlords and displacement. CRA credit should be given for
financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and operated by mission-
driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI tenants, and the
bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are compliant
with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents can
reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
ratings downgrades.
The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and
redline should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or
"Outstanding" ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen
banks that passed their CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal
will only increase that number by narrowing what constitutes evidence of
discrimination that may be considered for the purpose of downgrading a
bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should consider any evidence that a
bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in discrimination, redlining, or
illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit, branching, or other
activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its source (public
or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based on data,
testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit
Opportunity Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once
again encourage banks to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that
have been redlined, excluded, and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient
information to allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on
 numerous types of entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the
communities that the CRA was meant to support. If finalized in substantially
the same form as proposed, communities will suffer significantly decreased
investment in affordable housing and CDFI support, more LMI branch
closures, higher bank account fees, fewer community serving nonprofit
organizations, and increased bank discrimination and redlining with no CRA
consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its purpose of
encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and the
OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Very Truly Yours,



Hal Russek
Executive Director
Two Valleys Community Land Trust

Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street NW,
Washington, DC 20429

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
