Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

Inland Equity Community Land Trust writes to object to the harmful changes
proposed to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by
Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for
banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities,
including low and moderate income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has
successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved
communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and
lack of access remain.

Inland Equity Community Land Trust (501c3) based in Adelanto, CA. Banks that
have complied with the CRA have offered financial literacy classes and general
operations funds for our housing project. We are members of Rise Economy and
California Community Land Trust Network.


The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift.
The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on
LMI communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional
60 days so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost
to communities because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not
conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing
and small businesses will drop dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development
projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as
they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large"
Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and
expectation to serve the community development needs of their communities.[1]
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70
California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development
Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a
key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity
equivalent investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach,
and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative
market.

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
 motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1
capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower
than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary
to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]

Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business
development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.

2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain
branches in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a
Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five banks in California will no longer be
subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their branches are serving
LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI
areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure
due to this proposal.[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities.
Fewer branches will result in less small business lending. These changes will be
particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our state where smaller banks originate a
larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to
offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are
a gateway to credit access, financial stability, and wealth building, especially for
families who are otherwise preyed upon by predatory financial institutions. As one
important example, the BankOn program has provided access to no or low fee bank
accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
 coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based
organizations, and local governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million
are underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of
dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone,
state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million) in OD and
NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm,
and community development lending activities. Such data is critical to
understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA
data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The
loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the Administration is
walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending data
under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make
up a larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.


4) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will
suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating
that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more
than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and
OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to
nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions
 to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps
in their own capacity – seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job
training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can
attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will
focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet
their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As
one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to
pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates
must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer
loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines
 from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater
trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from
scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit
middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments
areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks
are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas
where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the
2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit
for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA responsibility. This
will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while
providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
 that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
ratings downgrades.
The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should
consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in
discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit,
branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its
source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based
on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage banks
to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined, excluded,
and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to
allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
 entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and
CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Very Truly Yours,
Maribel Nunez

Maribel Nunez
Executive Director
Inland Equity Community Land Trust

moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income communities.9
The proposed rule would eliminate the "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks
could earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or
improves jobs for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income
communities. Instead, financing could qualify as economic development based primarily
on the type and size of the business and whether the financing expands, improves or
preserves the business's productive capacity, physical presence or employment base.10
We are concerned that this change would weaken the connection between CRA
economic-development credit and the people and communities CRA is intended to
benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying business expand does not necessarily
create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an underserved neighborhood or address
the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.

to demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or
neighborhoods.11 The agencies themselves acknowledge that eliminating the purpose test
would expand the universe of activities eligible for CRA credit.12

whether bank financing could shift away from activities that create or retain jobs for low-
and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. The agencies

proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in
assets. Over 400 banks with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to
annually collect and report CRA data on small business loans, small-farm loans, and
community development loans.

information to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand
whether local credit needs are being met.

lending reporting nationwide.
Before reducing reporting requirements, the agencies should analyze the impact of doing
so will have for people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income
communities, including whether it could result in a reduction in small business, small
farm, or community development lending. In addition, the agencies should explain why
changing the standard is consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records
of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
communities. Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
●
identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
scrutiny under the proposal;
●
quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community

●
assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or

●
consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and

 impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs
considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.

do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to
comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and
extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and
support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being

income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination
and disinvestment.

BANKS
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1
capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough
to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the
percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the
largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the
OCC and FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these
banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development
loans and investments inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of
annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital,
and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments.3 If each
bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625%
of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined activity
would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1
billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make
their CRA compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set
strategic plan benchmarks for CRA performance well-below historical levels of
community development activity.4
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments
and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be
accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for

The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small

community development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have

limited administrative capacity. The agencies must also determine whether those effects

should also explain why eliminating the existing connection to these outcomes is
consistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs
of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities.

LMI communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional
60 days so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost
to communities because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not
conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing
and small businesses will drop dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development
projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as
they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large"
Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and
expectation to serve the community development needs of their communities.[1]
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70
California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development
Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a
key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity
equivalent investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach,
and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative
market.

housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
 adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1
capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower
than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary
to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]

Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business
development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.

2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain
branches in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a
Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five banks in California will no longer be
subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their branches are serving
LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI
areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure
due to this proposal.[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities.
Fewer branches will result in less small business lending. These changes will be
particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our state where smaller banks originate a
larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to
offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are
a gateway to credit access, financial stability, and wealth building, especially for
families who are otherwise preyed upon by predatory financial institutions. As one
important example, the BankOn program has provided access to no or low fee bank
accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based
organizations, and local governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million
are underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of
dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone,
state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million) in OD and
NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm,
and community development lending activities. Such data is critical to
understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA
data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The
loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the Administration is
walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending data
under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make
up a larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.

4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see
sufficient benefits.
The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs
of Native American communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served
by banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations in areas where banks have
branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near Tribal lands and in
rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this
CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related
activities in "Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of
bank CRA assessment areas. But many members of Tribes in California will not
benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or
Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within
particular geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with historic
dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should also consider
whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct
benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes.
Non-federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access
programs and contracts with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes
exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit
organizations or other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses
that are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by
providing:
●​ Active outreach and engagement
●​ Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and
economic development projects
●​ Small farm and small business loans
●​ Home mortgage loans
●​ Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes
and support for Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
●​ Support for cultural, health and other programs
●​ Bank branches
●​ Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
●​ The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship
programs and technical assistance support

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities
outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to
encourage banks to engage in CRA related activity to directly benefit Tribes,
nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned
businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks
whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with Tribes, Tribally
controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work
with Tribes.

suffer.

requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating
that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more
than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and
OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to
nonprofits entirely.

 Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment

reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal

sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps

compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest

from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for

workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide

middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.

smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an

attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will
focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet
their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As
one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to
pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

 The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates
must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer
loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines
from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater
trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from
scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit
middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
 childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments
areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks
are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas
where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the
2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit
for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA responsibility. This
will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while
providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
ratings downgrades.
 The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should
consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in
discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit,
branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its
source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based
on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage banks
to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined, excluded,
and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to
allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and
CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Very Truly Yours,

Zella Knight

Zella Knight
Board President
Altadena Earthseed Community Land Trust

Dear Comptroller Gould:

I am writing on behalf of Beyond Shelter, Inc. (Beyond Shelter) to share our concerns about
the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). My perspective comes
from more than three decades working in affordable housing and community development,
including more than two decades with Beyond Shelter. I have seen affordable housing
developments move forward when the right bank partners, equity investors, and public
resources come together. I have also seen how quickly a viable development can become
difficult or infeasible when one part of the capital stack falls short.

Beyond Shelter is a mission-driven nonprofit affordable housing developer based in Fargo,
North Dakota, focused on Impacting Lives through the Power of Housing. Since I joined
the organization in 2003, I have helped lead the development of more than 1,800 affordable
homes across North Dakota, South Dakota, and Minnesota. Our work includes senior, family,
supportive, rural, and homeownership housing, as well as preservation, rehabilitation, and
new construction.

For Beyond Shelter, the proposed CRA changes are not simply a regulatory matter. They
could directly affect our ability to continue developing and preserving quality, safe, affordable
housing. Low-Income Housing Tax Credit equity, bank construction and permanent financing,
grants, public resources, and subordinate financing each serve a different purpose. If one
source is reduced or becomes more expensive, the entire development can be delayed,
reduced in scope, or become financially infeasible.


Fewer banks subject to an investment test could reduce LIHTC equity available to
Beyond Shelter
The proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion and would
treat banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than
large banks. Banks between the current large-bank threshold of $1.649 billion and $10 billion
would no longer be evaluated under a separate investment test.

That change is especially concerning to Beyond Shelter because lending and equity are not
interchangeable. A bank may be willing to provide a construction or permanent loan, but a
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit development still needs an equity investor. Without sufficient
equity proceeds, the development has a funding gap. In rural and smaller markets, there are
often fewer investors available to fill that role and less competition among them.

When LIHTC equity proceeds fall short, Beyond Shelter must find another source to fill the
gap. That can require us to seek additional state or local resources, restructure debt, reduce
the scope of a development, delay closing, or determine that the development is no longer
feasible. Each of those outcomes consumes time and organizational capacity. More
importantly, each delays or reduces the delivery of affordable homes to people who need
them.

Approximately 80 percent of annual Housing Credit equity investment is reported to come
from CRA-motivated bank investors. The proposed threshold would reportedly reduce the
number of banks classified as large from 642 to 256. Banks in the affected asset range
invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity from 2021 through 2025, with an
estimated market-wide total of up to $2 billion during that period. Reducing the number of
banks subject to a separate investment test creates a real risk of fewer active investors, less
competition, lower credit pricing, and larger financing gaps.
Buffalo Manor demonstrates the challenge Beyond Shelter already faces
Beyond Shelter's recent experience with Buffalo Manor Apartments (Buffalo Manor) in
Jamestown, North Dakota, shows how limited the rural equity market already is. Buffalo
Manor is a proposed 39-unit affordable housing development for adults age 62 and older.
The development received a conditional commitment of $1,427,888 in 9 percent Low-Income
Housing Tax Credits (Housing Credits) from the North Dakota Housing Finance Agency.

In early 2026, Beyond Shelter issued a Request For Proposals (RFP) seeking an investor to
purchase the credits and serve as the limited partner. We sent the RFP to ten LIHTC investors
and received only one response from an investor interested in purchasing the credits. We
expected the RFP process to create competition and allow us to compare pricing, terms,
timing, and the overall strength of potential investment partners. Instead, we had one option.

With only one interested investor, we had very little negotiating leverage. Our practical choice
was to negotiate the best terms possible with that investor because it was our only available
path to keep Buffalo Manor moving forward. This was not a theoretical concern about how
the equity market might operate. It was a recent BSI development with public commitments


in place and a clear community need, yet nine of the ten investors we contacted chose not to
submit a proposal.

This occurred before the proposed CRA changes. If the proposed rule further reduces the
number of banks motivated to invest in Housing Credits, Beyond Shelter could face this same
challenge more often. The likely result would be lower equity pricing, larger funding gaps,
greater reliance on already limited public resources, development delays, or developments
that do not move forward.

For the communities we serve, those outcomes are consequential. They can mean fewer
affordable homes for seniors, families, and people with limited incomes; lost opportunities to
preserve existing affordable housing; and longer periods in which identified housing needs
remain unmet.
Grant restrictions could weaken the capacity Beyond Shelter needs to deliver housing
I am also concerned about the proposed treatment of community development grants. The
proposal would limit CRA consideration to grants directly used for a community development
plan, project, or initiative and would require large banks to document that grant recipients do
not have overhead costs exceeding 15 percent.

At Beyond Shelter, there is no clean line between organizational capacity and housing
production. Our staff identifies sites and community needs, secures local support, prepares
funding applications, assembles financing, negotiates with investors and lenders, oversees
design and construction, manages compliance, and stewards the housing for the long term.
Technology, accounting, audits, legal services, insurance, compliance systems, and asset
management are part of that work. They are not separate from our mission; they are
necessary to carry it out responsibly.

If banks are discouraged from providing flexible operating or capacity-building support,
Beyond Shelter may have fewer resources to undertake difficult projects, respond to
emerging housing needs, and maintain the systems required to develop and preserve
housing. The impact is likely to be greatest in rural and smaller communities, where
developments are often more difficult to finance and nonprofit development capacity is
already limited.
Reduced reporting would make North Dakota's capital gaps harder to identify
The proposal would also exempt newly classified intermediate banks from certain CRA data
collection and reporting requirements. Published analysis estimates that North Dakota is
among six states that would lose nearly one-quarter of currently reported CRA small-
business lending data.

Beyond Shelter does not rely on data for its own sake. Reliable information helps
communities, policymakers, housing organizations, and financial institutions understand
where capital is flowing, where gaps remain, and whether rural and low- and moderate-
income communities are being served. Less reporting would make it more difficult to identify

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57]

Dear Comptroller Gould:

I, Jimmy Duran, submit this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, I also request that the OCC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agency identifies supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.

I am a Dominican-American U.S. Army veteran based in Philadelphia with a background in SBA financing and commercial lending. Through my bilingual English/Spanish business advisory work, I work daily with aspiring and operating small-business owners - many of them Latino and immigrant entrepreneurs in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods - who depend on mainstream bank credit to start, sustain, and grow. When banks pull back from these neighborhoods, the owners I serve feel it first, which is why the strength of the Community Reinvestment Act is personal to me and central to the communities I work in.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. I am concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia metro area, from 2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small businesses. Investments such as these benefited our community by expanding access to affordable mortgages for working families, small-business loans that let neighborhood entrepreneurs hire and grow, and investments in affordable housing development and preservation that keep Philadelphia's neighborhoods stable.

I am concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote to community investments and loans and I fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually, but under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million - an 80% loss.

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example, in our community, such a reduction would mean first-time homebuyers - including the Latino and immigrant families I serve - facing steeper barriers to affordable homeownership; small-business owners in North and South Philadelphia's commercial corridors unable to obtain affordable financing to expand or hire; and continued disinvestment in neighborhoods that are already fighting to rebuild.

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities like ours.

passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote to
community investments and loans and I fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling
instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually, but
under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million - an 80% loss.
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and
loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to
the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For
example, in our community, such a reduction would mean first-time homebuyers - including the
Latino and immigrant families I serve - facing steeper barriers to affordable homeownership;
small-business owners in North and South Philadelphia's commercial corridors unable to obtain
affordable financing to expand or hire; and continued disinvestment in neighborhoods that are
already fighting to rebuild.

like ours. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.
The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
 banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the
less demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests
applied to large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and
reporting requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-
business, community development lending.
A number of banks that operate in Philadelphia will now be considered either intermediate or
small banks under the proposed rule and therefore subject to less rigorous requirements. These
reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development obligations for over 800
banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks across the country, may worsen the
housing crisis by reducing investor interest in buying Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC),
and reducing access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers or access to credit for home
repairs.
Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank
service test. Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and
information about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this
criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts
from direct evaluation under the service test. As such, examiners would no longer evaluate
whether those products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though
approximately 15% of Philadelphians - over 100,000 households - remain unbanked or
underbanked. Moreover, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, these
households are overwhelmingly low-income, black, or disabled. CRA review of the cost and
features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to address these
disparities by providing affordable products, and it must continue to do so.
For the people I serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from
access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely
receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit. I
have watched bank branches close in the very neighborhoods where the entrepreneurs I work
with operate, leaving residents to travel across the city for basic banking or to rely on check
cashers and other high-cost alternatives. For the families and small-business owners I serve, an
affordable checking account is often the first rung toward building savings, establishing a
banking relationship, and qualifying for responsible credit.
This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-
income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable
mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-
business financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small
businesses and other community development.
The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
 would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-
income communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and
disinvestment.
I am also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-
based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit
organizations. These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have
deep relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.

new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller
organizations. For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff,
rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to
deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and
funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based
nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial records or program
documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks

supporting community development. I have seen how bank grants and partnerships sustain the
housing counselors, small-business advisors, and corridor managers who turn capital into real

available.

development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond

would weaken the connection between CRA economic-development credit and the people and
communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying business
expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an underserved
neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities. In my work I
have watched small businesses - corner stores, bakeries, contractors - create stable local jobs
when they can access affordable expansion capital. Under the proposal's eliminated purpose
test, a bank could earn the same CRA credit for business financing that creates no jobs for low-
and moderate-income people at all, severing the link between the credit and the communities it
was meant to serve.
Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a
qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to
demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.
I am also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and
report data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while
the proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets.
Banks with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and
report CRA data on small business loans and community development loans.
Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less
information to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local
credit needs are being met. Local community leaders and elected officials depend on this data
for decision making and for ensuring that the needs of residents are being addressed. This
proposed change is inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the
credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and
should not be in the final rule.
Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
•
identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
under the proposal;
•
quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
•
assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
including rural communities and communities of color; and
•
consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability.

should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and
released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent
significant declines in CRA-related activity. The CRA remains an essential mechanism for
 ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting community credit needs. The agencies should
not finalize changes that materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that
the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire
communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. I also urge the OCC and FDIC
to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The proposal is more than 100
Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to bank classifications,
community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core
elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not
have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected
organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the
communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to
base any final rule. I therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment
deadline by at least 60 days.
Sincerely,
Jimmy Duran
Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

I am a Dominican-American U.S. Army veteran based in Philadelphia with a background in SBA

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring

income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic

The proposed rule would eliminate this 'purpose test' and thus under the proposal, banks could
