the Dodd-Frank Act, issued on May 1, 2026, limiting the scope of small business loan reporting
for financial institutions. Together, these measures will result in significant loss of data that is
critical to effectively track trends, including early warning signs of systemic disinvestment.
Proper data collection is a necessary tool to ensure modern-day redlining does not persist and
that regulators can intervene when institutions fail to serve the communities they are located in.
More than 50 years removed from the enactment of the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act
("HMDA"), it is imperative that we recall the fight that ensued to even gain access to lending
data. It was in Chicago that Gale Cincotta galvanized communities, partnering with local and
federal elected officials to advocate against redlining, a practice that was outlawed in 1968 with
the Fair Housing Act. But years after it was outlawed, LMI communities were still being denied
credit to buy homes, start businesses, and revitalize their neighborhoods. The passage of HMDA
in 1975 was the first-of-its-kind legislation that lifted the veil, providing transparency on where
lenders were and were not lending. This acted as a catalyst to the CRA in 1977, which
encouraged financial institutions to lend in communities they acquired and chartered deposits in.
The loss of small business and other investment data under the Proposed Rules will prevent
researchers, state regulators, and the public from being able to effectively determine whether
institutions are lending in their communities. This is a profound setback in the advocacy for data
transparency and fair lending. The Department urges the agencies to maintain CRA data
reporting requirements to ensure access to this vital information is retained.
 3

Disruptions to the Dual Charter System
In response to changes in consumer lending behavior and reporting that the federal CRA alone
does not address lending disparities in LMI communities,2 Illinois enacted the Illinois
Community Reinvestment Act ("Illinois CRA"), 205 ILCS 735, in 2021. The Illinois CRA
applies not only to Illinois-chartered banks, but also to Illinois-licensed mortgage companies and
Illinois-chartered credit unions. The Illinois CRA builds off the federal CRA and utilizes HMDA
data, in addition to community development, small business, and investment reporting to assess
an institution's record.
Federal changes that significantly reduce the scope of CRA could impact charter decisions.
While the dual banking system allows for divergence in state and federal supervision, those
differences should not create incentives for institutions to select a particular charter based solely
on reduced community investment obligations. State and federal CRA frameworks complement
one another, with the federal CRA providing a baseline for assessing community investment and
the state CRA framework supplementing it. The Proposed Rules will put banks operating in
similar markets with materially different CRA expectations. Charter choices should not come at
the expense of communities' access to credit and reinvestment opportunities.
Threats to Community Development Funding
Additionally, the increased asset size thresholds would substantially reduce requirements for
banks to invest in LMI communities. In Illinois, from 2010-2024, banks contributed $124 billion
in federal CRA-qualified mortgage lending and $68 billion in federal CRA-qualified lending to
businesses in LMI communities. These investments financed affordable housing, small business
loans, essential funding for Community Development Financial Institutions, and more. For
example, CRA-qualified investments funded mobile home park improvements in Chicago's only
manufactured housing community, start-ups that led to job growth and retention, and food
pantries that serve LMI communities. Federal CRA investment requirements create a regulatory
incentive that cannot be undermined. When banks are moved into less rigorous CRA evaluation
categories, that incentive may diminish, posing a direct threat to CD funding in Illinois.
Several of the proposed amendments to CD run contrary to the purposes of the federal CRA and
its effective implementation. For example, the limits on CD grants would pose a significant
burden to both banks and organizations. Imposing a 15 percent cap on indirect costs of grant
recipients from large banks is based on a "de minimis rate" that is not supposed to serve as a cap.
See 91 Fed. Reg. 52129 n. 131. If implemented, this cap would, notwithstanding the agencies'
stated intent, reduce overall CD investments under federal CRA. This would require institutions
to collect additional reporting metrics on grant recipients, ensuring that the funding does not
exceed 15 percent in indirect costs. This places unnecessary burden on both the recipient and the

2 Linda Lutton, Andrew Fan & Alden Loury, Where Banks Don't Lend, WBEZ (June 3, 2020),
https://interactive.wbez.org/2020/banking/disparity/.
 4

institution. The proposed cap would also not account for organizations and intermediaries with
diverse structures and multi-service programs and, therefore, would impose unnecessary and
unwieldy data collection requirements in an attempt to track indirect costs. For example, many
organizations adhere to complex compliance reporting requirements and grant funding may
cover, in part, expenses such as staffing, rent, technology infrastructure, and other administrative
costs. Ultimately, the proposed requirement will significantly reduce the number of organizations
able to receive funding and deter banks from issuing CD grants and funding opportunities to
high-impact organizations.
Effect of Discrimination on Ratings
The Proposed Rules would also diminish or possibly eliminate the negative impact of a bank's
discriminatory or otherwise unlawful credit practices on the bank's federal CRA rating. Under
Option 1, the agencies would limit consideration of evidence of discriminatory practices unless
cited by a public enforcement action or a judicial ruling in a case involving a federal or state
agency—the latter expressly rejecting consideration of judicial rulings in private lawsuits. This
heightened standard serves no legitimate purpose and should be rejected. Public enforcement
actions are governed by different legal standards and therefore should not be necessary to
establish discriminatory practices for purposes of a bank's CRA rating. Even Option 2, which
would permit a finding of discrimination based upon an examination report, would still weaken
this framework by eliminating the requirement that examiners consider "the nature, extent, and
strength of the evidence" of the illegal practices.
Unlawful credit practices are antithetical to the purposes of federal CRA and should always have
the fullest adverse impact on the rating. For example, the federal CRA rating shapes an
institution's supervisory cycle, including how frequently it is examined, its public image and
credibility, and its ability to expand and operate across markets. If a bank's discriminatory or
otherwise unlawful credit practices do not negatively impact its federal CRA rating, this bank
may unfairly benefit by operating for additional years between evaluations, exacerbating the
harm to consumers and communities. Delaying corrective action enables exclusionary and
predatory practices and erodes public trust—the very ill the federal CRA is intended to
ameliorate. If banks can game the system and score passing ratings while engaging in
discriminatory practices, the federal CRA's core purpose will begin to unravel. The Department
urges the agencies to retain the current administrative rule language for the effect of
discrimination when considering a bank's federal CRA rating.
Conclusion
The federal CRA remains a bulwark against redlining and other unfair or exclusionary lending
practices. The Proposed Rules threaten to upend fifty years of economic and civil rights progress.
They represent a stark reversal in data transparency, community investment expectations, and
supervisory oversight that acts as a safeguard against discriminatory lending practices. These
changes also pose significant threats to the dual charter system. When federal CRA standards
 5

diverge sharply, a fragmented regulatory landscape incentivizes institutions to switch charters
based on which legal framework is advantageous, rather than choosing a charter based on a
framework that meets an institution's needs and aligns with the communities it serves. This
undermines the parity between state and federal charters that both federal and state law are
designed to preserve. The FDIC and OCC have a responsibility to consider such effects when
seeking to amend the federal CRA rules. For these reasons, the Department urges the agencies to
withdraw the Proposed Rules. At a minimum, the administrative rules implementing CRA should
not be amended unless adequate time is afforded to analyze the potential impacts to ensure CRA
delivers on its intent of ensuring equitable access to credit across all communities.

Sincerely,

/s/ Susana Soriano

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hilt:

NeighborWorks Salt Lake (NWSL) submits this comment letter in strong opposition to the
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). We believe the
proposed changes would significantly undermine the foundational intent of the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) by sharply curtailing bank community development
obligations and shrinking capital flows to underserved neighborhoods. Given the sweeping
scope and complexity of this rule, we urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw or substantially
revise the proposal, conduct rigorous empirical analysis of its effects on low- and
moderate-income (LMI) communities, and immediately extend the comment deadline by at
least 60 days.

 For over four decades, NeighborWorks Salt Lake has worked across the Salt Lake Valley to
build strong, vibrant, and equitable neighborhoods through affordable housing
development, community land trusts, neighborhood revitalization, and community lending.
As achartered member of the NeighborWorks network and an allied member of the
National Community Reinvestment Coatition (NCRC), NWSL operates at the front lines
where private bank capital is converted into tangible community stability. For nearly fifty
years, the CRA has served as an essential pillar ensuring that depository institutions meet
the credit and capital needs of their entire service areas, including LMI neighborhoods that
have historically endured redlining, underinvestment, and systemic barriers to wealth
creation.

The proposed rule threatens to dismantle vital incentives that sustain local community
development ecosystems. We focus our comments on the areas where the proposal will
directly impair community-based housing and revitalization efforts:

1. Drastic Reductions in Community Investment Expectations and Capital Flows

The proposal drastically lowers performance expectations, suggesting that allocating a
mere 0.625% of Tier 1 capital toward community development loans or investments would
suffice for a passing rating. According to NCRC's analysis of the 69 OCC- and FDIC-
supervised institutions in the top 100 banks by assets, large institutions currently maintain
median commitments of 6.8% of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and
3.6% for CRA-qualified investments. Lowering the compliance threshold to 0.625% creates
a regulatory floor that could cut up to $87.1 billion annually—an 85% drop—in private
capital directed to affordable housing, Community Development Financial Institutions
(CDFls), and neighborhood stabilization nationwide.

In the Salt Lake metropolitan area and across Utah's Wasatch Front, housing affordability
has reached crisis levels as rapid home price escalation has severely outpaced local wage
growth. Community developers rely directly on patient bank equity and subordinated
financing to make deep, lasting affordability viable. For example, in community land trust
developments like our Maltair Lanes and Stanbridge townhome projects, CRA-motivated
bank investments bridge vital pre-development, construction, and long-term affordability
gaps. If banks are evaluated merely against an aggregate 0.625% Tier 1 capital floor,
institutions will inevitably retreat from complex, highly impactful community land trusts
and local lending consortia in favor of simpler, standardized transactions.

2. Elimination of Community Development Scrutiny for Hundreds of Institutions
 By dramatically lifting asset thresholds—raising the small-bank threshold to $1 billion and
reclassifying institutions between $1 billion and $10 billion into an intermediate
framework—the proposal completely relieves more than 800 banks of mandatory
community development evaluations. Furthermore, roughly 417 banks moving from the
large to intermediate tier would no longer be subject to a standalone CRA investment test.
Regional and mid-sized commercial banks play an indispensable role in community
financing across the Salt Lake metropolitan area and adjacent Intermountain markets.
Under current rules, these institutions actively compete to participate in community
development loan consortia, sponsored equity poois, and local affordable housing
partnerships to satisfy their investment tests. Removing standalone Investment obligations
and community development scrutiny for banks under $10 billion will disincentivize
institutions from backing complex, locally rooted housing developments. Regulators have
provided no evidence that community credit needs diminish simply because an institution
holds less than $10 billion in assets.

3. Severe Restrictions on Nonprofit Grants and Community Operating Support

We strongly object to the provisions that restrict grant eligibility for community
development organizations. The proposed rule would disqualify CRA credit for bank grants
that fund general operating support, requiring all contributions to be tied to narrow, project-
specific activities. Additionally, it would bar CRA credit for contributions to nonprofit
organizations that report indirect or administrative costs exceeding 15% on their Form 990.
These provisions demonstrate a fundamental misunderstanding of community-based
operations:

« The Operational Reality of High-Touch Community Work: Independent research,
including analysis by the MacArthur Foundation, confirms that healthy, fiscally
sound nonprofit organizations maintain average administrative and operational
expense rates around 29%—nearly double the proposed 15% cap. Like many
community developers providing comprehensive HUD-certified homeownership
counseling, resident financial education, intake coordination, and ongoing
community land trust stewardship, NWSL's operational infrastructure requires
robust financial management, accounting, auditing, and skilled personnel. These
expenditures are not dispensable "overhead"; they are the foundational delivery
mechanism for community programs. An arbitrary 15% cap threatens to disqualify
community-anchored organizations like NWSL from bank partnership simply
because we invest in the necessary infrastructure and compliance to steward public
and private resources responsibly.
 e The Importance of General Operating Support: Restricting bank support solely to
project-level grants deprives community organizations of the flexible, predictable
capital necessary to retain qualified personnel and sustain community initiatives.

¢ Disproportionate Harm to Local Nonprofits: Requiring banks to audit grantee 990
forms and enforce rigid indirect-cost caps will create unnecessary compliance
burdens for both lenders and community partners. Banks seeking path-of-least-
resistance CRA credit will inevitably shift grant capital away from high-impact
grassroots nonprofits toward large, balance-sheet-heavy national intermediaries.

4. Loss of Regulatory Consensus and Procedural Concerns

We must also highlight that the Federal Reserve has declined to join the OCC and FDIC in
this rulemaking. Issuing divergent, fragmented CRA standards across banking regulators
undermines regulatory consistency, breeds confusion among community development
practitioners, and undermines the legal durability of the proposed framework. A regulation
of this significance requires interagency consensus grounded in measurable, transparent
data.

Conclusion and Request for Extension
Before issuing this proposal, the OCC and FDIC failed to demonstrate how these drastic
rollbacks align with the statutory mandate of the CRA. The agencies did not:
1. Identify the specific LMI communities that will experience diminished investment
and branch scrutiny;
2. Model the geographic or economic impact of shifting over 1,200 institutions into
less rigorous evaluation tiers; or
3. Account for the market-wide impact of disqualifying general operating support and
imposing unworkable 15% indirect-cost restrictions on nonprofit partners.

NeighborWorks Salt Lake urges the OCC and FDIC to withdraw this proposed rule. At
minimum, we respectfully request an immediate extension of the public comment
deadline of at least 60 days beyond the current October 13, 2026 cutoff. Community
practitioners, local governments, and neighborhood residents must be granted adequate
time to analyze local data and place the real-world costs of this proposal on the public
record.

1. Purpose
This comment concerns the proposed rule published August 12, 2026 (Federal Register
document 2026-16454, 91 FR 52114).
BRIP — Banking Reference & Intelligence Platform — measures the CRA examination record,
investment authority and balance-sheet capacity of FDIC-insured banks from public sources:
Call Reports, the Summary of Deposits, published CRA performance evaluations, and federal
and state banking law. This comment responds to the agencies' request for comment on the
proposed asset-size thresholds and the alternatives to them (§ IV.A, 91 FR 52120–52123;
Question 1, 91 FR 52122–52123). BRIP computes, for every FDIC-insured institution it can
classify, the examination tier each threshold set would assign; this comment reports the results.
It takes no position on whether the agencies should adopt the proposal or any alternative.
Under the proposal's thresholds, 410 of the 512 OCC- and FDIC-supervised institutions that are
large banks today would become intermediate banks, and 843 intermediate small banks would
become small banks. The alternatives the agencies asked about would leave between 49 and
280 institutions in the large tier.
2. Method and data
BRIP applies the proposal's two-observation rule (§ IV.A, 91 FR 52121) to total assets reported
at December 31, 2024 and December 31, 2025, using the Call Reports as republished by the
FFIEC on September 15, 2026. The current thresholds are those in effect for 2026, $412 million
and $1.649 billion (OCC Bulletin 2025-48, December 23, 2025; 91 FR 509, January 7, 2026).
Each alternative changes one threshold and keeps the proposal's other; the $10 billion / $30
billion set, as Question 1 poses it, changes both. Every threshold is applied as stated, without
inflation adjustment. The population is the 4,431 FDIC-insured institutions in the FDIC's
Summary of Deposits as of June 30, 2025. The 87 institutions with a single December report
are classified on that report, and the 10 with neither are not classified.
 No institution reported total assets exactly equal to any threshold examined here at either
December, so every count in this comment is the same whether a threshold is read as "less
than" or "or less".
Capital and surplus is BRIP's measure at December 31, 2025. For institutions that elect the
community bank leverage ratio framework, it is tier 1 capital plus the allowance for credit losses
on loans and leases; for all others, it is total capital. The instruments quoted in section 7 apply
their own definitions. The 94 institutions without a December 31, 2025 Call Report are counted
in every tier figure and excluded from every capital figure.
3. The proposal
Under the proposal's $1 billion and $10 billion thresholds, 1,253 of the 3,728 OCC- and
FDIC-supervised institutions would be in a lower tier than today, and none would be in a higher
one. Of the 1,253, 843 would move from intermediate small to small, and 410 from large to
intermediate (130 OCC-supervised, 280 FDIC-supervised). Under the current rules, large banks
are "evaluated under separate lending, investment, and service tests" (91 FR 52116); smaller
banks may elect those tests if they collect the required data (91 FR 52122, footnote 104). The
410 hold $191.9 billion of capital and surplus; 8 of them have no December 31, 2025 Call
Report and are excluded from that sum. The other 102 large institutions would remain large.
4. The alternatives the OCC and the FDIC asked about
The agencies asked about three alternatives:
● an $850 million small-bank threshold (91 FR 52121);
● a $3.252 billion intermediate-bank cap (91 FR 52122);
● a $30 billion intermediate-bank cap, with or without a $10 billion small-bank threshold
(Question 1, 91 FR 52122–52123).

aggregate outstanding investments under this part exceed 15 percent of its capital and

investments of any such bank exceed 5 percent of the capital and surplus of the bank"
(15 U.S.C. 682(b)(1)).
● Rural business investment companies: investments may not be "greater than 5
percent of the capital and surplus of the bank, association, or institution" (7 U.S.C.
2009cc-9(b)).
8. Questions for the agencies
1. Did the agencies examine, from the performance evaluations of the institutions that
would leave the large tier, the qualified investments those institutions have reported, by
type and by the geographies where they were made? Did they examine how the
standards proposed for intermediate banks would consider the same activity?
2. S. 2223 and H.R. 754, each titled the Investing in Main Street Act of 2025, would amend
15 U.S.C. 682(b) by striking "5 percent" and inserting "15 percent". Did the agencies
consider how the proposed tiers interact with that amendment?
3. Will the final rule reconcile the following statements in the notice?
○ The $3.252 billion line: it appears as a "cap of $3.252 billion" (91 FR 52122).
Intermediate banks are those with "less than $3.252 billion" (91 FR 52166), and
large banks those "greater than $3.252 billion" (91 FR 52167). Read together, the
last two place an institution at exactly $3.252 billion in neither tier.
○ The current large-bank line: it appears as "over $1.649 billion" (91 FR 52121),
"$1.649 billion or more" (91 FR 52166, 52167) and "greater than or equal to
$1.649 billion" (91 FR 52156).
○ The SBA's proposed size standard: it appears as $925 million in footnote 100
(citing 90 FR at 41271) and as $940 million in footnote 244 (citing 90 FR 41168).
9. Data available
BRIP will provide the institution-level figures behind Tables 1 and 2 to agency staff on request.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency’s (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation’s (FDIC) proposed amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. The Colorado Health Foundation (“CHF” or “the Foundation”) is a statewide, nonprofit and nonpartisan philanthropic organization with a mission to improve the health and well-being of Coloradans. The Foundation recognizes the agencies’ stated goals of reducing regulatory burden for community banks and providing greater clarity in the CRA framework. This proposed rule, however, would substantially narrow CRA examination and reporting requirements by raising the small-bank threshold from less than $412 million to less than $1 billion, establishing an intermediate-bank category of $1 billion to $10 billion, and limiting the full large-bank framework to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. These changes would move hundreds of banks into less intensive examination categories and reduce separate scrutiny of community-development lending, investments, branches, and services. The Foundation is concerned that the proposal could weaken accountability for whether banks are meeting 
local credit and investment needs, particularly in smaller and rural markets where community and regional banks can play an especially important role. 
For these reasons, the Foundation respectfully urges the agencies to withdraw these proposed changes that would significantly narrow community-development, investment, service, and data-reporting requirements. Please see attached letter for our full comments.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill,

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's
(OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed amendments to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. The Colorado Health Foundation ("CHF" or "the Foundation") is a
statewide, nonprofit and nonpartisan philanthropic organization with a mission to improve the health
and well-being of Coloradans. Through community engagement, research, grantmaking, and private
sector investments, the Foundation works to ensure that everyone in Colorado has what they need to be
healthy. The Foundation has a particular interest in ensuring that communities across Colorado have
access to the capital, affordable housing, financial services, and economic opportunities that support
good health and well-being.

The Foundation recognizes the agencies' stated goals of reducing regulatory burden for community
banks and providing greater clarity in the CRA framework. This proposed rule, however, would
substantially narrow CRA examination and reporting requirements by raising the small-bank threshold
from less than $412 million to less than $1 billion, establishing an intermediate-bank category of $1
billion to $10 billion, and limiting the full large-bank framework to banks with more than $10 billion in
assets.




These changes would move hundreds of banks into less intensive examination categories and reduce
separate scrutiny of community-development lending, investments, branches, and services. The
Foundation is concerned that the proposal could weaken accountability for whether banks are meeting
local credit and investment needs, particularly in smaller and rural markets where community and
regional banks can play an especially important role.

For these reasons, the Foundation respectfully urges the agencies to withdraw these proposed changes
that would significantly narrow community-development, investment, service, and data-reporting
requirements. As outlined below, the Foundation is concerned that:

•
Raising the asset thresholds would move hundreds of banks into less intensive CRA
examination categories, reducing separate scrutiny of community-development lending,
investments, branches, and services and limiting CRA data collection and reporting to the public.
•
The proposed geographic-flexibility standard could establish a benchmark for local community-
development activity substantially below current levels and weaken incentives for banks to
remain responsive to needs within individual assessment areas.
•
Narrowing consideration of deposit products and branch services could reduce accountability for
forms of financial access that remain important to low- and moderate-income households and
communities.
•
The proposed restrictions on community-development grants, including the 15 percent indirect-
cost standard, could make it more difficult for smaller nonprofit and community-based
organizations to obtain general operating, capacity-building, and other flexible support.

Raising the asset thresholds would substantially reduce community-development accountability and
transparency.

According to the agencies' regulatory analysis, 604 FDIC-supervised banks and 194 OCC-supervised
banks would move from the intermediate category to the small-bank category and would no longer
have a separate community-development test if this proposed rule is implemented. Another 250 FDIC-
supervised banks and 126 OCC-supervised banks would move from large-bank to intermediate-bank
treatment and would no longer be subject to the existing large-bank data collection, maintenance, and
reporting requirements.

Under existing policy, intermediate banks are separately evaluated on community-development lending,
investments, and services, while large banks are evaluated under distinct lending, investment, and
service tests. The proposal would eliminate the separate community-development test for banks below
$1 billion and apply a less rigorous evaluation to institutions between $1 billion and $10 billion.

The National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) estimates that approximately 814 banks
nationwide would no longer receive a separate community-development evaluation and another 417



would move out of the large-bank framework, leaving only the largest approximately 6 percent of banks
subject to separate reviews of community-development investments and branch services. NCRC also
estimates that the proposal would eliminate approximately 11 percent of currently reported CRA small-
business lending data nationally. These estimates illustrate the scale of the potential reduction in
community-level accountability and publicly available information.

The reduction could be particularly important in Colorado. In the Federal Reserve Banks' 2025 Small
Business Credit Survey, 52 percent of the 98 Colorado employer firms surveyed reported using a small
bank for financial services, compared with 42 percent nationally. The survey defines a small bank as an
institution with less than $10 billion in assets—the same general asset range that the proposed CRA
rule would remove from the large-bank framework.

Reducing the amount of small-business, small-farm, community-development, and assessment-area
data available for these institutions could make it more difficult for regulators, community organizations,
researchers, and financial institutions to identify unmet credit needs and lending gaps. The Foundation
urges the agencies to withdraw this proposal and to preserve meaningful community-development
evaluation and data transparency for institutions that would otherwise move into less intensive CRA
categories.

Reduced scrutiny of community-development investment could have particular consequences for
affordable housing in Colorado.
Access to affordable housing is closely connected to health and economic stability, and Colorado
continues to face substantial affordability pressures. According to the Colorado Housing and Finance
Authority (CHFA), 46.8 percent of Colorado renters are housing cost-burdened and 22.9 percent are
severely cost-burdened. More than one in five Colorado homeowners are also cost-burdened.
Community-development capital is an important part of Colorado's response. Housing Tax Credits have
helped build or preserve more than 83,500 affordable rental homes in Colorado since 1986. In the first
2026 funding round, CHFA awarded credits to 14 developments expected to support 634 affordable
rental homes and generate more than $219 million in private-sector equity across urban, rural, and
Tribal communities.
Moving hundreds of banks out of separate investment evaluations could weaken incentives for
investments such as Low-Income Housing Tax Credits, particularly in smaller markets. Because
affordable-housing projects depend on multiple public and private financing sources, the Foundation
urges the agencies to more fully analyze how reduced investment scrutiny could affect the availability of
private capital before eliminating separate investment evaluations for banks that are currently treated as
large institutions.



The proposed geographic-flexibility standard could become a ceiling on local community-
development activity.
The proposal would allow a large bank, under one option, to receive CRA consideration for community-
development activity outside an assessment area after reaching annual levels within that area equal to
0.625 percent of allocated Tier 1 capital for community-development loans and a separate 0.625
percent for investments and grants. Intermediate, wholesale, and limited-purpose banks would be
subject to a combined 1.25 percent standard.
Although the agencies describe these figures as geographic-flexibility standards rather than CRA
passing scores, NCRC found a substantial gap between the proposed benchmark and recent activity. In
its review of 69 of the 100 largest banks supervised by the OCC or FDIC, NCRC calculated
approximately $102 billion in annual assessment-area community-development lending, investments,
and grants. Applying the proposed 0.625 percent benchmark to those institutions produced
approximately $14.8 billion, about 85 percent below their observed annual activity.
That approximately 85 percent difference raises concern that the threshold could establish a
substantially lower benchmark for local community-development activity and influence bank and
examiner expectations regarding what constitutes an adequate local commitment. This is particularly
important in communities where projects may be smaller, more complex, or more difficult to finance but
where unmet housing, small-business, infrastructure, and community-development needs remain
significant.
The Foundation urges the agencies to withdraw this proposal and to ensure that any geographic-
flexibility provision preserves strong expectations for responsiveness within each assessment area and
does not reduce incentives for banks to invest above the regulatory minimum where local needs support
greater activity.
Deposit products and branch access remain important components of financial access in Colorado.
The proposal would narrow the large-bank service test to focus on credit services and would no longer
consider deposit services such as checking and savings products. The agencies describe this change as
part of an effort to focus CRA more directly on lending and credit needs. The Foundation is concerned,
however, that affordable and accessible transaction accounts are closely connected to households'
ability to enter and remain in the financial mainstream.
Colorado has made a concerted effort to expand access to safe and affordable banking. Through Bank
On Colorado, the Colorado Office of Financial Empowerment works with financial institutions, local
governments, and community organizations to connect residents to accounts that meet national
standards. According to the Office's January 2026 report, more than 58,780 Bank On accounts were



opened by Coloradans in 2024 based on data from only about one-third of participating financial
institutions, and approximately 87 percent were opened by customers new to the institution.
The substantial use of these accounts underscores the importance of affordable transaction products to
financial access in Colorado. Removing deposit products from the CRA service evaluation would
therefore eliminate an important mechanism for assessing whether large banks' retail banking services
are responsive to community needs.
NCRC also estimates that more than 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts and
more than 4,000 branches in majority-people-of-color census tracts nationwide are operated by banks
that would no longer be subject to a separate large-bank branch evaluation. These figures demonstrate
the scale of branch networks that would lose separate scrutiny and underscore the need to evaluate the
state and local effects of the proposed thresholds, not only the share of national banking assets held by
affected institutions.
The proposed restrictions on community-development grants could reduce flexible support for
nonprofit organizations.
The Foundation is also concerned about the proposed treatment of community-development grants.
Under the proposal, CRA consideration would generally be limited to grants directly used for a specific
program, project, or initiative with a community-development purpose. For grants made by large banks,
recipient organizations would also have to demonstrate that indirect costs associated with administering
the grant do not exceed 15 percent, supported by documentation that could include an IRS Form 990
and annual operating and program budgets.
If implemented, this provision would be especially impactful to community-based organizations that use
operating support and capacity-building resources to maintain staff, develop programs, administer
financing, and deliver services. Importantly, the agencies' own regulatory analysis recognizes this
possible effect. It states that the direct-use requirement, 15 percent operating-cost condition, and
related documentation requirements could mean that general operating support, capacity-building
grants, intermediary grants, and grants to smaller nonprofits receive less CRA-motivated funding.
The 15 percent standard also warrants reconsideration. In explaining its proposal, the agencies point to
OMB's Uniform Guidance. Yet, as the proposed rule itself acknowledges, OMB describes its 15 percent
de minimis indirect-cost rate as a mechanism intended to permit a more reasonable and realistic
recovery of overhead costs, particularly for organizations without the capacity to negotiate a formal
indirect-cost rate. A de minimis rate designed to ensure some recovery of indirect costs does not
necessarily establish that 15 percent is an appropriate ceiling for determining whether a community-
development grant should receive CRA consideration.



As a philanthropic organization that works with communities and nonprofit organizations across
Colorado, the Foundation recognizes the importance of ensuring that community-development
resources reach their intended beneficiaries. At the same time, project delivery necessarily requires
sufficient administrative capacity within an organization. The Foundation urges the agencies to withdraw
this proposed categorical 15 percent ceiling and to preserve CRA consideration for reasonable general
operating, capacity-building, and intermediary support where the underlying activity has community
development as its primary purpose. The agencies should seek to prevent misuse of CRA credit without
inadvertently creating a standard that makes it more difficult for smaller community organizations to
obtain flexible resources necessary to carry out qualifying work.
Conclusion
The Community Reinvestment Act remains an important framework for assessing whether federally
supervised banks are helping meet community credit needs. The Foundation supports efforts to make
CRA requirements clearer and reduce unnecessary burden, but the proposed changes could
substantially reduce scrutiny of community-development activity, investments, services, public data, and
flexible nonprofit support.
These concerns are especially relevant in Colorado, where communities face significant affordable-
housing needs, small businesses rely on banks below $10 billion in assets, and tens of thousands of
residents are using affordable accounts designed to expand access to mainstream banking.
The Foundation therefore respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the proposed asset
thresholds and related reductions in CRA requirements; to preserve meaningful consideration of
affordable deposit products and branch access; to ensure that geographic flexibility does not weaken
responsiveness within individual assessment areas; and to revise the proposed grant restrictions so that
reasonable operating and capacity-building support remains eligible for CRA consideration. The
agencies should more fully assess the effects of these changes on low- and moderate-income
communities, smaller and rural markets, affordable-housing investment, small-business credit, and
community-based organizations before finalizing policy changes of this magnitude.
The Foundation appreciates your consideration of our comments. If you have any questions, please
contact Kyle Rojas Legleiter, Colorado Health Foundation Senior Director of Policy, at
klegleiter@coloradohealth.org or 303-953-3618.
Sincerely,

Kyle Rojas Legleiter
Senior Director of Policy



The Colorado Health Foundation

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

On behalf of National Housing Trust (NHT), a national affordable housing nonprofit organization, we
appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment
Act (CRA) regulations issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation (together, the agencies). For nearly 50 years, the CRA has helped
attract private capital to communities across the country and strengthen partnerships between
banks and the community development organizations that serve them. However, several aspects
of the recent proposal would reduce the availability of capital by decreasing the number of banks
subject to meaningful CRA obligations, limit consideration for grants that spur innovation and
catalyze private investment, and redirect investment away from deeply affordable housing that the
CRA is intended to support without durable affordability protections. Together, these changes
would leave low-income residents and communities with fewer resources to build and preserve
affordable housing for generations to come.

Summary of Comments
We urge the agencies to revise the proposal in three principal ways:
•
Maintain community development investment and service obligations for banks of all sizes;
•
Protect flexible grants and operating support to mission-driven nonprofit organizations as
qualifying community development activity; and
•
Ensure meaningful, enforceable, and durable affordability and tenant-protection
requirements for naturally occurring affordable housing (NOAH) investments receiving CRA
credit.

1. Maintain Community Development Investment and Service Obligations for Banks of All Sizes
The proposal to raise CRA asset-size thresholds across small, intermediate, and large banks would
reduce the community development obligations and more comprehensive CRA evaluations that
small, medium, and large banks participate in today. From the perspective of affordable housing
practitioners, these shifts in asset thresholds risk removing important sources of financing from the
community development ecosystem.

For instance, according to the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL)1, if the
agencies finalize the rule that defines small banks as those with less than $1 billion in assets, more
than 813 banks, or 19% of all banks nationwide, would no longer be subject to separate lending,
investment and service test to determine their CRA rating, rather solely a retail lending test and
community development test. This would, in our view, no longer incentivize small banks to provide
community development loans or investments in the places where they currently do business as a
strong retail lending test would offset a small bank's performance. Smaller and regional banks often
play an outsized role in smaller, rural markets as they are best situated and willing to evaluate
mission-focused projects that may not fit the underwriting preferences or scale requirements of the
largest institutions. Removing the community development evaluations for small banks will mean
that those with total assets less than $1 billion will no longer have comparable incentives to make
direct community development loans or investments. This will result in no obvious substitute
source of capital to fill the gap in places where affordable housing is greatly needed.

Increasing the thresholds for intermediate banks would reduce the number of banks that are
subject to a separate community development investment test and therefore reduce the number of
banks willing to provide project-level investment. This would drive more borrowers toward the same
pool of large-bank capital and weaken pricing and availability for mission-driven borrowers. These
impacts would be especially significant for Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit)
transactions and other deeply affordable housing developments. The Housing Credit program, the
country's most important tool for the production and preservation of affordable rental housing,
relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. According to a 2025 study by the
accounting firm CohnReznick,2 approximately 80% of equity investments in the Housing Credit
each year come from CRA-motivated bank investors. Removing the investment test would
substantially weaken CRA incentives to make equity investments in Housing Credit properties,
especially outside the largest metropolitan markets, meaning affordable housing developers may
face higher costs and less willingness from capital providers to support innovative or mission-
driven deals. At a time when Congress and the President have expanded LIHTC through HR 1 (2025)
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, this rule change goes counter to their priorities and threatens to
weaken the country's most powerful housing production and preservation tool.

For nonprofit Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFI) lenders such as our subsidiary,
NHTCDF, the impact may vary depending on the composition of each organization's bank lender
base. Even where only a subset of current bank lenders are directly reclassified, we believe that the
broader market effect could still be meaningful. If the agencies reclassify large banks as those with
assets over $10 billion, this will reduce the number of large banks by 416, impacting approximately
10% of all banks and reducing the number of banks subject to the full CRA exam.3 These banks may

face greater demand from borrowers and intermediaries, while banks with reduced obligations may
have less reason to provide flexible, mission-oriented capital. Increasing the large bank

recommend that the agencies retain meaningful CRA obligations for banks with demonstrated
capacity to engage in community development lending, investment, and services, and avoid
changes that would reduce the number and diversity of capital providers supporting affordable
housing.

2. CRA Should Continue to Protect Operating Grants and Nonprofit Capacity Building
The agencies propose to narrow consideration for community development operating grants. While
we support accountability and transparency, we are concerned that an overly restrictive approach
would discourage banks from providing the flexible resources that nonprofit affordable housing
organizations need to serve low- and moderate-income communities effectively. Operating grants
that offer capacity-building support are essential to community development as they allow
nonprofit developers, CDFIs, and policy organizations to respond to emerging community needs
that cannot be financed through project-specific grants alone. Flexible support gives community-
oriented organizations the opportunity to identify unmet needs, develop creative solutions, and
build organizational infrastructure needed to bring promising solutions to scale. If CRA credit is
limited only to grants directly used for a narrow plan, project, or initiative, banks may reduce
support for the very organizations that create and sustain the pipeline of affordable housing and
community development activity. The risk is particularly acute for smaller and rural communities,
where nonprofit capacity is limited and flexible resources can determine whether a project moves
forward at all.

We recommend that the agencies protect and preserve CRA consideration for grants, donations,
and operating support to mission-oriented nonprofit organizations where the recipient's mission,
activities, and use of funds are substantially directed toward community development. Preserving
CRA consideration for this flexible support will enable organizations to develop creative responses
to community needs, test and scale innovative approaches, undertake the early-stage work
necessary to attract private investment, and build a durable pipeline of financeable community
development projects.

3. CRA Credit for NOAH Should Require Meaningful Affordability Protections
NHT is encouraged to see that affordable housing now includes naturally occurring affordable
housing (NOAH), and affordability is determined by rent levels. However, we are deeply concerned
that recognizing naturally occurring affordable housing without strong affordability requirements
could shift CRA-motivated activity away from low-income communities and toward effectively
market-rate middle-income rental housing. While middle-income households face real housing
affordability challenges in many markets, expanding CRA eligibility to NOAH without enforceable
affordability limits could reward activity that does not produce durable community development
benefits, conflicts with the purpose of CRA, and could dilute scarce bank investments that are
needed for deeply affordable homes.

The agencies should avoid a framework in which banks can receive CRA credit for homes affordable
to households well above low-income levels such as 80% of area median income (AMI), particularly
in high-cost markets where lenders are already willing to invest. Broad NOAH eligibility would
reduce the capital available to populations that the CRA is intended to serve. LIHTC and other
restricted affordable housing developments, serving households at 60% AMI or below, would have

For example, the broad definition, proposed by the agencies, ties to income levels as high as 120%
AMI and could permit credit for properties serving households far above the income levels CRA is
meant to prioritize. In a high-cost market such as Washington, D.C., that could include rents of
greater than $5000 per month and incomes of more than $196,700 for a family of four – statistics
that bear little relationship to the housing needs of low- and moderate-income families. CRA credit
should focus on activity targeted to the low-income households and communities it was intended
to benefit.

If the agencies decide to recognize NOAH activity, they should require clear safeguards that, at
minimum, should include recorded or otherwise enforceable affordability restrictions, rent-growth
limits designed to prevent displacement, income targeting that prioritizes low- and moderate-

sponsor-imposed restrictions or comparable mechanisms where public subsidies are not present.
CRA credit should be calibrated to encourage preservation that would not otherwise occur, deepen
affordability where possible, and prevent tenant displacement. It should not create a higher-return
alternative that draws bank capital away from permanently restricted affordable housing, Housing
Credit developments, and projects serving residents with the greatest needs.
Conclusion
The Community Reinvestment Act has long been a critical tool for directing bank capital toward
communities that have faced disinvestment and unequal access to credit. For nonprofit affordable
housing developers and CDFI lenders such as NHT, CRA-motivated lending, investment, and grants
help make deeply affordable housing possible. The proposed changes should strengthen, not
weaken, that ecosystem. We respectfully urge the agencies to reconsider the changes to eligible
CRA activity based on proposed asset-size threshold increases, preserve CRA consideration for
operating grants and nonprofit capacity-building support, and ensure that any recognition of
naturally occurring affordable housing includes meaningful, enforceable, and durable affordability
protections. Thank you for considering these comments.

October 13, 2026

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations

As Greater Boston's oldest and largest community foundation, the Boston Foundation is committed
to closing the gaps that drive the region's greatest disparities. Through our civic leadership,
research, grantmaking, partnerships, and advocacy, we work to expand opportunity, advance
equity, and build thriving communities.

Central to this work is the Foundation's Community Wealth pathway, which focuses on increasing
economic mobility and building long-term wealth in historically marginalized communities.
Through this effort, the Foundation advances strategies that advance affordable housing and
homeownership, strengthen community development, and expand access to capital and technical
assistance for underserved small business owners. Together, these investments help create more
equitable, resilient, and prosperous communities throughout Greater Boston.

On behalf of the Boston Foundation, we respectfully urge the withdrawal of the proposed
amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The proposed changes would weaken
a longstanding and highly effective framework that helps ensure financial institutions meet the
credit, investment, and service needs of low- and moderate-income communities. Collectively,
these changes would reduce transparency, diminish accountability, and weaken incentives for
banks to make meaningful investments in historically underserved communities.

The CRA is one of the nation's most important tools for promoting equitable access to capital,
financial services, and community investment. Enacted to address decades of discriminatory
lending practices and disinvestment, it requires federal regulators to regularly evaluate banks
serving low- and moderate-income communities. Since receiving a poor CRA grade can hinder a
bank's ability to expand, the law incentivizes financial institutions to lend in underserved
communities. These investments have generated billions of dollars in economic activity and
community development financing, expanded pathways to homeownership and entrepreneurship,
and strengthened local economies by providing residents with opportunities that the private market
alone has often failed to deliver.

CRA review requirements vary by bank size, with larger institutions subject to more comprehensive
regulations. The proposed increase in CRA asset thresholds would move roughly 800 banks into the
"small bank" category, eliminating their community development obligations and reducing the
banks subject to those requirements by 40%. More than 400 currently large banks would also be
reclassified as intermediate institutions with less rigorous community development standards,
leaving only 86 banks subject to the highest level of scrutiny. As a result, communities across the
country could face substantial reductions in the investments and services that support economic
mobility and neighborhood stability.

 These investments often fill financing gaps that would otherwise go unmet. Community
development projects and small business lending programs frequently rely on CRA capital to move
forward, including affordable housing projects financed through the Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit program. Weakening community development obligations would likely diminish investment
in these projects, slowing progress toward economic equity, limiting opportunities for wealth
creation, and widening existing racial and economic disparities in addition to a worsening housing
crisis.

The proposal would also weaken oversight of bank branches and financial services in underserved
communities. The over 400 banks that would lose branch evaluation requirements as a result of
being reclassified as intermediate operate approximately 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-
income census tracts (30% of all branches in those communities) and 4,000 branches in majority
people-of-color census tracts (23%). Reducing branch evaluation requirements and eliminating
incentives tied to important banking products could limit access to financial services and further
disadvantage communities.

Nearly five decades after its enactment, the CRA remains a critical safeguard to ensure banks meet
the credit needs of all communities. The proposed rule departs from that foundational purpose by
lowering expectations, reducing accountability, and weaking incentives for meaningful community
reinvestment. At a time of growing housing affordability challenges and persistent racial and
economic inequities, federal regulators should preserve and strengthen this framework that has
helped direct billions of dollars to communities that have been historically excluded from
investment.

Sincerely,


Courtney Brunson
Senior Director, Economic Equity Initiatives


Soni Gupta
Associate Vice President, Community Wealth

II.
Indirect Effects that Could Alter Certain Bank LP Incentives

SBIA acknowledges that the primary statutory purpose that underpins the CRA is to ensure that
federally regulated financial institutions meet the credit needs of the communities from where they
take deposits, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Those credit needs generally
revolve around retail lending for home mortgages and small business needs.

Federal regulators concentrate this Proposal on streamlining retail lending metrics and revising
formulas and tests used to evaluate a financial institution's lending performance against this
statutory purpose. While community development investments by financial institutions are a
material component, we acknowledge that retail lending is a far more expansive component of the
CRA evaluation process.

The FDIC and OCC recommend revisions to asset thresholds that define small banks (below $1
billion in assets), intermediate banks ($1 billion to $10 billion) and large banks (more than $10
billion in assets). Because of the Proposal's streamlining effects there would be more small and
intermediate-sized financial institutions with total assets below $10 billion subject to fewer CRA
requirements. Regulators also recommend an evaluation realignment to focus on major product
lines (e.g., consumer, home mortgage, small business, and small farm loans) under the Retail
Lending test used to evaluate a financial institution's CRA credit eligibility.

SBIA takes no position on the Proposal's streamlining recommendations, but we warn that these
changes may trigger potential indirect effects that could alter the economic calculus among certain
small and intermediate-sized banks from making new investments in SBICs/RBICs or growing
their existing investment portfolios in these funds.

(a) Higher Bank Asset Thresholds May Discourage Bank Investment in SBICS/RBICs

The Proposal is positive because it expressly confirms that investments in licensed SBICs and
RBICs fall within the "government programs" category of economic development. This reduces
uncertainty concerning threshold eligibility for CRA consideration. The proposed realignment of
bank asset thresholds, however, may reduce the marginal CRA value of SBIC and RBIC
investments for certain community and regional banks.

Banks that move from the large-bank framework to the intermediate-bank framework would no
longer be evaluated under a separate investment test, although qualifying investments may continue
to receive consideration under the Community Development (CD) test. The practical concern is not
that such investments become irrelevant, but that they may become less important to the bank's
overall CRA result.

Based on the role CRA treatment plays in some banks' fund-allocation decisions, SBIA is
concerned that reducing the distinct rating significance of qualified investments could affect
whether some community and regional banks make commitments, the amounts committed, and the
range of strategies considered.

The final rule should confirm that qualifying SBIC and RBIC investments: (i) receive meaningful
consideration under the Community Development test for intermediate-sized banks and, (ii) for
small banks, may enhance the determination whether otherwise satisfactory lending performance

Introduction

CBAI and its member community bankers support the CRA, which was enacted by Congress in
1977 and is intended to encourage depository institutions to meet the needs of the communities
in which they operate, including low- and moderate-income ("LMI") neighborhoods, consistent
with the safe and sound operation of such institutions. The CRA requires that each insured
depository institution's record in helping meet the needs of its entire community is evaluated

banking regulators that are responsible for supervising their depository institutions, which are,

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

The California Community Land Trust Network writes to object to the harmful
changes proposed to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was
passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative
obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of
communities, including low and moderate income (LMI) communities. While the
CRA has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in
underserved communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination,

working to support the growth of permanently affordable, community controlled

●​ The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship
programs and technical assistance support

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities
outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to
encourage banks to engage in CRA related activity to directly benefit Tribes,
nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned
businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks
whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with Tribes, Tribally
controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work
with Tribes.

4) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will
suffer.




The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating
that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more
than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and
OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to
nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions
to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps
in their own capacity – seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job
training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can
attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will
focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet
their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As
one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to




pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

5) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates
must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer
loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines
from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater
trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from
scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit




middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments
areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks
are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas
where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the
2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit
for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA responsibility. This
will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while
providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.





Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

6) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
ratings downgrades.
The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should
consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in
discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit,
branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its
source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based
on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage banks
to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined, excluded,
and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to
allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and




CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Sincerely,

Maddie Ribble
Co-Director
California Community Land Trust Network

October 9, 2026

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
