The need for affordable housing remains most acute among LMI households. The number
of cost-burdened rental households has reached an all-time high, with 22.7 million
households spending more than 30 percent of their income on rent and utilities (defined as
"cost burdened"), and that percentage is even higher for poorer households. Over 80
percent of households making under $30,000 are cost burdened, and over 70 percent of
households making between $30,000 and $45,000 are cost burdened.

We support extending CRA credit to debt financing provided to naturally occurring
affordable housing. However, we believe some sort of standard should be in place to
ensure that CRA credit is not extended for the acquisition of NOAH property that is then
converted — with or without some rehabilitation expenditures — to market-rate housing. A
standard should be adopted that requires a LURA for rents at 30% of 80% of AMI and
provides full or partial credit based on the affordability of the property's rents during the
term of the loan that is receiving CRA credit.

While we support efforts to increase affordable housing development in high opportunity
areas, we don't agree that providing CRA credit to loans on housing for middle income
individuals in high opportunities areas merits special CRA recognition absent some
evidence that the debt and equity markets are not fully functioning to provide capital for
middle income housing in these areas. Given scarce resources and the relative difficulty of
attracting capital to housing dedicated to LMI households, any CRA related incentives for
affordable housing should be focused on properties supporting LMI communities

Conclusion

Thank you again for the opportunity to provide comments on the NPR. We are grateful to
the regulators for their efforts to modernize CRA rules and solicit comments on ways to
ensure that CRA continues to drive investment to underserved communities, especially
the rural markets that we serve.

Despite its shortcomings, CRA has been successful at achieving its objectives, increasing
the level of bank activity serving LMI communities. Since CRA has absolutely critical to the
success of the LIHTC program, we encourage the regulators to reduce potential negative
impacts on LIHTC investment that could undermine rural communities' ability to respond
to the housing affordability crisis.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
OCCH appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed amendments to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. OCCH supports the agencies' goals of improving clarity,
consistency, predictability, and proportionality in CRA supervision. We also recognize the
importance of reducing unnecessary regulatory burden while preserving a durable framework that
continues to direct private capital toward communities with unmet credit and investment needs.
OCCH is a mission-driven nonprofit aƯordable housing organization and Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit (Housing Credit or LIHTC) syndicator. Since its founding, OCCH has closed approximately
$7.226 billion of equity with equity from 84 unique investors. Our work supports aƯordable housing
and community development in urban, suburban, smaller-city, and rural markets. Community and
regional banks are essential partners in that work, often serving simultaneously as equity investors,
construction and permanent lenders, deposit partners, grant providers, New Markets Tax Credit
participants, and long-term civic partners. OCCH is an active member in the LIHTC, CDFI and
aƯordable housing communities with board and participation among a number of federal, state and
local organizations including National Association of State and Local Equity Funds (NASLEF), the
AƯordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), and the National Association of AƯordable
Housing Lenders (NAAHL).
 OCCH CRA Comment Letter | October 13, 2026 | 2

OCCH is concerned that several provisions of the proposal, particularly the proposed $10 billion
large-bank threshold, the resulting removal of the standalone Investment Test for many community
and regional banks, changes to the intermediate-bank Community Development Test, and
restrictions on qualifying grants, could unintentionally reduce aƯordable housing and community
development activity in markets that already have the greatest diƯiculty attracting capital. Our
comments are informed by OCCH's direct experience and data, as well as the analyses and
recommendations developed by NASLEF, AHTCC, and NAAHL.
CRA and the Housing Credit are complementary public-private partnerships
CRA has played a central role in building a deep, competitive, and eƯicient Housing Credit equity
market. Banks provide approximately 75 to 85 percent of Housing Credit equity, and AHTCC reports
that at least 71 percent of total Housing Credit equity surveyed in 2025 was CRA-motivated. The
standalone Investment Test creates a clear incentive for community development investment while
preserving banks' discretion to select appropriate investments, sponsors, and markets.
That demand directly aƯects aƯordable housing production. Housing Credit equity and debt serve
diƯerent functions in a development's capital stack, and additional lending cannot substitute for
lost equity. A broad investor base supports competitive pricing, increases the private capital
generated by each allocation of Housing Credits, reduces financing gaps, and allows limited public
resources to support more aƯordable homes.
Congress recently expanded the Housing Credit to increase aƯordable housing production. CRA
policy should reinforce that action by maintaining strong demand for Housing Credit investments,
not oƯset the intended production increase by diminishing the incentives for community and
regional banks to participate.
The proposed $10 billion threshold would remove an important investment incentive
Under the proposal, banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would be classified as
intermediate banks and would no longer be evaluated under a separate Investment Test. AHTCC's
survey found that 108 OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks below the proposed $10 billion threshold
invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity during the 2021-2025 survey period.
Extrapolated to the broader Housing Credit market, AHTCC estimates that banks below the $10
billion threshold invested approximately $2 billion over those five years.
The eƯect would extend beyond the direct loss or reduction of individual commitments.
Community and regional bank investments frequently complete multi-investor funds that also
include large banks, government-sponsored enterprises, insurance companies, and other
institutional investors. Because many investors limit their ownership to a stated percentage of a
fund or require a diversified investor roster, the loss of smaller-bank commitments can also reduce
the amount that larger investors are able or willing to commit. The resulting contraction may exceed
the amount of the departing investment.
 OCCH CRA Comment Letter | October 13, 2026 | 3

OCCH has experienced this dynamic directly. 36 of OCCH's 84 historical investors fall within the
$412 million to $10 billion asset range. Although these relationships represent approximately 10
percent of OCCH's historical equity volume, they represented approximately 14 percent of OCCH's
volume during the most recent five-year period analyzed, demonstrating the growing participation
of community and regional banks in aƯordable housing investment.
OCCH's analysis identifies 19 active bank investors with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion
that could be aƯected by the proposed structure. These investors represented approximately 10
percent of OCCH's investment activity during the period reviewed. Their reclassification could
aƯect not only their direct commitments, but also other investors whose commitments are
constrained by ownership limits or diversification requirements.
The potential impact is illustrated by OCCH's most recently closed multi-investor fund, which
closed with $300 million of committed LIHTC equity, which financed the construction or
rehabilitation of 1,743 units. OCCH's analysis indicates that, if only banks with assets above $10
billion had participated, the fund size would have been decreased to approximately $244.5 million,
which would have financed the construction or rehabilitation of 1,421 units. Under a $3.252 billion
threshold, the fund size would have decreased to approximately $276.5 million, which would have
financed the new construction or rehabilitation of 1,606 units. This diƯerence demonstrates why
the impact should not be measured solely by subtracting the commitments of reclassified banks.
Adopt the $3.252 billion alternative if the large-bank threshold is increased
OCCH joins NASLEF and AHTCC in recommending that, if the agencies increase the large-bank
threshold, they adopt $3.252 billion rather than $10 billion.
AHTCC's survey indicates that a $3.252 billion threshold would substantially reduce disruption.
Compared with the proposed $10 billion threshold, it would reduce the number of aƯected Housing
Credit investors by approximately 63 percent, from 108 banks to 40, and reduce the estimated five-
year Housing Credit equity aƯected from approximately $2 billion to $272 million. AHTCC also
found that approximately 86 percent of the Housing Credit equity invested by OCC- and FDIC-
regulated banks with assets between $1.65 billion and $10 billion came from banks with assets
above $3.252 billion.
The $3.252 billion alternative also has a clear policy basis. It is the inflation-adjusted equivalent of
the OCC's 2020 $2.5 billion threshold, which was calibrated to preserve the relative distribution of
banks among regulatory categories.
OCCH's analysis indicates that a threshold at this level would still provide substantial regulatory
relief. Approximately 90 percent of banks would remain subject to a more limited regulatory scope,
while the standalone Investment Test would be preserved for institutions responsible for the
substantial majority of active Housing Credit investment in the aƯected asset bands.
 OCCH CRA Comment Letter | October 13, 2026 | 4

OCCH strongly opposes a $30 billion large-bank threshold. AHTCC found that more than 140 banks
below that threshold captured in its survey invested at least $3.575 billion of Housing Credit equity
during the five-year survey period, with an estimated broader-market impact of approximately $4.5
billion. NAAHL also reports that banks with less than $30 billion in assets made nearly $53.5 billion
in community development loans in 2024, representing more than one-third of bank community
development lending by dollar volume and 64 percent by number of loans.
Rural and smaller markets would bear a disproportionate impact
The proposed threshold would create particularly serious consequences for rural communities,
smaller cities, and other markets with limited large-bank presence. AHTCC's survey found that
approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity from banks below $10 billion supported rural
markets. By comparison, approximately 8 percent of Housing Credit equity in the cited industry-
wide sample was invested in nonmetropolitan counties. Community and regional banks therefore
play an outsized role in rural Housing Credit investment.
OCCH's experience is consistent with that conclusion. Fifteen of the 27 OCCH investors examined
in the broader aƯected asset bands are headquartered in rural or smaller markets, and additional
banks headquartered in larger markets serve substantial rural areas. OCCH also found that
investment from potentially aƯected banks has increased, representing approximately 15 percent
of OCCH equity raised during the most recent five-year period studied.
Rural developments are often smaller, have fewer potential investors, and receive less pricing
competition than developments in highly sought-after CRA markets. In these communities, a
relatively modest commitment from a locally-aligned bank can determine whether a development
is financially feasible. The loss of one investor can also impair an entire multi-investor fund that
provides diversification and access to smaller rural transactions.
Local banks bring knowledge and relationships that cannot be replicated simply by shifting the
same opportunity to a national investor. They understand local employers, housing conditions,
sponsors, public partners, and residents. Their Housing Credit investments are frequently
connected to construction loans, permanent financing, deposits, financial education, credit-
building services, homeownership counseling, and other community activities.
Accordingly, the key question is not whether the national Housing Credit market might eventually
replace a portion of the lost capital in aggregate. It is whether capital will remain available on
workable terms in the specific rural and smaller markets served by the banks being reclassified.
Preserve a meaningful Community Development Test for intermediate banks
If the final rule places more institutions in the intermediate-bank category, the Community
Development Test should remain a meaningful and independent component of the CRA evaluation.


 OCCH CRA Comment Letter | October 13, 2026 | 5

The proposed changes would permit stronger retail lending performance to oƯset weaker
community development performance. OCCH recommends retaining the current requirement that
an intermediate bank achieve at least a Satisfactory rating on both its retail lending and community
development performance to receive an overall Satisfactory rating. NASLEF, AHTCC, and NAAHL
have identified the same concern.
Community development loans, investments, grants, and services perform related but distinct
functions. A bank should not be able to replace Housing Credit equity, grants, or patient community
development capital solely by increasing conventional lending. Housing Credit equity is not
interchangeable with debt, and excessive debt can undermine rather than improve a development's
feasibility and long-term stability.
Protect community-based organizations and nonprofit capacity
OCCH shares NAAHL's and NASLEF's concerns regarding the proposed restrictions on community
development grants, including the proposed 15 percent limitation on administrative costs.
AƯordable housing and community development require capable local organizations. StaƯ,
technology, compliance, resident outreach, financial counseling, grant administration, and
organizational infrastructure are necessary to deliver measurable outcomes. An organization's
administrative expense ratio, standing alone, does not determine the eƯectiveness or community
impact of its work.
Restricting consideration to grants tied narrowly to a particular program, project, or initiative,
combined with a rigid administrative-cost cap, could reduce organizational capacity and
discourage bank grantmaking. The limitation would be especially diƯicult for smaller nonprofits and
organizations serving rural or high-need communities, where staƯing and operating capacity are
already constrained.
OCCH therefore urges the agencies to maintain current CRA eligibility for grants that support
qualifying community development purposes and to evaluate grants based on demonstrated
outcomes, responsiveness, accountability, and community need rather than a fixed overhead
percentage.
Maintain CRA's focus on LMI households and recognize each component of community
development finance
OCCH supports clearer treatment of naturally occurring aƯordable housing, but CRA incentives
should remain focused on low- and moderate-income households and communities. Any standard
for naturally occurring aƯordable housing should include meaningful aƯordability protections and
should avoid diverting scarce CRA-motivated capital from households and communities with the
most acute needs. Seeting clear parameters around what qualifies (ie. More than 50% of the
community serves 80% AMI or lower) and making sure the aƯordability of the property is
 OCCH CRA Comment Letter | October 13, 2026 | 6

maintained for a period of time (similar to a LIHTC LURA) would help provide a framework for what
qualifies.
The final regulation should recognize the separate roles of loans, investments, grants, and services.
AƯordable housing projects frequently require all four. Complexity and responsiveness should be
evaluated based on community impact and the diƯiculty of assembling and executing the
financing, not primarily on whether an investment is tied to a loan. LIHTC and CDFI investments can
be highly responsive and complex even when they are not part of a transaction that includes a loan
from the same bank.
OCCH supports providing consideration for qualifying community development loans that remain
outstanding from prior evaluation periods, similar to the treatment of prior-period investments. This
approach should encourage banks to structure patient financing around community needs rather
than examination cycles, while maintaining expectations for a meaningful overall level of
community development activity.
Recommendations
Thank you for letting us comment on the potential changes. Below are OCCH's recommendations
in order to remove some regulatory burden and continue to benefit the communities LIHTC serves:
• If the large-bank threshold is increased, adopt $3.252 billion rather than $10 billion.
• Do not adopt a $30 billion large-bank threshold.
• Require intermediate banks to achieve at least a Satisfactory rating on both retail lending
and community development performance to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
• Design geographic flexibility to produce additional investment in rural and underserved
markets after local assessment-area needs are met.
• Maintain current CRA eligibility for grants that support qualifying community
development purposes and do not impose a rigid 15 percent administrative-cost cap.
Conclusion
OCCH supports targeted CRA modernization that improves clarity, reduces unnecessary burden,
and preserves flexibility. Those goals can and should be achieved without weakening the
investment incentives that help make aƯordable housing and community development possible.
The proposed changes should be evaluated not only by the number of banks receiving regulatory
relief, but also by what communities could lose if local and regional institutions have less incentive
to invest. Community banks may provide a smaller share of national Housing Credit equity by dollar
volume, but their participation can have an outsized eƯect on rural developments, multi-investor
funds, local partnerships, and the ability to attract additional private capital.
 OCCH CRA Comment Letter | October 13, 2026 | 7

OCCH believes the $3.252 billion alternative provides a reasonable and constructive balance. It
oƯers substantial regulatory relief while preserving CRA investment incentives for the institutions

Chief Counsel's Office, Attention: Comment Processing

-218

-52218 , August 12, 2026)

Dear Comptroller Jonathan Gould and
Chairman Travis Hill
:
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce's
(the Chamber) Center for Capital Markets
Competitiveness (CCMC) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)
1
issued jointly by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC).

The Chamber and its members reaffirm our unwavering support for the CRA's
vital statutory mission: to expand access to credit, capital, and financial services in
low- and moderate -income (LMI) and underserved communities. For decades, the
banking industry
has demonstrated an enduring commitment to community
development, investing hundreds of billions of dollars into affordable housing, small
business growth, and critical municipal infrastructure. We appreciate the agencies'
fundamental decision in this NPRM
 to recognize and adhere to statutory limits
—as
highlighted by the agencies' July 2026 motion to vacate the enjoined 2023 rule. We
specifically commend the agencies for correcting
course by anchoring evaluations to

1 https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/12/2026
-16454/community -reinvestment -act -
regulations .
 2

physical facility geographic footprints and properly excluding deposit products from
the lending assessment
 as necessitated by statute
.
To ensure institutions have adequate time to properly operationalize these
rules, we strongly urge the agencies to provide a realistic, two
-year implementation
period, with all rule changes
and required data collection and reporting
taking effect
on January 1st of the third calendar year following the effective date of the final rule.
Moreover, for any given bank, changes should take effect at the start of its next
evaluation period to avoid different rules applying to different portions of
said given
bank's evaluation.
This specific, extended timeframe is not merely a preference; it is a
vital operational necessity. Institutions require extensive time to build new operational
processes, update complex data reporting systems with third
-party processing
vendors, train comp liance personnel, adjust long -term CRA strategies,
 and account
for the outcome of any potential ongoing litigation.
 The agencies should ensure that
institutions' plans for existing evaluation periods are not
disrupted and that banks are
not assessed under two different frameworks for the same evaluation period.

While the NPRM provides critical regulatory relief and appropriately respects
key statutory guardrails, other elements of the proposal threaten to unnecessarily
disrupt the historically proven 1995 framework. The ultimate success, workability, and
durabili ty of any finalized rule rely on preserving the predictable structure of which
business lines are evaluated, achieving interagency consistency, prioritizing
meaningful qualitative performance context over rigid quantitative formulas, and
retaining the curr ent Service Test framework's focus on physical branch networks
while providing positive consideration for modern delivery channels.

I. Overarching Principles & Procedural Concerns

The Necessity of Interagency Consistency and Rule Durability

The Chamber is deeply concerned by the fractured, multi
-track rulemaking
process currently unfolding among the federal banking agencies.
2 A cornerstone of
the CRA's historical success has been the unified regulatory front presented by the

2 See U.S. Chamber of Commerce,
Comment Letter on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
 (April
8, 2020), available at
https://www.uschamber.com/assets/documents/ccmc/4.8.20_CCMC_CommunityReinvestmentActReg
ulations_FDIC -_OCC.pdf (detailing the Chamber's longstanding advocacy for a unified interagency
approach).
 3

OCC, FDIC, and the Federal Reserve Board. Inconsistent rules across banking
charters invite regulatory arbitrage, drastically compound compliance challenges, and
disrupt the secondary markets for community development financing. When
community groups and s
yndicators must navigate
different regulatory incentives
depending on a partner bank's charter, the entire community development ecosystem
suffers from friction and delay.
While the Chamber acknowledges the complex political and structural hurdles
currently separating the agencies' rulemaking tracks, regulators must prioritize
unified action. Proceeding with a fragmented approach fundamentally weakens the
legal and political
 durability of the final rule, perpetuating market uncertainty rather
than resolving it.
To achieve a unified, durable framework, the Chamber strongly recommends a
consensus -first approach. If the Federal Reserve cannot align with the entirety of the
OCC and FDIC proposal, all three agencies should work together to issue a consensus
rule or continue to operate under the 1995 framework until a three
-agency consensus
rule is achieved. Issuing separate, competing regulatory frameworks is an
unacceptable outcome that will ultimately harm the LMI communities the agencies
seek to protect.
Establishing a Durable, Defensible Framework

A highly functioning regulatory framework must be capable of enduring legal
challenges and administration changes, giving banks and community partners the
certainty needed for long
-term capital commitments. The foundational 1995
framework still works. It h
as successfully increased access to credit, spurred vital
investments in LMI communities, boosted affordable housing creation, and set clear
performance standards that allow banks to predictably integrate community
development (CD) into their core business models.
3
The Chamber strongly cautions against any categorical shift away from the
1995 framework's core focus on mortgage, small business, and small farm lending.
The proposal to aggressively expand the scope of evaluations risks diluting the CRA's
original intent . While wider consumer lending promotes general financial convenience,

3 ee U.S. Chamber of Commerce,
Comment Letter on 2022 CRA NPRM
 (August 5, 2022), available at
https://www.fdic.gov/system/files/2024
-06/2022 -community -reinvestment -act -3064 -af81-c-226.pdf
(defending the foundational stability and predictability of the existing CRA framework).

 4

it is the core commercial and mortgage credit products that drive the long
-term
wealth creation, generational equity, and structural economic gains for LMI
households that the CRA was designed to catalyze. Further necessary enhancements
to the CRA should be achieved
 through non-binding interagency guidance, updated
Q&As, and industry bulletins rather than continuous, highly disruptive formal
rulemakings.
Transition, Reliance, and the Protection of Existing Commitments

In the business of community development
—particularly concerning Low
-
Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC), New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC), and large
-
scale infrastructure projects
—capital deployment is inherently long
-term. Regulators
must recognize that bank
s establish multi
-year CRA strategies, targets, and
community capital commitments based on existing rules. These projects require years
of underwriting, co-investment structuring
, and phased funding.

Therefore, the agencies must ensure that material methodological changes are
not applied retroactively to existing evaluation periods. Specifically, institutions
operating under approved CRA Strategic Plans must be explicitly protected from
shifting regula tory goalposts. These long
-term, agency -approved commitments must
be honored so that banks are not retroactively penalized for executing on
 community
investments that are already in progress. Any final rule must include robust transition
periods and grandfathering provisions for existing community development
commitments and approved Strategic Plans.

II. Recognizing Regulatory Relief & Defining the Scope of Evaluations

Modernized Asset
-Size Thresholds

While the Chamber generally supports providing sensible regulatory relief to
community institutions and updating asset
-size criteria to reflect inflation, we are
deeply concerned by the sheer magnitude of the proposed jump to a $10 billion large
bank thres hold. The Chamber supports maintaining the current large bank threshold
of $1.649 billion. If the agencies are determined to increase the threshold to reflect
macroeconomic realities, such an increase should be capped at $3.252 billion
 5

(reflecting the OCC's 2020 intermediate bank cap of $2.5 billion, adjusted for
inflation). 4
The Chamber opposes increasing the large bank threshold to $10 billion, and
strongly oppose s any alternative proposals to raise it even further to $30 billion.
Drastically increasing the threshold to $10 billion
—and certainly anything
approaching $30 billion
—would have severe, unintended consequences for
Community Development financing, particula
rly in the LIHTC and NMTC markets.
Mid-sized and regional banks operating below the proposed $10
billion and
$30 billion thresholds are frequently the primary purchasers of these tax credits in
localized markets and rural areas. Removing them from the large bank requirements
by arbitrarily elevating the threshold would significantly reduce aggregate
community
development activity, destabilize critical tax credit syndication channels, diminish
funding for local nonprofits, and heavily curtail necessary investment in structural
rural banking deserts.
 Requiring fewer data collection and reporting requirements
from intermediate banks, combined with the proposal allowing intermediate banks to
receive an overall "Satisfactory" rating despite a less
-than -"Satisfactory" Community
Development Test when the L
ending Test standard is met, would weaken incentives
for community development activity and directly contribute to this decline in funding.

Furthermore, unjustifiably raising the threshold creates an unsustainable
dynamic where community development expectations are shifted and
disproportionately concentrated onto a shrinking pool of the largest banks. Expecting
a handful of the largest instit
utions to continually "fill in the gaps" left by exempted
regional and mid -size banks is analytically flawed and geographically impossible,
ultimately undermining the practical durability of the final rule and directly harming
the LMI communities it intend
s to support.
Retaining 1995 Standards Over "Major Product Lines"

The Chamber strongly recommends abandoning the proposed "major product
line" framework . The agencies should retain the predictable structure of the 1995 rule
regarding which business lines are evaluated. Consistent with the longstanding
framework, consumer lending
, including any specific subtype of consumer lending

such as auto loans
, should remain entirely optional and be evaluated only at a bank's

4 https://www.occ.gov/news
-issuances/bulletins/2020/bulletin
-2020 -99.html
 6

affirmative request. Specifically, the Chamber strongly supports Option C presented in
Question 5 of the NPRM: consumer loans should be evaluated solely at the
institution's option, regardless of whether they constitute a "major product line" or any
specif ic percentage of a bank's portfolio. Forcing the mandatory inclusion of
consumer lending introduces
significant new data collection and compliance costs.
Furthermore, as detailed below, consumer lending data simply does not provide a
reliable or accurate basis for evaluating a bank's local geographic lending distribution.

Maintain the Existing Limited Purpose and Wholesale Bank Designations

The Chamber strongly recommends maintaining the existing limited purpose
and wholesale designations and continuing to evaluate limited purpose and wholesale
banks under existing guidance.
Agencies have long recognized that no single CRA
test can apply to all banks.
The limited purpose and wholesale designations under the
existing regulations have served many banks and their communities well for 30 years,
the elimination of which would be a step backward in tailoring CRA obligations to
banks' various business models.
These designations have given banks with different
or unique business models, including banks with a limited physical presence and a
national business model, the ability to focus their CRA activities on community
development lending, investment, and servic
es. The proposed changes should be
withdrawn, and the limited purpose and wholesale bank designations should be
maintained in their existing form.

Crucially, the agencies must reject the flawed premise that identifying
consumer lending as a "major product line" eliminates the need for specialized
regulatory treatment. The proposal conflates two separate CRA paradigms: identifying
which loans should b
e reviewed versus determining whether a specialized institution
should be evaluated under a traditional lending framework. The Chamber strongly
opposes the narrowing or elimination of the "Limited Purpose Bank" designation.

The existing 1995 framework already permits consumer lending to be evaluated
when it constitutes a substantial majority of a bank's business, yet in adopting that
framework, the agencies expressly preserved the Community Development
Assessment for limited
purpose banks. Adding a product line test does not solve the
fundamental geographic mismatch of evaluating a narrow
-product, nationwide,
branch -light institution (such as a national credit card issuer) against a facility
-based
assessment area. The proposed
 elimination of the limited purpose category would
evaluate specialty banks against a localized geographic concentration their national
 7

business models were never designed to serve, effectively establishing criteria under
which they are designed to fail. It would impose severe compliance costs, require
immense new data reporting infrastructure, and subject these banks to the retail
lending rating gate without
actually increasing capital deployment to LMI
communities.
Furthermore, the Chamber cautions the agencies against attempting to replace
the stable, established Limited Purpose designation with a reliance on the specialized
Strategic Plan process. A strategic plan is an institution
-specific, approval
-dependent
proc ess requiring measurable goals, public participation, and individual agency
negotiation. Guiding an entire class of recurring, specialized business models away
from a consistent regulatory framework and into individualized strategic plan
negotiations creat
es unnecessary recurring costs, supervisory uncertainty, and
significant timing and public
-process risks.

Evaluating consumer loans (such as credit cards, auto loans, and unsecured
credit) on an equal footing with mortgages and small business loans fundamentally
departs from the core intent of the
CRA . As previously noted, while these products
provide liquidity, they are not the primary drivers of community revitalization or long
-
term wealth creation. Consumer loans also depreciate in value
, distinguishing them
from the asset -building nature of homeownership and entrepreneurship.

Moreover, consumer loans are a uniquely poor fit for the CRA Lending Test's
geographic distribution analysis. In the modern financial system, these products are
often distributed nationwide through centralized digital algorithms, automated
underwriting, or third -party fintech partner channels. Consequently, there is virtually
no localized peer data available to conduct an accurate geographic distribution
analysis. This stands in stark contrast to mortgage or small business lending, where
there is substantia
l localized peer data available through established Home Mortgage
Disclosure Act (HMDA) and Section 1071 reporting regimes. Mandating loan
-level data
collection for consumer loans would be incredibly burdensome, requiring the costly
development of entirely new reporting capabilities,
causing potential data integrity
concerns, forcing banks to aggregate fundamentally different products into distorted
metrics, and actively destroying the predictability of CRA evaluations. Accordingly, the
agencies should revise the consumer loan data collection requirements to apply only
when a b ank voluntarily elects to have its consumer lending evaluated, rather than
triggering these requirements automatically whenever an institution crosses an
arbitrary major product line threshold.

 8

Proportionate Methodologies & Unique Business Models

To ensure fairness, examiners must be required to consider each bank's
specific local circumstances when evaluating its performance. Banks vary
significantly in how they operate
. S ome rely heavily on large corporate or wholesale
deposits, others hold deposits from outside their local area, and some have major
international operations.
Without taking these structural differences into account
,
rigid, one -size -fits -all formulas will produce misleading results
—making it harder to
accurately measure how well a bank is actually serving the local communities where it
operates.
Rejecting Arbitrary Incidental Lending Limits


The Chamber strongly opposes the proposal to replace the flexible, facts
-and -
circumstances standard regarding "incidental" lending with a rigid, mechanical 5%
quantitative limit. Furthermore, the Chamber opposes the categorical restriction on
advertising o r marketing an ancillary product
to maintain a specialized designation.

Converting the current examiner
-driven analysis into an inflexible conduct,
marketing, and volume test means a specialized bank could lose its eligibility purely
because of a comparatively small ancillary consumer accommodation. This rigid
standard would a ctively discourage banks from offering customer accommodations,
exploring complementary products, or engaging in responsible product innovation,
even when such activities do not meaningfully alter the institution's fundamental
business model.
III. Modernizing the Service Test & Evaluating Retail Activities

The banking industry has clearly shifted toward a digital ecosystem,
fundamentally changing how consumers access their finances since the rules were
last significantly overhauled in 1995.
However, the Chamber strongly urges the
agencies to reject any recommendations from commenters that advocate for the
creation of new, standardized requirements or mandatory evaluation metrics for
digital and omnichannel delivery within the Service Test.

The agencies must resist any pressure to mandate the forced tracking of digital
accessibility metrics, language option usage, or digital adoption rates segmented by
specific LMI populations. Attempting to force digital banking into a rigid, quantitative
framework will invite severe data privacy concerns, demand massive IT overhauls, and
 9

create misleading metrics (e.g., penalizing banks if LMI customers in weak broadband
areas do not adopt mobile apps at high rates).

Instead of imposing blunt requirements or untested data collection burdens,
examiners should retain the current Service Test framework's focus on physical
branch networks while allowing institutions to
electively highlight their mobile
banking, digital lending platforms, and fintech partnerships as positive, qualitative
performance context.
 Crucially, consistent with the statute, this positive consideration
must remain tethered to how these digital channels enhance the reach and delivery of
retail services to LMI individuals within the bank's established, facility
-based
assessment areas.
 Recognizing digital reach through proactive performance context
rather than rigid mandates protects the stability of the 1995 framework. It provides a
flexible, future -proof mechanism for banks to receive positive consideration for
innovative delivery cha
nnels without subjecting them to punitive metrics.

Additionally, the Chamber highly supports the proposal to transition CRA public
files to online website hosting, which effectively modernizes the regulation and
severely reduces administrative paper tracking burdens for the industry.

IV. Optimizing Community Development (CD) Standards and Preserving Capital
Flows
Qualifying Activities and Evaluating Complexity

The Chamber supports maintaining a transparent, regularly updated illustrative
list of qualifying CD activities to provide the industry with greater ex
-ante certainty.
However, the agencies must be absolutely explicit in the text of the final rule that thi
s
list is strictly illustrative and non
-exhaustive , and it must explicitly cover CD loans,
investments, and services . A rigid, exhaustive list would stifle innovation, acting as a
ceiling rather than a floor. It would prevent banks from rapidly responding to newly
emerging local needs or innovative municipal partnerships simply because the novel
activity has not yet bee
n formally cataloged by Washington regulators.

The final rule should also preserve CRA consideration for impactful community
development services delivered through nonprofit partners, intermediaries, affiliates,
and other third -party delivery models. Eligibility should continue to be based on the
servi ce's community development purpose and impact, not on whether bank
personnel deliver the service directly.

 10

Regarding the proposed "Advance Confirmation" process, agencies must
ensure this formal petition mechanism reduces friction rather than acting as a new
bureaucratic bottleneck that delays capital deployment.
 The agencies should provide
a response to a confirmation request within 30 days and be permitted one additional
30 -day period to evaluate a request if it notifies the requestor of the need for
additional time. This would ensure that institutions do not mi
ss windows of
opportunity for CRA activities while it waits on an agency to respond.
 The final rule
should make clear that
 a lack of pre -approval, or an activity's absence from the
illustrative list, should never warrant negative performance context or automatic
denial by an examiner in the field.

Furthermore, the Chamber opposes artificially narrowing the definition of
"complex" CD activities to only those involving "multicomponent financing with a
loan." Complexity in community development takes many forms; innovative equity
investments, technical
 capacity -building grants, and flexible workforce programs
require immense expertise and should securely earn qualitative enhancements. The
Chamber also supports an elective
pro rata pathway for activities that partially
advance CD purposes (such as mixed
-income housing), provided the final rule
ensures this pathway preserves full consideration for activities that already qualify
under existing primary
-purpose standards, rather than i
nadvertently reducing credit.

Affordable Housing and High
-Cost Markets


The Chamber supports the proposal's express recognition of naturally
occurring affordable housing and urges the agencies to expand affordable housing
eligibility to include middle
-income and mixed -income rental housing in high
-cost
markets. These activitie
s can preserve housing supply and affordability where market
conditions place substantial pressure on households that may not satisfy traditional
LMI thresholds.
The final rule should avoid a single, one
-size -fits -all methodology for
identifying high -cost markets. Banks should be permitted to demonstrate high
-cost
conditions using objective, supportable measures appropriate to the transaction,
including housing
-cos t burden data, affordability metrics, housing development cost
indicators, HUD Difficult Development Areas, FHFA High Opportunity Areas, and
other established federal designations.

 11

If the agencies retain a county
-based housing
-cost -burden methodology, the
threshold for the proposed high -cost area standard should be reduced from 40%
to
30% of households with housing costs exceeding 30%
 so that markets facing
significant affordability challenges are not unintentionally excluded. The final rule
should also include grandfathering and transition provisions so that a change in a
market's designation does not affect CRA consideration for exis
ting loans,
investments, or legally binding commitments.

Preserving Flexible Geographic Recognition of Community Development Activity


The final rule must preserve the longstanding standard of recognizing
qualifying broader statewide and regional community development activities once a
bank has demonstrated that it is adequately serving the needs of its communities. The
agencies should us
e a bank's most recent CRA rating as the primary mechanism for
determining whether the bank has adequately met the needs of its assessment areas
and thus may receive such recognition.
A bank that received a Satisfactory or
Outstanding rating on its most recent CRA evaluation should be presumed to be
meaningfully serving those areas and therefore eligible to receive consideration for
qualifying statewide and regional development activiti
es. This approach would provide
certainty throughout the examination cycle, avoid the complexity and volatility of
ongoing capital
-based threshold calculations, and reinforce the purpose of the CRA
rating framework. The agencies should therefore decline to
 adopt a rigid prerequisite
such as 1.25% of allocated Tier 1 capital before broader activities receive
consideration. If the agencies nevertheless establish a minimum threshold,
performance should be aggregated over the bank's full examination period rath
er than
measured annually, and the threshold should apply across
a majority of a bank's
assessment areas rather than every assessment area.
This approach is essential to
directing capital toward underserved areas with significant unmet needs.

Opposition to the 15% Cap for Indirect CD Grant Costs

Philanthropic grants are the lifeblood of community development. The
refore,
the Chambe r strongly opposes the proposed 15% cap on a recipient nonprofit's
indirect (overhead) costs
 and the definition's limitation to grants that are directly used
by the recipient for a specific program, project, or initiative
. This strict cap
 does not
align with the reality of
 nonprofit operations and will have the unintended
consequence of steering CRA funding away from smaller, local community
organizations and toward large, national nonprofits.

 12

Local, neighborhood
-level charities inherently lack the economies of scale that
larger, national organizations possess. Their overhead costs (rent, utilities,
compliance, salaries) naturally represent a higher percentage of their operating
budgets. Penalizing them for this economic reality harms the very bespoke community
organizations the C
RA intends to support. Furthermore, grants are often a vital tool
for meeting CRA obligations in certain rural or under
-resourced assessment areas
that lack the market parameters for complex investments like LIHTC.
 Limiting
consideration to grants that support a discrete program, project, or initiative excludes
grants that can be especially impactful for organizations engaged in community
development activities.
General operating and capacity
-building support grants
provide these organizations with
the flexible funding needed for staffing, technology,
facilities, and other organizational capacity that are often essential to achieving
meaningful community outcomes.

Passing heavily audited documentation burdens down to small nonprofits will
overwhelm their already -strained administrative capacities and directly chill
philanthropic bank grants.
If the agencies insist on finalizing an indirect cost cap, it
should only apply to multi
-million -dollar, national grants (e.g., those exceeding $5
million).
Additionally , for grants that remain subject to the cap,
 documentation
requirements must be drastically streamlined via a safe harbor. Banks must be
permitted to rely on a simple self
-affirmation or attestation from the grantee that their
indirect costs comply with the threshold. The grantee possesses the relev
ant financial
information that the agencies can readily obtain
; banks should not be forced to act as
shadow -auditors required to independently recreate and verify a nonprofit's internal
cost analysis. This would align with the agencies' stated goals of reducing
unnecessary bank burden and minimizing duplicative data collection.

V. Preserving Performance Context & Limiting Data Burdens

CRA evaluations must prioritize meaningful community impact over sheer
activity volume or rigid formulaic thresholds. The true value and complexity of a
community development
activity is often rooted in its localized, qualitative impact,
which formulaic volume thresholds and strict quantitative demographic tests fail to
capture. Examiners must retain sufficient judgment to consider differences in market
opportunities, competiti
on, local economic constraints, and a bank's unique capacity
footprint. We echo a universal call from across the financial industry for clear pre
-
 13

examination guidance, transparent escalation processes for interpretive disputes
during exams, and the timely publication of final performance evaluations.

Finally, the Chamber urges regulators to recognize that the current data
collection and reporting processes are already working effectively
—giving examiners
the information they need to fairly evaluate CRA performance
. Imposing new, untested
data tracking systems will
create unnecessary administrative work and significantly
increase compliance costs for banks. This directly contradicts the
agencies explicitly
stated policy goal in this NPRM of reducing regulatory burden. By attempting to
establish new data tracking mandates where existing systems already suffice, the
agencies are imposing immense costs without commensurate benefits. Regulators
must conduct rigorous
 cost -benefit assessments under the Administrative Procedure
Act regarding operational viability and IT implementation costs before mandating any
new data tracking systems.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce appreciates the OCC and FDIC's thorough
consideration of these comments. We stand ready to serve as a resource and partner
as the agencies evaluate this proposal and work toward a highly functional, unified,
and durable final r
ule.
Sincerely,

Foxhall Parker
Senior Director, Center for Capital Markets

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Previously I have sent a detailed list of comments about various aspects of the NPR. I am submitting these comments because they focus on the most consequential impact of the NPR and the public should be aware of the serious implications regarding mandatory CRA reporters.

I have been advising banks since 1994 about their CRA responsibilities. So I have a very good understanding of the regulation. Some of the proposed changes, such as specifying performance standards for community development and providing a process whereby banks will be able to confirm if a proposed community development activity will be recognized as a qualified loan, investment or grant will be very helpful. 

However, I believe the proposed changes with respect to bank size categories will be extremely harmful, not so much because of their impact on the CRA examination standards, but because of the impact on the number of reporters and the consequences of the reduction in CRA reporters. Some of the most critical performance benchmarks applied for CRA examinations (geographic dispersion tests and borrower characteristics tests)  are determined by the reported CRA lending activity of banks that report under CRA. For 2024 there were 565 OCC- and FDIC-regulated lenders who reported under CRA. The NPR estimates that the number of reporters under the NPR will be reduced to only 86 lenders. As I ,mentioned in my first set of previously submitted comments the two most active small business lenders (JPMorgan Chase and American Express) reported about 53% of all the small business loans originated during 2024. Those two lenders had an extreme impact on the "borrower characteristics" tests skewing the "market benchmarks" substantially (see those comments and supporting documentation) The statistical bias in market benchmarks will be magnified substantially if the number of reporters is reduced as proposed under the NPR.

BTW, there were two lenders (WebBank with $2.5 billion of assets that originated 356,567 small business loans and Lake Forrest Bank with $8.1 billion of assts that originated 259,236 small business loans) in the 2024 data who originated hundreds of thousands of loans who will not be large banks under the $10 billion definition. There are also other lenders that originated tens of thousands of small business loans that also will be exempted from reporting (e.g., WEX Bank, 49,625 small business loans, Pathward NA with 28,014 originations and Cross River with 22,775 small business originations to name but a few) that will not be required to report their lending under the $10 billion asset threshold). Do the agencies intend for such active small business lenders to no longer be required to report their CRA lending activity?

Community banks already are handicapped by the lack of true peer data for comparison. This handicap will be magnified by the elimination of 85% of the existing mandated reporters if the NPR is approved as proposed. We respectfully suggest that it would be a very big help for community banks to report their activity under CRA. At the very least, Intermediate Banks as well as Large Banks should be mandatory reporters. Any bank that is serious about fulfilling its CRA responsibilities ought to be collecting and monitoring its CRA-related activity. The FFIEC offers free CRA software. Reporting under CRA for prudent and serious banks therefore should be a matter of hitting the "upload" button. Relief from reporting is not relief from performing. 

The consequences of the draconian reduction in the number of CRA reporters will actually be harmful to community banks, distorting the performance benchmarks and making any peer comparisons impossible for all but the largest institutions This really increases the regulatory burden for many community banks. At the very least, intermediate banks and large banks should be mandatory reporters under CRA.

On behalf of Habitat for Humanity of Greater Cincinnati (HFHGC), thank you for the opportunity to comment on

How banks partner with Habitat in Greater Cincinnati

participations in the affordable mortgages we originate, which recycles capital so we can serve the next family.

HFHGC are real but modest and usually tied to specific builds and neighborhood projects, including in
Cincinnati's West End. These partnerships exist because the CRA gives banks a clear reason to do this work in

Recommendations

clear enough that affordable housing done in partnership with nonprofit organizations falls within the proposed

mortgages are one of the bank's major product lines, and the proposal's carve-out for "home mortgage loans

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,
Central California Land Trust (CCLT) writes to object to the harmful changes proposed to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in
response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the credit,
deposit, and banking needs of communities, including low and moderate income (LMI)
communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide
services in underserved communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination,
underinvestment, and lack of access remain.
CCLT is a nonprofit community land trust in Fresno, California, incorporated in 2017 and a
member of the California Community Land Trust Network. In 2026 CCLT completed its first two
permanently affordable homes in Southwest Fresno. We acquired and fully rehabilitated both
homes with City of Fresno ARPA funds, and we are selling them for $220,000 each, roughly
30% below market, to first-time buyers earning at or below 80% of area median income. CCLT
keeps the land under a 99-year ground lease, so each home stays affordable for every family
that buys it after the first.
Our work sits on the history the CRA was written to address. When we bought these two homes,
the recorded documents on title for both carried racially restrictive covenants from the 1940s.
One, recorded in 1945, provides that no property it covers may be occupied "by any of the
following described person, or persons, or races, or lineal descendants of such person or
persons, or races, to-wit: Negro, Chinese, Japanese, Filipino, Indian, Hindu, Korean, Malayan or
Mexican." Those covenants are void today, and CCLT is formally removing them from the
record. But the disinvestment they helped create in Southwest Fresno has not been undone,
and the CRA remains one of the few tools that asks banks to help repair it.
The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift. The
proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on LMI communities.
We request an extension of the comment period for an additional 60 days so we have time to
 better understand how much CRA activity may be lost to communities because of this proposal,
an analysis the regulators did not conduct or provide.
1) Affordable homeownership in our community depends on bank participation.
The greatest unmet need in Southwest Fresno is affordable, stable homeownership, and the
financing to reach it. A community land trust home only works if a buyer can get a mortgage on
it, and few lenders in the Central Valley are set up to lend on a home sold under a ground lease.
Each willing lender must first take the time to understand and accept the structure. That work
has a cost for the bank, and the CRA gives banks a reason to take it on. If banks can ignore this
need and still pass their CRA examinations, the lenders who have begun to build these products
will have less reason to continue, and the families we serve will have fewer paths to a home
they can afford.
2) Community development activities for affordable housing will drop dramatically.
The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large" Banks, such
that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and expectation to serve the
community development needs of their communities.[1] According to National Community
Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70 California banks would see their reinvestment
obligations reduced under the proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their
Community Development Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer
be subject to the Investment Test.[2]
The Investment Test has driven investment into programs with large impacts in LMI
communities, including equity equivalent investments in Community Development Financial
Institutions and in Community Land Trusts that take property off of the speculative market. The
proposal also suggests that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just 0.625% of its Tier
1 capital were devoted to community development loans and investments. If each bank
conducted only the amount necessary to meet the proposed thresholds, community
development activity would decrease by approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%.[3]
We believe loosening these standards will lead directly to less reinvestment in our region. The
capital that land trusts and other affordable housing developers need to acquire and rehabilitate
homes is already scarce in the San Joaquin Valley. When a regulator signals that banks can do
far less and still pass, less is what our communities will receive. Asset thresholds should not be
raised.
3) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring a
demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating that large banks and
their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more than 15% of these grants on
overhead.[4] The regulators also ask whether CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to nonprofits
should end entirely.
These requirements would fall hardest on organizations like ours. CCLT delivered its first two
homes with one full-time employee, its Executive Director. Flexible general operating support
from a philanthropic partner is what sustained that capacity: the leadership, outreach, partner
development, and legal and policy groundwork that turned a restricted capital grant into
permanently affordable homes. Project-tied grants with a 15% overhead cap would not pay for
that work, because for a lean organization the staff who deliver the project are the overhead. A
rule that steers bank grants away from general operating and capacity-building support will steer
them toward larger organizations, and away from the local groups that know their
neighborhoods best.
 Nonprofits are key partners for banks trying to bring credit and investment products into
communities that trust long established local organizations. Land trusts, homebuyer education
providers and down payment assistance programs help residents become stable and bankable
so that banks can make new loans in LMI communities. The regulators acknowledge that
community groups, including smaller groups, may be affected,[5] yet they offer no analysis of
that harm.
Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to allow for
meaningful public comment, and will harm the communities that the CRA was meant to support.
If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed, communities like Southwest Fresno will
see less investment in affordable housing, fewer lenders willing to learn models like ours, and
fewer community serving nonprofit organizations. We urge the FDIC and the OCC to reconsider
this proposal.
Thank you for your consideration.
Very truly yours,
John Wellman
Executive Director

New Chapter Ventures (NCV) submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

NCV is a North Carolina nonprofit placemaking incubator. We partner with churches and
communities to repurpose underutilized assets through training, capital and operational support. Our
work includes teacher and essential-workforce housing on church-owned land, a church campus
redevelopment, and a commercial kitchen project, and we run cohort programs that help
congregations evaluate and plan the reuse of their property. Our projects are located in Salisbury,
Manteo, Durham and Statesville.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that
banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and
deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that have
experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial
services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change
how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit

have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
1. The proposal's treatment of community development grants would disadvantage small
community-based organizations
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new
documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.2 For
smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology,
accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the underlying
program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources over which to
spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may
not maintain financial records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would
need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more
difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose
activities are easier to verify.

reuse of underutilized property for workforce housing, community kitchens and other community
facilities typically operate with part-time or volunteer administrative capacity and do not maintain
grant-compliance systems. To date, our projects in Salisbury and Manteo have been supported by

which banks can document and receive CRA consideration for support of small organizations will
affect whether those partnerships are practical.

smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with limited administrative capacity. The agencies
must also determine whether those effects would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and
moderate-income communities. More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule
primarily in terms of reducing perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also
determine what the changes mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. From 2010 through 2024,
banks made approximately $81.1 billion in CRA-qualified mortgage lending to low- and moderate-

of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development loans or
