Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould,

On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide loans,
investments, grants, and services in communities that have historically lacked access to capital.

As the statewide coalition for Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) in
Minnesota, we are proud of the investments and impact that CDFIs have in expanding
opportunity and access across the state. Minnesota is home to almost 40 certified and emerging
CDFIs providing loans and capital investments to communities. CDFIs supplement capital with
critical training and technical assistance for small businesses, childcare providers, home buyers,
affordable housing developers, and community organizations. In the five-year period 2017 –
2022, CDFIs in Minnesota invested $3.463 billion in capital in rural, suburban, urban, and tribal
communities across the state.



Page 2
CRA partnerships are critical to that success, and the changes that the agencies are
proposing would fundamentally alter these partnerships. We have profound concerns with the
increases in the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA and the
restrictions on operating grants, as well as the impacts to bipartisan tools like Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC). Weakening community
development incentives will impair the flow of much needed capital in the most underserved
communities, and remove the promise of economic mobility and investment from Americans.


Minnesota will be uniquely impacted by proposed changes to community development
obligations

Minnesota has an active CDFI sector that is vital to ensuring capital moves to
communities. According to original research aggregating the work of CDFIs across Minnesota,
in the year from July 2024 to June 2025, Minnesota CDFIs closed on over 2,399 loans totaling
more than $282M. As of June 30th, 2025, Minnesota CDFIs had Loan Funds totaling more than
$944M and Loans Outstanding totaling more than $700M. Small business development and
affordable housing development simply does not happen in Minnesota at the same scale without
CDFI participation.

Bank partnerships through the CRA are important sources of capital for CDFIs. The
Minnesota CDFI Coalition's research shows that 74% of Coalition members receive capital from
bank partners. The provisions of the CRA that enable these partnerships would be fundamentally
altered under the proposed changes. According to research from the National Community
Reinvestment Coalition,1 Minnesota would be the second-most impacted state under the
proposed changes. In Minnesota, NCRC estimates:

● 50 of 107 banks, or 46.7%, would lose community development obligations
● 19 of 36 banks, or 52.8%, would lose large-bank status,
● 170 of 343 LMI branches, or 49.6% would be jeopardized

Based on current asset sizes, NCRC estimates this would roll back all community
development requirements for over 800 banks nationally, reducing the total number of all banks
with CRA-related community development requirements by about 40%, as well as reclassifying
over 400 large banks as intermediate.2 This would change the CRA's framework from one

where roughly the largest half of all banks have community development requirements, to a
regulatory system where less than one third are evaluated for community development.

In addition to raised asset thresholds, the OCC and FDIC have also proposed to remove
the requirement that intermediate banks pass both their community development test and their
lending test in order to receive an overall passing CRA rating.3 The OCC and FDIC make a
broad claim that this will lead to banks performing better on both tests without the "artificial
constraint" of having to pass both.4 It is counterintuitive at best to expect intermediate banks to
increase their community development even though they no longer have to prove satisfactory
community development performance; and a de-emphasis of community development seems far
more likely.

The loss of community development obligations and large bank status would remove the
requirements for investing in community that are critical to expanding access to capital across
the state. Without the strong framework of the CRA, the agencies undercut the intent of the
legislation to expand opportunity to all Americans and remove effective community
development and investment tools.


New grant restrictions will harm collaboration and partnerships between banks and
community nonprofits

The OCC and FDIC are proposing new restrictions on CRA-eligible philanthropy. All
banks will be required to show that grants are "directly used by the recipient for a program,
project, or initiative with a primary purpose of community development" and large banks will
also have to prove that no more than 15% of a grant or donation goes to indirect or
administrative costs, including collecting IRS Form 990s from grant recipients.5 The OCC and
FDIC are proposing a 15% cap on indirect costs since that is the standard the federal government
uses for its grants.

Banks often support affordable housing, small business development, financial
counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based
services through grants to nonprofit organizations. Grants can be particularly important to local
organizations that have deep relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of

that are central to community work. Payroll, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other
operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself, and smaller

The MacArthur Foundation analyzed data from over 130,000 nonprofits and "found that

smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward

more than 15% of a grant goes toward indirect costs. IRS Form 990s do not provide that level of
detail for each grant a nonprofit receives, instead 990s report high-level revenue categories,
general functional expenses, and broad descriptions of program accomplishments.


In Minnesota and across the nation, grants often support the organizations and
infrastructure needed to turn capital into tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what
kinds of grants receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond the
banks themselves. The agencies justify these restrictions in part by asserting that grants and
donations may be susceptible to "rent extraction," particularly when intermediaries are involved,
but they provide no data showing how common or significant this problem is.9 Before imposing
a categorical 15% limit on large-bank grants and dictating banks business and community
strategies, the agencies should provide evidence demonstrating the extent of the problem and
explain why existing CRA examination and supervisory practices are insufficient to address it.

Misalignment with Congressional priorities on Affordable Housing and New Markets Tax
Credit (NMTC)
The proposed changes also undermine Congress's recent efforts to strengthen Low-
Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) which are two
bipartisan, popular federal tax tools with a long track record of success in our communities.
CDFIs working to close the affordable housing crisis use LIHTC and NMTC extensively, and
NMTC is also critical for commercial development projects. While Congress expanded LIHTC
and made NMTC permanent, the proposal undermines functioning of these important investment
tools.

LIHTC and NMTC are considered equity investments that are evaluated under the
standalone investment test for large banks which currently have a distinct 25%-weighted
component of their CRA evaluation devoted to qualified investments. Moving banks into the
lower size category would mean these transitioned banks would only be subject to a diluted
evaluation that considers all CD in one test. This means a bank may have greater ability to
emphasize CD lending rather than maintain the same level of LIHTC or NMTC investment
because investment performance no longer receives a separate rating. Through this weakened
regulatory incentive, bank demand for these investments would decrease, taking vital community
projects out of pipelines for funding.


Rulemaking with two of three regulators creates a fractured regulatory environment
Finally, the form of this rulemaking is ill-conceived. Moving forward with rule changes
with only two of the three bank regulators participating would create inconsistent regulatory
frameworks across the OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve Board. This can and will lead to
substantial confusion for banks, CDFIs, communities, and the regulators themselves.

We welcome and encourage changes that provide clarity on CRA-eligible activities, but
not at the expense of the good work of bank and CDFI partnerships, or the overall health and

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The Washington State Housing Finance Commission is submitting this comment in opposition to the
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Regulations because these rules
would significantly weaken the CRA's ability to drive private investment in affordable housing.

Given the complexity of the rule and scope of the proposed changes, we request that the OCC and FDIC
carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an
opportunity to contribute evidence to and comment on the analysis, and extend the current comment
deadline by 60 days.

As the housing finance agency for Washington state, we are concerned about the negative impacts of
these changes on both affordable rental housing and affordable homeownership. Most critically, the
Community Reinvestment Act is a key driver for investment in the federal Low Income Housing Tax
Credit (LIHTC).

The housing credit, established by Congress in 1986, is a highly effective financing tool that brings
millions of dollars in private capital to build and preserve rent- and income-limited apartments across the
country. In Washington state alone, more than 110,000 affordable apartments have been built and
preserved in communities of all sizes for all kinds of renters, from working families to those experiencing
homelessness to seniors.

In the housing credit program, housing developers are allocated credits to sell to investors in return for
capital investment in their projects. Approximately 85 percent of this housing credit investment comes
from banks that are incentivized by the CRA investment test to purchase the credits.

But by raising the asset thresholds for banks, the proposed CRA changes would reduce the number of
banks subject to the investment test requirement, erasing their incentive to invest. The higher the
threshold, the greater the risk to billions of dollars in equity, according to a December 2023 survey of
housing-credit syndicators by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition.





Page 2 of 2

Here in Washington state alone, the proposed regulations could result in the loss of $3 billion of
investment for community development. Rural areas and smaller communities would be the most
negatively affected. In these areas, where attracting investment has historically faced challenges, banks
under the $10 billion threshold would no longer play a critically needed role as housing credit investors.

What is more, the proposed changes are in direct conflict with efforts by the Trump Administration and
Congress to expand the LIHTC program and increase investment in affordable housing. The "One Big
Beautiful Bill" established the largest expansion of the LIHTC program since it was created, while the
21st Century Road to Housing Act increased the Public Welfare Investment (PWI) cap for banks from
15% to 20%, creating the opportunity for billions more of investment into affordable housing. Without
sustained demand to purchase the housing credit, the full benefits of these two key legislative actions will
not be realized.

It is also important to note that maintaining a robust demand for the Housing Credit reduces demand for
other scarce public resources for housing. In the midst of a national housing affordability crisis, CRA
policies should incentivize private investment instead of creating barriers, as even the lowest proposed
increase of the CRA investment threshold would do.

We support OCC & FDICs proposal for greater geographic flexibility, allowing banks to invest outside
their assessment area in underserved communities with little to physical bank presence. This positive
change is an example of a proposal that both strengthens and streamlines the continued implementation of
CRA. Stakeholders across the spectrum can inform other such ideas.

For this reason, we urge OCC and FDIC to extend the comment deadline by at least 60 days and to
conduct a thorough analysis of potential impacts before considering implementation of any proposed
changes.

Hopefully, we share the goal of meeting the core spirit of the act: ensuring that all communities have
access to investments that create the opportunity for wealth building – most importantly an affordable
home. Thank you for your consideration.


Sincerely,



Steve Walker, Executive Director
Washington State Housing Finance Commission

RE: NDC OPPOSES THE PROPOSED CRA RULES 2026
The National Diversity Coalition ("NDC") is a national non-profit organization including the
leadership of our nation's major African American, Asian, and Latino organizations as well as major
minority- and women-oriented national nonprofits, and businesses advocating for economic
empowerment and financial equality for low-moderate income ('LMI'), minority, and other
disadvantaged communities.
NDC submits comments opposing the proposed rulemaking ("the CRA proposal"), which aims to
retain the structure of regulations applicable to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
("OCC") and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") supervised banks, but has proposed
major changes in the size of the banks, assessment area, and revised criteria for Community
Development Grants.
Background
Congress enacted the Community Reinvestment Act in 1977 to meet the credit needs of low-income
communities in a manner consistent with banks' safe and sound operations. There is no doubt that
CRA has been one of the transformative laws that has pushed financial institutions to respond to the
credit needs of low-income communities long ignored by traditional institutions.
For a long time, NDC has had concerns about the existing CRA rules, including that almost 90% of
banks received a 'satisfactory rating' in CRA examinations.1 However, NDC strongly believes the
proposed changes to the CRA rules would negatively affect low-income communities ("LMI") and
reduce the flow of capital and credit to them.

1 Josh Silver & Jason Richardson, Do CRA Ratings Reflect Differences in Performance: An Examination Using
Federal Reserve Data, NCRC, See at https://ncrc.org/do-cra-ratings-reflect-differences-in-performance-an-
examination-using-federal-reserve-data/


At the outset, NDC recommends that OCC and FDIC should not proceed with the proposed CRA
rules for the following reasons.
1. NDC Opposes reevaluation of Bank Asset Size Categories
NDC opposes reevaluating asset thresholds used for performance tests. The CRA proposal wants to
define the asset threshold of a 'small bank' with assets of 1 billion or less, an intermediate bank with
assets between 1 billion and 10 billion, and a large bank with more than 10 billion in assets. In the
current framework, a small bank has assets of $412 million, intermediate banks have assets between
$412 million and $1.649 billion, and large banks have assets of more than $1.649 billion.
NDC is concerned that the proposed reclassification of assets for large banks and intermediate
banks will exclude many banks currently assessed between $1.649 billion and $10 billion from the
full large bank examination, including the lending, investment, and service tests.2 The impact of
these proposed CRA rules will be devastating for many rural and small-town communities that
heavily rely on these banks for community development initiatives. NDC works closely with LMI
income communities that rely on large banks with assets between $ 1.649 billion and $ 10 billion; we
are seriously concerned that reclassifying asset size for large banks will reduce their regulatory
obligation to report community development investments and small-business lending. NDC strongly
believes this proposed rule would end up treating nearly 80% of OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks
as small banks, while only about 2% would be treated as large banks. As a result, there will be less
money for affordable housing, small businesses, consumer lending, and financial literacy for low-to-
moderate income communities, especially in small towns and rural areas.
Therefore, NDC opposes the proposed CRA rules that reclassify the asset size of small,
intermediate, and large banks.
2. NDC Opposes Revised Criteria for Community Development Grants as it harms Small
and Medium Community Based Organizations
NDC opposes the CRA proposal that would change community development grants, including the
rule requiring large banks to obtain a written commitment regarding the qualifying use of the
proceeds and to provide documentation sufficient to establish CRA eligibility. NDC also opposes
the rule proposal that would limit consideration for large banks to grant recipients whose indirect
cost for administering a grant or donation does not exceed 15%. This proposed rule would harm
small and medium community-based organizations that provide valuable services to low income
communities, such as affordable housing, small business support, financial literacy, and first-time
homeownership initiatives. Many small community-based organizations operate with fewer than 10
staff members and undertake multiple responsibilities and tasks to provide services for low-income
communities. These small community-based organizations are mostly based in low-income

2 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters, https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/

communities and have grassroots connections to their needs. The proposed CRA rule limiting
indirect costs to 15% will severely affect their operations and reduce low-income communities'
access to capital and community development benefits. More importantly, the proposed CRA rule
would lead large banks to prefer large nonprofit organizations that can comply with the
documentation and administrative-cost limits, and thereby refuse to provide community
development grants to small, community-based organizations.
Finally, there is no legal or policy rationale for narrow circumstances in which community
development grants receive CRA consideration. In many federal grants, legal mandates or policy
objectives limit the indirect costs incurred when selecting recipients. However, for community
development grants provided by the financial institution, banks' guiding rationale is to provide
community development funding after understanding the unique needs of low-income communities
and evaluating the competence of community-based organizations. The narrowing of the indirect
cost to 15 percent and the additional requirement of documentation of the grant would result in
reducing the community development initiatives in the low-income communities,
The NDC has a long history of partnering and collaborating with various small community-based
organizations in California, and we all provide important services, including affordable housing,
bridging small business loans, and financial literacy in our communities. Therefore, the NDC
strongly opposes the proposed CRA rules on the revised criteria for community development grants.
3. The proposed CRA Rules would negatively affect the availability of bank branches in
low-income communities
The proposed CRA rule reclassifying the asset threshold for large banks will harm bank branches in
low-income communities. NDC has always been vocal against closing bank branches in low-income
communities. Closing bank branches creates a 'bank desert' in the community, ultimately reducing
access to capital and financial opportunities for small businesses and lending in low-income
communities. In recent years, the number of people living in banking deserts has increased from
11.5 million to 12.3 million.3 Previous studies also show a clear pattern of financial institutions
disproportionately closing bank branches in low-income communities. 4
For the last decades, NDC has been able to challenge banks' attempts to close branches in low-
income communities by using the rules. The CRA branching obligations are the main reason banks
have maintained local branches in low-income communities, fearing that community-based
organizations will challenge their mergers before regulators. However, with the revised classification
of the asset threshold for 'large bank', many banks would have less incentive to maintain a fair share

3 Alaina Barca and Harry Hou, US Bank Branch Closures and Banking Deserts, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia,
https://www.philadelphiafed.org/-/media/frbp/assets/community-development/reports/banking-deserts-report-feb-
2024.pdf
4 Jason Richardson, Bank Branch Closures Slow, But Shifting Demographics Cloud the Picture, https://ncrc.org/bank-
branch-closures-slow-but-shifting-demographics-cloud-the-picture/

of branches in low-income communities, which could accelerate branch closures in LMI areas.
NCRC notes that "large-bank threshold to $10 billion would eliminate separate branch evaluations for 417
banks. More than 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts — 30% of all LMI branches
nationwide — and more than 4,000 branches in majority-people-of-color census tracts — 23% of all such branches
—would lose these needed accountability measures."5
NDC also believes that meaningful access to banking services should be evaluated not only through
branch presence and distribution, but also through an institution's commitment to community
engagement, financial education, and the development of banking relationships that address local
credit needs. The proposed or current model of evaluating service test does not properly adequate
the needs of a banking branch operating in the LMI areas.
Therefore, NDC recommends that the OCC and FDIC reevaluate the impact of the proposed rules
on LMI areas and refrain from reclassifying the asset size of large banks.
4. Proposed CRA Rules Reduce the Scope of Challenge to Poor Performing Banks in
Mergers and Acquisitions
The proposed CRA rule that reclassifies the asset threshold for large banks could negatively affect
community-based organizations' ability to challenge bank mergers that harm low-income
communities. The NDC, along with many other community-based organizations, relies on the CRA
reports to understand the bank's commitment to the credit needs of low-income communities,
including providing capital for small business and community development. Consequently, these
CRA reports play a pivotal role in analyzing bank mergers and acquisitions. However, proposed
changes to large bank asset size would reduce scrutiny of banks, particularly under the service and
investment tests and; community-based organizations would lack sufficient information and
evidence to challenge a bank merger that harms LMI communities.
NDC recommends that the OCC and FDIC not reclassify or change the asset threshold for large
banks, because diluting scrutiny would let poorly performing large banks avoid substantial challenges
to their mergers and acquisitions under CRA.
5. NDC Raises Concern on Continuing Exclusion of Credit Unions from CRA Review
NDC understands the legal limit on including credit unions in the CRA review, as federal statute
excludes credit unions from the CRA. Nevertheless, we still want to highlight the continuing
unfairness of excluding credit unions from the CRA review. Today, credit unions increasingly
operate like big banks. 445 credit unions have assets of more than $ 1 billion. Credit unions are
highly consolidated in the market; the average credit union size has jumped 186% in the past 10

5 Supra note 2

years. More importantly, in 2025 alone, the National Credit Union Administration approved 157
credit union mergers.
These figures clearly indicate growth and expansion in the credit union sector over the last 10 years.
Nevertheless, credit unions are extremely reluctant to address the credit needs of low-income
communities. CRA regulations require large banks to address the credit needs of low-income
communities, but similarly situated credit unions refuse to do so because they lack those obligations.
In a large bank merger, community-based organizations use their CRA periodic reports to support
or oppose the merger by considering its impact on low-income communities. However, because
there is no legal requirement to invest in low-income communities, community-based organizations
find it extremely difficult to have productive discussions with credit unions to address the credit
needs of low-income communities.
While we acknowledge that this specific issue is beyond the scope of the OCC and FDIC, we submit
this comment to raise awareness of one negative implication of excluding obligations to low-income
communities.
6. Proposed CRA rules do not factor in the importance of institutional investment in long-
term sustainability of branches in LMI Communities
Establishing a physical banking presence in an LMI community is only the beginning. Sustainable
success requires a strategic commitment to building brand awareness, cultivating community trust,
and developing meaningful relationships with local stakeholders.
Newly established branches, particularly those entering markets where the institution has limited
brand recognition, need adequate corporate marketing support, community engagement resources,
and sufficient time to establish themselves. Without these investments, even well-intentioned branch
expansion efforts risk falling short of their intended community impact.
NDC believes that meaningful access to banking services should be evaluated not only through
branch presence and distribution, but also through an institution's commitment to community
engagement, financial education, and the development of banking relationships that address local
credit needs. The proposed or current model of evaluating service test does not properly adequate
the needs of a banking branch operating in the LMI areas.
CONCLUSION
NDC opposes the OCC and FDIC proposed rewrite of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)
regulations. The proposed CRA rules will reduce community development and economic
development for low-income communities and reduce lending to small businesses. Moreover,
proposed rulemaking attempts to reduce the scrutiny of the existing large banks in their
performance in responding to the credit needs of the LMI communities

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Detroit Hispanic Development Corporation (DHDC) submits this comment in opposition to the OCC and FDIC proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). We believe the proposal would weaken CRA accountability and oversight of how banks serve low- and moderate-income communities.

DHDC is a community-based nonprofit rooted in Southwest Detroit and a member of the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC). We serve more than 5,000 people annually through housing counseling, entrepreneurship and wealth-building, family services, youth development, adult education, and violence prevention programs. Our HUD-certified housing counselors help residents navigate homeownership, housing stability, credit improvement, and financial decision-making. Through this work, we see how access to responsible banking products, mortgage credit, small-business financing, and community partnerships affects household stability and neighborhood opportunity.

For nearly 50 years, the CRA has helped ensure that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. These protections remain important in communities that have experienced disinvestment and unequal access to mainstream financial services.

The proposed rule would reduce CRA scrutiny of banks and change how regulators evaluate bank services and community development activities. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without adequate analysis of their likely impacts on low- and moderate-income communities.

By raising the large-bank threshold to $10 billion, the proposal would reduce the number of banks subject to the current large-bank CRA examination, including the separate service test that evaluates delivery systems and banking services. As a result, regulators would apply less scrutiny to branch networks and banking services at institutions that currently receive more comprehensive CRA evaluations.

The proposal would also narrow what regulators examine under the service test. Examiners currently evaluate factors such as branch distribution, branch openings and closings, alternative delivery systems, and the range of banking services provided. The proposal would place greater emphasis on credit-related services and reduce consideration of deposit products such as checking and savings accounts that are currently evaluated under the service test.

DHDC works with Detroit residents who are preparing for homeownership, establishing or repairing credit, creating household budgets, and seeking stable financial relationships. Through our housing counseling programs, we assist residents who depend on accessible bank branches and affordable financial products to build stability and achieve long-term financial goals. Access to a nearby branch and an affordable checking account is often a critical first step toward receiving income, building savings, documenting financial history, and qualifying for responsible credit. Limited-English-proficient households that need hands-on assistance can be especially affected when branches close or in-person services become less available. For the people DHDC serves, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from access to credit and economic opportunity. By reducing CRA scrutiny of branch performance and banking services, the proposal could weaken incentives for banks to maintain accessible branches and offer products that meet the needs of low- and moderate-income households.

We further request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026, comment deadline by at least 60 days. Given the proposal's scope and potential impact, additional time is necessary to allow stakeholders to evaluate it and provide meaningful feedback.

Sincerely,

Detroit, Michigan

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
I am a student earning an MPA and I lead a nonprofit, formed after Hurricane Helene, this rule will affect. I am addressing three parts of the proposal: the new limit on indirect costs for community development grants, the rules for disaster areas, and the higher bank size thresholds.
The 15 percent limit on indirect costs could hurt the groups that need help most. The agencies took the 15 percent number from federal grant rules. In those rules, 15 percent is a rate that new and small organizations are guaranteed to be able to use. In this proposal, it transforms from protection to a cutoff that can make a small group ineligible for a grant. 
In a disaster, a lot of the real work gets counted as overhead, like coordinating volunteers, running supply sites, and managing logistics. In a crisis, like Hurricane Helene, the overhead can prove to be a valuable service. 
Documentation requirements hit new and small organizations the hardest. The rule requires an IRS Form 990 with budgets. Many groups formed in response to a disaster have no 990 history. Very small groups file a shorter form without budgets, and groups with fiscal sponsors report through the sponsor. Well established organizations that file a Form 990 often already have funding and resources available, while small, new organizations are often the first to respond when disaster and crisis occur. 
I support counting disaster preparedness and resilience work. I also support removing the exclusion for counties that only received certain early FEMA help (Question 31). But the 36-month window is too short for a disaster like Helene. Recovery in western North Carolina will take longer than three years. The agencies have extended the window before, after Hurricane Katrina, and they should be able to do that again for major disasters.
Higher size thresholds could mean less community investment in rural areas. The agencies estimate that about 600 FDIC banks and 194 OCC banks would no longer be required to do community development work. In rural areas, community banks are often the main source of this funding. Fewer reporting requirements would also make it harder for the public to see where the money goes.
I recommend:
1.Keep grants in the rule. Do not eliminate them.
2.Do not use 15 percent as a hard cutoff. Treat it as a guide, and let organizations explain higher costs. Count volunteer coordination and logistics as direct costs.
3.Do not require a Form 990 for small grants. Accept other proof, such as financial statements, a board-approved budget, or a letter from a fiscal sponsor.
4.In disaster areas, waive or raise the limit while recovery is happening.
5.Make extending the 36-month window the normal practice for major disasters.
6.Let smaller banks earn credit for disaster-area work, and require public reporting of grant data.
I agree that grants should reach communities and not be eaten up by overhead. The organization I lead models this in our own budgeting practice, but this rule would punish the small, volunteer-led groups that respond first in a disaster. Please keep grants, replace the hard limit with a flexible one, and protect the groups the original federal rule was meant to protect.

To the Comptroller of the Currency and the Board of Directors of the Federal Deposit Insurance

Dear Comptroller and FDIC Leadership:
On behalf of the Texas Association of Community Development Corporations (TACDC), I
respectfully submit this comment letter opposing significant elements of the proposed revisions
to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. TACDC urges the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to
reconsider provisions that would weaken accountability for meeting community credit needs,
diminish transparency, and undermine investment in affordable housing, small businesses, and
economically distressed communities.
TACDC is a statewide nonprofit trade association representing community-based organizations
working to expand economic opportunity and improve the quality of life for low- and moderate-
income Texans. Our members include Community Development Corporations (CDCs) that
develop affordable housing, revitalize neighborhoods, and provide essential community services,
as well as Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) that finance small businesses,
entrepreneurs, and other borrowers who often face barriers to conventional credit. Our members
work in urban, suburban, rural, and economically distressed communities throughout Texas.
Our members understand firsthand that community development depends on a functioning
partnership among banks, nonprofit organizations, public agencies, and mission-driven financial
institutions. The CRA is a foundational mechanism for encouraging banks to participate in these
partnerships and help meet the credit needs of the communities they serve. Although we support
reasonable efforts to simplify regulations and provide greater clarity to financial institutions, the
 Texas Association of Community Development Corporations
3301 Northland Dr. Ste. 410 | Austin, Texas 78731 | Phone: 512.916.0508 |
www.tacdc.org
proposed rulemaking is not reasonable, and regulatory efficiency must not come at the expense
of meaningful community investment and public accountability.
I. The CRA Must Continue to Promote Meaningful Investment in Affordable Housing and
Community Development
Affordable housing remains a critical need across Texas. CDCs develop and preserve affordable
rental housing, support homeownership, rehabilitate deteriorating properties, and revitalize
neighborhoods where private capital alone frequently fails to meet community needs. These
activities often depend on complex financing structures that combine bank loans, grants,
philanthropic resources, public funding, and specialized financing from CDFIs.
The CRA helps encourage banks to participate in these transactions by recognizing the value of
lending, investments, and services that support community development. Weakening that
incentive could make it more difficult for nonprofit developers to assemble viable financing
packages, increase the cost of affordable housing production, and limit the ability of
communities to preserve existing affordable units.
TACDC is particularly concerned that changes intended to narrow or redirect qualifying
community development activities could create uncertainty for banks and their nonprofit
partners. Banks need clear, predictable rules that recognize the full range of legitimate
community development activities, including affordable housing development and preservation,
rehabilitation of distressed neighborhoods, and financing for community facilities serving low-
income populations.
We urge the agencies to preserve broad, practical eligibility for activities that demonstrably
benefit low- and moderate-income communities. Any qualifying-activity framework should be
transparent, sufficiently flexible to accommodate local needs, and responsive to the realities of
financing affordable housing and community development projects.
II. Excluding Deposit Services Would Overlook an Important Dimension of Community
Reinvestment
The proposed rule would narrow the range of retail banking services considered in CRA
evaluations by excluding deposit services. TACDC opposes this approach.
Access to safe, affordable banking is an important component of economic stability. Low-
income households and small businesses need accessible deposit accounts to receive income,
save for emergencies, manage expenses, and establish financial relationships that can support
future borrowing. In communities where traditional banking access is limited, the availability
and affordability of deposit services can be particularly important.
 Texas Association of Community Development Corporations
3301 Northland Dr. Ste. 410 | Austin, Texas 78731 | Phone: 512.916.0508 |
www.tacdc.org
Although deposit services are not a substitute for responsible lending, they are an essential part
of a bank's relationship with its community. Removing them from consideration risks
overlooking whether financial institutions are providing meaningful access to basic banking
services in the neighborhoods they serve.
TACDC urges the agencies to retain a comprehensive assessment of retail banking services,
including deposit access, affordability, accessibility, and responsiveness to the needs of low- and
moderate-income communities. CRA evaluations should encourage banks to expand responsible
banking relationships, not limit the definition of community service to a narrower set of
activities.
III. Preserve Transparency and Accountability Through Meaningful Data Collection
TACDC is concerned about the proposal to exempt banks with $10 billion or less in assets from
certain CRA data collection, maintenance, and reporting requirements. We recognize that smaller
institutions have fewer resources to devote to compliance. However, reducing reporting
requirements without adequate safeguards could make it harder for regulators and the public to
determine whether community credit needs are being met. TACDC and our members do not
want to see any changes to the current bank asset-size classifications.
Reliable data help identify underserved neighborhoods, evaluate lending patterns, measure
access to credit, and determine whether community development investments are reaching the
people and places with the greatest need. For nonprofit housing developers and CDFIs,
transparent information about lending and investment patterns can also support effective
partnerships with financial institutions.
Texas includes large metropolitan areas alongside rural communities, smaller cities, and regions
experiencing persistent economic challenges. Aggregate information can obscure significant
differences in access to capital within these areas. Without appropriate data, gaps in mortgage
lending, small-business financing, and community development investment may be more
difficult to identify and address.
IV. Protect the Role of CDFIs and Community-Based Lending Partnerships
CDFIs are essential partners in expanding access to capital for small businesses, entrepreneurs,
and communities that are underserved by conventional financial institutions. TACDC members
use specialized lending, technical assistance, and local knowledge to support businesses that
create jobs, strengthen neighborhood economies, and provide goods and services in underserved
areas.
These institutions frequently collaborate with banks to structure financing, extend credit to
borrowers with limited collateral or credit histories, and support projects that may not proceed
 Texas Association of Community Development Corporations
3301 Northland Dr. Ste. 410 | Austin, Texas 78731 | Phone: 512.916.0508 |
www.tacdc.org
through conventional underwriting alone. CRA incentives can encourage banks to provide loans,
investments, and other support that enable these partnerships to operate effectively.
The agencies should ensure that the regulations recognize the community development value of
financing delivered through qualified CDFIs and other mission-driven intermediaries. The
proposed rules do not accomplish this. Community development lending should not be
evaluated so narrowly that it discourages banks from partnering with organizations that possess
specialized expertise and established relationships with underserved borrowers.
The final rule should clearly recognize qualifying loans, investments, and other eligible support
that help CDFIs finance affordable housing, small businesses, and community revitalization. It
should also preserve a workable process for confirming eligibility so that banks can make
informed commitments without unnecessary uncertainty or delay.
V. Ensure Community Development Grants Reach Communities Without Undermining
Effective Organizations
TACDC supports appropriate safeguards to ensure that community development grants benefit
their intended recipients and produce meaningful community outcomes. However, rules
governing grants and donations should recognize that effective nonprofit organizations require
qualified staff, sound financial management, compliance systems, and other reasonable operating
resources to deliver those outcomes.
Restrictions that fail to distinguish between excessive administrative costs and necessary
organizational capacity will weaken the organizations responsible for delivering affordable
housing, small-business financing, and essential services. Smaller community-based
organizations will be especially vulnerable to rules that impose rigid requirements without
accounting for differences in organizational size, mission, and operating model.
We encourage the agencies to adopt clear, practical standards that prevent misuse of grant
funding while recognizing reasonable administrative and operational expenses necessary to
achieve community development objectives. The focus should remain on measurable community
benefits, sound stewardship, and effective delivery of services to underserved populations.
VI. Recommendations and Conclusion
TACDC respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to revise the proposed rule to:
1. Preserve strong CRA accountability by ensuring that regulatory simplification does not
diminish banks' responsibility to meet the credit needs of their entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
 Texas Association of Community Development Corporations
3301 Northland Dr. Ste. 410 | Austin, Texas 78731 | Phone: 512.916.0508 |
www.tacdc.org
2. Retain consideration of deposit services as part of a comprehensive evaluation of
access to affordable, responsible retail banking.
3. Maintain meaningful data transparency through proportionate reporting requirements
and appropriate safeguards that allow regulators and the public to identify unmet credit
needs and disparities in access to capital.
4. Protect community development financing partnerships by recognizing qualifying
activities conducted through CDFIs, CDCs, and other mission-driven organizations that
serve low-income communities and small businesses.
5. Support effective nonprofit capacity by ensuring that grant and donation standards
distinguish necessary operating expenses from improper diversion of funds.
6. Provide clear and inclusive qualifying-activity standards that recognize the diversity
of affordable housing, community revitalization, and economic development needs across
Texas.
The Community Reinvestment Act is more than a regulatory framework. It is an important
public policy tool for encouraging the financial resources of the banking system to help meet
community needs. For Texas communities facing housing shortages, limited access to small-
business capital, and persistent economic disparities, a strong and effective CRA remains
essential.
TACDC urges the OCC and FDIC to reconsider the proposed changes identified in this letter and
adopt a final rule that preserves meaningful incentives for community investment, supports
effective partnerships between banks and community-based organizations, and maintains
transparency and accountability for the communities the CRA was enacted to serve.
Thank you for considering our comments and for the opportunity to represent the perspectives of
Texas's community development sector.
Sincerely,
Matt Hull
Executive Director

To Whom It May Concern,
On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). CRA has created a vital incentive for our bank partners to make a variety of loans,
investments, and grants to CDFIs like Housing Development Fund ("HDF") that have provided a
pipeline of capital to persons, projects and communities that may not otherwise be served by
the private finance market.
HDF applauds the agencies' efforts to revise and update the CRA regulations, and we support
some proposed provisions that could improve the CRA framework. Broadly though, we have the
increases in the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated and the restrictions
on operating grants will likely have major negative outcomes for the work CDFIs alike HDF does.
These changes, if implemented, would have a negative impact with a potential net loss of tens
of millions in leveraged capital investments and thousands fewer low and moderate-income
households assisted with housing opportunities at a time when we can all agree that more
housing is needed across the country and particularly in high-cost areas like Connecticut and
New York.

hdfconnects.org











HDF is a community development finance institution (CDFI) working in Connecticut and New
York for over 30 years. Our work focuses on supporting first-time low and moderate-income
homebuyers and housing developers creating new rental and ownership opportunities in
Connecticut in low and moderate-income communities and to low-income households. HDF
offers free one-on-one pre-purchase counseling with HUD-certified counselors, free homebuyer
and landlord education classes and outreach events across CT and NY. We also offer a host of
downpayment and closing cost assistance programs to assist buyers across the finish lines.
Finally, we providing flexible, low interest loans of all types- pre-development through
permanent, for developers of affordable and mixed-income single and multifamily housing. To
date, and in one of the highest-cost housing markets in the country, we have helped an
estimated 3,676 households purchase their first home and created more than 3,200 units of
mixed-income rental and homeownership housing. We achieve all of this work with the
assistance and investment of partner banks, philanthropic foundations, and public entities like
the CDFI Fund, Connecticut Housing finance Authority, Connecticut Department of Housing,
local municipalities and Neighborworks America.
Banks are by far our most critical partners in this work. In the last two years alone, our bank
partners have committed and/or advanced more than $53 million in the form of low-interest
capital to HDF or our borrowers. This has come in the form of approximately $14.5 million in
low-interest second mortgages for first time homebuyers and $38.5 million in low-interest
capital for housing developers. During the same two-year period, HDF has leveraged these
funds with 1) our own revolving resources and interest income totaling nearly $5M, 2) major
gifts from philanthropic partners totaling over $8 million, and 3) $5M of lending capital from
public resources. We currently work with more than 20 banks in a variety of different ways to
achieve results.
In addition to being financing partners, our bank partners are deeply involved in our work.
They assist us with reviewing and approving each loan we make and sit on our board and
various loan committees. Banks often lend alongside HDF as first mortgage lenders or as
partner lenders in a housing development. We are thought partners in how to best and most
efficiently create housing opportunities. We regularly join our bank partners in public outreach
and education events across our area and they join ours. Their deep understanding,
participation and investment in our work also often leads to small grant support for operations.
This operational support is vital to covering our overhead and also for outreach and marketing

hdfconnects.org











to reach underserved markets. This support is also highly incentivized by CRA requirements.
Our bank partners rely on CDFIs to reach underserved communities, educate and counsel
homebuyers, cultivate new developer borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers. While
banks undoubtedly appreciate our efforts and benefit from better educated homebuyers with
lower delinquency rates, $400 million in interest on first mortgages that were made possible by
our mutual programs, developers that seek mainstream finance products for other projects and
future repeat homebuyers, it is CRA that drives their substantial and vital financial
commitments. Weakening these incentives would directly and substantially impact our work,
reducing bank engagement and outreach partnerships and drastically reducing the amount of
households we are able to serve.
Concern #1: Raised Asset Thresholds Threaten Available Capital for Attainable Housing
Development Finance (Section IV.A, "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 1-3)
The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate
banks as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as institutions
with more than $10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate community
development test as intermediate small banks would become small banks and lose that
requirement. Another approximately 400 banks that are currently evaluated as large banks
would become intermediate banks, losing the separate large-bank lending, investment, and
service tests and many associated data-reporting requirements.
In the state of Connecticut where we do the most work, it is estimated that nine of 43 banks,
comprising 20.9% of all the banks in the state would no longer be required to reinvest in local
community development projects such as affordable housing, small business support,
workforce development, community healthcare and education services. About 19 banks,
comprising 46% of all banks in the state would lose their large bank status.
In Connecticut where there are fewer local banks the loss of even a couple of CRA-motivated
bank partners will directly reduce the number of projects we can finance and homebuyer
households we can support. Many of the larger banks that do cover our region already spread
their CRA commitment dollars wide and more often do not work substantially with smaller and
mid-sized CDFIs in the area. In a state like Connecticut which consistently falls in the top 10 for
housing costs, and particularly in our office footprint in Fairfield County, CT and adjacent to

hdfconnects.org











Westchester County, NY and NYC, the financial resources needed to build new housing and
finance affordable rentals or assist households in purchasing a home are double and in many
cases triple what they are in other locations.
HDF estimates that of the 15 banks that do currently actively work with HDF, only three would
retain their Large or Intermediate size status. Seven would see their size drop from large to
Intermediate – threatening more than $24,000,000 in current funding commitments from those
banks. The remaining three would drop from Intermediate to Small. Of those three small banks
who would no longer have CRA investment requirements, their current $5.5 million collective
partnership with HDF would likely be reduced if not entirely eliminated.
Community Would Result from Loss of Community Development Finance
The CRA asset size thresholds determine not just how much a bank is investing in CD activities,
but also how a bank's community development performance is evaluated. The agencies
acknowledged in their proposal that when banks become subject to a CD test under the existing
CRA requirements, that evaluation typically results in banks adjusting their CRA programs.
Banks moving down asset size thresholds and losing incentives for community development
activities would have a direct impact on our partnerships. We estimate that more than $30
million of our grants and investments would be at risk from our bank funders that are currently
considered large or intermediate that would transition into lower asset categories. This
represents roughly 55% of our total bank funding. The loss of this much funding would
drastically reduce our ability to serve households that need us and further would reduce our
ability to leverage that funding with other resources.
HDF recently approved a low-interest construction loan to a local nonprofit to create attainable
homeownership opportunities in Sharon - a rural town in the Northwest corner of Connecticut.
This loan structure combined HDF's own equity, gap grant funds from the State Department of
Housing to close the gap between the cost to build and the affordable sale price, and several
hundred thousand of low-cost lending capital from multiple local partner banks. A future low-
income homebuyer household could be supported by our HUD-certified pre-purchase
counseling department – funded by grants from CitiBank and Neighborworks America.
Homebuyers would then be eligible for downpayment and closing cost assistance programs
from our residential lending team funded by our partnership of 15 banks. Loosing even just a

hdfconnects.org











few of these banks or reductions in investment as a result of changes to asset threshold would
mean these types of smaller projects in rural areas would be much less likely to occur.
Significance of CRA data and transparency: Section IV.G, "Data Collection, Reporting, and
Disclosure"
We also note that the asset size thresholds would cause a reduction in the number of banks
that are subject to the CRA data requirements. This data is critical for community development
operations. Reducing the requirements would make it harder for organizations like HDF to
assess where, how and whether community credit needs are being met. Community
development data tracking is already an area that is under resourced and insufficient. The
proposed changes would exacerbate these challenges, making it difficult to determine where
credit is flowing and what impact it might be having downstream.
Recommendation
We strongly urge the agencies to maintain the current thresholds and reject alternatives
including the substantially higher thresholds considered in Question 1. As the thresholds are
annually indexed to the consumer price index, they are appropriate for the current year. There
is, therefore, no reason to "restore proportionality to 1995." It is also worth noting that the
small bank threshold proportionality metric rests on the distribution of the number of banks so
that 80% of all banks would be considered small, very close to the number in 1995. However,
nearly 20% of banks in 1995 met the large bank threshold but while the new threshold would
leave only 2% at the same level. Moreover, the banking industry has changed drastically since
1995 with considerable consolidation and geographic footprint shifts. Matching a 1995
distribution through either method does not necessarily demonstrate that the resulting
categories are appropriate for the modern banking system.
Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community Development
Activities — CD Grants"; Questions 9–11
The proposed changes to CRA imposes new restrictions on community development grants that
will have a negative outcome on CDFIs like HDF and the individuals we serve. Most critically, we
oppose the changes that requires a qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a
program, project, or initiative with a primary purpose of community development. While we
agree that funds must be carefully allocated to ensure they are benefitting

hdfconnects.org











community development targets, the proposed changes, as write, would restrict other forms of
grantmaking including operational grants that support activities that are otherwise challenging
to find funding for. This includes data reporting and record-keeping, technology upgrades,
overhead including staff salaries and benefits, financial management, compliance and
accounting, and more. These activities are not only critical for making community lending
happen, but they also are vital in ensuring that funding is implemented according to regulatory
requirements and that data is collected to measure impact.
HDF also opposes the proposed change capping large banks' grant recipient's indirect
administrative costs to 15%. Again, HDF supports the goal of ensuring that as many dollars as
possible go to community development activities. As federally regulated lending institutions,
CDFIs must still fund servicing, compliance, underwriting, risk management, data security,
insurance and financial auditing and oversight along with considerable federal data reporting
requirements. These elements of our work, along with staffing require considerable financial
support that is often not covered by grants or by the interest we receive on our low-cost
lending products. These costs also vary within our own organization from year to year and
nationally based on product types, geography and much more. HDF, located near New York City
and serving Connecticut and New York experiences higher staffing and benefits costs, for
example, than many other areas of the country – creating administrative costs that may be
higher than organizations in other areas. Bank grants, and their flexibility when it comes to
operational costs are a critical piece of our operating, compliance and administrative picture. As
such, we also strongly oppose artificially limiting them as well as the alternative contemplated
in Question 10 to eliminate grants and donations from CRA consideration entirely.
Recommendation
Preserve the existing 1995 CRA framework as it relates to general operating and capacity
building grants. Banks are in the best position to evaluate how and where their grant dollars
should be used and to evaluate grant recipients according to criteria specific to their
community development activities and geography.

hdfconnects.org











Proposed Provisions That Could Further Reduce Community Development Incentives
Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance: Section IV.B,
"Performance Tests — Intermediate Bank Ratings"
Under the current framework, an intermediate-small bank must achieve a Satisfactory rating on
both their lending test and the CD test while the proposed standards only require the
Satisfactory rating on the lending test, allowing for compensation for weaker CD performance.
When considered alongside the change in asset thresholds which allows for many banks
currently classified as large to be evaluated under the intermediate-small standards, the result
could be that many banks that CDFIs work with, would have less incentive to make investments
and loans with CDFIs if a weak CD performance doesn't otherwise prevent an overall
Satisfactory rating. We request that agencies keep the requirement that intermediate banks
meet the Satisfactory standard for CD performance in order to achieve a Satisfactory rating
overall.
Complexity definition anchored to lending is too narrow: Section IV.C, "Qualitative Factors";
Questions 12–17
At HDF, our commercial lending practice involves a variety of different types of housing loans.
The goal is to be as flexible as we can to provide the financial feasibility for affordable rental
and homeownership development. In many projects, we are the only lender. Sometimes we
finance the much-needed rehabilitation of older, run down properties. Occasionally we make
risker, predevelopment or acquisition loans to nonprofit or emerging developers that
eventually go on to utilize public funding sources for affordable development. Sometimes they
are construction loans for single family homeownership units on vacant lots that don't pencil
out without gap grant funding we're providing on the back end. Sometimes we are a
subordinate gap lender in a larger capital stack for a more traditional affordable housing project
utilizing LIHTC or voucher funding. These projects occasionally combine resources with private
financing but just as frequently, do not. The proposal at hand would define complexity for CD
investments, grants, and services largely by whether an activity is a necessary or beneficial
component of a multicomponent financing transaction involving a loan. We oppose establishing
a lending-centric definition of complexity. Investments in CDFIs like HDF can involve specialized
expertise, layered capital, subordinate positions, public subsidies, risk sharing, guarantees, tax-

hdfconnects.org











credit structures, patient repayment terms, or other features that make transactions complex
even when they are not directly paired with a particular bank loan. We also oppose requiring
CD investments or services to be complex as contemplated in Question 14 or treating
complexity as categorically more responsive than innovation, flexibility, or impact as
contemplated in Question 15.
Essential community infrastructure and facilities should retain a meaningful CD nexus: Section
IV.D, "Community Development Definition — Revitalization and Stabilization", Question 25
The proposed changes threaten to broaden eligibility for essential community infrastructure
and facilities serving targeted areas without needing to demonstrate that the activity helps
attract or retain businesses, residents or without allocating a share of benefit to low and
moderate-income individuals. Standard lending/investment in infrastructure and facilities
projects that do not otherwise demonstrate substantial community benefit – especially to low
and moderate-income individuals should not replace critical housing needs or CDFI financing –
especially where they are not required to demonstrate community benefits including benefits
to LMI individuals. Flexibility for these types of CD activity should only be considered genuine
CRA-eligible investments when they address a financing gap and do not replace or displace
more targeted CD projects.
Strategic plans require strong guardrails: Section IV.F, "Strategic Plan"; particularly Questions
38–53
HDF believes that the goal to provide more clarity around strategic plans and metrics is a
laudable one. Our concern lies in the fact that such strategic plans allow banks to develop
individualized CRA standards and as such, it is critical that guardrails are present to avoid
circumvention. It is vital that strategic plans be responsive to actual, demonstrated community
needs. The goals under such plans should be rigorous, transparent and measurable. Moreover,
the goals should be subject to public input and evaluated against their efficacy in meeting the
aforementioned demonstrated community needs. We request that the agencies to establish
strong standards in responding to Question 53, regarding when measurable goals should be
considered inadequate to address assessment-area needs.

hdfconnects.org











Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas: Section IV.E, "Consideration
of Community Development Activities — CD Activities Outside Assessment Areas"; proposed §
__.13(e); Question 34
HDF supports the goal of allowing CRA investments in communities that have significant capital
needs but which do not currently fall in a bank assessment area. This type of flexibility could
help serve more communities. HDF has often encountered banks interested in working with
HDF but for small assessment areas that don't provide enough significant overlap with our
current lending borders. Broadening these boundaries would allow banks to work with HDF in
areas that might fall just outside of assessment areas. This expansion or flexibility should not,
however, replace CD activity in banks own assessment areas.
With respect to Question 34, HDF supports more geographic flexibility –especially where it can
help rural communities, Indian County and other underserved areas that often fall outside
standard assessment areas. greater geographic flexibility where it can help direct CRA-
motivated capital to rural communities, Indian Country, and other underserved areas that may
fall outside traditional assessment areas.
Recent research by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition demonstrates the gap
between the new, proposed thresholds and current bank activity. Of the 69 large banks
examined by NCRC, annual assessment-area CD lending, investments, and grants totaled
approximately $102 billion. Applying the proposed 0.625% Tier 1 capital thresholds to those
same institutions would yield only $14.8 billion. Median assessment-area community
development lending was also found to equal to 6.83% of Tier 1 capital and median qualified
investments and grants equal to 3.5%, both substantially above the proposed 0.625%
benchmarks.
We request that the agencies adopt a more rigorous standard that that proposed which
considers both the level of activity and its responsiveness to identified community needs. We
are very concerned that allowing a broadly defined "substantially met" standard would weaken
this safeguard.
Allocation of CD activities across assessment areas: Section IV.E, "CD Activities in Assessment
Areas, Assessment Area Allocation, Assigning Assessment Area Weights"

hdfconnects.org











We support greater flexibility in allocating CD activities that benefit or serve multiple
assessment areas. HDF's primary office is located in Stamford, Connecticut, but approximately
66% of our resources are deployed outside of Fairfield County CT and we also lend in New York.
This change could better accommodate statewide and regional CDFIs whose community impact
is not accurately represented by the physical location of their headquarters. If an entire bank
assessment area was tied to our headquarters, this would not accurately represent the
communities and states benefitting from the investments.
Support for Provisions That Could Strengthen Community Development Finance
Consider prior-period community development loans: Section IV.C, "CD Loans"; Question 8
HDF strongly supports providing CRA consideration for qualifying CD loans that remain
outstanding from prior evaluation periods, similar to the existing treatment of prior-period
investments. Our borrowers frequently need long-term, permanent or revolving financing for
housing development. This is an example where the CRA evaluation would better match
community need. The agencies could base the consideration on outstanding exposure and
account for duration and repeat renewals of the same loan as a single exposure.
Establish an illustrative list and advance-confirmation process: Section IV.E, "Illustrative List"
and "Confirmation of CD Activity Eligibility"; Questions 32–33
We stand with many other CDFIs in supporting a publicly available non-exhaustive list of eligible
CD activities. Ideally, the OCC, FDIC and Federal Reserve should maintain an single interagency
list.

hdfconnects.org











With respect to Questions 32–33, we support requiring banks retain eligibility determinations
for as long as the applicable activity remains on their balance sheet and establishing a maximum
30-day extension beyond the proposed 90-day review period. Please ensure the confirmation
process ensures accountability for genuine community development impact. Ideally, agencies
should identify a process for reconsideration where banks or community development partners
can provide additional information and community stakeholder input or raise concerns about
eligibility of activities. We also urge that nonconfidential or anonymized determinations and the
reasoning behind them should be made public to promote transparency.
Recognize Indian Country and other Tribal and native lands: Section IV.D, "Revitalization and
Stabilization"; Section IV.I, "Indian Country and Other Tribal and Native Lands"; Question 54
We strongly support expressly recognizing Indian Country and other Tribal and native lands as
targeted geographies within the revitalization and stabilization component of community
development.
Recognize disaster preparedness and resilience: Section IV.D, "Revitalization and Stabilization
— Designated Disaster Areas"; Question 31
We support recognizing qualifying activities that help communities prepare for, adapt to, and
withstand natural disasters. CDFIs, including HDF, sometimes provide financing before and after
disasters to affordable housing developments and homeowners. CRA should encourage these
types of investments that strengthen vulnerable communities.
Conclusion
The Community Reinvestment Act has had a tremendous impact in increasing access to capital
for people and in places where it otherwise might not be available. Partnerships between banks
and CDFIs, like those we have fostered at HDF, are the lifeblood of our work and have mutually
beneficial outcomes for banks, CDFIs and the people we jointly serve. While we understand the
agencies' attempts to modernize the thresholds and standards by with CRA goals are met, we
share the concerns outlined in this letter with many partners across the county. Perhaps most
importantly, we request that the OCC and FDIC withdraw the proposed asset threshold changes
and the restrictions on operating grants.

hdfconnects.org











Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed
changes on the communities we serve.
Sincerely,

Kiley A. Gosselin
President & CEO
Housing Development Fund, Inc.
