II.
AFC Supports a Materiality Based Major Product Line Framework that Focuses
CRA Evaluation on Meaningful Consumer Lending and Related Bank Activities

AFC appreciates the agencies' consideration of both quantitative and qualitative approaches to
identifying major product lines for CRA evaluation. The quantitative approach offers greater
objectivity and predictability, while the alternative approach appropriately recognizes the
importance of institutional business strategies, lending capacity, and responsiveness to
community credit needs. Although both approaches incorporate meaningful elements, neither, as
currently proposed, provides sufficient flexibility to accommodate the diversity of business
models and product offerings among innovative banks. Accordingly, AFC encourages the
agencies to incorporate the benefits of both approaches into a framework that allows for greater
consideration of an institution's particular lending activities and the communities it serves.8

The final rule should establish a clear materiality principle for determining which consumer
lending activities warrant CRA evaluation. Consumer lending products should be evaluated when
they constitute a meaningful component of an institution's lending activity, not merely because
the bank originates some volume of loans within a particular regulatory product category.
Accordingly, the agencies should identify major product lines by considering the significance of
the relevant lending activity to the institution's overall consumer lending operations and should
preserve the ability to evaluate related consumer lending activities on an aggregate basis where
separate product level conclusions would not materially improve the assessment of CRA
performance.

A product-by-product methodology would risk substituting regulatory categorization for a
meaningful assessment of consumer lending performance. Credit cards, automobile loans, other
revolving credit, and other consumer loans may differ in their underwriting, duration, collateral,
and customer use, but those distinctions alone should not require each product to receive an
independent CRA evaluation. Where individual products form part of a broader consumer
lending business, mandatory separate evaluations could fragment the agencies' analysis and
produce disproportionate supervisory consequences from changes in individual product volumes
that do not reflect a meaningful change in the institution's overall consumer lending activity. The
agencies should therefore require separate evaluations only where a product line is sufficiently
material to provide meaningful information about whether the institution is meeting community
credit needs.


8 AFC's recommendations in this section are also intended to address the agencies' requests for comment concerning the proposed quantitative
and qualitative approaches to identifying major product lines, as discussed in the Proposed Rule's Supplementary Information.
 7

The same materiality principle should govern the establishment of measurable consumer lending
goals under a strategic plan. Rather than requiring goals for every category of consumer credit
offered by an institution, the agencies should permit a strategic plan bank to identify the
consumer product line or lines that constitute the principal components of its consumer lending
activity. That determination should be supported by objective measures of lending volume and
supplemented by relevant performance context, including the extent to which particular products
serve LMI borrowers or respond to identified community credit needs. This approach would
preserve meaningful accountability while ensuring that strategic plan goals are concentrated on
lending activities sufficiently significant to provide a reliable measure of CRA performance.

Materiality, however, should not be reduced exclusively to a quantitative determination. Loan
count and dollar volume can provide useful indicators of whether a product line is sufficiently
significant to warrant evaluation, but those measures do not necessarily capture the extent to
which a product responds to identified community credit needs or serves LMI borrowers. The
final rule should therefore preserve an appropriate role for qualitative responsiveness and
performance context alongside quantitative measures. Doing so would allow examiners to
distinguish between lending activity that is significant principally by volume and activity that,
although different in scale, may be particularly responsive to the financial needs of LMI
consumers and communities and therefore provide meaningful information regarding an
institution's CRA performance.

Responsiveness to the needs of LMI consumers and communities is not limited to the specific
provision of credit. For many unbanked and underbanked consumers, access to safe, affordable,
and appropriately designed deposit products can represent an important point of entry into the
regulated financial system and a meaningful means of addressing barriers to financial inclusion.
Moreover, appropriately designed deposit products can help consumers establish a record of
responsible financial management over time, potentially strengthening their ability to qualify for
responsible credit products and supporting their broader financial stability. This is particularly
relevant for institutions that have developed business strategies, including responsible bank-
fintech partnerships, centered on expanding access to deposit products rather than extending
credit. AFC recognizes that the Proposed Rule would not provide for the assessment of deposit
products, consistent with the agencies' position in pending litigation, and does not ask the
agencies to revisit that position.9 Within that framework, however, examiners should be
permitted to take into account, as performance context, such institutions' efforts to expand access
to safe and affordable financial services for LMI, unbanked, and underbanked consumers.

The agencies should further clarify that the channel through which a qualifying consumer loan is
originated or distributed does not independently determine whether the activity receives CRA
consideration. Where a bank is the originating institution and the lending otherwise satisfies
applicable CRA standards, lending conducted through a responsible bank fintech partnership
should be evaluated consistently with comparable lending conducted through the bank's
proprietary channels. A channel neutral approach would prevent examination methodology from
drawing artificial distinctions between economically comparable lending activity and would

2026), ECF No. 93.
 8

ensure that CRA evaluation remains focused on whom the bank serves and the credit needs being
addressed rather than the technology or distribution arrangement used to reach the borrower.

The agencies should also consider how the CRA evaluation framework treats institutions lending
to LMI borrowers occurs predominantly outside a bank's facility-based assessment areas. For
institutions that originate consumer credit through nationwide or predominantly digital channels,
a substantial portion of lending that serves LMI borrowers may occur outside the geographic
areas associated with the institution's main office or any physical deposit-taking facilities. AFC
recognizes the agencies' position that the CRA does not permit assessment of retail lending
outside those areas and does not ask the agencies to extend CRA consideration to such lending.
Under the proposed small and intermediate bank lending test, a satisfactory rating generally
contemplates that a majority of a bank's loans are in its assessment areas, and the meaningful
assessment provision may cause examiners to rely principally on that percentage where in-area
loan volume is limited. Applied mechanically, that criterion would penalize an institution whose
business model is nationwide by design, even where it responsively serves its facility-based
communities. The final rule should therefore clarify that an institution will not receive an adverse
lending conclusion solely because a nationwide or digital business model produces a low
percentage of loans in its assessment areas, and that performance context will account for such
business models in applying this criterion.

Relatedly, the agencies should retain the existing formulation of the loan-to-deposit ratio
criterion. The current rule evaluates a bank's loan-to-deposit ratio adjusted for seasonal variation,
and, as appropriate, other lending-related activities, such as loan originations for sale to the
secondary markets, community development loans, or qualified investments. The Proposed Rule
would delete the reference to other lending-related activities without explanation. That language
is important for institutions that originate loans for sale or to partners and therefore carry a lower
ratio on their balance sheets despite substantial lending activity. This concern is closely related to
the one described above: just as an institution whose business model is nationwide or digital
should not be penalized solely because a structural feature of that model produces a low
percentage of loans in its assessment areas, an institution whose lending activity flows through
originate-to-distribute or partnership channels should not be penalized solely because that
structural feature produces a low on-balance-sheet ratio. In both cases, the framework should
look at actual lending activity. The final rule should restore the lending-related activities
language so that the loan-to-deposit ratio continues to reflect the full scope of an institution's
lending engagement.

By anchoring the major product line framework in materiality, the agencies can maintain a
rigorous assessment of consumer lending without dispersing examination and compliance
resources across product categories that provide little additional insight into CRA relevant
performance. The final rule should therefore concentrate consumer lending evaluation on product
lines that are sufficiently significant to the institution's lending activity to warrant independent
consideration, while permitting aggregation where separate product level analysis would not
materially enhance the agencies' assessment of how effectively the institution serves community
credit needs.

 9

III.
AFC Supports Flexible Community Development Standards and Greater
Regulatory Certainty to Direct Resources Toward High Impact Activities

Effective CRA implementation requires sufficient flexibility for banks to allocate community
development resources among lending, investments, grants, and services according to
demonstrated community needs and the activities through which an institution can most
effectively address those needs. Because community development priorities vary considerably
across markets, the form of activity best suited to address a particular need will likewise differ
among communities and institutions. The agencies should avoid requirements that prescribe,
either expressly or in practice, separate or predetermined allocations among community
development activity categories. Separate goals may be appropriate where they reflect an
institution's community development strategy but combined or otherwise tailored goals should
remain available where they provide a more meaningful measure of overall community
development performance. Preserving this discretion would allow CRA considerations to guide
the deployment of resources without permitting the structure of the evaluation methodology itself
to dictate how those resources are deployed.

Geographic treatment of community development activities warrants similar flexibility. The final
rule should preserve a practical pathway for banks to receive CRA consideration for qualifying
community development activities outside their facility-based assessment areas, particularly
where the institution has demonstrated meaningful responsiveness to the needs of its assessment
areas. Although a threshold may appropriately ensure that institutions remain attentive to the
communities surrounding their deposit-taking facilities, that threshold should not operate so
rigidly that it discourages otherwise responsive community development activity in areas with
substantial unmet needs. This concern is particularly significant in so-called CRA deserts, where
community development needs may be acute but the number of institutions with assessment
areas encompassing those communities may be limited. The agencies should therefore ensure
that any geographic flexibility standard is sufficiently attainable and appropriately tailored to an
institution's business model, capacity, and community development activity. The final rule
should also preserve meaningful qualitative consideration where a purely quantitative threshold
would fail to capture the responsiveness or impact of an activity. This approach would maintain
the CRA's statutory focus on the communities surrounding a bank's deposit-taking facilities
while allowing institutions that have meaningfully served those communities to deploy
additional resources where community development needs are substantial. For banks serving
customers across broader geographic markets through digital channels, such flexibility is
particularly important to avoid concentrating CRA-eligible capital in markets primarily because
qualifying opportunities are more readily identifiable there. Greater geographic flexibility would
also help mitigate market distortions arising from excessive competition for CRA-eligible
activities in areas with a high concentration of bank headquarters, allowing institutions to direct
resources toward underserved communities where those resources may have a more meaningful
impact.

Flexibility in the deployment of community development resources, however, is considerably
less valuable if institutions cannot determine with reasonable confidence whether contemplated
activities will receive CRA consideration. A publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of
qualifying community development activities, coupled with a formal process for confirming
 10

novel or less established activities, as contemplated by the Proposed Rule and consistent with the
OCC's existing practices, would provide important regulatory certainty. AFC supports this
approach in the Proposed Rule, provided that the illustrative list remains searchable and regularly
updated and that the agencies expressly clarify that omission from the list does not indicate
ineligibility. Treating the list as effectively exhaustive could discourage institutions from
pursuing innovative community development structures that respond to emerging needs simply
because those activities have not previously received formal regulatory recognition. The list
should instead operate as a source of reliable guidance while preserving examiners' ability to
recognize new structures that satisfy the regulatory definition and advance qualifying community
development objectives.

For the confirmation process to provide comparable value, institutions also need timely decisions
and reasonable assurance that they may rely upon them. The agencies should establish a firm
outer limit on any extension beyond the proposed response period, absent the requesting
institution's consent, and require a written explanation identifying the issue necessitating
additional review. Equally important, written confirmation that an activity qualifies for CRA
consideration should remain reliable for the relevant activity, including during subsequent
evaluation periods while a qualifying loan or investment remains outstanding or on the bank's
balance sheet. A confirmation mechanism that remains subject to unpredictable reconsideration
after an institution has committed capital or entered into a community partnership would provide
little practical certainty and could discourage precisely the types of longer-term commitments
that the CRA framework seeks to encourage.

The agencies should apply the same principles of clarity and flexibility to community
development grants and donations. AFC supports ensuring that grant funding meaningfully
advances qualifying community development purposes, but the final rule should avoid rigid
requirements that could exclude otherwise impactful grants based principally on the
administrative structure through which funds are deployed. In particular, grants should remain
eligible for CRA consideration where funds are provided through intermediary organizations that
can demonstrate a qualifying community development purpose and appropriate use of the
proceeds. Additionally, consideration should be given as to whether a fixed 15 percent limitation
on a recipient's indirect costs provides an appropriate measure of a grant's community
development impact. Administrative expenses can vary materially based on the nature of the
organization, the community served, and the activity being supported, and a uniform threshold
may exclude organizations that deliver meaningful community benefits but necessarily incur
greater administrative costs. Accordingly, AFC recommends that the agencies treat the proposed
15 percent indirect cost threshold as a safe harbor rather than an absolute limitation, permitting
grants with higher indirect costs to qualify for CRA consideration where the institution can
demonstrate that the funds advance qualifying community development purposes. Any
documentation requirements associated with grant eligibility should likewise be proportionate
and should provide institutions with a practical means of establishing that funds support
qualifying purposes without requiring burdensome monitoring of a recipient's internal cost
structure. The final rule should also provide appropriate grandfathering treatment for existing
community development grant commitments, including multiyear agreements entered into before
the rule's applicability date. Preserving CRA consideration for these commitments would protect
established community partnerships and prevent changes in eligibility requirements from
 11

disrupting funding arrangements undertaken in reasonable reliance on the existing regulatory
framework. A more flexible standard focused on the grant's primary purpose and demonstrated
community development benefit would better preserve bank discretion while providing
reasonable safeguards against activities that do not meaningfully advance CRA objectives.

Taken together, these reforms would better align regulatory incentives with the underlying
objective of directing resources toward demonstrated community needs. Banks should be able to
select the form and geographic allocation of qualifying community development activity based
on where their resources can generate meaningful value, while receiving sufficient advance
certainty to make those commitments responsibly. Pairing substantive flexibility with predictable
qualification standards would enable institutions to commit capital, establish durable
partnerships, and pursue responsive community development initiatives with greater confidence
that qualifying activities will receive appropriate CRA consideration while substantively
addressing identified financial needs of their communities.

IV.
AFC Supports Streamlined Data Requirements and Sufficient Implementation Time
to Reduce Duplicative Compliance Burdens

CRA data collection should be governed by a straightforward principle: an institution should not
be required to collect and report information unless that information materially contributes to its
CRA evaluation or serves a distinct and identifiable supervisory purpose. New reporting
obligations can require substantial modifications to data architecture, internal controls, validation
procedures, governance processes, vendor relationships, and reporting systems. Those burdens
are difficult to justify where substantially similar information is already available to regulators
through another federal reporting regime or where the requested information does not bear
directly on the activities being evaluated. The agencies should therefore calibrate data
requirements to the information necessary to administer the CRA framework and refrain from
imposing collection obligations that lack a clear nexus to CRA performance evaluation or an
identified supervisory need.

Section 1071 data presents an important opportunity to reduce unnecessary duplication in CRA
reporting. In determining whether to maintain separate CRA collection and reporting
requirements for small business lending, the agencies should assess the extent to which
information collected pursuant to section 1071 can satisfy the same CRA evaluation or
supervisory purposes. Where existing section 1071 data provides the information necessary for
CRA purposes, institutions should not be required to collect or report substantially similar
information through a separate CRA process. Conversely, any additional CRA specific data
requirement should serve a distinct supervisory purpose that cannot reasonably be satisfied
through information already collected under section 1071. Applying this principle would
promote a more efficient reporting framework while ensuring that the agencies continue to
receive the information necessary to conduct meaningful CRA evaluations.

Comparable discipline is warranted for consumer lending and community development data.
Consumer lending information should be collected for CRA purposes only when the relevant
lending activity is actually subject to evaluation as a major product line or is affirmatively
incorporated into an approved strategic plan. Likewise, community development reporting
 12

should be confined to information necessary to establish qualification, geographic allocation, and
performance. Requiring broader data sets untethered to the examination methodology would
impose systems and validation costs without materially improving the agencies' assessment of
CRA performance. Aligning reporting obligations with the activities actually evaluated would
instead ensure that data collection remains an instrument of effective supervision rather than an
independent compliance exercise.

The proposed waiver authority can provide an additional safeguard against unnecessary
reporting, but its practical value will depend on the standards governing its availability. Rather
than treating waivers as exceptional relief reserved for unusual circumstances, the agencies
should establish objective criteria identifying when a reporting requirement may be waived
because the information is unnecessary to evaluate an institution's CRA performance or provides
no material additional value to aggregate agency analysis. Published examples of circumstances
warranting a waiver would further promote consistency across examinations and allow
institutions to assess eligibility before devoting resources to collecting information of limited
supervisory utility. A transparent and administrable waiver process would therefore complement
appropriately calibrated reporting requirements by providing a mechanism to address
circumstances in which a generally applicable requirement produces little corresponding
regulatory benefit.

Even appropriately tailored data requirements require adequate time to implement. Any new or
materially revised reporting obligation should carry an applicability date that affords banks
sufficient time to design, test, validate, and govern the systems necessary for accurate
compliance. Importantly, that implementation period should account for the timing of technical
specifications, file formats, validation rules, and examination guidance necessary to
operationalize the requirement. Banks should not be expected to begin building reporting
systems against incomplete specifications or to repeatedly modify those systems as
implementation instructions evolve. A sequenced implementation schedule, measured with
reference to the availability of the technical information necessary for compliance, would
promote data accuracy, reduce avoidable implementation costs, and allow institutions to devote
greater resources to substantive community reinvestment rather than repeated systems
remediation.

*
*
*

AFC appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Proposed Rule and supports the agencies'
efforts to establish a CRA framework that provides meaningful regulatory certainty while
recognizing the diversity of institutions, business models, and communities subject to the Act. As
the agencies finalize these reforms, the framework should preserve the flexibility that enables
CRA evaluations to account for how institutions actually operate and serve their communities,
while maintaining clear and meaningful standards for assessing performance.

To achieve that balance, AFC encourages the agencies to preserve strategic plan flexibility and
the limited purpose bank designation, focus consumer lending evaluations on material product
lines, afford institutions appropriate discretion in directing community development resources
toward demonstrated needs, provide greater certainty regarding qualifying activities, and ensure
 13

that data collection requirements are appropriately tailored and nonduplicative. These
refinements would promote a more predictable and administrable CRA framework while
allowing institutions to devote greater attention and resources to the credit and community
development needs that the Act is intended to address.

AFC appreciates the agencies' consideration of these comments and stands ready to serve as a
resource as the final rulemaking unfolds.

Sincerely,



Ian P. Moloney
Chief Policy Officer
American Fintech Council

To Whom It May Concern:
Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. Developers Collaborative (DC) is a
Portland-based real estate developer and Maine's leading producer of affordable housing.
Through the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit) program, and in partnership
with MaineHousing and private equity investors, DC has developed nearly 1,200 Housing
Credit homes across the state. Housing Credit equity, paired with other public and private
financing, is what makes those housing projects feasible at restricted rents, allowing DC to
produce safe, stable homes for Maine families.
For nearly half a century, CRA has driven banks to extend private capital financing to local
communities they serve, combating the legacy of redlining, promoting equitable lending,
and facilitating reinvestment in low- and moderate-income places and people. CRA has
spurred lending and investments in homeownership, small businesses, healthcare,
childcare, and other community needs, but nowhere is its impact more pronounced than in
the effect CRA has had on the production of affordable rental housing through the Housing
Credit program.
The Housing Credit, our nation's most important tool for the production of affordable rental
housing, relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. In fact, approximately 80
percent of equity investments in the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated
bank investors, according to a 2025 study by the accounting firm CohnReznick.1 Banks
make these investments not only to receive the modest return provided by the tax
advantages associated with investing in Housing Credit properties, but also because the
full CRA examination for large banks includes a distinct investment test. Because Housing
Credit investment yields are typically modest, large banks often could get a more

1 2025 Affordable Housing Credit Study, CohnReznick


631 Stevens Avenue, Suite 203, Portland, ME 04103
substantial yield from making other forms of investment, but often still choose to invest in
the Housing Credit because Housing Credit investments help banks meet their CRA
obligations.

We are concerned that OCC and FDIC's proposal to reclassify banks with assets ranging
from $1.649 billion to $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than large banks subject to
the full CRA examination, including the investment test, could reduce competition in the
Housing Credit equity market, leading to lower pricing on credits and less housing
produced. Of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks, only 256 would maintain
that designation under the proposal—a decline of over 60 percent, according to the
National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL). This leaves only 6 percent of
banks in the current large bank classification subject to the full CRA exam. According to a
survey by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), banks with assets in the
$1.649 billion to $10 billion range invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over
the five-year survey period. Extrapolating these results to the full Housing Credit market,
banks in this asset range invested up to $2 billion in Housing Credit equity over the past five
years.

If the OCC/FDIC proposal is made final, newly classified intermediate banks would no
longer need to invest in the low and moderate-income communities they are supposed to
serve because they would no longer be subject to the investment test, despite still having
more general community development obligations as an intermediate-sized bank. This is
because, for various reasons, it is often easier for banks to support community
development activities through lending rather than equity investment.
Moreover, the CRA Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) undercuts recent congressional
action to strengthen and expand the Housing Credit and facilitate more bank investment in
the program. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (also known as the Working Families Tax Cuts
Act) included a substantial increase in Housing Credit authority and expanded the 4
Percent Housing Credit program to increase supply, while the 21st Century ROAD to
Housing Act raised the limit on banks' public welfare investments (PWI) to allow them to
increase their Housing Credit investments. The provision lifting the PWI cap would mostly
impact many of the same banks that would be reclassified as intermediate banks. Thus,
the CRA changes under consideration by the OCC and FDIC could greatly dilute these
legislative accomplishments and undercut congressional goals of providing more
affordable rental homes.
The consequences of this proposal would be most damaging to smaller communities that
now benefit from being in the CRA assessment area of one or more large banks but may no
longer be if the OCC and FDIC change the definition of large bank as proposed. A survey by
AHTCC finds that approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity invested through
syndicators by banks in the $412 million – $10 billion asset range supported rural markets
between 2021 and 2024, indicating that these banks play an outsized role in investing in
smaller communities. Credit pricing for properties in many urban areas—which are more
likely to have at least one and often multiple banks competing to invest in Housing Credit

631 Stevens Avenue, Suite 203, Portland, ME 04103
developments because of overlapping assessment areas—tends to be much higher than
pricing in rural and other smaller communities that are not part of assessment areas for
large banks subject to the investment test.

We have seen this pricing dynamic on a 9% Housing Credit development in southern Maine.
The project is a 48-unit senior community in a market MaineHousing has designated as among
the highest need for senior affordable housing. A CRA-motivated bank investor with that
community in its assessment area committed to a substantial share of the equity at a price
above the economic market. However, that commitment was capped, so when MaineHousing
adjusted the mix of Housing Credit and subsidy, the development required additional equity
and the balance had to be placed in a multi-investor fund. With a larger share of the equity
outside the CRA commitment, pricing on the full investment fell by two cents and created a gap
in the development budget. If banks that currently invest in the Housing Credit to meet the
investment test are no longer examined on those investments, more deals will be priced as
economic product. The result is lower credit pricing, larger gaps in the capital stack, and fewer
affordable homes delivered.

Alternatives to the Primary Proposal

The OCC and FDIC included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new thresholds or
various bank size classifications related to CRA. The first would raise the large bank
asset threshold from $1.649 billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would still have far-
reaching negative consequences compared to the current large bank threshold but is
substantially less disruptive to Housing Credit investment than the primary proposal to raise
the large bank threshold to $10 billion.

According to AHTCC's survey of bank investment in the Housing Credit, 108 banks would be
reclassified as intermediate banks rather than large banks if the threshold is set at $10
billion, while just 40 would be reclassified as intermediate banks if the large bank threshold is
set at $3.252 billion. Moreover, the banks that would remain subject to the separate
investment test under a $3.252 billion threshold account for approximately 86 percent of the
Housing Credit equity investment by OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks captured in the AHTCC
survey with assets between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.
The second alternative proposal would be far more damaging for affordable rental housing
production than either the primary or first alternative proposals. NAAHL estimates that, under a
$30 billion large bank threshold, 17 states would see the number of large banks with
investment requirements cut by half or more. According to AHTCC, banks with assets between
$10 billion and $30 billion account for more than twice as much Housing Credit debt and equity
investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.

Conclusion
Developers Collaborative has seen the impact of CRA firsthand. If banks now subject to the
investment test are reclassified and no longer examined on equity investments, more Housing
Credit equity will price on economic terms. As the pricing gap on our southern Maine
development demonstrates, this means larger budget gaps and fewer affordable homes built at
a time when our communities desperately need them.
We strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand under
the 1995 CRA rule, consistent with the direction the Federal Reserve—the third bank
regulator—appears to be taking. If the OCC and FDIC move forward with changes to CRA
regulations, we strongly urge maintaining the lowest possible threshold for large banks and
adopting policies to strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including rural
and smaller markets.

RE: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations - Proposed Rule

Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould:

On behalf of Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe Housing Authority, we appreciate the opportunity to
comment on the proposed Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.

Our organization is responsible for supporting housing opportunities for members of the Leech
Lake Band of Ojibwe. We work to develop, preserve, and maintain housing that meets the needs of
our community, including through partnerships with private financial institutions and federal
housing programs.

Access to private capital is essential to meeting our housing needs. However, attracting bank
financing and investment to Indian Country can be particularly difficult because of our rural
location, unique land ownership structures, and the limited number of financial institutions actively
investing in Tribal communities.

We recognize the agencies' stated goals of reducing regulatory burdens and improving clarity.
However, we are concerned that certain proposed changes could further limit the private capital
available for Tribal housing development.

We respectfully offer the following recommendations.

Recommendation #1: Preserve strong incentives for banks to invest in Tribal housing
(Question 1 and Appendix A(d)(3)).

We oppose proposed changes that would substantially reduce the number of banks subject to
meaningful community development investment requirements.
 Tribal housing developments frequently depend on multiple funding sources, including federal
housing funds, LIHTC equity, and other private financing. These resources are essential to
constructing new homes, rehabilitating existing housing, and addressing significant housing
shortages.

The CRA encourages banks to participate in these investments. Weakening community
development requirements could reduce the number of financial institutions willing to invest in
Tribal housing projects.

We urge the agencies to retain the current large-bank asset threshold and preserve meaningful
Community Development Test requirements for intermediate banks.

Recommendation #2: Allow banks to receive CRA consideration for investments in Indian
Country regardless of their assessment-area boundaries (Question 34).

Many Tribal communities are located outside the traditional assessment areas of banks that have
the financial resources and experience to invest in affordable housing.

This geographic mismatch can make it difficult to attract private financing even when our
communities have substantial unmet housing needs and viable development opportunities.

We recommend that qualifying investments benefiting Indian Country and other Tribal and Native
lands receive CRA consideration outside a bank's assessment areas without requiring the bank to
first satisfy the geographic flexibility standard in every assessment area.

Banks should continue to serve the communities within their assessment areas, but those
obligations should not discourage additional investments in underserved Tribal communities.

Recommendation #3: Recognize Tribal housing development as an important form of
economic development and community revitalization (Question 30).

Housing development in Indian Country supports much more than the construction of homes. It
creates jobs, supports local businesses, strengthens community infrastructure, and enables Tribal
citizens and families to remain in or return to their communities.

We support recognizing residential development in Indian Country as presumptively promoting
economic development when applicable requirements are met.

We also recommend that housing development, rehabilitation, and preservation qualify as
revitalization and stabilization activities in Indian Country and other Tribal and Native lands.

Housing needs in Tribal communities extend across income levels, and federal CRA regulations
should recognize the broader economic and community benefits of Tribal housing development.

Recommendation #4: Recognize Tribal Indian Housing Plans under NAHASDA (Question 30).
 Tribal governments and their housing entities develop Indian Housing Plans (IHPs) under the Native
American Housing Assistance and Self-Determination Act (NAHASDA) to identify housing needs,
establish priorities, and guide housing activities.

We recommend that the agencies expressly recognize an approved IHP as a bona fide Tribal
government revitalization or stabilization plan.

Doing so would recognize Tribal planning processes and provide banks with a clear basis for
determining whether housing investments advance documented community priorities.

Recommendation #5: Ensure comprehensive recognition of Tribal and Native lands (Question
55).

We support using the broader 2023 Native Land Area framework, or an equally inclusive approach,
to ensure that Tribal and Native communities are appropriately recognized under CRA.

Definitions should encompass relevant trust lands, restricted-fee lands, Alaska Native areas, and
other Tribal and Native geographies.

Regulatory definitions should not unintentionally exclude otherwise qualifying housing
developments simply because of the unique land ownership or geographic circumstances of Native
communities.

Conclusion

Tribal communities face substantial housing needs and significant challenges attracting private
capital. CRA should help address those challenges by encouraging financial institutions to invest in
communities that have historically received limited bank investment.

We urge the agencies not to finalize the proposed rule in its current form. Any revised rule should
preserve meaningful community development investment incentives, recognize Tribal housing
priorities, and provide practical opportunities for banks to invest in Indian Country.

Sincerely,

AD Pluar"

The CRA encourages banks to participate in these investments. Weakening community
development requirements could reduce the number of financial institutions willing to invest
in Tribal housing projects.

We urge the agencies to retain the current large-bank asset threshold and preserve
meaningful Community Development Test requirements for intermediate banks.

Recommendation #2: Allow banks to receive CRA consideration for investments in Indian
Country regardless of their assessment-area boundaries (Question 34).

Many Tribal communities are located outside the traditional assessment areas of banks that
have the financial resources and experience to invest in affordable housing.

This geographic mismatch can make it difficult to attract private financing even when our
communities have substantial unmet housing needs and viable development opportunities.

We recommend that qualifying investments benefiting Indian Country and other Tribal and
Native lands receive CRA consideration outside a bank's assessment areas without requiring
the bank to first satisfy the geographic flexibility standard in every assessment area.

Banks should continue to serve the communities within their assessment areas, but those
obligations should not discourage additional investments in underserved Tribal communities.

Recommendation #3: Recognize Tribal housing development as an important form of
economic development and community revitalization (Question 30).

Housing development in Indian Country supports much more than the construction of homes.
It creates jobs, supports local businesses, strengthens community infrastructure, and enables
Tribal citizens and families to remain in or return to their communities.

We support recognizing residential development in Indian Country as presumptively
promoting economic development when applicable requirements are met.

We also recommend that housing development, rehabilitation, and preservation qualify as
revitalization and stabilization activities in Indian Country and other Tribal and Native lands.

Housing needs in Tribal communities extend across income levels, and federal CRA
regulations should recognize the broader economic and community benefits of Tribal housing
development.

Recommendation #4: Recognize Tribal Indian Housing Plans under NAHASDA (Question 30).

Tribal governments and their housing entities develop Indian Housing Plans (IHPs) under the
Native American Housing Assistance and Self-Determination Act (NAHASDA) to identify
housing needs, establish priorities, and guide housing activities.

We recommend that the agencies expressly recognize an approved IHP as a bona fide Tribal
government revitalization or stabilization plan.

Doing so would recognize Tribal planning processes and provide banks with a clear basis for
determining whether housing investments advance documented community priorities.

Recommendation #5: Ensure comprehensive recognition of Tribal and Native lands (Question
55).

We support using the broader 2023 Native Land Area framework, or an equally inclusive
approach, to ensure that Tribal and Native communities are appropriately recognized under
CRA.

Definitions should encompass relevant trust lands, restricted-fee lands, Alaska Native areas,
and other Tribal and Native geographies.

Regulatory definitions should not unintentionally exclude otherwise qualifying housing
developments simply because of the unique land ownership or geographic circumstances of
Native communities.

Conclusion

Tribal communities face substantial housing needs and significant challenges attracting
private capital. CRA should help address those challenges by encouraging financial
institutions to invest in communities that have historically received limited bank investment.

We urge the agencies not to finalize the proposed rule in its current form. Any revised rule
should preserve meaningful community development investment incentives, recognize Tribal
housing priorities, and provide practical opportunities for banks to invest in Indian Country.

Sincerely,


Pete Delgado
Executive Director
Tohono O'odham Ki:Ki Association

Dear Deputy Executive Secretary Jones and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency:
Northern Initiatives (NI) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the OCC and FDIC proposed revisions to
the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations, published in the Federal Register on August 12, 2026.
NI is a certified Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) and Michigan's largest small business
lending CDFI. We are an SBA Microlender and Community Advantage lender, and USDA's rural lending programs
have long been our most consistent source of capital for rural small businesses. Over our history, we have made
nearly 2,000 loans totaling more than $120 million, helping create or retain nearly 7,900 jobs. We pair financing
with hands-on coaching, with a strong focus on rural communities.
We support the agencies' goals of clarity and reduced burden. However, the proposed asset thresholds, grant
restrictions, and weaker community development standards would arrive just as consolidation has made the
remaining banks' partnerships more important than ever to rural Michigan. Together, these changes would
weaken the bank partnerships that small businesses in our region depend on.
Proposed changes would negatively impact rural communities
Rural communities have seen a wave of bank closures and consolidation over the past two decades. As local banks
merge into larger institutions and branches close, fewer lenders remain who know local businesses and markets.
In many of the small towns we serve, NI is one of the few sources of small business credit left.
That makes CRA more important in rural markets, not less. CDFIs like NI fill the gap that consolidation leaves, but
we do so in partnership with the banks that remain, through capital, referrals, and shared customers. With fewer
banks left, each one's incentive to invest in rural small business carries more weight. Bank capital also multiplies


federal investment: banks look for CDFI Fund awards on our balance sheet, and CRA gives them reason to invest
alongside those public dollars.
The proposed asset thresholds would weaken that incentive just when it matters most. Hundreds of banks would
move into lower CRA categories, and many regional and community banks would face weaker community
development expectations or none at all. These are the banks most likely to serve rural Michigan and to partner
with organizations like ours.
Small businesses depend on bank–CDFI partnerships
Small businesses are the backbone of rural Michigan's economy, and bank partnerships are how NI reaches many
of them. Banks refer business owners who need more flexibility than a conventional loan allows. Our financing
and coaching then help those owners build the track record to return to a bank as they grow.
Northland Precision, a CNC machining shop in Traverse City, is one example. When a move to a larger facility
strained the company's cash flow, Dart Bank's vice president of lending connected the owner with NI. We
financed raw materials and inventory so the shop could keep up with growing demand from its largest customer.
CRA encourages exactly this kind of partnership.
We urge the agencies to keep small business lending a meaningful CRA activity, even when it is not one of a bank's
largest product lines. We also oppose the proposed 15% indirect-cost cap on grants. For a lender, underwriting,
servicing, compliance, and technology are not overhead separate from community impact; they are what make
small-dollar, high-touch lending possible in rural markets.
Recommendations
Northern Initiatives respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to:
●​ Retain the current asset thresholds, indexed to inflation, and require intermediate banks to perform at
least Satisfactory on both lending and community development.
●​ Keep small business lending, and bank partnerships with CDFIs that expand small business credit, a
meaningful CRA activity.
●​ Provide geographic flexibility that directs capital to rural CRA deserts, without displacing activity within
assessment areas.
CRA has helped build durable partnerships that bring private capital to rural small businesses without new
federal spending. As consolidation leaves rural communities with fewer banks, the final rule should strengthen
those incentives, not weaken them. Thank you for considering our comments.
Sincerely,

Elissa Sangalli
CEO/President

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed modifications to the Community
Reinvestment Act regulations.
Evernorth respectfully urges the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation to retain the current Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) asset thresholds. If the
agencies nevertheless decide to increase the Large Bank threshold, we urge adoption of the $3.252
billion alternative rather than the proposed $10 billion threshold.

The proposed changes could threaten the future supply of affordable housing in Maine, Vermont and
New Hampshire by significantly reducing the amount of Housing Credit Equity available from the
network of active bank investors in Northern New England in three significant ways:
-
Reclassifying 27 of the banks currently providing Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) equity
through the CRA framework.
-
Weakening incentives for Intermediate Banks to provide equity investments across the rural
markets we serve; and
-
Reducing the available capital raised through multi-investor funds by removing investors and
constraining the commitments of the banks that remain.
Evernorth is a mission-driven Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) syndicator and community
development organization serving Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont. Created by the state Housing
Finance Agencies more than 35 years ago to facilitate the use of the LIHTC program in our rural states,
Evernorth works with community and regional banks to bring private investment to affordable housing
developments in markets that often face significant barriers to attracting capital.
Over our 35-year history, we have raised and invested more than $1.6 billion in affordable housing and
more than $300 million in community and economic development initiatives. These investments have

helped create or preserve more than 17,000 affordable homes, support more than 5,000 quality jobs,
and expand access to critical services for more than 125,000 people across Northern New England.
The proposed thresholds could significantly reduce LIHTC investment from banks that provide
affordable housing capital in Northern New England.
Banks that would be reclassified under the proposal are important sources of affordable housing capital
for the region. From 2021 through 2025, these institutions invested approximately $97.75 million in
Housing Credit equity through Evernorth's multi-investor funds, nearly one-third of all the equity raised
through those funds during that period.
If changes to CRA reduce their incentive to invest, the impact could reach well beyond these individual
banks, reducing the capital available to finance affordable housing across Northern New England. Given
the significant role these institutions play in our investor base, Evernorth does not believe an increase in
the Large Bank threshold is warranted. If the agencies nevertheless increase it, the $3.252 billion
alternative would affect fewer of our current Large Bank investors and be less disruptive to our existing
LIHTC investor base than the proposed $10 billion threshold.
The proposed thresholds would weaken community development incentives for a significant share of
banks serving Northern New England.
The impact extends beyond banks that invest directly through Evernorth. Analysis by Partnership for
Financial Equity shows how broadly the proposed changes would affect banks based in Maine, New
Hampshire, and Vermont.
-
In Maine, 12 of the 17 Maine-based banks regulated by the OCC or FDIC would move to a
smaller asset category, including 11 moving from Large to Intermediate and one from
Intermediate to Small.
-
In New Hampshire, nine of the 12 covered state-based banks would move to a smaller category,
including three moving from Large to Intermediate and six from Intermediate to Small.
-
In Vermont, 6 of the 10 covered state-based banks would face different CRA requirements,
including four moving from Large to Intermediate and two from Intermediate to Small.
These reclassifications would reduce community development requirements for many of these
institutions. We are concerned that the proposal would allow lending performance by Intermediate
Banks to offset weaker community development performance. Loans alone will not make an affordable
housing development feasible.
Evernorth recommends continuing to require Intermediate Banks to demonstrate satisfactory
performance in both Lending and Community Development to receive an overall satisfactory rating.
Taken together, the proposed changes would weaken community development investment incentives for
a significant share of the community and regional banks serving Northern New England. In rural markets
with fewer sources of private capital, maintaining these incentives is especially important because

without CRA incentives there are few alternative sources of investment to build and preserve these
critically needed homes and community services.
Multi-investor funds amplify the impact of losing even a small number of investors.
Evernorth's analysis indicates that the proposed thresholds could have reduced the capacity of our multi-
investor funds by more than $236 million in Housing Credit equity, enough to support approximately
1,432 affordable homes.
Multi-investor funds are Evernorth's primary vehicle for raising Housing Credit equity for affordable
housing developments throughout Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont. These funds are particularly
important in smaller and rural markets, where individual projects often cannot attract investment from
large national banks.
Large bank investors are generally subject to ownership concentration limits within individual multi-
investor funds. For example, individual investors may be limited to 20 or 25 percent ownership of a fund.
These ownership limits also mean that lost investment dollars from a departing smaller investor cannot
necessarily be replaced by increasing the commitments of the remaining large bank investors.
If smaller institutions withdraw or materially reduce their participation, an entire fund becomes smaller,
which in turn, reduces the amount our largest investors can contribute as the total fund size diminishes.
Based on our fund activity from 2021 through 2025, more than $236 million in Housing Credit equity
could be affected, representing more than 70 percent of the capital raised through our multi-investor
funds during that period. That includes the $97.75 million invested directly by the affected institutions
and approximately $125 million in additional equity from other investors whose participation could be
constrained by a smaller fund size.
This dynamic is especially important in rural communities, where there are fewer investors and fewer
options for replacing lost capital. Multi-investor funds bring together investments from banks of different
sizes to finance rural affordable housing developments that might otherwise struggle to attract
institutional investment. When even a few community or regional banks reduce their participation, the
impact can ripple through the fund, reducing the capital available to build and preserve affordable
homes across rural communities.
Responses to Selected Questions:
Question 1: To better align with agency policies that establish an asset size of less than $30 billion as a
threshold for certain supervisory approaches, such as being considered a community bank or being
subject to the continuous examination process, 108 should the agencies consider adjusting the
intermediate bank asset size threshold to include all banks with an asset size of less than $30 billion that
do not qualify as small banks? If the agencies establish $30 billion as the appropriate threshold to
delineate between intermediate banks and large banks, should the agencies also adopt a larger
threshold for small banks, such as the $10 billion currently proposed as the intermediate bank threshold?

Evernorth strongly recommends against adopting a $30 billion Large Bank threshold. AHTCC survey data
show that banks with assets between $10 billion and $30 billion account for more than twice as much
LIHTC debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion. Given the direct and
fund-level impacts described above, raising the threshold to $30 billion would further increase the
amount of affordable housing capital potentially affected.
Question 18: Should the definition of affordable housing be expanded to include rental housing for
middle-income individuals in high-cost areas as proposed? For example, should banks be
incentivized to support affordable workforce housing that would allow public servants, such as
teachers, firefighters, and police officers, to live in the communities they serve?
Evernorth recognizes the need for workforce housing across Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont. In
many communities, teachers, health care workers, first responders, and other working households
struggle to find homes they can afford near where they work. We support efforts to increase the supply
of housing for these households and to bring additional private capital to communities facing significant
housing shortages.
At the same time, we believe CRA incentives for affordable housing should remain focused on low- and
moderate-income (LMI) households, for whom housing needs are significant and attracting private
capital can be especially challenging. Expanding CRA consideration to middle-income housing in high-
cost areas should not divert investment away from LIHTC developments or other affordable housing
serving LMI households. Instead, these investments should complement existing efforts to meet the
housing needs of those with the fewest affordable options

We also believe that housing receiving CRA consideration based on affordability should be subject to
meaningful protections to ensure it remains affordable over time. This is particularly important for
Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing (NOAH), where rents may be affordable at the time of financing
but can increase over time without long-term affordability restrictions, potentially displacing residents
and putting homes out of reach for the people they were meant to serve. CRA considerations should
therefore be tied to defined affordability periods, with compliance requirements to ensure those
protections remain in place

Evernorth supports using CRA to address workforce housing needs in high-cost areas, as long as
protections keep that housing affordable and strong incentives remain in place for investment in housing
serving LMI households.
Based on our experience raising and deploying private capital in Northern New England, Evernorth
respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to:
1. Retain the current Large and Small Bank asset thresholds. If the agencies nevertheless increase the
Large Bank threshold, adopt the $3.252 billion alternative rather than the proposed $10 billion
threshold. Do not adopt the $30 billion Large Bank threshold or a $10 billion Small Bank threshold
raised in Question 1.

2. Preserve meaningful community development investment incentives for Intermediate Banks,
including the current requirement that banks achieve at least satisfactory performance on both the
Lending and Community Development tests to receive an overall satisfactory rating.
3. Consider the effect of reclassification on multi-investor funds as a whole, rather than considering
only the investment supplied directly by reclassified banks. Evernorth's experience demonstrates that
reduced participation by some institutions can also constrain commitments from other investors.
Evernorth supports appropriately targeted efforts to reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens for
community banks. Our experience, however, shows that the proposed thresholds would affect
institutions that currently provide significant affordable housing capital in Northern New England and
could reduce the capacity of the multi-investor funds that bring this capital to rural communities.
Thank you for considering Evernorth's comments and our experience raising and deploying private
capital throughout Northern New England.
Sincerely,
Nancy Owens

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill,

On behalf of more than one million members and supporters of Public Citizen, we
provide the following comment on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking issued by the
Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC) regarding the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). We strongly
oppose this proposal because it would sharply reduce credit to low- and moderate-income
(LMI) communities and decimate one of the nation's foundational laws enacted to
combat redlining and racial discrimination in finance. Public Citizen members live in
communities across the nation and benefit when local banks responsibly recirculate
deposits collected locally into commercial and retail credit in those same communities.
When they export those deposits into loans elsewhere, that community may decay.
 2
Background
The Community Reinvestment Act serves as one among a constellation of laws aimed at
combating discriminatory lending. Perversely, the federal government itself built
discrimination into the loan-making process. In response to the many foreclosures during
the Great Depression, Congress established the Home Owners' Loan Corporation
(HOLC) in 1933. This entity provided government support for loans, but it drew red lines
on the maps of certain neighborhoods, denoting them as higher risk. These
neighborhoods had lower-income residents and large minority populations. This became
the basis for the process referred to as "redlining."1 The harmful impact of that policy has
persisted for decades, with neighborhoods of color suffering lower mortgage approval
rates.
Congress began to address the problem with the 1968 Fair Housing Act and the 1974
Equal Credit Opportunity Act. In 1975, Congress approved the Home Mortgage
Disclosure Act (HMDA) to quantify where and to whom banks made loans. The law
required banks to make their annual lending public, delineated by recipients'
neighborhood, income, and race.
In 1977, Congress built on these laws and passed the Community Reinvestment Act,
authored by Sen. William Proxmire (D-Wisc.), then chair of the Senate Banking
Committee. Sen. Proxmire explained: "By redlining, let me make it clear what I am
talking about. I am talking about the fact that banks and savings and loans will take their
deposits from a community and instead of reinvesting them in that community, they will
actually or figuratively draw a red line on a map around the areas of their city, sometimes
in the inner city, sometimes in the older neighborhoods, sometimes ethnic and sometimes
black, but often encompassing a great area of their neighborhood."
The CRA went beyond the data collection required by earlier laws by adding a
mechanism to promote fair lending. As the law states, banks must demonstrate "a
continuing and affirmative obligation to help meet the credit needs of the local
communities in which they are chartered."2 If banks fail to demonstrate such a record of
fair lending, regulators will "take such record into account in its evaluation of an
application for a deposit facility by such institution."3 (The regulators are the Federal
Reserve Board, the Comptroller of the Currency, and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corp.)
To implement this law, regulators identified factors they would consider including:
efforts by the bank to ascertain the credit needs of the community such as communication
with members of the community; geographic distribution of the bank's credit extensions,
credit applications, and credit denials; evidence of prohibited discriminatory or other
illegal credit practices; and bank participation in local community development (CD)

1 Amy E. Hillier, Redlining and the Homeowners' Loan Corporation, 29 JOURNAL OF URBAN HISTORY 394-
395 (2003)
2 12 U.S.C. §2901(a)(3)
3 12 U.S.C. §2903(a).
 3
projects.4 (CD loans and investments involve larger scale projects such as multi-unit
affordable housing.) The statute provided that regulators also assign banks a rating–
Outstanding, Satisfactory, Needs to Improve, or Substantial Noncompliance. Regulators
also required banks to produce a written report that became part of the institution's
supervisory record.5
Over its history, the CRA led to important investments. Since 1996, banks have issued
more than $1 trillion in loans for community development, and $1 trillion for small
businesses located in low- and moderate-income census tracts.

Trump's CRA Proposal
In a blatant abuse of the nation's effort to combat redlining and the CRA's successes, the
two agencies whose officials serve at the pleasure of President Trump now propose to
undermine this law. (The Federal Reserve (Fed) did not advance a CRA rule. The
Supreme Court ruled the president can remove certain agency leaders but blocked a
Trump effort to remove Fed governors.)
Low Numerical Goal
Perhaps most harmful, this proposal sets a witheringly low threshold for community
reinvestment funding that would put a large financial institution in good standing. The
proposal calls for community investments totaling 0.625 percent of a bank's primary
capital standard (Tier 1 capital). This is some 85 percent less than the nation's 100 largest
banks now devote to this sector, according to one analysis. Capital, or the level of assets
that exceeds a bank's liabilities, generally hovers at less than 10 percent of total assets. In
other words, this proposal asks not that 0.625 percent of the bank's total funding be
reinvested in the community, but only about a half-percent of that 10 percent. Out of
every $100 million in assets at a large bank, it could devote as little as $62,500 to CRA-
qualified projects.

4 43 Fed. Reg. 47144, 47152 (Oct. 12, 1978).
5 Congress has modified the CRA several times. In 1989, as part of the Financial Institutions Reform,
Recovery, and Enforcement Act (FIRREA), banks were required to prepare a written evaluation,
which includes a public section as well as a confidential section. In 1994, as part of the Riegle-Neal
Interstate Banking and Branching Efficiency Act of 1994, Congress required banks to provide
separate analysis for each metropolitan area where the bank maintains a branch. It also required a
report for each state where it operated, and an overall report for the entire region of a bank's
operation. In 1995, the regulators implementing that law issued a rule designed to emphasize
performance, as critics contended that the CRA previously overemphasized process. The agencies
introduced the concepts of "assessment area" and "performance context." The assessment area
describes the geographic area within which the performance criteria in the rule would be assessed.
The performance context is a measure of how a bank performs compared to its peers in the
assessment area.

 4
This will represent an historic retreat from efforts to provide credit to LMI communities,
which have already suffered decades of disinvestment.
Excuses Banks from Scrutiny
The proposal also raises the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated
under CRA. Banks with less than $1 billion in assets would now be considered "small"
and face little scrutiny. Those with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would be
evaluated as "intermediate" and also face less comprehensive scrutiny than larger banks.
The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements for institutions with $10 billion or less in assets, including reporting on
small-business, small-farm, and community development lending.
This means that some 800 banks would no longer receive a community development
evaluation. Again, this will reduce incentives for banks to meet CRA goals. Among other
problems, this may reduce demand for the Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC),
an important driver of affordable housing development. This proposal exacerbates the
nation's housing crisis.
Fewer Products Reviewed

This proposal also reduces the number of products examiners will consider at larger
banks. Currently, examiners might review deposit products and transaction fees. The
proposal would limit examination to credit services. This ignores the fact that too many
citizens remain unbanked.

Community Development Grants Threatened
This proposal also threatens the viability of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Through CRA, banks may support affordable housing, small-
business growth, and other programs through grants. This proposal imposes a 15 percent
limit on indirect costs such as staff, rent, accounting compliance, and other expenses
ancillary to affordable housing construction. This could threaten many nonprofits,
especially smaller ones with few projects.
Undermining the "Purpose" and "Benefits" Tests
Under the current regime, simply extending credit to a small business does not
necessarily satisfy CRA guidance. It must also satisfy a "purpose" test, meaning it must
promote economic development for the LMI community. Funding the data centers, for
example, provides little ongoing employment relative to the cost of construction. But
under the new proposal, such investments might qualify as a CRA project.
Similarly, regulators propose weakening the "benefits" test, allowing credit that might
flow to an affluent community to count toward CRA investment.
 5
Promoting Bank Mergers
The CRA's enforcement mechanism rests on a banker's motivation to consummate a
merger. Without a satisfactory CRA rating, a merger proposal may be denied. Sharply
reducing CRA standards will lead to more mergers. This means losing more community
banks that understand local communities better than regional or mega-banks. Community
banks hold only 11 percent of total bank assets, but account for 37 percent of small
business loans, according to the Conference of State Bank Supervisors.
More mergers also threaten greater concentration among the larger banks. The 2008
financial crash followed concentration among large banks that proved not only too big to
fail, but too big to regulate.

Ignores Growing Risks from Climate Change
Given the growing impacts of climate change, which disproportionately harm LMI
communities, the CRA can and should be used as a tool to combat disinvestment related
to these impacts. Worsening climate disasters and chronic climate change impacts
threaten the availability of financial services in climate-vulnerable geographies. Financial
institutions are increasingly withdrawing from climate-vulnerable communities to
manage risk, a practice expected to accelerate as climate change impacts grow. At a
hearing before the U.S. Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs last
year, former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell testified, "If you fast forward 10 or 15
years, there will be regions of the country where you can't get a mortgage, there won't be
ATMs, banks won't have branches and things like that." While withdrawing from
communities can help financial institutions manage their exposure to climate risks in the
short run, withdrawal does nothing to reduce climate risk in the financial system over the
long term. Moreover, this practice deprives communities of essential financial services
that they need to build climate resilience or rebuild following a disaster.
The impact of climate change on the availability of financial services is not felt equally
across communities. Due to a history of systemic exclusion, including redlining, low-
income communities and communities of color are overrepresented in climate-vulnerable
areas. LMI communities face greater flood risk and are more exposed to extreme heat
than their middle- and upper-income counterparts. After a climate disaster, LMI
communities have fewer resources and less access to credit to make needed repairs.
Bluelining, or the practice of limiting credit creation and investment in climate-
vulnerable areas, often deepens financial exclusion and magnifies existing inequalities
and barriers to traditional finance for LMI communities and communities of color. As
such, a financial institution's attempts to manage climate-related financial risk by
withdrawing credit and other essential financial services from climate-vulnerable
communities can violate fair lending laws and exacerbate economic and racial inequality.
 6
Managing climate-related risks is appropriate, but using the cover of growing climate
risks to discriminate unfairly is not.
Given the disproportionate impacts of climate change on LMI communities and the role
of bluelining in exacerbating existing credit barriers, lending and investment in LMI
communities related to mitigating the impacts of climate change should be explicitly
eligible for CRA credit. Eligible loans and investments should extend to both climate
mitigation, which reduces greenhouse gas emissions, and climate adaptation, which
makes property and communities more resilient to the impacts of climate change.
Under the proposed rule, consideration of climate change impacts on LMI communities is
limited. Eligible community development includes activities that help individuals and
communities prepare for, adapt to, or withstand natural disasters, but only in designated
disaster areas. Rather than limit these eligible community development activities to
designated disaster areas, the rule should include disaster preparedness and adaptation
activities as eligible community development for all CRA-eligible areas. Activities that
mitigate climate change to reduce the frequency, severity, and cost of disasters should
also be eligible community development activities in all CRA-eligible areas. However,
the impact of any expansion of eligible community development activities will be greatly
diminished if the agencies proceed with the current proposal to increase the asset
thresholds that determine how banks are analyzed for CRA compliance or reduce the
required community development financing banks must do overall. Additionally,
activities related to disaster preparedness and adaptation—whether or not they occur in a
designated disaster area—should only be considered eligible for CRA credit if the
benefits of these activities accrue to LMI individuals or communities. Failing to consider
whether an investment benefits LMI individuals so long as it occurs in CRA-eligible
areas can incentivize banks to finance activities that do not further the underlying purpose
of the CRA. In designated disaster areas, this can be particularly perverse, siphoning
resources away from needed rebuilding efforts toward unrelated projects.

Conclusion
In its half-century of application, the CRA helped address some of the most intractable
problems with credit discrimination. This proposal insults that history. Ideally,
responsible bankers will remain committed to helping meet the credit needs of the
communities where they collect deposits. Unfortunately, this proposal invites
irresponsible actors to reduce such efforts and invites other ill-intentioned actors to
exploit the federal guarantees and imprimatur to divert those deposits to exacerbate
economic inequity.
We oppose this proposal and ask regulators to withdraw it.

 7
For questions, please get in touch with Bartlett Naylor at bnaylor@citizen.org and/or
Elyse Schupak at eschupak@citizen.org.

Sincerely,

Public Citizen
