Dear Deputy Executive Secretary Jones and OCC Comment Processing Staff:
On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).
CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide loans, investments, grants, and services
in communities that have historically lacked access to capital.
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations, and we support some of the agencies'
provisions that could improve the CRA framework and increase responsible capital in underserved
communities. However, we have grave concerns with the increases in the asset thresholds that
determine how banks are evaluated under CRA and the restrictions on operating grants. We also have
concerns with several interacting provisions that could further weaken community development
incentives that could impair the flow of much-needed capital in the most underserved communities.
The Virginia CDFI Coalition is a statewide network of Community Development Financial Institutions
(CDFIs) working to expand access to capital and financial services for underserved communities across
Virginia. Coalition members serve low- and moderate-income communities throughout the
Commonwealth, including rural and other communities that have historically faced barriers to accessing
affordable credit and investment. The Coalition brings together CDFIs and other community-based
lenders to advocate for policies that strengthen their ability to support affordable housing, small
businesses, community facilities, and other community development initiatives.
Banks are critical partners in our members' work. Virginia CDFIs maintain relationships with banks that
provide loans, investments, grants, deposits and other forms of support. These partnerships help
finance affordable housing, small businesses, community facilities and other community development
projects across Virginia. Bank support also helps CDFIs leverage additional public and private capital
and reach borrowers and communities that face barriers to conventional financing.
These partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing capital and resources to CDFIs,
banks rely on CDFIs to reach underserved communities and help borrowers prepare for future
financing. People Incorporated Financial Services, for example, pairs access to capital with business
guidance and referrals through the Small Business Development Center network. Its published account
of a home inspector's franchise purchase illustrates how financing and advisory support together can
help an entrepreneur establish a business. [1] The CRA helps sustain the incentives behind bank-CDFI
relationships. We are concerned that several provisions in the proposal could weaken those incentives
and reduce the flow of capital to the communities our members serve.
 Virginia CDFI Coalition | CRA comments
Page 2
Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance
Section IV.A, "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 1–3
The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate banks
as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as institutions with more than
$10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate community development test as
intermediate small banks would become small banks and lose that requirement. Another approximately
400 banks that are currently evaluated as large banks would become intermediate banks, losing the
separate large-bank lending, investment, and service tests and many associated data-reporting
requirements.
In Virginia, NCRC estimates that nine banks would lose their separate community development
evaluation and 16 would lose large-bank status under the proposed thresholds. These changes would
reduce the regulatory incentives and scrutiny associated with community development lending,
investment and services. They would not eliminate all CRA obligations for the affected banks.
The consequences may be especially significant in rural and smaller markets, where fewer financial
institutions and alternative sources of capital can make a single financing relationship particularly
important. People Incorporated Financial Services began serving Southwest Virginia and has expanded
into the Northern Piedmont, Northern Shenandoah Valley and Greater Prince William regions. Its
services include business and consumer loans, technical assistance and community facility financing. [2,
3] That combination reflects the work required to serve borrowers across different local markets.
Weakening incentives for bank partnerships could make it harder to sustain that reach.
Harm to Communities from Loss of Community Development Finance
These thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development performance is
evaluated and therefore affect the strength of banks' incentives to engage in community development.
The agencies acknowledge in the proposal that when banks become subject to a CD test under the
current framework, the explicit evaluation of their CD activities typically results in banks adjusting their
CRA programs.
Reclassifying banks into categories with less demanding community development evaluations could
affect the loans, investments and grants available to our members. Each member's exposure depends on
its funding relationships, the institutions that would be reclassified and the role those institutions play
in its capital structure. The agencies should evaluate those relationships before weakening the
incentives that support them.
CDFIs frequently rely on regional and community banks for patient debt, deposits, investments, lines of
credit and grants. The value of a bank relationship is not captured by the size of a single commitment. A
line of credit can support lending between funding cycles; patient capital can accommodate a
borrower's repayment capacity; and operating support can sustain the staff needed to originate,
underwrite and service smaller loans. Reductions in any of these forms of support could affect whether
a community project or business receives financing.
Misalignment with Congressional Priorities on Affordable Housing and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC)
The change also undermines Congress's recent efforts to strengthen Low-Income Housing Tax Credit
(LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) which are two bipartisan, popular federal tax tools with a
long track record of success in our communities. While Congress expanded LIHTC and made NMTC
permanent, the proposal undermines these important investment tools.
 Virginia CDFI Coalition | CRA comments
Page 3
LIHTC and NMTC are considered equity investments that are evaluated under the standalone
investment test for large banks which currently have a distinct 25%-weighted component of their CRA
evaluation devoted to qualified investments. Moving banks into the lower size category would mean
these transitioned banks would only be subject to a diluted evaluation that considers all CD in one test.
This means a bank may have greater ability to emphasize CD lending rather than maintain the same
level of LIHTC or NMTC investment because investment performance no longer receives a separate
rating. Through this weakened regulatory incentive, bank demand for these investments would
decrease.
Virginia's tax-credit financing provides a concrete example. In November 2025, VCDC reported raising
$53.4 million for Housing Equity Fund 29 from nine investment partners, including eight banks and
Fannie Mae. The fund was expected to help create or restore more than 523 affordable homes across
Norfolk, Lebanon, Manassas, Richmond, Saltville, Orange, Wytheville and Charlottesville. VCDC
identified units for low-income veterans, formerly homeless and very low-income residents and low-
income seniors. [4] These figures describe the whole fund, not the banks' individual contributions. They
show the housing activity supported by a financing structure in which banks are major partners.
Significance of CRA data and transparency
Section IV.G, "Data Collection, Reporting, and Disclosure"
The threshold changes would also substantially reduce the number of institutions subject to large-bank
CRA data requirements. This would make it harder for communities, CDFIs, policymakers, and
regulators to identify credit gaps, compare bank performance, assess geographic disparities, and
understand whether community credit needs are being met. We are concerned that aggregate
community development finance data is already difficult to track and the proposal would further reduce
data coverage, making it difficult to identify and understand where credit is flowing.
For the Coalition, bank lending data is needed to distinguish a shortage of available capital from gaps in
geographic coverage, product design or borrower access. Our policy and impact work needs evidence
showing where lending reaches low- and moderate-income communities and where gaps remain.
Comparable bank data can help members and public partners identify underserved markets and assess
whether financing is reaching the communities it is intended to serve. Removing reporting institutions
would reduce the evidence available for that work.
Recommendation
For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and reject all
alternatives offered (including the substantially higher thresholds raised for consideration in Question
1). The current thresholds are already annually indexed to CPI-W, so they are not beholden to 1995
asset levels. Moreover, the justification of "restoring proportionality to 1995" that the agencies use in
the proposal does not adequately explain why raising asset thresholds better serves the statutory intent
of the CRA, which is to ensure that credit needs of LMI communities are met. For the small bank
threshold, the proportionality metric rests on the distribution of the number of banks such that nearly
80% of all banks would be considered small, similar to what it was in 1995. While that's true, by the
same logic, nearly 20% of banks in 1995 were considered large whereas under the proposed large bank
threshold, only a little over 2% of all banks would be considered large. Instead, the agencies selectively
use total banking industry share to justify the large bank threshold saying large banks would under this
proposal, and similar to 1995 cover about 85% of all total bank industry's assets. Matching a 1995
distribution through either method does not necessarily demonstrate that the resulting categories are
appropriate for the modern banking system. The industry has consolidated dramatically, bank business
 Virginia CDFI Coalition | CRA comments
Page 4
models and geographic reach have changed. Banks with several billion dollars in assets today may have
substantially greater lending, investment, data, and operational capacity than institutions that were
treated as small or intermediate, three decades ago. The fact that assets happen to sit above a chosen
threshold does not by itself establish that banks below that threshold should lose the separate
investment/service tests or associated data requirements.
Restrictions on Community Development Grants
Section IV.C, "Community Development Activities , CD Grants"; Questions 9–11
We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants which: 1) require a
qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a
primary purpose of community development; 2) for large banks, cap a grant recipient's indirect
administrative costs at 15%; 3) require that large banks obtain documentation from grant recipients
including written commitments regarding use of funds, indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and
operating and program budgets. We also strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10 to
eliminate grants and donations from CRA consideration entirely.
While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit
communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of effective grantmaking and
misunderstand the role that flexible operating support plays in community development finance. For
CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, risk management, data systems,
financial management, technical assistance, and product development are not ancillary to community
development. They are the infrastructure that makes community development lending possible.
People Incorporated Financial Services' published programs illustrate the combination of lending and
borrower support that requires sustained organizational capacity. In a public announcement, it
described a $300,000 Commonwealth's Capital for Communities Fund award to support accessible
financial products, coaching, business lending and technical assistance for women entrepreneurs across
its service area. [3] This state-funded example illustrates why funding for the work around a loan
matters. CRA rules should preserve banks' ability to support that capacity through flexible operating
grants rather than limit consideration to narrowly defined project expenditures.
Moreover, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA eligibility. An
organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for community impact. Costs
vary depending on an organization's size, geography, product mix, regulatory obligations, technical-
assistance model, and populations served. The cap could disproportionately affect small and emerging
CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-dollar loans, organizations providing intensive borrower
technical assistance, CDFIs developing new products or entering underserved markets and
organizations making necessary investments in technology, compliance, data, and risk management.
Recommendation
The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building grants as
currently provided under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage flexibility for banks to provide
the form of support that best responds to the identified community needs instead of imposing undue
compliance burdens.
 Virginia CDFI Coalition | CRA comments
Page 5
Interacting Provisions That Could Further Reduce Community Development Incentives
Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance
Section IV.B, "Performance Tests , Intermediate Bank Ratings"
Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a Satisfactory
rating on both its lending test and its CD test to receive an overall Satisfactory rating. The proposal
would require a Satisfactory or better lending-test rating but would allow lending performance to
compensate for weaker CD performance.
This change is particularly concerning when combined with the proposed asset thresholds, which would
move hundreds of banks currently evaluated under the large-bank framework into the intermediate
category. If weak CD performance does not prevent an overall Satisfactory rating, banks may have less
regulatory incentive to make CDFI loans and investments, provide grants, or undertake other
community development activities. We urge the agencies to retain a requirement that intermediate
banks demonstrate at least Satisfactory CD performance to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
VCDC's public description of its relationship with Atlantic Union Bank identifies a long-standing
partnership in CRA investment and affordable housing finance. [5] This illustrates that CRA
considerations are part of the bank-CDFI partnership model. Our concern is prospective: allowing
weaker community development performance to be offset by retail lending could reduce the incentive
to sustain specialized partnerships.
Complexity definition anchored to lending is too narrow
Section IV.C, "Qualitative Factors"; Questions 12–17
The proposal would define complexity for CD investments, grants, and services largely by whether an
activity is a necessary or beneficial component of a multicomponent financing transaction involving a
loan. We oppose establishing a lending-centric definition of complexity. Investments in CDFIs can
involve specialized expertise, layered capital, subordinate positions, public subsidies, risk sharing,
guarantees, tax-credit structures, patient repayment terms, or other features that make transactions
complex even when they are not directly paired with a particular bank loan. We also oppose requiring
CD investments or services to be complex as contemplated in Question 14 or treating complexity as
categorically more responsive than innovation, flexibility, or impact as contemplated in Question 15.
For example, an investment in a pooled affordable housing fund may require analysis of tax-credit
delivery, developer capacity, long-term affordability obligations and performance across multiple
properties. The community value and complexity of that investment should be assessed on those
features, even when the investing bank is not also making a loan to each underlying project.
The agencies should assess complexity, innovativeness, flexibility, impact, and responsiveness based on
the characteristics and community value of the activity itself, rather than its association with a lending
transaction.
Prevent ordinary retail lending from substituting for specialized CD lending
Section IV.B, "Retail Lending Product Lines," Questions 4–7; and Section IV.C, "CD Loans"
The proposal would evaluate retail lending only in a bank's major product lines. It would also allow a
loan in a retail product line that is not evaluated as a major product line to receive consideration as a CD
loan if the loan otherwise satisfies the community development definition. We agree that genuinely
 Virginia CDFI Coalition | CRA comments
Page 6
community-development-oriented financing should not lose CRA consideration simply because a
product line is excluded from the retail evaluation.
However, this interaction creates a risk that ordinary-course small-business, small-farm, or other retail
lending could substitute for more specialized community development lending that depends more
directly on CRA incentives. The agencies should require a meaningful community development nexus
and ensure that the provision does not allow banks to satisfy CD expectations primarily through activity
they would undertake in the ordinary course of business.
Essential community infrastructure and facilities should retain a meaningful CD nexus
Section IV.D, "Community Development Definition , Revitalization and Stabilization", Question 25
We support CRA consideration for essential community facilities and infrastructure, particularly in rural
communities, Indian Country, distressed areas, and other markets with limited access to conventional
capital. The proposal, however, would broaden eligibility for essential community infrastructure and
facilities serving specified targeted areas. These activities would no longer necessarily need to
demonstrate that they help attract or retain businesses or residents, and community-wide
infrastructure may receive consideration without allocating a particular share of the benefit to LMI
individuals.
We are concerned that large infrastructure transactions routinely financed in the conventional market
could compete with affordable housing, CDFI financing, small-business lending, and other activities
more dependent on CRA incentives. The agencies should preserve flexibility where infrastructure
addresses a genuine community development or financing gap while ensuring that ordinary-course
infrastructure transactions do not displace more targeted CD activity.
The agencies should require evidence of the intended community benefit, such as the low- and
moderate-income population served, affordability of the service, documented financing gaps and the
project's contribution to access in an underserved community. A project's location in a targeted area
alone should not substitute for evidence of whom it serves. These standards would allow consideration
of genuinely needed infrastructure while limiting displacement of activities that depend more directly
on CRA incentives.
Strategic plans require strong guardrails
Section IV.F, "Strategic Plan"; particularly Questions 38–53
We support efforts to provide greater clarity regarding strategic plans and measurable goals. However,
because strategic plans allow banks to develop individualized CRA performance standards, strong
guardrails are essential to ensure that banks do not circumvent rigorous and reasonably consistent
expectations applied to similarly situated institutions.
The agencies should require strategic-plan goals to be responsive to demonstrated community needs,
sufficiently rigorous to approximate performance expected under the standard CRA tests, transparent
and measurable, subject to meaningful public engagement and evaluated against clear standards for
determining whether the goals adequately address assessment-area credit needs.
We particularly urge the agencies to establish strong standards in responding to Question 53, which
asks when measurable goals should be considered inadequate to address assessment-area needs.
 Virginia CDFI Coalition | CRA comments
Page 7
Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas
Section IV.E, "Consideration of Community Development Activities , CD Activities Outside Assessment Areas"; proposed §
__.13(e); Question 34
We support the goal of enabling CRA-motivated capital to reach communities with significant unmet
needs but relatively few bank assessment areas. Greater geographic flexibility could be particularly
beneficial for reaching CRA deserts.
Coalition members serve communities across Virginia that may have difficulty attracting CRA-motivated
capital because they fall outside the geographic footprints of many banks. This includes rural
communities, smaller markets, and communities where there may be limited access to bank branches or
other traditional sources of capital. CDFIs can help bridge these gaps by bringing financing and
investment to communities that may otherwise receive less attention from conventional financial
institutions.
However, flexibility should supplement rather than displace CD activity in banks' own assessment areas.
The agencies are considering both quantitative and qualitative approaches for determining when a bank
has sufficiently served its assessment areas to receive consideration for outside-AA activity.
With respect to Question 34, we support greater geographic flexibility where it can help direct CRA-
motivated capital to rural communities, Indian Country, and other underserved areas that may fall
outside traditional assessment areas. However, that flexibility should only become available after a bank
has demonstrated meaningful community development performance within its own assessment areas.
We are concerned that the quantitative standard proposed under Option 1 is too low to meet that
objective. For large banks, the proposal would allow outside-assessment-area consideration once a bank
reaches 0.625 percent of allocated Tier 1 capital in community development loans and 0.625 percent in
community development investments and grants. The agencies themselves explain that these thresholds
generally reflect the minimum level of activity needed to avoid a "Needs to Improve" rating and are not,
by themselves, sufficient to demonstrate satisfactory community development performance.
Recent analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition further illustrates the gap between
the proposed thresholds and current bank activity. Among 69 large OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks
analyzed by NCRC, current annual assessment-area community development lending, investments, and
grants totaled approximately $102 billion. Applying the proposed 0.625% Tier 1 capital thresholds to
those same institutions yielded a benchmark of approximately $14.8 billion, roughly 85% below current
activity. NCRC also found median assessment-area community development lending equal to 6.83% of
Tier 1 capital and median qualified investments and grants equal to 3.5%, both substantially above the
proposed 0.625% benchmarks.
A standard intended to determine when a bank has adequately served its own communities should
therefore be calibrated to meaningful, satisfactory community development performance, not merely
the minimum necessary to avoid a failing rating. We encourage the agencies to adopt a more rigorous
standard that considers both the level of activity and its responsiveness to identified community needs.
We further caution against allowing a broadly defined "substantially met" standard to weaken this
safeguard. Any exception should be narrowly tailored to circumstances in which a documented lack of
community development opportunities or other performance-context factors explain the shortfall,
rather than simply allowing weaker community development performance in individual assessment
areas to be offset by activity elsewhere.
 Virginia CDFI Coalition | CRA comments
Page 8
Allocation of CD activities across assessment areas
Section IV.E, "CD Activities in Assessment Areas, Assessment Area Allocation, Assigning Assessment Area Weights"
We support greater flexibility in allocating CD activities that benefit or serve multiple assessment areas.
This could better accommodate statewide and regional CDFIs whose community impact is not
accurately represented by the physical location of their headquarters.
People Incorporated Financial Services offers a practical example of why a headquarters address is an
incomplete measure of community benefit. Established to meet financing needs in Southwest Virginia, it
now also serves the Northern Piedmont, Northern Shenandoah Valley and Greater Prince William
regions. [3] Assigning a bank investment entirely to the institution's headquarters location would fail to
reflect that regional reach. Allocation should follow documented lending and service activity, using
information on the communities receiving the benefit.
Support for Provisions That Could Strengthen Community Development Finance
Consider prior-period community development loans
Section IV.C, "CD Loans"; Question 8
We strongly support providing CRA consideration for qualifying CD loans that remain outstanding from
prior evaluation periods, similar to the existing treatment of prior-period investments. Community
development borrowers frequently need long-term, patient financing. CRA should encourage banks to
structure loans around community needs rather than examination cycles.
With respect to Question 8, we recommend evaluation period-based consideration because it better
recognizes patient, long-term CD financing and provides a more representative measure of capital
committed throughout the CRA examination period than an annual snapshot and brings parity to the
treatment of loans and investments. The agencies should base consideration on the average outstanding
balance or otherwise account for both the amount and duration of the outstanding exposure, and should
treat repeated renewals of substantially the same loan as a single exposure.
Requested agency action
CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities we serve. We
appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and flexibility in the CRA framework. Modernization,
however, should result in more responsible capital reaching communities with unmet credit needs, as
the CRA statute was intended.
We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to reconsider the proposed increases to the asset thresholds and
the restrictions on community development operating grants. We also encourage the agencies to
preserve meaningful community development performance requirements for intermediate banks,
maintain robust data collection and reporting requirements, and ensure that strategic plans and
geographic flexibility are structured with appropriate accountability and transparency. The agencies
should also ensure that changes to the CRA framework do not undermine the partnerships between
banks and CDFIs that help bring capital to communities that have historically faced barriers to accessing
financing.
 Virginia CDFI Coalition | CRA comments
Page 9
Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed changes on
the communities we serve.
Respectfully,




Casey Bell
Coalition Director
The Virginia CDFI Coalition

These comments are submitted on behalf of Grow America, one of the oldest national community

reaching rural markets, providing capital to service enriched projects and areas often overlooked by large
LIHTC syndicators.
In addition to our work financing LIHTC developments, we are involved in other community development
activities that rely on bank participation incentivized by the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), including
training for community develop practitioners, New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) investment and
Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) lending.
Grow America welcomes the opportunity to comment on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR)
regarding CRA, a law which we believe is critically important to the continued success of the LIHTC
program. In our view the current proposal, to increase the limit at which a bank becomes a large bank
would disincentivize banks below the limit from investing in LIHTC and other CRA qualified investments.
This runs contrary to the recent increase by congress of the LIHTC allocation to each state and the
expansion of the projects that would qualify for LIHTC utilizing tax exempt debt. In those increases the
supply of credits was increased, but this proposal will decrease the demand for credits by banks, the
majority of investors in the current market, and decrease the capital available to projects in general, and
significantly undermine capital raise for LIHTC syndicators like Grow America. These mission driven,
non-profit syndicators often are working with smaller more locally focused financial institutions, who now
would be excluded from the investment test requirement. For our Fund specifically, the proposal to raise
the small bank limit to $10 billion would result in the loss of three investors totaling approximately $15
million a year and would result in the loss of an additional $7.50 from leveraged large bank investment.
Combined this would be a $22.5 million loss for the communities we serve.
As a former banker responsible for CRA compliance for 16 years at KeyBank, I believe this change would
eventually lead to the decrease in LIHTC investment outlined. Over time banks will revert to their most
comfortable product, which are primarily lending products. This decrease may not be immediate, but as
time passes and priorities change at banks, it will be the eventual outcome. As such, we outline below
the NASLEF observations and recommendations.

New York, NY 10017
growamerica.org
2
If Regulators Increase the Large Bank Threshold, Adopt a $3.252 Billion Threshold to Prevent
Unintended Negative Consequences on Rural Affordable Housing Development and Preservation
As noted above, CRA has helped create a competitive and efficient market for LIHTC. For
nonmetropolitan areas, banks below $10 billion in assets play an outsized role in ensuring the efficient
delivery of capital for LIHTC developments. According to the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition's
(AHTCC) survey of tax credit syndicators, over 108 banks below the $10 billion threshold invested at least
$1.6 billion in LIHTC equity over a five-year survey period. Extrapolating these results to the full LIHTC
market, banks under the $10 billion threshold invested approximately $2 billion in LIHTC equity over
those five years.
These investments are particularly important in rural areas: Approximately one-third of LIHTC equity
invested through syndicators by banks with $412 million to $10 billion in assets supported rural markets
from 2021–2024, indicating that banks in this asset range play an essential role in investing in rural
communities. By comparison, 8.1% of Housing Credit equity in a CohnReznick industry-wide sample was
invested in USDA-defined nonmetro counties, a proxy for rural and small-town markets.
Unlike large metropolitan areas with CRA hotspots, smaller cities, nonmetropolitan areas, and rural
communities rely on smaller investors with CRA obligations driven by the standalone Investment Test to
support LIHTC projects. Without the Investment Test for the smaller banks that serve these markets, we are
concerned that these communities will face even more severe disadvantages in accessing capital that will
reduce the production and preservation of the desperately needed affordable housing that they need.
Outsize Impact of Smaller Banks on Making Rural LIHTC Developments Possible
The loss of these smaller investors would jeopardize not just the total amount of investment in rural LIHTC
projects, but also the outsize impact that these investors have on the financial feasibility of rural affordable
housing developments.
In rural markets that are not served by large banks and do not enjoy strong CRA demand, smaller banks are
often the only CRA-motivated capital available for LIHTC developments. As a result, even small investments
by these banks have a major impact because they help even out the pricing disadvantages rural communities
face. Investments by these banks can make the difference on whether a project moves forward and a
community's affordable housing needs are met.
Without a standalone Investment Test, there will be reduced incentives for banks to play this role, creating a
gap for rural communities. Without this transformative capital, it will be exceedingly difficult for rural LIHTC
projects to find alternative investors with equity pricing that makes projects financially feasible. That will
deepen rural communities' disadvantages compared to urban areas with strong CRA-driven demand and
threaten their ability to create and preserve affordable housing.
Key Recommendation: If Regulators Increase the Large Bank Threshold, Adopt a $3.252 Billion Large Bank Asset
Threshold
We believe a primary goal of CRA regulatory reform should be driving investment and lending into rural
communities that are too often struggle to get access to mainstream finance. The Investment Test under
CRA has proved to be an effective way of driving high-impact activities in the communities these banks serve.
CRA has also helped community banks directly see the value of activities like LIHTC investments since the
leadership of those banks see their impact, spurring additional investment in the LIHTC program.
If regulators increase the large bank threshold, the $3.252 billion alternative large bank threshold would
be substantially less disruptive to LIHTC investment than the proposed $10 billion large bank threshold.
Based on AHTCC survey data, using a $3.252 billion threshold instead of $10 billion would reduce the
number of affected Housing Credit investors by approximately 63 percent, from 108 banks to 40 banks,
and reduce the estimated five-year LIHTC equity affected from roughly $2 billion to $272 million.
Moreover, the banks that would remain subject to standalone Investment Test under a $3.252 billion
threshold account for approximately 86 percent of the LIHTC equity investment by OCC- and FDIC-
regulated banks captured in AHTCC's survey with assets between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.

New York, NY 10017
growamerica.org
3
Preserve Meaningful Incentives for Banks to Prioritize Community Development Financing
In addition to the large bank threshold change, we are concerned that changes to how intermediate banks are
evaluated will diminish impactful community development financing activity. Intermediate banks are
evaluated separately on retail lending and on community development activities, including community
development loans, investments, and services.
Under the NPR, intermediate banks would no longer be required to achieve at least a Satisfactory rating on
both their lending test and Community Development (CD) test. Given the high impact of CD activities and the
increased number of banks that will fall in this category, we recommend against allowing weak CD
performance to be offset by lending. We encourage the agencies to retain the current requirement that banks
demonstrate at least a Satisfactory CD rating to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
In addition to raising equity capital for LIHTC developments, our organizations work to raise flexible lending
capital for affordable housing and community development projects. These high-impact loans play a
particularly important role in increasing the supply of affordable housing. Preserving meaningful incentives
through the CD test will help us ensure the flow of lending capital to affordable housing developments.
Remove Restrictions on Community Development Grants
We appreciate the agencies' goals of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit communities.
However, we caution against imposing new and burdensome restrictions on banks and community partners,
which would increase costs and regulatory complexity. New red tape would not only hurt banks, but also
community-based organizations that have become particularly important for responding to the affordable
housing needs of the communities we serve. We urge the agencies to recognize the important work of
local nonprofits in helping to meet community credit needs and to maintain the current CRA eligibility for
grant funding in the final rule.
RESPONSE TO SELECTED QUESTIONS
Question 1: To better align with agency policies that establish an asset size of less than $30 billion as a
threshold for certain supervisory approaches, such as being considered a community bank or being
subject to the continuous examination process, 108 should the agencies consider adjusting the
intermediate bank asset size threshold to include all banks with an asset size of less than $30 billion that
do not qualify as small banks? If the agencies establish $30 billion as the appropriate threshold to
delineate between intermediate banks and large banks, should the agencies also adopt a larger threshold
for small banks, such as the $10 billion currently proposed as the intermediate bank threshold?
We strongly recommend against the adoption of a $30 billion large bank threshold, which would be much
more damaging to LIHTC developments. AHTCC survey data show that banks with assets between $10
billion and $30 billion account for more than twice as much LIHTC debt and equity investment as banks
between $1.65 billion and $10 billion. Banks below the $30 billion threshold captured in the AHTCC
survey invested at least $3.575 billion in LIHTC equity over a five-year survey period. Extrapolating these
resuls to the full LIHTC market, these banks invested approximately $4.5 billion in LIHTC equity over the
past five years.
As we note above, these banks play an outsize role in rural areas and supporting the viability to rural
housing developments. As the asset threshold moves higher, the potential negative impact broadens.
Under the $30 billion threshold, more than 140 banks would no longer be subject to the Investment Test,
extending the impact to smaller cities in states that are not well served by major financial institutions. This
would also further concentrate LIHTC investment in large financial institutions that often have less of a
presence in smaller cities as well as nonmetropolitan areas.
Question 12: Does the proposed definition of "complexity" enhance the rule's focus on meeting
community credit needs by providing greater consideration to CD investments, grants, and services that
are linked to CD lending activities or are otherwise the functional equivalent of loans?
The proposal would require community development activities to be or be tied to a lending activity to be
considered "complex." While we appreciate the agencies' efforts to add clarity, this revised standard does
 633 Third Avenue 19th Floor, Suite J
New York, NY 10017
growamerica.org
4
not necessarily enhance the rule's focus on community credit needs. Investments – including investments
in CDFIs and LIHTCs – can be extremely responsive to community credit needs and complex to execute,
yet not directly tied to a loan as part of the transaction.
To maximize impact, the definition of complexity should not restrict the form of financing banks provide
and instead retain flexibility for banks to meet identified community needs using the most effective
products. We also recommend that the concept of complexity be communicated through interagency
guidance or as part of the illustrative list of qualifying activities, rather than adding complexity as a
definition in the regulation. Maintaining the explanation of complexity in subregulatory guidance preserves
the ability for the agencies to make adjustments and add examples of complex activities in response to
innovations in CD finance.
Question 18: Should the definition of affordable housing be expanded to include rental housing for
middle-income individuals in high-cost areas as proposed? For example, should banks be incentivized to
support affordable workforce housing that would allow public servants, such as teachers, firefighters, and
police officers, to live in the communities they serve?
The need for affordable housing remains most acute among LMI households. The number of cost-
burdened rental households has reached an all-time high, with 22.7 million households spending more
than 30 percent of their income on rent and utilities (defined as "cost burdened"), and that percentage is
even higher for poorer households. Over 80 percent of households making under $30,000 are cost
burdened, and over 70 percent of households making between $30,000 and $45,000 are cost burdened.
We support extending CRA credit to debt financing provided to naturally occurring affordable housing.
However, we believe some sort of standard should be in place to ensure that CRA credit is not extended
for the acquisition of NOAH property that is then converted – with or without some rehabilitation
expenditures – to market-rate housing. A standard should be adopted that requires a LURA for rents at
30% of 80% of AMI and provides full or partial credit based on the affordability of the property's rents
during the term of the loan that is receiving CRA credit.
While we support efforts to increase affordable housing development in high opportunity areas, we don't
agree that providing CRA credit to loans on housing for middle income individuals in high opportunities
areas merits special CRA recognition absent some evidence that the debt and equity markets are not fully
functioning to provide capital for middle income housing in these areas. Given scarce resources and the
relative difficulty of attracting capital to housing dedicated to LMI households, any CRA related incentives
for affordable housing should be focused on properties supporting LMI communities
Conclusion
Thank you again for the opportunity to provide comments on the NPR. We are grateful to the regulators for
their efforts to modernize CRA rules and solicit comments on ways to ensure that CRA continues to drive
investment to underserved communities, especially the rural markets that we serve.
Despite its shortcomings, CRA has been successful at achieving its objectives, increasing the level of bank
activity serving LMI communities. Since CRA has absolutely critical to the success of the LIHTC program, we
encourage the regulators to reduce potential negative impacts on LIHTC investment that could undermine
rural communities' ability to respond to the housing affordability crisis.
If you would like further information, please contact me at mgriffin@growamerica.org
Sincerely,

New York, NY 10017
growamerica.org

To Whom It May Concern:
I. Introduction and Scope of Comments
The Community Opportunity Alliance (COA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency's and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's proposed amendments to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. The proposal would make significant changes to how banks
are categorized and evaluated, how community development activities receive CRA consideration, how grants
are treated, and how banks' geographic responsibilities are defined.
COA is a national field builder for community development. Through our network of state and regional
associations, we support a field of almost 6,000 community development organizations (CDOs) working in
urban, rural, and suburban communities across the country. These organizations develop and preserve
affordable housing, support small businesses and economic opportunity, provide essential community
services, strengthen neighborhoods, and help residents shape the futures of their communities.
COA's role is not simply to represent those organizations in Washington. We work to strengthen the
infrastructure of the community development field itself. We build the capacity of state and regional networks;
connect leaders and organizations across markets; develop and spread effective practices; conduct research
and build knowledge about the field; convene practitioners, funders, financial institutions, and policymakers;
and help ensure that local CDOs have the relationships, resources, and voice they need to succeed. In that
sense, COA is a field builder for a national system of locally rooted organizations.
Our members - state and regional community development associations - occupy a particularly distinctive
place in that system. They sit between individual CDOs and the larger institutions that shape community
development capital and policy. They connect local organizations to one another and to banks, public agencies,
funders, and policymakers; identify needs that may not be visible through lending data alone; strengthen
organizations so they are prepared to deploy capital effectively; and help successful approaches spread from
one community to another.
This network and field-building perspective is particularly important to understanding CRA. State and regional
associations convene practitioners, provide training and technical assistance, coordinate research, policy, and
data work, connect smaller and rural organizations to resources, and build relationships between banks and
community partners. COA (formerly NACEDA) has made this point in prior CRA proceedings: investments in
these networks are themselves investments in community development capacity.
 Page 2
Put together, these organizations form an ecosystem. Local CDOs turn capital into housing, businesses,
services, and stronger neighborhoods; state and regional associations build their capacity and connect them to
resources and institutions; and COA strengthens and connects that infrastructure nationally. CRA is one of the
most important sources of private-sector partnership and capital within that ecosystem.
This perspective matters in evaluating the proposed rule. CRA does not operate only through individual loans
or investments. Its impact also depends on relationships, organizational capacity, local knowledge, technical
assistance, and institutions capable of connecting capital with community needs. A rule that recognizes
transactions while weakening the organizations and networks that make those transactions possible risks
measuring community development too narrowly.
COA therefore approaches CRA modernization from a straightforward starting point: the regulatory framework
should strengthen banks' responsibility to understand and respond to identified community needs, with the
needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) people and places at the center. Before asking what activities
should count, CRA should preserve the responsibility of banks to know the communities they serve and to
respond to their needs.
Our comments are intentionally focused. COA and our members have particular experience with banks'
community development responsibilities and with the organizations, partnerships, grants, investments, and
services through which those responsibilities are carried out. We focus primarily on community development
activities and tests, bank asset thresholds and community development obligations, grants and nonprofit
capacity, assessment areas, strategic plans and community engagement, economic and affordable housing
development, racial disparities and discriminatory practices, and interagency consistency. We generally defer
to organizations with deeper expertise on the technical design of retail lending tests and individual retail
product evaluation.
Several parts of the proposal offer opportunities for greater clarity and modernization. COA supports clearer
rules where they make CRA easier for banks, regulators, and communities to understand and implement. But
simplification should not come at the expense of meaningful community development responsibility. Nor
should greater objectivity substitute for community impact, local accountability, or the judgment necessary to
distinguish an activity that genuinely meets an identified LMI need from one that merely satisfies a regulatory
definition.
This concern is particularly acute in the proposal's treatment of grants. Flexible grants and operating support
sustain not only individual CDOs, but also the state and regional associations that provide training, technical
assistance, coordination, research, advocacy, and connections across an entire community development
ecosystem. A CRA framework that narrowly distinguishes project expenses from organizational infrastructure
risks undermining precisely the institutions that help banks identify community needs, develop effective
partnerships, and put capital to work successfully.
Accordingly, COA asks the agencies to evaluate the proposed rule against three basic questions: Does it
preserve meaningful community development responsibility? Does it direct bank activity toward identified
needs of LMI people and places? And does it strengthen, rather than weaken, the community institutions and
relationships necessary to turn capital into lasting community benefit?
In developing these comments, COA also asked our members to share examples of how the proposal could
affect their organizations, their bank partnerships, and the communities they serve. We include several of
those examples below. They are practical examples of how the proposed changes could play out on the
ground.
