avoiding analyses that are not meaningful. At the same time, a product line that is not among a bank's
largest nationally can be important to small businesses in a particular local market. The agencies
acknowledge that the approach may reduce CRA incentives for non-major product lines even where
those products matter to low- and moderate-income borrowers, small businesses, small farms, or local
communities. 91 Fed. Reg. at 52164-65.
The final rule should ensure that material small-business lending does not escape evaluation solely
because two other product lines are larger. AEO recommends an assessment-area-level materiality
backstop that requires evaluation when small-business lending reaches a defined level of local
significance, when community input identifies an unmet credit need, or when the bank represents a
meaningful share of local deposits or small-business credit. Examiners also should consider loan size,
borrower revenue, product terms, approval and denial patterns, and the distribution of lending across
neighborhoods and business types.
The rule should preserve attention to the smallest loans and smallest firms. Aggregate dollar volume
can mask whether a bank is serving microbusinesses or concentrating activity in larger transactions.
Public data should allow communities to distinguish smaller-dollar loans and lending to businesses
with gross annual revenue of 1 million dollars or less, consistent with privacy protections.
VI Data Relief Should Not Precede Reliable Replacement Data
The agencies request comment on whether CRA small-business and small-farm data collection could
be reduced or discontinued in reliance on data collected under Section 1071 of the Dodd-Frank Act.
AEO supports eliminating true duplication, but only after the replacement data are fully operational,
stable, comparable across institutions and time, and publicly accessible in a form that communities
can use.
The final rule should not create a transition gap in which CRA data disappear before Section 1071 data
can perform the same accountability function. Before discontinuing any CRA field, the agencies should
publish a field-by-field comparison, identify differences in institutional and transaction coverage,
evaluate the effect of exemptions, and provide an implementation period with overlapping data. Any
waiver authority should be narrow, documented, time-limited, and disclosed publicly in a manner that
allows stakeholders to understand its effect on comparability.
AEO supports the proposed public database for community development grant data, with appropriate
safeguards. The database should include the bank, grant amount, recipient, geography served,

1310 L STREET NW
SUITE 820
WASHINGTON, DC 20005
www.aeoworks.org


community development purpose, and whether the grant supports direct service, general operations,
capacity building, or an intermediary function. When a recipient serves multiple areas, the database
should permit reporting of the actual service area rather than relying solely on the recipient's
headquarters address.
VII Geographic Rules Should Reach Underserved Markets
The CRA's place-based responsibilities remain essential, and banks should first demonstrate that they
are meeting needs in their assessment areas. At the same time, many rural, Tribal, and persistently
underserved communities have limited branch presence and fewer institutions for which they fall within
an assessment area. The final rule should preserve a practical path for community development activity
in these markets after local obligations are met.
The agencies should allow banks to receive consideration for well-documented statewide, regional, and
multi-community activities that reach underserved entrepreneurs, including activities delivered through
CDFIs and nonprofit intermediaries. Examiners should evaluate whether the activity responds to a
demonstrated credit or capacity need, not merely whether the recipient's office is located within a
particular boundary. Geographic flexibility should expand investment in underserved markets, not
redirect resources toward projects that are larger or easier to document but less responsive to
community needs.
VIII Implementation Should Be Clear and Informed by Community Stakeholders
AEO supports clearer definitions, a timely process for confirming whether an activity will receive CRA
consideration, standardized public information, and an illustrative list that can evolve with market
practice. These tools will be useful only if they are accessible to community partners as well as banks.
Before implementation, the agencies should conduct listening sessions with CDFIs, nonprofit lenders,
technical-assistance providers, rural and Tribal organizations, small banks, large banks, researchers,
and entrepreneurs. Guidance should include examples involving microenterprise lending, loan funds,
loan-loss reserves, technical assistance, capacity building, general operating support, regranting,
shared technology, rural service areas, and multi-state intermediaries. The agencies should publish
responses on confirmation requests promptly and in a manner that protects confidential information
while improving consistency for all stakeholders.
The final rule also should include a reasonable transition period and should not discourage existing
bank-community partnerships while new documentation systems are developed. Community
organizations should not be required to redesign their accounting systems solely to fit a bank's CRA
process when existing records can reasonably document use, purpose, and outcomes.
Conclusion
For nearly five decades, the Community Reinvestment Act has reinforced the responsibility of regulated
financial institutions to help meet community credit needs. That responsibility remains vital for
America's entrepreneurs. Very small businesses rely on an interconnected system of banks, CDFIs,
nonprofit lenders, business-support organizations, and technical-assistance providers. A CRA
framework that recognizes only the final financing transaction, while discounting the capacity required

to originate, deploy, and sustain that financing, will not reflect how responsible capital reaches
communities.

thresholds, preserving meaningful community development evaluation, retaining grants and donations
as qualifying activities, replacing the 15 percent indirect-cost ceiling with a flexible and documented
standard, protecting capacity-building and intermediary support, ensuring that small-business lending
remains visible, and maintaining reliable public data.
The appropriate measure of the final rule is whether it expands responsible access to capital,

opportunity for entrepreneurs and communities. AEO welcomes continued engagement with the

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
(NPR) on the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).
Cinnaire is a Michigan-based organization working to raise capital for affordable housing
and community development across the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic regions. With deep ties
to the communities we serve, Cinnaire has leveraged the federal Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit (LIHTC), New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC), and Community Development Financial
Institution (CDFI) lending to raise $5.7 billion in total investments, supporting the creation
or preservation of more than 76,000 affordable homes across fourteen states.
Founded to bring capital to overlooked communities, we have maintained our focus on
driving investment to rural communities that struggle to get access to capital for affordable
housing and community development projects compared to large metropolitan centers
with major bank presence. Through the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, for example,
Cinnaire has raised $395 million to support the creation or preservation of more than 3,300
affordable homes in rural areas over the past five years.




2

CRA has been a critical driver of our ability to bring this transformative private capital to the
communities we serve, helping make possible high-impact developments in areas that are
not well served by the mainstream financial sector. For example, CRA has driven
investment in projects that have empowered our communities to respond to severe
workforce housing shortages, created life-changing housing communities for veterans that
have fought for our country, helped individuals and families in rural communities struggling
with opioid abuse, and provided stable housing for seniors.

By creating a competitive market for LIHTC investment, especially through the separate
investment test, CRA has helped drive investment in transformative projects like these. As
we seek to help our communities meet their housing needs, CRA will also be instrumental
in helping realize the full benefits of the recent expansion of the LIHTC program and
provisions in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which Congress enacted to respond to
the unprecedented affordable housing crisis affecting communities across the country.
According to the National Low Income Housing Coalition, there is a shortage of more than
7 million homes affordable and available to extremely low-income renters in the U.S. As
the demand has grown, so too has the difficulty of creating affordable homes that our
communities need due to high construction, materials, labor, and borrowing costs.
The NPR includes changes to the CRA regulatory framework that could negatively impact
LIHTC investment, especially in rural communities that struggle to attract LIHTC capital.
Specifically, by increasing the large bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion in
assets, the NPR would result in hundreds of OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks no longer
having a separate investment test. We fear that this threshold could inadvertently
undermine the LIHTC program's ability to respond to the housing crisis, especially in rural
areas that should be prioritized for affordable housing investment. Should the agencies
adopt a new threshold for large banks, we recommend a reasonable alternative in our
comments below. We also strongly oppose a $30 billion large bank threshold, which would
have even more significant negative impacts.
We appreciate the agencies' work to develop the NPR and provide relief to smaller
institutions, which have been critical partners of ours in helping meet the housing and
community development needs of the communities we serve. We also support several
changes that would provide more clarity and consistency, which will support the efficient
deployment of capital to communities. In our comments below, we provide our
perspective on additional changes in the NPR and responses to selected questions.



3

Key Recommendation: If Regulators Increase the Large Bank Threshold, Adopt a
$3.252 Billion Threshold to Prevent Unintended Negative Consequences on Rural
Affordable Housing Development and Preservation
CRA has contributed significantly to Cinnaire's ability to bring capital to the communities
we serve, including underserved rural markets and areas without major bank presence.
Commercial banks, encouraged by CRA requirements, typically provide more than 80
percent annually of the equity capital for LIHTC developments. For that reason, any change
in CRA that inadvertently reduces that demand could undercut efforts to create and
preserve affordable housing. LIHTC pricing can vary by up to 20% ($0.20) in areas with high
CRA need versus low CRA need, including rural areas that struggle to attract investment.
This pricing matters because it determines the amount of equity invested into LIHTC
properties, with lower pricing leading to more financially strained developments.
Banks below $10 billion in assets play an important role in ensuring the efficient delivery of
capital for LIHTC developments. According to the Affordable Housing Tax Credit
Coalition's (AHTCC) survey of tax credit syndicators, more than 108 banks below the $10
billion threshold invested at least $1.6 billion in LIHTC equity over a five-year survey period.
Extrapolating these results to the full LIHTC market, banks under the $10 billion threshold
invested approximately $2 billion in LIHTC equity over those five years.
These investments disproportionately serve rural areas. According to AHTCC,
approximately one-third of LIHTC equity invested through syndicators by banks with $412
million to $10 billion in assets supported rural markets from 2021–2024, indicating that
banks in this asset range play an essential role in investing in rural communities. By
comparison, 8.1% of Housing Credit equity in a CohnReznick industry-wide sample was
invested in USDA-defined nonmetro counties, a proxy for rural and small-town markets.
Unlike large metropolitan areas with CRA hotspots, smaller cities, nonmetropolitan areas,
and rural communities rely on smaller investors with CRA obligations driven by the
standalone Investment Test to support LIHTC projects. Without the Investment Test for the
community and regional banks that serve these markets, we are concerned that these
communities will face even more severe disadvantages in accessing capital that will
reduce the production and preservation of desperately needed affordable housing.
Outsize Impact of Community and Regional Banks on Making Rural Developments Possible
Under the NPR, 376 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks currently classified as large would
move to the intermediate bank framework and would no longer be subject to a separate
investment test. The loss of community and regional bank investors would jeopardize not



4

just the total amount of investment in rural LIHTC projects, but also the outsize impact that
they have on the financial feasibility of rural affordable housing developments.
In rural markets that are not served by the largest banks and do not enjoy strong CRA
demand, community and regional banks are often the only CRA-motivated capital
available for LIHTC developments. As a result, even small investments by these banks
have a major impact because they help even out the pricing disadvantages rural
communities face. Investments by these banks can make the difference on whether a
project moves forward and a community's affordable housing needs are met.
Without a standalone Investment Test, there will be reduced incentives for banks to play
this role, creating a gap for rural communities. As a result, it will be exceedingly difficult for
rural LIHTC projects to find alternative investors with equity pricing that makes projects
financially feasible. That will deepen rural communities' disadvantages compared to urban
areas with strong CRA-driven demand and threaten their ability to create and preserve
affordable housing. Consequently, we fear that far fewer rural affordable housing
developments will be completed. In addition, preservation of existing affordable housing
stock in rural areas – a major challenge in the coming years – will be far more difficult to
finance, jeopardizing already scarce affordable housing supply.
Further compounding the problem, small developments in rural areas typically receive
equity investment through multi-investor funds. Multi-investor funds are particularly
important for rural projects, which are often smaller in scale and thus struggle to find bank
investors. They also help leverage additional capital from large banks and other LIHTC
investors, bringing more capital to rural communities. To mitigate investor risk, multi-
investor funds have proportionate share limits, meaning an individual investor's equity
investment is capped as a percentage of the overall fund size. As a result, the loss of these
investors in multi-investor funds will have a compounded effect, resulting in less equity in
funds that disproportionately serve rural areas.
We believe a primary goal of CRA regulatory reform should be driving investment and
lending into rural communities that are too often struggle to get access to mainstream
finance. The Investment Test under CRA has proved to be an effective way of driving high-
impact activities in the communities these banks serve. CRA has also helped community
banks directly see the value of activities like LIHTC investments since the leadership of
those banks see their impact, spurring additional investment in the LIHTC program.
If regulators increase the large bank threshold, the $3.252 billion alternative large bank
threshold would be substantially less disruptive to LIHTC investment than the proposed



5

$10 billion large bank threshold. Based on AHTCC survey data, using a $3.252 billion
threshold instead of $10 billion would reduce the number of affected LIHTC investors by
approximately 63 percent, from 108 banks to 40 banks. Moreover, the banks that would
remain subject to standalone Investment Test under a $3.252 billion threshold account for
approximately 86 percent of the LIHTC equity investment by OCC- and FDIC-regulated
banks captured in AHTCC's survey with assets between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.
This threshold also has a clear policy basis since it is the inflation-adjusted version of the
OCC's 2020 $2.5 billion threshold, which was calibrated to preserve the relative shares of
banks classified as small and intermediate when the categories were established in 2005.
In addition, the agencies specifically request comment on treating banks with less than
$30 billion in assets as intermediate banks. Based on our experience serving our markets,
we strongly recommend against the adoption of a $30 billion large bank threshold, which
would be significantly more damaging to LIHTC investment. The more than 140 banks
below the $30 billion threshold captured in AHTCC's survey invested at least $3.575 billion
in LIHTC equity over the five-year survey period. Extrapolating these results to the full
LIHTC market, these banks invested approximately $4.5 billion in LIHTC equity over the
past five years – more than twice as much LIHTC debt and equity investment as banks
between $1.65 billion and $10 billion, as shown in the chart below.

Preserve Meaningful Incentives for Intermediate Banks to Prioritize Community
Development Financing
In addition to LIHTC investment, CRA is also a critical driver of investor interest in
partnering with Cinnaire Lending, our affiliated, certified Community Development
Financial Institution (CDFI) that provides flexible lending for affordable housing and
community development projects. CDFIs have become increasingly important for
affordable housing lending as borrowing, construction, and labor costs have risen. Like the



6

LIHTC investor market, small and intermediate banks also play a disproportionate role in
serving rural communities. These partnerships with CDFIs can help banks reach
underserved communities and meet complex needs, such as affordable housing lending.
Under the NPR, about 800 banks that currently face a separate community development
test as intermediate small banks would become small banks and lose that requirement. In
addition, we are concerned that changes in the NPR governing how intermediate banks are
evaluated will diminish impactful community development financing activity. Intermediate
banks are evaluated separately on retail lending and on community development
activities, including community development loans, investments, and services. However,
under the NPR, intermediate banks would no longer be required to achieve at least a
Satisfactory rating on both their lending test and Community Development (CD) test.
Given the high impact of CD activities and the increased number of banks that will fall in
this category, we recommend against allowing weak CD performance to be offset by
lending. We encourage the agencies to retain the current requirement that banks
demonstrate at least a Satisfactory CD rating to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
Ensure Geographic Flexibility Leads to Increased Activity, Especially in Underserved
Rural Markets
As an organization working to support rural areas, we appreciate the potential for allowing
geographic flexibility to help capital reach these underserved markets, including CRA
"deserts." The NPR would allow banks to receive CRA credit for activities outside their
assessment areas after satisfying assessment area needs.
We encourage regulators to adopt strong quantitative and qualitative approaches to
ensure that banks first meet the needs of their assessment areas and that this flexibility
results in more, not less, CRA-driven activities. In addition, this activity should
meaningfully help direct CRA-motivated capital to reach rural areas. This will be especially
important to help mitigate the impact of the loss of CRA-motivated small bank investors
that play a disproportionate role in rural communities, as noted above.
Provide Credit for Prior Period Loans Should Receive Credit
We support providing CRA consideration for qualifying CD loans that remain outstanding
from prior evaluation periods, similar to the existing treatment of prior-period investments.
Community development borrowers frequently need long-term, patient financing. CRA
should encourage banks to structure loans around community needs rather than
examination cycles.



7

Establish a Publicly Available, Illustrative List of Eligible CD Activities
We support all banking regulators establishing a publicly available, non-exhaustive
illustrative list of eligible CD activities and a formal process for advance confirmation of
eligibility. The OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve should seek to maintain consistent
standards and, ideally, a single interagency illustrative list.
Remove Restrictions on Community Development Grants
We appreciate the agencies' goals of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully
benefit communities. However, we caution against imposing new and burdensome
restrictions on banks and community partners, which would increase costs and regulatory
complexity. Community-based organizations have become particularly important for
responding to affordable housing needs. We urge the agencies to recognize the important
work of local nonprofits in helping to meet community credit needs and to maintain the
current CRA eligibility for grant funding in the final rule.
RESPONSE TO SELECTED QUESTIONS
Question 1: To better align with agency policies that establish an asset size of less than $30
billion as a threshold for certain supervisory approaches, such as being considered a
community bank or being subject to the continuous examination process, should the
agencies consider adjusting the intermediate bank asset size threshold to include all
banks with an asset size of less than $30 billion that do not qualify as small banks? If the
agencies establish $30 billion as the appropriate threshold to delineate between
intermediate banks and large banks, should the agencies also adopt a larger threshold for
small banks, such as the $10 billion currently proposed as the intermediate bank
threshold?
We strongly recommend against the adoption of a $30 billion large bank threshold, which
would be much more disruptive to LIHTC developments. AHTCC survey data show that
banks with assets between $10 billion and $30 billion account for more than twice as
much LIHTC debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.
Banks below the $30 billion threshold captured in the AHTCC survey invested at least
$3.575 billion in LIHTC equity over a five-year survey period. Extrapolating these results to
the full LIHTC market, these banks invested approximately $4.5 billion in LIHTC equity over
the past five years.



8

As we note above, these banks play an outsize role in rural areas and supporting the
viability of rural housing developments. As the asset threshold moves higher, the potential
negative impact broadens to smaller cities in states that are not well served by major
financial institutions, including in the Midwest markets we serve. This would also further
concentrate LIHTC investment in large financial institutions that often have less of a
presence in smaller cities as well as nonmetropolitan areas.
Question 12: Does the proposed definition of "complexity" enhance the rule's focus on
meeting community credit needs by providing greater consideration to CD investments,
grants, and services that are linked to CD lending activities or are otherwise the functional
equivalent of loans?
The proposal would require community development activities to be or be tied to a lending
activity to be considered "complex." While we appreciate the agencies' efforts to add
clarity, this focus on lending does not necessarily enhance community credit needs.
Investments in LIHTC, NMTC, and CDFIs can be extremely responsive to community credit
needs and complex to execute, yet not directly tied to a loan as part of the transaction.
Conclusion
CRA has been successful at increasing the level of bank activity that serves LMI
communities and has been essential to the success of the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit
program, the New Markets Tax Credit program, and the growth of our CDFI activities and
partnerships in underserved communities. To meet the housing affordability crisis our
country faces, including the communities we serve in the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic
regions, it is critical that any changes to CRA rules do not unintentionally reduce incentives
that drive investments and loans to often overlooked communities, especially rural areas.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the NPR. We would be happy to
provide any additional information or expertise based on our experience working with
financial institutions and the communities intended to be served by CRA.
Respectfully submitted,

Mark McDaniel

RE: Comment on Proposed Revisions to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)
Regulations (RIN 3064-AG31)
To Whom It May Concern:
On behalf of the Sonoma County Community Development Commission, a governmental
agency dedicated to expanding affordable housing opportunities and supporting community
development, we appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed revisions to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.
Our agency works to address critical housing needs by financing the development and
preservation of affordable homes, supporting community-based organizations, and leveraging
public resources with private capital. Banks are essential partners in this work. Through
investments in Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) developments, purchases of affordable
housing bonds, community development lending, and grants to nonprofit organizations,
financial institutions help make projects financially feasible, preserve long-term affordability,
and strengthen the communities we serve.
We are concerned that several elements of the proposed revisions could reduce the availability
of this critical support, particularly for lower-income households and communities with the
greatest housing needs.
The Role of Bank Investments in Affordable Housing Finance
Bank participation is a cornerstone of affordable housing finance. Investments in LIHTC
developments and affordable housing bonds help close financing gaps, attract additional
public and private capital, and make it possible to build and preserve homes at rents affordable
to households with limited incomes. These investments are particularly important in high-cost
regions, where development costs are substantial and market rents often exceed what working
families, seniors, people with disabilities, and other vulnerable residents can afford.
Raising the threshold for full CRA requirements from $1.649 billion to $10 billion in assets—
and potentially to $30 billion—could reduce incentives for a significant number of banks to
participate in community development investments. Eliminating a separate investment test for
 these institutions could further diminish incentives to invest in LIHTC projects and affordable
housing bonds.
For governmental housing finance agencies, a reduction in bank participation would make it
more difficult to assemble competitive financing packages, stretch limited public resources,
and meet the demand for affordable homes. Fewer participating investors could also increase
financing costs and uncertainty, potentially delaying or preventing projects from moving
forward.
The Importance of Nonprofit Capacity and Community Partnerships
Nonprofit organizations are indispensable partners in affordable housing and community
development. They provide resident services, help identify and address local housing needs,
build organizational capacity, and connect public agencies with the communities they serve.
Many smaller organizations rely on bank grants to sustain their operations, develop projects,
build expertise, and serve populations that may otherwise be overlooked.
Restricting CRA credit to grants that are directly tied to a specific community development
program could exclude essential operating support, capacity-building grants, and funding for
intermediaries and collaborative efforts. Eliminating CRA consideration for grants altogether
could further reduce the resources available to these organizations.
Although these activities may not always be attributable to a single housing development or
measurable program outcome, they are often necessary to make affordable housing and
community development possible. Without adequate organizational capacity, nonprofit
partners may be less able to identify development opportunities, navigate complex financing
requirements, deliver resident services, or sustain projects over time.
A reduction in grant support would therefore affect more than nonprofit budgets. It could
weaken the broader network of organizations that governmental agencies depend on to
advance housing stability and equitable community development.
Maintaining a Meaningful Definition of Affordable Housing
We are also concerned that allowing unsubsidized, market-rate apartments to qualify as
affordable housing based on current rents, without adequate protections for continued
affordability, could divert investment from housing that serves lower-income households.
In high-cost communities, rents that are below prevailing market levels may still be
unaffordable to households with very limited incomes. Moreover, affordability based solely on
current rents does not guarantee that homes will remain affordable following a sale,
renovation, or lease turnover.
Public resources and CRA-motivated private investment should support housing outcomes that
are measurable, durable, and responsive to local affordability needs. For governmental housing
finance agencies, enforceable affordability restrictions are a key mechanism for ensuring that
investments deliver lasting public benefits. A broader definition that does not adequately
 account for household income or long-term affordability could make it more difficult to direct
capital toward housing with the deepest and most enduring affordability protections.
Preserving Local Investment and Community Development Impact
The proposed minimum investment threshold for activities outside a bank's local assessment
areas also raises concerns. If banks can satisfy local community development expectations by
committing only 0.625 percent of Tier 1 capital to local community development lending and
an equivalent amount to local investments and grants, the minimum could become a practical
benchmark rather than a floor for institutions that currently provide greater support.
This could result in less community development capital remaining in the regions where banks
operate and where housing needs are acute. For communities such as those in California's
North Bay, where housing affordability is a significant challenge, maintaining access to locally
invested capital is essential. Local investment supports not only housing production and
preservation, but also the nonprofit infrastructure and community partnerships necessary to
sustain thriving, inclusive communities.
We encourage the agencies to ensure that CRA evaluation standards continue to incentivize
meaningful investment in the communities from which financial institutions draw deposits and
conduct business, while recognizing the importance of sustained, place-based partnerships.
Recommendations
We respectfully encourage the agencies to consider the following modifications to the
proposed revisions:
1. Maintain meaningful CRA investment incentives across bank sizes. Avoid raising
asset thresholds in ways that remove significant numbers of banks from meaningful
community development and investment evaluations. Preserve incentives for
investments in LIHTC developments, affordable housing bonds, and other activities that
support the production and preservation of affordable homes.
2. Recognize the full range of effective nonprofit support. Continue to award
appropriate CRA consideration for general operating support, capacity building,
intermediary organizations, and collaborative community development activities when
they contribute to eligible community development outcomes. These investments build
the infrastructure required to deliver and sustain affordable housing.
3. Preserve a meaningful, income-sensitive definition of affordable housing. Ensure
that CRA-eligible affordable housing activities demonstrate affordability relative to
household incomes and, where appropriate, include enforceable mechanisms to
maintain affordability over time. Current rents alone should not determine whether
housing meets the needs of lower-income households.
4. Encourage sustained local community development investment. Establish evaluation
standards that recognize the value of banks maintaining or expanding their existing
 levels of local lending, investment, and grantmaking, rather than treating a low
minimum threshold as sufficient community reinvestment.
5. Assess the cumulative effects on housing supply and community capacity. Before
finalizing the rules, carefully evaluate how the proposed changes could affect the
availability, cost, and geographic distribution of affordable housing capital, as well as the
operational capacity of nonprofit organizations and intermediaries.
Conclusion
The Community Reinvestment Act is an important framework for encouraging financial
institutions to help meet the credit and community development needs of the communities
they serve. For governmental housing and community development agencies, bank lending,
investments, and grants are not peripheral sources of support; they are integral components of
the financing and partnership structures that make affordable housing possible, even in the
high cost, disaster impacted areas we serve. Further, CRA investments allows our agency to
leverage public resources at a 24:1 ratio, activating private capital that might otherwise be
sitting on the sidelines.
Changes that reduce incentives for these activities could constrain the resources available to
develop and preserve affordable homes, weaken nonprofit capacity, and make it more difficult
to ensure that public investments produce lasting benefits for lower-income households.
We urge the agencies to adopt a framework that continues to encourage meaningful bank
participation, recognizes the essential role of nonprofit partners, and prioritizes housing
affordability that is both income-appropriate and durable. Maintaining strong CRA incentives
will help governmental housing finance agencies and their partners leverage public resources,
attract private capital, and advance the shared goal of ensuring that every community has
access to safe, stable, and affordable housing.
Thank you for considering our comments.
Sincerely,
Michelle Whitman
Executive Director
Sonoma County Community Development Commission

RE: Comments on Proposed Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
Dear Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
On behalf of North Lawndale Employment Network (NLEN), we appreciate the opportunity to provide
comments on the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.
For 25 years, NLEN has advanced economic mobility through workforce development, financial
empowerment, fair-chance employment, and social enterprise. Our experience demonstrates that
sustainable community development depends not only on funding individual programs but also on
investing in the organizational infrastructure that makes those programs effective.
We are concerned that the proposed changes to CRA regulations could discourage banks from
providing unrestricted operating support and capacity-building investments to community-based
nonprofit organizations, potentially undermining the very economic outcomes the CRA is intended
to advance.
1. Sustained investment in nonprofit organizations produces measurable economic impact
NLEN's FY24–FY25 Impact Report demonstrates the value of sustained investment in community-
based workforce development. Over this two-year period, NLEN achieved the following outcomes:
2,300 residents served, including 421 program graduates.
50% employment placement within 90 days, with an average starting wage of $19.51 per hour.
70% of participants increased their net worth, and more than 500 new household bank accounts
were opened.
A recidivism rate below 10%, compared with a cited national range of 44–68%.
Our impact extends beyond individual participants. A Mastercard study commissioned by We Rise
Together, an initiative of The Chicago Community Trust, documented a 59% increase in consumer
spending in the area surrounding NLEN's campus, representing $1.85 million in new local economic
activity.
These results illustrate how sustained investment in workforce development, financial capability,
and organizational infrastructure can contribute to employment, household financial stability, and
broader economic revitalization.
2. Unrestricted funding is essential to achieving community-development outcomes
The proposed CRA regulations could create incentives for banks to prioritize narrowly defined
projects over unrestricted operating support and institutional capacity building.
For organizations like NLEN, this distinction has significant operational consequences.

2
Our ability to produce measurable economic outcomes depends on an integrated service-delivery
model that combines workforce training, paid transitional employment, financial coaching,
employer partnerships, and individualized support.
Delivering these services requires substantial organizational infrastructure, including qualified staff,
financial management, technology, data collection, program evaluation, compliance, and strategic
leadership.
These functions cannot always be attributed to a single project, yet they are essential to the success
of every program.
Unrestricted funding allows organizations to allocate resources strategically, respond to changing
community needs, strengthen operational efficiency, and sustain services when project-specific
funding is insufficient.
A regulatory framework that discourages unrestricted funding risks weakening the very institutions
responsible for translating community investment into measurable economic outcomes.
3. The proposed 15% indirect-cost threshold may undermine nonprofit effectiveness
We are particularly concerned about the proposed requirement that large banks document that
indirect costs associated with qualifying community-development grants do not exceed 15%.
A uniform threshold does not necessarily reflect the actual cost of operating a community-based
nonprofit or delivering comprehensive workforce-development services.
Financial management, human resources, technology, data infrastructure, compliance, evaluation,
and organizational leadership are not peripheral expenses. They are essential components of
responsible program delivery and effective stewardship of philanthropic and public resources.
Restricting the amount of funding available for these functions could create incentives for nonprofits
to underinvest in their infrastructure, potentially weakening their ability to deliver services,
demonstrate outcomes, and maintain long-term financial sustainability.
We encourage the agencies to consider a more flexible approach that recognizes reasonable and
documented indirect costs rather than establishing a uniform ceiling.
4. CRA should preserve incentives for banks to invest in institutional capacity
Banks have long served as important partners in community development, providing philanthropic
support, financial services, and investments that help community-based organizations expand
economic opportunity.

3
These partnerships are particularly valuable when they extend beyond individual transactions and
support the long-term capacity of organizations to serve their communities.
NLEN's experience illustrates the importance of this approach. Our workforce-development
programs, financial coaching, employer partnerships, and social enterprises operate as an
integrated system designed to help individuals secure employment, increase earnings, build assets,
and achieve lasting economic stability.
The effectiveness of this model depends on our ability to maintain the institutional capacity that
connects these activities.
We encourage the agencies to preserve meaningful CRA consideration for unrestricted operating
grants, organizational capacity-building investments, and other forms of flexible philanthropic
support that strengthen community-based nonprofit institutions.
Such investments should be recognized as contributing to community-development outcomes
when they support organizations with demonstrated missions and measurable results serving low-
and moderate-income communities.
5. Recommendations
We respectfully encourage the agencies to consider the following as they finalize the proposed CRA
regulations:
Preserve CRA consideration for unrestricted operating support provided to qualifying community-
development nonprofit organizations.
Recognize organizational capacity building as an eligible community-development activity, including
investments in technology, staffing, financial management, data infrastructure, evaluation, and
operational sustainability.
Allow reasonable and documented indirect costs rather than imposing a uniform 15% threshold that
may not reflect the actual cost of delivering effective community-development services.
Maintain incentives for long-term bank-nonprofit partnerships that support institutional
sustainability alongside direct programmatic investments.
Recognize measurable economic outcomes as evidence of the value of sustained investment in
community-based institutions, including employment placement, increased earnings, household
wealth building, and neighborhood economic activity.
Conclusion
The Community Reinvestment Act plays an important role in connecting financial institutions with
the communities they serve. Its effectiveness depends on recognizing that meaningful community
development requires both direct investment in programs and sustained investment in the
institutions responsible for delivering them.

4
NLEN's experience demonstrates that community-based organizations can generate measurable
employment, financial, and economic outcomes when they have the resources and institutional
capacity to operate effectively.
We respectfully encourage the agencies to ensure that the final CRA regulations preserve incentives
for banks to provide unrestricted operating support, recognize reasonable indirect costs, and invest
in the long-term sustainability of nonprofit organizations.
Thank you for considering our comments and for your commitment to strengthening economic
opportunity in communities across the country.
Sincerely,

On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation

regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide
loans, investments, grants, and services in communities that have historically lacked access to capital.
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations, and we support some of the agencies' provisions that
could improve the CRA framework and increase responsible capital in underserved communities. However, we have grave
concerns with the increases in the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA and the
restrictions on operating grants. We also have concerns with several interacting provisions that could further weaken
community development incentives that will undoubtedly impair the flow of much needed capital to the most under-
resourced small businesses and communities.
Community Reinvestment Fund, USA (CRF) is a national nonprofit and Community Development Financial Institution
(CDFI) with a mission to expand economic opportunity by reimagining the way capital and resources flow to small
businesses and communities. CRF partners with community stakeholders to deliver sustainable, tailored financial solutions
that support long-term economic growth with the goal of building a just economy where small businesses and local
communities thrive. Since 1988, CRF has provided nearly $4 billion in funding to transform local economies across the
country.
Banks are critical collaborators and partners in our work. CRF currently has relationships with banks that provide vital
grants, investments, loans, and technical assistance in the form of invaluable board representation. These partnerships are
essential to our programmatic work. For example, Fifth Third Bank recently partnered with CRF to launch the Small
Business Catalyst Fund, a $7.85M investment that empowers small businesses across Fifth Third's footprint to grow and

create jobs in their communities and build a more robust small business ecosystem. The program is designed to connect
small business owners with capital through trusted CDFI partners. These mission-driven lenders provide both funding and
guidance to help businesses scale operations, purchase inventory, cover operating expenses, and invest in growth
initiatives. This impactful and scalable program would not have happened without Fifth Third Bank's investment and
commitment to community.
These partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical capital and resources to CDFIs, banks rely on
CDFIs to reach under-resourced communities, develop borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers. CRF's work
focuses on expanding access to capital and opportunity for under-resourced small businesses - particularly those owned
by entrepreneurs who have historically faced barriers to traditional financing - helping them grow, create jobs, and
strengthen their communities, ultimately graduating to the financial mainstream. The CRA has long helped create the
incentives for banks to build and sustain these relationships with CDFIs, strengthening the broader community
development ecosystem. We are therefore concerned that several provisions in the proposal could weaken these
incentives, reducing aggregate bank engagement with CDFIs and ultimately the flow of capital to the communities we
serve.
Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance: Section IV.A, "Asset Thresholds";
Questions 1–3
The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate banks as institutions with
between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as institutions with more than $10 billion. As a national CDFI, we serve
communities across the country. It is estimated that about 800 banks that currently face a separate community
development test as intermediate small banks would become small banks and lose that requirement. Another
approximately 400 banks that are currently evaluated as large banks would become intermediate banks, losing the
separate large-bank lending, investment, and service tests and many associated data-reporting requirements. 1

These thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development performance is evaluated and therefore
affect the strength of banks' incentives to engage in community development. The agencies acknowledge in the proposal
that when banks become subject to a CD test under the current framework, the explicit evaluation of their CD activities
typically results in banks adjusting their CRA programs.

our partnerships and the critical work of local and regional CDFIs. CDFIs frequently rely on regional and community banks
for patient debt, deposits, investments, lines of credit, grants, and other forms of capital that allow us to reach borrowers
and projects that conventional financial institutions cannot efficiently serve directly.

The threshold changes would also substantially reduce the number of institutions subject to large-bank CRA data

compare bank performance, assess geographic disparities, and understand whether community credit needs are being
met. We are concerned that aggregate community development finance data is already difficult to track and the proposal

For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and reject all alternatives offered
(including the substantially higher thresholds raised for consideration in Question 1). The current thresholds are already
annually indexed to CPI-W, so they are not beholden to 1995 asset levels. Moreover, the justification of "restoring
proportionality to 1995" that the agencies use in the proposal does not adequately explain why raising asset thresholds
better serve the statutory intent of the CRA—which is to ensure that credit needs of LMI communities are met. For the
small bank threshold, the proportionality metric rests on the distribution of the number of banks such that nearly 80% of all

saying large banks would under this proposal, and similar to 1995 cover about 85% of all total bank industry's assets.

geographic reach have changed. Banks with several billion dollars in assets today may have substantially greater lending,

management, data systems, financial management, technical assistance, and product development are not ancillary to
community development. They are the infrastructure that makes community development lending possible.

We support expressly recognizing qualifying activities that help communities prepare for, adapt to, and withstand natural
disasters. When Hurricane Helene devastated western North Carolina in September 2024, small businesses faced
unprecedented challenges—from destroyed storefronts to disrupted supply chains. CRF partnered with Appalachian

CDFIs frequently provide financing before and after disasters to affordable housing developments, homeowners, small

Kentucky Housing Corporation (KHC) respectfully submits these comments in response to the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency, Department of Treasury (OCC), and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). By this notice, these federal agencies
propose changes intended to "refocus on the statutory objective of encouraging banks to meet the credit needs of
their communities; to better ensure that community development grants reach the communities they are intended
to benefit; to reduce unnecessary burden, particularly for community banks; and to provide greater clarity for how
to obtain CRA consideration." The OCC and the FDIC also propose technical changes to their rules implementing the

KHC wishes to state our opposition to these reforms, as we believe they will rule that would weaken bank
obligations to invest, lend, and provide services in low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. We are
particularly concerned that by raising the asset thresholds that determine a bank's size classification and associated
CRA assessment requirements, fewer banks would be assessed for their community development lending and
investments. This proposed regulatory change would undermine the principal driver of bank investment in
affordable housing, with particularly adverse effects on smaller and rural markets. KHC has endorsed the national
"sign on" letters that will be submitted by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition and the National
Association of Affordable Housing Lenders. While we strongly support the positions taken in both letters, we also
wanted to submit comment given our role as a state housing finance agency.

Created in 1972 by the General Assembly, KHC is a quasi-governmental agency-a self-supporting, public corporation
of the Commonwealth of Kentucky- administratively attached to the Kentucky Finance and Administration Cabinet.
The corporation receives income from interest earned through the sale of tax-exempt mortgage revenue bonds and
fee income for administering federal programs. In addition to mortgage finance, KHC is responsible for
administration of the following programs: Low Income Housing Tax Credits; Tax-Exempt Bond Multifamily Financing;
HUD Continuum of Care; HUD Emergency Solutions Grants; HUD HOME Investment Partnerships; HUD HOME
American Rescue Plan, HUD Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS (HOPWA), HUD National Housing Trust
Fund; HUD Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program; HUD Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance Program;
HUD 811 Rental Assistance Program; HUD Preservation and Reinvestment Initiative for Community Enhancement
(PRICE) program; US Department of Energy (DoE) Weatherization Assistance Program; the U. S. Department of
Health and Human Services (HHS) Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP); Kentucky Affordable
Housing Trust Fund; and Kentucky Rural Housing Trust Fund.
 2
Since 1977, the CRA has played a critical role in encouraging financial institutions to meet the credit needs of the
communities they serve. By helping to address the historic effects of redlining, expanding equitable lending
opportunities, and fostering reinvestment in low- and moderate-income communities, the CRA has supported a
broad range of community development activities. Although its benefits extend to homeownership, small business
growth, healthcare, childcare, and other community priorities, its impact has been particularly significant in the
financing and development of affordable rental housing through the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC)
program.
The LIHTC program, which has been the cornerstone of affordable rental housing production for nearly four
decades, relies heavily on capital from banks regulated under the CRA. According to a 2025 CohnReznick study,
CRA-motivated banks account for roughly 80 percent of annual LIHTC equity investments.1 These institutions invest
not only to obtain the tax benefits associated with LIHTC transactions, but also because CRA examinations for large

Don't Let a Consent Judgment Write CRA's Future: An Invitation to Pro Bono Counsel

Second Comment of Kenneth H. Thomas, Ph.D., on OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 and FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

My full comment letter and six supporting documents are attached. This summary is for attorneys, law firms, legal clinics, and public interest organizations that may be interested in a narrow pro bono collaboration.

THE ISSUE. On July 31, 2026, the OCC and FDIC moved for entry of judgment in Texas Bankers Association v. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, No. 2:24-cv-00025 (N.D. Tex.), ECF No. 93. Their Proposed Judgment, ECF No. 93-1, declares the 2023 Retail Lending Test unlawful insofar as it reached beyond "the geographic areas where the institution operates physical facilities and accepts deposits." The agencies say the judgment will "set a clear table for future potential amendments." That language could be read to foreclose future CRA assessment areas based on where banks gather deposits, including targeted deposit-based assessment areas for branchless banks.

WHY IT MATTERS. Branchless banks, such as fintech, credit card, and other internet banks, hold an estimated $2 trillion of deposits nationwide gathered electronically, but they have no corresponding CRA reinvestment obligation other than the area around their distant headquarters. Addressing this "weblining," the modern form of redlining, requires keeping open the option of deposit-based assessment areas, which the OCC itself adopted in its 2020 CRA Final Rule. A consent judgment should not close that door without public comment.

MY REQUEST TO THE AGENCIES. Clarify, through a revised proposed judgment or in the preamble to any final rule, that the judgment does not decide whether the CRA permits assessment areas based on the geographic source or concentration of deposits. That clarification takes nothing from the plaintiffs.

MY INVITATION TO PRO BONO COUNSEL. I am a banking economist, not a lawyer. I supported the challenge to the 2023 CRA Final Rule and was the only individual to file an Amicus Brief in the Fifth Circuit appeal (No. 24-10367, Document 100). With the assistance of generative artificial intelligence, I have prepared three draft court documents: a proposed supplemental Amicus Brief, a motion for leave, and a proposed order. The brief asks the Court to add one sentence to the judgment:
"ORDERED AND DECLARED that nothing in this Judgment shall be construed to address or determine whether the Community Reinvestment Act permits the OCC or FDIC to delineate assessment areas based upon the geographic source or concentration of deposits received by a regulated institution, including deposit-based assessment areas."

CONCLUSION. I welcome pro bono counsel's independent review of these drafts and possible representation in seeking leave to file in the District Court. I bring nearly five decades of CRA experience, including congressional testimony, two books on CRA, and training federal bank examiners. I regularly provide pro bono CRA assistance to community organizations and even banks, and I offer this collaboration in the same spirit.

The draft court documents have not been filed and are attached for independent legal review only. Because the motion for entry of judgment remains pending, timing matters.

I respectfully request that the agencies include this comment and its attachments in the public comment record. 

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment.

(CRA) reform proposal, OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 and FDIC RIN 3064-AG31, for two
purposes: to ask the agencies to address a court judgment issue that bears directly on this rulemaking,

research, policy analysis, and practical experience, including congressional testimony, two books on
CRA, numerous articles, training federal bank examiners, and an Amicus Brief before the Fifth
Circuit. Because I am not a lawyer, I used generative artificial intelligence to help prepare this
comment and the draft court documents described below.
My first public comment on this Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR), OCC-2026-0694-0002,
submitted August 12, 2026, explained my opposition to the agencies' July 31, 2026 proposal,
particularly its failure to address digital and branchless banking.
Meaningful modernization, the central goal of CRA reform, must recognize the communities from
which banks gather substantial deposits electronically. To address this modern form of redlining,
which I have termed "weblining" in the context of branchless banks, like fintech, credit card, and
other internet banks, I urged the agencies to consider targeted assessment areas based on deposit con-
centrations, using my 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule.
Former Comptroller Joseph Otting adopted a variant of this 5% Rule in his 2020 CRA Final Rule.
The current NPR, however, keeps a framework centered on physical branches and does not address
weblining at all, a result welcome to branchless banks holding an estimated $2 trillion of deposits na-
tionwide, much of it from my home state of Florida. It should be noted that some branchless banks
are voluntarily following the spirit of deposit reinvestment, and they deserve credit for that effort.
As with my previous comments opposing the 2023 CRA Final Rule, I am not responding to the indi-
vidual questions in the present reform proposal, because its basic framework does not address this
central issue.
Nor do the current NPR's proposed Community Development (CD) metrics work. They are set artifi-
cially low, and most are based on a capital denominator instead of the proper asset one. That penal-
izes well-capitalized banks, which runs counter to CRA's requirement that banks meet credit needs
consistent with safe and sound operations. An asset-based benchmark would be more appropriate,
such as the 1% of Assets rule of thumb for CD loans and investments developed in The CRA Hand-
book.
I was the only individual filing an Amicus Brief regarding the 2023 CRA Final Rule, where I op-
posed it in the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit in Texas Bankers Association, et
al. v. Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, et al., No. 24-10367. That brief is attached.
The agencies' current CRA reform proposal raises a separate concern about the scope of the proposed
judgment in that litigation and its potential effect on future CRA reform. The issue concerns the OCC
and FDIC's July 31, 2026 Motion for Entry of Judgment in Texas Bankers Association v. Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency, No. 2:24-cv-00025 (N.D. Tex.), ECF No. 93, and the accompanying
Proposed Judgment, ECF No. 93-1.
Its declaration on the Retail Lending Test refers to "the geographic areas where the institution oper-
ates physical facilities and accepts deposits." That language could be interpreted to foreclose future
CRA assessment areas based on the geographic source or concentration of deposits.
 Such an interpretation could unnecessarily restrict future CRA modernization, particularly the ability
to address weblining by branchless banks through targeted deposit-based assessment areas. This
would be counter to the entire purpose of CRA reform.
This question belongs in this docket. The agencies' motion states that the judgment will "set a clear
table for future potential amendments" (ECF No. 93 at 5) and provide "clear judicial direction on
certain outer-bounds" of what the CRA allows (id. at 9). In footnote 3, the agencies distinguish
Arizona v. City and County of San Francisco, 596 U.S. 763 (2022) (Roberts, C.J., concurring), on the
ground that they sought public comment on rescinding the 2023 Rule. That forward-looking limit on
future rulemaking, however, was never itself proposed for public comment.
This NPR is the agencies' opportunity to receive that comment.
This is not a new position. My September 25, 2024 Amicus Brief, filed through counsel in the United
States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, No. 24-10367, Document 100, supported the challenge
to the 2023 CRA Final Rule while expressly distinguishing its expansive lending-based framework
from more targeted approaches for online banking. Footnote 16 specifically identified the OCC 2020
CRA Final Rule's deposit-based assessment area framework and its 5% geographic deposit threshold.
I continue to support the challenge to the 2023 CRA Final Rule. My present objective is simply to
preserve the distinction between invalidating that Rule's expansive lending-based assessment areas
and leaving open the separate question of targeted deposit-based assessment areas for future
rulemaking.
I therefore ask the OCC and FDIC to clarify, either through a revised proposed judgment or in the
preamble to any final rule, that the judgment does not decide whether the CRA permits assessment
areas based on the geographic source or concentration of deposits. That clarification would take
nothing from the plaintiffs and could make a supplemental amicus filing unnecessary.
To give interested counsel a concrete starting point toward moving this CRA reform effort in the right
direction, I used generative artificial intelligence to prepare three draft court documents:
1. Proposed Supplemental Brief of Amicus Curiae Kenneth H. Thomas, Ph.D., Regarding the
Scope of Proposed Judgment
2. Proposed Motion for Leave to File Supplemental Amicus Brief
3. Proposed Order Granting Leave to File Supplemental Amicus Brief
The proposed supplemental brief asks the Court to add one sentence to the judgment: "ORDERED
AND DECLARED that nothing in this Judgment shall be construed to address or determine whether
the Community Reinvestment Act permits the OCC or FDIC to delineate assessment areas based
upon the geographic source or concentration of deposits received by a regulated institution,
including deposit-based assessment areas." It does not disturb any relief the plaintiffs obtained
against the 2023 CRA Final Rule.
I welcome collaboration involving an independent assessment of the legal arguments, verification of
authorities and procedural requirements (including the Local Rules on leave to file an Amicus Brief
and on conferring with the parties), revision of the drafts where appropriate, and possible

I have worked extensively with banking regulators, financial institutions, and community
