 INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
Amicus curiae Dr. Kenneth H. Thomas is a banking economist who has
focused his scholarship and professional activities on the Community
Reinvestment Act ("CRA") since its enactment in 1977. He previously appeared as
amicus curiae in support of Plaintiffs in the Fifth Circuit appeal arising from this
action. His September 25, 2024 brief supported the challenge to the 2023 CRA
Final Rule and argued that the Rule's nationwide lending-based framework
exceeded the proper scope of CRA. See Brief for Amicus Curiae Kenneth H.
Thomas, Ph.D., No. 24-10367, Doc. 100 (5th Cir. Sept. 25, 2024) ("Thomas Fifth
Circuit Brief").
Dr. Thomas continues to support Plaintiffs' challenge to the 2023 Rule. This
supplemental submission does not ask the Court to restore the Retail Lending Test,
reconsider the preliminary injunction, or require the OCC or FDIC to adopt any
particular future regulation. It addresses only the scope of the proposed final
judgment now before the Court. Dr. Thomas has also raised this issue in public
comments on the OCC and FDIC's pending CRA rulemaking, Docket ID OCC-
2026-0694.
The issue is important to Dr. Thomas because his prior amicus brief
expressly distinguished the 2023 Rule's expansive lending-based assessment areas
from a narrower, targeted response to online banking. Near the conclusion of that
1
 brief, Dr. Thomas stated that the "subset" of online banks "could and should have
been addressed with targeted amendments to the existing regulations." Thomas
Fifth Circuit Brief at 22. Footnote 16 then identified the OCC's 2020 deposit-based
assessment-area framework and its five-percent geographic deposit threshold as the
specific example. Id. at 22-23 & n.16.
Dr. Thomas therefore has a direct interest in ensuring that the final judgment
does not inadvertently foreclose the very distinction his prior amicus brief placed
before the courts: invalidating an expansive lending-based assessment-area regime
does not require adjudicating whether the CRA permits a future, targeted deposit-
based assessment-area framework for a subset of institutions that gather material
concentrations of deposits outside their physical branch networks.
No party or counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in part, and no
person other than amicus contributed money intended to fund its preparation or
submission.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The Court can grant the OCC, FDIC, and Plaintiffs the relief they seek
against the 2023 Rule without deciding a separate question that is unnecessary to
resolve that Rule's legality: whether CRA categorically prohibits the agencies from
ever delineating an assessment area based on the geographic source or
concentration of deposits.
2
 The distinction matters because the OCC and FDIC are not merely asking
the Court to vacate the 2023 Rule. Their July 31, 2026 Motion for Entry of
Judgment states that the agencies seek a "clear table for future potential
amendments," with those future amendments subject to judicially defined limits.
ECF No. 93 at 5. The motion later states that the proposed judgment would provide
"clear judicial direction on certain outer-bounds of what the CRA allows." Id. at 9.
The proposed judgment itself would declare unlawful the assessment of retail
lending outside geographic areas where an institution "operates physical facilities
and accepts deposits." ECF No. 93-1 at 2.
Amicus does not challenge the judgment's separate treatment of deposit
products. Nor does Amicus challenge the conclusion that the 2023 Rule's Retail
Lending Test went too far. The concern is narrower: the physical-facilities
language, coupled with the agencies' stated intention to establish prospective
"outer-bounds," could be read to resolve the legality of deposit-based assessment
areas even though those areas were not the 2023 Retail Lending Test challenged
here.
That result is unnecessary. The OCC itself previously adopted a targeted
deposit-based assessment-area approach in its 2020 Final Rule under Comptroller
Joseph Otting. The OCC explained that increasing use of internet platforms for
collecting deposits made deposit-based assessment areas "increasingly relevant."
3
 85 Fed. Reg. 34,734, 34,757 (June 5, 2020). The rule required certain institutions
receiving 50 percent or more of retail domestic deposits outside facility-based
assessment areas to delineate separate deposit-based assessment areas in
geographies accounting for at least five percent of retail deposits. Id. That rule was
later rescinded, but its existence demonstrates that deposit-based assessment areas
are a distinct regulatory concept, not merely another name for the 2023 Rule's
lending-based framework.
The narrow solution is a savings clause. The Court can leave the proposed
declaration concerning the 2023 Retail Lending Test intact while expressly stating
that the judgment does not address or determine whether CRA permits future
assessment areas based upon the geographic source or concentration of deposits.
Such language preserves Plaintiffs' victory, does not reinstate any rescinded
regulation, and leaves a separate statutory question for a future case if it ever
becomes necessary to decide it.
ARGUMENT
I. THE PROPOSED JUDGMENT GOES BEYOND VACATING THE 2023
RULE AND IS EXPRESSLY INTENDED TO ESTABLISH PROSPECTIVE
"OUTER-BOUNDS."
The OCC and FDIC's Motion for Entry of Judgment makes clear that they
seek more than vacatur of the 2023 Rule. The motion asks the Court to declare that
their CRA regulations may not permit assessment of retail lending outside
4
 geographic areas where an institution operates physical facilities and accepts
deposits. ECF No. 93 at 1. The proposed judgment uses substantially the same
formulation. ECF No. 93-1 at 2.
Most importantly for present purposes, the agencies expressly describe the
judgment as prospective. After discussing the 2025 rescission proposal and public
comments, the OCC and FDIC state:
"Given the wide disparity in views, the OCC and FDIC believe the
best path forward is to request vacatur of the 2023 Rule and set a clear
table for future potential amendments, acknowledging those
amendments can neither be based on (1) an expansive view of 'entire
community' that provides for or permits the assessment of regulated
institutions' retail lending activities outside the geographic areas
where they operate and maintain deposit-taking facilities; nor (2) an
expansive view of 'credit needs' that provides for or permits the
assessment of regulated institutions' deposit products." ECF No. 93 at
5.
The motion then explains that vacatur would allow the agencies to return to
rulemaking "with a clear judicial direction on certain outer-bounds of what the
CRA allows as to the Retail Lending Test and deposit products." Id. at 9.
Amicus does not dispute that a final judgment can resolve the claims
actually presented. But those statements make it particularly important that the
judgment be precise about what it does not decide. If the phrase "operates physical
facilities and accepts deposits" is treated as establishing the exclusive permissible
geographic basis for all future CRA assessment areas, the judgment could reach
5
 beyond the challenged lending-based test and into a distinct deposit-geography
question.
The agencies anticipate, and attempt to distinguish, this very concern. In a
footnote to their argument that the proposed judgment is a reasonable resolution,
they cite Arizona v. City and County of San Francisco, 596 U.S. 763, 766 (2022)
(Roberts, C.J., concurring). ECF No. 93 at 9 n.3. In that concurrence, the Chief
Justice cautioned against using confessed judgments to accomplish through
litigation what would otherwise require notice-and-comment rulemaking, a tactic
he described, quoting a Ninth Circuit dissent, as "rulemaking-by-collective-
acquiescence." The agencies state they avoid that concern because they solicited
public comment on rescinding the 2023 Rule generally. That process, however, did
not solicit comment on the specific, forward-looking declaration at issue here,
which would constrain future CRA rulemakings, including the proposal the OCC
and FDIC issued the same day. See Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91
Fed. Reg. 52,114 (Aug. 12, 2026). The agencies' own citation therefore does not
resolve the concern Amicus raises here; if anything, it confirms that the agencies
recognized the risk and addressed only part of it.
II. AMICUS PREVIOUSLY DISTINGUISHED THE 2023 LENDING-
BASED FRAMEWORK FROM TARGETED DEPOSIT-BASED
ASSESSMENT AREAS.
6
 This concern is not a new litigation position. Dr. Thomas's 2024 Fifth
Circuit brief expressly opposed the 2023 Rule's expansion of CRA evaluation
through retail lending assessment areas. At the same time, the brief recognized that
changes in online banking could justify targeted modernization rather than
wholesale regulatory expansion.
"This 'subset' of online banks could and should have been addressed
with targeted amendments to the existing regulations or through the
traditional process of providing guidance through interagency
questions-and-answers." Thomas Fifth Circuit Brief at 22.
Footnote 16 immediately identified the OCC's 2020 rule as the example. It
quoted the OCC's observation that the increase in internet banks and internet
platforms for collecting deposits made "deposit-based assessment areas
increasingly relevant," and described the requirement that qualifying banks
delineate separate deposit-based assessment areas in geographies where they
received five-percent concentrations of retail deposits. Id. at 22-23 & n.16.
Thus, Amicus's original position contained two complementary
propositions: first, the 2023 Rule's nationwide lending-based expansion was
impermissibly broad; second, a subset of online banks could instead be addressed
through a targeted deposit-based mechanism. A supplemental clarification would
preserve that distinction rather than alter it.
7
 III. DEPOSIT-BASED ASSESSMENT AREAS ARE FUNDAMENTALLY
DIFFERENT FROM THE LENDING-BASED ASSESSMENT AREAS
CHALLENGED IN THIS CASE.
The 2023 Rule's Retail Lending Test defined additional assessment
geography by reference to where certain lending occurred. See ECF No. 93 at 3.
Plaintiffs challenged that framework because it assessed retail lending outside
areas where banks maintained facilities and accepted deposits. Id. The Court
agreed at the preliminary-injunction stage that Plaintiffs were likely to succeed on
that statutory claim. Texas Bankers Ass'n v. Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency, 728 F. Supp. 3d 412, 419-23 (N.D. Tex. 2024).
A deposit-based assessment area asks a different question. It does not make
every location where a bank happens to lend part of its CRA community. Instead,
it asks whether an institution has established a sufficiently material deposit
relationship with a particular geography that the geography should be recognized
for CRA purposes even though deposits are gathered electronically rather than
through a traditional branch.
That distinction is tied to CRA's statutory premise. Congress found that
regulated financial institutions have a "continuing and affirmative obligation to
help meet the credit needs of the local communities in which they are chartered."
12 U.S.C. § 2901(a)(3). The agencies must assess an institution's record of
meeting the credit needs of its "entire community." 12 U.S.C. § 2903(a)(1). Dr.
8
 Thomas's prior brief emphasized Senator Proxmire's concern that deposits could
flow out of communities without adequate local reinvestment. Thomas Fifth
Circuit Brief at 8-14.
Internet banking changes how deposits can enter an institution; it does not
eliminate the underlying relationship between deposit gathering and community
reinvestment. Whether CRA permits the agencies to recognize that relationship
through a narrowly drawn deposit-based assessment area is a question distinct from
whether the 2023 Rule could follow retail lending nationwide.
The Court need not decide that distinct question now. The only point
necessary here is that invalidating the 2023 lending-based framework does not
logically require a declaration that deposit geography can never be relevant to the
delineation of a CRA community.
IV. THE OCC'S 2020 FINAL RULE DEMONSTRATES THAT A
TARGETED DEPOSIT-BASED APPROACH IS NEITHER NOVEL NOR
UNTESTED.
The distinction is reinforced by the OCC's own regulatory history. In 2020,
under Comptroller Joseph Otting, the OCC adopted a final CRA rule that expressly
addressed the growing separation between physical branches and electronic deposit
gathering. The OCC stated:
"The OCC has observed an increase in the number of internet banks
and the use of internet platforms for collecting deposits, making
deposit-based assessment areas increasingly relevant." Community
9
 Reinvestment Act Regulations, 85 Fed. Reg. 34,734, 34,757 (June 5,
2020).
The rule required certain banks receiving 50 percent or more of their retail
domestic deposits from outside facility-based assessment areas to delineate
separate deposit-based assessment areas in geographies where they received at
least five percent of their retail domestic deposits. Id. at 34,757. The OCC
rescinded the 2020 rule in 2021, but the regulatory history remains relevant for the
limited purpose presented here: it confirms that a deposit-based assessment area is
a distinct, targeted concept that predates the 2023 Rule and can be analyzed
separately from the lending-based assessment areas challenged in this case.
Indeed, Amicus's 2024 brief cited that 2020 framework precisely because it
represented a narrower response to online banking than the 2023 Rule. The Court
therefore should not inadvertently transform the successful challenge to the 2023
Rule into a prospective ruling against a different framework that the parties did not
need to litigate to resolve this case.
V. A NARROW SAVINGS CLAUSE WOULD PRESERVE PLAINTIFFS'
RELIEF WITHOUT DECIDING A SEPARATE QUESTION NOT
NECESSARY TO THIS CASE.
Amicus does not ask the Court to rewrite the parties' substantive resolution
of the 2023 Rule. The simplest approach is to leave the declaration concerning the
Retail Lending Test intact and add one clarifying paragraph stating what the
judgment does not decide.
10
 PROPOSED SAVINGS CLAUSE
ORDERED AND DECLARED that nothing in this Judgment
shall be construed to address or determine whether the
Community Reinvestment Act permits the OCC or FDIC to
delineate assessment areas based upon the geographic source or
concentration of deposits received by a regulated institution,
including deposit-based assessment areas.
Alternatively, the Court could incorporate the same reservation directly into
the existing declaration concerning the Retail Lending Test. The separate savings
clause is preferable, however, because it does not alter any word of the declaration
that Plaintiffs, OCC, and FDIC have already accepted. It merely makes explicit
that the judgment does not adjudicate a different question.
That clarification would impose no deposit-based rule, restore no rescinded
regulation, and diminish none of Plaintiffs' relief from the 2023 Rule. It would
simply preserve the ordinary principle that a court should not decide more than is
necessary to resolve the dispute before it, particularly where the agencies
themselves seek to use the judgment as prospective guidance concerning the
"outer-bounds" of future CRA regulations.
CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Amicus respectfully requests that, if the Court enters the
proposed final judgment against the OCC and FDIC, it clarify that the judgment
does not address or determine whether the CRA permits appropriately tailored
11
 assessment areas based upon the geographic source or concentration of deposits
received by a regulated institution.

SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

Plaintiffs-Appellees have convincingly demonstrated that the district court
properly granted a preliminary injunction to enjoin the Final Rule promulgated by
Defendants-Appellants, the federal banking agencies ("FBAs"), which radically
rewrites the CRA and displaces the intent of Congress. Dr. Thomas provides
additional context and data to support Plaintiffs-Appellees' arguments regarding the
Final Rule's historic overreach and contradiction of congressional intent, its
substantial adverse economic impacts on banks and the communities they serve, and
the practical consequences of replacing the well-functioning existing regulations that
have been in place since 1995 with the overly complex Final Rule.
First, the Final Rule departs from the CRA and the intended meaning of the
word "entire" as used to modify the word "community" by establishing a Retail
Lending Test to evaluate bank CRA performance in areas geographically removed
from the local communities where banks maintain facilities and accept deposits. As
the district court summated, in "modifying 'community,' the word 'entire' merely
clarifies that the whole community must be served—it does not change what a
'community' is." ROA.594 (original emphasis). The CRA's legislative history

5 Community Reinvestment Act Final Rule, 89 Fed. Reg. 6574 (Feb. 1, 2024) (to
be codified at 12 C.F.R. pts. 25, 228, 345) ("Final Rule").
Case: 24-10367 Document: 100 Page: 12 Date Filed: 09/25/2024

5

demonstrates that the phrase "entire" as applied to "community" was intended as a
demographic directive for banks to help meet the credit needs of all income-level
segments within the bank's community as a whole. The FBA's 1978 CRA
regulations and 1993 CRA guidance confirm this meaning. The CRA's well-
documented intent cannot be displaced by a claimed need to address changes in the
geographic scope of lending activities. The CRA's legislative history establishes that
Congress understood in 1977 that banks engaged in lending away from the local
communities where they maintained facilities. The Final Rule would be legislating
nationwide credit allocation through agency rulemaking by requiring examiners to
evaluate and rate lending outside a bank's local community—a requirement that
Congress never intended and purposely avoided in enacting the CRA.

Second, data published by the FBAs projects that the Final Rule will
unnecessarily and arbitrarily deflate bank ratings on CRA performance evaluations
under the new Retail Lending Test by significantly increasing the percentage of
"failing" (i.e., Substantial Noncompliance and Needs to Improve) ratings and greatly
decreasing the percentage of Outstanding ratings for larger banks. The projected
ratings deflation on the Retail Lending Test implicates matters of economic
significance relating to bank business because that test drives the bank's overall
CRA rating, and the FBAs generally restrict banks that receive Substantial
Noncompliance or Needs to Improve ratings from opening new branches or

6

participating in mergers and acquisitions. Conversely, the remarkable reduction of
Outstanding ratings for larger banks with the greatest ability to move the needle in
low- and moderate-income communities may negatively impact an incentive to
implement aggressive community reinvestment and development strategies. These,
and other harmful effects, including reputational damage, would be artificially
imposed because the ratings reductions would not necessarily reflect lower levels of
community reinvestment.
Third, the complexity of the Final Rule and inevitable compliance costs
support injunctive relief. The public interest is not served by overly complicated
rulemaking spanning 649 pages of triple-column text and 60,000 words, particularly
given that the existing regulations are generally working well and are only in need
of simple modernization. The overcomplexity raises serious concerns regarding the
consistent application of the rewritten standards, undercutting a primary purpose of
rulemaking to achieve an increase in efficiency and predictability. Any need to
address the CRA obligations of "a subset" of online banks could have been
accomplished through targeted amendments to the existing regulations, and the
modernization rationale functioned as a Trojan Horse. Appellants' Br. 2, 9-10.
The Final Rule is irreconcilable with the documented intent of the CRA, and it
will create unintended and serious economic consequences for banks and low- and
moderate-income communities. Importantly, based on their extensive personal

ARGUMENT
I. The CRA's Usage of the Phrase "Entire" to Modify "Community"
Requires Banks to Serve All Income-Level Segments Within the Bank's
Delineated Local Community, Not All Geographies in the Nation
The CRA recognizes that banks have an "affirmative obligation to help meet
the credit needs of the local communities in which they are chartered" and requires
the FBAs to "assess the institution's record of meeting the credit needs of its entire
community, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with
the safe and sound operation of such institution." 12 U.S.C. §§ 2901(a)(3),
2903(a)(1). The FBAs wrongly argue that the CRA's usage of the phrase "entire
community" authorizes the Final Rule to establish tests for assessing bank CRA
performance in a "nationwide area" that extends beyond the communities in which
banks have a physical presence and accept deposits to reach "other geographic areas
where the bank conducts retail lending." Appellants' Br. 11, 19, 22. Rejecting this
strained interpretation, the district court found that "[i]n modifying 'community,' the
word 'entire' merely clarifies that the whole community must be served — it does
not change what a 'community' is." ROA.594 (original emphasis).
The term "entire" does not geographically expand what a community is.
Rather, the CRA's usage of the word "entire" to modify the word "community"
Case: 24-10367 Document: 100 Page: 15 Date Filed: 09/25/2024

8

underscores a demographic mandate requiring banks to help meet the credit needs
of all income-level segments contained within their delineated local communities
and restricts them from serving the credit needs of middle- and upper-income
segments to the exclusion of any low- and moderate-income segments that comprise
the community as a whole.
The legislative history of the CRA provides strong evidence of this meaning.
During three days of hearings in 1977 before the Senate Committee on Banking,
Housing, & Urban Affairs on the proposed CRA, the Chairman and sponsor of the
bill, Senator Proxmire, repeatedly explained that the basis for the bill derives from
data demonstrating a lack of credit services and investments in lower income, less
affluent, and minority neighborhoods:
You have a situation here in the District of Columbia, for instance,
where the loans by banks and savings and loan instiutions [sic] in the
District are very light and they make big investments outside the
District in the suburbs in mortgages, and where they do invest in the
District it's by and large in the northwest section and the white section
and they don't invest in the inner-city. They don't invest in the black
neighborhoods, with some exceptions where one or two banks have
done it and done extremely well.
***
My problem is the flow has been the other way. It has been from the
depressed communities. You get deposits there and then you invest in
the outside thriving communities.
***
We have a record establishing the fact that there is a market here, a
need. You can see that there is a need. It isn't being met now. [. . .] The
testimony of the banking commissioner of Massachusetts was that a
great deal of loans for low income census tract areas were made with
private mortgage lenders at much higher rates on terms which required
Case: 24-10367 Document: 100 Page: 16 Date Filed: 09/25/2024

9

much higher monthly payments because the term was shorter, much
higher down payments in spite of the fact she said her experience was
that the default rate was the same in all of the census tracks regardless
of income."

The CRA's use of the term "safe and sound operation" serves as another
powerful indicator of this intent. During the 1977 legislative hearings, Senator
Proxmire addressed concerns regarding the perceived credit quality of loans in low-
income neighborhoods and the bill's provisions for lending in those neighborhoods:
This bill says where there is a local credit need, where the need is sound,
that it should be provided for. We had [. . .] the commissioner of
banking in Massachusetts, and she found in the lowest income census
tracts there was no worse record of delinquency than in the highest
income census tracts.

Community Credit Needs: Hearings on S. 406 Before the Sen. Comm. On Banking,
Hous. & Urban Affs., 95th Cong. 1st Sess. 321 (1977) (statement of Chairman
Proxmire). Senator Proxmire emphasized that the CRA would not "require that you
make loans that aren't sound. Every loan should be sound. We are not saying that
you should make a loan that has any greater prospect of default in the community."
Id. at 323. Echoing the congressional hearings and Senator Proxmire's assurances,
the FBAs observed in the 1978 CRA regulation that "[s]ome commenters believed
that institutions attempting to comply with the CRA would be forced to make
imprudent credit decisions. However, the Agencies will always conduct their
assessments giving consideration to the safety and soundness of the institution." 43
Fed. Reg. at 47145. The CRA's usage of the term "safe and sound operation" serves
Case: 24-10367 Document: 100 Page: 19 Date Filed: 09/25/2024

12

no purpose other than to mitigate concerns that requiring banks to lend in low- and
moderate-income segments of the "entire community" would impose unacceptable
levels of credit risk. 12 U.S.C. § 2903(a)(1).
Perhaps most persuasively, the 1993 Q&A undermines the argument that the
word "entire" can been read as geographically expanding what a community is. It
states:
[Q:] What do the financial supervisory agencies expect from
institutions that have voluntarily limited or specialized their services to
target particular markets?

[A:] Such an institution has the same continuing and affirmative
obligation as a 'full service' institution to help meet the credit needs of
its entire local community, consistent with safe and sound operations.
An institution's self-imposed service or market limitations may not be
used as a justification for the failure to define its local community or to
help, directly or indirectly, meet the credit needs within that community,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

58 Fed. Reg. at 9182 (emphasis added). This confirms that the FBAs understood the
statutory directive: to evaluate whether banks adequately helped meet the credit
needs of low- and moderate-income segments falling within the "entire local
community."

The FBAs cannot override congressional intent by arguing that, "since the last
comprehensive update to the regulations in 1995, a subset of banks, such as primarily
online banks, are now conducting substantial shares of their retail lending away from
these physical facilities." Appellees' Br. 2 (emphasis added). Banks engaged in
Case: 24-10367 Document: 100 Page: 20 Date Filed: 09/25/2024

13

nationwide lending away from their physical facilities long before technological
advancements permitted online banking. The CRA's legislative history confirms
that Congress was well aware of nationwide lending practices at the time of the
statute's enactment in 1977. During the congressional hearings, data was presented
showing that "about 11 percent of the money deposited in Brooklyn remains, and 89
percent is invested elsewhere" and Senator Proxmire observed that some banks "take
money from the community and reinvest it elsewhere, in some cases abroad, in some
cases in other parts of the country," while other banks "sometimes ship their funds
to the major money markets." 123 CONG. REC. 17603, 17630 (June 6, 1977). Yet,
Congress did not address the issue by authorizing the FBAs to review bank lending
activity across the entire country. Instead, to encourage banks "to help meet the
credit needs of the local communities in which they are chartered," Congress

§§ 2901(a)(3), 2903(a)(1).

encouraging credit services in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods within a
bank's local community into a geographic concept for nationwide credit allocation.

to address 'redlining'—the practice of refusing credit in neighborhoods 'deemed

LEGAL STANDARD
I.
Motions for Judgments on the Pleadings
Rule 12(c) provides that "[a]fter the pleadings are closed—but early enough not to delay
trial—a party may move for judgment on the pleadings." Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(c). "A motion brought
Case 2:24-cv-00025-Z-BR Document 93 Filed 07/31/26 Page 5 of 11 PageID 728
 - 6 -
pursuant to [Rule] 12(c) is designed to dispose of cases where the material facts are not in dispute
and a judgment on the merits can be rendered by looking to the substance of the pleadings and any
judicially noticed facts." Great Plains Tr. Co. v. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Co., 313 F.3d
305, 312 (5th Cir. 2002) (citations omitted). Indeed, "[l]itigation in which the sole question is the
applicability or interpretation of a statutory provision is another context in which judgment on the
pleadings may be appropriate." 5C Charles Alan Wright & Arthur R. Miller, Fed. Prac. & Proc.
Civ. § 1367 (3d ed. Apr. 2022 update) (collecting citations). While a typical Rule 12(c) motion
seeks a judgment in favor of the movant, the Rule is flexible and permits a party to seek a judgment
against itself. See, e.g., Meggs v. Colo. Hosp. Grp., LLC, Civ. A. No. 21-2971, 2022 WL 1810597,
at *6 (D. Colo. June 2, 2022) (granting motion by defendant for entry of judgment against itself
under Rule 12(c) over plaintiff's objection); Cuesta v. DTC Lodging LLC, Civ. A. No. 21-3092,
2022 WL 2077940, at *2 (D. Colo. June 8, 2022), R. & R. adopted, 2022 WL 3212924 (D. Colo.
Aug. 9, 2022) (same).
Where a motion seeks the entry of judgment in favor of a plaintiff, "the court should grant
the motion only if a defendant's answer or other pleading admits, alleges, or fails to deny facts
which, taken as true, show the plaintiff is entitled to judgment as a matter of law against that
defendant." Atl. Specialty Ins. Co. v. Bindea, 632 F. Supp. 3d 681, 694 (W.D. Va. 2022) (granting
motion for judgment on the pleadings); see also Alexander v. City of Chicago, 994 F.2d 333, 336
(7th Cir. 1993) (In contrast to using Rule 12(c) to assert Rule 12(b) dismissal grounds after
pleadings have closed, when a party uses Rule 12(c) "in its customary application to attempt to
dispose of the case on the basis of the underlying substantive merits . . . the appropriate standard
is that applicable to summary judgment, except that the court may consider only the contents of
the pleadings."). In so doing, a court accepts as true the factual allegations admitted by defendants
Case 2:24-cv-00025-Z-BR Document 93 Filed 07/31/26 Page 6 of 11 PageID 729
 - 7 -
in the pleadings but not "legal conclusion[s] couched as a factual allegation[s]." Garza v. Escobar,
972 F.3d 721, 727 (5th Cir. 2020) (citations omitted; affirming grant of motion for judgment on
the pleadings); see also Kohen v. H.S. Crocker Co., 260 F.2d 790, 792 (5th Cir. 1958) ("in the state
of the pleadings it is sufficient to refer to the rule that a motion for judgment on the pleadings
admits facts but does not admit conclusions of law"). The court should grant a judgment on the
pleadings when a party establishes that no material issue of fact remains to be resolved and a party
is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. See Lowery v. Gonzales, No. 2:22-cv-0016, 2023 WL
2636727, at *1 (N.D. Tex. Feb. 27, 2023), R. & R. adopted, 2023 WL 2634500 (Mar. 23, 2023),
aff'd, No. 23-10366, 2023 WL 8449215 (5th Cir. Dec. 6, 2023). "When there remains no
legitimate question left to be decided as to whether a claim is valid, judgment is appropriate." Id.
II.
Final Judgments Dispensing of Fewer Than All Claims.
Rule 54(b) provides that "when multiple parties are involved" in an action "the court may
direct entry of a final judgment as to one or more, but fewer than all, claims or parties only if the
court expressly determines that there is no just reason for delay." Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b). Whether
there exists "no just reason for delay" is "is left to the sound judicial discretion of the district court
and is to be exercised in the interest of sound judicial administration." Ginett v. Computer Task
Grp., Inc., 962 F.2d 1085, 1092 (2d Cir. 1992) (citation modified; quoting Curtiss-Wright Corp.
v. Gen. Elec. Co., 446 U.S. 1, 8 (1980), and Sears, Roebuck & Co. v. Mackey, 351 U.S. 427, 437
(1956)); see also Fed. Sav. & Loan Ins. Corp. v. Cribbs, 918 F.2d 557, 559 (5th Cir. 1990)
(Rule 54(b) determination is reviewed for abuse of discretion). In finalizing a judgment that
dispenses with some, but not all, claims, courts have suggested that a district court "provide a brief
reasoned statement in support of its determination that 'there is no just reason for delay where the
justification for the certificate is not apparent." Ginett, 962 F.2d at 1092 (affirming grant of
Rule 54(b) relief to finalize judgment on one claim).

DISCUSSION
A judgment against the OCC and FDIC on the terms set forth in the proposed judgment
enclosed herewith is appropriate in light of the pleadings and applicable law. Additionally, there
exists no just reason to delay in finalizing that judgment even though this action continues to
proceed against the Federal Reserve.
I.
The Entry of the Proposed Judgment is Appropriate.
The entry of judgment against the OCC and FDIC as set forth in the enclosed proposed
judgment is plainly appropriate. The OCC and FDIC have admitted the material facts in Plaintiffs'
Complaint, which largely presents questions of law regarding the permissibility of the 2023 Rule
in light of the CRA's statutory text. Having done so, the OCC and FDIC have no further factual
defenses in this action as to the relief sought in Plaintiffs' Complaint, which the proposed judgment
fully encompasses. As such, judgment, primarily in the form of vacatur of the 2023 Rule as it
applies to the OCC and FDIC, is appropriate. Indeed, there is no basis to deny this motion.
First, even were it a requirement, the requested judgment is fair and adequate considering
the circumstances. The Court has already assessed the threshold merits of Plaintiffs' claims,
finding them likely to succeed on the ground that the Agencies exceeded their statutory authority.
Such a ruling on the merits would undoubtedly lead to the vacatur of the 2023 Rule—i.e., the
primary term of the proposed judgment enclosed herewith. See Rest. Law Ctr. v. Dep't of Lab.,
120 F.4th 163, 177 (5th Cir. 2024) (when an agency action is contrary to law, the "default rule is
that vacatur is the appropriate remedy" (collecting citations and quoting Data Mktg. P'ship, LP v.
Dep't of Lab., 45 F.4th 846, 859 (5th Cir. 2022)).
Second, the proposed judgment is a reasonable resolution to the claims against the OCC
and FDIC in this action. Not only has the Court found that Plaintiffs are likely to succeed in their
challenges to the 2023 Rule and 2016 Guidance, but the Agencies have sought comment on

rescinding that rule, eliciting a wide range of views. Thus, vacating the rule not only resolves the
claims against the OCC and FDIC in this action (and concomitantly avoids the expenditure of
additional government resources to litigate it), it also positions the OCC and FDIC to return to the
rulemaking process anew to consider the public's views with a clear judicial direction on certain
outer-bounds of what the CRA allows as to the Retail Lending Test and deposit products. This is
plainly a reasonable resolution of this matter.3
Ultimately, the proposed resolution serves the interests of the OCC and FDIC and does so
in a manner that is fair, adequate, and reasonable to all involved.
II.
The Court Should Finalize the Proposed Judgment Against the OCC and FDIC
Under Rule 54(b).
Not only should the Court enter the proposed judgment against the OCC and FDIC, it
should also find that there exists no just reason to delay finalizing that judgment under Rule 54(b).
Undoubtedly, this motion will not resolve all claims against all parties in this action—the Federal
Reserve does not join in this motion, and Plaintiffs' claims against it remain pending. As such,
without a Rule 54(b) finding, the judgment against the OCC and FDIC would not be final.
But finalizing the resolution of this case against them is exactly what the OCC and FDIC
seek through this motion. Finalizing the vacatur of the 2023 Rule and the challenged portions of
the 2016 Guidance as they pertain to the OCC and FDIC will allow them and the institutions they
supervise to return to the prior CRA regulatory state. It will also permit the OCC and FDIC to

To Whom it May Concern:

Valley National Bank ("Valley") values the opportunity to comment on the joint notice of proposed
rulemaking (the "NPR") issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (the "OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation (the "FDIC") concerning the Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA"). Valley
is a national bank supervised by the OCC and a regional financial institution with a longstanding
commitment to meeting the credit, investment, and community development needs of the communities it
serves. Valley views CRA not only as a regulatory framework, but an important mechanism for aligning
bank activity with measurable community benefit, particularly for low- and moderate-income ("LMI")
individuals and communities, small businesses, affordable housing providers, nonprofits, and underserved
communities. This commitment is deeply embedded in Valley's culture and guides how the Bank
approaches community partnerships, lending, investments, philanthropy, and volunteerism. Valley believes
banks play a vital role in supporting economic opportunity and strengthening communities. A successful
CRA framework should encourage meaningful, long-term engagement that responds to community needs
and creates lasting impact.
The OCC and FDIC released the NPR on July 31, 2026, and published it in the Federal Register on August
12, 2026. Valley appreciates the agencies' efforts to provide greater regulatory clarity, reduce uncertainty
regarding qualifying activities, and better align CRA implementation with the goal of directing community
development capital where it can achieve meaningful and lasting impact. Valley, however, strongly supports
preserving the CRA's core mission and ensuring that the final rule does not unintentionally dilute support
for LMI communities or disrupt sustained community development activity. In that regard, clear and stable
asset thresholds are an important part of an effective framework because they recognize differences in
bank size and business models while allowing institutions to plan for and maintain long-term community
investments. Changes to those thresholds could redirect resources away from activities that strengthen LMI
communities. The recommendations below identify areas where Valley believes the final rule can further
balance accountability for community outcomes with the clarity and flexibility banks need to address
community needs effectively.
•
Maintain the current primary-purpose standard for CRA-eligible grants rather than adopting a
bright-line indirect-cost limitation. Flexible grant funding provides critical support to mission-driven
nonprofits and intermediaries, helping them sustain essential programs, strengthen organizational
capacity, and respond to growing community needs.
•
Preserve CRA consideration for digital services, alternative delivery channels, and deposit products
that expand access, inclusion, and future credit readiness.
•
Modernize retail branch distribution analysis in the Service Test to reflect both physical access and


2


how customers use digital, workplace, and community-based banking channels.
•
Use the average quarterly Tier 1 capital over the examination period when establishing community
development performance expectations.
•
Support the qualitative framework reflected in Option 2 for geographic flexibility, measuring
compliance over the full examination period with appropriate consideration of performance context.
•
Support Option 1's approach of identifying major retail product lines at the institution level and
evaluating individual consumer lending products when a single product becomes a substantial
majority of the bank's retail lending, is responsive to serving LMI individuals, or when the bank
elects to have that product evaluated.
•
Recognize meaningful community development loan and line renewals, extensions, and ongoing
credit commitments that continue to support qualifying community development purposes.
•
Promote alignment among the federal banking agencies so CRA standards remain clear,
consistent, and administrable.
Valley is a regional financial institution with over $66 billion in assets and more than 220 branch locations
and commercial offices across New York, New Jersey, Florida, Alabama, California, Illinois, Pennsylvania,
and Arizona, while serving clients nationwide. As reflected in our current Outstanding CRA rating, Valley
has developed a comprehensive CRA program that integrates lending, investment, grant-making, volunteer
service, and community development activities across its footprint. Our comments are informed by direct
experience working with community organizations, affordable housing partners, small business support
providers, and public-sector stakeholders, as well as by the need for a CRA framework that remains
rigorous, transparent, and administrable for banks and regulators.
Valley strongly supports the principal goal of CRA, which is to encourage banks to help meet the credit
needs of their entire communities, including LMI neighborhoods, consistent with safe and sound banking
practices. Valley's commitment to community reinvestment has evolved alongside our growth and business
model. While CRA provides an important framework, our commitment extends beyond regulatory
requirements by focusing on activities that expand access to housing, credit, financial services, nonprofit
capacity, and economic opportunity. In 2025 alone, Valley originated, funded, invested, or otherwise
provided more than $3.6 billion in qualifying lending, investment, and community-support activities. This
included $1.8 billion in community development loans, $816 million in community development investments,
which includes $380 million in highly catalytic New Markets Tax Credit investments that support economic
revitalization in underserved communities and Tribal Lands, $371 million in residential mortgages to LMI
borrowers and LMI neighborhoods, and $319 million in small business loans. In addition, Valley provided
more than $4 million in CRA qualified grants, charitable contributions, and over 7,200 board service and
volunteer hours in support of LMI individuals, communities, nonprofits, and small businesses. While the
examples above are based on 2025 activities, they are representative of the sustained community
development efforts undertaken throughout Valley's 2022-2024 examination period, which contributed to
the Bank earning its third consecutive Outstanding CRA rating and demonstrate our longstanding
commitment to strengthening the communities we serve through both capital deployment and direct
engagement.
 The Need for CRA-Eligible Flexible Grant Funding is Critical
Community development grants are critical because they provide nonprofits with the flexible resources
needed to address urgent local needs and deliver measurable benefits to LMI individuals and
communities. A fixed 15 percent indirect-cost threshold could unintentionally reduce support for
effective organizations providing affordable housing, small business assistance, workforce

3


development, financial capability, housing stability, and other essential services.
Flexible and unrestricted grants help nonprofits retain staff, sustain programs, meet compliance
obligations, invest in technology, and respond as community needs evolve. These costs are integral to
responsible service delivery, particularly for smaller organizations and at a time when operating costs
are rising and public resources are constrained.
Funding organizations that expand the reach and effectiveness of community development efforts is
important because they provide data, research, training, technical assistance, capacity building, and
other shared resources that strengthen local nonprofit organizations. These services enhance program
quality, build organizational capacity, and help community-based organizations respond more
effectively to community needs.
Valley recommends maintaining the current primary-purpose standard for CRA-eligible grants rather
than adopting a bright-line indirect-cost limit. Banks should be permitted to demonstrate that a grant
has a bona fide community development purpose, appropriate oversight, and a reasonable expectation
of benefiting LMI individuals and communities, small businesses, affordable housing, or other qualifying
needs.
Valley also encourages the agencies to consider the reputational, competitive, and privacy implications
of publicly disclosing recipient-level grant information. This disclosure may provide little additional
regulatory insight while potentially discouraging the bank-community partnerships that help drive
meaningful community impact.
 Recognize That Deposit and Digital Services Remain Critical Gateways to Responsible Credit
Access
Valley encourages the agencies to clarify that the NPR's proposed elimination of consideration for
deposit services does not preclude consideration of deposit accounts that provide a demonstrable
pathway to credit, as well as services delivered through alternative delivery systems and digital
channels. Valley recognizes the agencies' objective of maintaining an appropriate nexus between CRA
consideration and community credit needs. While the proposal focuses on meeting credit needs,
deposit accounts and related banking services often serve as the foundation for future access to and
responsible use of credit products. Low-cost transaction accounts, Bank On-certified products, digital
banking services, remittance products, financial education, and similar offerings help consumers
establish savings, build assets, strengthen financial stability, and develop relationships with mainstream
financial institutions. These relationships can help consumers move beyond basic transaction services
and into the responsible use of credit products, supporting greater financial inclusion and economic
opportunity. Over time, access to banking services through physical branches and digital channels can
expand access to affordable credit, enabling individuals and families to finance major purchases,
navigate financial shocks, build wealth, and achieve long-term economic security.
Accordingly, Valley recommends retaining consideration for deposit products and alternative delivery
systems that demonstrate a meaningful connection to credit access, credit readiness, or the effective
delivery of credit-related services to LMI individuals or communities. Recognizing these activities would
encourage banks to invest in practical tools and services that help LMI households establish and
maintain banking relationships, build financial capability, manage household cash flow, and become
better positioned to access responsible credit as their financial needs evolve. It would also provide
regulators and community stakeholders with a clearer framework for evaluating how these services

4


expand participation in the banking system, strengthen financial inclusion, and support long-term
community and economic outcomes.
Valley further encourages the agencies to continue supporting innovative approaches to expanding
financial inclusion and access to banking services. As consumer banking preferences evolve, financial
institutions increasingly utilize digital platforms, fintech partnerships, online small business lending
capabilities, and other technology-enabled solutions to reach underserved populations. The final rule
should preserve flexibility for institutions to receive appropriate CRA consideration for innovative
delivery models that responsibly expand access to financial services and credit opportunities for LMI
individuals and communities.
 Modernize Branch Distribution to Better Reflect Customer Behavior
Valley encourages the agencies to modernize branch distribution analysis by continuing to recognize
the importance of physical access while also considering how individuals, small businesses, and
community organizations access banking and credit-related services through digital channels,
alternative delivery systems, and community-based partnerships.
While branch presence remains important, the banking industry has evolved significantly since CRA
was enacted in 1977. Today, customers increasingly access banking services through digital channels,
remote deposit capture, call centers, online account opening, and mobile lending platforms. In addition,
banks often reach LMI individuals and communities through partnerships with community-based
organizations that provide financial education, housing counseling, small business support, and other
critical services. As a result, branch location alone may not provide a complete measure of whether
and how a bank provides meaningful access to banking and credit-related services. The final rule
should therefore recognize meaningful activity delivered beyond traditional physical branch networks,
including alternative delivery systems, collaborations with community-based organizations, and other
channels that expand access to mainstream banking, credit, and community development resources.
Branch distribution analysis should recognize that customers do not always bank where they live.
Individuals may choose a branch near where they work, attend school, receive services, shop, conduct
business, or otherwise engage in daily activities. Small businesses and nonprofit organizations may
also maintain banking relationships near commercial corridors, service locations, administrative offices,
or community partners. A Service Test analysis that considers only branch locations in an LMI census
tract may not fully capture how customers and community organizations access banking and credit-
related services. The final rule should provide flexibility to allow examiners to consider customer
behavior, digital access, and community activity centers when assessing meaningful access to banking
services. Moreover, branch distribution analysis is heavily dependent on census tract classifications
that change periodically as economic conditions evolve. A bank may establish a branch in an LMI
census tract and invest substantial resources into helping that community prosper. Where a bank has
maintained a branch and made sustained investments in a community that is later reclassified, the
evaluation should consider the bank's historical presence, continuing service to LMI customers, and
the circumstances surrounding the tract's reclassification.
Valley recommends that branch distribution remains a meaningful component of the Service Test but
be evaluated together with demonstrated customer access, the effectiveness of alternative delivery
systems, credit-related services, and applicable performance context. Greater emphasis should be
placed on measurable outcomes, including access to banking services and affordable deposit and
credit products, digital and alternative delivery systems, and the extent to which banks successfully

5


serve LMI individuals and communities within their assessment areas. This approach would continue
to recognize the importance of branches where they are critical to community access, while avoiding
an overly narrow analysis that may not capture the full range of ways banks meet community needs. It
would also help prevent disincentives to expansion into new markets or operating in markets with limited
branch coverage.
 Clarifying the Use of Tier 1 Capital in Community Development Performance Metrics
The NPR continues to rely on Tier 1 capital as a key benchmark for assessing community development
lending and investment activity. Valley supports the use of a capital-based metric because it provides
a transparent measure of institutional capacity; however, additional clarity regarding the methodology
would help ensure that performance expectations are fair, stable, and appropriately aligned with a
bank's ability to support community development activities over time.
Valley does not believe that Tier 1 capital measured at a single point in time is the most appropriate
benchmark for evaluating activity over a multi-year examination period. Capital levels may fluctuate
significantly due to acquisitions, economic conditions, balance sheet management decisions, and other
factors unrelated to community development performance. As a result, an end-of-period measurement
may not accurately reflect a bank's capacity or level of activity throughout the evaluation cycle.
Accordingly, Valley recommends that the agencies use average quarterly Tier 1 capital over the
examination period. This approach would reduce point-in-time volatility and better align the
denominator with the period during which the relevant community development activities were
conducted.
 Evaluate Geographic Flexibility in a Manner That Allows Banks to Deploy Capital Where It Will
Have the Greatest Impact
Valley strongly supports geographic flexibility within the community development framework, including
recognition of qualified community development loans and investments made outside a bank's
assessment areas when those activities support community development. Because community
development opportunities are not evenly distributed across markets, banks should retain the ability to
deploy capital, resources, and expertise where they can have the greatest impact while continuing to
meet local needs. CRA evaluations should incorporate qualitative factors and performance context that
recognize circumstances where geographic flexibility thresholds are not met due to limited
opportunities, market characteristics, project timing, or competition for eligible activities. Valley believes
geographic flexibility should be measured over the entire examination period, using average quarterly
Tier 1 capital, and supports the qualitative framework reflected in Option 2, which evaluates whether a
bank has adequately served its assessment areas over the full evaluation period while considering
responsiveness, market opportunities, project timing, and other relevant performance-context factors.
Properly structured geographic flexibility can help ensure that smaller markets, rural areas, Tribal lands,
and other underserved communities benefit when banks are able to deploy capital beyond traditional
assessment area boundaries, while still maintaining accountability for meeting local needs. This
approach helps direct community development capital to areas that often lack sufficient financing
opportunities and local funding sources, rather than concentrating activity solely in larger, more active
markets.
Large metropolitan areas typically offer numerous CRA-qualified lending and investment opportunities,
while smaller, rural, and less densely populated markets may have only a limited number of eligible

6


projects in any given year. Competition for available opportunities can also be significant, and project
timing is often driven by factors outside a bank's control. As a result, annual measurement may create
unintended challenges for institutions operating in markets with fewer community development
opportunities. Evaluating performance over a multi-year period better reflects how community
development projects are sourced, underwritten, approved, and funded, while supporting a more
consistent flow of capital to communities over time. When combined with appropriate geographic
flexibility, this approach helps ensure community development resources are deployed where they can
have the greatest impact.
Valley supports the qualitative framework reflected in Option 2 because it would evaluate whether a
bank has adequately served an assessment area over the full evaluation period and would permit
consideration of responsiveness, market opportunities, project timing, and other performance-context
factors.
 Assessing Major Product Line Determinations at the Institution Level, Which Ensures
Consistency and Meaningful Outcomes
Valley supports the institution-level approach reflected in Option 1 for identifying a bank's major retail
product lines. Determining major product lines at the institution level would promote consistency across
assessment areas, align the evaluation with the bank's overall business model, and reduce volatility
associated with localized product concentrations that may not be material to the institution's overall
lending strategy or local credit needs. An institution-level approach would provide greater certainty for
banks and examiners while keeping evaluations focused on the products most representative of a
bank's lending activity. Valley recommends adopting Option 1 rather than identifying major retail
product lines separately within each assessment area.
Additionally, Valley recommends that individual consumer product categories be evaluated separately
when a product represents a substantial majority of the institution's retail lending activity, consistent
with longstanding CRA practice, rather than being subject to a prescriptive percentage threshold or
evaluated in the aggregate. Product line determinations should be targeted, meaningful, and reflective
of the significance of each product within the bank's overall lending strategy and community impact.
This approach is particularly important for products that help low- and moderate-income individuals and
communities build wealth, accumulate assets, and improve long-term financial stability.
Unlike mortgage lending or small business lending, consumer lending encompasses a broad spectrum
of products with significantly different purposes, risks, and community impacts, including auto loans,
recreational vehicle loans, boat loans, unsecured consumer loans, and cash-value lines of credit.
Treating these products as a single major retail product category could obscure their distinct
characteristics and produce an evaluation that is less transparent and less useful in assessing whether
a bank is meeting community credit needs.
 Community Development Loan Renewals, Extensions, and Ongoing Credit Commitments When
They Involve Reflect the Need for Ongoing Credit Availability
Valley supports the agencies' proposal to recognize community development loans over multiple
examination cycles because it better reflects the long-term nature of community development finance.
Additionally, in response to the agencies' invitation to comment on whether to consider CD loans or
lines only once per evaluation period, we recommend that renewals count where they continue to
support a bona fide community development purpose. Typically, renewals are not simply passive or

7


automatic extensions of prior activity. Banks must continue to allocate capital, maintain credit exposure,
monitor borrower performance, satisfy underwriting and risk management expectations, devote capital
and resources that could be deployed elsewhere, manage concentration limits, and devote relationship,
servicing, and compliance resources to these facilities. In many cases, renewing a community
development loan or line of credit reflects a continuing commitment of institutional capacity and balance
sheet resources to a borrower or project that continues to meet community development needs.
For many nonprofit organizations, affordable housing developers, community facilities, and small
businesses, the ongoing availability of credit is often more important than the initial loan origination.
Annual renewals of revolving lines of credit and working capital facilities frequently reflect a borrower's
continuing need for financing rather than a bank's desire to generate additional CRA consideration. A
framework that limits CRA recognition to a single occurrence during an examination period may
unintentionally discourage banks from maintaining long-term credit relationships. In certain cases,
institutions may be incentivized to originate new facilities rather than continuing existing successful
relationships, even when renewal is the most prudent, cost-effective and efficient course for both
borrowers and lenders.
CRA should encourage sustained commitments to communities and borrowers. Valley recommends
recognizing a renewal or extension where the transaction reflects a continuation or expansion of
community development support. Relevant factors could include a new underwriting determination, an
extension of maturity, a recommitment or increase of available funds, modification of material terms,
additional capital exposure, or continuation of a legally binding commitment responsive to a
documented community development need.
 Alignment Among the Federal Banking Agencies Is Critical to a Sustainable CRA Framework
Valley encourages the OCC and FDIC to continue coordinating with the Board of Governors of the
Federal Reserve System toward consistent and administrable CRA standards across the federal
banking agencies. CRA has historically functioned most effectively when the federal banking agencies
apply consistent standards, definitions, and examination expectations. Divergent regulatory
approaches can create uncertainty, complicate compliance planning, and produce inconsistent
outcomes for similarly situated institutions and the communities they serve.
A durable CRA rule should provide clarity and stability for banks, regulators, community organizations,
advocacy groups, and the communities the statute is intended to benefit. Lack of alignment may
increase operational complexity, foster interpretive disputes, and heighten the risk of future challenges
to the framework. Valley therefore recommends that the agencies prioritize a consistent approach in
the final rule to ensure CRA implementation remains transparent, predictable, and effective while
maintaining strong expectations for community-focused performance.
Valley believes alignment in CRA standards, definitions, examination methodologies, and
implementation expectations remains essential to promoting transparency, consistency, and regulatory
efficiency while reducing unnecessary compliance burden and uncertainty.
Examination Guidance and Supervisory Consistency
Valley encourages the agencies to retain and as needed, update the Interagency Q&As through the
existing rulemaking process as a reliable source of CRA eligibility and supervisory guidance. In order
to promote consistent implementation of the final rule, the agencies should also publish examination

8


procedures, illustrative examples, Q&A's, and other supervisory materials concurrently with the rule.
Providing this guidance at the outset would clarify regulatory expectations, support consistent
interpretations across agencies and examination teams, and give financial institutions greater certainty
regarding the treatment of qualifying activities. In turn, institutions would be better positioned to plan
and deploy community development resources effectively while reducing unnecessary compliance
uncertainty.
Implementation Timeline and Transition Period
Valley respectfully requests that the agencies provide a reasonable implementation period following
adoption of any final rule. Changes to CRA requirements often necessitate significant updates to
policies, procedures, data systems, reporting processes, employee training programs, vendor
relationships, governance frameworks, and strategic planning efforts. Providing adequate time for
implementation will promote more effective compliance, facilitate accurate reporting, and ultimately
enable institutions to focus resources on delivering meaningful community benefits rather than
operational adjustments.
Conclusion
As the agencies finalize the CRA framework, Valley encourages close attention to how the final rule will
affect the communities CRA is intended to benefit. Certain provisions in the NPR, if applied too rigidly, could
unintentionally reduce the flow of credit, investments, grants, services, and nonprofit support to LMI
individuals, small businesses, affordable housing providers, and underserved communities. A durable CRA
framework should promote accountability while preserving the flexibility banks need to respond to real
community needs and deliver measurable local impact.
Valley remains committed to supporting the nonprofit partners, local organizations, borrowers, and
neighborhoods that drive community development outcomes. The final rule should strengthen, not
constrain, the ability of banks to work alongside these organizations to expand opportunities, promote
economic stability, and meet the evolving needs of the communities they serve.
At the same time, we encourage the agencies to ensure that CRA evaluations remain focused on actual
community outcomes rather than proxy measurements, avoid creating unintended incentives, and
recognize the realities of modern banking and community development activity. Specifically, we
recommend that the agencies:
•
Maintain the current primary- purpose standard for qualification of CRA-eligible grants rather than
imposing a strict indirect-cost limit and preserving high-impact nonprofits that strengthen
development capacity.
•
Retain CRA consideration for deposit products, digital services, alternative delivery systems, and
innovative delivery models that expand financial inclusion and provide meaningful pathways to
responsible credit.
•
Modernize branch distribution analysis by evaluating physical locations alongside demonstrated
customer access, alternative delivery systems, credit-related services, customer behavior, and
relevant performance context.
•
Use average quarterly Tier 1 capital over the full examination period to establish stable and
appropriately aligned community development performance expectations.
•
Adopt Option 2's qualitative framework for geographic flexibility, evaluated over the full examination
period with appropriate consideration of responsiveness, market opportunities, project timing, and
 9
other performance-context factors.
•
Implement Option 1's institution-level approach for identifying major retail product lines, while
providing separate consideration for consumer products that are responsive to the needs of LMI
individuals and communities, represent a substantial majority of the institution's retail lending
activity, or are elected to be evaluated by the bank.
•
Recognize community development loan and line renewals, extensions, and ongoing credit
commitments, as these activities support ongoing community needs and reflect a sustained
commitment of capital to communities.
•
Promote interagency alignment through clear, consistent, and administrable CRA standards,
definitions, examination methodologies, and implementation expectations. Retain and update the
Interagency Q&As as needed, issue supervisory guidance concurrently with any final rule, and
provide a reasonable implementation period.
Valley remains committed to serving the credit and community development needs of the communities in
which we operate and appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments. We believe a clear,
consistent, and impact-oriented CRA framework can support strong bank performance, effective regulatory
oversight, sustainable nonprofit partnerships, and meaningful outcomes for the communities CRA is
intended to benefit. We look forward to continued engagement with the agencies as the rulemaking process
moves forward.
Thank you again for the opportunity to comment on this important proposed regulatory change.
Sincerely,

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
The Low Income Housing Institute is a nonprofit affordable housing organization based in Seattle that
serves a six county region in Washington State. We are one of the largest housing nonprofits in the state.
We rely heavily on the Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) program, tax exempt bonds,
community development loans, CDLF resources, charitable donations, and equity equivalent investments
from financial institutions to finance and develop low-income housing for families and individuals at/or
below 50% and 80% of the Area Median Income.
We are submitting this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above
(CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we request that the OCC
and FDIC extend the current comment deadline by 60-days before making any proposed changes. We are
most concerned with the likely impacts and consequences for low- and moderate-income communities.
We believe the CRA changes would drastically affect bank investments in LIHTC projects and the current
pace of addressing the nation's housing affordability crisis will be curtailed.
CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of
their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized
that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain
especially important in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss, and
unequal access to mainstream financial services.


The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how
regulators evaluate community development, bank services, and support for nonprofit organizations. We
are concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects
on low- and moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic
discrimination and disinvestment.
The Low Income Housing Institute focuses on lifting up communities that directly experience the impact
of these hardships. We own and operate over 3,700 units of affordable housing, with the overwhelming
majority financed through the LIHTC program. Due to the high rate of homelessness in our region, we
provide emergency housing and tiny house villages to shelter vulnerable families and individuals from the
elements. In 2025 we sheltered 1,663 adults and children in tiny houses. Given the housing and homeless
crisis, we need stronger reinvestment from financial institutions, not less!
REDUCTION IN COMMUNITY INVESTMENT EXPECTATIONS
Currently, CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their communities. In Washington State—where
LIHI operates—from 2010-2024, banks made $100,862,714,000 in CRA qualified mortgage lending to
LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and $25,369,880,000 in CRA qualified lending to small
businesses.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our communities.
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination cannot
withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans.
SUPPORT FOR LOCAL ORGANIZATIONS
We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit
organizations.
Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling, workforce
programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through grants, investments,
loans, and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These resources can be particularly important to
local organizations that have deep relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their
communities.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can play in
supporting community development. We receive favorable rates on construction loans, term debt and
equity equivalent investments. Banks have financed our projects for first-time low-income homebuyers.
We have benefited from investments in New Market Tax credits. Charitable donations have helped our
residents with supportive services, financial literacy, and skills building.

focus on meeting local credit needs. We support a clearer lending-focused and proportionate
framework that recognizes differences in bank size, business model, and market.

suburban communities and may be the only nearby source of credit and in-person financial

community development activities. These measures would improve predictability and
reduce inconsistencies among examiners and across charter types.
•
Allow practical assessment area flexibility. Keep assessment areas grounded in
physical presence, replace the ambiguous "substantial portion" standard with an objective

boundaries. Maine's geography and travel patterns do not conform to rigid boundaries.
