Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Appalachian Community Capital (ACC) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed
amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.
ACC is a regional CDFI intermediary and membership organization representing 46 community
development financial institutions serving communities across Appalachia. The Appalachian region spans
13 states and 423 counties, of which 103 are classified as persistent poverty counties. Our members, with
$6 billion of combined assets, finance small businesses, affordable housing, community facilities, health
care, Main Street development, and other essential economic activity. They work in communities where
distance, smaller markets and transactions, persistent economic distress, and limited access to
conventional financial institutions can make capital more difficult and expensive to deliver. Our
perspective on the proposed CRA changes comes from this distinctly Appalachian experience.
In Appalachia, CRA works through a network. Banks provide loans, investments, grants, and other
financial support to local CDFIs and regional intermediaries such as ACC. Those institutions, in turn,
move capital into communities and projects that conventional financial institutions may not reach directly.
Changes that reduce incentives for banks to participate in this system therefore can have effects far
beyond an individual bank's direct lending or branch footprint.
CDFIs are part of Appalachia's financial infrastructure
The importance of community-based financial institutions in Appalachia has been documented for
decades. Research commissioned by the Appalachian Regional Commission found that mid-sized
community banks played an important role in small-business financing in rural and economically
distressed Appalachian communities and identified continued CRA effectiveness, stronger CDFIs, and
access to bank branches as important components of expanding access to capital in the region.
That research also found that CRA generated substantial community development lending and investment
in Appalachia while documenting persistent disparities in access to capital in nonmetropolitan and
distressed communities.
Those findings remain relevant because the economics of rural community finance remain challenging.
CDFIs often make smaller loans, work with borrowers requiring more intensive underwriting or technical
assistance, and finance projects in markets where scale and geography make conventional financial
delivery more difficult.

110 Peppers Ferry Road NW | Christiansburg, VA 24073 | (202) 547-5155

ACC's intermediary model is designed for this environment. ACC raises and deploys capital through
locally rooted CDFIs that understand their markets and maintain relationships with borrowers and
communities. This allows capital raised at regional and national scale to reach places where an individual
financial institution may have little or no direct presence.
Current member experience shows how important bank partnerships remain
To understand how changes to CRA could affect this system today, ACC conducted a rapid data request
among its members in October 2026. Twenty-two ACC members provided responses. Of the 20
organizations for which an impact assessment was available, 15 or 75% indicated that reduced CRA-
motivated bank support would have a significant impact on their organization or the communities they
serve.
Members reported extensive relationships with banks through loans, investments, grants, and other forms
of financial support. Importantly, responding members identified at least 50 relationships with banks in
the $1 billion to $10 billion asset range, the range that includes banks whose CRA treatment would
change under the proposed rule. Several respondents were unable to provide complete information about
the asset size of their bank partners, so this figure is conservative.
The responses also illustrate what these relationships mean on the ground. One member reported that
banks have specifically identified CRA as a reason for investing in its equity-equivalent, or EQ2, product.
Without CRA consideration, the member expects comparable capital would become more expensive and
substantially shorter-term—three to five years rather than ten to fifteen—reducing the amount and quality
of capital available for community lending.
Another reported that seven bank capital partners provide approximately $9 million in debt and equity-
equivalent capital, including $6.7 million in EQ2 investments. This capital supports small-business
lending across 26 western North Carolina counties, including Hurricane Helene recovery lending, as well
as technical assistance serving more than 2,000 entrepreneurs annually.
And another member reported receiving little direct support from large banks in its market yet described
the CRA-related resources it receives indirectly through ACC and other intermediaries—including low-
cost lending capital, affordable housing financing, and grants—as meaningful to its work.
That last example is particularly important. In rural Appalachia, the impact of CRA cannot be
measured solely through direct relationships between banks and the communities they ultimately
benefit. Capital often moves through networks, from banks to regional intermediaries and CDFIs, and
from those institutions to businesses, housing projects, community facilities, and borrowers.
Appalachian CDFIs are already facing substantial capital needs
ACC's broader 2026 member survey provides important context for these bank relationships. All 37
members responding to a question about near-term capital needs anticipated needing additional capital
during the next 12–14 months. Nearly one-quarter (24%) expect to need more than $10 million, and just
over half (51%) expect to need at least $5 million.

110 Peppers Ferry Road NW | Christiansburg, VA 24073 | (202) 547-5155

At the same time, 67% of the 36 respondents to a question about organizational challenges identified cost
of capital as one of their greatest current challenges.
When asked about their greatest unmet organizational needs, 69% of 36 respondents identified grant or
operating support, 64% affordable lending capital, and 50% investor development or capital raising.
Members also identified substantial opportunities to put additional capital to work. Survey respondents
reported approximately $121.5 million in anticipated need for small-business lending and working capital,
along with substantial needs for housing, commercial real estate and Main Street development,
community facilities and health care, manufacturing and business expansion, energy projects, and disaster
recovery.
CRA is not the sole source of capital needed to meet these needs, and bank relationships vary
considerably across ACC's membership. But the findings show why the potential loss or deterioration of
affordable bank capital and flexible support matters in this region.
Rural markets require a networked approach to community investment
ACC recognizes the agencies' interest in reducing regulatory burden and providing greater clarity and
predictability for financial institutions.
We urge the agencies, however, to consider the cumulative effects that changes in CRA expectations
could have on rural community finance.
In Appalachia, the significance of an investment cannot always be measured by its size. A relatively
modest operating grant can support the staff and systems needed to originate and service millions of
dollars in community loans. A long-term, low-cost investment can strengthen a CDFI's balance sheet and
allow it to leverage additional capital. An investment in a regional intermediary can ultimately reach
multiple CDFIs and communities across a large rural geography.
The relevant question is therefore broader than whether a particular bank makes a particular loan in a
particular community. It is whether CRA continues to encourage financial institutions to participate in
the financial infrastructure through which capital reaches rural and economically distressed places.
What ACC urges the agencies to preserve
As the OCC and FDIC consider changes to CRA implementation, ACC urges the agencies to preserve:
•
Meaningful incentives for banks of different sizes to provide capital to and partner with
CDFIs, including through loans, long-term and patient investments, grants, and other forms of
community development support.
•
Strong recognition of regional intermediaries and CDFI networks that aggregate and move
capital into rural markets where individual banks may have limited direct presence.
•
CRA consideration for flexible grants and operating support that build the institutional
capacity necessary for CDFIs to deploy larger amounts of lending capital effectively.

110 Peppers Ferry Road NW | Christiansburg, VA 24073 | (202) 547-5155

•
Community development expectations that recognize the economics of rural markets,
including the importance of smaller transactions and institutions whose impact may be
disproportionate to the dollar size of an individual investment.
•
Sufficient transparency and data to understand whether community development capital is
reaching rural and economically distressed communities and to identify changes in access
over time.
For decades, CRA has helped connect the resources of regulated financial institutions with the credit and
community development needs of the places they serve. In Appalachia, that connection often operates
through a network of banks, CDFIs, intermediaries, public agencies, philanthropy, and other partners.
ACC sees this system from a regional vantage point. Our experience—and the experience reported by our
members—is that this network can move capital effectively into communities that have historically had
less access to it. It is also a system in which the loss of affordable capital, patient investment, or flexible
grant support at one point can have consequences much farther downstream.
We encourage the agencies to ensure that changes to CRA preserve the incentives and flexibility
necessary for this rural community finance infrastructure to function and grow.

communities across Appalachia.

RE: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
To the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation:
On behalf of the East Central Iowa Housing Trust Fund (ECIHTF), I appreciate the
opportunity to comment on the proposed amendments to the Community Reinvestment
Act (CRA) regulations.
ECIHTF serves Benton, Iowa, Jones, and Washington Counties in eastern Iowa. Our
mission is to expand and preserve affordable housing opportunities for low- and moderate-
income households through partnerships with local governments, financial institutions,
developers, nonprofit organizations, and other community stakeholders.
We recognize the importance of reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens on financial
institutions, particularly smaller community banks. However, we are concerned that
several proposed changes could unintentionally reduce incentives for financial institutions
to support affordable housing and community development activities in rural communities.
1. Changes to Bank Asset Thresholds and Community Development Evaluations
The proposed increase in the small-bank threshold to $1 billion and the intermediate-bank
threshold to $10 billion would significantly reduce the number of financial institutions
subject to comprehensive community development evaluations and reporting
requirements.
In rural Iowa, regional and community banks are essential partners in financing housing
development, rehabilitation, and neighborhood revitalization. Many of these institutions
serve communities where development opportunities are relatively small and financial
returns may not justify conventional lending without additional incentives.
We are concerned that removing community development lending and investment
activities from separate evaluation and reporting requirements could diminish incentives
for financial institutions to participate in these projects.
We encourage the agencies to retain meaningful consideration of community development
lending, investment, and service activities across bank asset categories, with appropriately
scaled reporting requirements.
 2
2. Treatment of Community Development Grants
We are particularly concerned about proposed changes to the treatment of community
development grants, including restrictions on eligible expenditures and the proposed 15
percent overhead-cost limitation for grant recipients.
Housing trust funds and nonprofit housing organizations frequently operate with limited
administrative resources. Successfully delivering housing programs requires activities
such as financial underwriting, applicant eligibility verification, construction oversight,
regulatory compliance, reporting, and program administration.
These functions are not incidental expenses. They are essential to ensuring that financial
assistance reaches eligible households and produces sustainable housing outcomes.
A rigid overhead threshold may discourage banks from supporting smaller organizations,
particularly in rural communities where administrative costs cannot be distributed across
large numbers of projects.
We recommend that the agencies recognize reasonable and necessary program
administration costs as legitimate components of community development activities and
avoid categorical overhead limitations that fail to account for organizational size, program
complexity, and demonstrated outcomes.
3. Geographic Flexibility and Rural Investment
We recognize that geographic flexibility can help financial institutions support worthwhile
community development activities beyond their immediate assessment areas. However,
this flexibility should not weaken incentives to invest in the communities where banks
maintain deposits and conduct business.
Rural communities frequently face challenges attracting private investment because
projects are smaller, development costs are relatively high, and financing opportunities are
limited.
We encourage the agencies to establish safeguards ensuring that expanded geographic
flexibility does not divert community development resources away from rural and
underserved communities.
4. Transparency and Accountability
Publicly available CRA performance information is an important resource for local
governments, housing organizations, and community development practitioners seeking
financial partners.
Reducing reporting requirements could make it more difficult to identify institutions actively
supporting affordable housing and to assess whether community credit needs are being
met.
We encourage the agencies to preserve accessible, meaningful reporting on community
development lending, investments, and grants while pursuing reasonable measures to
simplify compliance.
 3
Recommendations
ECIHTF respectfully requests that the agencies:
1. Preserve meaningful community development evaluation standards for financial
institutions of all sizes, proportionate to their capacity.
2. Reconsider the proposed 15 percent overhead-cost limitation and recognize reasonable
program administration as an eligible community development expense.
3. Maintain strong incentives for banks to support affordable housing development,
rehabilitation, and preservation in rural communities.
4. Ensure that geographic flexibility does not reduce investment in underserved
assessment areas.
5. Retain sufficient public reporting to allow communities to evaluate bank performance
and identify potential investment partners.
The Community Reinvestment Act has long provided an important framework for
encouraging private-sector participation in meeting local housing and community
development needs. Regulatory modernization should preserve that purpose while
recognizing the unique challenges facing rural communities.
Thank you for considering these comments.
Sincerely, Deanna Robinson

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, Docket ID OCC-2026-0694, RIN 1557-AF57 (OCC), RIN 3064-AG31 (FDIC)

I am submitting this comment as an individual with about 27 years in affordable housing finance and development. I spent 13 years underwriting Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac multifamily loans, and 14 years in affordable housing development, policy advocacy, and resident services, most of it across the Southeast. The views below are my own.

I have seen what CRA does in markets like mine. In much of the Southeast, the banks that invest in Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) properties and make the construction loans are regional and community banks, not only the largest national institutions. I am concerned that parts of this proposal would weaken that incentive just as Congress has expanded the Housing Credit and is counting on private capital to deliver it.

In my experience, the largest bank investors focus their Housing Credit equity on high-growth, high-demand markets. Rural Alabama, and even midsize cities like Montgomery, compete for that capital at a disadvantage. In these places, the investor that makes a deal work is often a community or regional bank whose CRA assessment area includes that community and that needs community development credit there. That local CRA need is often the difference between a deal closing or not. The proposal would end community development evaluation entirely for banks under $1 billion and let banks up to $10 billion earn Satisfactory on lending alone, removing the incentive from exactly the banks that serve these markets. The Alabama Housing Finance Authority recently shared the story of Betty, a senior who moved from rural Wilcox County, where she drove up to two hours each way to see her doctors, to Magnolia Trace, a new affordable community here in Montgomery a few miles from her care. Housing Credits generated $14.2 million in equity for that property. Homes like hers, in markets like mine, depend on banks with a local reason to invest. I urge the agencies to keep the current asset size thresholds, keep the requirement that intermediate banks receive at least Satisfactory on both the lending and CD tests, and reject the $10 billion and $30 billion thresholds.

Banks provide roughly 80 percent of Housing Credit equity, and the track record is exceptional. IRS data show the recapture rate averaged 0.08 percent from 2008 to 2021, and annual Housing Credit foreclosure rates stayed below 0.1 percent even through the Great Recession. Encouraging banks to keep making these investments fits squarely within the statute’s direction to meet community credit needs consistent with safe and sound operation.

On the proposed 15 percent indirect cost cap for grants, I agree that grants should reach communities. But in resident services, the service is a person: a coordinator who helps an older resident stay housed, connects a family to food or job resources, or works with management to prevent an eviction. Supervision, outcome tracking, compliance, and insurance are what make that work effective and accountable. A hard 15 percent cap would steer banks away from smaller, local groups, especially in rural areas. The agencies should clarify that program staff and the supervision and data systems needed to deliver and measure services count as direct costs, accept a recipient’s federally negotiated indirect cost rate where one exists, and keep documentation simple for smaller grants.

I support codifying that naturally occurring affordable housing can qualify when rents are affordable to low- and moderate-income households, and a definition of complexity that recognizes multicomponent financing, which describes most affordable housing transactions. A clear process for confirming eligibility in advance would also help.

Thank you for considering these comments. CRA has financed a large share of the affordable housing in communities like mine. I ask the agencies to preserve the incentives that make that possible.

Patti Adams
Montgomery MSA, Alabama

Dear Comptroller Gould:
The Beekman Corridor Coalition is a group of 5 working-class and low-income neighborhoods in Cincinnati
Ohio. We are submitting this comment in strong opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced
above issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In
addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC,
before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income
communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting
any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.
The five neighborhoods in our Coalition have benefitted greatly from the active enforcement of the Community
Reinvestment Act. Thanks to the CRA, one of our neighborhoods, South Cumminsville, has a 52% home
ownership, compared to Cincinnati's 36% homeownership rate overall. We have also benefitted from banks
investing in home repair and home ownership education programs in our communities. Through these efforts,
we have been able to help our senior citizens remain in their homes, and we have been able to help our young
people purchase their first homes.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks
meet the credit needs of their entire communities, particularly the needs of low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods. Congress recognized that communities depend on equal access to fair and non-predatory credit
and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that have experienced
 redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial services. The proposed rule
would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks. We are concerned that these changes are being
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and
on communities that have historically experienced discrimination and disinvestment.
The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. In Ohio, eighteen banks representing 20.9% of all banks operating in the
state would lose community development obligations and would no longer have to invest in
critical local projects. Moreover, 43.2% of large-banks operating in Ohio would no longer be
considered large-banks under these new regulations. These large-banks would no longer be
required to maintain branches in low-moderate income neighborhoods, volunteer with local
nonprofits, or report small business lending data each year. These reclassifications and resulting
eliminations of community development obligations jeopardize access to key resources that
organizations like ours depend on, particularly when it comes to serving communities that have
experienced historic and persistent disinvestment.
Moreover, these reduced regulations would permit the closure of 176 branches serving LMI
communities in Ohio, representing a loss of over 25% of all LMI branches in the state.
Communities of color are similarly at risk with the proposed regulations jeopardizing nearly 10%
of bank branches located in their communities. These branches serve as a critical resource in
underserved communities, and their loss would be extremely consequential. Ohio already lags
behind the national average of branches in these communities, and the proposed rule would
further exacerbate this issue.
From 2010-2024, banks issued $29,547,297,000 in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI
borrowers and borrowers in LMI census tracts in the Cincinnati MSA. These considerable
investments are essential to correcting the historic disinvestment these communities experienced
and would not have occurred without the CRA as it stands today. Under the current rule, large
banks are generally evaluated on their home mortgage, small business and small farm lending.
The new proposal outlines two options for regulators to focus on products designated as a bank's
"major product lines." Either option would allow weak performance in a lower volume product
to escape meaningful scrutiny even when that lending is important locally. For example, in the
Beekman Corridor, we are trying to attract younger families to purchase homes in the area. If
home mortgages programs for first-time home buyers is not a major part of a bank's business,
regulators will not evaluate whether the bank is meeting this crucial community need. Absent
such evaluation, the bank will likely deprioritize making these loans.
Under the current regulations, infrastructure projects in an LMI area receive CRA credit only
when they help keep or attract residents or businesses. The proposal allows credit for
infrastructure that "benefits or serves" a targeted area, even when the project delivers few
meaningful benefits to LMI residents and does not preserve or strengthen the community. This
means that a bank could seek CRA credit for a large regional infrastructure project that only
incidentally serves an LMI neighborhood, even if the project's benefits primarily flow to wealthy
communities or private companies. For example, a data center located in or connected to an LMI
 community could qualify despite providing little direct benefit to residents.
We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other communitybased
services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
These resources are incredibly important to local organizations that have deep relationships with
residents and understand the specific needs of their communities. We have seen firsthand the role
that bank grants, investments and partnerships can play in supporting community development.
Under the current CRA regulations, banks have provided funding for the development of several
single-family homes that were sold to first-time home owners. Banks have also sponsored
Individual Development Accounts to help senior citizens finance needed home repairs. Both of
these programs have benefitted the Beekman Corridor greatly.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed
documentation requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or redirect bank
support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with limited administrative
capacity. The agencies must also determine whether those effects would ultimately reduce
resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.
More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of reducing
perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine what the changes
mean for the communities that the CRA is intended to serve. Given their failure to do so and the
concerns described above, my organization believes that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this
proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public
comment. This proposal needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRArelated
activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not
have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. We therefore request that the
agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.
Sincerely,
The Beekman Corridor Coaltion
Cc: The National Community Reinvestment Coalition

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-
AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]

Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould,

The National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) and the organizations signed
on to this letter insist that the OCC and FDIC rescind the proposed changes to the regulations
that implement the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The proposed rule would substantially
alter how the OCC and FDIC evaluate community development, bank services, and support for
nonprofit organizations. These changes will dramatically reduce both the quantity and quality of
CRA-related community development and philanthropy to the detriment of community
development practitioners, low-and-moderate-income (LMI) communities, small businesses,
small farms, as well as banks. We are also very concerned these changes are being considered
without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on LMI communities and on communities that
have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment such as communities of color and
Native Lands.
NCRC is a network of more than 700 community-based organizations dedicated to
creating a nation that not only promises but delivers opportunities for all Americans to build
wealth and attain a high quality of life. We work with community leaders and policymakers to
advance solutions and build the will to solve America's persistent racial and socio-economic
wealth, income, and opportunity divides, and to make a Just Economy a national priority and a
local reality.
The CRA is key to the nation's economic well-being. Congress passed the CRA in
response to redlining to ensure that all communities have opportunities to build wealth.
Redlining occurs when communities of color and low-income neighborhoods are intentionally
cut off from lending and investment. One of the main goals of the CRA is to prevent redlining by

2

regularly evaluating banks on the level and quality of their loans, investments, and services to
borrowers and communities with LMI. The accountability the CRA creates has been successful
at ensuring borrowers and neighborhoods with LMI have access to homeownership and
entrepreneurship, with nearly $5 trillion in CRA-qualifying mortgages and small business loans
made since 2010.1 The CRA also benefits renters, with the CRA often referred to as the primary
motivator of bank investment in Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC), with banks
accounting for 85% of LIHTC investment dollars.2
In order for the CRA to remain an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks meet
community credit needs, the OCC and FDIC (the agencies) must not finalize regulations that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that changes are consistent
with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including LMI
neighborhoods. As discussed in more detail, NCRC and the organizations signed on to this letter
believe that this proposal would significantly scale back CRA coverage, drastically reduce
regulatory expectations of CRA activity, and weaken the CRA's mechanisms for holding banks
accountable for serving the needs of the entire communities they operate in. To summarize,
NCRC and the organizations signed on to this letter oppose the OCC and FDIC's proposed
changes to the CRA regulations because they would:
● Raise asset thresholds to significantly roll back CRA requirements;
● Decrease the quantity and quality of community development financing from banks of all
sizes;
● Decrease the importance of public participation, and the OCC's strategic plan guidance
proposed last year also threatens to significantly reduce community development
financing;
● Define major product lines to roll back how lending performance is evaluated for all large
banks;
● Fail to provide enough of an incentive to address heightened needs of Native Lands;
● Remove deposit products from CRA performance evaluations despite being a critical part
of serving credit needs;
● Impose new grant restrictions that will impair collaboration and partnerships between
banks and nonprofits;
● Use this rulemaking and parallel litigation to foreclose future CRA modernization;
● Improperly treat physical deposit-taking facilities as the outer boundary of a bank's
"entire community"; and
● Reduce consideration of discriminatory and illegal credit practices.

Raised asset thresholds significantly roll back CRA requirements
Summary: The OCC and FDIC offer several proposals to significantly increase the asset
thresholds that determine how most banks are analyzed for CRA compliance. Raising the small
bank asset threshold by 142% from $412 million to $1 billion, as well as increasing the large
bank threshold by over 500% from $1.649 billion to $10 billion, is a significant rollback of long
established CRA performance factors. The agencies misleadingly claim that their proposed asset
thresholds realign the distribution of large and small banks with the percentage of banks that fell
into these categories when the current framework for evaluating a bank's CRA performance was
finalized in 1995. The agencies also fail to analyze the impact a reduction in community
development, services, and small business lending data could have nationally, as well as in
states with larger numbers of reclassified banks. NCRC and the organizations signed on to this
letter implore the agencies to reconsider this proposal and leave the CRA's asset thresholds
intact in order to prevent a significant loss of community development loans and investments, a
reduction in bank branches in LMI census tracts and tracts that are majority people of color,
and diminished transparency in small business lending.

Beyond raised asset thresholds, the proposed rule would also substantially decrease the
quantity and quality of community development financing from banks of all sizes
Summary: The OCC and FDIC propose eliminating community development requirements and
drastically reducing expectations of how much community development loans and investments a
bank should aim for to receive a passing rating. In addition, changes to how economic
development, revitalization and stabilization, and affordable housing are considered will
diminish the impact and benefits of CRA-eligible community development.

As already discussed, community development has always been a significant component
of the agencies' evaluations of the extent to which banks serve the credit needs of entire
communities. However, the OCC and FDIC's proposal explicitly and implicitly minimizes
regulatory expectations of community development performance. This comment has already
covered at length how NCRC opposes the proposal to raise asset thresholds which would
dramatically scale back the number of banks with any community development requirements,
and allow more banks to have a simplified community development test.
In addition to raised asset thresholds, the OCC and FDIC have also proposed to remove
the requirement that intermediate banks pass both their community development test and their
lending test in order to receive an overall passing CRA rating.32 There is no support for the OCC
and FDIC's claim that this will lead to banks performing better on both tests without the
"artificial constraint" of having to pass both.33 It is counterintuitive at best, if not just plain naïve,
to expect intermediate banks to increase their community development even though they no
longer have to prove satisfactory community development performance; and a de-emphasis of
community development seems far more likely. NCRC and the organizations signed on to this
letter urge the OCC and FDIC to keep the requirement that intermediate banks pass both tests.

Besides these obvious changes that eliminate or modify current requirements, the
proposed rule could justify banks of all sizes sharply reducing their community development
financing due to signaling from the OCC and FDIC that they will accept levels of community
development financing far below current levels.
One of the ways the proposal would do this is through the geographic flexibility standard
suggested for determining when banks may receive credit for community development outside of
their branch networks. Current guidance states banks may receive favorable consideration for
community development activities that benefit broader statewide or regional areas that include

were determined. NCRC and the organizations signed on to this letter demand that the OCC and

NCRC would support an alternative method for determining how banks can get
community development credit outside of branch networks. As mentioned earlier, NCRC has
heard that a lack of clarity around when banks can get credit outside of their assessment areas is
often a hurdle for community development practitioners serving Native and rural communities
that have less bank branches.
NCRC proposes a three part proposal for considering community development outside of
assessment areas:
First, NCRC would favor allowing all large and intermediate banks to do 25% of their
community development loans outside their assessment areas, as well as 25% of qualified
investments and CRA-eligible grants, as long as banks do not decrease their previous average
level of community development loans or investments in their assessment areas observed during
their last evaluation period. Banks that decrease their average levels of community development
financing would be eligible for ratings downgrades in the relevant assessment areas or states

16

after considering performance context and the impact and responsiveness of the remaining
community development loans, investments, or services.41
Second, banks that do more than 25% of their retail loans outside of their assessment
areas, as well as wholesale banks that are not retail lenders, would be eligible to do more than
25% of their community development outside of branch networks provided they also did not
decrease community development within their assessment areas.
Third, all banks would also be eligible to do 50% of their community development
outside of assessment areas, provided they maintain average levels inside their assessment areas,
as long as at least 50% of their outside community development was in high need areas. High
need areas would include communities with less bank branches, which are markets less likely to
be included in bank assessment areas. Specific types of high need areas would include rural
counties, Native lands, persistent poverty counties, and census tracts with poverty rates of 40%
or more.
For example, a bank that averaged $1 billion a year in community development loans
inside its assessment areas during its last CRA evaluation period would be eligible for as much
as $333 million per year in community development loans outside its assessment area as long as
it maintained its average of $1 billion a year inside in its assessment areas. The same bank would
also be eligible for as much as $1 billion per year on average outside its assessment areas, as
long as at least $500 million per year was in high need areas and the bank maintained $1 billion
per year within its assessment areas.

This would increase transparency for when banks are eligible for community
development outside of their branch networks since banks are able to track how much of their
community development is inside or outside assessment areas, as well as their historical levels of
community development inside assessment areas. This also avoids any unintended consequences
of setting a benchmark that banks above that threshold could use to justify reducing their
community development since this approach uses previous performance levels as institution
specific baselines. Finally, our proposal provides more flexibility for banks that do more
business outside of their branch networks, as well as greater flexibility to serve high need areas.

The proposed rule would also reduce the quality and impact of CRA eligible community
development. The OCC and FDIC have proposed to expand the definition of economic
development by eliminating the "purpose test" that requires loans or investments to create jobs
for workers with LMI, or in LMI communities, to qualify. The proposal focuses on businesses,
not communities. Financing could qualify as economic development based primarily on the size
of the business and whether the financing expands, improves, or preserves the business's
productive capacity, physical presence, or employment base.42 NCRC is concerned this change
weakens the connection between economic development and the people and communities the
CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying business expand does not
necessarily create jobs or address the needs of LMI communities.
The OCC and FDIC justify eliminating the purpose test in part on their conclusion that
the current standard is subjective and does not adequately account for job quality.43 Those
concerns may justify improving the existing standard, but they do not support eliminating the
connection between economic development credit and demonstrated benefits for workers or
communities. Under the proposal, the OCC and FDIC would assume financing that expands or
strengthens a qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the
bank to demonstrate that those benefits reach workers or LMI neighborhoods. The OCC and
FDIC attempt to maintain some of the employment considerations by including "employment
bases" as one option for what the financing must benefit, as well as adding that financing must
be "not reasonably likely to result in a reduction in jobs at the business or farm."44 However,
financing would now qualify regardless of whether it benefits "employment bases" as long as it
enhances or preserves either a business's productive capacity or physical location. Furthermore,
the OCC and FDIC offer that "financing for the purpose of purchasing technology that would
replace employee functions without simultaneously resulting in hiring new employees" would
not qualify. However, it appears that such financing would qualify if new employees were hired,
even if new employees were paid less and received fewer benefits. Finally, the OCC and FDIC
appear to minimize the effect of this change by inaccurately claiming that eliminating the
purpose test is "consistent with the language in the current rules (which do not expressly
reference the purpose test in the Interagency Questions and Answers)," when the Interagency
Questions and Answers explicitly discuss the purpose test as a requirement for qualifying as
economic development.45

Both proposed options for defining major product lines roll back how lending performance
is evaluated for all large banks
Summary: The agencies are proposing to only review a bank's largest two product lines, or to
review different product lines in particular assessment areas determined by factors such as a
bank's business strategy and capacity. Both approaches result in less lending being evaluated
for how well it reaches borrowers with LMI, LMI census tracts, small businesses, and small
farms. The OCC and FDIC have offered very little analysis of the effects of minimizing lending
reviews, in particular the effect that only analyzing a bank's largest two product lines could have
on small farm lending. A better approach would be to maintain the current practice of evaluating
a large bank's mortgage, small business, and small farm lending across their assessment areas
based on demographics of the assessment area and performance of other lenders. The OCC and
FDIC's proposed definition of lending done on an incidental basis could also be applied to
defining major product lines. This approach is preferred over the major product line options
offered by the OCC and FDIC since it would avoid the potential for disincentivizing loans and
reducing transparency of how banks will be evaluated locally.

Under the current rules, a large bank's lending test includes an evaluation of three types
of retail loans: mortgage, small business, and small farm – as well as consumer lending if it
makes up a majority of a bank's overall lending or a bank opts for consumer lending to be

25

included.63 The OCC and FDIC are proposing two options for defining a bank's "major product
lines," with the goal of minimizing both the type and amount of lending reviewed for CRA
performance.64 Neither should be adopted.
The first option would define a bank's largest two categories of loans as their major product
lines. For example, a bank would no longer be evaluated for small farm lending if mortgage and
small business lending were their largest categories of loans. The two largest loan categories
would be calculated based on total lending, not in reference to a specific assessment area. The
second option would define major product lines at the assessment area level and allow for
different types of lending to be reviewed in different assessment areas, such as small farm
lending in rural assessment areas and small business lending in urban ones. Neither option would

The proposal improperly treats physical deposit-taking facilities as the outer boundary of a
bank's "entire community"
Summary: Congress intended for the CRA to review a bank's record of serving credit needs of
their "entire communities," not just the credit needs of those that live close to a bank's branches.
The OCC and FDIC want to limit the CRA's ability to review retail lending outside of branch
networks, while also allowing institutions to get credit for community development financing
conducted outside of branch networks. The OCC and FDIC must explain why the CRA's analysis
of retail lending cannot be updated to account for modern banking practices.
The proposed rule rests on an unduly narrow interpretation of the CRA's geographic scope.
The OCC and FDIC should not adopt a rule that categorically excludes substantial banking
markets from a CRA evaluation simply because a bank does not maintain a physical deposit-
taking facility there.
The CRA does not use the regulatory term "assessment area" in defining the geographic
scope of an institution's CRA obligation. Instead, Congress directed the agencies to assess each
institution's record of meeting the credit needs of its "entire community, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods."98 Congress also found that the "convenience and needs of
communities include the need for credit services as well as deposit services."99 Although CRA
expressly refers to branches and deposit facilities in several provisions, it does not expressly state
that the absence of a branch or other deposit-taking facility excludes a local community from an
institution's "entire community."100 Moreover, although CRA uses branch locations to determine
how certain geographic evaluations are presented, it does not state that branch locations define
the exclusive outer boundary of a bank's "entire community."101
The distinction regarding the entire community matters increasingly as banks conduct
material portions of their business outside their physical branch networks. A bank can
systematically solicit borrowers in a local market, originate substantial amounts of credit there,
develop longstanding customer relationships there, and earn substantial revenue from those
customers without establishing a traditional branch. Banks may also accept deposits from those
customers through digital channels. Under the approach reflected in the proposal, however, the
absence of a physical deposit-taking facility can prevent that market from receiving meaningful
place-specific CRA scrutiny regardless of the scale or duration of the bank's activity there.

qualify. A nationally operating institution can conduct substantial banking business in multiple
identifiable local communities. At minimum, where an institution has established a substantial,
sustained, and geographically concentrated retail banking presence in a local market, the
agencies should not treat the absence of a physical deposit-taking facility as dispositive of
whether that market forms part of the institution's "entire community." Such a presence could be
identified through objective measures such as lending volume, market share, customer
relationships, deposits, or the duration and concentration of the institution's activity in the
market.
The proposal's treatment of geography also points in only one direction. When CRA is being
used to hold a bank accountable for its retail lending, the proposal treats the bank's physical
footprint as defining the communities in which that lending is evaluated. But when a bank seeks
CRA consideration for beneficial community development activity, the proposal permits
qualifying activity outside those assessment areas to count once the bank satisfies specified
conditions within them.102 The proposal makes it clear that communities beyond a bank's
branch-based assessment areas can matter when their inclusion improves the bank's CRA
performance, while substantial retail lending in those same communities may remain outside
place-specific CRA scrutiny. The OCC and FDIC should explain why geography may be flexible
for purposes of awarding CRA consideration for community development lending and investing,
but rigid when determining where a bank's lending record is evaluated.
This question is not resolved merely by pointing to the agencies' longstanding use of facility-
based assessment areas. Assessment areas are a regulatory mechanism for implementing CRA,
not a term enacted by Congress. Historical practice may inform interpretation of the statute, but
it does not eliminate the agencies' obligation to determine whether their current regulations give
effect to the statutory requirement to evaluate an institution's entire community in a banking
system that has changed substantially since the existing framework was adopted.
Consider two banks operating in the same metropolitan area. Bank A maintains one branch
there and makes $200 million in loans annually; Bank B has no branch but makes $1 billion in
loans annually and has served thousands of customers there for several years. Under a
framework in which the physical facility controls CRA geography, Bank A's local lending would

102 Federal Register / Vol. 91, No. 154 / Wednesday, August 12, 2026 / Proposed Rules. Page 52119.
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-12/pdf/2026-16454.pdf

37

receive place-specific CRA scrutiny while Bank B's much larger and more sustained lending
presence might not. The OCC and FDIC should explain why that distinction follows from CRA's
text.
The OCC and FDIC should address the statutory basis for treating physical facilities as
controlling. In particular, they should explain how that interpretation gives effect to Congress'
use of "entire community;" how it accounts for Congress's separate recognition of credit and
deposit services; why substantial, sustained banking activity outside a branch footprint may be
excluded from place-specific retail lending evaluation even when community-development
activity outside those same assessment areas may receive CRA consideration; and whether
reasonable alternatives could recognize significant non-branch local markets suitable for a
review of an institution's retail lending performance to ensure banks are serving credit needs of
LMI borrowers in every community in which they conduct business.
The OCC and FDIC should preserve meaningful consideration of discriminatory and
illegal credit practices
Summary: Under current CRA practice, examiners may consider discriminatory or other
illegal credit practices identified through the supervisory process, including violations cited in
examination reports, when determining whether a bank's CRA rating should be adversely
affected. The current framework therefore does not require a separate public enforcement action
before illegal conduct can matter for CRA purposes. The proposal's Option 1 would change that
by limiting consideration to violations reflected in a public federal or state enforcement action or
qualifying judicial order. As a result, a serious violation identified by examiners but resolved
through nonpublic supervision could no longer affect the bank's CRA rating under Option 1. The
proposal is also concerning in light of recent changes to fair-lending enforcement. Because
ECOA's applicant-based framework has been narrowed for certain pre-application conduct,
importing similar "applicant" language into CRA treatment of Fair Housing Act violations
could make it harder for traditional redlining conduct to affect a bank's CRA rating. NCRC and
the organizations signed on to this letter urge the OCC and FDIC to reject Option 1, and to
maintain the current regulatory language directing the agencies to consider the "nature, extent,
and strength of the evidence of the practices'' when considering a bank's CRA rating.
The OCC and FDIC have proposed two options for changing the consideration of
discriminatory or other illegal credit practices on a bank's CRA ratings.103 Option 1 would
improperly make CRA consequences depend not only on whether discriminatory or illegal
conduct occurred, but also on whether an agency chose to pursue a public enforcement action.

103 Id. at Page 52151.

38

Enforcement decisions may reflect resource constraints, supervisory strategy, settlement posture,
or other considerations unrelated to the seriousness of the underlying conduct. CRA examiners
should not be required to disregard a substantiated violation simply because the matter was
resolved through supervision rather than a public case.
Option 2 would continue to allow consideration of violations cited in examination reports,
enforcement actions, or qualifying judicial orders. However, even Option 2 would weaken the
current framework by eliminating the explicit requirement that examiners consider the "nature,
extent, and strength of the evidence" of the illegal practices.
The proposal is especially troubling in light of recent changes to fair-lending enforcement.
ECOA prohibits discrimination against an "applicant," and the CFPB recently narrowed
Regulation B's protections for prospective applicants by substantially limiting when pre-
application conduct constitutes unlawful discouragement.104 The Fair Housing Act is broader and
has long provided an independent basis for traditional redlining cases, including where
discrimination occurs before a consumer applies for credit. Against that backdrop, proposed
§__.28(c)(1)'s reference to "discrimination against applicants" under either ECOA or the Fair
Housing Act risks importing Regulation B's narrower applicant-based framework into the CRA
treatment of FHA violations. If that interpretation is combined with Option 1's requirement that
a violation be cited in a public federal or state enforcement action before it can affect a CRA
rating, traditional redlining conduct could be excluded from consideration even though it remains
prohibited by the Fair Housing Act.
The OCC and FDIC reason that discrimination can be captured through consideration of "any
other relevant information." But that is an inadequate substitute for an explicit factor directing
examiners to evaluate the seriousness, breadth, and evidentiary basis of the conduct. A narrowly
confined or weakly supported violation should not necessarily have the same CRA consequence
as a widespread, well-substantiated pattern of discrimination affecting large numbers of
borrowers or communities. Retaining the existing factor would also promote more disciplined
and transparent CRA evaluations. It gives examiners a clear framework for distinguishing among
violations and determining when conduct is serious enough to warrant a ratings consequence.
NCRC and the organizations signed on to this letter therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to
reject Option 1, and preserve explicit consideration of the nature, extent, and strength of the
evidence in Option 2 when determining how discriminatory or other illegal credit practices affect
a bank's CRA rating.

104 Equal Credit Opportunity Act (Regulation B), 91 Fed. Reg. 21620, 21644–46 (Apr. 22, 2026)

Other Recommendations
● The OCC and FDIC should not remove language from the rating factors that require
specific consideration of serving credit needs of highly disadvantaged areas and people
with low incomes.105 The OCC and FDIC propose to eliminate this text because "highly
disadvantaged areas is not a defined term and the agencies believe this factor is already
considered in factors related to borrower and geographic characteristics."106 It is
inconsistent of the OCC and FDIC to remove highly disadvantaged areas because it lacks
a definition, while a similar lack of a definition of high-cost areas has not prevented the
OCC from developing a method the agency already uses to determine where banks will
receive credit for financing housing that benefits individuals with middle incomes.107 Just
as the OCC was able to come up with an approach for identifying high-cost areas, a
technique for identifying highly disadvantaged areas can also be developed and should be
proposed for public feedback. NCRC recommends the agencies conduct periodic
statistical studies to identify metropolitan areas and rural counties that exhibit significant
disparities in access to credit. One method would be to identify underserved census tracts
that receive the lowest amount of loans per housing units and number of small
businesses, and to then factor into performance ratings an institution's level of lending,
community development, and services in these tracts. Finally, NCRC disagrees that
highly disadvantaged and low income is already covered by referring to "individuals of
different income levels." Since CRA's purpose has been to rectify redlining and increase
lending in neglected neighborhoods, it is appropriate for CRA ratings to more explicitly
reflect how a bank serves highly disadvantaged areas that currently benefit the least from
our banking system, as well as people with low incomes that have heightened economic
vulnerabilities.

have proven to be quite beneficial for local communities, borrowers, and businesses.
These programs have helped strengthen the mortgage banking sector, expanding
opportunities for consumers, and increasing the breadth of mortgage products lenders can
offer to people. From 2022-2024, special purpose credit programs backed by Fannie Mae
and Freddie Mac helped nearly 58,000 economically disadvantaged persons fairly access

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
The Council for Affordable and Rural Housing ("CARH") appreciates the opportunity to comment on the
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (the "NPR") issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
("OCC") and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (together, the "Agencies") regarding
the Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA").
CARH represents for-profit and nonprofit companies providing affordable rural rental housing throughout
America. For more than 30 years, CARH has served as the nation's premier association for participants
in the affordable rural housing profession, including owners, developers, managers, syndicators, lenders,
builders and companies that supply goods and services to the industry. CARH is the only association that
solely represents the needs of the entire rural affordable housing industry. Our members regularly obtain
loans and seek equity investments from financial institutions regulated under the CRA, and many of the
properties they own and manage are financed and rehabilitated by utilizing the Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit (the "Housing Credit") and the U.S. Department of Agriculture ("USDA") Rural Development
("RD") multifamily housing programs.
CARH supports the Agencies' efforts to make the CRA clearer, more consistent, and more workable for
institutions of different sizes, and we appreciate the Agencies' targeted interest in providing relief to
smaller institutions. We write, however, because several elements of the NPR, taken together, could
reduce the bank investment on which rural affordable housing depends. Our comments focus on the
proposed large bank asset threshold, the evaluation of intermediate banks, geographic flexibility, and the
definition of affordable housing.
The CRA Is Central to Rural Housing Credit Investment
The Housing Credit is the nation's primary tool for creating and preserving affordable rental housing and
has financed more than four million homes. Congress recently enacted the most significant expansion of
Council for Affordable and Rural Housing
 the Housing Credit in the program's history as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which is projected
to support more than 1.2 million additional affordable rental homes over the next decade. Through the
"21st Century ROAD to Housing Act", Congress also raised the Public Welfare Investment cap from 15
percent to 20 percent, expanding banks' capacity to invest. CRA policy should help realize the full benefit
of these reforms, not offset them.
Banks provide roughly 75 to 80 percent of Housing Credit equity, and approximately 71 percent of the
Housing Credit equity surveyed in 2025 was considered CRA-motivated. The "Separate Investment Test"
has helped create a deep, competitive, and efficient market for the Housing Credit. That market is not
equally deep everywhere. In our 2021 comments on CRA modernization, CARH members reported that
Housing Credit equity pricing in rural areas not covered by the CRA was about 10 cents per credit dollar
below non-rural areas. Others in the industry report that pricing can vary by up to 20 percent between
areas of high and low CRA demand. Lower pricing means less equity for each development, more
financially strained properties, and fewer affordable homes.
Equity investment and lending serve different functions. Housing Credit equity is a distinct part of the
financing stack and cannot simply be replaced with additional debt. This is especially true in rural
communities, where rents are typically lower than urban areas. For aging USDA Section 515 and other
rural rental properties, Housing Credit equity is frequently the only way to finance the rehabilitation
needed to responsibly preserve existing affordable units in rural communities.
The need is urgent. Most USDA-financed rural multifamily properties are more than 40 years old and in
need of modernization, and USDA's own capital needs assessment estimated that portfolio-wide
rehabilitation would cost approximately $5.6 billion. The Section 514/515 portfolio, which recently
consisted of 12,912 properties containing 406,290 units, continues to shrink every year. Over the next
decade, as many as three-quarters of all Section 515 mortgages will mature, ending the related Section
521 Rental Assistance contracts and putting more than 250,000 families and elderly residents at risk of
losing affordable housing.
After years of advocacy by CARH and other housing organizations, Congress responded by passing the
"21st Century ROAD to Housing Act" which preserved this critical subsidy by permanently authorizing
Section 521 Rental Assistance to be decoupled from Section 514/515 mortgages set to mature, through
Stand Alone Rental Assistance ("SARA") contracts, and also permanently authorized the Multifamily
Housing Preservation and Revitalization program ("MPR"). SARA contracts keep residents' rents
affordable, but they do not pay for the capital improvements these aging properties desperately need.
Owners entering SARA will depend heavily on Housing Credit equity to recapitalize and rehabilitate their
properties. Considering there is no longer adequate federal funding for new construction, preservation of
the Section 514/515 portfolio is critical, and the Housing Credit is the lifeblood of rural rehabilitation. In
the rural markets where most of these properties are located, that equity often comes from the community
and regional banks whose Investment Test obligations would be removed under the NPR. Weakening
CRA incentives for those banks would undercut the preservation tools Congress just put in place.
The alternative is stark. When owners cannot finance needed capital improvements, many will prepay or
allow their mortgages to mature and leave the program, ultimately resulting in market rate units. Residents
of those properties must then rely on Section 542 vouchers, a program that has run out of federal funding
before the end of the fiscal year for two years in a row and has not kept pace with demand. Every rural
property that can be recapitalized with Housing Credit equity and kept in the affordable portfolio avoids
that outcome.
Rural rental housing is also an economic engine. Building 100 apartment units creates an estimated 161
local jobs in the first year, about half in construction, along with $11.7 million in local income and $2.2
 million in local taxes and government revenue. Substantial rehabilitation produces comparable impacts.
CRA-motivated investment in rural preservation therefore supports local employment as well as housing.
If the Agencies Raise the Large Bank Threshold, They Should Adopt a $3.252 Billion Threshold
Under the proposed $10 billion threshold, 376 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks currently classified as
large banks would move to the intermediate bank framework and would no longer be subject to a separate
investment test. According to a survey1 of Housing Credit syndicators conducted by the Affordable
Housing Tax Credit Coalition ("AHTCC"), more than 108 banks in this group invested at least $1.6 billion
in Housing Credit equity over the five-year survey period. Extrapolated to the full market, banks under
the $10 billion threshold invested approximately $2 billion in Housing Credit equity over those five years.
These banks matter most in rural America. AHTCC survey data shows that approximately one-third of
Housing Credit equity from banks under $10 billion in assets supported rural markets. By comparison,
roughly 8 percent of all Housing Credit equity in a CohnReznick industry-wide sample2 was invested in
USDA-defined nonmetropolitan counties. In many rural markets that are not served by large national
banks, community and regional banks are often the only CRA-motivated investors available. Even modest
investments by these banks can determine whether a rural development moves forward.
The loss of these investors would also have a compounding effect. Small rural developments typically
receive equity through multi-investor funds, and commitments from community and regional banks often
complete those funds and leverage additional capital from larger investors. Because larger investors are
commonly subject to proportionate share limits, a reduction in smaller bank participation can shrink the
fund as a whole. When funds shrink, the smallest and most remote rural properties are the first to go
without capital. Community and regional banks have also become an increasingly important and growing
source of Housing Credit investment, with many entering the market in recent years and becoming repeat
investors. Removing their incentive to invest now would reverse that progress just as Congress has
expanded the program.
CARH therefore recommends that, if the Agencies raise the large bank threshold, they adopt the $3.252
billion alternative. Based on AHTCC survey data, a $3.252 billion threshold would reduce the number of
affected Housing Credit investors by approximately 63 percent, from 108 banks to 40 banks, and reduce
the estimated five-year Housing Credit equity affected from roughly $2 billion to $272 million.
Approximately 86 percent of the Housing Credit equity from OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks with assets
between $1.65 billion and $10 billion come from banks with assets above $3.252 billion. This alternative
also has a clear policy basis: it is the inflation-adjusted version of the OCC's 2020 $2.5 billion threshold,
which was calibrated to preserve the relative shares of small and intermediate small banks established in
2005.
Response to Question 1: The Agencies Should Not Adopt a $30 Billion Threshold or a $10 Billion
Small Bank Threshold
CARH strongly opposes a $30 billion large bank threshold. The more than 140 banks below the $30 billion
threshold captured in the AHTCC survey invested at least $3.575 billion in Housing Credit equity over
the five-year survey period, or potentially up to $4.5 billion when extrapolated to the full market. A

1 Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition, Survey Results and Responses to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) Proposal on the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) (Sept. 30,
2026).
2 CohnReznick, 2025 Affordable Housing Credit Study, accessed September 18, 2026,
https://creditstudy.cohnreznick.com/credit-study.

 threshold at this level would extend the loss of the Investment Test to a much larger segment of the market,
broaden the harm from rural areas to smaller cities in states not well served by major financial institutions,
and further concentrate Housing Credit investment in the largest institutions, which often have the least
presence in nonmetropolitan areas.
CARH also opposes the companion proposal in Question 1 to raise the small bank threshold to $10 billion.
Small banks are not evaluated on community development at all. If the small bank definition were raised
to banks with less than $10 billion in assets, more than 1,500 banks, or 36 percent of all banks, would no
longer be incentivized to provide community development loans or investments. In 2024, these banks
reported nearly $27 billion in community development loans, representing 35 percent of all community
development loans made that year.
That loss would fall hardest in rural America. Rural areas have a built-in credit barrier because they are
small markets with limited lending opportunities, and smaller banks are frequently the only institutions
with a local presence. CARH has consistently cautioned that changes to how smaller banks are evaluated
must not create gaps in CRA activity in rural communities where those banks predominate. Removing
community development expectations from banks of this size would create exactly that gap, just as rural
owners need financing partners to preserve maturing Section 514/515 properties.
Preserve a Meaningful Community Development Test for Intermediate Banks
Under the NPR, an intermediate bank would no longer need at least a "Satisfactory" rating on both its
lending test and its community development test to receive an overall "Satisfactory" rating. Instead,
stronger lending performance could make up for weaker community development performance. The
Agencies themselves acknowledge that this change may increase banks' relative incentive to devote CRA
resources to lending.
This concern grows considerably if hundreds of additional banks are moved into the intermediate bank
framework. If those banks lose the Separate Investment Test, the community development test will be the
only remaining CRA incentive for Housing Credit equity and other community development investment.
CARH urges the Agencies to retain the current requirement that an intermediate bank demonstrate at least
Satisfactory community development performance to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
Geographic Flexibility Should Direct Capital to Underserved Rural Markets
CARH has long supported giving banks CRA credit for qualifying activities outside their assessment
areas, and we welcome the NPR's proposal to do so. Rural communities with few bank branches are
among the clearest examples of the CRA "deserts" the Agencies have identified. In 2021, CARH
recommended that banks receive credit for Housing Credit investments in properties located in the same
state as their assessment areas, and we continue to support a clear pathway for qualifying activities
conducted on a statewide or regional basis.
To make this flexibility work in practice, CARH supports a presumption that a bank that received a
Satisfactory or Outstanding rating on its most recent CRA evaluation has adequately served its assessment
areas and may receive consideration for qualifying activities outside those areas throughout its next
examination cycle. CARH also encourages the Agencies to give priority to activities in underserved rural
areas, so that geographic flexibility results in more, not less, CRA-motivated investment in the vulnerable
rural communities that most need it and helps offset the potential loss of smaller bank investors.
 Response to Question 18: Keep Affordable Housing Credit Focused on Low- and Moderate-
Income Households
The need for affordable housing remains most acute among low- and moderate-income ("LMI")
households. CARH supports clear standards defining when housing is affordable, which helps banks
invest and lend in programs that provide critical resources to rural communities, including the Housing
Credit and RD rental housing loan and subsidy programs. We are concerned, however, that expanding
CRA credit to middle-income rental housing could shift scarce CRA-motivated capital away from LMI
households and rural communities that already struggle to attract investment. If the Agencies extend credit
to naturally occurring affordable housing, CARH recommends a meaningful standard, such as a recorded
use agreement, to ensure that properties receiving CRA credit remain affordable to LMI households rather
than converting to market-rate housing.
Additional Recommendations
CARH supports a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of CRA-eligible activities, ideally
maintained on a consistent interagency basis. Consistent with our 2021 comments, CARH recommends
that the list expressly include Housing Credit investments; loans and investments supporting properties in
the Section 514 and 515 programs, including properties preserved through the MPR program; and loans
guaranteed under the USDA Section 538 Guaranteed Rural Rental Housing program. The Section 538
program is a fee-based, revenue-neutral tool used for both new construction and preservation, and it is a
natural fit for CRA-motivated lending in rural markets. The list should make clear that it is non-exhaustive
so that activities not listed are not overlooked.
CARH further requests that the final rule confirm that loans and investments used to recapitalize and
preserve RD properties transitioning to SARA contracts, including properties whose Section 514/515
mortgages have matured or been prepaid, qualify as affordable housing activities, provided the properties
remain subject to rental assistance or recorded affordability restrictions. Express recognition would give
banks and examiners certainty as this permanent program is implemented.
CARH also supports CRA consideration for qualifying community development loans that remain
outstanding from prior evaluation periods, because rural preservation transactions often require long-term,
patient financing. Finally, CARH cautions against new restrictions and documentation requirements on
CRA-qualifying grants, which could reduce support for the small nonprofit and community-based
organizations that serve vulnerable rural communities.
Because the Federal Reserve is not participating in this proposal, banks could face different CRA
frameworks depending on their regulator. CARH encourages the Agencies to work toward a durable and
consistent interagency framework that gives long-term certainty for affordable housing investment.
Conclusion
The CRA has created tremendous opportunities for affordable housing in rural America. CARH supports
the Agencies' efforts to modernize and simplify the CRA, and we urge the Agencies to do so in a way that
preserves the incentives that bring private capital to rural communities. Specifically, if the Agencies raise
the large bank threshold, they should adopt a $3.252 billion threshold rather than $10 billion; they should
reject a $30 billion large bank threshold and a $10 billion small bank threshold; they should preserve a
meaningful community development test for intermediate banks; and they should expressly recognize the
USDA rural housing programs and SARA preservation transactions that will keep rural families housed
for decades to come.
We appreciate your time and attention to this matter.
 Sincerely,



Colleen M. Fisher
Executive Director
