To the Comptroller of the Currency and the Board of Directors of the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation:

Dear Comptroller and FDIC Leadership Officials,
I submit these comments based on our work at Business & Community Lenders of Texas (BCL), a
nonprofit Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) with 36 years of experience, and our
subsidiary, Texas Community Builders, an affordable housing development and real estate management
nonprofit. BCL is headquartered in Austin, with our North Texas office in Dallas. Our work also reaches
smaller cities and rural communities across Central Texas, South Texas, the Middle Rio Grande region,
and the I-10 corridor between San Antonio and Houston, stopping short of Katy.
Thank you for the opportunity to share how the proposed CRA changes could affect the people and
communities we serve. My comments focus on affordable housing, access to responsible financing, and
practical ways for community and regional banks to participate in this work.
Our responsibility is to help families, business owners, and communities move from preparation to
opportunity. That may mean helping a household prepare for homeownership, helping an entrepreneur
become ready for financing, or assembling the resources necessary to develop and manage affordable
housing. Each requires capital, qualified people, and partners willing to stay engaged.
CRA helps bring banks into these relationships. Yet attracting sustained bank participation in South Texas
and smaller communities remains difficult. In our experience, CRA investment is more visible in major
urban markets and financial centers such as Dallas. We spend considerable effort keeping banks engaged
in communities where transactions may be smaller, preparation takes longer, and financing options are
limited.
I ask the agencies to consider what the proposed changes would mean for those communities. A bank may
meet its examination requirements while a family, business owner, or housing development in another
community continues to struggle for financing. The regulations should help identify and address that gap.


1. Keep affordable housing central to the evaluation of community needs.
The National Low Income Housing Coalition's 2026 Texas Housing Profile reports only 26 affordable
and available rental homes for every 100 extremely low-income renter households, with a statewide
shortage of 708,661 homes. Behind that shortage are households trying to find a home they can afford
while meeting their other basic expenses.
I recommend that examinations clearly assess how a bank's community development activities respond to
documented affordable housing needs. Housing production, rehabilitation, preservation, and responsible
homeownership financing should be identifiable within the evaluation.
Examiners should consider households served, income levels reached, affordability commitments where
applicable, and the financing barriers addressed. Consideration should include qualifying subsidized
housing and naturally occurring affordable housing that serves low- and moderate-income households.
Through Texas Community Builders, affordable housing development and real estate management are
part of our work. Financing decisions must account for both creating housing and keeping it affordable
and financially sustainable over time. The examination framework should recognize contributions across
that process.
2. Recognize financing approaches that expand access.
In response to Questions 12–17, I recommend evaluating innovation and flexibility by the financing
problem an activity solves and the people it reaches.
A smaller community may need acquisition financing to secure a property before it is lost to another
buyer. A housing development may need predevelopment funds before it can qualify for construction
financing. An existing affordable property may need rehabilitation financing that can be repaid without
making rents unaffordable.
The agencies should provide clear examples covering qualifying acquisition and predevelopment
financing, preservation loan pools, loan participations, appropriately structured credit enhancements, and
flexible financing through CDFIs.
A straightforward transaction can make a substantial difference in a community with few alternatives.
Innovation should be considered in relation to a bank's capacity and local circumstances, with appropriate
underwriting and safety and soundness standards.
3. Make community and regional bank participation easier to carry out.
Community and regional banks bring local knowledge and relationships that matter to this work. They
also have staff and resource constraints. Clear rules and practical documentation would help them make
informed commitments.
I recommend facilitating bank consortia, pooled affordable housing funds, and participation arrangements
with CDFIs. These approaches can allow banks to share resources and participate at a scale consistent
with their capacity.


Each bank should receive consideration for its documented contribution. Standard templates and
appropriate shared project records could reduce repeated administrative work while preserving
responsibility for due diligence.
BCL and other CDFIs can help prepare borrowers, structure transactions, and connect banks with
opportunities in underserved communities. The regulations should recognize the value of those
partnerships and make their treatment predictable.
4. Provide eligibility answers in time for financing decisions.
The proposed process for confirming community development eligibility could be useful if it provides
timely, clear answers.
I recommend a published response timeframe, a standard request form, and written determinations that
banks can rely on when an activity is carried out as described. Anonymized examples would also help
banks and community organizations understand how the standards apply.
Housing transactions have deadlines. Uncertainty can affect whether a property is acquired, whether
financing closes, or whether a development proceeds. An eligibility process should provide answers early
enough to inform those decisions.
5. Pay attention to the communities receiving the financing.
Methodist Healthcare Ministries' 2024 Central and South Texas CDFI Landscape report identifies
funders' preference for urban areas as a disadvantage for rural-serving CDFIs. It also identifies inadequate
operating resources and higher capital costs as barriers to affordable financing. Although the report does
not quantify bank CRA investment by geography, it documents challenges relevant to the communities
BCL serves.
The need for sustained investment is clear in the Middle Rio Grande region. Census Bureau estimates for
2020–2024 show poverty rates of 41.1 percent in Dimmit County, 33.9 percent in Zavala County, and
22.8 percent in Maverick County. All three experienced poverty rates of at least 20 percent in each of four
five-year periods spanning 2005–2024.
I recommend that evaluations distinguish financing in major metropolitan centers, smaller cities, rural
communities, and underserved areas within metropolitan regions. Being located within a metropolitan
area does not mean a household or business has adequate access to financing.
For investments through regional or statewide CDFIs, the record should identify where funds are
ultimately deployed. An investment in an Austin-headquartered organization may finance housing or a
business in South Texas. The evaluation should capture the community receiving that benefit.
Meaningful data collection and public reporting are necessary to understand these patterns. Standard
formats, appropriate privacy protections, and use of existing records where feasible would help make
reporting practical.
6. Recognize the resources required to deliver affordable housing and responsible financing.


Affordable housing transactions may require loans, equity, grants, and flexible capital, each serving a
different purpose. Adding debt cannot resolve every financing gap while keeping housing affordable.
I recommend maintaining meaningful consideration for the full range of qualifying contributions,
including funding that allows nonprofit developers and CDFIs to prepare and deliver transactions.
The proposed 15 percent indirect-cost ceiling for grants from large banks raises concerns about how
organizations would maintain the capacity to do this work. Accounting, compliance, technology, and
management are necessary to administer funds responsibly. Housing counseling, borrower preparation,
and technical assistance also require qualified staff and reliable systems.
For residents, these resources can determine whether someone is available to help them understand a
mortgage, prepare a business loan application, or work through a financial obstacle. In smaller
communities, maintaining that assistance takes sustained organizational capacity.
I recommend standards that recognize reasonable, documented operating costs, with clear safeguards
against misuse and accountability for community development results.
7. Consider local consequences when changing bank classifications.
As the agencies evaluate asset thresholds, including the alternatives raised in Question 1, I recommend
retaining the current classifications and associated community development requirements while
addressing compliance costs through simpler procedures.
A bank that represents a small share of national banking assets may be one of the few financing partners
available in a Texas community. Before changing its examination requirements, the agencies should
consider the affordable housing needs, financing alternatives, and community development relationships
in the markets it serves.
Standard documentation, shared records, clearer eligibility guidance, and procedures proportionate to
institutional capacity would help community and regional banks participate without losing meaningful
attention to local needs.
8. Include access to affordable banking services in the assessment.
Preparing for homeownership and business ownership includes building savings, managing expenses, and
establishing a dependable banking relationship. Affordable deposit accounts are part of that preparation. I
recommend continuing to consider the accessibility and affordability of deposit services for low- and
moderate-income households and small businesses. This is especially relevant where residents have
limited banking choices or difficulty accessing services. For BCL, these services connect directly to the
work of helping people become ready for responsible financing and maintain financial stability afterward.
I respectfully ask the OCC and FDIC to consider these recommendations as they develop the final
regulations. BCL's experience points to the need for clear eligibility standards, practical participation by
community and regional banks, and sustained attention to affordable housing and underserved
communities.
The people we serve are working toward a stable home, a viable business, and greater financial security.
Texas. Thank you for considering these recommendations.


Sincerely,


Raquel Valdez Sanchez
President & CEO

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Consumers Council of Missouri (CCM) submits these comments regarding the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) proposed
changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.
Consumers Council of Missouri is a Missouri nonprofit organization that works collaboratively to
build a more inclusive and equitable community for Missouri low- and moderate-income households
and communities. CCM has extensive experience working on banking access, financial
empowerment, affordable credit, community investment, and consumer financial issues. CCM is a
member and leader within the St. Louis Equal Housing and Community Reinvestment Alliance
(SLEHCRA) and the St. Louis Regional Financial Empowerment Coalition (STLRFEC). CCM is
also a member of the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC).
CCM has participated in efforts to examine how banks meet their obligations under the CRA and fair
lending laws. Through our collaborative work, we have submitted public comments concerning
individual banks and worked directly with financial institutions to identify opportunities to improve
services and investment in low- and moderate-income and minority communities and worked to
brings together financial institutions, nonprofit and community organizations, government
representatives, and other stakeholders to promote financial education, affordable banking, asset
building, financial inclusion, and economic mobility
These experiences over the years have led CCM to have significant concerns about proposed changes
that could lower expectations for community development activity, reduce transparency, and make it
 more difficult for communities to determine whether financial institutions are adequately serving the
communities in which they do business.
For decades, the CRA has provided an important framework for ensuring that federally insured and
regulated financial institutions help meet the credit needs of the communities they serve, including
low- and moderate-income communities.
The need for this oversight has not disappeared. In the St. Louis region, community organizations
continue to work with banks on issues involving affordable mortgage credit, small-business
financing, access to banking services, financial inclusion, and investment in communities that have
experienced historic disinvestment.
The proposed rule should therefore be evaluated not only in terms of administrative efficiency for
financial institutions, but also in terms of what communities may lose if regulatory scrutiny and
public accountability are reduced.
1. Concern regarding reduced community investment expectations
The proposed rule would establish substantially lower benchmarks for certain community
development lending and investment activity. CCM is concerned that a benchmark intended as a
minimum could become a practical ceiling for community investment.
If banks respond to the new benchmark by reducing their community development activity toward
the proposed threshold, the amount of capital available for affordable housing, small businesses,
nonprofit organizations, and other community development activities could decline significantly.
For St. Louis communities, the potential consequences are important. Community organizations rely
on partnerships with financial institutions to help expand access to affordable financial products,
homeownership opportunities, small-business financing, and community development resources.
CCM therefore encourages the agencies to carefully analyze whether the proposed benchmarks
would reduce actual lending and investment in low- and moderate-income communities before
adopting them.
2. Concern regarding reduced CRA scrutiny of banks
CCM is also concerned about the proposed increase in the asset thresholds used to determine how
banks are evaluated under the CRA.
Reducing the amount of information available to regulators and community organizations could make
it more difficult to identify gaps in lending, services, and investment.
CCM recommends that the agencies identify which institutions would move into less rigorous
examination categories under the proposal and analyze the communities those institutions serve. The
agencies should specifically examine whether the proposed changes would reduce oversight in low-
and moderate-income communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment.
CCM's experience also demonstrates the importance of community organizations as partners in the
CRA process. As a leader in SLEHCRA, CCM has worked for many years to bring community
organizations and financial institutions together to identify community needs and develop strategies
for improving bank performance. Its work includes both accountability and partnership: community
 organizations review bank performance, raise concerns when necessary, and work with banks to
identify ways they can better serve the community.
This approach is complementary to regulatory oversight. Community organizations often have direct
relationships with residents, nonprofit organizations, small businesses, and neighborhood leaders and
therefore can identify needs that may not be apparent from financial institution data alone.
Similarly, CCM's participation in STLRFEC provides direct experience with the importance of
affordable banking products, financial education, asset building, and financial inclusion. Community
organizations provide an important link between financial institutions and unbanked and underbanked
consumers.
Any changes to the CRA regulations should preserve meaningful opportunities for these
organizations to provide information to regulators and financial institutions. Given the extent of the
proposed changes, CCM urges the OCC and FDIC to conduct and make public a careful analysis of
the likely effects of the proposal on low- and moderate-income communities. The proposed changes
would most likely lead to reduced community development in LMI communities, potential effects on
affordable housing availability, less small business financing, and potential setbacks in communities
with a history of redlining, discrimination or disinvestment are likely to experience disproportionate
effects.
In Conclusion, the Community Reinvestment Act remains an important mechanism for connecting
the banking system with the needs of the communities in which financial institutions operate. CCM's
work through SLEHCRA and STLRFEC has demonstrated the value of strong CRA oversight,
transparent information, meaningful community participation, and constructive partnerships between
financial institutions and community organizations.
CCM respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to carefully consider the potential consequences of the
proposed changes for low- and moderate-income communities and communities that have
experienced historic disinvestment. Before finalizing significant changes to the CRA regulations, the
agencies should provide additional evidence demonstrating that the proposed reductions in scrutiny,
reporting, and community development expectations will not diminish access to credit, banking
services, and community investment.
CCM also supports extending the comment period by 60 days to allow community organizations,
financial institutions, local governments, and residents sufficient time to understand and respond to
the substantial changes contained in the proposal.
Thank you for considering the experience and perspective of Consumers Council of Missouri and the
communities we serve.
Sincerely,
Ed Bryant,
Executive Director,
Consumers Council of Missouri
St. Louis, Missouri

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
We at First Step House, a community-based, 501(c)3, in Salt Lake City, Utah, are deeply
concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit
organizations.
Banks often support development of single-family and multi-family affordable housing and
deeply affordable housing for community members that struggle with serious mental and
physical health conditions and homelessness, as well as small-business development, financial
counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based
services, including substance use disorder and mental health treatment, through grants,
investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These resources can be
particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships with residents and
understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.1
For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology,
accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the
underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources
over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with
limited staff and may not maintain financial records, budgets or program documentation in the
precise format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to
1 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward
larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can
play in supporting community development. Specifically, as a community-based non-profit
organization, grants from banking institutions have been key to our ability to execute on our
mission to help people build lives of meaning, purpose and recovery. CRA grants, loans and
investments from banking institutions have enabled First Step House to:
•
Develop an internationally recognized supportive employment program that links
motivated individuals struggling with serious mental health conditions, including
substance use disorder, to employers and allows them to return to the workforce, with
meaningful work and a living wage.
•
Open four supportive housing projects targeting individuals struggling with serious
mental illness, allowing us to pull 228community members out of homelessness.
•
Embed an in-house medical clinic directly on-site at our main treatment campus,
providing accessible healthcare to over 800 people a year
•
Operate a 72-bed transitional housing facility for veterans experiencing homelessness
•
Provide case management services to over 900 community members annually,
connecting them to the support and resources needed to secure stable
housing/employment and achieve lasting self-sufficiency
Bank grants are often the first money in on our mission-driven initiatives, empowering First Step
House to use that funding as a point of leverage to secure other philanthropic grants that prefer to
be last money in.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into
tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community
development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond
the banks themselves.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed
documentation requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or redirect bank
support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with limited administrative
capacity. The agencies must also determine whether those effects would ultimately reduce
resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.
More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of reducing
perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine what the changes
mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.
Respectfully,
Shawn M. McMillen, ASUDC, MPA
Executive Director
First Step House
Salt Lake City, Utah

On behalf of Habitat for Humanity Greater San Francisco, please accept the attached comment letter in opposition to the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act Regulations.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0385_09000064b9668938.pdf:
October 13, 2026


Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street NW,
Washington, DC 20429
RIN 3064-AG31
Via email: comments@FDIC.gov

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, DC 20219
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
Via: https://regulations.gov/


Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Docket ID
OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57; RIN 3064-AG31)


Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

On behalf of Habitat for Humanity Greater San Francisco (Habitat GSF), I write in opposition
to the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed
by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to
help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities, including making the
purchase of a home possible for low and moderate income (LMI) communities. While the CRA
has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved
communities, it has a long way to go to fulfill its mission in the San Francisco Bay Area.

Since 1989, Habitat GSF has made the dream of homeownership a reality for more than 300
families in one of California's the nation's most challenging and expensive regions for
affordable home building and buying – Marin, San Francisco, and San Mateo Counties. We can
only make this possible through our partnerships with banks who volunteer their time to help
build homes alongside our team, through generous philanthropy of our bank partners, and
through securitization and sale of our mortgage notes. To state this simply, the CRA is the
investment engine that drives banks to invest in Habitat GSF and opens the door to
homeownership to LMI families in the communities we serve.

The scale of housing need across the three counties of our service area makes the stakes of
this proposal especially high. At the state level, the California Department of Housing and
Community Development (HCD) estimates in its statewide housing plan that California needs
one million more homes affordable to lower-income households who cannot afford market-


rate homes due to their historic lack of access to capital and financial services.1 Further,
homeownership in our area is often considered well out of reach due to both the increasingly
high cost to build and the cost to purchase a home where the median sale price of a single-
family home exceeds $2 million.

According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70 banks active in
California would see their CRA reinvestment obligations reduced under the proposal, with 25
banks active in California shedding their CRA community development responsibilities
entirely.2 Forty-five banks active in California would no longer be subject to the investment
test, which critically supports affordable homeownership development in part through the
purchase of mortgage-backed securities like Habitat GSF's mortgage notes.3

Accordingly, we urge you to ensure that the final rule addresses each of the concerns detailed
below.


I. Reclassification of Banks with $1.649 Billion to $10 Billion in Assets as Intermediate
Banks No Longer Subject to the Investment Test

This is the single most consequential negative change in the proposed rule for California's
affordable housing supply, and its scale is not a theoretical concern, it is a specific,
documented, and immediate shift in the market. According to the National Association of
Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL), of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks
nationally, only 256 would retain that designation under the proposal, a decline of more than
60 percent, leaving only an estimated 6 percent of all CRA-regulated banks subject to the full
CRA exam, including the standalone investment test.4 A survey by the Affordable Housing Tax
Credit Coalition (AHTCC) found that 376 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks nationally (126 OCC-
supervised and 250 FDIC-supervised) would move from the large bank framework to the
intermediate bank framework, and that more than 108 of those banks are currently active
Housing Credit investors, having invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over a
five-year survey period, projected to be approximately $2 billion in Housing Credit equity
across the full market over that period.5 In California specifically, NCRC analysis finds that 45
California banks would no longer be subject to the investment test.


1 Statewide Housing Plan. (n.d.). Statewide-Housing-Plan-Cahcd.Hub.Arcgis.Com. Retrieved September 30, 2026,
from https://statewide-housing-plan-cahcd.hub.arcgis.com/
2 NCRC. Stop CRA Rollback, Keep Banks Accountable to Communities with Strong CRA. (2026),
https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending
3 NCRC. Stop CRA Rollback, Keep Banks Accountable to Communities with Strong CRA. (2026),
https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending
4 The Center for Affordable Housing Lending. (2026). Incentive to Impact. The Center for Affordable Housing Lending.
https://static1.squarespace.com/static/67dd69627071be10fb7c3fb4/t/6a6296c2f95fab4060bd8828/1784846018733/NAAHL_CR
A_Report_072326_V4-Web.pdf
5 Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition, Survey Results and Responses to the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) Proposal on the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). (2026)


The proposal weakens how community development performance is scored for the banks that
remain in the intermediate tier. Under the current framework, an intermediate bank
generally must receive at least a "satisfactory" rating on both its lending test and its
community development test to earn an overall satisfactory rating. Under the proposal,
strong lending performance could compensate for weak community development performance
in the overall rating. Because Housing Credit equity serves a function that cannot be replaced
with additional debt, allowing lending to substitute for investment removes the last structural
reason many mid-sized banks would continue making Housing Credit investments at all.

We ask the agencies to:

1. Retain the current $1.649 billion large bank threshold, consistent with the 1995 CRA
framework and the direction the Federal Reserve, the third federal bank regulator,
appears to be taking.

2. If the agencies proceed with raising the large bank threshold, instead adopt the $3.252
billion alternative rather than the proposed $10 billion threshold. AHTCC survey data
show this alternative would reduce the number of affected Housing Credit investors by
approximately 63 percent (from 108 banks to 40 banks) and reduce the estimated five-
year Housing Credit equity impact from roughly $2 billion to approximately $272
million because banks with assets above $3.252 billion already account for
approximately 86 percent of the Housing Credit equity investment made by banks
between $1.65 billion and $10 billion. The $3.252 billion threshold is also the inflation-
adjusted successor to the OCC's 2020 $2.5 billion threshold and has a clearer
regulatory basis than an untested $10 billion cutoff.

3. Reject the $30 billion alternative threshold discussed in the proposal outright. NAAHL
estimates that a $30 billion threshold would cut the number of large banks with
investment requirements by half or more in 17 states, and AHTCC survey data show
that banks between $10 billion and $30 billion in assets account for more than twice as
much Housing Credit debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and
$10 billion, meaning this alternative would be dramatically more damaging than the
primary proposal.

4. Require intermediate banks to receive a passing rating on both the lending test and
the community development test independently, rather than allowing strong lending
performance to compensate for weak community development investment in a
blended overall score.

5. Phase in any threshold increase rather than implementing it as a single cutover, to
avoid a sudden, market-wide repricing shock as a large share of investment-test
demand exits simultaneously.





II. The Proposed 0.625% Tier 1 Capital Floor Would Sanction a Historic Drop in Community
Development Finance

The proposed rule changes would allow a bank devoting just 0.625 percent of its Tier 1
capital to community development loans, and separately 0.625 percent to community
development investments, to receive a passing CRA rating. This bar is set far below what
banks currently do. NCRC found that among the largest 100 OCC and FDIC supervised banks,
the median bank devotes 6.8 percent of Tier 1 capital annually to community development
lending in its assessment areas, and a median of 3.6 percent of Tier 1 capital to CRA-qualified
investments.6 If banks instead did only the minimum necessary to meet the proposed 0.625
percent thresholds, NCRC estimates that combined community development lending and
investment activity would fall to approximately $14.8 billion annually, a decrease of
approximately $87.2 billion, or 85 percent, from current levels. There is no justification
consistent with CRA's purpose for setting a floor this far below current market performance;
doing so functions less as a minimum standard than as a signal to banks that current levels of
community development activity are unnecessary.

We ask the agencies to:

1. Reject the proposed 0.625% Tier 1 capital floor or set any minimum activity threshold
at a level consistent with current market performance rather than a fraction of it.

2. Maintain separate, independently binding minimums for community development
lending and community development investment, so that a bank cannot satisfy its
entire community development obligation through lending alone.


III. Preserve CRA-Qualifying Grants and Nonprofit Capacity

The proposal would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring an
established nexus to a specific community development project and capping grantee
overhead and administrative costs at 15 percent, with new documentation requirements to
demonstrate compliance. The agencies also ask whether CRA eligibility for grantmaking
should be eliminated entirely. The effect of removing this eligibility as a tool to encourage
partnerships and support for nonprofit affordable housing developers would be detrimental to
our ability to address our region's ongoing housing crisis.

Habitat GSF uses flexible general operating and capacity-building support from our bank
partners to bridge funding gaps and respond quickly when affordable housing opportunities
arise. Public funding often arrives late in an affordable housing development or preservation
project and is considered "last-dollar-in" funding. Flexible grants and sponsorships from banks

6 NCRC. (2026, September 14). New NCRC analysis: 85% Of community development activity at risk with proposed CRA
rule changes – NCRC. Ncrc.Org. https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-
development-activity-at-risk/



provide the early capital needed to advance housing production and preservation, strengthen
homeownership programs, and expand our development pipeline. Habitat GSF is also able to
leverage flexible investments, alongside homeowner mortgage payments, creating a
sustainable funding cycle that helps build and preserve more homes and serve more families.
Adding any such restrictions would be felt disproportionately by the organizations like Habitat
GSF that are best positioned to do the hardest preservation and community development
work in underserved parts of California and our region.

We ask the agencies to preserve CRA eligibility for general operating support, capacity-
building grants, and sponsorships to nonprofit organizations engaged in community
development, without imposing new project-level nexus or overhead-tracking requirements
that fall hardest on smaller and rural organizations.

Habitat for Humanity Greater San Francisco has seen firsthand what CRA-motivated
investment makes possible in in the San Francisco Bay Area, and what is put at risk when that
investment weakens. We urge the OCC and FDIC to preserve the standalone investment test,
reject the proposed activity floor, and ensure that any final rule strengthens, rather than
diminishes, the effectiveness and positive investment that CRA has made possible in
California for nearly 50 years.


Thank you for your consideration of this request.


Very Truly Yours,

Holden Weisman
Director of Policy and Advocacy
Habitat for Humanity Greater San Francisco

Ladies and Gentlemen:
Dauntless Capital Management submits these comments on the proposal by the Office of the Comptroller of
the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (the "Agencies") to amend their Community
Reinvestment Act ("CRA") regulations.
Dauntless is an SBA-licensed Small Business Investment Company. We invest venture capital equity in
small businesses developing critical and dual-use technologies, including secure communications,
autonomous systems, advanced materials and resilient logistics, all areas the Department of Defense has
identified as priorities. Many of our portfolio companies are early-stage manufacturers. They are capital-
intensive, rarely qualify for bank credit in their first years, and create skilled engineering and production jobs
as they scale. Over the last 18 months alone, we have invested in 12 companies in seven states that
together employ more than 1,000 people.
Banks provide a substantial share of our limited partner capital, including wholesale and limited purpose
banks, and CRA consideration is a principal reason they commit. We welcome the Agencies' decision to
write the long-standing SBIC presumption into the rule itself. Our comments focus on the provisions that will
decide whether that presumption keeps bank capital flowing to small businesses like those in our portfolio.
1. SBIC investments are economic development in the plain sense of the CRA
For a critical-technology startup, SBIC equity often funds the first production line, the first hires and the first
government contract. That is the small business financing and job creation the economic development
definition is meant to capture. We ask the Agencies to confirm that a bank's investment in a licensed SBIC
qualifies in full under the proposal's category for government programs that serve small businesses
(proposed § __.12). SBA licenses, examines and collects detailed reporting from every SBIC, so that federal
oversight already does the verification work. Asking each bank to repeat it for every portfolio company would
add cost and discourage participation in commitments that run ten years or more.
2. Credit should follow SBIC capital beyond a single assessment area
Critical-technology companies grow where engineering talent, suppliers and test facilities are, which rarely
coincides with where a bank investor is headquartered. A fund like ours invests nationally by design, and
SBA diversification rules reinforce that. Many of our bank investors, by contrast, operate from one office with
one assessment area.
The proposal's geographic flexibility standards would allow credit outside a bank's assessment areas after
its needs there are met. We support that approach. We ask that the final standard credit the full amount of a

bank's SBIC commitment when the fund invests in a broader statewide or regional area that includes the
bank's assessment area, without requiring the fund to place capital inside that area.
We also ask the Agencies to keep the limited purpose bank designation, on which the preamble invites
comment. Limited purpose banks are among the most active investors in critical-technology SBICs. Moving
them to the general asset-size tests would pull their CRA resources toward retail activity in a single market
and away from fund investments that reach small businesses across the country.
3. Stability for existing commitments and across regulators
SBIC commitments outlast most rule cycles. Commitments made before the effective date should keep their
current CRA treatment for their full term, including for banks that move between the new asset-size
categories. Our funds also draw capital from banks supervised by all three federal banking agencies. We
encourage the OCC to work with the FDIC and the Federal Reserve Board toward consistent treatment, so
that two banks investing in the same fund receive the same consideration.
Conclusion
Bank capital invested through SBICs helps critical-technology startups become domestic manufacturers
and employers. We ask that the final rule keep that capital moving, and we would welcome the opportunity
to share more detail about our portfolio companies and the jobs they support.

To Whom It May Concern:
CRA Today LLC appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposal. CRA Today provides
on-demand and live CRA training and the CRA Hub, a membership community where bank CRA officers
and compliance professionals master the CRA, prepare for examinations, and put capital to work for
community benefit. Our members design CRA programs, collect and validate data, and respond to
examiner requests. This letter draws on their practical experience and on more than three decades of
CRA compliance, community development finance, and CDFI partnership work at the core of CRA
Today.
We support the agencies' stated goals of greater clarity and reduced burden. A rule meets those goals
only if the materials that make it workable exist on the day it applies. This letter addresses those
materials: the transition provisions (Question 59), the future of the Interagency Questions and Answers
(Question 58), and the data provisions of proposed section __.42.We will address the substantive
provisions of the proposal in a separate comment letter.
What banks are asked to build, and what does not yet exist
The proposal changes how community development activities qualify, how strategic plans work, what
large banks must collect and report, and how public notice is given. Banks are being asked to comment
on, and eventually build to, a framework whose supporting materials have not been written.
We looked for a commitment to publish revised examination procedures, performance evaluation
templates, a data file specification, or examiner training. We did not find one. The phrase "examiner
training" does not appear in the proposal. The phrase "examination procedures" appears four times,
each time describing existing procedures or stating that they are unlikely to change. The Interagency
Questions and Answers, on which practitioners rely daily, are discussed throughout the proposal.
Among other changes, the proposal would eliminate the purpose test for economic development, one
of the two tests a loan must meet today to qualify as a community development loan under that
category. That change alone would require revised examination procedures and new guidance for
practitioners. What remains of the Questions and Answers after codification is not stated.
The materials that practitioners and examiners use today were issued between 2005 and 2019: the
performance evaluation templates in September 2005, four sets of examination procedures in July 2007,
the large institution examination procedures in April 2014, the Interagency Questions and Answers in
July 2016, a data collection guide for 2015 data, and agency examination manuals, including the OCC's

Comptroller's Handbook booklet on CRA examination procedures (June 2018) and the FDIC's Consumer
Compliance Examination Manual, whose CRA data review section was last updated in March 2019.
The agencies also once answered unclear questions through Interagency Interpretive Letters, issued, in
the FFIEC's words, to ensure consistency in answering public inquiries about the CRA regulations. The
FFIEC lists 58 of them, from 1995 through 2006, with the most recent dated January 11, 2006. They
include letters that clarify the definition of affordable housing (October 30, 1997) and that discuss
similarly situated lenders and performance context (June 11, 1996). Those are two of the questions this
proposal and this letter raise again. That practice is a model the agencies can return to.
Much of the clarity the agencies seek could be achieved by reviewing and updating all of these
resources, and by issuing new interpretive guidance where the rule leaves a question open, under the
existing framework and through notice and comment where required. Updated guidance carries no
applicability date, requires no data build, and preserves the flexibility banks use to respond to the credit
needs of their communities. We encourage the agencies to treat a comprehensive update as a first step
that stands on its own merits, whatever the outcome of this rulemaking.
Summary of recommendations
1.​ Pursue a single interagency rule, and issue every implementation resource on an interagency basis.
2.​ Tie the applicability date to publication of six named resources, and begin a transition period of at
least twelve months only after the last of them is published (Question 59).
3.​ Complete each bank's current evaluation period under the framework in place when it began, so
that no examination applies two sets of criteria to one record (Question 59).
4.​Reissue or replace the Interagency Questions and Answers with a disposition table showing which
entries and Interagency Interpretive Letters survive, and make future changes through notice and
comment (Question 58).
5.​ Publish a file specification, field definitions, edit validations, and a resubmission protocol for the
section __.42 data before collection is required. Publish a coding guide for the complexity and
community development purpose indicators, and confirm that good-faith coding later revised at
examination is a data correction and not a violation.
6.​ Address the interaction between the two rule sets, so that banks do not build and maintain
duplicate processes.
7. Address the interaction between CRA data and Section 1071 data, so that banks do not build and
maintain duplicate processes.
1. Why an interagency approach matters
The agencies have said the purpose of this proposal is to reduce unnecessary burden, particularly for
community banks, and to provide greater clarity for how to obtain CRA consideration. We support both
goals. In our experience, neither can be fully achieved while the rules are split between two sets of
agencies.
The 1995 regulations have lasted three decades in part because the federal banking agencies issued
them together. One rule, one set of interagency Questions and Answers, and one body of examination
procedures meant that a bank, a vendor, and an examiner at any agency worked from the same text.
Practitioners built programs, systems, and training around that common reference point.
A bifurcated approach works against simplification in concrete ways. Two sets of definitions require a
bank with affiliates under different charters to maintain two compliance programs. Two sets of
Questions and Answers leave practitioners unsure which guidance applies to which institution. Two sets
of examination procedures and two data specifications require vendors to build and support parallel

products, and those costs reach banks, including community banks, through higher prices and slower
updates. Examiners who move between agencies must work from different rulebooks, which makes
consistent treatment harder to achieve. Every added layer of difference adds burden and subtracts
clarity, which is the reverse of what the proposal intends.
We respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to work with the Federal Reserve Board toward a single
interagency rule. We recognize that the Board's next steps rest with its Governors. Where a single rule is
not yet possible, we ask the agencies to issue the implementation materials described in this letter on
an interagency basis, and to align the definitions that drive CRA consideration, so that the differences
banks must manage are as few as possible. Every recommendation below is easier to carry out, and less
likely to confuse the people who must follow it, if it is issued jointly.

A transition period of at least twelve months should begin only after the last of these resources is
published. For the new data collection, maintenance, and reporting requirements that apply to large
banks, the period should be the longer of twelve months after the last resource is published and two
years after the final rule. New data obligations should start on January 1, so that a bank collects a full year
of data under one specification.
3. Completing current evaluation periods (Question 59)
A bank's current evaluation period should be completed under the framework in place when it began. If
an evaluation period straddles the applicability date, examiners would have to apply two sets of criteria
to a single record, and the bank could not know in advance how the pieces would be weighed. ​
​
Banks already face a version of this problem. A bank's size category depends on its year-end assets for
two consecutive years, and an evaluation period is often three years, so a bank that changes category
can find that part of its period falls under one set of expectations and the rest under another. Members
report that they resolve it by contacting the examiner, who decides the treatment case by case. We
found no discussion of this situation in the proposal or in the current Questions and Answers. ​
​
The proposal would reclassify banks at the same time the new framework applies, so the question would
arise for many banks at once. Whichever approach the agencies choose, we ask them to state it in the
rule or the examination procedures, so that every bank and examiner applies the same one. If the
agencies allow a bank to elect between completing its evaluation period under the existing rules and
moving to the new framework on January 1 of the following year, we ask that the election, its deadline,
and its effect on the bank's rating be stated in the rule, and that the same options be available to every
similarly situated bank.
4. The Interagency Questions and Answers (Question 58)
Question 58 asks how the agencies should address the Interagency Questions and Answers going
forward. The Questions and Answers are an essential resource. Practitioners and examiners rely on them
daily to apply the rule to specific loans, investments, and services. The proposal codifies some of this
guidance but does not say how the remaining entries will be treated. Even under the current rule, some
entries leave banks and examiners to reach different conclusions on the same facts, as the two examples
below show. We recommend that the agencies retain the Questions and Answers, clarify the entries
where practice has diverged, and commit to updating them on a stated schedule.
Our members' experience with naturally occurring affordable housing shows why. The current
Questions and Answers say that low- or moderate-income individuals must benefit from the housing,
but they set no rent standard, and the agencies acknowledge in the proposal that the Questions and
Answers are not sufficiently clear on how to demonstrate it. Members report using three different
methods for the same kind of loan, which are rents measured against 30 percent of 80 percent of area
median income, HUD Fair Market Rents, or rent rolls, and individual examiners have been known to
accept one while others have asked for another. The proposal settles the 30 percent standard but not
whose median rent counts or how it is documented. A reissued Question and Answer would close that
gap with no change to the rule text.
Economic development shows a similar gap. The current Questions and Answers mention Bureau of
Labor Statistics wage data only in the entry on community services (section __.12(g)(2)-1). Members
report that they use BLS wage data to show that jobs created or retained through an economic
development activity benefit low- or moderate-income individuals. Most examiners accept that
evidence, but some ask the bank to go back to the borrower for actual wage data, and banks cannot
know in advance which standard will apply. A reissued Question and Answer should confirm that BLS

wage data are acceptable documentation, so that banks are not expected to obtain actual wage data
from borrowers, information that banks do not ordinarily collect when underwriting a loan.
We recommend that the agencies:
●​
Publish a disposition table that lists every Question and Answer entry as retained, codified, modified,
or superseded. Include the Interagency Interpretive Letters in the same table, since some address
the same topics as Question and Answer entries, such as affordable housing and gross annual
revenue.
●​
Issue the replacement on an interagency basis, and make any future change through notice and
comment, as the agencies have done in the past.
●​
State where a practitioner will find the applicable set of resources, and which set applies to which
bank. The Board's next steps rest with its Governors (proposal, footnote 31), and we do not ask the
agencies to speak for the Board. We ask only that the agencies tell banks supervised by each agency
where to look.
●​
Provide a feedback channel for bank-specific questions during the transition, with a stated response
commitment.
5. Data integrity and the section __.42 requirements
What the proposal requires
Under proposed section __.42(a)(2), a large bank would collect and maintain, in machine-readable form
"as prescribed by" its agency, the following for each community development loan, investment, and
grant: a unique identifier, the recipient's name, the dollar amount, the recipient's address, the activity
location, an indicator whether a loan or investment involves complexity, an indicator of community
development purpose, and an indicator of activity type. Section __.42(a)(3) adds, for each grant, the
recipient's written commitment, its attestation on indirect costs, and supporting documentation
including IRS Form 990 with budgets. Section __.42(a)(4) adds loan-level consumer lending data for a
bank with consumer lending as a major product line. Section __.42(b)(2) requires annual reporting.
What is missing
The rule text defers the format to the agencies, but the proposal does not prescribe one. It contains no
file specification, no field definitions, no edit validations, and no resubmission protocol. The phrase "data
integrity" does not appear in the proposal. The agencies' own burden analysis describes what banks and
vendors would do: design, project planning, development, validation testing, and controlled escalation
to production, with independent verification at each stage. That sequence cannot begin until the
specification exists.
Field definitions matter even for familiar data. Under the current rule, one small business data field,
gross annual revenue, has needed guidance in more than one place. The Questions and Answers direct
a bank to report the revenues it considered in making its credit decision (section __.42(a)(4)-1), and to
report gross, not adjusted, annual revenue (section __.42(a)(4)-4). An Interagency Interpretive Letter
dated January 27, 1998 reached the same conclusion on gross revenue and stated that banks need not
verify it. The new section __.42 fields, including the complexity and community development purpose
indicators, will need the same kind of definitions. They should be published before collection begins,
rather than settled one question at a time afterward.
Two indicators are judgments
The complexity indicator and the community development purpose indicator are conclusions that
banks and examiners reach today through discussion of the specific facts. Under the proposal they
become coded values in a file that examiners will test. The FDIC's Consumer Compliance Examination
Manual (section XI-11, CRA Data Review Timeframes and Sampling Guidelines, last updated March 1,
CRA Today and the CRA Hub | www.cratoday.com | Page 5 of 7

2019) already directs examiners to validate data fields including loan type, amount, location, and income
or revenue. The proposal does not say what happens when an examiner disagrees with a bank's coding.
Consumer lending data and the major product line determination
Section __.42(a)(4) applies to a large bank that has consumer lending as a major product line under
section __.21(g). Under section __.21(g)(2), consumer lending is evaluated only if consumer loans exceed
50 percent of retail lending by both dollar volume and loan count, or at the bank's option. A bank near
that line can know whether the threshold is met only after the lending has occurred, but collection is
required as the loans are made. A bank in that position would collect defensively, which is the burden
the major product line approach was meant to reduce.
What we recommend
If the final rule includes any new data collection, maintenance, or reporting requirements, including
those in proposed section __.42, we recommend the following.
●​
Publish a file specification, field definitions, edit validations, and a resubmission protocol before the
collection applicability date.
●​
Publish a coding guide for the complexity and community development purpose indicators, with
worked examples.
●​
State in the examination procedures how data integrity will be tested, including whether review is by
sample or in full, and whether the approach differs for community development data and lending
data.
●​
Confirm that good-faith coding of a subjective indicator, later revised at examination, is a data
correction and not a violation.
●​
For consumer lending, provide a bright-line test with details on determination and collection start
times, or confirm that a bank may rely on its own prior-period calculation and make its election at
the start of an evaluation period.
●​
Issue the optional template the agencies have asked about as a file specification. In the discussion of
how banks demonstrate a community development primary purpose, the agencies invite comment
on an optional template for collecting community development activity information. We support it.
It will be most useful as a machine-readable specification with field definitions covering all of section
__.42(a)(2), and not as a form.
6. Two rule sets
The proposal amends only the OCC and FDIC rules. Banks supervised by the Federal Reserve Board
remain under the 1995 regulations. For practitioners, this affects holding companies with banks under
both frameworks, vendors that build to one specification, and examiners who move between them. We
do not ask the agencies to resolve the Board's choices. We ask the agencies to address what is within
their control:
●​
Issue an interagency statement on how examiners will treat similarly situated lender analysis and
performance context across the two rule sets.
●​
Coordinate with the Board on the definitions of community development, complexity, and primary
purpose, so that the two frameworks do not drift further apart.
●​
Address how affiliate activity is treated across charters within a single holding company, and how a
merger or charter conversion during an evaluation period is handled.

7. Section 1071 and CRA data
The agencies state that, to the fullest extent feasible, they intend to leverage Section 1071 data and
discontinue duplicative CRA data collection and reporting. We support avoiding duplication. We ask for
a sequencing commitment: that the agencies announce any discontinuation, with a timeline, before

banks are required to build or revise a CRA small business or small farm specification. Banks should not
be asked to build to two specifications for the same loans in the interim.
Conclusion
The agencies have stated two goals for this proposal: greater clarity and reduced burden, particularly for
community banks. Much of that clarity can be achieved without changing the rule text. Updated
examination procedures, current performance evaluation templates, a reissued and regularly updated
Interagency Questions and Answers, and interpretive guidance where questions remain open would
give banks and examiners a shared, current reference point. These resources can be issued under the
existing framework, with notice and comment where required. They carry no applicability date, require
no new data systems, and would benefit banks and examiners alike, whatever the outcome of this
rulemaking. Where the agencies do change the rule, these same resources are what make the change
workable, and the applicability date should follow them.
Uncertainty has a cost beyond compliance burden. When a bank cannot determine in advance whether
an activity will receive consideration, or what documentation an examiner will require, it is more likely to
favor familiar activities whose treatment is settled. Complex and less common transactions, often the
ones that CDFIs, nonprofits, and community organizations bring to banks, are the most likely to be
delayed, reduced, or declined. Members already report examiners reaching different conclusions on the
same facts under the current guidance. Without updated resources in place before the new framework
applies, that uncertainty would extend to every activity whose treatment the proposal changes.
For us, these resources matter most because of community development. Partnerships between banks
and CDFIs, nonprofits, and community organizations are where a bank's capital becomes housing, small
business credit, and financial capability for the people the CRA was written to serve. A rule that is clear,
stable, and well supported by guidance makes it easier for banks to say yes to the community
development transactions their partners bring to them.​
​
We would be glad to provide further detail on any point in this letter.

Summary of recommendations
1. Reporting threshold and comparative data (Question 1)
a. Publish the method examiners use to compare a bank with similarly situated lenders, and
how that comparison translates into each rating level, before the reporting threshold changes.
b. Keep the comparison pool intact. Banks that report today and would be reclassified as

1. The reporting threshold and the benchmark for how much is enough
What the proposal does
Under proposed section __.42, only large banks, those with more than $10 billion in assets, would
collect, maintain, and report small business and small farm data. The proposal states that, using 2024
and 2025 Call Report data, about 2.4 percent of banks (86 banks) would have been large banks under
that definition, holding 85.4 percent of industry assets. The agencies acknowledge the effect on
comparative data. They state that the threshold increases "may reduce the amount of standardized
CRA data available" and that more tailored evaluations "may reduce comparability across banks."
Neither "benchmark" nor "peer" appears in the proposal, and "similarly situated" appears twice. No
numbered question asks how comparative analysis will work afterward. We raise the issue under
Question 1 on asset thresholds, because the reporting population changes with them.
The 86 banks hold most of the industry's assets, but a community bank's comparison pool is local.
The aggregate that matters to a bank in a particular market is made up of the lenders that report in
that market.
The burden is in the data, not the transmittal
A bank evaluated as a large bank and a bank evaluated as an intermediate bank face the same core
work. Examiners test the accuracy of the loan-level data a bank collects, whether or not it is reported.
The FDIC's procedures for large banks direct examiners to test a sample of loan files to verify the
accuracy of data collected and reported (Consumer Compliance Examination Manual, section XI-4),
and the same manual directs examiners to validate collected data even when it is not reported, and
to sample when it is not collected (section XI-11). The intermediate small bank procedures likewise
direct examiners to test the accuracy of a bank's loan reports or to sample (section XI-3). Both are
evaluated on their lending and on the same types of community development activity. The
difference is structure: intermediate banks under one community development test, large banks
across the lending, investment, and service tests. In our experience, what changes when a bank
moves from large to intermediate is the final step of formatting and transmitting the data. The
agencies estimate an 86 percent reduction in burden hours for intermediate banks, including banks
that move from large. We ask the agencies to publish how much of that estimate reflects reporting,
and how much reflects collection and maintenance, which continue.
What reporting provides is the benchmark
Two problems compound each other. The standard for each conclusion is unstated, and the
aggregate data that examiners start from would shrink if fewer banks report. In a recent public FDIC
evaluation of a large bank, each assessment area narrative states a conclusion in a single word,
adequate, good, excellent, or poor, after describing the bank's position relative to aggregate lending.
For small business lending in one assessment area, the narrative notes that performance in
low-income tracts was below aggregate in one year, improved the next, and exceeded aggregate in

moderate-income tracts, and concludes, "Overall, the bank's performance is adequate." The
evaluation does not say how far above or below aggregate separates adequate from good or
excellent, or how conclusions on different products combine into one. In the same evaluation, the
2023 aggregate figure for small business lending is shown as not available. Banks encounter the
same gap during examinations. When asked, examiners have not been able to articulate the
difference between High Satisfactory and Outstanding performance in terms a bank can measure. A
bank that does not know where the next level begins cannot manage toward it. Without a clear
target, the bank may purchase loans at a premium or take on other activity as a precaution, and
learns which standard applied only at the end of the examination. That uncertainty is a primary
source of regulatory burden.

Figure 1 represents the evaluation's narrative and delineates small business lending in one

The benchmark arrives too late to use
The value of the aggregate also depends on when it arrives. Banks report small business and small
farm data by March 1, but the agencies released the 2024 aggregate and disclosure data on
November 13, 2025, more than ten months after the close of the year the data describe. By then,
most of the following year's lending is complete. HMDA shows that a faster turnaround is possible.
HMDA requires roughly four times as many data points and significantly more fields per loan from a
larger and more varied pool of reporters, including nondepository lenders. Yet HMDA data are
available to banks for self-evaluation by the end of March each year. If CRA data followed a similar
schedule, a bank could measure its prior-year performance against the aggregate early in the
current year and adjust its lending while it can still affect that year's results. Examiners would also
work from current data rather than the gaps shown in Figure 1. Faster release would increase
certainty and reduce burden without any change to the rule text. It works only if the pool of reporters
stays stable, so that the aggregate continues to represent similarly situated lenders in each market.
Section 1071 is not a ready substitute
The agencies state that, to the fullest extent feasible, they intend to leverage Section 1071 data. That
data cannot yet serve as a substitute. The CFPB's revised rule, issued in May 2026, covers only lenders
that meet a volume threshold of 1,000 covered credit transactions in each of the two preceding
years, and compliance begins on January 1, 2028. A lender below that threshold would not
contribute to a Section 1071 data pool, so Section 1071 cannot supply the comparison data that CRA
reporting supplies for banks outside its coverage. The threshold also limits the duplication the
agencies seek to avoid. Only banks that report CRA small business data and also exceed the Section
1071 volume threshold would report the same loans twice. Banks below that threshold face no
duplication, yet they would lose the CRA comparison data they rely on. The proposal does not say
how many banks fall into each group.
Before narrowing or discontinuing CRA data collection or reporting, we ask the agencies to publish
an analysis of the number and type of institutions subject to both regimes and of the extent to
which Section 1071 data would be an adequate substitute for CRA data.
