Intermediate banks are evaluated on the same loan products as large banks, and examiners
already test the accuracy of their loan data or sample their loan files (Consumer Compliance
Examination Manual, section XI-3). For banks that already maintain this data for examination,
reporting is the final step of formatting and transmitting it, not a new collection. A uniform
reporting population would give each market a complete and stable aggregate and make the
comparison to similarly situated lenders more reliable for every bank, not only those that report
today. This would preserve comparative data, while the higher asset thresholds we support in
Section 4 would still reduce burden through the streamlined performance test.
●​
Apply the agencies' own test. The proposal would excuse an individual bank from reporting
only if the data are not necessary to evaluate its performance and would not have more than a
minimal effect on aggregate data (proposed section __.42(h)). We ask the agencies to apply that
test to the threshold change, to publish the analysis, and to state how many banks would be
reclassified.
●​
Keep the aggregate current. Commit to continued publication of the aggregate and disclosure
reports, and release them on a schedule comparable to HMDA, within one month of the March 1
reporting deadline, so banks can use prior-year results to self-correct during the current year
starting in April as opposed to November or December.
●​
Address thin pools. State how an examiner will evaluate a bank when the comparison pool is
small, and consider a documented peer analysis supplied by the bank as performance context.
2. The 15 percent condition on community development grants (Questions 9 and 10)
The condition inverts its source
Under proposed section __.42(a)(3), a large bank would obtain, for each community development
grant, the recipient's written commitment, a written attestation that its indirect costs for
administering the grant will not exceed 15 percent, calculated consistent with the Uniform Guidance,
2 CFR part 200, "or a comparable standard," and supporting documentation including IRS Form 990
with annual operating and program budgets. The agencies took the 15 percent figure from the Office
of Management and Budget. Their own footnote explains that OMB "guarantees" a de minimis rate
of 15 percent "to allow for a more reasonable and realistic recovery of indirect costs, particularly for
new or inexperienced organizations that may not have the capacity to undergo a formal rate
negotiation but still deserve to be fully compensated for their overhead costs" (91 Fed. Reg. 52129
n.131, citing 89 Fed. Reg. 30046, 30093 (Apr. 22, 2024)). The proposal turns a rate OMB guarantees to
grantees into a ceiling.
The condition raises further practical questions. "Comparable standard" is not defined. A Form 990
reports an organization's expenses by function for its fiscal year, not an indirect cost rate for a
particular grant, and the Form 990-EZ and 990-N filed by many smaller nonprofits contain no
functional expense breakdown at all. The proposal does not say whether the test applies at the grant
date or at expenditure, or how multi-year grants, pooled funds, and small sponsorships are treated. It
flags grants to intermediaries as a concern without explaining how the test would apply to them. The
preamble's own example, a grant to a nonprofit that provides homeownership counseling and
health care to people experiencing homelessness and directs about 25 percent of the grant to
internal expenses, would not qualify under the proposal.
An alternative that uses tools already in place
Question 9 asks whether there are alternative standards. We suggest one that uses frameworks
Congress and the agencies already administer and that focuses scrutiny where the concern is
greatest:
CRA Today and the CRA Hub | www.cratoday.com | Page 5 of 8

●​
Drop the 15 percent condition, the recipient attestation and Form 990 requirements, and the
grant-by-grant reporting under proposed section __.42.
●​
For ordinary grants, keep primary purpose as the test, confirmed through a simple
certification modeled on the OCC's public welfare investment process. Under 12 CFR 24.5, a
national bank gives an after-the-fact notice within 10 working days that includes a statement
certifying compliance, and may use a standard form. Examiners already understand it.
●​
Where the concern is greatest, rely on the CRA Sunshine provisions (12 U.S.C. 1831y; 12 CFR
parts 35 and 346). Covered written agreements, those tied to the CRA with a value above $10,000
a year, must be publicly disclosed. The nongovernmental party must file an annual accounting of
the use of funds, itemized by category including compensation and administrative expenses, and
the statute provides penalties for diversion of funds. If the agencies want more accountability,
this is the targeted place to add it.
●​
For all other nonprofits, rely on IRS oversight. Treasury announced a Form 990 Transparency
Initiative on April 23, 2026, under which the IRS plans to revise the form, with public comment, to
improve reporting on government grants, government contracts, and fiscal sponsorship. If
current reporting is insufficient, that is the appropriate venue.
This approach serves the agencies' stated purpose of making sure that grants reach the
communities they are meant to benefit, and it avoids placing a documentation burden on the broad
base of community nonprofits that receive modest grants.
Question 10 asks whether the agencies should eliminate all grants and donations from CRA
consideration. They should not. Grants are often the most flexible and least available form of support
for nonprofit partners, and removing them would reduce the resources reaching the organizations
that carry out community development. The agencies state that they expect to maintain a public
database of grant recipients, street addresses, and amounts. We ask that the database identify
recipients by census tract rather than street address. Some recipients, such as domestic violence
shelters, keep their locations confidential for the safety of the people they serve, and a tract-level
identifier still allows the public to see where grant dollars are going.
3. Geographic flexibility (Questions 8 and 34)
Under proposed section __.13(e), a large bank must, for each year in the evaluation period, expend at
least 0.625 percent of its tier 1 capital, allocated to each assessment area by deposit weight, on
community development loans, and the same percentage on investments and grants together, to
receive consideration for activities outside its assessment areas. Intermediate, wholesale, and limited
purpose banks must expend 1.25 percent. The standard is calculated for each assessment area, and a
bank must meet it in every assessment area in a rated area. Section __.13(e)(3) lets an agency find,
based on performance context, that a bank with a lesser amount may still receive consideration.
The percentages should govern eligibility only. The agencies state that section __.13(e) does not
require a bank to conduct activities outside its assessment areas and that a bank may receive
Satisfactory or Outstanding based solely on assessment area activities. We appreciate that
statement. Our concern is that a number printed in the Code of Federal Regulations does not stay
optional. Boards, auditors, and examiners will read 0.625 percent and 1.25 percent as the agencies'
view of expected volume, and banks will measure against them whether or not they seek
outside-area consideration. We ask the agencies to state in the rule text, and not only in the
preamble, that the standard governs eligibility for outside-area consideration and is not a
performance expectation, a floor for a Satisfactory conclusion, or a safe harbor.
Measure across the evaluation period (Question 8). An annual measurement standard does not
reflect how community development transactions are structured and funded. A Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit or New Markets Tax Credit transaction may close in one year with no comparable
activity in the following two years, and the bank's program may be stronger as a result. These
CRA Today and the CRA Hub | www.cratoday.com | Page 6 of 8

transactions often involve layered capital stacks, construction-to-permanent financing, and equity
installments paid through capital calls tied to construction milestones and placed-in-service dates.
As a result, a single commitment may fund over several years. CRA practitioners track both
commitments and fundings because those amounts rarely line up within one calendar year. We ask
that the standard be measured across the full evaluation period, or that the agencies permit
multi-year averaging. The annual measurement weighs most heavily on banks with a single
assessment area. With no other market to balance a slow year, such a bank may feel pressure to buy
whatever qualifying activity is available locally, often in a market already saturated with CRA
investment, simply to meet the threshold each year.
Measure at the rated area level (Question 34). Requiring the standard to be met in every
assessment area, every year, means that strong performance in three markets and a shortfall in a
fourth forfeits geographic flexibility for the entire institution. Community development pipelines do
not move on an annual schedule. Affordable housing, infrastructure, and similar projects come up
unevenly depending on local conditions, and a market with little qualifying activity in a given year is
not evidence that a bank is neglecting it. An annual, market-by-market threshold also discourages
participation in regional and national funds that deploy capital across many geographies. It would
push banks, particularly institutions with a single assessment area, to concentrate capital in markets
that are already saturated with CRA activity rather than in communities with the greatest need.
We ask that the standard be applied at the rated area level. We also ask the agencies to publish the
allocation worksheet so a bank can reproduce the calculation before examination, and to specify the
tier 1 capital measurement date and averaging convention. In response to the agencies' question
about when tier 1 capital is an insufficient measure of capacity, additional examples include a high
ratio of securities to loans, a recent capital raise, a de novo institution, and a bank carrying large
unrealized securities losses.
A simpler alternative that we would also support: make a bank eligible for consideration of qualifying
activities outside its assessment areas if it received an overall rating of Satisfactory or better on its
most recent examination. This approach is predictable, ties flexibility to demonstrated performance
in the bank's own communities, and avoids the complexity of a quantitative test. A bank rated below
Satisfactory would remain ineligible for the next examination cycle.
If the agencies keep an annual, assessment area by assessment area standard without a published
worksheet, we believe the simpler alternative is the better outcome. The agencies describe it as
consistent with the level of performance historically considered Low Satisfactory, and it evaluates
activity over the evaluation period rather than year by year. Consistent with our concern above, we
ask that this description not be read as a performance expectation or a floor for any conclusion. The
standard should determine only whether a bank is eligible for consideration of activities outside its
assessment areas.
4. An alternative path
The agencies identify four purposes for this rulemaking: increasing the focus on lending, ensuring
that community development grants benefit communities, reducing burden, and increasing clarity
and objectivity. We support each of these goals. We believe they can be achieved through targeted
changes to the current framework, which banks, examiners, and data vendors already understand,
rather than through a new structure that would require new systems, procedures, and training
across the industry.
We recommend that the agencies retain the current framework and add the following:
●​
Update the supporting resources, as described in our companion comment letter: examination
procedures, performance evaluation templates, the Interagency Questions and Answers, the data
guide, and examination manuals, with a disposition table, issued on an interagency basis.
CRA Today and the CRA Hub | www.cratoday.com | Page 7 of 8

●​
Publish the illustrative list of qualifying activities the proposal contemplates, and the
confirmation process.
●​
Count financial education for people at all income levels. The proposal's definition of civic
assistance requires service to low- or moderate-income people.
●​
Replace the 15 percent condition with the approach in Section 2.
●​
Offer a streamlined strategic plan option for banks without branches. The agencies state that
customer bases are increasingly geographically dispersed but that the statute focuses on areas
around physical facilities. A strategic plan pathway designed for banks without branches would
give those banks a clear way to be evaluated that fits their business model, and it is consistent
with the agencies' stated aim of making strategic plans more viable and less burdensome.

This path addresses each of the agencies' purposes. Lending already carries the greatest weight
under the current framework; the proposal itself notes that the lending test generally accounts for
50 percent of a large bank's rating, so an increased focus on lending does not require a structural
overhaul. The approach in Section 2 ensures that grants benefit communities without imposing a
rigid percentage condition. Updated interagency resources and a published list of qualifying
activities provide the clarity and objectivity banks need to plan with confidence. Finally, burden
would be reduced by adopting the proposal's increased asset thresholds, $1 billion for small banks
and $10 billion for intermediate banks, with both indexed for inflation, so that more community
banks are evaluated under the streamlined tests designed for their size.
Conclusion
The recommendations in this letter share a common thread. Community development does not
happen on an annual cycle or within neat geographic lines, and a CRA framework works best when it
measures performance the way community development activity actually unfolds. Measuring across
the evaluation period, applying flexibility standards at the rated area level, and linking out-of-area
consideration to a bank's demonstrated record would let examiners evaluate what a bank
accomplished rather than when a transaction happened to close or where a qualified project
happened to be located. Replacing the 15 percent condition with a clear standard for grant eligibility
would protect the purpose of grants without discouraging the operating support that community
organizations depend on.
These changes are modest, and each fits within the current framework. Together they would
advance the agencies' stated purposes while preserving what already works: a bank's ability to
commit capital to a multi-year housing transaction, support a CDFI serving several markets, or fund a
local nonprofit's core operations with confidence that the activity will be recognized. When the rules
reflect how community development is financed, banks can respond to the needs their partners
bring to them, and the communities the CRA was written to serve benefit most.
We appreciate the agencies' consideration of these comments and would be glad to provide further
detail on any point in this letter.
Respectfully submitted,
Linda Ezuka​
Founder, CRA Today and the CRA Hub​
32+ years in CRA compliance and community development finance

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0388_09000064b9668a9d.pdf:
The Honorable Travis Hill
Chairman
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
The Honorable Jonathan V. Gould
Comptroller of the Currency
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould:
On behalf of the National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals® (NAHREP®),
thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed amendments to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations issued jointly by the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC) and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). The proposal
seeks to make targeted revisions to the CRA framework to reduce regulatory burden, improve
clarity, and refocus supervision on the statutory objectives of the CRA.
NAHREP is the nation's largest Latino business organization advancing sustainable Hispanic
homeownership and wealth creation. Our network of real estate professionals, mortgage
originators, brokers, title professionals, appraisers, builders, and housing advocates works every
day with Hispanic families pursuing the American Dream through homeownership. As a result,
we have a unique perspective on the policies that effectively expand access to responsible credit
and those that inadvertently create barriers to opportunity.
The Community Reinvestment Act remains one of the most important federal laws promoting
equitable access to credit and investment in underserved communities. Since its enactment, the
CRA has helped create incentives for lenders to build relationships in communities that
historically lacked access to affordable financial services and mortgage credit. For Hispanic
families, CRA-supported lending activities, affordable mortgage products, homebuyer education
initiatives, and community partnerships have played a significant role in expanding
homeownership opportunities and wealth-building pathways.
While NAHREP appreciates many aspects of the proposal, we have significant concerns that
certain provisions could weaken incentives for institutions to engage in mortgage lending,
homeownership promotion, and community investment activities that have historically benefited
Latino households and other underserved populations.
I. CRA Must Continue to Prioritize Sustainable Homeownership and
Mortgage Lending
 NAHREP has consistently maintained that CRA examinations should encourage activities that
directly expand access to sustainable homeownership for working families. In prior comments,
we warned against frameworks that could shift attention away from mortgage lending and
toward larger, less targeted investments that may not directly expand opportunities for first-time
or underserved homebuyers.
Today, Hispanic households continue to drive a disproportionate share of America's
homeownership growth and future housing demand. Yet Hispanic homebuyers remain more
likely to be first-generation homebuyers, more likely to rely on affordable mortgage products,
and more likely to benefit from community-based lending initiatives. Policies that support
responsible mortgage credit are therefore essential not only for Latino families but for the long-
term health of the American housing market. In 2024, banks financed over 500,000 CRA-
qualifying mortgage loans, which on average totaled less than $200 thousand per loan. In
comparison, the average for all mortgage loans was approximately $378 thousand. Any
amendment to CRA regulations should continue to prioritize providing low-income and
underserved communities with affordable financing options that help families achieve
homeownership.
Accordingly, NAHREP urges the agencies to:
•
Preserve strong CRA incentives for mortgage lending activities.
•
Continue to recognize home mortgage lending as one of the most impactful CRA
activities.
•
Ensure institutions receive meaningful consideration for first-time homebuyer lending.
•
Prioritize activities that facilitate sustainable homeownership and wealth-building.
•
Avoid examination structures that incentivize large-scale investments at the expense of
direct lending to working families.
•
Retain the CRA incentives that encourage banks to support homebuyer education and
housing counseling.
The most effective way to build intergenerational wealth remains homeownership. CRA
implementation should reflect that reality.
II. Special Purpose Credit Programs Should Be Explicitly Recognized
NAHREP strongly supports explicit CRA recognition for Special Purpose Credit Programs
(SPCPs) authorized under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act.
The FDIC and OCC previously recognized SPCPs within the 2024 CRA framework, and support
for that recognition was widespread among stakeholders. The current proposal omits express
reference to SPCPs, creating regulatory uncertainty and risking reduced utilization of one of the
most effective tools available for responsibly expanding access to mortgage credit.
 SPCPs provide lenders with a lawful mechanism to address documented barriers faced by
economically disadvantaged populations while maintaining safe and sound lending standards.
Recent federal findings demonstrate the significant potential of these programs. According to the
Federal Housing Finance Agency, SPCPs supported by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac helped
nearly 58,000 economically disadvantaged borrowers access homeownership between 2022 and
2024 and generated approximately $17.2 billion in economic impact.
NAHREP therefore urges the agencies to explicitly include:
"Programs authorized under 15 U.S.C. §1691(c)(1), (2), or (3)"
within the non-exhaustive list of civic assistance and qualifying community development
activities. This change would align CRA regulations with ECOA, provide certainty to lenders,
and encourage innovative approaches to expanding sustainable homeownership opportunities in
underserved communities.
As Hispanic households continue to face affordability challenges and wealth gaps, SPCPs
represent one of the most practical and effective tools available to responsibly expand access to
credit.
The agencies should encourage banks to assess opportunities to make lawful SPCPs, affordable
mortgage products, and down payment assistance reasonably accessible through the wholesale
channel, where independent mortgage brokers originate loans that the bank itself underwrites and
funds directly. Clear eligibility guidance, workable underwriting and purchase processes, and
partner training can improve program reach. Availability should remain subject to applicable
law, program requirements, and appropriate oversight; this recommendation does not require
every program to be offered through every channel.
III. Proposed Asset Threshold Increases Risk Weakening CRA Accountability
and Reducing Investment in Underserved Communities
NAHREP is deeply concerned that the proposal to substantially increase the asset thresholds for
small and intermediate banks may weaken CRA accountability and reduce investment in
underserved communities.
The proposal would classify institutions with less than $1 billion in assets as small banks and
institutions with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion as intermediate banks. As a result,
many institutions currently subject to more rigorous CRA evaluation standards would receive
reduced examination requirements and fewer CRA investment and reporting obligations.
While NAHREP supports efforts to reduce unnecessary regulatory burden, burden reduction
cannot come at the expense of CRA's central purpose. Congress did not enact the CRA to
 minimize compliance responsibilities. Congress enacted the CRA to ensure that banks maintain a
continuing and affirmative obligation to help meet the credit needs of the communities they
serve.
We are concerned that the proposed threshold increases could significantly reduce incentives for
institutions to maintain strong performance in:
•
Mortgage lending.
•
Community development financing.
•
Affordable housing initiatives.
•
Homebuyer education programs.
•
Community-based partnerships.
•
First-time homebuyer assistance efforts.
•
Pre-purchase housing counseling.
•
Housing counseling for distressed loans.
This concern is particularly significant for Latino communities.
Hispanic households accounted for nearly 93% of new household formation in 2025, yet Latino
families continue to face challenges related to down payment accumulation, affordability, credit
access, and housing supply constraints. CRA-driven investments have played an important role
in helping lenders develop products and partnerships that address these barriers. A reduction in
CRA accountability risks reversing progress at precisely the moment when expanding
sustainable homeownership opportunities is most needed.
NAHREP is especially concerned that institutions with several billion dollars in assets could
receive substantially lighter CRA treatment despite maintaining meaningful influence within
local housing and credit markets. Banks of this size possess substantial capacity to originate
mortgage loans, support affordable housing production, invest in community development
initiatives, and implement innovative lending programs.
The agencies should carefully evaluate whether the proposed threshold changes could diminish
incentives for these activities.
Accordingly, NAHREP recommends that the agencies:
•
Reconsider the proposed increases in the small and intermediate bank asset thresholds.
•
Publish a comprehensive analysis of how many institutions and communities would be
affected.
•
Evaluate the likely impacts on mortgage lending, homeownership programs, and
community development activity.
•
Consider a narrower and more incremental adjustment to the thresholds.
 •
Retain meaningful transparency and reporting requirements even for banks receiving
regulatory relief.
If threshold increases are ultimately adopted, institutions benefiting from reduced examination
obligations should still be required to demonstrate meaningful responsiveness to local credit
needs through mortgage lending and community development activities.
Institutions receiving regulatory relief should continue to demonstrate meaningful mortgage
responsiveness, including through qualifying activity originated via the wholesale channel.
Proportionate transparency should help identify whether access to affordable programs and
assistance declines in affected communities, using existing reliable information where possible.
The future of American homeownership growth depends heavily on the success of Hispanic
households in achieving sustainable homeownership. Weakening CRA incentives at a time of
persistent affordability challenges would be inconsistent with both the intent of the statute and
the nation's broader economic interests.
IV. CRA Evaluations Should Continue to Reflect Local Community Needs
The strength of the CRA lies in its recognition that credit needs vary by community.
NAHREP supports maintaining an examination framework that recognizes local conditions and
rewards institutions that respond to unique community needs through innovative and responsive
lending products, investments, and community partnerships.
CRA evaluations should continue to recognize activities that support:
•
Down payment assistance.
•
Affordable mortgage products.
•
Housing counseling programs.
•
Financial education initiatives.
•
Housing supply investments.
•
Community development partnerships.
•
First-generation homebuyer programs.
Community-based organizations and local stakeholders are often best positioned to identify
barriers to homeownership and access to credit. The agencies should continue encouraging banks
to work collaboratively with community organizations that possess direct knowledge of local
housing market conditions.
Community-needs discussions should draw on residents and local mortgage brokers, real estate
professionals, housing counselors, and nonprofit organizations working directly with
 underserved households. Their firsthand experience with both successful homebuyers and people
unable to obtain financing can help identify recurring product-access, affordability,
documentation, and language barriers and practical solutions. This input should complement
broader community evidence and reflect local needs. Accurate multilingual resources, qualified
interpretation, and culturally responsive homebuyer education can help eligible households
understand and use available programs.
V. CRA Should Encourage Partnerships That Expand Hispanic
Homeownership
Many Hispanic households pursuing homeownership today are first-generation homebuyers
navigating the mortgage process for the first time. In 2025, 64% of Hispanic homebuyers were
Millennials or Generation Z, with an average buying age of 31 years old. Partnerships between
financial institutions and trusted community organizations often play a critical role in helping
these families successfully prepare for and sustain homeownership.
NAHREP urges the agencies to continue providing favorable CRA consideration for partnerships
with:
•
HUD-approved housing counseling agencies.
•
Community development financial institutions.
•
Minority-serving nonprofit organizations.
•
Community-based homeownership programs.
•
Organizations advancing financial capability and housing access.
These partnerships help ensure that mortgage lending is accompanied by education, support, and
housing counseling that improve long-term outcomes for both borrowers and lenders.
Expanding access through the wholesale channel
The agencies should encourage banks to make their CRA-eligible products more widely
available through the wholesale channel. A significant share of the boots-on-the-ground
mortgage originators serving the communities where they live and work are independent
mortgage brokers rather than bank employees. When a wholesale lender underwrites and funds a
broker-originated loan directly, in its own name, that lending reflects the bank's own qualifying
activity and should be eligible for CRA consideration on the same basis as any other loan the
bank funds. Expanding wholesale access to CRA products can increase their reach and
utilization, helping more Hispanic households and other underserved borrowers achieve
homeownership through affordable financing.
In the wholesale channel, the broker originates and processes the loan but does not fund it. The
lender underwrites the loan, makes the credit decision, and funds it directly at closing. Because
the bank is the funding institution and bears the lending decision, loans originated through
 approved wholesale broker relationships are appropriately attributed to that bank for CRA
purposes.
Any CRA consideration should remain tied to the covered institution's own underwriting,
funding, and qualifying activity under applicable rules. This recommendation does not seek to
extend federal CRA obligations to mortgage brokers, who do not fund loans. It also does not
extend to loans a bank purchases after closing through correspondent arrangements, where the
funding decision was made by another institution; CRA consideration should continue to reflect
only the covered institution's direct underwriting and funding activity, whether through retail,
broker, or wholesale channels.
Conclusion
The Community Reinvestment Act remains one of the nation's most effective tools for promoting
access to credit, expanding homeownership opportunities, and supporting economic mobility.
NAHREP appreciates the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and reduce unnecessary burden.
However, any modernization of the CRA framework must preserve the law's fundamental
purpose: ensuring that banks meaningfully serve the credit needs of their communities,
particularly those communities that have historically faced barriers to accessing capital and
mortgage financing.
For the reasons outlined above, NAHREP respectfully urges the FDIC and OCC to:
1. Maintain a strong emphasis on mortgage lending and sustainable homeownership.
2. Explicitly recognize ECOA-authorized Special Purpose Credit Programs as qualifying
CRA activities.
3. Reconsider the proposed increases in small and intermediate bank asset thresholds.
4. Preserve accountability and transparency for institutions with significant market
presence.
5. Continue encouraging partnerships that expand responsible homeownership
opportunities.
6. Ensure CRA examinations remain focused on the needs of local communities and
working families.
7. Encourage broader access to bank-funded affordable mortgage programs through the
wholesale channel, recognizing that loans a bank underwrites and funds directly through
approved broker relationships reflect the institution's own qualifying activity under CRA.
As Hispanic households continue to drive future homeownership growth in the United States,
preserving strong CRA incentives for responsible mortgage lending is both a community
imperative and an economic necessity.
Thank you for your consideration of these comments.
 Respectfully submitted,
Gary Acosta
Co-Founder & CEO
NAHREP

 SPCPs provide lenders with a lawful mechanism to address documented barriers faced by
economically disadvantaged populations while maintaining safe and sound lending standards.
Recent federal findings demonstrate the significant potential of these programs. According to the
Federal Housing Finance Agency, SPCPs supported by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac helped
nearly 58,000 economically disadvantaged borrowers access homeownership between 2022 and
2024 and generated approximately $17.2 billion in economic impact.
NAHREP therefore urges the agencies to explicitly include:
"Programs authorized under 15 U.S.C. §1691(c)(1), (2), or (3)"
within the non-exhaustive list of civic assistance and qualifying community development
activities. This change would align CRA regulations with ECOA, provide certainty to lenders,
and encourage innovative approaches to expanding sustainable homeownership opportunities in
underserved communities.
As Hispanic households continue to face affordability challenges and wealth gaps, SPCPs
represent one of the most practical and effective tools available to responsibly expand access to
credit.
The agencies should encourage banks to assess opportunities to make lawful SPCPs, affordable
mortgage products, and down payment assistance reasonably accessible through the wholesale
channel, where independent mortgage brokers originate loans that the bank itself underwrites and
funds directly. Clear eligibility guidance, workable underwriting and purchase processes, and
partner training can improve program reach. Availability should remain subject to applicable
law, program requirements, and appropriate oversight; this recommendation does not require
every program to be offered through every channel.
III. Proposed Asset Threshold Increases Risk Weakening CRA Accountability
and Reducing Investment in Underserved Communities
NAHREP is deeply concerned that the proposal to substantially increase the asset thresholds for
small and intermediate banks may weaken CRA accountability and reduce investment in
underserved communities.
The proposal would classify institutions with less than $1 billion in assets as small banks and
institutions with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion as intermediate banks. As a result,
many institutions currently subject to more rigorous CRA evaluation standards would receive
reduced examination requirements and fewer CRA investment and reporting obligations.
While NAHREP supports efforts to reduce unnecessary regulatory burden, burden reduction
cannot come at the expense of CRA's central purpose. Congress did not enact the CRA to
 minimize compliance responsibilities. Congress enacted the CRA to ensure that banks maintain a
continuing and affirmative obligation to help meet the credit needs of the communities they
serve.
We are concerned that the proposed threshold increases could significantly reduce incentives for
institutions to maintain strong performance in:
•
Mortgage lending.
•
Community development financing.
•
Affordable housing initiatives.
•
Homebuyer education programs.
•
Community-based partnerships.
•
First-time homebuyer assistance efforts.
•
Pre-purchase housing counseling.
•
Housing counseling for distressed loans.
This concern is particularly significant for Latino communities.
Hispanic households accounted for nearly 93% of new household formation in 2025, yet Latino
families continue to face challenges related to down payment accumulation, affordability, credit
access, and housing supply constraints. CRA-driven investments have played an important role
in helping lenders develop products and partnerships that address these barriers. A reduction in
CRA accountability risks reversing progress at precisely the moment when expanding
sustainable homeownership opportunities is most needed.
NAHREP is especially concerned that institutions with several billion dollars in assets could
receive substantially lighter CRA treatment despite maintaining meaningful influence within
local housing and credit markets. Banks of this size possess substantial capacity to originate
mortgage loans, support affordable housing production, invest in community development
initiatives, and implement innovative lending programs.
The agencies should carefully evaluate whether the proposed threshold changes could diminish
incentives for these activities.
Accordingly, NAHREP recommends that the agencies:
•
Reconsider the proposed increases in the small and intermediate bank asset thresholds.
•
Publish a comprehensive analysis of how many institutions and communities would be
affected.
•
Evaluate the likely impacts on mortgage lending, homeownership programs, and
community development activity.
•
Consider a narrower and more incremental adjustment to the thresholds.
 •
Retain meaningful transparency and reporting requirements even for banks receiving
regulatory relief.
If threshold increases are ultimately adopted, institutions benefiting from reduced examination
obligations should still be required to demonstrate meaningful responsiveness to local credit
needs through mortgage lending and community development activities.
Institutions receiving regulatory relief should continue to demonstrate meaningful mortgage
responsiveness, including through qualifying activity originated via the wholesale channel.
Proportionate transparency should help identify whether access to affordable programs and
assistance declines in affected communities, using existing reliable information where possible.
The future of American homeownership growth depends heavily on the success of Hispanic
households in achieving sustainable homeownership. Weakening CRA incentives at a time of
persistent affordability challenges would be inconsistent with both the intent of the statute and
the nation's broader economic interests.
IV. CRA Evaluations Should Continue to Reflect Local Community Needs
The strength of the CRA lies in its recognition that credit needs vary by community.
NAHREP supports maintaining an examination framework that recognizes local conditions and
rewards institutions that respond to unique community needs through innovative and responsive
lending products, investments, and community partnerships.
CRA evaluations should continue to recognize activities that support:
•
Down payment assistance.
•
Affordable mortgage products.
•
Housing counseling programs.
•
Financial education initiatives.
•
Housing supply investments.
•
Community development partnerships.
•
First-generation homebuyer programs.
Community-based organizations and local stakeholders are often best positioned to identify
barriers to homeownership and access to credit. The agencies should continue encouraging banks
to work collaboratively with community organizations that possess direct knowledge of local
housing market conditions.
Community-needs discussions should draw on residents and local mortgage brokers, real estate
professionals, housing counselors, and nonprofit organizations working directly with
 underserved households. Their firsthand experience with both successful homebuyers and people
unable to obtain financing can help identify recurring product-access, affordability,
documentation, and language barriers and practical solutions. This input should complement
broader community evidence and reflect local needs. Accurate multilingual resources, qualified
interpretation, and culturally responsive homebuyer education can help eligible households
understand and use available programs.
V. CRA Should Encourage Partnerships That Expand Hispanic
Homeownership
Many Hispanic households pursuing homeownership today are first-generation homebuyers
navigating the mortgage process for the first time. In 2025, 64% of Hispanic homebuyers were
Millennials or Generation Z, with an average buying age of 31 years old. Partnerships between
financial institutions and trusted community organizations often play a critical role in helping
these families successfully prepare for and sustain homeownership.
NAHREP urges the agencies to continue providing favorable CRA consideration for partnerships
with:
•
HUD-approved housing counseling agencies.
•
Community development financial institutions.
•
Minority-serving nonprofit organizations.
•
Community-based homeownership programs.
•
Organizations advancing financial capability and housing access.
These partnerships help ensure that mortgage lending is accompanied by education, support, and
housing counseling that improve long-term outcomes for both borrowers and lenders.
Expanding access through the wholesale channel
The agencies should encourage banks to make their CRA-eligible products more widely
available through the wholesale channel. A significant share of the boots-on-the-ground
mortgage originators serving the communities where they live and work are independent
mortgage brokers rather than bank employees. When a wholesale lender underwrites and funds a
broker-originated loan directly, in its own name, that lending reflects the bank's own qualifying
activity and should be eligible for CRA consideration on the same basis as any other loan the
bank funds. Expanding wholesale access to CRA products can increase their reach and
utilization, helping more Hispanic households and other underserved borrowers achieve
homeownership through affordable financing.
In the wholesale channel, the broker originates and processes the loan but does not fund it. The
lender underwrites the loan, makes the credit decision, and funds it directly at closing. Because
the bank is the funding institution and bears the lending decision, loans originated through
 approved wholesale broker relationships are appropriately attributed to that bank for CRA
purposes.
Any CRA consideration should remain tied to the covered institution's own underwriting,
funding, and qualifying activity under applicable rules. This recommendation does not seek to
extend federal CRA obligations to mortgage brokers, who do not fund loans. It also does not
extend to loans a bank purchases after closing through correspondent arrangements, where the
funding decision was made by another institution; CRA consideration should continue to reflect
only the covered institution's direct underwriting and funding activity, whether through retail,
broker, or wholesale channels.
Conclusion
The Community Reinvestment Act remains one of the nation's most effective tools for promoting
access to credit, expanding homeownership opportunities, and supporting economic mobility.
NAHREP appreciates the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and reduce unnecessary burden.
However, any modernization of the CRA framework must preserve the law's fundamental
purpose: ensuring that banks meaningfully serve the credit needs of their communities,
particularly those communities that have historically faced barriers to accessing capital and
mortgage financing.
For the reasons outlined above, NAHREP respectfully urges the FDIC and OCC to:
1. Maintain a strong emphasis on mortgage lending and sustainable homeownership.
2. Explicitly recognize ECOA-authorized Special Purpose Credit Programs as qualifying
CRA activities.
3. Reconsider the proposed increases in small and intermediate bank asset thresholds.
4. Preserve accountability and transparency for institutions with significant market
presence.
5. Continue encouraging partnerships that expand responsible homeownership
opportunities.
6. Ensure CRA examinations remain focused on the needs of local communities and
working families.
7. Encourage broader access to bank-funded affordable mortgage programs through the
wholesale channel, recognizing that loans a bank underwrites and funds directly through
approved broker relationships reflect the institution's own qualifying activity under CRA.
As Hispanic households continue to drive future homeownership growth in the United States,
preserving strong CRA incentives for responsible mortgage lending is both a community
imperative and an economic necessity.
Thank you for your consideration of these comments.
 Respectfully submitted,
Gary Acosta
Co-Founder & CEO
NAHREP

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The Utah Bankers Association ("UBA") appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency's and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's proposed amendments to the
Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA") regulations ("Proposal"). UBA is a supporting signer of the American
Bankers Association's comment letter and endorses its recommendations. UBA submits this separate comment to
provide Utah-specific market information illustrating a significant unintended consequence of the Proposal's
alternatives for considering community development ("CD") activity outside a bank's assessment areas.
Utah is home to an unusual concentration of banks that serve regional or national markets while
maintaining only one or a small number of banking offices and facility-based assessment areas. Many operate
under approved strategic plans or are evaluated as wholesale or limited purpose banks under the CD test. Others
are large banks with specialized, predominantly national business models. Their limited physical footprints can
concentrate institution-wide CRA expectations in the Salt Lake City–Murray, Utah Metropolitan Statistical Area
("Salt Lake City MSA"), even though their customers, lending, deposits, and community relationships extend
nationwide.
UBA supports consideration of qualifying CD activity outside assessment areas. Geographic-flexibility
standards, however, should not concentrate institution-wide expectations in one market without regard to local
needs, available opportunities, or the aggregate expectations imposed on all banks serving that market. Such a
result would affect not only limited-footprint institutions, but also community, regional, and national branch-
based banks competing to serve Utah communities and underserved markets outside Utah that benefit from
broader CD activity.
 Page 2 of 4

I. Utah's Banking Market Requires a Business-Model-Sensitive CRA Framework
The June 30, 2026 FDIC Deposit Market Share Report identifies 57 institutions in the Salt Lake City
MSA. Small banks would not be subject to the Proposal's CD thresholds. Among the intermediate and large
banks that would have CD responsibilities, however, many of the institutions with the largest potential Tier 1
capital-based thresholds are Utah-headquartered or otherwise limited-footprint banks serving regional or national
markets.
The distinction between these institutions and conventional branch-based banks is important. A branch-
based bank operating across multiple markets ordinarily would have only a portion of its Tier 1 capital allocated
to the Salt Lake City MSA based on its deposits in the market. By contrast, a nationwide bank with one Utah
office and no other deposit-taking offices may have all or nearly all its Tier 1 capital allocated to a single Utah
assessment area, even though its operations are national in scope.
The CRA framework has long recognized that wholesale and limited purpose banks frequently draw
resources from and serve areas well beyond their immediate communities. The CD test provides a rigorous and
comparable evaluation of those institutions without forcing national or specialized business models into a
geographically concentrated retail test. Strategic plans likewise should remain a flexible alternative for institutions
whose products, delivery channels, customers, or geographic footprints are not represented accurately by the
standard size-based tests.
UBA therefore urges the Agencies to retain the wholesale and limited purpose designations and the CD
test, preserve strategic plans as a genuinely flexible alternative, and evaluate each institution through a method
that reflects its business model and performance context.
II. Option 1 Would Create an Aggregate Market-Capacity Problem in Salt Lake City
In Question 34, the Proposal requests comment on two alternatives for considering CD activity outside
assessment areas. Under Option 1, a bank generally would need to satisfy annual assessment-area thresholds
based on Tier 1 capital before receiving consideration for activity elsewhere. The threshold would be 1.25% for
wholesale, limited purpose, and intermediate banks. Large banks would be subject to separate 0.625% thresholds
for CD lending and CD investments, or 1.25% to satisfy both components.
UBA analyzed the Proposal using the June 30, 2026 FDIC Deposit Market Share Report and June 30,
2026 Call Report Tier 1 capital data. The analysis allocates each bank's Tier 1 capital to the Salt Lake City MSA
based on the percentage of its deposits assigned to the market. It excludes small banks because their examination
method would not impose a CD threshold, as well as institutions with no allocated market deposits or no
applicable threshold.
The analysis identifies 42 intermediate or large banks with a potential threshold: 12 banks subject to a
combined 1.25% threshold through the CD, intermediate-bank, or strategic-plan framework, and 30 large banks
subject to the two 0.625% components. Their aggregate allocated Tier 1 capital is approximately $155.8 billion.
Applying a combined 1.25% threshold produces an aggregate annual amount of $1,947,512,000, appropriately
rounded to $1.95 billion.
The concentration is even more pronounced among the institutions with the largest calculated amounts.
Twenty-one institutions account for approximately $1.93 billion of the aggregate total. Only three of those
institutions appear to be conventional branch-based banks; the remaining 18 principally serve regional or national
markets through limited Utah office footprints. The largest potential amounts are associated with Utah-
headquartered national or specialized banks and Goldman Sachs Bank USA, which has a significant Utah
presence but is headquartered elsewhere.
The $1.95 billion figure does not measure Utah's annual CD needs or the available inventory of
qualifying transactions. It results from allocating bank capital based principally on deposit and office geography.
 Page 3 of 4

The Proposal does not demonstrate that such an allocation reliably corresponds to the annual amount, timing,
type, or financing structure of qualifying opportunities in a particular market.
Utah has substantial needs, including affordable housing, small-business financing, community services,
and rural development. Those needs warrant sustained bank engagement. But a requirement that numerous
institutions collectively place approximately $1.95 billion each year into one metropolitan market before
receiving predictable consideration elsewhere could exceed the market's capacity to generate additional
responsive transactions on that schedule. A capital formula does not create additional developments, tax-credit
allocations, qualified sponsors, public subsidies, or finance-ready projects. Nor does it account for the multi-year
timing of complex affordable-housing, economic-development, and community-facility transactions.
III. The Potential Harm Extends to Branch-Based Banks and Communities Outside Utah
The consequences would not be confined to specialized or limited-footprint institutions. Utah community
and regional banks, as well as national banks with substantial Utah branch networks, would compete for
responsive CD opportunities alongside institutions whose national capital bases are allocated disproportionately to
the Salt Lake City MSA.
Increased competition may not produce a corresponding increase in meaningful community benefit. It
instead could concentrate financing in a finite pipeline of large, readily scalable transactions; distort pricing
without increasing the number of viable projects; disadvantage smaller, rural, innovative, or layered-finance
transactions; and make it more difficult for branch-based institutions to identify opportunities proportionate to
their local operations and longstanding community relationships.
This result could be particularly counterproductive for traditional branch-based banks. Those institutions
maintain broad local obligations and ongoing relationships throughout Utah. Requiring them to compete against
the institution-wide capacity of numerous national, single-office, or limited-office banks could crowd out activity
that otherwise would reflect the branch-based banks' local knowledge, deposit presence, and continuing
engagement.
The harm also extends beyond Utah. If banks cannot determine before an examination whether responsive
activity outside their assessment areas will receive consideration, they may reduce commitments in rural areas,
CRA deserts, Native communities, and underserved markets in other states. The Proposal therefore could shift
activity toward a regulatory hotspot without increasing the total amount of responsive CD financing, while
reducing capital available where unmet needs are greater and fewer banks are present.
IV. The Final Rule Should Preserve Performance-Based Geographic Flexibility
UBA recommends retaining the current performance-context approach under which a bank may receive
consideration for qualifying activity in broader statewide, regional, or national areas after adequately addressing
needs within its assessment areas. That standard appropriately prioritizes local responsibility while recognizing
that community needs and effective financing structures do not end at assessment-area boundaries.
If the Agencies conclude that greater specificity is necessary, the final rule should provide an objective
and predictable safe harbor. For example, a bank receiving a Satisfactory or Outstanding rating in an assessment
area during its most recent CRA evaluation should be able to receive consideration for qualifying activity outside
that assessment area during the next evaluation period. Such a standard would preserve local accountability while
giving banks and community partners sufficient certainty to plan multi-year transactions.
At a minimum, the Agencies should not adopt a capital-based threshold without conducting and
publishing an empirical market-capacity analysis. That analysis should assess the cumulative thresholds
applicable to all banks sharing an assessment area, distinguish conventional branch-based banks from regional or
national limited-footprint institutions, and compare the resulting expectations with demonstrated community
needs and the volume and types of qualifying opportunities in the market.
 Page 4 of 4

UBA respectfully requests that the final rule:
1. retain the existing wholesale and limited purpose designations and the CD test;
2. preserve strategic plans as a flexible, voluntary evaluation method rather than a mandatory substitute for
wholesale or limited purpose treatment;
3. permit strategic plans to omit retail lending goals or other components that would not meaningfully
measure the bank's CRA responsiveness;
4. preserve consideration for responsive CD loans, investments, and services in broader statewide, regional,
and national areas;
5. apply performance context, including the bank's business model, office footprint and capacity, local
market capacity, and the aggregate activity expected of other banks in the same assessment area; and
6. avoid standards that require an institution to alter its lawful business model, product mix, customer base,
or geographic footprint to fit an evaluation method designed for a conventional branch-based bank.

Conclusion
Utah demonstrates why CRA regulations must account for both individual bank performance and
aggregate market effects. The Salt Lake City MSA contains an unusual concentration of nationally operating
banks whose institution-wide capital may be allocated to one or two Utah offices. Under Option 1, 42
intermediate and large banks could collectively face approximately $1.95 billion in annual local CD thresholds
before receiving predictable consideration for activity elsewhere, with approximately $1.93 billion attributable to
21 institutions, only three of which appear to be conventional branch-based banks.
That result could exceed the available pipeline of qualifying transactions, distort competition,
disadvantage branch-based banks serving Utah communities, and divert financing from rural and underserved
markets in Utah and nationwide. The Agencies should preserve the current performance-based geographic-
flexibility standard, retain business-model-sensitive evaluation methods, and ensure that any new standard reflects
demonstrated community needs, market capacity, and performance context rather than capital concentration
alone.
UBA appreciates the Agencies' consideration of these comments.
Sincerely,


Howard Headlee
President & CEO
Utah Bankers Association

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill,
On behalf of the National Community Stabilization Trust (NCST) and the Homeownership Alliance, we
appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)
regulations.1 NCST is a national nonprofit organization dedicated to restoring distressed single-family homes,
strengthening neighborhoods, and expanding affordable homeownership opportunities.2 The Homeownership
Alliance, established by NCST in 2021, is a practitioner-led coalition of Community Development Financial
Institutions (CDFIs) and nonprofit housing developers working across the nation to build wealth and housing
stability for low- and moderate-income (LMI) families.
As organizations on the frontlines of addressing the nation's shortage of an estimated 3-4 million homes, our
primary focus is expanding the supply of affordable single-family for-sale housing.3 While we support regulatory
efforts that increase clarity and objectivity under CRA, these proposed revisions risk substantially reducing the
bank capital available and incentivize to support single-family affordable homeownership development.
To protect and expand affordable homeownership opportunities in underserved communities, we urge your
offices to address the following critical areas in the final rule:
Protecting Local Community Development (CD) Capital by Maintaining Bank Assessment Obligations
Proposed increases to asset thresholds—such as categorizing banks under $10 billion in assets as small
banks—could eliminate community development expectations for more than 1,500 institutions, representing
36% of all banks nationwide. Intermediate and regional banks are important financing partners for
Homeownership Alliance members, providing essential acquisition, construction, and line-of-credit financing
3 Recent estimates of the national housing shortage range from approximately 3.7 million to 4.0 million homes. Freddie Mac estimated
a shortage of 3.7 million units as of the third quarter of 2024, while Realtor.com estimated a gap of 4.03 million homes in 2025.
2 About, (2026). The National Community Stabilization Trust.
1 Proposed Rule, Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, (August 12, 2026). Federal Register.

needed to acquire distressed properties, undertake complex rehabs, and construct new for-sale homes.
Removing CD obligations for these institutions could significantly diminish access to capital for regional
single-family housing developers, particularly in smaller markets and rural areas where local banks are the
primary source of credit.
Safeguarding NMTC and Single-Family Development Capital
Unlike rental housing supported by tax credits like the Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC), affordable
for-sale housing lacks a dedicated federal tax credit, making flexible subsidies and equity mechanisms
essential. The New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) and specialized single-family development loans are critical
tools that enable mission-driven developers to address the severe value and affordability gaps that can occur
when development costs exceed market appraisals in distressed neighborhoods. For CRA-motivated banks,
the proposed rule threatens to disincentivize current and potential bank investment in NMTC-backed
homeownership projects and single-family production funds by shifting CRA evaluation weight away from
community development investments.
Preserving Operational and Capacity Support for Nonprofit Developers
Mission-driven nonprofit housing developers operate on tight margins while working to deliver affordable
homes to LMI families. CRA-qualifying grants provide critical flexible funding for activities such as capacity
building and housing counseling costs that enable local developers to sustain and scale single-family
production. The proposed rule's restrictive eligible-use definitions, administrative fee caps, and heightened
documentation burdens could discourage banks from providing the flexible operational support that nonprofit
developers rely on to build capacity and deliver affordable housing.
Balancing Geographic Flexibility with Assessment Area Accountability
We support introducing geographic flexibility to encourage CRA-motivated capital in historically underserved
"CRA deserts," persistent poverty areas, and Tribal lands where homeownership capital remains limited.
However, this flexibility must include clear guardrails to ensure that institutions continue to meet the needs of
their primary assessment areas. Banks should remain incentivized to meet the single-family homeownership
and neighborhood stabilization needs of LMI communities within their primary service footprint before receiving
CRA consideration for community development investments outside those areas.
At a time when LMI buyers face unprecedented affordability barriers, CRA must remain a strong, active
mechanism for steering private capital into single-family home production and neighborhood revitalization. We
urge the OCC and FDIC to adjust the proposed framework to ensure it strengthens, rather than weakens, the
public-private partnerships that make affordable homeownership possible.
Thank you for your leadership and consideration of our recommendations. If you have any questions or would
like additional information, please contact NCST's Policy Department at policy@ncst.org. We look forward to
continuing our work with your agencies to advance affordable homeownership across the country.
Sincerely,
National Community Stabilization Trust (NCST)
The Homeownership Alliance

CohnReznick appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform Community Reinvestment
Act (CRA) regulations. CohnReznick is a national accounting and advisory firm with a longstanding
leadership position in the affordable housing industry. For more than four decades, we have combined
deep technical expertise with active advocacy on behalf of affordable housing initiatives. This unique
blend of practitioner experience and industry leadership has enabled CohnReznick to play a significant
role in advancing the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) program and the broader community
development finance sector.
CohnReznick was an active contributor to the development of industry comment letters submitted by the
Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition ("AHTCC") and the ACTION Campaign, and we support the
recommendations contained therein. We submit these additional comments to provide market-based
observations drawn from our extensive work across the affordable housing industry, including insights
from our annual LIHTC Equity Market Survey1 and biennial LIHTC Industry Study2.
A stable and predictable CRA framework is critical to the continued production and preservation of
affordable housing. Based on CohnReznick's annual LIHTC Equity Market Survey, approximately $30.1
billion of housing credit equity was invested in affordable housing transactions during 2025, representing
a substantial source of capital for affordable housing development nationwide. Our survey further found
that bank investors accounted for approximately 81% of total LIHTC equity investment volume, reaffirming
that CRA-motivated institutions remain the primary source of affordable housing equity capital. Banks

1 CohnReznick and Tax Credit Advisor, Housing Tax Credit Monitor, Mar. 2026, https://www.taxcreditadvisor.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/03/TCA-Housing-Tax-Credit-Monitor_March-2026.pdf.
2 CohnReznick, 2025 Affordable Housing Credit Study, https://creditstudy.cohnreznick.com/credit-study.
 make these investments not only to manage their tax liabilities; but also because the full CRA
examination for large banks includes a distinct investment test.
History demonstrates the importance of maintaining a broad and active CRA-motivated investor base.
During the 2008-2009 financial crisis, many investors reduced or withdrew from the LIHTC market,
causing equity investment volume to decline by approximately 50 percent and significantly constraining
affordable housing production. As banks continued to invest under the CRA framework and market
confidence returned, equity volumes recovered and housing production resumed. This experience
highlighted the critical role that consistent participation by CRA-motivated investors plays in sustaining
affordable housing development.
At the same time, affordable housing needs continue to grow. The National Low Income Housing
Coalition estimates a nationwide shortage of approximately 7.1 million affordable and available rental
homes for extremely low-income households and reports that only 35 affordable and available units exist
for every 100 extremely low-income renter households3. No state currently has an adequate supply of
affordable housing for this population.
Given these realities, the primary policy challenge is not generating demand for affordable housing
investment, but ensuring sufficient private capital is available to convert that demand into housing
production and preservation. We are concerned that OCC and FDIC's proposal to reclassify banks with
assets ranging from $1.649 billion to $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than large banks subject to
the full CRA examination, including the investment test, could lead to less equity supply, lower pricing on
credits and less housing produced. According to the AHTCC survey that CohnReznick contributed to,

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
The Low Income Investment Fund (LIIF) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed
changes to the regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).
LIIF is a certified Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) that mobilizes capital and
partnerships to expand access to funding for more Americans. Since 1984, LIIF has deployed more than
$3.8 billion to serve more than 2.6 million people in communities across the country through investments
in affordable housing, early care and education, and community facilities.
As a national CDFI, LIIF has decades of experience working with CRA-motivated banks across both the
community development lending and investment components of the CRA framework. We rely on bank
partners to provide hundreds of millions of dollars in financing to serve low- and moderate-income (LMI)
people and communities, as well as critical grant funding that supports our ability to deliver impact. This
capital enables public-private partnerships and helps finance critical community assets.
LIIF supports efforts to make CRA clearer, more consistent, and workable for banks of different sizes and
business models. However, we are concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule, taken together,
could significantly reduce the incentives for banks to provide the lending, investment, grants, and other
resources that communities need. CRA has played a critical role for nearly 50 years in bringing private
capital into LMI communities and strengthening partnerships between banks and community
development organizations. In 2024 alone, CRA incentivized more than $430 billion in loans and
investments in LMI communities.
At a time when communities face significant affordable housing shortages, rising costs, limited public
resources, and continued need for child care, community facilities, and economic development, it is
critical that changes to CRA strengthen rather than diminish this source of private capital.
We respectfully urge the agencies to consider the following recommendations:

 I. Maintain meaningful CRA responsibilities for banks of all sizes
We are concerned that raising the asset thresholds used to determine how banks are evaluated under CRA
could substantially reduce the number of institutions with meaningful community development
responsibilities.
Banks of all sizes play an important role in meeting community development needs. In particular, smaller
and midsize banks can be critical sources of capital in rural communities, smaller markets, and other
places where there may be fewer financial institutions or community development partners.
Raising the "small bank" threshold to institutions with less than $10 billion in assets could remove more
than 1,500 banks—approximately 36 percent of all banks—from meaningful community development
expectations. These institutions reported nearly $27 billion in community development loans in 2024,
representing approximately 35 percent of all community development loans made that year.
From LIIF's perspective, the concern is not simply the number of institutions subject to CRA
examinations. It is the potential loss of incentives for banks to seek out and maintain relationships with
CDFIs and other community development organizations.
LIIF currently has a bank lender that provides us with a $20 million below-market-rate loan. This product
enables LIIF to deploy more affordable capital to underserved communities and supports projects that
may not otherwise be financially feasible. While the bank's CRA obligations are an important incentive
for providing this financing, the benefits extend well beyond regulatory compliance. The below-market-
rate allows LIIF to stretch its resources further, finance more projects, and increase the reach and impact
of its investments. Under the proposed changes to CRA asset thresholds, this bank would no longer be
subject to its current CRA requirements and would likely have less incentive to renew the loan when it
matures. The loss of this below-market capital could significantly affect the communities LIIF serves and
the projects financed through this loan.
The $20 million loan is currently deployed across a range of projects, including:

$4.4 million loan to a startup charter school to support the development of a new 520-seat K–5
charter school in Douglas County, Georgia.

$1.3 million loan to a Community Development Corporation for the acquisition of a 72-unit
scattered-site property in Houston, Texas.

$3.25 million loan to a nonprofit affordable housing developer for the acquisition of a 3.53-
acre vacant parcel in Manteca, California. The site will be developed into a 100-unit affordable
multifamily project serving households earning between 30% and 60% of Area Median Income
(AMI).
These projects illustrate the types of investments supported by the below-market capital LIIF receives
from bank partners. Like many CDFIs, LIIF provides financing to borrowers and projects that can face
challenges directly accessing conventional financing from large mainstream banks.
If the proposed CRA changes result in this bank being classified as a "small bank" and no longer subject
to its current CRA requirements, LIIF could lose access to an important source of below-market capital.
This would not only affect LIIF's ability to finance similar projects in the future, but could also make it
 more difficult for borrowers in undercapitalized communities to access the capital they need to develop
affordable housing, schools, and other community-serving projects.
We therefore urge the agencies to reconsider the proposed asset thresholds and ensure that banks of all
sizes continue to have meaningful incentives to support community development lending and investment.
II. Preserve a strong and balanced role for community development lending and investment
We support the proposal's recognition of the importance of lending, but we are concerned that placing
greater emphasis on lending could inadvertently diminish the role of community development
investments.
Loans and investments are not interchangeable forms of capital. Different community development needs
require different forms of financing, and investments can play a critical role in projects that cannot be
supported through conventional lending alone. Equity investments and other forms of capital support
affordable housing through the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, economic development through the
New Markets Tax Credit, CDFI financing, and other community development activities.
LIIF's experience demonstrates the importance of maintaining this flexibility. CRA-motivated bank
investments enable LIIF to leverage private capital and deploy financing into projects and communities
that may otherwise face significant barriers to accessing capital. In many cases, the ability of a CDFI to
structure a financing package depends on having access to multiple forms of capital, including
investments, lending, grants, and other flexible resources.
The final rule should therefore preserve a strong and balanced role for both community development
lending and investment. CRA should recognize the value of the full range of capital structures that enable
CDFIs and other community development organizations to finance affordable housing, child care
facilities, community facilities, and other critical community needs.
III. Protect CRA consideration for grants and flexible capital
LIIF is also concerned about proposed changes that would narrow the types of grants eligible for CRA
consideration and impose additional restrictions and documentation requirements.
Grants and flexible capital are particularly important to CDFIs and community-based organizations
because they can support activities that cannot be financed through lending alone. Flexible grant capital
can help organizations build capacity, provide technical assistance, develop projects, cover
predevelopment costs, de-risk investments, and leverage additional public and private capital.
For LIIF, grant funding from CRA-motivated bank partners has been an important component of our
ability to maximize the impact of our lending and investment activities. Grants can help make projects
feasible and enable CDFIs to serve borrowers, projects, and communities that may otherwise be difficult
to reach.
We urge the agencies to preserve CRA consideration for grants and contributions that advance eligible
community development purposes and respond to demonstrated community needs. The final rule should
recognize that operating support and capacity building are often essential to achieving measurable
community development outcomes and should avoid overly prescriptive requirements that could reduce
the availability of this critical capital.

IV. Preserve CRA's focus on low- and moderate-income people and communities
Finally, LIIF urges the agencies to maintain a clear and meaningful focus on the LMI people and
communities that CRA was enacted to serve.
CRA has helped address persistent gaps in access to credit and investment by encouraging banks to build
partnerships with organizations that have specialized expertise and relationships in undercapitalized
communities. Through these partnerships, banks have supported affordable housing and homeownership,
small businesses, community facilities, health care, child care, and other essential community needs.
Changes to income targeting, community development definitions, evaluation standards, and other
provisions should not unintentionally shift CRA-motivated capital away from LMI households and
communities. The final rule should preserve a clear connection between CRA obligations and the
communities that continue to experience the greatest barriers to accessing capital.
Conclusion
LIIF supports efforts to create a CRA framework that is clear, consistent, and workable for banks.
However, modernization should not come at the expense of the community development activity that
CRA has helped make possible for nearly 50 years.
LIIF appreciates the agencies' consideration of these comments and looks forward to continuing to work
with the OCC, FDIC, banks, CDFIs, and community partners to ensure that CRA remains a meaningful
tool for bringing private capital to communities across the country.
Sincerely,

Daniel A. Nissenbaum
Chief Executive Officer
Low Income Investment Fund

stages of development. None of these LIHTC investments, representing well over $100

Act.

For nearly half a century, CRA has driven banks to extend private capital financing to local
communities they serve, combating the legacy of redlining, promoting equitable lending,
and facilitating reinvestment in low- and moderate-income places and people. CRA has
spurred lending and investments in homeownership, small businesses, healthcare,

the effect CRA has had on the production of affordable rental housing through the Low-
Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit) program.

The Housing Credit, our nation's most important tool for the production of affordable rental
housing, relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. In fact, approximately 80
percent of equity investments in the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated
bank investors, according to a 2025 study by the accounting firm CohnReznick.1 Banks
make these investments not only to receive the modest return provided by the tax
advantages associated with investing in Housing Credit properties, but also because the
full CRA examination for large banks includes a distinct investment test. Because Housing

If the OCC/FDIC proposal is made final, newly classified intermediate banks would no
