Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Rebuilding Together Philadelphia (RTP) submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller
of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would
significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the
complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before
making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-
income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the
agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.
Rebuilding Together Philadelphia (RTP) provides free, critical home repairs to income-eligible
homeowners, helping long-time residents stay safely and affordably in the homes and
neighborhoods they've anchored for generations. By preserving existing housing stock, RTP
 protects one of the most important sources of family wealth in Philadelphia's legacy
neighborhoods and stabilizes entire blocks against disinvestment and displacement. We direct
public, philanthropic, and financial-institution dollars straight into neighborhood homes.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-
income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both
credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that
have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream
financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia
metro area, from 2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to
LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small
businesses. Banks are key partners in RTP's work, providing grant funding, sponsoring
applications to programs like the Federal Home Loan Bank's Affordable Housing
Program, and contributing employee volunteers to our repair projects. These partnerships
help financial institutions meet their Community Reinvestment Act commitments in a direct,
visible way, channeling capital into low- and moderate-income neighborhoods where it preserves
affordable homeownership and keeps families rooted in their communities.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a
passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote
to community investments and loans and we fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling
instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually,
but under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million – an 80% loss.
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If
regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the
communities they serve, there would be harmful consequences for communities. It is imperative
that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities like ours. Before
finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce
 lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether
communities that have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would be
disproportionately affected.
The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less
demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to
large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business,
community development lending.
A number of banks that operate in Philadelphia will now be considered either intermediate or
small banks under the proposed rule and therefore subject to less rigorous requirements. These
reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development obligations for over 800
banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks across the country, may worsen the
housing crisis by reducing investor interest in buying Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC), and reducing access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers or access to credit for
home repairs.
Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service
test. Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and
information about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this
criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts
from direct evaluation under the service test. As such, examiners would no longer evaluate
whether those products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though
approximately 15% of Philadelphians – over 100,000 households – remain unbanked or
underbanked. Moreover, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, these
households are overwhelmingly low-income, black, or disabled. CRA review of the cost and
features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to address these
disparities by providing affordable products, and it must continue to do so.
For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from
access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely
receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit.
This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-
income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable
mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business
financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small
businesses and other community development.
 The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income
communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-
based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships
with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.
For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology,
accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the
underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources
over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with
limited staff and may not maintain financial records or program documentation in the precise
format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller
organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.

play in supporting community development. If banks pulled back their investment, RTP would
have to serve fewer homeowners, leaving more low-income and elderly residents living with
unsafe conditions like failing roofs, broken heat, and hazardous wiring. Over time, deferred
repairs would push more families toward displacement, tangled title, or tax foreclosure,
eroding generational wealth and destabilizing the very neighborhoods that community
reinvestment is meant to strengthen.

report data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while
the proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Banks
with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report CRA
data on small business loans and community development loans.

to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs
are being met. Local community leaders and elected officials depend on this data for decision
making and for ensuring that the needs of residents are being addressed. This proposed change is
inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and should not be in the
final rule.

● identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
under the proposal;
● quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
● assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
including rural communities and communities of color; and
● consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability.

that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its
impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs
considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
 examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely,

Stefanie F. Seldin, CEO
Rebuilding Together Philadelphia

protections remain especially important in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch

Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. Diamond & Associates (Diamond) is a
skilled, successful provider of development advisory services focused upon the planning,
packaging, financing, structuring, closing, construction, leasing and/or sale of affordable,
multifamily housing development projects. Since 1990, it has supported the development of over
15,000 completed affordable housing units, comprising $2.8 billion in development work, for
low-income seniors, families, and vulnerable populations.

Diamond's clients include national, regional, and local, non-profit developers, for-profits, and
public entities. Diamond has supported affordable housing developments in many states
including Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, New York, Illinois, Iowa, Maryland, Ohio,
Kentucky, and Virginia.

For nearly half a century, CRA has driven banks to extend private capital financing to local
communities they serve, combating the legacy of redlining, promoting equitable lending,
and facilitating reinvestment in low- and moderate-income places and people. CRA has
spurred lending and investments in homeownership, small businesses, healthcare,




diamondandassociates.com

childcare, and other community needs, but nowhere is its impact more pronounced than in
the effect CRA has had on the production of affordable rental housing through the Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit) program.

The Housing Credit, our nation's most important tool for the production of affordable rental
housing, relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. In fact, approximately 80
percent of equity investments in the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated
bank investors, according to a 2025 study by the accounting firm CohnReznick. Banks
make these investments not only to receive the modest return provided by the tax
advantages associated with investing in Housing Credit properties, but also because the
full CRA examination for large banks includes a distinct investment test, which incentives
investment in affordable housing. Since Housing Credit investment yields are typically modest,
large banks often could receive a more substantial yield from making other forms of investment.
However, banks often still choose to invest in Housing Credits because these investments help
banks meet their CRA obligations.

We are concerned that OCC and FDIC's proposal to reclassify banks with assets ranging
from $1.649 billion to $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than large banks, which are
subject to the full CRA examination, including the investment test, could reduce competition in
the Housing Credit equity market and subsequently lead to lower credit pricing and less housing
produced. Of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks, only 256 would maintain that
designation under the proposal—a decline of over 60 percent, according to the National
Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL). This leaves only 6 percent of banks in
the current large bank classification subject to the full CRA exam. According to a survey by the
Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), banks with assets in the $1.649 billion to
$10 billion range invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over the five-year survey
period. Extrapolating these results to the full Housing Credit market, banks in this asset range
invested up to $2 billion in Housing Credit equity over the past five years.

If the OCC/FDIC proposal is made final, newly classified intermediate banks would no
longer need to invest in the low and moderate-income communities they are supposed to
serve because they would no longer be subject to the investment test, despite still having
more general community development obligations as an intermediate-sized bank. This is
because, for various reasons, it is often easier for banks to support community
development activities through lending rather than equity investment.

Moreover, the CRA Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) undercuts recent congressional
action to strengthen and expand the Housing Credit and facilitate more bank investment in
the program. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (also known as the Working Families Tax Cuts
Act) included a substantial increase in Housing Credit authority and expanded the 4
Percent Housing Credit program to increase supply, while the 21st Century ROAD to
Housing Act raised the limit on banks' public welfare investments (PWI) to allow them to
increase their Housing Credit investments. The provision lifting the PWI cap would mostly
impact many of the same banks that would be reclassified as intermediate banks. Thus,
the CRA changes under consideration by the OCC and FDIC could greatly dilute these
legislative accomplishments and undercut congressional goals of providing more




diamondandassociates.com

affordable rental homes.

The consequences of this proposal would be most damaging to smaller communities that
currently benefit from being in the CRA assessment area of one or more large banks, but may no
longer be if the OCC and FDIC change the definition of large bank as proposed. A survey by
AHTCC finds that approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity invested through
syndicators by banks in the $412 million – $10 billion asset range supported rural markets
between 2021 and 2024, indicating that these banks play an outsized role in investing in
smaller communities. Credit pricing for properties in many urban areas—which are more
likely to have at least one and often multiple banks competing to invest in Housing Credit
developments because of overlapping assessment areas—tends to be much higher than
pricing in rural and other smaller communities that are not part of assessment areas for
large banks subject to the investment test.

The Housing Credit plays a role in an overwhelming majority of projects Diamond supports,
which are located in both CRA and non-CRA areas. The credit pricing difference between CRA
and non-CRA areas can be staggering, especially in today's market. Diamond has seen how
CRA-motivated investors are continuing to pay more per credit by a margin of $0.10-$0.20.
Projects in non-CRA areas are currently struggling to attract investment as the market has
tightened, even without these proposed changes in effect. The proposed changes would create
more problems for more projects.

Alternatives to the Primary Proposal

The OCC and FDIC included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new thresholds
for various bank size classifications related to CRA. The first would raise the large bank
asset threshold from $1.649 billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would still have far-
reaching negative consequences compared to the current large bank threshold, but is
substantially less disruptive to Housing Credit investment than the primary proposal to
raise the large bank threshold to $10 billion.

According to AHTCC's survey of bank investment in the Housing Credit, 108 banks would
be reclassified as intermediate banks rather than large banks if the threshold is set at $10
billion, while just 40 would be reclassified as intermediate banks if the large bank threshold
is set at $3.252 billion. Moreover, the banks that would remain subject to the separate
investment test under a $3.252 billion threshold account for approximately 86 percent of
the Housing Credit equity investment by OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks captured in the
AHTCC survey with assets between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.

The second alternative proposal would be far more damaging for affordable rental housing
production than either the primary or first alternative proposals. NAAHL estimates that,
under a $30 billion large bank threshold, 17 states would see the number of large banks
with investment requirements cut by half or more. According to AHTCC, banks with assets
between $10 billion and $30 billion account for more than twice as much Housing Credit
debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.





diamondandassociates.com

Conclusion

Diamond and Associates has seen the impact of CRA firsthand. As noted above, Diamond is
seeing substantial pricing differences from CRA areas to non-CRA areas. In addition, non-CRA
areas are struggling to attract investors, even prior to the changes proposed. Many factors are
contributing to the downturn in the equity market. The federal government should not exacerbate
conditions further by changing CRA for the worse.

We strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand
under the 1995 CRA rule, consistent with the direction the Federal Reserve—the third bank
regulator—appears to be taking. If the OCC and FDIC move forward with changes to CRA
regulations, we strongly urge maintaining the lowest possible threshold for large banks and
adopting policies to strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including
rural and smaller markets.

Sincerely,
Diamond and Associates

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Reinvest Toledo, Inc. submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it
would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given
the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and
FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences
for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the
analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the
current comment deadline by 60-days.
Reinvest Toledo is a 501(c)(3) non-profit community coalition representing nine
neighborhoods and over 30,000 residents in Toledo, Ohio's low to moderate income
(LMI) neighborhoods. Reinvest supports leadership and neighborhood development. We
train community leaders to advocate and apply their new skills to a range of matters that
include youth development and civic engagement, brownfield redevelopment, nuisance
property receivership, tenant advocacy, and community safety. Reinvest equips leaders
with the strategic insight and perspective necessary to make sustainable decisions about
where and how to invest social and financial resources.

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.
There is a lack of analysis of the proposal's effects on LMI communities that have
experienced historic discrimination and divestment.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and
support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination
and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In our
community, from 2010-2024, banks made $4,360,321,000 in CRA qualified mortgage
lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and $2,142,714,000 in CRA qualified
lending to small businesses.

On a local level, banks have provided tens of thousands of vital operational dollars to
support Reinvest Toledo's work.
 3
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1
capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough
to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the
percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the
largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the
OCC and FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these
banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development
loans and investments inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of
annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital,
and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments.3 If each
bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625%
of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined activity
would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1
billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make
their CRA compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set
strategic plan benchmarks for CRA performance well-below historical levels of
community development activity.4
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments
and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be
accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for
communities. For example, in our community, families will struggle to obtain affordable
mortgage credit, first-time homebuyers will face barriers, neighborhoods will continue to
experience divestment, and residents will have even more limited relationships with
mainstream financial institutions. It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize
banks to meet community needs. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze
whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or investment available to

low- and moderate-income communities and whether communities that have experienced

The proposal will result in less community development scrutiny of banks.
The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks
are evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small

Approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation

In Ohio, 20.9% of banks will lose their community development obligations (18 of 86

This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and
moderate-income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to
affordable mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain
responsible small-business financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in
affordable housing, small businesses and other community development.
The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the
CRA obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify
the banks that would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the
communities those institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development

activity that would receive less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be
concentrated in low- and moderate-income communities or communities that have

Toledo already is an underbanked community.
By raising the large-bank threshold to $10 billion, 417 banks would no longer receive the
full large-bank examination, including a separate service test that evaluates branch
delivery systems and banking services. We are concerned that approximately 5,000
branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts would no longer be evaluated as part
of the large-bank CRA service test under the proposal, and more than 4,000 branches in

The proposal would also narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service

this criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings

Our organization works with communities where access to mainstream banking services
remains a serious concern. We recently lost one of the last branches remaining in

For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate
from access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families
can safely receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain

We are therefore concerned that under the proposal, examiners will no longer evaluate
whether banks that are still subject to the service test offer affordable checking and

performance in CRA evaluations, the proposal eliminates incentives for banks to offer
basic products that help unbanked and underbanked households. Before finalizing these
changes, the agencies should identify which communities would receive less scrutiny of
bank branches and services, determine whether the effects would fall disproportionately
on low- and moderate-income communities or communities of color, and explain why the
changes are justified despite those consequences.
The impact on nonprofits will be significant and harmful.
We are extremely concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development
grants and nonprofit organizations.
Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial
counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based
services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep
relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect
costs and new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for
smaller organizations.11 For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be
unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses
are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also
have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition,
many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain
financial records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would
need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations
are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and
partnerships can play in supporting community development. As Reinvest Toledo has
grown, local banks have provided CRA dollars for operational expenses, which have
been invaluable. Without it, Reinvest would not be where it is today, and our community
would not be where it is today. https://reinvesttoledo.org/
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn
capital into tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and

11 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 7
community development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have
consequences well beyond the banks themselves.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed
documentation requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or
redirect bank support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with
limited administrative capacity. The agencies must also determine whether those effects
would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.
More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of
reducing perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine
what the changes mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.
The proposal eliminates the "purpose" test and weakens connection to the LMI
community benefits.
Under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business does not
automatically constitute economic development. The activity must also satisfy a
requirement known as the "purpose test," meaning it must promote economic
development by supporting permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for low- or
moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income communities.12
The proposed rule would eliminate the "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks
could earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or
improves jobs for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income
communities. Instead, financing could qualify as economic development based primarily
on the type and size of the business and whether the financing expands, improves or
preserves the business's productive capacity, physical presence or employment base.13
We are concerned that this change would weaken the connection between CRA
economic-development credit and the people and communities CRA is intended to
benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying business expand does not necessarily
create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an underserved neighborhood or address
the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens
a qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank
to demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or

12 Federal Reserve Board, Interagency Questions and Answers Regarding Community Reinvestment, §
__.12(g)(3)-1 (explaining that CRA economic-development activities must satisfy both a "size" test and a
"purpose" test, and identifying permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for LMI persons or in
LMI geographies as qualifying purposes).
13 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,133-34 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 8
neighborhoods.14 The agencies themselves acknowledge that eliminating the purpose test
would expand the universe of activities eligible for CRA credit.15
Before eliminating the purpose test, the agencies should analyze what additional activities
would qualify under the new definition, where those activities are likely to occur, and
whether bank financing could shift away from activities that create or retain jobs for low-
and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. The agencies
should also explain why eliminating the existing connection to these outcomes is
consistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs
of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities.
The proposal expands what infrastructure projects qualify for CRA credit.
Under current guidance, infrastructure projects in an LMI area generally receive CRA
credit only when they help keep or attract residents or businesses. The proposal
would change the standard by allowing credit for infrastructure that "benefits or serves" a
targeted area, even when the project delivers little meaningful benefit to LMI residents
and does not help preserve or strengthen the community.16
This means that a bank could seek CRA credit for financing a large regional
infrastructure project that only incidentally serves an LMI neighborhood, even if most of
the project's benefits flow to affluent communities or private companies. For example, a
data center located in or connected to an LMI tract could qualify despite creating few
permanent jobs and providing little direct benefit to residents.
Before expanding what infrastructure projects qualify for CRA credit in this way, the
agencies should analyze the impact of expanding the types of projects that qualify for
CRA credit on people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income
communities, including whether it could result in a reduction in projects that preserve or
strengthen LMI communities. In addition, the agencies should explain why changing the
standard is consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting
the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
communities.
The proposal will narrow the activities subject to CRA examination and hide lending
gaps.
Under the current rule, large banks are generally evaluated on their home mortgage,
small business and small farm lending. The proposal outlines two options for regulators
to focus on products designated as a bank's "major product lines" based either on the
largest two product lines by all lending volume, or based on the type of lending a bank

14 Id.
15 Id. at 52,133.
16 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,1335 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 9
does more of in a particular assessment area.17 Either option would allow weak
performance in a lower volume product to escape meaningful scrutiny even when that
credit is important locally.
For example, in my community, there is a strong need for home mortgage lending. But if
that type of lending is not a major part of a large bank in my community's business,
regulators will not evaluate whether the bank is meeting this crucial community need.
Absent such evaluation, the bank will likely deprioritize making such loans. Also,
analyzing only a bank's largest two product lines will tend to excuse a bank's failure to
offer mortgage loans from CRA reviews.
Before narrowing the activities subject to CRA examination and eliminating data
reporting requirements, the agencies should analyze the impact of doing so will have for
people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income communities,
including whether it could result in a reduction in the types of lending that would meet
community needs. In addition, the agencies should explain why this change would be
consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit
needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
The proposal will make it harder to hold banks accountable.
Under the current rule, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and report
data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans. The
proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in
assets. Over 400 banks with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to
annually collect and report CRA data on small business loans, small-farm loans, and
community development loans.
Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less
information to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand
whether local credit needs are being met. This data has been vital as our coalition
members as they decide how best to advocate for solutions to community needs.
According to NCRC, the proposal would eliminate 11% of CRA small business data
lending reporting nationwide, and 8.7% in Ohio.
Before reducing reporting requirements, the agencies should analyze the impact of doing
so will have for people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income
communities, including whether it could result in a reduction in small business, small
farm, or community development lending. In addition, the agencies should explain why
changing the standard is consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records

 10
of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
communities.
Conclusion
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
● identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
scrutiny under the proposal;
● quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
● assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities and communities of color;
● consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, Reinvest Toledo, Inc.
believes that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough
analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely
needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.
Sincerely
Reinvest Toledo, Inc.

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
On behalf of the Financial Empowerment Network of Washington, which includes hundreds of organizations across our state, I am submitting our comments in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). Please see our attached letter detailing our concerns: 

1. Reduction in community investment expectations for all banks
2. Less community development scrutiny of banks
3. Bank branches and access to banking services
4. Support for local organizations
5. Proposal eliminates "purpose test" for economic development
6. Proposal expands what infrastructure projects qualify for CRA credit
7. Proposal will narrow the activities subject to CRA examination and hide lending gaps
8. Proposal will make holding banks accountable harder

We believe that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity. Any decline in CRA-related activity will have real-world impacts, causing harm to vulnerable communities across Washington state and the country.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0400_09000064b9665a3a.pdf:
1


October 9, 2026
Jonathan V. Gould
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219
Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community
Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57]
Dear comptroller Gould:
The Financial Empowerment Network of Washington State (FEN) and Bank On Washington submit this
comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by
the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1
because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the
complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making
any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income
communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify
supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.
FEN is a nonprofit organization dedicated to promoting financial thriving across Washington state,
through connecting and equipping providers and advocates. We work across sectors to build capacity and
promote financial health initiatives, creating accessible routes to generational wealth. As the lead
organization for Bank On WA, we focus on building partnerships across sectors that center and support
low- and moderate-income individuals and families, especially the un- and under-banked. The CRA
supports the engagement of banks through accessible accounts, small business support, homeownership
initiatives, bank volunteerism, financial education, and grant funding for nonprofits – both for FEN and
the hundreds of nonprofits within our network.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that
banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit
services. These protections remain especially important in communities that have experienced redlining,
disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how
regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. We
are concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 2
on low- and moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic
discrimination and disinvestment.

CONCERN #1: REDUCTION IN COMMUNITY INVESTMENT
EXPECTATIONS FOR ALL BANKS
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In Washington state, from 2010-
2024, banks made over $100B in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census
tracts and $25B in CRA qualified lending to small businesses. Investments such as these benefited our
community by building financial stability and wealth in communities who are furthest from opportunity,
dovetailing with the work of the Washington State Community Reinvestment Project and Black Home
Initiative, among others, who reach low- to moderate-income Washingtonians.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in communities. For
example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community
development loans or investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that
percentage is far lower than the percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC)
determined the largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the OCC and FDIC
supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these banks currently conduct
approximately $102 billion annually in community development loans and investments inside their
assessment areas, and that the median percentage of annual community development lending in
assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital, and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for annual CRA
qualified investments.3 If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate
thresholds of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined
activity would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1 billion, or
85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make their CRA compliance

2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks surpass a
benchmark of 0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625% for investments.
91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical effect of this proposal is
that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
3 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk, (Sept. 10,
2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-activity-at-
risk/.
 3
easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set strategic plan benchmarks for CRA
performance well-below historical levels of community development activity.4
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination cannot
withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If regulators lower the
expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the communities they serve, there could
be harmful consequences for communities. We could lose ground we have made on reducing the wealth
gap in communities of color, through additional barriers for first-time homeowners, small business
owners, and increases in the rates of un- and under-banked. It is imperative that the CRA continues to
incentivize banks to meet community needs. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze
whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and
moderate-income communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

CONCERN #2: LESS COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT SCRUTINY OF
BANKS
The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under
CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while banks with assets
between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less demanding intermediate-
bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to large banks.5 The proposal would
also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting requirements currently applicable to large banks
for institutions with $10 billion or less in assets, including reporting on small-business, small-farm and
community development lending.6
Approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation because the
proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion.7 The 417 banks newly
classified as intermediate rather than large would no longer be examined under separate CRA investment
and services tests and instead would be evaluated based on their combined community development
loans, investments and services. These reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community

4 NCRC, The Proposed CRA Rule's Strategic Plans: A More Predictable Path to Doing Less (Sept 1, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/the-proposed-cra-rules-strategic-plans-a-more-predictable-path-to-doing-less/.

5 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,120–23 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
6 Id. at 52,120.
7 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.
 4
development obligations for over 800 banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks, may
worsen the housing crisis by reducing the demand for Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC).
In Washington state, 4 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation, and 9 banks
would lose large-bank status.
This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-income
communities remains substantial. In communities across Washington, families continue to face barriers to
affordable mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-
business financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small
businesses and other community development.
The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply because a bank
falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA obligations and scrutiny
applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that would move into less rigorous
examination categories, determine the communities those institutions serve, analyze the lending and
community development activity that would receive less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be
concentrated in low- and moderate-income communities or communities that have experienced historic
discrimination and disinvestment.

CONCERN #3: BANK BRANCHES AND ACCESS TO BANKING
SERVICES
By raising the large-bank threshold to $10 billion, 417 banks would no longer receive the full large-bank
examination, including a separate service test that evaluates branch delivery systems and banking
services. We are concerned that approximately 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts
would no longer be evaluated as part of the large-bank CRA service test under the proposal, and more
than 4,000 branches in majority-people-of-color census tracts would also lose CRA consideration. In 28
states, at least one-third of branches located in LMI census tracts would no longer receive any CRA
evaluation.8

In Washington state, 79 branches located in LMI tracts would be at risk, including 31 branches in
communities of color. This would impact both urban and rural communities in all corners of our state.

The proposal would also narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service test. Today,
examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information about the costs and
features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this criterion to credit services, removing deposit

8 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.
 5
products such as checking and savings accounts from direct evaluation under the service test.9 As such,
examiners would no longer evaluate whether those products are affordable and responsive to community
needs even though 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million are
underbanked.10 CRA review of the cost and features of deposit products has played an important role in
encouraging banks to address these disparities by providing affordable products.
As the lead organization for Bank On Washington, our organization works with communities where
access to mainstream banking services remains a serious concern. We have worked incredibly hard to
address the challenges faced by individuals who have been marginalized and excluded from mainstream
banking services. This would undermine our gains and make it harder for individuals and families to
access safe, affordable banking services in their own communities. This puts vulnerable people at risk of
higher-cost, predatory financial services that will undermine their financial stability.
For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from access to
credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely receive income, build
savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit. Bank On-certified accounts are an
excellent example of low-barrier access into the financial mainstream that allows many Washingtonians
to move from financial vulnerability into stability. The CRA supports and encourages institutions to work
towards making banking more accessible for these communities.
We are therefore concerned that under the proposal, examiners will no longer evaluate whether banks that
are still subject to the service test offer affordable checking and savings accounts. By reducing the
importance of deposit services and branch performance in CRA evaluations, the proposal eliminates
incentives for banks to offer basic products that help unbanked and underbanked households. Before
finalizing these changes, the agencies should identify which communities would receive less scrutiny of
bank branches and services, determine whether the effects would fall disproportionately on low- and
moderate-income communities or communities of color, and explain why the changes are justified despite
those consequences.

CONCERN #4: SUPPORT FOR LOCAL ORGANIZATIONS
We are concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit
organizations.
Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling, workforce
programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through grants, investments,
loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These resources can be particularly important to local

9 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,126 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
10 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.

 6
organizations that have deep relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their
communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new
documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.11 For smaller
nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting,
compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself.
Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In
addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial
records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA
eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document,
they may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can play in
supporting community development. Our organization receives nearly one quarter of our funding from
financial institutions who are seeking opportunities to invest and engage in our work with low- and
moderate-income communities. We council our nonprofit partners on how to develop similar meaningful
partnerships and engagement opportunities for banks. These efforts support access to financial education
and financial coaching, foreclosure prevention, and banking access, and this investment supports the
operating capacity of critical nonprofit organizations across Washington state.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into tangible
benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community development activities
receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond the banks themselves.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed documentation
requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or redirect bank support away from
smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with limited administrative capacity. The agencies must
also determine whether those effects would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-
income communities.
More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of reducing perceived
regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine what the changes mean for the
communities CRA is intended to serve.
CONCERN #5: PROPOSAL ELIMINATES "PURPOSE TEST" FOR
ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT, WEAKENING CONNECTION TO LMI
COMMUNITY BENEFITS
Under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business does not automatically constitute
economic development. The activity must also satisfy a requirement known as the "purpose test,"

11 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 7
meaning it must promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation, retention, or
improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income communities.12
The proposed rule would eliminate the "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could earn CRA
credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs for low- and
moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. Instead, financing could qualify
as economic development based primarily on the type and size of the business and whether the financing
expands, improves or preserves the business's productive capacity, physical presence or employment
base.13
We are concerned that this change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-development
credit and the people and communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a
qualifying business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an
underserved neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a qualifying
business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to demonstrate that those
benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.14 The agencies themselves
acknowledge that eliminating the purpose test would expand the universe of activities eligible for CRA
credit.15
Before eliminating the purpose test, the agencies should analyze what additional activities would qualify
under the new definition, where those activities are likely to occur, and whether bank financing could
shift away from activities that create or retain jobs for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and
moderate-income communities. The agencies should also explain why eliminating the existing connection
to these outcomes is consistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit
needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities.


12 Federal Reserve Board, Interagency Questions and Answers Regarding Community Reinvestment, § __.12(g)(3)-1
(explaining that CRA economic-development activities must satisfy both a "size" test and a "purpose" test, and
identifying permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for LMI persons or in LMI geographies as qualifying
purposes).
13 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,133-34 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
14 Id.
15 Id. at 52,133.
 8
CONCERN #6: PROPOSAL EXPANDS WHAT INFRASTRUCTURE
PROJECTS QUALIFY FOR CRA CREDIT
Under current guidance, infrastructure projects in an LMI area generally receive CRA credit only when
they help keep or attract residents or businesses. The proposal would change the standard by allowing
credit for infrastructure that "benefits or serves" a targeted area, even when the project delivers little
meaningful benefit to LMI residents and does not help preserve or strengthen the community.16
This means that a bank could seek CRA credit for financing a large regional infrastructure project that
only incidentally serves an LMI neighborhood, even if most of the project's benefits flow to affluent
communities or private companies. For example, a data center located in or connected to an LMI tract
could qualify despite creating few permanent jobs and providing little direct benefit to residents.
Washington state is working hard to build infrastructure for marginalized communities, tying workforce
development and economic development together. CRA should continue to support these efforts, not
work at odds.
Before expanding what infrastructure projects qualify for CRA credit in this way, the agencies should
analyze the impact of expanding the types of projects that qualify for CRA credit on people with low- and
moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income communities, including whether it could result in a
reduction in projects that preserve or strengthen LMI communities. In addition, the agencies should
explain why changing the standard is consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities.

CONCERN #7: PROPOSAL WILL NARROW THE ACTIVITIES
SUBJECT TO CRA EXAMINATION AND HIDE LENDING GAPS
Under the current rule, large banks are generally evaluated on their home mortgage,
small business and small farm lending. The proposal outlines two options for regulators to focus on
products designated as a bank's "major product lines" based either on the largest two product lines by all
lending volume, or based on the type of lending a bank does more of in a particular assessment area.17
Either option would allow weak performance in a lower volume product to escape meaningful scrutiny
even when that credit is important locally.
In addition, under the current rule banks above the large bank threshold generally collect and report on
small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans and assessment areas. But
because of the proposed change in the threshold, banks with $10 billion or less in assets would no longer
be required to collect and report such CRA data. Nationwide, that will result in a 11% reduction in CRA

16 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,1335 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
17 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52123 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 9
small business lending data. Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers will not
be able to identify credit deserts, compare performance or understand whether local credit needs are being
met.
Before narrowing the activities subject to CRA examination and eliminating data reporting requirements,
the agencies should analyze the impact of doing so will have for people with low- and moderate-incomes
or low- and moderate-income communities, including whether it could result in a reduction in the types of
lending that would meet community needs. In addition, the agencies should explain why this change
would be consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

CONCERN #8: PROPOSAL WILL MAKE HOLDING BANKS
ACCOUNTABLE HARDER
Under the current rule, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and report data on
small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans. The proposal would limit
these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Over 400 banks with assets of $10
billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report CRA data on small business
loans, small-farm loans, and community development loans.
Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information
to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs are being
met. Bank On relies on this data as we focus on identifying gaps and meeting the needs for marginalized,
low- and moderate-income communities.
According to NCRC, the proposal would eliminate 11% of CRA small business data lending reporting
nationwide, including 8.9% of data in Washington state.
Before reducing reporting requirements, the agencies should analyze the impact of doing so will have for
people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income communities, including whether it
could result in a reduction in small business, small farm, or community development lending. In addition,
the agencies should explain why changing the standard is consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess
banks' records of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
communities.

CONCLUSION
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
 10
●
identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under
the proposal;
●
quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development
activities subject to CRA evaluation;
●
assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
including rural communities and communities of color;
●
consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability; and
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the OCC and
FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released
for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in
CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting
the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The
proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to bank
classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core
elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from community
organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not have dedicated
regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected organizations to
evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the communities they serve, and
provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request
that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely,

Jennifer Quiróz
Executive Director
Financial Empowerment Network

I oppose your agencies’ proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules.

Please withdraw this proposal and keep banks accountable to the communities they profit from.

Thank you.

Thank you for considering these comments opposing proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act.

Sincerely, 
Samantha Wines
NRDC
National Digital Advocacy Campaign Manager
