Markets Tax Credit (NMTC)
The change also undermines Congress's recent efforts to strengthen Low-Income Housing
Tax Credit (LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) which are two bipartisan, popular
federal tax tools with a long track record of success in our communities. While Congress
expanded LIHTC and made NMTC permanent, the proposal undermines these important
investment tools.
LIHTC and NMTC are considered equity investments that are evaluated under the
standalone investment test for large banks which currently have a distinct 25%-weighted
component of their CRA evaluation devoted to qualified investments. Moving banks into the
lower size category would mean these transitioned banks would only be subject to a diluted
evaluation that considers all CD in one test. This means a bank may have greater ability to
emphasize CD lending rather than maintain the same level of LIHTC or NMTC investment
because investment performance no longer receives a separate rating. Through this
weakened regulatory incentive, bank demand for these investments would decrease.

Reporting, and Disclosure"

large-bank CRA data requirements. This would make it harder for communities, CDFIs,
policymakers, and regulators to identify credit gaps, compare bank performance, assess
geographic disparities, and understand whether community credit needs are being met. We
are concerned that aggregate community development finance data is already difficult to
track and the proposal would excerbate the coverage of data, making it difficult to identify
and understand where credit is flowing.
Recommendation
For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and
reject all alternatives offered (including the substantially higher thresholds raised for
consideration in Question 1). The current thresholds are already annually indexed to CPI-
W, so they are not beholden to 1995 asset levels. Moreover, the justification of "restoring
proportionality to 1995" that the agencies use in the proposal does not adequately explain
why raising asset thresholds better serve the statutory intent of the CRA—which is to ensure
that credit needs of LMI communities are met. For the small bank threshold, the
proportionality metric rests on the distribution of the number of banks such that nearly 80%
of all banks would be considered small, similar to what it was in 1995. While that's true, by
the same logic, nearly 20% of banks in 1995 were considered large whereas under the
proposed large bank threshold, only a little over 2% of all banks would be considered large.
Instead, the agencies selectively use total banking industry share to justify the large bank
threshold saying large banks would under this proposal, and similar to 1995 cover about
85% of all total bank industry's assets. Matching a 1995 distribution through either method
does not necessarily demonstrate that the resulting categories are appropriate for the
modern banking system. The industry has consolidated dramatically, bank business models
and geographic reach have changed. Banks with several billion dollars in assets today may
have substantially greater lending, investment, data, and operational capacity than
institutions that were treated as small or intermediate, three decades ago. The fact that
assets happen to sit above a chosen threshold does not by itself establish that banks below
that threshold should lose the separate investment/service tests or associated data
requirements.
Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C,
"Community Development Activities — CD Grants"; Questions 9–11
We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants which: 1)
requires a qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or
initiative with a primary purpose of community development; 2) for large banks, caps grant
recipient's indirect administrative costs to 15%; 3) requires that large banks obtain
documentation from grant recipients including written commitments regarding use of funds,
indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and operating and program budgets. We also
strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and
donations from CRA consideration entirely.
 While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully
benefit communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of effective
grantmaking and misunderstand the role that flexible operating support plays in community
development finance. For CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology,
risk management, data systems, financial management, technical assistance, and product
development are not ancillary to community development. They are the infrastructure that
makes community development lending possible.
The Nebraska Enteprise Fund uses operating grants to hiring more staff for the delivery of
lending and technical assistance.
Moreover, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA
eligibility. An organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for
community impact. Costs vary depending on an organization's size, geography, product
mix, regulatory obligations, technical-assistance model, and populations served. The cap
could disproportionately affect small and emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-
dollar loans, organizations providing intensive borrower technical assistance, CDFIs
developing new products or entering underserved markets and organizations making
necessary investments in technology, compliance, data, and risk management.
Recommendation
The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building
grants as currently is in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage flexibility
for banks to provide the form of support that best responds to the identified community
needs instead of imposing undue compliance burdens.

Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance:
Section IV.B, "Performance Tests — Intermediate Bank Ratings"
Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a

rating. The proposal would require a Satisfactory or better lending-test rating but would
allow lending performance to compensate for weaker CD performance.
This change is particularly concerning when combined with the proposed asset thresholds,

 Satisfactory CD performance to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
Complexity definition anchored to lending is too narrow: Section IV.C,

The proposal would define complexity for CD investments, grants, and services largely by

The agencies should assess complexity, innovativeness, flexibility, impact, and

We support CRA consideration for essential community facilities and infrastructure,

particularly Questions 38–53

Assessment Areas"; proposed § __.13(e); Question 34

The Nebraska Enteprise Fund serves multiple rural and urban communities that have

The Housing Justice Center submits these comments in response to the above-referenced
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) jointly issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the

bank's CRA rating. As set out in more detail below, the Housing Justice Center strongly

About the Housing Justice Center
The Housing Justice Center is a Minnesota public interest advocacy and legal organization
whose primary mission is to preserve and expand affordable housing for low-income
individuals and families. For more than twenty-five years, the Housing Justice Center has
worked to ensure that people have access to safe, stable, affordable dignified places to call

bears on a bank's CRA rating. The agencies offer two alternatives. Option 1 would count a
violation only where it is cited in a public enforcement action brought by a federal or state

the existing factor directing examiners to weigh the nature, extent, and strength of the

The Housing Justice Center opposes Option 1. Whether a bank is downgraded should turn
on whether the bank broke the law, not on whether an agency elected to bring a public case.
Charging decisions reflect staffing and settlement posture, neither of which bears on the
harm to the borrowers and neighborhoods affected. The agencies themselves expect that
nonpublic citations will seldom warrant a downgrade.31 If that is so, Option 1 forecloses the
agencies' flexibility and provides little in return. Option 2 is the better alternative.
In addition, the agencies should retain the instruction that examiners weigh the nature,
extent, and strength of the evidence. The agencies reason that this factor is subsumed within
the consideration of any other relevant information.32 A residual catch-all is not an express
directive. The existing factor is what allows an examiner to distinguish an isolated violation,
promptly corrected, from a sustained pattern affecting thousands of borrowers, and to
match the rating consequence to the conduct. Removing it leaves examiners with less
guidance about when a downgrade is warranted.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

I am the Managing Director of Renaissance Economic Development Corporation (REDC), writing to
oppose the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) by the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). These
changes risk weakening banks' obligations to invest in the communities they serve, reducing
accountability, and limiting critical resources for low- and moderate-income (LMI) households, small
businesses, and community development organizations.

REDC is a 30-year-old nonprofit Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) dedicated to
serving low to moderate income (LMI) communities across New York and New Jersey. Through
affordable small business financing and business training, we help aspiring and growing entrepreneurs
overcome financial barriers, build sustainable businesses, and create pathways toward economic stability
and a better future for their families.

For three decades, we have brought together public and private resources to give entrepreneurs
opportunities otherwise out of reach. For every $1 in public funding we raise, we are able to leverage
approximately $5 from the private banking sector, in part because of banks' Community Reinvestment
Act (CRA) obligations. This partnership has enabled us to deploy nearly $70 million in capital to more
than 2,800 entrepreneurs, helping small businesses grow, support families, and strengthen the economic
fabric of their communities over the last 30 years. These investments have also contributed to job
creation, with over 7,000 jobs created and retained through our lending.

The proposed changes to the CRA would weaken this essential partnership. By reducing banks'
incentives to invest in community development, these changes could significantly limit the capital
available to organizations like REDC and the entrepreneurs who depend on us. For entrepreneurs in low-
income communities, access to affordable financing is often the difference that allows them to turn a
dream into a viable business. When capital becomes harder to access, businesses lose opportunities to
grow, jobs are not created, and already struggling neighborhoods risk further economic decline.

Equally concerning is the proposed rule changes' potential impact of restricting community development
grants to narrowly defined projects while limiting support for essential operating costs. As a nonprofit, the
majority of the funding we receive is restricted to specific programs and activities, leaving limited
resources to cover the day-to-day costs of delivering our services. Yet meaningful community impact
requires more than funding individual programs. It requires qualified staff, strong operational capacity,
and the flexibility to respond to the evolving needs of entrepreneurs and the communities they call home.
Flexible operating support allows us to sustain these essential functions, build trusted relationships with
business owners, and provide consistent guidance beyond the initial loan.

Without this support, even well-funded programs can struggle to reach the people who need them most.
Limiting flexible operating grants would not simply create an administrative burden for organizations like
ours; it could mean fewer entrepreneurs receiving assistance, fewer small businesses accessing the
resources they need to survive and grow, and fewer opportunities for families to build lasting financial
security.

For 30 years, REDC has witnessed firsthand how access to capital and trusted business support can
change lives and strengthen communities. We urge policymakers to recognize that CRA investments are
not merely financial transactions or regulatory obligations. They are investments in people, livelihoods,
local businesses, and the future of our neighborhoods. Preserving strong CRA incentives and maintaining
access to flexible community development funding are essential to ensuring that all entrepreneurs
continue to have a fair opportunity to succeed.

First, we urge the OCC and FDIC to preserve meaningful CRA obligations for banks of all sizes.
The proposal would significantly raise the asset thresholds determining which CRA tests apply to banks,
potentially classifying approximately 80% of CRA-covered banks as small banks. As a result, more than
75% of banks could be exempt from community development tests, substantially reducing incentives for
banks to invest in underserved communities. These changes could leave many neighborhoods with fewer
resources and less access to the financing needed to support economic growth and financial stability.

Second, the OCC and FDIC should maintain strong incentives for banks to invest in Community
Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs). CDFIs play a vital role in expanding access to responsible
and affordable capital for small businesses, entrepreneurs, and communities that traditional financial
institutions often underserve. Strong CRA incentives encourage banks to partner with CDFIs, leveraging
their local expertise and lending capacity to reach borrowers who might otherwise be excluded from
conventional financing. Weakening these incentives would threaten an important source of capital for
community development and small business growth.

Third, we strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants and
donations. Requiring grants to be directly tied to specific programs, projects, or initiatives, while capping
indirect and administrative costs at 15% for large banks, would shift funding away from flexible operating
support toward narrowly restricted, project-specific grants. Community development organizations need
flexible resources to maintain essential operations, retain qualified staff, respond to emerging community
needs, and provide sustained support to the people they serve. Restricting these resources could
undermine organizational capacity for non-profits and reduce the effectiveness and long-term impact of
community development efforts.

Finally, we urge the OCC and FDIC to preserve robust reporting requirements for small business,
small farm, and community development lending. Transparent and comprehensive lending data are
essential for identifying credit gaps, evaluating whether banks are meeting community needs, and holding

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
referenced above issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to amend the regulations of the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). 1

The National Association of IOLTA Programs (NAIP) is a nonprofit, non-partisan
membership organization for funders of civil legal aid throughout all United States
jurisdictions and the Canadian provinces and territories. Since 1986, NAIP has supported
the growth and development of Interest on Lawyers Trust Account (IOLTA) programs as
effective grantmaking organizations.

NAIP members across the United States work closely with the financial institutions in their
jurisdictions. Many IOLTA programs offer documentation recognizing their partner banks'
relevant, voluntary activities that the banks may submit toward CRA consideration.
However, as set out in greater detail below, the proposed rule's provision to removing
deposit products from CRA consideration and cap grantee indirect costs at 15% will make
it substantially more difficult for banks to receive CRA credit for actions that nonetheless
have a substantial, positive impact on their local assessment areas.



1 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52114 (Aug. 12, 2026).
 NAIP Comment
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694/FDIC RIN 3064-AG31


Page 2 of 3
I. Negative Impact of Removing Deposit Products from CRA Consideration

Offering deposit products is a core way in which banks can benefit their local communities.
Individuals, families, and businesses of all sizes need a safe and affordable way to store
and access their money. Attorneys use deposit products that benefit low- and moderate-
income (LMI) communities to securely store client funds and meet their ethical obligations
under states' various rules of professional conduct. Banks not only offer a vital service
when offering deposit products, but many also choose to invest more money in their
communities by paying favorable interest rates on the deposits of LMI individuals or the
client funds deposited in attorney accounts.

The large-bank service test under the CRA has traditionally considered the availability,
costs and features of deposit products. Limiting the test to credit products, as the
proposed rule recommends, would result in banks not receiving consideration for being
responsive to community needs through offering deposit products.

In light of the foregoing, we urge the agencies to remove the proposed changes omitting
deposit accounts from consideration in the large-bank service test deposit products.

II. Reducing Indirect Costs Negatively Impacts Nonprofit Compliance & Effective
Management

NAIP is also concerned about the impact of the proposed changes to the consideration of
grantmaking under the CRA. The narrowing of the definition of a community development
grant and the addition of an indirect cost cap for large bank grants, along with the
administrative work that cap entails, run counter to the agencies' stated goals for the
proposed rulemaking to reduce burden and increase clarity.

The proposed rules would eliminate CRA consideration for grants made to intermediary
organizations in the pursuit of increasing efficiency. But on the contrary, such intermediary
organizations may actually result in multiplier effects, pooling funds from multiple funders
to support significant projects. They may also have dedicated staff who can research and
connect with direct service nonprofits, freeing up bank staff time for other activities.

The rulemaking additionally proposes capping indirect costs at 15 percent to match the
standard in the Uniform Guidance for Federal Awards, 2 CFR part 200. However, federal
funds subject to the Uniform Guidance are most likely awarded to large nonprofit
organizations with other funding sources to absorb vital administrative costs. Banks, on the
other hand, may be most interested in funding small, local nonprofits who are the
community development experts in their assessment areas. As an association of
grantmakers, we know that these smaller nonprofits can sometimes be the most effective
at delivering services, as they often have the most direct connections to community
members and the most expertise in local needs. However, a 15 percent indirect cost cap

can be difficult – if not impossible – for them to overcome. Indirect costs are not
unnecessary; rather, they are essential for tasks like compliance and monitoring. As
described in a large-scale MacArthur Foundation study conducted in 2022, a higher
indirect cost rate is often essential to ensure healthy compliance and allow oversight
systems to function effectively.2

In addition to the difficulties the indirect cost cap would cause for grant recipients, it would
also significantly increase the burden on grantmaking banks. The sheer amount of
paperwork and staff time needed to undertake the proposed documentation may lead
some banks to ultimately redirect funding away from community development activities
altogether, contravening the purposes of the CRA. We urge the agencies to remove the
proposed indirect costs cap and prohibition on general operating support grants as
qualifications for CRA consideration.

Thank you for considering this comment. Should the agencies proceed with finalizing the
proposed rule changes, we respectfully urge you to amend the final rule such that deposit
products will continue to be an avenue for CRA credit and that organizations serving low-
income communities are not subject indirect cost limits that degrade their internal
oversight systems. NAIP opposes the proposed rulemaking as drafted and believes the
agencies would be better served by withdrawing it and submitting a new proposal for
consideration.

through CDCs, and borrower equity. It enables small businesses to acquire, build,
or improve owner-occupied commercial facilities and purchase eligible long-term
equipment. Clear CRA treatment for qualifying bank financing associated with

encourage continued participation in small-business economic development.

development activities. Recognizing qualifying loans made through an expressly

Dear Regulators:

On behalf of Dallas City Homes, Inc. (DCH), I write to express strong support for the Community Reinvestment Act and to raise concerns about proposed regulatory changes that could weaken incentives for financial institutions to invest in affordable housing and resident services in underserved communities.
CRA plays a critical role in encouraging financial institutions to invest in communities that have historically faced barriers to capital. Affordable housing development requires more than traditional lending. Construction financing, community development investments, grants, and other flexible funding sources are essential to closing financing gaps and sustaining nonprofit development capacity.

While we recognize the importance of regulatory efficiency, we are concerned that the proposed changes could reduce incentives for grants, community development investments, and other forms of support critical to affordable housing. We are particularly concerned about restrictions on qualifying nonprofit grants, as reasonable administrative and operating expenses are necessary to responsibly manage public and private investments. Proposed changes to bank asset thresholds also warrant careful consideration of their potential impact on community investment.

We respectfully urge the agencies to preserve strong CRA incentives for affordable housing development, community development financing, nonprofit capacity building, and investment in low- and moderate-income communities.

CRA’s effectiveness should be measured not only by regulatory efficiency, but by its ability to expand economic opportunity, strengthen neighborhoods, and ensure access to capital for communities that need it most.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The New York City Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) and New York City
Housing Development Corporation (HDC) welcome the opportunity to provide comments on the
above-referenced notice of proposed rulemaking to amend the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) regulations (Proposed Rule). HPD and HDC represent the largest municipal housing agency
and housing finance agency in the nation, respectively. The Agencies jointly administer low-income
housing tax credits (LIHTC) to finance the development and preservation of affordable housing in
New York City.

Since 1977, the CRA has generated trillions of dollars in loans, investments, and services for
communities with low and moderate-income (LMI) residents nationwide and billions annually in
New York City. In particular, the CRA has been a major driver of investment in LIHTC, the most
important federal source of affordable housing financing today. Any reforms to the CRA should not
weaken the effectiveness of LIHTC or dilute the law's emphasis on LMI households and
communities, especially in light of a growing nationwide affordable housing crisis. To ensure the
CRA continues to generate critical affordable housing investments, we strongly encourage you to
consider the following:

Protect current incentives to invest in affordable housing through LIHTC

LIHTC is the most significant federal source of financing for affordable housing serving LMI
residents and communities in New York City and nationally. The LIHTC program provides tax credit
equity to owners and developers to acquire, rehabilitate, or construct new rental housing for lower-
income households. The CRA is a primary driver of LIHTC investment, and without financial
 institutions as investors, the capacity to provide affordable housing in New York City and nationally
would be greatly diminished.
For this reason, we urge you to maintain the current asset-size thresholds for banks, or at a
minimum, ensure that any changes to asset-size thresholds preserve existing levels of
affordable housing investment. Specifically:

•
By recategorizing banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion from "large banks" to
"intermediate banks," the Proposed Rule would reduce incentives for many banks to
continue making LIHTC investments. The Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition projects
the $10 billion threshold would reduce the number of LIHTC investors from 108 to 40 banks,
which could reduce LIHTC equity raised over a five-year period from roughly $2 billion to
$272 million.

•
Raising the asset-size threshold for large banks could also reduce competition in the LIHTC
market, lowering credit pricing, decreasing available equity, and risking the financial
feasibility of countless affordable housing projects, ultimately slowing national production.

•
Weakening current incentives to invest in LIHTC would also diminish the impact of
Congress's recent expansion of LIHTC.

Keep the emphasis on LMI households and communities

The CRA must maintain its emphasis on serving the LMI communities it was intended to support.
Any proposals that would expand the current definition of affordable housing or allow exemptions
for certain types of housing risk shifting resources away from LMI households.

For this reason, we do not support exemptions from the LMI requirement or from the current
definition of affordable housing. Specifically:

•
While middle-income families in high-cost areas face difficulties in today's housing market,
the challenges are greatest for families with lower incomes. The Joint Center for Housing
Studies has reported that while lower-income renters continue to experience high rates of
cost burden in all 50 states, the overall supply of low-rent units is shrinking. In New York
City, the 2023 Housing and Vacancy Survey reported a vacancy rate of 0.65% for units
renting below $1,650 (a rent considered affordable for a two-person household earning
slightly less than 60% of AMI). This severe shortage of housing affordable to lower income
households underscores the importance of preserving the CRA's emphasis on this
population.

 •
Naturally occurring affordable housing partnerships should not be exempt from
requirements that median rents not exceed 30% of 80% of AMI, or 30% of 120% of AMI in
high-cost areas.

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Proposed Rule and urge the OCC and FDIC to
ensure the CRA continues to meet the most pressing housing needs of LMI communities. We also
strongly believe meaningful reform requires joint rulemaking by all three federal regulators to
provide a consistent evaluation framework. We therefore respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to
pause this proposal and work with the Federal Reserve on a unified approach that maintains the
CRA's longstanding focus on the communities it was created to serve.

Dear members pf Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
I appreciate the opportunity to submit comments regarding the Office of the Comptroller of
the Currency's (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed
amendments to the regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).
The agencies' efforts to clarify regulatory expectations, reduce unnecessary compliance
burdens, and preserve a consistent framework for evaluating bank performance are
important objectives. A well-designed CRA framework should promote meaningful access
to financial services, encourage responsible lending and community development, and
provide banks with clear, proportionate, and predictable regulatory expectations.
While the proposed rule seeks to retain much of the established CRA framework, several
aspects warrant further consideration to ensure the regulations reflect the diversity of the
banking industry and the evolving ways consumers and businesses interact with financial
institutions.
Specifically, I respectfully recommend that the agencies consider four modifications:
1. Establish a graduated bank asset classification framework consisting of small,
intermediate-small, large, and large national or regional banks, rather than relying
on a single $10 billion threshold to distinguish intermediate and large institutions.
2. Remove administrative cost considerations as a determining factor in the CRA
eligibility of charitable donations and grants.
3. Modernize assessment area delineation to account for banks' actual service areas,
including digital and other non-branch delivery channels, rather than relying
primarily on physical branch locations.
4. Retain and strengthen consideration of the geographic and demographic
distribution of bank deposit products as part of CRA performance evaluations.
 These recommendations are intended to strengthen the connection between CRA
evaluations and the statutory objective of encouraging financial institutions to help meet
the credit needs of the communities in which they operate.
I. Establish a Graduated Asset Classification Framework
The agencies should reconsider the proposed reliance on a single $10 billion asset
threshold to distinguish intermediate banks from large banks. Although asset size is a
useful measure of institutional capacity, a single threshold does not adequately reflect the
significant differences in operational complexity, geographic reach, business models,
staffing, and community development capacity among institutions of varying sizes.
The banking industry includes community institutions serving a limited number of local
markets, regional institutions operating across multiple states, and large national
institutions with extensive branch networks, digital platforms, and diversified lending
operations. These institutions do not have equivalent resources or face equivalent
challenges in implementing CRA programs. A regulatory framework should recognize these
differences without compromising the expectation that every covered institution meet the
credit needs of its communities.
I recommend that the agencies establish four distinct classifications: small banks,
intermediate-small banks, large banks, and large national or regional banks. The
framework should preserve proportionate expectations for community institutions while
providing additional differentiation among institutions currently grouped together under the
large-bank category.
The small and intermediate-small classifications should continue to recognize the limited
resources and operational capacity of community banks. The large-bank classification
should apply to institutions with greater lending capacity, broader service delivery systems,
and more extensive compliance infrastructure. A separate large national or regional
classification should address institutions whose scale, geographic reach, and
organizational complexity warrant a more comprehensive evaluation of their CRA activities.
The agencies should establish objective asset thresholds for each classification, informed
by industry data, inflation, institutional complexity, and the distribution of assets across
the banking system. The thresholds should be periodically reviewed so that they remain
meaningful as the industry changes. The agencies should also consider whether
geographic reach, the number of states served, business model, and operational
complexity should supplement asset size in determining the appropriate performance
framework.
 A graduated approach would avoid the disproportionate regulatory consequences that can
arise when an institution crosses a single asset threshold. Two banks with similar asset
levels may have substantially different capacities to maintain specialized CRA personnel,
develop community development investments, collect and analyze performance data, and
manage activities across multiple assessment areas. Conversely, institutions with assets
just below a threshold may operate in ways that resemble substantially larger institutions.
The proposed framework should therefore establish proportionate requirements that
reflect actual institutional capacity and complexity. This would promote consistency,
reduce unnecessary burden on smaller institutions, and preserve meaningful expectations
for banks with broader resources and geographic reach.
Further, the expansion would not be inconsistent with current review procedures in which
non-asset based performance evaluations are conducted on Strategic Plan and Limited-
Purpose banks. The agencies should strongly consider more thresholds, not fewer, to
establish meaningful performance metrics.
The objective should not be to exempt larger institutions from meaningful CRA scrutiny.
Rather, it should be to align the scope and rigor of regulatory expectations with the
institution's capacity, operating model, and potential impact on the communities it serves.
II. Remove Administrative Cost Considerations as a Determining Factor in CRA
Donation Eligibility
The agencies should reconsider the extent to which administrative costs associated with
charitable donations and grants affect eligibility for CRA consideration. Ensuring that
community development funding reaches its intended beneficiaries is an appropriate
regulatory objective. However, administrative costs should not serve as a determining
factor that disqualifies otherwise eligible grants or donations supporting legitimate
community development purposes.
Nonprofit organizations and community development intermediaries require administrative
infrastructure to operate effectively. Personnel, accounting, compliance, technology,
reporting, and program management expenses are often necessary to ensure that funds
are appropriately managed and that community programs achieve their intended
objectives. These expenses do not necessarily represent a diversion of resources from
community development. In many cases, they are integral to the successful delivery of
services.
For example, an organization providing affordable housing assistance may require qualified
staff to evaluate applicants, administer funding, coordinate with housing partners, monitor
program performance, and satisfy reporting requirements. Similarly, a community
 development financial institution may incur operational expenses necessary to originate
and service loans to small businesses and underserved borrowers. Treating such expenses
as a basis for restricting CRA consideration could discourage banks from supporting
organizations that possess the infrastructure and expertise necessary to deliver effective
community development outcomes.
A regulatory approach that places excessive emphasis on administrative expenses may
also favor organizations with minimal overhead rather than those with the capacity to
manage complex, sustained, and accountable programs. Low administrative costs are not,
by themselves, evidence of effectiveness, just as reasonable operating expenses are not
evidence that a grant fails to benefit its intended community.
I recommend that the agencies remove administrative cost considerations as a categorical
or determining eligibility criterion for CRA-qualifying donations and grants. Instead,
eligibility should be based primarily on whether the recipient, purpose, and use of funds
satisfy the applicable CRA community development criteria and whether the activity
demonstrably benefits eligible communities or populations.
This approach should not eliminate appropriate safeguards. Banks should continue to
conduct reasonable due diligence, verify the charitable or community development
purpose of the proposed activity, maintain documentation supporting CRA eligibility, and
monitor the use of funds where appropriate. Regulators may also consider whether a grant
has a legitimate community development purpose and whether its intended benefits are
reasonably supported by available evidence.
The distinction is between evaluating the substance and effectiveness of an activity and
treating administrative expenses as an independent barrier to eligibility. A focus on
purpose, accountability, and community benefit would preserve regulatory oversight while
allowing banks to support organizations with the operational capacity to deliver meaningful
results.
Removing administrative cost considerations as a determining factor would provide greater
clarity, avoid discouraging productive partnerships, and direct regulatory attention toward
whether community development activities actually serve eligible needs.
III. Modernize Assessment Area Delineation Beyond Physical Branch Locations
The agencies should establish a more flexible and objective methodology for delineating
CRA assessment areas that reflects how banks deliver services and where they conduct
meaningful business. Assessment areas remain fundamental to CRA evaluations because
they define the communities against which a bank's performance is assessed. However, a
 methodology primarily tied to physical branch locations may not accurately capture the
geographic footprint of many institutions.
Banking has evolved substantially since the existing framework was established.
Consumers increasingly open accounts, maintain deposits, apply for loans, and conduct
transactions through online and mobile platforms. Banks also serve customers through
centralized lending operations, remote relationship management, digital account-opening
systems, and other delivery channels that are not necessarily associated with a traditional
branch.
As a result, a bank's actual service area may extend well beyond the geographic
boundaries suggested by its branch network. A community may provide a meaningful
source of deposits, borrowers, and banking relationships without containing a physical
branch. Conversely, the presence of a branch does not necessarily establish that the
institution meaningfully serves all surrounding communities.
A branch-centered assessment area methodology can therefore produce an incomplete
picture of a bank's activities. It may fail to recognize communities that contribute to a
bank's deposit base or receive substantial lending and financial services through non-
branch channels. It may also create inconsistencies in the evaluation of banks with
different business models, particularly when comparing traditional community banks with
institutions that rely more heavily on digital delivery.
I recommend that the agencies establish a modernized assessment area methodology
incorporating multiple objective indicators of a bank's geographic footprint. Relevant
indicators should include branch locations, the geographic distribution of deposits, the
location of borrowers and loan originations, customer account activity, and the geographic
reach of digital and other non-branch delivery channels, where reliable data are available.
The methodology should distinguish between a bank's primary assessment areas and
other areas in which it has a meaningful presence. For example, an institution could be
required to delineate assessment areas around its physical branches while also identifying
additional geographic markets where its deposit-taking or lending activities meet
established materiality criteria. Regulators should establish clear standards for identifying
these additional markets so that assessment area delineation remains consistent,
transparent, and administratively manageable.
The agencies should also consider a methodology that recognizes the geographic
distribution of a bank's deposits and lending activity without requiring institutions to
designate every location in which an individual customer resides as a separate assessment
area. Materiality thresholds, aggregation rules, and documented methodologies could
 prevent unnecessary fragmentation while ensuring that significant markets are not
overlooked.
Importantly, this approach should not allow banks to select assessment areas solely to
improve their CRA performance ratings. Assessment areas should be based on objective,
consistently applied criteria, and banks should document the data and rationale
supporting their delineations. Regulators should retain the ability to evaluate whether the
designated areas reasonably reflect the institution's actual operations and community
impact.
Modernizing assessment area delineation would improve the accuracy of CRA evaluations,
better align regulatory expectations with contemporary banking practices, and strengthen
accountability for communities that meaningfully participate in a bank's business model.
IV. Include the Geographic and Demographic Distribution of Deposit Products in CRA
Evaluations
The agencies should retain and strengthen consideration of the geographic and
demographic distribution of deposit products as part of CRA performance evaluations. The
proposed rule's approach to narrowing retail banking services to credit services, thereby
excluding deposit services, warrants reconsideration.
The CRA's statutory foundation recognizes the importance of both credit and deposit
services in meeting community needs. Deposit accounts are often the primary point of
entry into the financial system. They provide consumers with a means of receiving wages
and public benefits, paying bills, maintaining savings, and establishing an ongoing
relationship with a financial institution. For small businesses, deposit accounts facilitate
the receipt of revenue, payment of operating expenses, and management of working
capital.
The availability and accessibility of appropriate deposit products can be especially
important for low- and moderate-income individuals and communities. Account fees,
minimum balance requirements, overdraft practices, identification requirements, account-
opening procedures, and access to convenient service channels can affect whether
consumers can establish and maintain a usable banking relationship. The geographic and
demographic distribution of deposit accounts can therefore provide useful information
about whether a bank's services are reaching the communities it serves.
Excluding deposit services from the evaluation of retail banking services could create a
significant gap in the assessment of a bank's overall responsiveness to community needs.
A bank may demonstrate substantial lending activity while providing limited access to
affordable, practical deposit products in certain communities. Conversely, a bank may
 offer accessible, low-cost accounts and other services that support financial inclusion,
even when those benefits are not fully reflected in its lending performance.
CRA evaluations should recognize these distinctions without substituting deposit activity
for the evaluation of responsible lending. Deposit products and credit products serve
different but complementary functions in household and business financial health. A
comprehensive assessment should consider both.
I recommend that the agencies explicitly incorporate the geographic and demographic
distribution of deposit products into CRA evaluations. Relevant measures could include
the number and distribution of accounts across census tracts and income categories, the
availability of low-cost or no-cost accounts, account-opening and retention patterns, and
the accessibility of deposit services through branches, ATMs, and digital channels. Where
reliable information is available and legally appropriate, the agencies should also consider
whether products are reaching low- and moderate-income customers and communities.
The agencies should develop a standardized, proportionate methodology for evaluating
this information. Small and intermediate-small banks should not be subjected to
unnecessarily burdensome data collection requirements. Regulators could rely on existing
supervisory data, institution-level account information, and appropriate sampling or
reporting methods to reduce compliance costs. Larger institutions with more extensive
operations could be expected to provide more detailed analyses consistent with their
capacity and the scale of their activities.
Deposit product distribution should be evaluated in context. Differences in customer
demographics, local economic conditions, institutional business models, and service
delivery systems should be considered when assessing performance. The purpose should
be to determine whether a bank's deposit services are reasonably accessible and
responsive to community needs, not to impose a uniform product mix on all institutions.
Incorporating deposit services would reinforce the CRA's broader purpose, recognize the
role of deposit-taking in financial inclusion, and provide regulators with a more complete
understanding of how banks serve their communities.
Conclusion
The proposed CRA amendments provide an opportunity to improve regulatory clarity and
proportionality while ensuring that CRA evaluations remain responsive to the needs of the
communities the statute was designed to serve. The four recommendations outlined in this
letter would strengthen that objective.
 First, a graduated asset classification framework would better align regulatory expectations
with institutional size, complexity, and capacity. Second, removing administrative cost
considerations as a determining factor in donation eligibility would allow banks to support
capable community development organizations while preserving appropriate due diligence
and accountability. Third, modernizing assessment area delineation would recognize the
realities of digital banking and geographically dispersed customer relationships. Fourth,
incorporating the geographic and demographic distribution of deposit products would
ensure that CRA evaluations reflect the importance of accessible deposit services
alongside responsible lending.
Taken together, these changes would support a CRA framework that is more adaptable to
the contemporary banking environment, more proportionate in its application, and more
comprehensive in its assessment of community needs. They would also help maintain a
meaningful connection between bank operations and the statutory expectation that
financial institutions help meet the credit and financial service needs of their communities.
I respectfully encourage the OCC and FDIC to consider these recommendations as they
finalize the proposed rule.
Thank you for your consideration.

(Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57; RIN 3064-AG31)

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

On behalf of Eden Housing, I am writing to express serious concerns with the updated
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations proposed by the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporations. We believe
these changes will severely undermine a program that has been one of the pillars of the
affordable housing financing system for decades — and that run contrary both to the plain
language of the CRA statute and to the recent expansion of the housing tax credit enacted
in H.R. 1.

Eden Housing is one of California's oldest non-profit housing developers, founded in 1968
by a group of volunteers concerned about a lack of affordable housing in Alameda
County. As the one of the first developers in California to use the Low Income Housing
Tax Credit, Eden has since relied on countless CRA-motivated investments, alongside
other state and federal programs, to develop, acquire, and preserve more than 10,000
affordable apartments — providing homes to 22,000 low-income Californians.

The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and creates an
affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of
communities, including low- and moderate-income communities. While the CRA has

successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved
communities, significant gaps still remain in access to capital and financial services.

Instead of addressing these gaps, however, the changes proposed by the OCC and FDIC
will make it much more difficult for non-profits like Eden to access the financing necessary
to build affordable homes — by raising asset thresholds for federal chartered banks in
ways that will pull investment and support away from the communities the statute directs
them to serve.

To state it plainly, this will make our affordable housing and homelessness crisis much
worse.

As a result of the 2025 federal tax bill (H.R. 1), California has doubled production of
affordable rental homes over the past year — with private banks playing a critical role in
the boost in dealmaking that has followed the legislation's historic expansion of the
housing tax credit.

The California Housing Partnership estimates that an additional $388.8 billion in CRA
loans and investments are needed to meet the state's affordable housing needs over the
next decade. But the proposed CRA rule changes would take the financing system in the
opposite direction: reducing the number of banks incentivized to make CRA loans and
investments in California and draining the expanded financing pool created by H.R. 1.

According to a National Community Reinvestment Coalition analysis, 70 banks active in
California would see their CRA reinvestment obligations reduced under the proposal,
with 25 banks active in California shedding their CRA community development
responsibilities entirely.1 Forty-five banks active in California would no longer be subject
to the investment test, which has successfully driven crucial investment in Low-Income
Housing Tax Credits.2 Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC
investors nationally, making this test a critical driver of affordable housing capital.3

Given these concerns, we urge you to consider these updates to the final rule to ensure
the CRA can continue supporting the production and preservation of affordable housing
that lower-income Californians are depending on:


1 NCRC. Stop CRA Rollback, Keep Banks Accountable to Communities with Strong CRA. (2026),
https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending
2 NCRC. Stop CRA Rollback, Keep Banks Accountable to Communities with Strong CRA. (2026),
https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending
3 NCRC. Stop CRA Rollback, Keep Banks Accountable to Communities with Strong CRA. (2026),
https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending


•
First and foremost, we strongly suggest using the alternative $3.252 billion
threshold instead of the $10 billion threshold for Large Banks that would be
subject to the investment test. The other alternative $30 billion threshold would
be disastrous for affordable housing, potentially reducing investment in
affordable housing by billions of dollars.

•
In addition, for intermediate banks, we urge retaining an independent
community development test as a key component of the CRA rating. As
proposed, allowing these banks to substitute lending for community
development activities could have a further damaging effect on affordable
housing development. If more Large Banks are categorized as Intermediate due
to a higher threshold, this test becomes even more important.

With that said, we appreciate the OCC and FDIC's proposal for greater geographic
flexibility on CRA assessment areas. Under the current framework, we have seen certain
distortions in investment activity (sometimes even within a single region) due to the
rigidity of the assessment areas. Creating greater flexibility for banks to get credit for
investments outside their assessment areas – assuming a baseline level of strong
performance within those areas – could help spread capital more efficiently into
communities in need.

Finally, though not part of the scope of these proposed changes, we would like to note
that the bank capital rules being finalized under the Basel III framework could also have
a major impact on investment in affordable housing. If the risk weight for low-income
housing tax credit investments is reduced – ideally to 20 percent but no greater than 50
percent, commensurate with the extremely low historical foreclosure and tax credit
recapture rates – we anticipate banks would be motivated to deploy additional sorely
needed investment.

Thank you for your consideration. If we can be of assistance, please contact me:
lmandolini@edenhousing.org.

Sincerely,



Linda Mandolini
President and CEO
Eden Housing

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The Urban Economic Development Association of Wisconsin, Inc. (UEDA) is submitting this comment in opposition
to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

In addition, given the complexity and of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that before making the
proposed changes, the OCC and FDIC carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income
communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting
any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.

UEDA is a 501(c)(3) membership organization dedicated to the professional development of individuals and groups
working in economic and community development in Wisconsin. Incorporated in 1997, we focus on and advocate
for sustainable homeownership and housing, financial empowerment and economic mobility, small business
growth, community investment, and regional workforce and transportation strategies.

We are an active member of the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) and National Low Income
Housing Coalition (NLIHC). On behalf of our members, we work in collaboration across sectors, and at local,
regional, and national levels to advocate for continued investment in lending products and services to individuals
and businesses in the communities we serve.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks meet
the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also
recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain
especially important in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss, and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
1915 North Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive, Suite 260 | Milwaukee, WI 53212
 tel. 414-562-9904 | www.uedawi.org
 Page 2 of 5

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how regulators
evaluate community development, bank services, and support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that
these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

UEDA leads and supports two coalitions that have active participation from financial institutions, community-based
organizations, and public entities: Take Root Milwaukee (sustainable homeownership & neighborhoods), and Bank
On Greater Milwaukee (banking access & financial education). These two programs exemplify how community
groups and banks can work together through public-private partnerships to have long-range impact by investing in
underserved communities – and this happens largely through the CRA.

Our chief concerns with the proposed rule include:
1. A reduction in community investment expectations for all banks.
2. Setting a low community development benchmark that effectively turns into a goal for financial services.
3. Putting affordable housing and community development investment and financing at risk.
4. Undermining the financial health of unbanked and underbanked communities.
5. Restricting CRA credit for grants that support local nonprofit operating costs.

REDUCING EXPECTATIONS, SETTING LOW BENCHMARKS, AND PUTTING MUCH-NEEDED INVESTMENT AT RISK
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In Wisconsin, from 2010-2024, banks made
over $63.16 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts – helping people
and families build wealth through homeownership. Banks also made over $27.74 billion in CRA qualified lending to
small businesses – a huge investment in both urban and rural communities in the State.

Investments such as these have benefited our community in many ways. For example, since 2013 UEDA has worked
with Take Root Milwaukee (TRM) members (takerootmilwaukee.com) on an annual analysis of Home Mortgage
Disclosure Act (HMDA) data for the City of Milwaukee and the Milwaukee-Waukesha Metropolitan Statistical Area
(MSA). In 2025, banks made over 35,000 home loans in the Milwaukee MSA; 42% of them were for home purchase.
In the City of Milwaukee, over 8,000 home loans were made in 2025 and 48% of them were for home purchase.
Additionally, 55% of the loans in Milwaukee were to LMI borrowers, and 46% of the loans were to borrowers of
color. TRM is a program that is strongly aligned with the CRA, and its bank members provide a greater percentage
of their home loans to LMI borrowers and people of color than their peers. This is critically important as the City of
Milwaukee has lower rates of homeownership compared to the MSA.

We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends the incentives for banks to invest in communities. For
example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development
loans or investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating2. However, that percentage is far lower than
the percentage that NCRC determined the largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.

For example, NCRC found that the median percentage of annual community development lending in CRA
assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital3. If banks chose to meet the 0.625% threshold, that would represent a
reduction of 85% in their community development lending activity. Setting such a low regulatory floor could lead to
a de facto benchmark – with significant and negative consequences for rural and urban communities.

2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks surpass a benchmark of 0.625% of
its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625% for investments. 91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
We are concerned that the practical effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
3 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk, (Sept. 10, 2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-
new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-activity-at-risk/.
 Page 3 of 5


For example, in our Take Root program, we continue to see persistent challenges in terms of low-income borrowers
and communities accessing credit in a challenging homeownership market. In the Milwaukee MSA this would likely
look like fewer LMI families obtaining affordable mortgage loans, or small business owners struggling to access
capital either directly through banks or Community Development Finance Institutions (CDFIs), who are a critical part
of the lending landscape for small and micro businesses in our state.

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs. Before finalizing the rule,
the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or investment available
to low- and moderate-income communities and whether communities that have experienced historic
discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

BANK BRANCHES AND ACCESS TO BANKING SERVICES
By raising the large-bank threshold to $10 billion, 417 banks would no longer receive the full large-bank
examination, which includes separate testing that evaluates branch delivery systems and banking services. We are
concerned that approximately 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts would no longer be
evaluated as part of the large-bank CRA service test under the proposal, and more than 4,000 branches in majority-
people-of-color census tracts would also lose CRA consideration.

In 28 states, at least one-third of branches located in LMI census tracts would no longer receive any CRA
evaluation.4 In Wisconsin, this would put nearly 46% of LMI branches and 33% of branches in communities of color
in jeopardy. This means that our state is the 4th highest out of 54 in terms of banks losing community development
obligations if the proposed threshold levels are put in place.

The proposal would also narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service test. Today, examiners may
consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information about the costs and features of deposit
accounts. The proposal would limit this criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and
savings accounts from direct evaluation under the service test.

As such, examiners would no longer evaluate whether those products are affordable and responsive to
community needs even though 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million are
underbanked. CRA review of the cost and features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging
banks to address these disparities and increase access to banking.

Since 2019, UEDA has hosted Bank On Greater Milwaukee (bankonmilwaukee.org/), joining over 100 coalitions
across the country to promote safe, affordable accounts and trustworthy financial education to consumers. We
work with 55 members (including 21 financial institutions) and assist banks to partner with service providers to
connect clients to safe and affordable accounts and provide financial education/resources.

For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from access to credit and
economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely receive income, build savings, establish
banking relationships, and obtain responsible credit. According to recent Prosperity Now and FDIC data, 7% of
Milwaukee County households are unbanked, and 16% are underbanked – nearly a quarter of households in the
County are not using safe, affordable bank products at all or paying more in fees to use alternative services.


4 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026), https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.
 Page 4 of 5

Cities for Financial Empowerment (CFE) Fund research indicates that unbanked Financial Empowerment Center
clients are half as likely to increase savings and more than one-third less likely to establish a credit score. Bank On
National Data Hub findings show that opening an account can lead to broader use of bank and credit union services,
supporting goals such as higher education and homeownership.

We strongly believe that regulators should review the quality of all bank credit and deposit products, especially in
the consumer arena, which changes rapidly. This includes marketing, language access, terms, rates, fees, defaults,
and collections. By reducing the importance of deposit services and branch performance in CRA evaluations, the
proposal eliminates incentives for banks to offer basic products that help unbanked and underbanked households.

SUPPORT FOR LOCAL ORGANIZATIONS
We are concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit organizations.
Banks are a significant source of support for affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling,
workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through grants,
investments, loans, and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. Through the CRA infrastructure, local
community-based organizations are able to build important and often transformative relationships with banks,
working with them to understand the specific needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new
documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations5. For smaller
nonprofit organizations, this limit may be unrealistic – they have fewer programs and funding sources over which to
spread necessary costs such as staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance, etc. If banks conclude that grants to
smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify, with detrimental impact to community-based organizations.

Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments, and partnerships can play in supporting
community development and smaller organizations. UEDA is a small nonprofit, with an annual budget of around
$500,000 and four full-time staff. Along with our Take Root homeownership and Bank On programs, we provide
capacity building and technical assistance to local nonprofits. Often CRA-focused grants from banks are how small
organizations are able to secure support for community initiatives that stabilize neighborhoods.

These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into tangible benefits
for residents. Many community-based organizations operate with limited staff and infrastructure – they may not
maintain program documentation in the format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. Rules governing
what kinds of grants and community development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have
consequences well beyond the banks themselves.

Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of reducing
perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine what the changes mean for the
communities CRA is intended to serve – there could be impacts that ultimately reduce resources available to low-
and moderate-income communities.

SUMMARY
Although progress has been made by banks in serving low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities and
communities of color as a result of CRA, there is still much work to be done to ensure that people have access to
fairly priced credit and financial services they can trust to serve their needs.

5 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 Page 5 of 5

Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
•
identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under the proposal;
•
quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development activities subject
to CRA evaluation;
•
assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations, including rural
communities and communities of color; and
•
consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing meaningful
community accountability.
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the OCC and FDIC
should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public
comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting community credit
needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that accountability without first
demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire
communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

Milwaukee's continues to be one of the most segregated cities and metro areas in the country due to a legacy of
past redlining practices that denied certain groups of people access to credit and underinvested in specific
geographic areas. UEDA works with a diverse cross-section of members and other partners that include nonprofits,
financial institutions, CDFIs, government agencies, small businesses, neighborhood associations, funders, and
individuals concerned with these issues. Working to reverse the impact of these historical disparities requires
consistency and intention, with contributions from the private, public, and nonprofit sectors – the CRA is a critical
tool that helps us develop relationships and innovative strategies to meet the needs of our community.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from community
organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates, and other stakeholders that do not have dedicated regulatory
staff, additional time is warranted. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit
grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. An extension would allow affected organizations to
evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the communities they serve, and provide the
agencies with a more complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days, for a total of 120 days.

Sincerely,

Kristi Luzar
Executive Director | (414) 562-9904 | kristi@uedawi.org

cc: National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC)

ABOUT UEDA
The Urban Economic Development Association of Wisconsin (UEDA) is a 501(c)(3) membership association dedicated to
facilitating cross-sector collaboration, meaningful connections, and strengthening individual and organizational capacity in
Wisconsin's community and economic development sector. Our vision is that the members and communities we serve are
inspired and thriving, with equitable access to investment and opportunity. Learn more at www.uedawi.org.

Ladies and Gentlemen:
American Express National Bank ("AENB" or the "Bank") appreciates the opportunity to
comment on the notice of proposed rulemaking issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (each, an
"Agency", and together, the "Agencies") to amend their Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA")
regulations (the "Proposal").1
AENB maintains a single corporate office in Sandy, Utah, operates no retail branches,
and is primarily a nationwide credit and charge card lender. Based on its corporate office,
AENB's single assessment area ("AA") is the Salt Lake City-Murray, Utah Metropolitan
Statistical Area. The OCC has designated AENB as a limited purpose bank because it offers
narrow product lines to regional and broader markets. The limited purpose designation
recognizes that structural reality and ensures that AENB is evaluated under a framework that
meaningfully measures how it meets community credit and development needs rather than under
retail metrics driven principally by the location of its single corporate office. The existing

1 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114 (Aug. 12, 2026).

framework has produced demonstrable results, with the most recent AENB CRA evaluation
recognizing $2.22 billion in total community development investments and loans.
AENB supports the Agencies' objective to refocus CRA implementation on the statute's
core principles, encouraging banks to help meet community credit needs in a safe and sound
manner. Achieving this objective does not require the elimination of longstanding features of the
CRA regulations that tailor the statute sensibly across materially different business models. The
final rule should preserve the limited purpose bank designation and the standalone community
development ("CD") test, which produce substantial and measurable community impact. The
Agencies should not replace that framework with one that would redirect existing limited
purpose banks' resources toward nationwide consumer-data infrastructure and geographically
mismatched retail metrics without benefiting low- and moderate-income ("LMI") communities.
I.
Executive Summary
Consistent with the Agencies' objectives of creating better alignment with the statute,
reducing unnecessary burden, and improving clarity, AENB respectfully recommends that the
Agencies make the following targeted changes to the Proposal:
• Retain the limited purpose designation and standalone CD test. Eliminating the
limited purpose designation would not encourage banks currently designated as limited
purpose to become more responsive to community needs. Instead, it would
inappropriately subject nationwide lenders with one physical location to an AA-based
retail test. In turn, this change, coupled with the Proposal's major product line ("MPL")
framework, would reduce currently-designated limited purpose banks' incentives and
resources to engage in meaningful CD activities that the CRA should encourage.
• Retain the current, qualitative approach to incidental lending. The proposed five
percent cap would create an arbitrary cliff unrelated to whether the CD test continues to
provide the more accurate assessment of CRA performance.
• Exempt limited purpose banks from any consumer loan data collection
requirement. The Proposal could require AENB to build and maintain systems to
collect, normalize, geocode, reconcile, retain, and produce data across more than 40
million consumer loan-level records nationwide. Even if AENB were evaluated on its
consumer lending – which it is not, under the CD test – less than one percent of that data
would inform an analysis of AENB's consumer lending in its AA. The data collection
would therefore impose substantial burden without purpose in AENB's CRA evaluation.
• Do not adopt the 1.25 percent Tier 1 capital threshold for banks with one AA. Under
Option 1 of the Proposal's geographic flexibility standard, AENB and the four other
largest banks in AENB's AA would be required to invest an aggregate of $1.03 billion of
CD activity in that single AA each year to meet the geographic flexibility standard. Such
a result would ignore whether there are available opportunities or needs in a single,
highly competitive market, and exacerbate the problem of CRA hotspots.
 3

II.
The Agencies Should Retain the Limited Purpose Bank Designation and Community
Development Test
AENB strongly opposes eliminating or narrowing the limited purpose bank designation.
The Agencies have not identified a deficiency in the existing framework that warrants
eliminating it, and AENB's experience demonstrates why the designation continues to serve an
important regulatory purpose. Under the standalone CD test, the OCC found that the Bank
exhibited excellent responsiveness to the credit and CD needs of its AA and recognized
approximately $2.22 billion in loans and investments.2 If the limited purpose bank designation is
not retained in the final rule, AENB would be evaluated primarily on its retail lending in a single
AA, instead of how it actually helps fulfill CD needs in LMI communities. As a result, the
Proposal would reduce AENB's ability and incentive to conduct CD activity outside of the AA,
potentially reducing over $869 million3 in CD activity relative to the activity recognized in
AENB's last performance evaluation.
The Proposal recognize that eliminating the limited purpose designation would be a
significant change for the small number of banks now evaluated solely under the CD test, but
suggest that the retail lending test ("RLT") would be suitable because those banks' consumer
lending would no longer be omitted from the retail evaluation.4 However, the limited purpose
designation was never intended to address this issue; indeed, under the existing CRA regulations,
the RLT can already evaluate consumer lending. Instead, the limited purpose designation
addresses a more fundamental and continuing structural mismatch: AENB conducts a nationwide
card business through a bank with one AA, and the RLT is focused on performance within a
bank's AAs. Adding credit cards to the categories of loans evaluated under the RLT does nothing
to resolve that structural mismatch. For AENB, designating consumer lending as a MPL would
mean that the Bank's nationwide portfolio would be evaluated through a framework centered on
its single AA, which accounts for less than one percent of AENB's consumer-lending activity.
The proposed RLT exacerbates the very geographic mismatch that the limited purpose
framework was designed to address.
A CRA evaluation framework should measure how a bank serves its community within
its established business model; it should not require the bank to redesign that model to avoid a
negative result driven by the structure of the test. AENB's nationwide card platform, single
office, and limited physical footprint are longstanding features of a business model that is subject
to ongoing prudential supervision. The Proposal could create incentives to alter lending, product,
or legal-entity decisions merely to improve CRA metrics, which would contradict Congress's
explicit statutory direction to the Agencies to evaluate performance consistently with safe and
sound operations.5 The most direct and administrable solution is to retain the limited purpose
designation and continue evaluating designated banks under the CD test.
