To Whom It May Concern,
On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act
("CRA"). CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide loans, investments, grants,
and services in communities that have historically lacked access to capital.
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations, and we support some of the
agencies' provisions that could improve the CRA framework and increase responsible capital in
underserved communities. However, we have grave concerns with the increases in the asset
thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA and the restrictions on operating
grants. We also have concerns with several interacting provisions that could further weaken
community development incentives that will undoubtedly impair the flow of much needed capital in
our most underserved communities.
The Catalytic Fund is a not-for-profit 501(c)(3) company and certified Community Development
Finance Institution ("CDFI") working in Boone, Kenton, and Campbell Counties, Kentucky ("Northern
Kentucky"), to provide nontraditional capital and related property development advisory services for
commercial real estate developments of all types and sizes. Since our founding in 2008, we have
grown a revolving loan fund to over $35 million, offering financing to developments that otherwise
would not qualify for traditional financing structures.
We focus on projects that are "catalytic" to the surrounding areas, meaning our leading investments
endeavor to establish comparables and history in disinvested areas which allows private capital to flow
where it once would not. The developments that we support cover all aspects of urban real estate,
from multifamily housing, condominiums, single family housing, income-aligned housing, commercial




2

and restaurant spaces, hospitality, community assets, and more. In total, we have invested more than
$53 million in over 110 Northern Kentucky developments, with an overall impact of over $630 million
to the Northern Kentucky region - representing a nearly 12× leverage on dollars invested.
Banks are critical partners in the results of that work. We currently have relationships with banks that
provide low, or zero, interest loans, lines of credit, EQ2 (equity equivalent) investments, and grants.
These partnerships with banks and financial institutions have provided approximately $21 million in
capital to our Investor Fund, capital that has been instrumental in reversing decades of disinvestment
in Northern Kentucky's urban core. Leveraging these resources, the Catalytic Fund has supported 113
catalytic real estate projects that have restored historic assets, attracted private investment, expanded
housing opportunities, and stimulated economic growth in communities that had long struggled to
attract conventional financing.
The resulting impact ultimately includes the preservation of 107 historic buildings; the creation of
more than one million square feet of commercial space; the opening of 23 new restaurants; the
development of 181 hotel rooms in disinvested downtown markets; the establishment of eight
community facilities; the creation of 1,808 residential units, including over 400 affordable units; and
the generation of more than 2,800 jobs. These outcomes demonstrate the critical role that bank-
supported community development capital plays in transforming distressed communities into
economically vibrant and sustainable neighborhoods.
These partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical capital and resources to
CDFIs, banks rely on CDFIs to reach underserved communities, develop borrowers, and cultivate
future bank customers. A substantial majority of the borrowers that we serve ultimately transition to
traditional financing sources, demonstrating how CDFIs help prepare projects and developers for
access to conventional capital markets.
The CRA has long helped create the incentives for banks to build and sustain these relationships,
strengthening the broader community development ecosystem. We are therefore concerned that
several provisions in the proposal could weaken these incentives, reducing bank engagement with
CDFIs and ultimately the flow of capital to the communities we serve.
Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance: Section IV.A, "Asset
Thresholds"; Questions 1–3
The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate banks
as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as institutions with more than
$10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate community development test as
intermediate small banks would become small banks and lose that requirement. Another
approximately 400 banks that are currently evaluated as large banks would become intermediate
banks, losing the separate large-bank lending, investment, and service tests and many associated
data-reporting requirements.
In the Commonwealth of Kentucky where we serve, it is estimated that 30 banks, comprising 38% of
all the banks in the commonwealth would lose their CRA obligation, and no longer be required to




3

reinvest in local community development projects such as affordable housing, small business support,
workforce development, community healthcare and education services. About 14 banks in the
Commonwealth would lose their large bank status, thereby jeopardizing 168 low-and moderate-
income ("LMI") census tracts in Kentucky alone.1
Harm to Communities from Loss of Community Development Finance
These thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development performance is
evaluated and therefore affect the strength of banks' incentives to engage in community
development. The agencies acknowledge in the proposal that when banks become subject to a CD
test under the current framework, the explicit evaluation of their CD activities typically results in banks
adjusting their CRA programs.
Banks moving down asset sizes and losing incentives for community development activities would
have a direct impact on our partnerships. We estimate that $10 million of support for our Investor
Fund would be at risk from our bank funders that are currently considered large or intermediate that
would transition into lower asset categories. This represents approximately 39% of our total bank
funding.
The current CRA asset thresholds have produced tangible benefits in Northern Kentucky by ensuring
that small and intermediate-sized banks remain active participants in community development. In
many communities across our region, particularly rural and non-urban areas, these local institutions
are often the primary source of capital for transformative projects. Their deep community relationships
and understanding of local market conditions position them uniquely to support complex
developments that larger institutions may overlook. CRA consideration helps bridge the gap between
mission and market reality, encouraging banks to deploy capital into projects that carry greater risk
but substantial community benefit. Working alongside subordinate financing from the Catalytic Fund,
these investments have helped catalyze projects that otherwise would not have reached completion.
CDFIs frequently rely on regional and community banks for patient debt, deposits, investments, lines
of credit, grants, and other forms of capital that allow us to reach borrowers and projects that
conventional financial institutions cannot efficiently serve directly.
Misalignment with Congressional Priorities on Affordable Housing and New Markets Tax Credit
("NMTC")
The change also undermines Congress's recent efforts to strengthen Low-Income Housing Tax Credit
("LIHTC") and New Markets Tax Credit ("NMTC") which are two bipartisan, popular federal tax tools
with a long track record of success in our communities. While Congress expanded LIHTC and made
NMTC permanent, the proposal undermines these important investment tools.
LIHTC and NMTC are considered equity investments that are evaluated under the standalone
investment test for large banks which currently have a distinct 25%-weighted component of their CRA
evaluation devoted to qualified investments. Moving banks into the lower size category would mean
these transitioned banks would only be subject to a diluted evaluation that considers all CD in one
test. This means a bank may have greater ability to emphasize CD lending rather than maintain the

1 National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) Interactive CRA Map. https://ncrc.org/cra/




4

same level of LIHTC or NMTC investment because investment performance no longer receives a
separate rating. Through this weakened regulatory incentive, bank demand for these investments
would decrease.
Northern Kentucky has spent years building the relationships, infrastructure, and local support
necessary to attract LIHTC investment to our region. Through the collaborative efforts of local
governments, the Northern Kentucky Area Development District, the Kentucky Housing Corporation,
and the Northern Kentucky Housing Fund, our region has intentionally positioned itself to support and
leverage LIHTC-financed developments. These efforts were undertaken precisely because LIHTC
remains one of the most effective tools available for addressing the shortage of affordable housing
facing Northern Kentucky. After years of work, Northern Kentucky is now poised to capitalize on
expanded LIHTC authority and attract additional affordable housing developments that can meet
demonstrated local demand.
The proposed changes would undermine that progress at the very moment communities like ours are
prepared to deliver results and tackle the housing crisis sweeping the nation. Congress and the
Administration have repeatedly recognized the importance of expanding affordable housing
production, including through bipartisan legislation such as the ROAD to Housing Act and other
initiatives designed to strengthen and expand the LIHTC program. We responded - Northern
Kentucky invested time, resources, and partnership capital to create a framework capable of attracting
and supporting more LIHTC developments. Imposing additional bank barriers now would make it
more difficult for our region to utilize the very housing tools federal policymakers have worked to
expand. Rather than limiting access, federal policy should reinforce and support communities that
have answered the challenge and are ready to deploy LIHTC financing to deliver needed housing.
These changes risk slowing production, discouraging investment, and denying growing communities
the opportunity to benefit from housing resources that Congress intended to make more accessible.
Significance of CRA data and transparency: Section IV.G, "Data Collection, Reporting, and
Disclosure"
The threshold changes would also substantially reduce the number of institutions subject to large-
bank CRA data requirements. This would make it harder for communities, CDFIs, policymakers, and
regulators to identify credit gaps, compare bank performance, assess geographic disparities, and
understand whether community credit needs are being met. We are concerned that aggregate
community development finance data is already difficult to track and the proposal would exacerbate
the coverage of data, making it difficult to identify and understand where credit is flowing.
Recommendation
For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and reject all
alternatives offered (including the substantially higher thresholds raised for consideration in Question
1). The current thresholds are already annually indexed to CPI-W, so they are not beholden to 1995
asset levels. Moreover, the justification of "restoring proportionality to 1995" that the agencies use in
the proposal does not adequately explain why raising asset thresholds better serve the statutory intent
of the CRA—which is to ensure that credit needs of LMI communities are met. For the small bank
threshold, the proportionality metric rests on the distribution of the number of banks such that nearly
80% of all banks would be considered small, similar to what it was in 1995. That comparison, however,
is not applied consistently. Nearly 20% of banks were considered large in 1995, but under the




5

proposed large-bank threshold, only slightly more than 2% of banks would be classified as large. To
justify this threshold, the agencies instead compare large banks' share of industry assets, noting that
the proposed category would cover approximately 85% of total banking industry assets, similar to the
share covered in 1995. Matching a 1995 distribution through either method does not necessarily
demonstrate that the resulting categories are appropriate for the modern banking system. The
industry has consolidated dramatically, bank business models and geographic reach have changed.
Banks with several billion dollars in assets today may have substantially greater lending, investment,
data, and operational capacity than institutions that were treated as small or intermediate, three
decades ago. The fact that assets happen to sit above a chosen threshold does not by itself establish
that banks below that threshold should lose the separate investment/service tests or associated data
requirements.
Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community Development
Activities — CD Grants"; Questions 9–11
We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants which: 1) requires
a qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a
primary purpose of community development; 2) for large banks, caps grant recipient's indirect
administrative costs to 15%; 3) requires that large banks obtain documentation from grant recipients
including written commitments regarding use of funds, indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and
operating and program budgets. We also strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question
10 to eliminate grants and donations from CRA consideration entirely.
While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit
communities, these requirements first would restrict many forms of effective grantmaking and second
misunderstand the role that flexible operating support plays in community development finance. For
CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, risk management, data systems,
financial management, technical assistance, and product development are not ancillary to community
development. They are the infrastructure that makes community development lending possible.
Furthermore, CDFIs have been tasked with providing technical assistance as a part of our purpose-
oriented work. While larger developments may be able to support a fee for technical assistance, that
can be used to cover operating expenses, the majority of developments we support cannot. Yet this
work is often what transforms a promising concept into a financeable project.
While the Catalytic Fund has achieved financial self-sustainability in recent years, that would not have
been possible without prior operating grants, which remain a critical component of our ability to
maximize impact in Northern Kentucky. These grants support the staff, overhead, underwriting, asset
management, compliance, and program administration functions necessary to operate a responsible
and effective community development lending organization. By covering these essential operating
costs, grants allowed us to recycle 100 percent of loan repayments and a portion of retained
investment earnings back into our lending and investment activities, increasing both the size and long-
term sustainability of our fund while decreasing our need to request operating grants. Without startup
operating grant support, a greater portion of our lending returns would need to be diverted to
administrative expenses and fundraising efforts, reducing the flexible capital available to finance
affordable housing, historic preservation, commercial revitalization, community facilities, and other
projects that strengthen the region's urban core. This approach not only enabled us to preserve and




6

grow a permanent source of community development capital, but will enable emerging CDFIs to do
the same well into the future. The flexibility provided by operating grants therefore multiplies the
impact of every dollar invested in the Catalytic Fund and helps ensure that community development
resources remain available for future generations of borrowers and projects.
For example, in connection with the redevelopment of 341 Pike Street in Covington, Kentucky—a
longtime vacant 1880s-era mixed-use historic building and neighborhood landmark—the Catalytic
Fund provided not only financing but also substantial technical assistance over three years without
compensation to ensure the deal's completion. Our staff worked tirelessly with the local emerging
developer on building design and unit configuration, financial feasibility, historic tax credit strategy
and application preparation, and other predevelopment matters necessary to position the
development for success. This type of hands-on support helps small and emerging developers
undertake substantial projects that might otherwise never advance beyond the evaluation stage.
Without the operating grants to support these services, many critically important community
development projects would struggle to move from concept to completion.
Moreover, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA eligibility.
An organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for community impact.
Costs vary depending on an organization's size, geography, product mix, regulatory obligations,
technical-assistance model, and populations served. The cap could disproportionately affect small
and emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-dollar loans, organizations providing intensive
borrower technical assistance, CDFIs developing new products or entering underserved markets and
organizations making necessary investments in technology, compliance, data, and risk management.
Recommendation
The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building grants
as currently is in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage flexibility for banks to
provide the form of support that best responds to the identified community needs instead of imposing
undue compliance burdens.
Interacting Provisions That Could Further Reduce Community Development Incentives
Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance: Section IV.B,
"Performance Tests — Intermediate Bank Ratings"
Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a Satisfactory
rating on both its lending test and its CD test to receive an overall Satisfactory rating. The proposal
would require a Satisfactory or better lending-test rating but would allow lending performance to
compensate for weaker CD performance.
This change is particularly concerning when combined with the proposed asset thresholds, which
would move hundreds of banks currently evaluated under the large-bank framework into the
intermediate category. If weak CD performance does not prevent an overall Satisfactory rating, banks
may have less regulatory incentive to make CDFI loans and investments, provide grants, or undertake
other community development activities. We urge the agencies to retain a requirement that




7

intermediate banks demonstrate at least Satisfactory CD performance to receive an overall
Satisfactory rating.
Support for Provisions That Could Strengthen Community Development Finance
Consider prior-period community development loans: Section IV.C, "CD Loans"; Question 8
We strongly support providing CRA consideration for qualifying CD loans that remain outstanding
from prior evaluation periods, similar to the existing treatment of prior-period investments.
Community development borrowers frequently need long-term, patient financing. CRA should
encourage banks to structure loans around community needs rather than examination cycles.
With respect to Question 8, we recommend evaluation period-based consideration because it better
recognizes patient, long-term CD financing and provides a more representative measure of capital
committed throughout the CRA examination period than an annual snapshot and brings parity to the
treatment of loans and investments. The agencies should base consideration on the average
outstanding balance or otherwise account for both the amount and duration of the outstanding
exposure, and should treat repeated renewals of substantially the same loan as a single exposure.
Establish an illustrative list and advance-confirmation process: Section IV.E, "Illustrative List"
and "Confirmation of CD Activity Eligibility"; Questions 32–33
We strongly support establishing a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of eligible CD
activities and a formal process for advance confirmation of eligibility. The OCC, FDIC, and Federal
Reserve should seek to maintain consistent standards and, ideally, a single interagency illustrative list.
With respect to Questions 32–33, we support requiring banks to retain eligibility determinations for as
long as the applicable activity remains on their balance sheet and establishing a maximum 30-day
extension beyond the proposed 90-day review period.
We also encourage the agencies to pair this with a confirmation process that provides timely certainty
while maintaining accountability for genuine community development impact. Eligibility
determinations should include a clear written rationale and, where appropriate, identify the facts or
conditions on which eligibility depends. The agencies should provide a process for reconsideration
where banks or community development partners can supply additional information, as well as a
mechanism for community stakeholders to raise material concerns regarding activities that have been
determined eligible. Nonconfidential or anonymized determinations and their rationales should be
made public to promote transparency and consistent treatment across institutions. Eligibility
determinations should also remain subject to verification during CRA examinations where the activity
is ultimately implemented differently than represented.
Conclusion
CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities we serve.
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and flexibility.




8

As the Catalytic Fund's results demonstrate, community development finance is a critical tool to a
community's success and something to be encouraged. We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to
withdraw the proposed increase in asset thresholds and preserve CRA consideration for community
development operating grants.
Innovative community development organizations need seed funding, operating support, and patient
investment to build the capacity, partnerships, and project pipelines necessary to deploy larger
amounts of capital. Operating grants from financial institutions have been critical to helping the
Catalytic Fund establish itself, develop expertise, provide technical assistance, and create a
sustainable platform that has catalyzed millions of dollars of investment in Northern Kentucky. These
grants are not ancillary to community development outcomes; they are often the foundation that
makes those outcomes possible.
We also urge the agencies to maintain a meaningful community development performance standard
for intermediate banks, and at the same time, we support provisions that recognize outstanding
community development loans from prior evaluation periods and provide greater certainty regarding
eligible activities through an illustrative list and advance-confirmation process.
Banks remain the Catalytic Fund's most important partners in advancing innovative community
development finance, and continued CRA incentives are essential to ensuring that local companies
can develop new tools, attract additional investment, and respond to evolving housing and economic
development needs in tandem with Congress and the Administration.
In closing, the Catalytic Fund exists today because financial institutions were empowered and willing
to invest not only in creative projects, but also in the organizational capacity required to make those
projects possible. CRA policy should continue to recognize and encourage that kind of forward-
looking investment in community development innovation.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Please find below the comments of the Hope Enterprise Corporation / Hope Credit Union / Hope
Policy Institute (HOPE) in response to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA), Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557 AF57; RIN 3064-AG31.

Submitting these comments is consistent with HOPE's long-standing support for increasing
meaningful investments in underserved communities in the Deep South. CRA-motivated
investments and partnerships have been critical to HOPE's work in expanding access to banking
services, affordable housing, homeownership, and other pathways for economic mobility.

Rooted in HOPE's more than 30 years of experience in serving the Deep South, this comment
outlines concerns about how the proposed rule will widen existing capital access gaps in the
region, particularly those in the most underserved and economically distressed rural
communities.

About HOPE

HOPE is a credit union, community development financial institution and policy institute that
provides affordable financial services; leverages private, public and philanthropic resources; and
engages in policy analysis to fulfill its mission of strengthening communities, building assets,
and improving lives in economically distressed areas throughout Alabama, Arkansas, Georgia,
Louisiana, Mississippi, Tennessee. Since 1994 HOPE has generated nearly $4 billion in
financing that has benefited over three million people.

Both HOPE's work and the region it serves significantly overlap with the intent and goals of the
Community Reinvestment Act. For example, HOPE has helped over 4,000 people become
 HOPE Comment Page 2

homeowners by providing accessible mortgage financing in underserved areas. And, since its
first small business loan to a cabinet manufacturer in the Arkansas Delta, HOPE has made over
6,800 business loans totaling over $1 billion. In 2025, 69% of HOPE business lending reached
businesses in economically distressed areas.

HOPE's footprint comprises a substantial portion of communities that struggle to gain access to
banking services and capital, and where HOPE serves as a critical capillary in the flow of
resources to these communities. HOPE's six-state footprint includes 45% (147) of all persistent
poverty counties in the country. Of these 147 counties, 83% (119) are rural, 39% (57) are
majority Black; one-third (49) have unemployment rate one and a half times higher than the
national rate; and 65% (95) are in the bottom quartile of health outcomes.1

The Community Reinvestment Act has been a critical, though imperfect, tool for HOPE to
leverage the resources it needs to serve low-income communities, rural communities, and
communities of color in the Deep South. CDFIs, like HOPE, are critical vehicles for receiving
and deploying that capital to underserved communities. For example, over the last ten years,
HOPE has leveraged more than $251.8 million in investments from FDIC and OCC banks, in the
form of low-cost debt, grants, and New Market Tax Credit equity investments to ensure access to
fair financial services for people and places in the region.

Impact of Proposed Changes on Deep South Communities

Rooted in our experiences in reaching underserved communities, HOPE seeks to strengthen the
CRA and its ability to significantly increase banks' lending, services, and investments in our
region. The proposed changes, however, risk reducing investments and hindering economic
opportunity in the Deep South for the following reasons:

1. Banks will have fewer obligations to serve their communities,
2. A smaller number of communities may fall in banks' assessment areas,
3. Resulting downward pressure on tax credit pricing in rural and underserved
communities will put affordable housing and other investments further out of reach,
4. Banks will have less flexibility for community development investments, including
into CDFIs, and
5. The proposed changes dilute banks' obligations to serve the communities at the heart
of the CRA's original statutory intent.

The cumulative impacts of the proposed changes will be profound in the Deep South. If
finalized, nearly 1 in 4 people in the region would live in places with few to no community
development reinvestment obligations by FDIC and OCC banks.2 Each of HOPE's concerns are
discussed in detail below.

1. Banks will have fewer obligations to serve their communities.

The proposal will significantly reduce Deep South banks' obligations to serve the very
communities in which they are located. Under the proposal, banks classified as "small" are
exempt from the community development services test, and those classified as "intermediate"
will have fewer reinvestment and reporting obligations than those classified as "large." Places
like the Deep South have a dearth of large national banks compared to other parts of the country,
 HOPE Comment Page 3

and therefore any changes for banks in the small and intermediate categories will have an
outsized impact on the region.

To understand the potential impact of the proposed asset size threshold changes in its six-state
footprint, HOPE analyzed the asset sizes of banks headquartered in Alabama, Arkansas, Georgia,
Louisiana, Mississippi, and Tennessee. See Figure 1. Currently, 57% (262) of FDIC and OCC
banks in the region are currently considered "small," with less than $412 million in assets. Under
this proposal banks would be considered small if they have fewer than $1 billion in assets, which
would mean 83% (379) of the banks would be considered small and therefore no longer have
community development obligations under the Community Reinvestment Act.3

Figure 1: Impact of Proposed Asset Size Threshold Changes for the Deep South

Just as concerning, the proposal would reduce the number of FDIC and OCC banks considered
"large" from 39 to 4, leaving only these 4 banks subject to the most robust CRA regulatory
structure. This means that 35 FDIC and OCC banks will be re-classified from "large" to
"intermediate" even though they have assets ranging between $1 and $10 billion. Under the
proposal, a bank that is re-classified from their current "large" status to "intermediate" will have
reduced oversight and obligations for reinvesting in their community such as:

• Being able to combine community development loans, investments, and services into one
evaluation – even though each these are very distinct models with different value
propositions for communities.
• No longer collecting and reporting CRA data on small business loans, small farm loans,
community development loans and assessment areas. For, Louisiana and Mississippi this
change would mean losing nearly a quarter of this reported data, reducing transparency in
capital gaps in the small business market.4
• Pass either rather than both their community development test and their lending test in
order to receive an overall passing CRA rating.
• No longer be subject to the service test, which otherwise takes branch locations into
consideration for their CRA evaluation.

In addition to the work that banks do to help people get access to safe, affordable banking
accounts, CDFIs like HOPE are critical in stepping into these financial services gaps, and often
with the support of CRA-motivated bank partnerships. More than 46% of HOPE's members
were unbanked or underbanked when they began their partnership with HOPE. The proposed
rule puts support for the work of CDFIs at risk both with the restrictions on grant-making for
community development purposes, as discussed further in Section 4, and the reduction in banks
that have any community development obligations at all.

2. A smaller number of communities may fall in banks' assessment areas.

HOPE is concerned that the proposal will accelerate the number of communities that fall outside
of banks' assessment areas, thus reducing the number of communities to which banks have
reinvestment obligations even if banks take deposits from those very same communities. The
proposal lands against a backdrop of already declining bank branches in the region. Between
2010 and 2025, the Deep South has lost more than 1,100 bank branches, a 12% decline. See
Figure 2. In rural counties in the Deep South over the same time period, there was an 18%
decline in bank branches.6 Under the current CRA framework in which assessment areas are

based on bank's physical locations, a loss of bank branches equates to a loss of CRA-related
obligations to those communities.

The proposal risks further reduction of CRA assessment areas by accelerating branch closure
decline. This is due to the dual impact of (1) large banks being re-classified to intermediate and
therefore no longer subject to the services test which would otherwise takes bank branch
locations into account for the purposes of their CRA rating and (2) the fact that a bank's
obligations are triggered by their branch facilities. Branches in harder to reach underserved
communities would no longer count positively or at all towards a bank's CRA rating, yet it
triggers obligations for investments into those communities.7 Given this calculation, banks may
choose to simply close these branches rather than undertake the work to serve those
communities. Without CRA incentives, the Deep South stands to lose as many as 896 branches
in low median income areas and 841 branches located in communities of color.8

As such, this proposal risks accelerating an existing trend of banking deserts in the region. From
2019 to 2025, every state in the Deep South except for Arkansas experienced an increase of
census tracts considered to be a banking desert, with a growing share of them in rural
communities in the region.9 See Table 2. Of these banking deserts, 26% are in low-moderate-
income census tracts and nearly 20% are in those where the majority of residents are people of
color.10 Given the current and proposed structure of the CRA, with some limited exceptions, a
banking desert also then becomes a reinvestment desert as CRA obligations will rarely flow to
those communities. In fact, recent analysis by NAAHL estimates that under the proposal, the
number of census tracts considered community development deserts in HOPE's six-state region
will increase from community development desert tracts from 58 currently to 122.11

Given the large swaths of the Deep South considered banking deserts, HOPE has long-supported
the development of additional assessment areas, in addition to those based on physical locations.
And, these additional assessments could be based on a mix of deposit and lending activity (not
just deposits alone). HOPE continues to support the creation of non-facility based assessment
areas and urges the regulators to consider this for future rulemaking.

3. Downward pressure on tax credit pricing in rural and underserved communities.

Downward pressure on tax credit pricing for the Low Income Housing Tax Credit and New
Markets Tax Credit in already underserved communities, particularly rural, will be the
compounding consequence of several elements of the proposed rule changes: fewer banks with
community reinvestment obligations, fewer communities falling within banks' assessment areas,
lower thresholds for community development activities needed for a passing grade, and non-
distinctive treatment between loans and equity investments. Fewer equity investments flowing to
purchase the credits generally, and in certain communities, may lead to less demand and lower
prices in those areas. Relatedly, a study by CohnReznick notes the strong relationship between
CRA assessment areas and supply of LIHTC equity investments from banks.12

In HOPE's experience, this is already evident given that a number of communities HOPE serves
fall outside of a CRA assessment area, often making it more difficult to attract bank investments
(equity or debt) in projects requiring Low Income Housing Tax Credits or New Market Tax
Credits for financing. Thus, it is subsequently difficult to garner competitive prices for those
credits even when there is interest. Here is a real-life example of what this may mean: In a recent
HOPE transaction for 38 affordable units in a small rural town of about 5,000 people, HOPE
provided a $1 million loan and a syndicator paid 87.5 cents on the dollar for the available
housing tax credits. This pricing was already 6.5 cents below the national average at that time
(93 cents).13 If the price had been in parity with the national average, it would have yielded
additional $412,500 in equity, making the overall financing less reliant on debt service and more
affordable. If there is further depressed tax pricing, particularly compared to other regions of the
country, transactions will be even further out of reach for the Deep South.

Recent data from the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition notes how much equity would be
at risk due to the reduced obligations flowing from the asset-size threshold changes: if banks up
to $10 billion are exempt from the community development obligations, this may risk up to $1.6
billion in tax credit equity investments.14 The Coalition also notes the outsized role banks under
 HOPE Comment Page 7

this size have in rural markets, accounting for approximately one-third of rural equity
investments. This has been true in HOPE's experience as well: there are a small but reliable
handful of banks which partner in either equity or debt participations in LIHTC deals and nearly
all of these banks are currently designated as large but will be re-classified as intermediate, thus
reducing this incentive for affordable housing investments particularly in underserved and hard-
to-reach areas.

The lower the price of the credits, the less equity that is available to complete a capital stack for
things like affordable housing, rural hospitals, and educational institutions such as HBCUs and
charter school lending. As discussed in Sections 1 and 2 above, given the reduced CRA footprint
being drawn by the FDIC and OCC proposed rule, HOPE is concerned that far more
communities in the Deep South will fall outside of CRA assessment areas and thus have
increased difficulties in leveraging federal tax credits to attract the private capital to meet their
communities' needs.

4. Reduced flexibility for community development investments, including CDFIs.

The CRA is one of the primary tools for catalyzing bank investments into underserved
communities, including via community development financial institutions (CDFIs) that reach
deep into communities that would otherwise be overlooked. HOPE's history is full of examples
of successful bank investments and partnerships to expand capital access. These investments can
take the form of deposits, low-cost patient debt, bank participation in a capital stack, or grants
which support the day-to-day work of CDFIs and other community partners.

In terms of deposits, HOPE is concerned that the proposal may lead to banks reducing or
eliminating mission driven deposit commitments since a greater share of banks would no longer
need to pass a community development test. This proposed change would apply to the new small
banks as well as the new intermediate banks that would still have a community development test
but would no longer need to pass it in order to receive an overall passing rating.

A reduction in CRA-driven bank deposits would directly impact HOPE's ability to provide
capital to the people and communities it serves, as loan demand from HOPE's members far
exceeds member deposit capacity. HOPE's current Loan to Shares ratio is 99%, compared to
peer credit unions at 83%. This high loan-to-deposit ratio is driven by lower incomes as 60% of
HOPE members have incomes of less than $50,000 a year (and an additional 21% earn less than
$75,000). By extension, there are lower levels of discretionary income that can be left or placed
into a checking or savings account among HOPE's membership The average deposit in HOPE's
checking / savings accounts is about $2,000, compared to $60,000 other depositories. As such
the ability to draw capital from institutional depositors is crucial to HOPE's ability to meet the
capital needs in the Deep South. Institutional deposits from private entities, such as banks, are
particularly critical given that every state in HOPE's footprint only permits banks, but not credit
unions, to serve as full-service depository for public funds.15

In terms of low-cost debt, grants, and equity investments for NMTC transactions, a significant
majority come from large banks that will remain large banks under the revised thresholds. In
looking just at these three types (low-cost debt, grants, and NMTC equity investment), HOPE
has leveraged more than $251.8 million of these investment types from large FDIC and OCC
banks over the last 10 years. The changes to the community development activities and
 HOPE Comment Page 8

subsequent evaluation for large banks will have a direct and significant impact on HOPE's
ability to catalyze development in the Deep South. As such HOPE is concerned about the
unintended consequences of the proposed changes related to evaluation of community
development activities for large banks, in addition to the reduced obligations for those re-
classified as small and intermediate.

For the large banks still subject to a rigorous community development evaluation, a significant
concern is the proposed restriction on grants being limited to specific community development
projects and then, even in such an instance, having the amount for administrative costs capped at
15% of the project. This is simply inconsistent with the flexible and innovative nature of CDFIs'
work that enables them to reach underserved people and places. For example, in several
instances HOPE has received an unrestricted bank grant alongside a project-specific investment,
such as the donation of a bank branch, in recognition that HOPE needs staff and systems to put
that bank branch to use. In other instances, HOPE has received flexible bank grants for the
purposes of carrying out certain goals, such as expanding access to homeownership. The flexible
funding allows HOPE to engage in more expensive manual underwriting leading to the
origination of smaller size mortgages that generate less revenue. As a result, HOPE is regularly
originating nearly 90% of its mortgage loans to first-time homebuyers who otherwise would not
have another option. Notably, HOPE's annual net charge off rate is historically and consistently
low, underscoring the need for this type of community development finance within the banking
ecosystem. In the community development financing context, the availability of grants allows
HOPE to structure its own debt financing to at a rate that is affordable to serve low-income
populations.

Additionally, the proposal dramatically reduces the thresholds of community development
investing in a bank's assessment area that would be enough to signal they could also receive
credit for investments outside of their assessment area.16 This threshold is therefore likely to be
interpreted as what would be considered necessary to receive a passing grade on the CRA exam.
NCRC estimates that the proposed threshold for large banks of .625% of Tier 1 capital for
qualifying community development activities would result in the loss of $87 billion in
community development loans and investments from just the top 100 banks (by assets).17 This
steep decline in community development flows from banks would have far reaching impacts
across sectors of affordable housing, CDFIs, and other critical pieces of the economic
development infrastructure for under-resourced communities. For the Deep South, the impact of
reduced community development obligations by large banks would be particularly acute, as there
would be more competition nationally for this smaller pool of large bank dollars, thus ultimately
reducing the overall supply of dollars for the Deep South especially since few large banks have a
physical presence in the region.

Beyond the impact to CDFIs, HOPE is concerned about the impact of these changes on
motivating community development activities to benefit other critical institutions, such as
HBCUs. Nearly half of the nation's HBCU's are located in HOPE's footprint, and serve as
critical engines for their local economy.18

HOPE has documented the persistent capital gap for HBCUs and heard multiple examples of
HBCUs unable to get the financing they need on fair terms from other financial
institutions.19 Reflecting the critical role of CDFIs in bridging this capital gap, HOPE has made
over $141 million in investments into Deep South HBCUs, such as New Market Tax Credit
 HOPE Comment Page 9

investments coupled with bank partner equity, affordable commercial debt financing, and grants
to support campus life at HBCUs.20 For example, HOPE completed a $7.5 million New Market
Tax Credit investment into Tuskegee University in rural Alabama, along with a bank equity
partner that completed the financing. The investment was part of the $14 million expansion of
Tuskegee's Carver Research Center to increase access to cancer research through the Center for
Genomics and Health Disparity Research.21 This fall, HOPE provided $12.5 million New
Market Tax Credit financing with the Xavier University Ochsner College of Medicine, along
with a bank partner, to serve approximately 400 medical students and create 88 full-time jobs. As
such, it is critical for public policies like the Community Reinvestment Act to help move private
capital to meet the needs of these and other institutions, both to improve the strength of local
economies and the prosperity of the people connected to them. This work and innovation would
be severely constrained by the proposed changes to community development activities.

5. Significant shifts from the original purpose of the Community Reinvestment Act.

In addition to the reductions described in the previous sections, the proposal dilutes requirements
that investments actually flow to underserved communities, such as rural, low-income or
communities of color, the very communities harmed by banks' redlining practices that the CRA
was intended to remedy. It does this through numerous provisions, with little justification or
explanation of how impacted communities will still be served. For example, the proposal
weakens the standards by which discriminatory lending activity would be considered part of a
bank's CRA exam. In a number of other ways, bank activities would not necessarily be required
to benefit low-income people or communities, for example with the removal of the purpose test
for economic development activities, changes to the standards for infrastructure projects such
that they are required to just "serve" low-income communities even if they do not otherwise
benefit, and the changed definition of "unsubsidized affordable housing" such that it could
include housing for middle-income families in high-cost markets.

Throughout its 30 years of providing financial inclusion and community development financing
for people and places throughout the Deep South, HOPE knows all too well that when given the
option, resources will most commonly flow to the easiest to serve rather than those hardest to
reach. This is true in private investments, such as philanthropy, as well as in public funding
streams. As such, HOPE is concerned that the cumulative impact of these proposed changes will
mean that much needed bank capital that could advance economic opportunity in the Deep South
will bypass the very communities that the CRA was intended to benefit.

Conclusion

The Community Reinvestment Act has the potential to unlock capital and opportunity for
communities across the Deep South. It has served as a critical tool in expanding financial access
to the people and places HOPE serves. Any changes or updates to CRA should work to increase
the reach of bank investments into historically underserved communities. Instead. the proposed
changes currently under consideration would move the CRA in the wrong direction by reducing
incentives to serve low income and rural communities, threatening vital community development
efforts that help Deep South communities thrive.

Dear Sir or Madam:

The Indiana Affordable Housing Council (IAHC) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the
proposed Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. We strongly oppose the proposal to
increase the large bank asset threshold from approximately $1.65 billion to $10 billion, which
would eliminate the separate investment test for banks with assets between those levels.

IAHC is a statewide membership organization dedicated to the preservation and expansion of
affordable housing throughout Indiana. Our members include developers, owners, property
managers, lenders, investors, syndicators, nonprofits, and other professionals involved in all
aspects of affordable housing. The developments our members finance, build, and manage
depend on Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) equity, and the CRA investment test is a key
reason for banks to be involved.

Removing the separate investment test for banks currently subject to it could weaken demand
for LIHTC and reduce the equity available for affordable housing developments. Weaker investor
 2 | P a g e

demand generally means lower prices for credits, so the same credit allocation generates less
equity for construction. For developers, that shortfall could create financing gaps, delay
construction, or prevent otherwise viable developments from moving forward. For Hoosiers, the
result will be fewer affordable homes.

Rural communities in Indiana would be particularly hard hit by this change. Banks with less than
$10 billion in assets play an outsized role in financing affordable housing in rural areas.
Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC) survey data shows that approximately one-third
of LIHTC equity investments from banks below this threshold supported rural markets. By
comparison, roughly eight (8) percent of all LIHTC equity in a CohnReznick industry-wide sample
was invested in nonmetro counties, a proxy for rural and small-town markets. Eliminating the
separate investment test for these banks could therefore disproportionately reduce the equity
available for affordable housing in rural communities.

This concern is particularly timely following the recent expansion of LIHTC through the One Big,
Beautiful Bill. Additional tax credits create an opportunity to address housing needs but realizing
that opportunity requires sufficient private investment. We recognize the agencies' goal of
reducing regulatory burden. However, we urge you to pursue that goal while preserving strong
incentives for affordable housing investment. We respectfully ask the agencies to retain the
existing asset threshold and the separate investment test.

Thank you for considering our comments and the potential effects of this proposal on affordable
housing development and the communities our members serve.
